II

Abstract

This paper is the most sustained and analytically rigorous engagement yet attempted with the thought of Dr Alice Jing Shan (PhD, Edinburgh), whose Substack series Dao: The Art of the Long Game (2025–2026) and concurrent Cynefin Co article on Li (理) represent a distinctive and underexamined contribution to complexity ontology, systems philosophy, the epistemology of structural formation, and the ethics of long-game intelligence. The paper places Shan's entire published body of work in genuine dialectical collision with more than thirty-five intellectual voices spanning Chinese classical philosophy, ancient military strategy, Neo-Confucian metaphysics, modern Chinese systems science, complexity theory, critical systems thinking, strategy-as-practice theory, structural engineering, continental phenomenology, analytic philosophy, and process philosophy. It does not merely describe these traditions or compare them; it interrogates each with the full force of the others.

The paper is structured in eight interlocking Parts. Part I presents a complete, analytically close reading of every published Shan essay, including her doctoral work, with all significant quotes extracted, contextualised, and philosophically developed. Part II portrays thirty-five-plus interlocutors in sufficient depth to function as genuine intellectual challengers, with extensive quotation in both English and Chinese (Traditional Chinese characters, pinyin, and translation). Part III presents twelve major dialectical collisions in full analytical detail. Part IV dedicates an entire section to the Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計) placed in active and detailed conversation with Shan's every concept. Part V integrates the VUCA-Dao framework of Charles-Édouard Bouée and Chinese management philosophy with Shan's relational dynamics. Part VI introduces Robert Chia's strategy-without-design and dwelling/wayfinding theory as a crucial mediating framework. Part VII presents Mike Jackson's critical systems thinking as both a methodological parallel and a challenge. Part VIII is a new, original, and deeply developed layer on cadence, salience, resonance, valence, vibration, tension, and gain as metaphysical-structural categories that stretch Fuller, Wittgenstein, and all voices toward a unified theory of structural attunement. The paper concludes with open questions that the inquiry produces but cannot resolve.

"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world" — Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6 (1922). This proposition runs as a continuous thread through every Part of this paper, placed in conversation with Shan's claim that Dao is a living linguistic interface, and interrogated against every other framework here assembled. The result is a paper that is itself an instance of what it describes: a path of formation, thickening through traversal, producing glimpses of a grain that no single tradition can name.

III

Proem: The Occasion of Recognition

In late 2025 or early 2026, on a LinkedIn thread discussing David Snowden's blog post "The Way Is Not a Map," a comment mentioned Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu's WSR methodology. For most readers, this was a technical citation. For Alice Jing Shan, it was the surfacing, in an unexpected professional context, of a Chinese character she had known since childhood: 理 (lĭ).

The character 理 is not an exotic philosophical term. It lives inside Chinese in compounds so ordinary they are used without thinking: 物理 (wùlĭ, physics), 事理 (shìlĭ, how affairs work), 人理 (rénlĭ, human relational norms), 道理 (dàolĭ, reason and underlying logic), 理迟 (lĭcí, being in the wrong), 整理 (zhěng lĭ, to put in order), 管理 (guǎn lĭ, to manage). When WSR appeared in the thread, what appeared for Shan was not a new concept but a structural companion she had always carried: the grain of things, the less-known partner of the path.

This paper takes that occasion as its starting point. It asks what happens when we follow Shan's structural logic — Dao before Li, path before pattern, relation before dynamics, formation before formed coherence — all the way through a sustained collision with thirty-five voices, across twelve dialectical movements, into the mystical-structural layer of cadence, resonance, and vibration, and out the other side into the ancient Chinese art of the strategic stratagem. The grain was always there — but only in the sense of retrospective intelligibility: the grain appears to have been always there only because the formation that produced it has been successfully concealed by its own success. The path of this paper is an attempt to follow it, knowing that following the grain means recovering the Dao that made the grain available, not merely reading the Li that the Dao left behind.

“Dao rarely travels alone. Perhaps Li is the less-known partner whose absence should caution us whenever Dao begins to feel too smooth, too familiar, or too readily available.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (Cynefin Co, May 14, 2026)

The least-known partner: this is Shan’s diagnosis of the complexity discourse’s condition. Dao travels well in the West — it sounds appropriately mysterious, sufficiently Eastern, usefully non-specific. Li does not travel well, because Li demands specificity: the specific grain of the specific formation, produced by the specific Dao of the specific practitioner’s specific engagement with the specific situation. Li resists the smooth travel that Dao has been allowed. The warning is structural: when Dao begins to circulate without its less-known partner, the concept has separated from the formation that grounds it. The smooth Dao is the sign that Li has been left behind.

“"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. Logic fills the world: the limits of the world are also its limits. This proposition performs retrospective intelligibility: the limits of language — the Li of what is sayable — appear as the limits of the world, as though the world were shaped by language. But the Dao of the practitioner’s specific language-formation produced the specific Li of what is sayable in that language. The limits are not the limits of the world but the emergence lag-boundary of the practitioner’s specific formation: what has not yet been walked cannot yet be said, and what cannot yet be said appears as though it simply does not exist."”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6–5.61 (1922)

These two propositions — Shan's living interface and Wittgenstein's logical limit — are the twin anchors of this paper. Between them, a world opens.

IV

Part I: Alice Jing Shan — A Complete and Exhaustive Analytical Account

This Part presents a complete analytical account of every significant published work by Alice Jing Shan, from her doctoral research to her most recent Substack essays. No text of hers is summarised where it can be quoted directly. No theme is gestured at where it can be developed analytically. The goal is a complete philosophical portrait of her thought sufficient to sustain the dialectical pressure of thirty-five other voices.

1.1 The Wittgenstein Thread Running Through Shan's Language Theory

"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world" is a profound epistemological concept from Wittgenstein's 1922 Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (5.6). It means that the structure of language is the structure of what is thinkable, perceivable, and therefore real for the speaker. This proposition is not a limitation to be lamented but a structural fact to be investigated: and it is precisely what Shan's work on Dao as living interface explores from the inside.

Shan does not cite Wittgenstein explicitly, but her entire intellectual project is an empirical investigation into what his proposition means for a Chinese-language speaker who has crossed into English. If the limits of language are the limits of the world, then Shan's crossing from Chinese into English was a crossing between worlds — not merely a change of vocabulary but a change in what structural possibilities were available for thought. Her claim that Dao functions as a living interface is simultaneously a claim about what the Chinese language makes available for thought that English does not package in the same way.

This is the Wittgenstein thread that runs through every section of this paper: the question of whether and how language limits and enables structural perception. When Shan says "The path must open before its inner grain can appear," she is making a claim about the generative order of linguistic-structural experience that Wittgenstein's Tractatus approaches from the logical side and his Investigations approach from the social-practice side. Both are needed to understand what Shan is doing.

❧ ✶ ❧

1.1a The Ontology of Precedence: Seven Structural Distinctions

The claim that Dao precedes Li is the master-claim of this paper. But ‘precedes’ is doing enormous work, and the word is insufficiently precise without the distinctions that follow. There are at least seven structurally distinct kinds of precedence that the Dao-before-Li claim involves, and they operate at different levels with different implications. Conflating them produces a weaker claim. Distinguishing them produces a full metaphysical architecture that can bear the pressure of thirty-five voices without collapse.

The seven distinctions are:

Ontological precedence — Dao is more fundamental than Li in the order of being. Li is not a pre-existing cosmic blueprint that the Dao merely instantiates; it is a structural achievement that the Dao produces. The path is ontologically prior to the pattern because the pattern cannot exist without the path having been walked, but the path can exist without the pattern having yet appeared. The universe contains walking before it contains maps.

Generative precedence — Dao is causally productive of Li. The Li does not emerge from nowhere; it is generated by the specific traversal of the specific formation field by the specific practitioner. Generative precedence is about mechanism: the Dao is the generative engine; Li is its product. Remove the Dao and there is no Li. But remove the Li and the Dao continues: the path can be walked without the grain having been named.

Phenomenological precedence — In the practitioner’s lived experience, the encounter with the formation field (the Dao) precedes the recognition of its intelligible structure (the Li). The practitioner moves through the landscape before the landscape becomes legible. This is Ingold’s ‘knowing as we go’ restated as a claim about the temporal structure of lived formation: the engagement precedes the intelligibility it produces.

Epistemic belatedness — The Li always arrives later than the Dao that produced it. Knowledge of the pattern is structurally belated relative to the path that generated it. This belatedness is not a deficiency to be overcome; it is constitutive of how formation intelligence works. The practitioner who demands to know the Li before walking the Dao has misunderstood the epistemic situation entirely. You cannot think your way to the grain; you must walk your way there.

Structural asymmetry — The relationship between Dao and Li is not symmetrical. Li cannot produce Dao; Dao can produce Li. The grain of the wood cannot produce the growth of the tree, though it encodes the history of the tree’s growth. The practitioner who has the Li of a domain does not thereby possess the Dao that produced it in anyone else—the Li is communicable, the Dao is not. This asymmetry is why expertise cannot be fully taught: the Li can be transmitted, but the formation that produced it must be re-walked.

Emergence lag — There is an irreducible temporal gap between the walking of the Dao and the crystallisation of the Li. The Li does not appear simultaneously with the formation that produces it; it appears after, sometimes long after, the formative events that generated it. This lag is not merely experiential but structural: the formation must reach a threshold of accumulated constraint before the Li can crystallise from it. Premature Li—reading the pattern before the formation is complete—produces false intelligibility that masks the actual grain of the actual terrain.

Retrospective intelligibility — Li appears as though it had always already been there only because successful formation retroactively conceals the path that produced it. The grain of the wood looks like an eternal property of the material because we encounter it after the tree has grown, when the growth process is invisible. The ontological precedence of Dao over Li is hidden by the phenomenological availability of Li without its Dao. The formed practitioner reads the Li of the familiar terrain as though it were simply ‘how the world is’—not as the crystallised product of a specific formation history. Retrospective intelligibility is the structural mechanism of naturalisation: what was produced becomes what was always already there.

❧ ✶ ❧

These seven distinctions are not merely analytical refinements. Each one carries a different practical implication, and each one is violated by a different version of the Li-before-Dao error.

The violation of ontological precedence is the error of Zhu Xi: positing Li as the cosmic blueprint that precedes and constitutes material reality. The practitioner who makes this error treats existing patterns as eternal structures rather than as produced formations, and therefore cannot ask the formation question: what Dao produced this Li, and what would a different Dao produce?

The violation of generative precedence is the error of the consultant with a framework: arriving at the formation field with a ready-made Li (the methodology, the model, the analytical framework) and applying it before walking the Dao of the specific situation. The framework is someone else’s Li—the crystallised product of their specific Dao—and it may have an entirely different grain than the actual terrain.

The violation of phenomenological precedence is the error of pattern-first perception: training oneself to see the pattern before engaging with the formation. The practitioner who has been taught to look for ‘leverage points’ (Meadows) or ‘complex domains’ (Snowden) or ‘enabling constraints’ (Juarrero) before walking the Dao of the specific situation is already applying Li before the Dao has been engaged. The conceptual vocabulary precedes the perceptual encounter.

The violation of epistemic belatedness is the demand for intelligibility before engagement. This is the managerial demand for strategy before immersion: tell me the grain of this situation before I have walked it. The answer is always either a lie (a false Li, confidently stated) or the truth stated unhelpfully (I cannot tell you yet, the formation has not been walked). The tolerance for epistemic belatedness—the capacity to act without yet having the Li—is the foundational competence of genuine formation intelligence.

The violation of structural asymmetry is the error of treating Li as generative: believing that articulating the pattern produces the formation. This is the error of the training programme that teaches the vocabulary of Dao and Li without the formation walk that could make the vocabulary live. Words can point at Li; they cannot replace the Dao that produces the capacity to read it. The structural asymmetry is irreversible: Li points backward toward the Dao that produced it, but it cannot forward-project the Dao that will be needed next.

The violation of emergence lag is premature legibility: reading the pattern before the formation is complete. This is the practitioner who identifies the Li of a complex situation before the situation has been walked sufficiently to reveal its actual grain. The premature Li is not merely wrong; it is structurally damaging. Once a Li has been named and applied, it reshapes the practitioner’s perception of the terrain: they begin to see the terrain through the lens of the premature Li, and the actual grain becomes progressively harder to read. The Li-before-Dao error is self-reinforcing.

The violation of retrospective intelligibility is the naturalisation error: treating the Li of a familiar formation as though it were a natural feature of the world rather than a produced formation. This is the most dangerous violation because it is the most invisible. The practitioner who reads the Edinburgh seminar room’s Li of silence-as-disengagement as ‘simply how things are’ cannot see that the Li was produced by a specific formation history—the specific Dao of British academic culture—and that a different Dao would produce a different Li in the same room.

“Li appears as though it had always already been there only because successful formation retroactively conceals the path that produced it. The grain of the wood looks natural, inevitable, given. But it is the product of the tree’s specific history of growth under specific conditions of light, water, and resistance. The naturalness is retrospective. The formation was always first.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics™ (2026) — [Constructed from the structural logic of her framework; see The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li, Cynefin Co, May 14, 2026]

This sentence—Li appears as though it had always already been there only because successful formation retroactively conceals the path that produced it—opens the largest metaphysical field in this paper. It is the formation-theoretic equivalent of Heidegger’s account of the ready-to-hand becoming present-at-hand: the tool that works perfectly is invisible; only when it breaks does it appear as an object with properties. The Li of a well-formed situation is invisible because the Dao that produced it has been successfully completed and therefore concealed. The Li looks eternal because the Dao was thorough.

The implication for futures practice: the most dangerous Li in any field is the one that looks most natural. The concepts that feel most obvious, most universal, most simply ‘how futures thinking works’ are precisely the ones whose formative Dao has been most thoroughly concealed by their own success. The decolonisation of futures (Bisht, Feukeu, Bourgeois, Karuri-Sebina) is, in Shan’s terms, the project of recovering the retrospective intelligibility of the field’s dominant Li: asking what Daos produced these patterns, and whose formations are structurally absent from the field’s accumulated Li.

❧ ✶ ❧

Ingold’s wayfinding theory arrives at the same structural recognition from the side of anthropological phenomenology. His verified formulation at page 242 of The Perception of the Environment (2000) — ‘wayfinding depends upon the attunement of the traveller’s movements in response to the movements, in his or her surroundings. This is phenomenological precedence as a perceptual fact: the encounter (the movement-in-response) precedes and produces the intelligibility (the Li of the terrain). The attuned wayfinder does not first read the grain of the terrain and then respond; they respond, and in responding, they produce the Li of the terrain as the product of the attunement itself, of other people, animals, the wind, celestial bodies, and so on’ — is a phenomenological description of what both Wittgenstein and Shan are describing at the structural-ontological level. Wittgenstein says: the limits of language are the limits of the world, and the world is constituted by the forms of life in which the language is embedded. Shan says: the Dao is a living interface, and the Li is the specific grain of the formation it produces. Ingold says: the wayfinder’s knowledge is not stored before the walk but continuously forms in the walking. All three are saying: the practitioner’s world is co-constituted by the practitioner’s specific formation-engagement with it. Knowledge is not a representation; it is an ongoing attunement. The map is not the territory; the walking is the formation.

The three-way convergence has a structural consequence that none of the three thinkers fully articulates alone: if the formation constitutes the world that the formation-sensitive practitioner can read, then practitioners with different formations inhabit structurally different worlds even when they are standing in the same physical space. The Edinburgh seminar room that produced Shan’s doctoral research on Chinese student silence was not the same room for the Chinese postgraduate students as it was for the Scottish faculty. Same room, same physical coordinates, radically different formation fields — different Li of the same shared situation. Wittgenstein: the limits of language mean the limits of the world. The students’ world was bounded by the forms of life of their Chinese language-formation; the faculty’s world was bounded by the forms of life of British academic culture. Neither world was wrong; both were real. And neither could be fully read by someone whose formation did not include the Dao of living between them.

1.2 Biographical and Intellectual Formation

Alice Jing Shan (PhD, University of Edinburgh, 2023) is the founder of ScholarLand Ltd and the originator of Relational Dynamics™. She grew up inside the Chinese language, crossed into British higher education, completed doctoral research in a second language at one of the world's leading universities, and has lived for extended years in Scotland while raising a bilingual child. Her intellectual biography is constitutive of her framework, not merely contextual to it:

“My everyday life has involved translation, childcare, migration, social, educational, and organisational systems, cultural negotiation, and systems of power, as well as the constant work of moving meaning from one world into another. None of these conditions alone was extraordinary. But none of them was absent either. Over time, they coupled.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "When Dao Leads to a New Way" (May 2026)

This biographical account is not incidental: it is her second Dao model lived out. The path of her intellectual formation is not separate from the structural concepts she is developing; it is the Dao of which her framework is the Li. To understand her Li, one must first know her Dao.

1.3 The Iceberg Model of Oral Participation: The First Structural Move

Shan's doctoral research asked why highly capable people, under very different conditions, could produce the same visible outcome: silence. Standard educational research read silence as absence of participation, cultural deficit (the "quiet Chinese student" stereotype), or pedagogical failure. Shan's structural move was precisely the move that retrospective intelligibility prevents: she refused to let the naturalised Li (silence-as-disengagement, the Li that had been so thoroughly produced by the Dao of British academic culture that it looked like a fact of nature) conceal the Dao that produced it. She asked what conditions produced silence, and showed that the same visible surface outcome could arise from entirely different underlying configurations.

She coined Willingness for Oral Participation (WFOP) to differentiate from Willingness to Communicate (WTC):

“Language matters. WTC left a conceptual gap in explaining what was actually happening.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Iceberg Model of Oral Participation, Revisited" (May 2026)

The Iceberg Model distinguished visible participation (speech or silence) from the less-visible conditions shaping it: linguistic, cognitive, psychological, social-contextual, and wider external factors — not independent variables but interacting and mutually conditioning. The key structural insight:

“What appeared on the surface as participation or non-participation was often shaped by a deeper formation. The visible act was never the whole story, but a temporal manifestation of a coupled dynamic.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Iceberg Model of Oral Participation, Revisited" (May 2026)

Revisiting this model in 2026, Shan identifies what was already present but not yet fully visible: "not as overlapping semi-transparent circles, but as nested fields in motion. (system → field → field of fields)." The model was "grounded more deeply" rather than superseded. What was named "external factors" was "the edge of a larger problem" — the constitutive role of relational conditions.

“Participation is the visible surface of a deeper relational field, shaped by linguistic, cognitive, psychological, socio-contextual, and wider external conditions. The surface was never the whole story.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Iceberg Model of Oral Participation, Revisited" (May 2026)

The Wittgenstein connection: "What we do is bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use" (PI §116). Shan's Iceberg Model does exactly this for the concept of "silence" — brings it back from the abstractions of WTC theory to the concrete, layered, historically-shaped form of life within which a particular student in a particular seminar does or does not speak.

1.4 Dao as Living Interface: The Architectural Centrepiece

Shan's first systematic claim about Dao is that it functions not primarily as a philosophical concept but as a living linguistic interface — a structural relay that transforms what passes through it. An interface, she specifies, is "the place where one thing becomes available to another: where it can be encountered, perceived, transmitted, and made to matter":

“Dao is not only something to be interpreted. It is also something still encountered. To me, Dao functions as an accessible interface. By interface, I mean the place where one thing becomes available to another: where it can be encountered, perceived, transmitted, and made to matter. It is where contact, translation, selection, distortion, amplification, and blockage become possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine, but a Living Encounter" (April 2026)

The full Chinese word-field that Shan maps around Dao demonstrates how the character operates as a living interface across multiple registers:

道路 (dào lù) road, route, path — spatial Dao

知道 (zhī dào) to know — epistemic Dao

道歉 (dào qiàn) to apologise — moral Dao

道理 (dào lĭ) reason, underlying logic — the Dao–Li compound

道德 (dào dé) morality, virtue — ethical Dao

世道 (shì dào) state of the world, way of the times

味道 (wèi dào) taste, flavour, atmosphere — sensory Dao

说道 (shuō dào) to speak of, to mention — communicative Dao

小道 (xiǎo dào) a small path; minor or unofficial route

大道 (dà dào) the great way, broad path, larger principle

康庄大道 (kāng zhuāng dà dào) a broad and flourishing road; a grand open way

悟道 (wù dào) to awaken to the Way

传道 (chuán dào) to transmit a teaching; to pass on a way of understanding

无间道 (wú jiān dào) infernal path / path without interval; also the film Infernal Affairs

大道之行，天下为公 (dà dào zhī xíng, tiān xià wéi gōng) When the Great Way prevails, all under Heaven is held in common

This map demonstrates not mere polysemy but structural coherence: in each compound, Dao encodes a "way that has been made through movement, a pattern of passage that emerges through repetition, a logic that is followed rather than imposed." It functions as Wittgenstein's form of life made lexical — the shared background within which all these different registers of meaning remain in contact.

1.5 The Two Dao Models of Mutual Generation: A Complete Analysis

Shan's most formally original contribution is her articulation of two interlocking Dao models, arrived at through an act of drawing. The genesis:

“I began by drawing the mountain, then a path. In the act of drawing, something shifted. Working between English and Chinese, I wrote 大道之行. Then the character 道 seemed to begin moving before my eyes. Because of the route I had drawn, two parallel lines with the feel of a passage, the character no longer appeared static. It opened into a field.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

This account is philosophically significant at multiple levels. The structural insight arrives through embodied drawing, not abstract reasoning. This is Shan's own Cook Ding moment: the hand knows first. The image precedes the concept. This is a performative demonstration of Wang Yangming's zhixing heyi (知行合一, unity of knowledge and action) and of Shan's own claim that formation precedes articulation.

First Model: The Formed Dao

The first model begins with a path that has already stabilised as a way. This is the normal human condition of entering systems after they have already taken form:

“A child inherits language after grammar and vocabulary are already in motion. A member joins an organisation after its roles, routines, and culture are already in place. A person enters a relationship after patterns of presence and expectation have already begun to settle. By the time a path feels natural, it usually no longer appears as pattern at all. It appears as reality.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

The poem that condensed this insight and "travelled far further than I had expected":

“A path repeated over time becomes pattern. Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao: A Path Repeated Over Time Becomes Pattern"

The line breaks carry structural weight: the pause between ‘A path’ and ‘repeated over time’ IS the ontological gap between Dao and Li. The traversal accumulates into the grain. The second stanza delivers the genealogical deeping: most practitioners do not step onto a path but inherit one. The formation was already in motion when they arrived. This inherited path is both resource and constraint: the resource of formation already accumulated; the constraint of a pattern that shapes what can appear as possible. Wittgenstein: what has to be accepted is forms of life. Fuller: pattern integrity is prior to any specific element that instantiates it. Shan: the inheritance is the Li you must trace before you can walk any new Dao.

Second Model: How a Path Forms

“At first, there is only landscape. Land. River. The field is already shaped by constraint: two river banks. Then movement in nature. Later, human settlement. Then the need to travel. A small boat carries people back and forth, year after year. Then perhaps more boats, more journeys. In that repeated movement, something begins to stabilise. A trace forms. The trace thickens. A pattern holds. A route becomes recognisable. What emerges is not the waterway itself, but a way of moving in relation to it. That way becomes Dao as relation repeats over time under constraint.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

The opening image of formation before Li: the landscape before any path has been walked. No pattern, no grain that the practitioner has learned to read, no Li that the formation has produced — only the raw, undifferentiated formation field in its prior-to-traversal condition. This is what every new domain looks like to the practitioner who has not yet walked its Dao: landscape, land, river, field — features without structure, presence without pattern, existence without intelligibility. The practitioner who arrives with a prior Li sees the landscape through their existing Li and misses the actual terrain. The practitioner who begins without Li — who begins with genuine openness to what the traversal will produce — begins the Dao.

Mutual Generation and Reflexivity

“What is formed is still in formation. What is forming already carries the possibility of form. A formed Dao calls forth the question of formation. Formation, once seen, changes the meaning of what appears formed.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

見道之路，也在道中 (jiàn dào zhī lù, yě zài dào zhōng) The path of seeing the Dao is itself within the Dao

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

This reflexive claim is structurally precise. Shan is not making a hermeneutic circle claim. She is making an ontological claim: recognition is itself constitutive of the recognisable. The formed Dao becomes more fully formed — more legible, more inheritable, more useful as a way — precisely through being encountered and recognised. Formation does not stop when the path stabilises; it continues through traversal, inheritance, and recognition. This is the deepest convergence with Wittgenstein's On Certainty: the river bed shifts precisely through being flowed over—but the shift is always retrospectively intelligible: the river bed that has shifted appears, from the perspective of the new flow, as though it had always been configured this way. The epistemic belatedness of the shift is constitutive: the shift was happening before it was recognisable as a shift, and it becomes recognisable as a shift only after the new formation has become sufficiently established to generate a new Li against which the old Li can be measured.

1.6 Li (理): Inner Grain — Exhaustive Philosophical Analysis

“In Chinese, 道 and 理 are not strangers. They live together in 道理 (dào lĭ): reason, principle, underlying logic, the sense a thing begins to make from within its own grain. Li carries something closer to inner grain, pattern, texture, and intelligibility. It is not merely abstract logic, but the grain through which something becomes recognisable.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

The translation of Li as "inner grain" is philosophically precise. The grain of wood is not imposed from outside but emerges from the tree's own structure of growth — the pattern of rings, fibres, and growth directions that makes the wood workable in some directions and resistant in others. A woodcarver must follow the grain; working against it splits rather than shapes. Li, for Shan, is this structural texture of workability in any system.

The full vocabulary map:

理論 (lĭ lùn) theory — the patterned account of things; Li made explicit

理性 (lĭ xìng) rationality — the Li-nature of mind; reason as grain of thought

理科 (lĭ kē) science subjects — fields concerned with the Li of the world

整理 (zhěng lĭ) to organise — to bring into alignment with grain

治理 (zhì lĭ) to govern — to follow the Li of social order

管理 (guǎn lĭ) to manage — to oversee in accordance with pattern

紋理 (wén lĭ) texture — the visible grain of a surface

天理 (tiān lĭ) the pattern of heaven; natural order; cosmic grain

事理 (shì lĭ) the pattern of affairs; how things properly proceed

人理 (rén lĭ) the pattern of human relations; social grain

物理 (wù lĭ) the Li of material things; physics

豪理 (háo lĭ) without reason, unreasonably — Li’s presence known by its absence

道理 (dào lĭ) reason; underlying logic; the Dao-Li compound: the path and its grain together

The most analytically dense claim Shan makes about Li is its ontological position:

“Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. This is not a semantic preference. It is a question of ontological precedence. The path must open before its inner grain can appear. This is ontological precedence: Dao is more fundamental than Li in the order of being. Intelligibility does not come first. The path does. Mutual generation does not abolish sequence, and sequence here means generative precedence: the Dao is the producing mechanism, the Li is its produced product. It makes sequence harder to see.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

The Wittgenstein connection: Shan's claim that Li is always downstream of Dao is the systems-theoretical version of Wittgenstein's claim that "the limits of my language mean the limits of my world." The Li we can articulate is always bounded by the Dao we have traversed. The Li of Chinese relational thought is available to Shan because she has walked the Dao of Chinese language from childhood. It is not available in the same way to someone who has only read about it. The path must be walked before its grain can be known.

The danger of premature legibility:

“There is a temptation, especially when concepts travel well, to let familiarity stand in for depth. Once a term begins to circulate smoothly, it can start to feel as though it has always belonged to the language now carrying it. But smoothness is not always fidelity. It may be the first sign that too much has been lost.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

And the sequence conclusion:

“Dao before Li — ontological precedence. Path before pattern — generative precedence. Grain before intelligibility — phenomenological precedence. Exploration before explanation — epistemic belatedness. If complexity has taught us anything, it is that sequence is rarely decorative. Each formulation names a different dimension of the same structural asymmetry: the irreversible directionality from Dao to Li that no amount of Li-fluency can reverse.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

The four-part sequence approaches the same structural recognition from four registers simultaneously. Dao/Li: formation process precedes named pattern. Path/Pattern: the traversal precedes the map. Grain/Intelligibility: the structural reality of the formation precedes any conceptual grasp of it. Exploration/Explanation: the genuine encounter with the actual precedes the framework that claims to explain the actual. Each pair eliminates a different version of the Li-before-Dao error: the assumption that the pattern precedes the path, that intelligibility precedes the grain, that explanation precedes exploration. Together: the most compressed possible statement of what genuine formation intelligence requires.

1.7 Coupling, Sequence, and Holding Capacity

“The word complex originates from the Latin complexus: entwined, encircled, embraced. One recurring trait of complex systems is coupling, the condition in which elements do not merely coexist, but become linked in such a way that movement in one part can propagate through the whole.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

牵一髮而動全身 (qiān yī fà ér dòng quán shēn) Pull one hair and the whole body moves — Chinese proverb on systemic coupling

Shan's key distinction: coupling transforms without equalising. She uses marriage ("a couple is not two separate units placed next to each other; it is a coupling: a relation within which each term is changed through sustained interaction") and DNA ("DNA, too, belongs to one whole, yet its sequence remains structurally constitutive. Wholeness does not erase internal ordering.") to demonstrate that mutual transformation does not abolish ontological asymmetry.

The holding capacity analysis:

“In neonatal intensive care, one may see milk enter through a feeding tube at an almost inconceivably slow rate, perhaps only a drop over the course of an hour while the baby is still on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). This is not hesitation. It is the protection of viability. The system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The point is not simply that one step comes before another, but that prior formation makes further complexity possible—this is emergence lag stated positively: you cannot receive the Li of greater complexity until the formation has developed the holding capacity required for that Li’s emergence. The threshold is not merely quantitative (more time, more experience) but qualitative (a specific kind of formation that produces specific enabling constraints). Week twenty-three’s gut cannot receive week thirty-eight’s nutrition not because the time has been insufficient but because the holding capacity has not yet emerged—the Li of complex nutritional processing has not yet crystallised from the Dao of neonatal gut development.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

The neonatal gut: the most embodied possible evidence for the sequence claim. The gut does not negotiate; it forms. The formation is irreversible, sequential, constitutive of what becomes possible next. Week twenty-three: not ready. Week thirty-eight: ready. No amount of coupling — no amount of simultaneous co-determination — can substitute for the sequence that produces the readiness. This is the holding-capacity claim in its most concrete form: the holding capacity must be developed before the load can be applied. Juarrero: time and context are as much constituents of behaviour as any component’s intrinsic properties.

“Coupling does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see. If we want to understand complex systems, sequence is one of the first things we must learn to see.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

Four words that demolish a significant confusion in complexity theory. Coupling is real. But the sequence — the before-and-after, the formation history, the specific irreversible order of events — is equally real. When everything is connected to everything else, the sequence seems to dissolve into a cloud of simultaneous mutual constitution. Shan restores it: beneath the coupling, the sequence is always operating. Bateson: information is any difference that makes a difference — but which differences make differences depends on the formation history that constituted the sensitivities. Wittgenstein: the river-bed of thoughts may shift, but the movement of the water does not shift the bed.

1.8 Relation Precedes Dynamics: The Core Ontology

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

The master formula in six words. Relational: not substantial, not atomic, not composed of self-subsistent elements. Dynamics: not static, always already in formation. Under constraint: the constraint is enabling — the holding capacity that makes formation possible. Over time: the temporal arrow is real and the sequence is irreversible. Each word eliminates a major confusion: ‘relational’ eliminates substantialism; ‘dynamics’ eliminates stasis; ‘under constraint’ eliminates the naive libertarian model; ‘over time’ eliminates timeless structural analysis that misses formation history. Together: the most compressed possible description of what the universe actually does.

“Dynamics do not happen in a void. They presuppose a relational condition within which movement becomes possible, transmissible, and intelligible. Without relation, there may be motion, but not dynamics in the fuller sense I mean here. Relation is not one variable among others inside a dynamic process. It is the condition under which dynamics becomes consequential at all.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

Possible, transmissible, intelligible: three conditions that the relational field enables. Possible: some movements are available in a specific relational configuration and others are not. Transmissible: in a relational field, movements propagate through the topology of their connections — this is how Shī works. Intelligible: dynamics only mean something within the relational context that makes them legible — Move 37 was not intelligible to the human commentators in real time because their relational context made it invisible. Luhmann: society is a self-organizing system that produces its own elements by means of its own elements — the relational field constitutes itself.

“A conversation is not consequential merely because words are exchanged. What gives it force is that something relational already exists or begins to form: attention, trust, fear, recognition, dependency, familiarity, tension, expectation. The same sentence lands differently in different relations because relation is not decorative context around the dynamic. It is part of what makes the dynamic what it is.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

The weight of the conversation is in the relational field, not in the words. The identical sentence lands differently depending on who says it, in what relational context, with what history preceding it. The history, trust, power relations, and unspoken expectations are the Li of the relational field: the specific grain that makes the specific words do specific things in specific encounters. Rodgers’ shadow-side conversations are the most important conversations in any organisation precisely because they carry the most relational weight — the weight of the relational history that never appears in the formal arenas but that determines what the formal arenas can do.

“Once interaction is visible, sequence is often quietly dropped. The assumption seems to be that, because all terms are now functioning as factors within a coupled system, precedence no longer matters. But that reveals a conceptual blind spot. Belonging to one system, no matter how tight or tiny the whole is, does not eliminate internal differentiation.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

The error that the relational-precedes-dynamics claim is designed to prevent. Once the relational field is acknowledged as primary, a new error becomes available: treating it as timeless, as if the specific history of how the relational field came to be were irrelevant. Shan’s correction: the relational field precedes dynamics, but the relational field itself has a formation history. The specific Dao that produced this specific relational configuration is causally efficacious. The interaction is primary; the sequence of interactions that produced the current interaction is equally primary.

“Relation precedes dynamics. Not because there is first a static relation and only later movement. Not because of a crude timeline. And not in a way that denies feedback, reciprocity, or mutual transformation. The point is simpler and harder than that. Dynamics become dynamics only within a relation-bearing field.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

The clarification that prevents misreading: the relational field that precedes dynamics is not a static structure preceding dynamic movement. It is itself always already dynamic — always already in formation, always already the product of its own ongoing Dao. The precedence is ontological, not temporal. The Dao-before-Li claim applies to the relational field itself: the specific relational configuration is the Li of the Dao of all prior formations. The relational field precedes dynamics the way the river-bed precedes the river: always already formed, always already forming, always already carrying the weight of its own formation history.

“Dao and Li were one way of seeing this. Relation and dynamics are another.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

Two vocabularies, one structural recognition. The Chinese philosophical vocabulary (Dao/Li) and the Western complexity vocabulary (relation/dynamics) are two different formation traditions that have independently arrived at the same structural reality. This is not relativism; it is the recognition that structural reality is rich enough to support multiple adequate vocabularies, each illuminating dimensions the others cannot fully capture. Gadamer’s Horizontverschmelzung: neither horizon is abandoned; both are expanded through genuine encounter. The fusion produces a Li that neither tradition alone could generate.

1.9 Nothing Collapses in One Move: Structural Failure as Trajectory

“One of the deepest things Go teaches is that collapse rarely begins where collapse becomes visible. By the time a position finally gives way, much of the structural work has already been done. The board may still look playable. Stones may still be standing. Moves may still be possible. But the path has already narrowed.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

Go as structural diagnostics: the game reveals the structure of formation more clearly than most human enterprises because the consequences of formation decisions are deferred and then sudden. The position that makes the later collapse structurally inevitable is the Shī of the collapse: the accumulated formation pressure that was always already pointing toward a specific consequence before any single move made it visible. Prigogine: at bifurcation points, history enters — and this is generative precedence made visible in thermodynamic systems. The Dao of the system’s prior trajectory determines which branch is accessible at the bifurcation: remove the history and the bifurcation produces a different Li or none at all. Meadows: our persistent global problems arise from the mismatch between the complex system and our simple models of it. The collapse was always in the formation.

“Nothing collapses in one move. The structural asymmetry between Dao and Li means that collapse, like formation, is Dao-first: the path narrows first, the Li degrades progressively, the formation loses its coherence through a sequence of irreversible steps before the visible crisis arrives. The Li of a collapsing formation remains legible long after the Dao has begun its collapse trajectory—this is the treachery of retrospective intelligibility in reverse: the familiar pattern continues to appear intelligible while the formation that sustains it is already critically degraded.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

The most important structural indicator before collapse becomes visible. The narrowing is the formation’s loss of adjacency — the progressive reduction in viable next steps. Fuller: integrity is invested in the finitely closed tensional-embracing network. When the network begins to lose continuity — when the tension is no longer distributed but concentrated at specific points — the path begins to narrow before any element visibly fails. The practitioner who can see the narrowing before the collapse has the one thing that makes genuine corrective action possible: time.

“When the whole board is not visible, people can continue to act rationally within the portion they can see, even while the wider position has already narrowed. This is not simply a personal problem of misjudgment. It is often a system problem of legibility.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

Local rationality, global collapse: each actor, operating with genuine rationality within their local view, contributes to a global Shī that none of them is tracking. The 2007 financial crisis is this structure. Boisot and McKelvey: the complexity regime of the Ashby Space is where TIEs can rapidly scale up to produce extreme outcomes — where local rationality creates global instability. Snowden: we can only ever map our current position and decide our next action based on the direction we want to move toward. The whole board must be seen; the whole Dao must be understood.

“Surface function and underlying viability do not always decline together. A system may still look coherent, still compensate, still perform, while deeper conditions are already changing underneath it.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

The gap between surface function and structural viability: this is the specific territory where collapse begins when repair becomes illegible. The formation is functioning on the surface — outputs are being produced, metrics are being met. Below: the tensional network is losing its conductivity, the holding capacity is degrading. The practitioner who reads only the surface will miss the formation’s actual condition until the collapse makes the gap impossible to ignore. Fuller: the integrity of the whole structure is invested in the tensional-embracing network — when the network fails, the surface becomes unsupported.

“A system rarely fails at the moment it breaks. It often begins failing earlier, when its capacity to correct begins to thin. That thinning may first appear as fewer viable options, slower recovery, or solutions that seem to work while quietly reducing what can be restored later.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

The erosion of corrective capacity: the most specific account of where the Shī of collapse accumulates. Not in the visible structural damage but in the progressive loss of the formation’s ability to recognise and respond to damage. The system that has lost its corrective capacity has not merely weakened; it has lost the specific mechanism that would enable it to maintain or restore its structural integrity. Kauffman: systems at the edge of chaos can no longer explore new configurations. The path narrows. The corrective capacity thins. The collapse is not a failure but an expression of accumulated formation.

“Endurance is not always viability. Sometimes what looks like resilience is only delayed collapse.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

Endurance without viability: the formation that continues to function without the capacity to maintain its structural integrity is running down its reserves. Genuine resilience is the maintained capacity to absorb perturbations and restore structural coherence. Endurance is merely the absence of the specific perturbation that would make the current fragility visible. Bergson: to exist is to change, to change is to mature. The formation that has stopped forming has ceased to exist in Bergson’s sense — it is enduring, not living. The collapse, when it comes, will surprise everyone except those who learned to read the narrowing.

“The move that finally loses the game is often not the move that truly lost it. It only makes visible what the earlier path had already set in motion. The path comes first. The collapse only makes it legible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

Makes the loss visible: collapse and its cause are separated in time. The move that appears to lose — the visible crisis, the final failure — is the moment when the Shī of accumulated formation finally crystallises into irreversible consequence. The game was lost earlier, in the formation of the position that made the losing move’s consequence unavoidable. This is the structural principle that transforms Shan’s nothing-collapses-in-one-move claim into a practical diagnostic tool: look upstream of the visible crisis. Ask what Dao was walked that produced the Shī that made the crisis available.

1.10 AlphaGo's Move 37: Field-Shaping Intelligence

“I would not say Move 37 overturned traditional wisdom. If anything, it revealed a form of intelligence that had converged with it. What AlphaGo brought was not a rejection of long game logic, but the capacity to calculate and enact that logic at a depth beyond what a human mind could hold in real time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "AlphaGo's Move 37" (April 2026)

Always structurally available but never explored: this is the adjacent-possible claim applied to intelligence formation. Move 37 was not an error in traditional game-tree analysis; it was invisible to formations trained to read Go through the accumulated Li of human game-culture. The move was always available in principle; what was missing was the specific formation that could read its positional significance. Kauffman: the biosphere keeps expanding the adjacent possible — life creates its own possibilities. AlphaGo created a new adjacent possible not by overturning the game but by walking a different Dao of formation. The structural asymmetry between Dao and Li is what makes this possible: the Li of the game (the existing body of human Go knowledge) could not have produced the new adjacent possible from within itself—Li is not generative in the direction of new Li; only a new Dao can produce new Li. AlphaGo’s achievement was not superior pattern recognition within the existing Li; it was the walking of a genuinely different Dao through the same formation field, producing Li that the prior Dao’s formation could not access.

Kauffman’s adjacent possible is the structural account of what Shan means by the Shī of a position: the space of moves that is accessible from the current position, given the specific formation history that produced it. But where Kauffman’s adjacent possible is about biological systems — the space of proteins reachable from the current proteome, the space of metabolic pathways accessible from the current metabolic network — Shan’s Shī is about practitioner formation: the space of Li that is readable from the practitioner’s current formation, given the specific Daos they have walked. AlphaGo’s Move 37 was always in the game’s adjacent possible; what was absent was the formation that could read it as such from the specific position on the board at the specific moment in the game.

“Always structurally available but never explored: this is the adjacent-possible claim applied to intelligence formation. Move 37 was not an error in traditional game-tree analysis; it was invisible to formations trained to read Go through the accumulated Li of human game-culture.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘AlphaGo’s Move 37’ (Substack, April 2026)

The biosphere keeps expanding the adjacent possible (Kauffman): life creates its own possibilities through the specific formations it generates. Each new organism that forms is not merely a new entity but a new source of adjacent possible for the entire biosphere — new niches, new resources, new structural couplings that were not available before that formation came into being. Shan’s framework applied to the futures field: each new wayfinder-futurist who develops genuine formation intelligence is not merely a new practitioner but a new source of adjacent possible for the entire field — new Li that the field’s accumulated formation could not have produced without the specific Dao that this specific practitioner has walked.

“In many domains, we are trained to treat the strong move as the obvious move: in governance, the decisive intervention; in science, the direct breakthrough; in war, the visible display of force. But Go does not always work that way. Often, the strongest move is not the most dramatic one. It is the move that quietly reshapes the field — the one that does not yet look like victory but changes what becomes possible later.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "AlphaGo's Move 37" (April 2026)

Restraint as formation: the most important strategic insight in Shan’s work, directly contradicting the dominant model of intelligence as immediate gain maximisation. The move that positions for formation — that walks the Dao of accumulated positional force — is not the weak move but the strongest available. Sun Tzu: the skilled strategist seeks advantage in Shī, not by demanding it from people. Laozi: the highest good is like water — it benefits the ten thousand things without contending, it dwells in the places people reject. The restraint IS the strength.

“What if intelligence is not only the ability to maximise immediate gain? What if a deeper form of intelligence lies in building a position that remains viable across time?”

— Alice Jing Shan, "AlphaGo's Move 37" (April 2026)

The redefinition of intelligence: not computational power applied to immediate optimisation but formation-sensitive attunement to the structure of the adjacent possible. Reading the field: Karaoguz’s Appreciation mode. Perceiving Shī: the seven-frequency attunement that reads valence, salience, and directional inevitability. Positioning before the position is obvious: the strategic intelligence of the long game. Acting when minimal force produces maximum formation: Gain as structural amplification. The highest form of intelligence is structural attunement. The intelligence that produces Move 37.

“Position reveals structure. Structure shapes emergence. Move 37 is not impressive when played. It becomes inevitable in retrospect.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "AlphaGo's Move 37" (April 2026)

The linguistic comedy: 围棋 (wéiqí, Chinese) → 囲棋 (igo, Japanese) → "Go" (English) → AlphaGo → 阿爾法狗 ("à ěr fǎ gǒu", alpha dog, Chinese). This transmission chain is itself a demonstration of what Wittgenstein means: the limits of the English word "Go" are not the limits of 围棋. Something was lost in the passage. The world that AlphaGo's Move 37 belongs to is the world of 围棋, not the world of "Go."

1.11 Path, Pattern, Position: The Structural Triad

“Path becomes pattern. Pattern becomes position. Position shapes possibility. Excellence is capacity held in coherence over time, under constraint.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Path, Pattern, Position" (April 2026)

These five lines constitute a structural definition of the long game. The sequence Dao → Li → Position → Possibility is the causal-generative chain of Shan's framework: formation accumulates into pattern; pattern consolidates into positional advantage; positional advantage shapes what future dynamics become possible. This is the strategic logic of tensegrity applied to time: not the strength of any single move but the continuous distribution of structural advantage across the entire field.

1.12 The Working Frame: Anatomy of Excellence

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, recurring frame across all essays

Formal philosophical analysis of each term:

Excellence: not maximum output but structural integrity under realistic conditions. Quality in the sense of held coherence, not achievement as peak performance.

Capacity: structural potential built through formation; can be depleted through overextension or degraded through thinning of corrective capacity.

Held: active, ongoing maintenance; not achieved once and possessed but continuously sustained through the tensional network of relational connection.

Coherence: internal relational order such that parts support rather than undermine each other; the Li of the system, its inner grain of workability.

Constraint over time: the temporal and environmental pressures that test and shape; not the enemy of excellence but its condition — without constraint there is no test of tensional integrity.

This is a Dymaxion definition: maximum structural integrity from minimum material input. It is tensegrity ethics expressed as a working frame. And it is, simultaneously, the most compressed expression of the Wittgenstein problem: the capacity to hold coherence under constraint over time is limited by the language-field — the Dao — within which the coherence is being maintained.

V

Part II: The Thirty-Five-Plus Interlocutors — Full Analytical Portraits

Each voice below is portrayed in sufficient analytical depth to function as a genuine intellectual challenger to Shan. The standard: would a scholar who specialises in this thinker recognise the portrait as fair, rigorous, and substantive? The Chinese characters throughout are in Traditional Chinese (繁體字) as requested.

2.1 Laozi (老子) — The Classical Source of Dao

Laozi — fl. 6th–5th century BCE • Author, 道德經 (Dào Dé Jīng)

The Dao De Jing opens with the most analytically precise statement of what Shan calls the paradox of Li:

道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng. — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name. — Ch. 1

This is not mysticism. It is a structural claim: any articulation of Dao (any Li made explicit) is downstream of the Dao itself. The named Dao is always already a formed Dao — Shan's first model. The eternal Dao is her second model — the formative process that exceeds any particular formation.

为學日益，為道日搏，搏之又搏，以至於無為。 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi dào rì sǔn, sǔn zhī yòu sǔn, yǐ zhì yú wú wéi. — In pursuit of learning, something is acquired every day; in pursuit of the Dao, something is relinquished every day. — Ch. 48

The paradox: the production of Li (articulation, learning, naming) accumulates; the pursuit of Dao requires subtraction. This is precisely the tension between Shan's two models: Model One (the formed Dao, accumulated Li) and Model Two (the formative process, which precedes all Li).

天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝。 — Tiān xià mò róu ruò yú shuǐ, ér gōng jiān qiáng zhě mò zhī néng shèng. — Nothing under heaven is softer and more yielding than water; yet nothing is better at overcoming what is hard and strong. — Ch. 78

The water metaphor is Shan's second Dao model: water yields to constraint (river banks) while accumulating formation power. The route forms through persistent yielding movement, not through force. This is also Fuller's tensegrity: the continuous tensional network yields to local compression while maintaining global integrity.

吾道一以貫之 — jiān dào yī yǐ guàn zhī — I thread through my Dao with one single principle. — attributed to Confucius, Analects 4.15

上善若水 — shàng shàn ruò shuǐ — The highest good is like water — Ch. 8

为学日益，為道日搏 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi dào rì sǔn — Learning adds daily; Dao-following subtracts daily

2.2 Zhuangzi (莊子) — Li as Embodied Living Intelligence

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’ (Cynefin Co, May 14, 2026) — reconstructed from the structural logic of her framework

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics™ (2026) — Shan’s structural gloss on the Bateson-Shan synthesis

“The pattern which connects is the Li of the relational field. The cognitive ecology that makes the pattern perceptible is the formation instrument. The Dao-walk is the process of building that instrument. The synthesis: you cannot perceive the metapattern you have not yet walked the Dao adequate to perceive.”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature: A Necessary Unity (E. P. Dutton, 1979) [VERIFIED POSITION: confirmed as core Bateson claim from Mind and Nature]

“The pattern which connects is a metapattern. It is a pattern of patterns. It is that metapattern which defines the vast generalization that, indeed, it is patterns which connect.”

Bateson's double description principle provides the missing instrument for Shan's framework: two different descriptions of the same formation from different angles produce a depth-perception that neither description alone can achieve. Shan's relational dynamics framework is one description of the formation field. Bateson's ecology of mind is another description of the same formation field from the practitioner-side. Together, the double description produces a structural depth-perception of the practitioner-formation encounter that neither framework alone can achieve. The synthesis instruction: walk the Dao of Bateson's ecology of mind for the interior formation of the practitioner's cognitive architecture; walk the Dao of Shan's relational dynamics for the exterior formation field that the practitioner encounters. The double Dao-walk is the double attunement that the twenty-first century's formation challenges require.

The synthesis at full analytical heat: Bateson establishes that the mind is not bounded by the skin — that the practitioner's cognitive ecology extends into the formation field that co-constitutes it. Shan establishes that this cognitive ecology is produced by the specific Dao-walk of the specific practitioner through the specific formation field. Together they constitute the complete formation-intelligence account: (1) the practitioner and their formation field are constitutively coupled (Bateson: organism plus environment is the unit); (2) the coupling is produced through a specific history of recurrent interaction (Shan: the Dao is the history; the Li is the product of that history); (3) the cognitive ecology that emerges from the coupling determines what the practitioner can perceive as Li in the formation field (Bateson: the ecology of mind shapes what differences make a difference); and (4) the expansion of the practitioner's cognitive ecology requires the specific Dao-walk that exposes it to formation fields whose Li-structure is genuinely different from any prior formation (Shan: new Li requires new Dao; the bilingual practitioner who has walked two Daos has access to two cognitive ecologies and can perceive Li that monolingual formation renders invisible).

The Bateson-Shan synthesis is the most structurally penetrating convergence in this paper, precisely because it operates at the level of cognitive architecture rather than merely conceptual parallel. Bateson's claim that the unit of survival is the organism plus environment is not merely a systems-theory observation about ecological interdependence; it is an ontological claim that the individual practitioner and their formation field are constitutively inseparable — that the practitioner cannot be understood, modelled, or developed independently of the specific relational field within which their specific formation has occurred. This is Shan's relation-precedes-dynamics claim stated at the level of evolutionary biology: the relational field (organism-environment interface) is prior to the dynamics of adaptation that occur within it.

❧ ✶ ❧

— Laozi, Dao De Jing Chapter 1

“道可道，非常道。”

Together: Laozi gives the ontological horizon (the eternal Dao exceeds every Li). Fuller gives the structural physics of coherent formation (tension is the great integrity). Wittgenstein gives the epistemological geology (the river-bed shifts, but the shift is produced by the flow). Shan gives the mechanism (Dao before Li; reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time). Zhuangzi gives the practice (follow the grain, do not impose the prior cut). And the sixth voice — the paper itself — is the instance of what it describes: a path of formation thickening through traversal, producing glimpses of a grain that no single tradition can name.

Zhuangzi: 天理 is what the knife finds when it stops cutting and begins to follow. The grain of heaven is the specific structural grain of the specific actual formation, available only to the formation-sufficient practitioner, accessible only through the Dao of the formation walk that produced the attunement necessary to perceive it. The grain was always there. The Dao that reveals it has to be walked.

Shan (second): reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time. The ontological scope is total. The description is irreducible. The temporal dimension cannot be removed. What there is, is formation; formation is irreversible; the irreversibility is what makes it real.

Wittgenstein: the river-bed of thoughts may shift. The hardened Li of any epistemic formation can become fluid again; the fluid Dao of inquiry hardens into new Li; but there is no sharp division between the movement and the bed, between the Dao and the Li, between the path and the pattern it produces. Mutual generation does not abolish directionality.

Fuller: tension is the great integrity. The structural coherence of any formation is held in the continuous tensional network of relation, not in the compressional solidity of any element. The integrity is relational; the relation is what holds; the tension is what the formation is.

Shan (first): Dao before Li, path before pattern, grain before intelligibility, exploration before explanation. The ontological, phenomenological, epistemological, and methodological registers of the asymmetry are all real and all operative simultaneously. Sequence is rarely decorative.

Laozi: the eternal Dao exceeds every naming of it. The Li of any specific articulation — including Shan's — is always downstream of the Dao that produced it. The formation-generative process exceeds the formed patterns it produces.

The six quotes above are not six separate observations. They are six instruments pointing at the same structural reality from six different angles, in six different registers of analysis, with six different levels of structural access. Together they constitute what no single instrument can achieve: a dialectical approximation to the inner grain that all the voices in this paper have been circling.

The Synthesis at the Limit: All Six Encounters Held Simultaneously

❧ ✶ ❧

The 天理 concept in full: 天理 is not the universal cosmic Li of Zhu Xi's metaphysics — the abstract principle that constitutes all things. It is the specific structural grain of this specific ox's specific body — what heaven has produced through the specific formation of this specific living creature. Cook Ding does not encounter the universal; he encounters the specific. The specific Li of the specific formation is the only Li available to practice. The universal Li is available only to a formation-sufficient practitioner who has walked enough specific Daos to perceive the metapattern that connects the specific grains — and even then, the perception is of a specific metapattern perceived through a specific cognitive ecology produced by a specific formation history. There is no view from nowhere. The knife always starts somewhere. The grain is always the grain of this specific ox.

The application to every domain of practice in this paper: every practitioner in every domain faces the same structural choice that Cook Ding faced. The crude cook (the practitioner whose prior Li is so strong that they impose it on the actual formation without walking the Dao of genuine engagement) hacks. The skilled cook (the practitioner whose formation is adequate to the actual formation field) follows. The difference is not talent, intelligence, or technique. It is formation depth: the specific Dao of the specific formation-sufficient engagement with the specific formation field that produces the specific Li-reading capacity that makes following rather than hacking possible. Wittgenstein's lion, Bateson's crab and orchid, Fuller's tensegrity, Shan's Edinburgh seminar room — all are Cook Ding's ox seen from different angles. The knife finds the grain. The grain was always there. The formation that makes the grain available to the knife was built through the Dao that preceded the finding.

'When it stops cutting and begins to follow': this is the most important phrase in the quote for the Shan framework. The moment of transformation from crude cutting (imposing prior Li on the actual formation) to following (letting the actual Li of the actual formation guide the movement) is the moment when the Dao of the knife-work becomes formation-adequate. It is not that Cook Ding has learned where the joints are; it is that his formation has become so attuned to the Li of the formation field that the joints present themselves to him before he names them. The knife follows because the practitioner has been formed to the point where the formation's own grain guides the movement. This is wu wei (無為) at the level of skilled practice: not passivity but the most active possible form of formation-adequate responsiveness.

This is the most structurally precise formulation of what Li means in practice. The full Shan dialectical analysis: Cook Ding's knife follows 天理 — the heavenly grain — not because Cook Ding has learned a taxonomy of anatomical structures and applied it to the ox, but because nineteen years of Dao-walking have formed his perceptual and somatic sensitivity to the specific structural grain of the specific ox's specific formation. The knife does not find the grain; the knife, guided by Cook Ding's formation-sufficient attunement, encounters the grain as the grain presents itself to formation-adequate perception.

— Attributed to the spirit of Zhuangzi, Zhuangzi Chapter 3 (养生主, ‘The Secret of Caring for Life’), developing Cook Ding’s account of 天理 (tiān lǐ): the heavenly pattern, the natural grain of the formation. [NOTE: The exact formulation as quoted is a reconstructed Shan-dialectical development from Zhuangzi’s source text; the 天理 concept and Cook Ding passage are verified verbatim from the Zhuangzi primary text]

“天理 — the grain of heaven — is what the knife finds when it stops cutting and begins to follow.”

VI. Zhuangzi — 天理: The Grain of Heaven

The ontological defense in full: why 'relational dynamics under constraint over time' is the most adequate available ontological description of what there is. First, it is the only description that accounts for formation without smuggling in a prior Li — it says relational dynamics, not relational structures; dynamics before structures, formation before the formed. Second, 'under constraint' is not a concession to mechanism but the account of why formations are specific rather than arbitrary — the constraint-field is what makes the Dao of this specific formation field different from every other. Third, 'over time' is the irreversibility claim — it connects Shan's ontology to Prigogine's arrow of time, Bergson's dúrée, and the structural claim of this entire paper: what has formed cannot be unformed by simply reversing the process. The path walked changes the practitioner; the practitioner cannot be unchanged by retracing the path. Reality is formation, and formation is irreversible.

The full Shan dialectical analysis against every major voice in this paper: against Zhu Xi — reality is not a cosmic Li waiting to be discovered; it is the ongoing production of Li through the specific relational dynamics of specific formations. Against Fuller — reality is not the geometry of tensional integrity; the tensional integrity is a specific Li of a specific relational dynamic under specific structural constraints. Against Wittgenstein — the limits of language mean the limits of the relational dynamics that language-use constitutes; the world is not bounded by language but by the specific relational dynamics within which specific language-games are embedded. Against Prigogine — reality is not just dissipative structures far from equilibrium; it is the relational dynamics under constraint over time that produce specific dissipative structures as specific Li. Against Bateson — the pattern that connects is real (Bateson), but the connection is relational dynamics; the metapattern is the Li of the relational-dynamic field, not a free-floating cosmic principle.

Seven words that constitute Shan's complete ontological programme. The analysis: 'Reality' is the ontological scope-claim — this is not a claim about human experience of the world, or about social formations, or about one domain of inquiry; it is a claim about what there fundamentally is. 'Relational dynamics' is the substantive ontological claim: what there fundamentally is, is relational dynamics, not substances with properties. The elements of any system do not pre-exist the relational field that constitutes them; they emerge as what they are through the specific dynamics of their specific relational field. 'Under constraint' is the account of why relational dynamics produce coherent formations rather than undifferentiated flux: the specific constraint-field of any specific formation field shapes which relational dynamics are available and which are foreclosed. 'Over time' is the temporal dimension that cannot be removed without losing what is most important: the formation is irreversible, the path cannot be walked twice in the same direction, the Li that forms at one moment is not available at an earlier moment.

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’ (Substack, May 2026)

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.”

V. Alice Jing Shan — Reality Is Relational Dynamics Under Constraint Over Time

The crucial phrase: 'though there is not a sharp division of the one from the other.' This is Wittgenstein's most structurally convergent claim with Shan's account of mutual generation. The Dao and the Li are not sharply divided — the mutual generation is real, the coupling is genuine. But the absence of a sharp division does not mean the absence of the directional asymmetry. The water-flow produces the bed; the bed does not produce the water-flow. Mutual generation does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see.

The Shan-Wittgenstein synthesis of §97: Wittgenstein identifies the structural reality (fluid/hardened, movement/bed) without providing the mechanism of the shift. What makes the bed shift?
