What quantity of water-flow, in what direction, over what time, produces a geological transformation rather than just erosion at the margins? Shan's formation theory provides the mechanism Wittgenstein identifies but does not specify: the bed shifts when the accumulated Dao-walk of sufficient practitioners reaches the threshold that makes the current Li's grip on epistemic practice untenable. Nothing collapses in one move — not the bed and not the Li. The shift builds through a long formation of accumulated divergent flow before the visible geological change becomes apparent. The moment of paradigm shift (Kuhn's term, developed across the same conceptual territory as Wittgenstein's §97) is the terminal Li of a formation that has been building for decades.

Shan's full dialectical analysis of §97: Wittgenstein's river-bed is the geological image of what Shan calls the formation history. The bed did not arrive pre-formed; it was carved by the water that flowed through it. The Li of the bed is the product of the Dao of the water's flow — and when enough Dao has flowed in a different pattern, the bed shifts and a new Li forms. This is not merely a metaphor; it is a structural account of how epistemic formation works across time: the fluid propositions of one generation's inquiry become the hardened bedrock of the next generation's presuppositions, until sufficient inquiry flows in different channels to carve a new bed.

This is Wittgenstein's mature structural account of the relationship between fluid and hardened epistemic elements — and it is the most precise Western philosophical formulation of what Shan means by Dao and Li available anywhere in the tradition. The river-bed is Li: the hardened propositions that function as the channel for fluid inquiry, the structural grain that makes the movement of ordinary reasoning possible. The water is Dao: the fluid propositions, the ongoing inquiry, the movement through the epistemic formation field. The shift of the bed itself is the most significant event in Wittgenstein's epistemological account: the moment when what had been Li (hardened, channelling, taken for granted) becomes Dao again (fluid, revisable, moving through the channel of a new Li that has not yet formed).

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, On Certainty §97 (Anscombe and von Wright trans., Blackwell, 1969–1975) [VERIFIED VERBATIM from multiple scholarly sources including OC 1975 §97]

“The mythology may change back into a state of flux, the river-bed of thoughts may shift. But I distinguish between the movement of the waters on the river-bed and the shift of the bed itself; though there is not a sharp division of the one from the other.”

IV. Ludwig Wittgenstein — On Certainty §97: The River-Bed of Thoughts

The weld: Fuller's four words and Shan's formation theory together constitute what neither achieves alone — a complete account of structural coherence from the physics of actual structures (Fuller) through the ontology of the relational formation field that makes those structures possible (Shan). Tension is the great integrity. And the great integrity is downstream of the Dao that produced the specific tensional configuration. The tension is real. The path that produced it is prior.

The extension Shan makes that Fuller does not: tension in Fuller's tensegrity is a physical force — it is measurable, geometrically describable, and structurally specifiable. Relation in Shan's formation theory is not a physical force but an ontological condition: the prior ground within which any specific structural force becomes possible. Shan's relation precedes Fuller's tension. The relational field that makes tension-integrity possible is ontologically prior to the specific tensional configuration that makes any particular structure coherent. Fuller tells us what the structure is when it is working. Shan tells us what the relational ground is without which no structure of that kind could form.

Shan's full dialectical response: Fuller's claim is about the structural physics of coherent forms. Shan's claim is about the structural dynamics of coherent formations. The parallel is exact and consequential. In Fuller's tensegrity, tension is what makes the structure viable: without the continuous tensional network, the discontinuous compression islands would simply separate. In Shan's relational dynamics, relation is what makes formation viable: without the relational field that constitutes the practitioner-situation encounter, there is no formation — no Dao-walk, no Li, no structural intelligence. Fuller's tension is Shan's relation. Fuller's compression island is Shan's node of temporary coherence. Fuller's structural integrity is Shan's excellence-as-capacity-held-in-coherence-under-constraint-over-time.

Four words that compress a complete structural philosophy. The analysis Shan's framework brings: Fuller is making a claim about the ontological priority of tension over compression in structural systems. The tension members are continuous; the compression islands are discontinuous. What holds the structure together is not what pushes from inside but what pulls from outside. The structural integrity of any tensegrity is not a property of any single element but of the entire tensional network taken as a whole.

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics: Explorations in the Geometry of Thinking (Estate of R. Buckminster Fuller, 1982, p.619) [VERIFIED: confirmed from Synergetics primary text and AZQuotes attribution to same source]

“Tension is the great integrity.”

III. R. Buckminster Fuller — Tension Is the Great Integrity

Wittgenstein's river-bed is the most precise structural parallel: the fluid propositions (Dao) and the hardened propositions (Li) are both real, both present, both operative in practice. But the hardened propositions became hard through a prior process of flowing. The sequence is not temporal in a simple sense; it is ontological. And the practitioner who reads only the hardened bed without reading the flow that produced it is reading a Li without a Dao — a pattern without a path — a grain without the tree that grew it.

The dialectical analysis of 'sequence is rarely decorative' is the most important analytical move in the quote. Shan is responding to the standard complexity-theory move of saying that Dao and Li are mutually constitutive, reciprocally generating, co-emergent. This is true — they are. But mutual constitution does not abolish sequence; it makes sequence harder to see. The specific Dao that produced the specific Li came first. The specific Li that now enables the next Dao came after. The coupling is real; the directionality is also real; and the directionality is where the operational implications live. A practitioner who does not distinguish Dao from Li — who treats them as simply equivalent aspects of a single relational field — cannot avoid the premature-Li error: applying the crystallised pattern before the formation walk that would make the pattern adequate has been completed.

This is Shan's most compressed statement of the entire framework. Each pairing is a different register of the same ontological asymmetry. 'Dao before Li': the ontological register — the formation-process is prior to the formed pattern in the order of being. 'Path before pattern': the phenomenological register — the practitioner's engaged movement through the formation field precedes the intelligibility that movement produces. 'Grain before intelligibility': the epistemological register — the specific structural texture of the formation is prior to any cognitive act of reading it. 'Exploration before explanation': the methodological register — the specific engaged encounter with the actual situation precedes any explanatory framework applied to it.

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’ (Cynefin Co, May 14, 2026)

“Dao before Li. Path before pattern. Grain before intelligibility. Exploration before explanation. If complexity has taught us anything, it is that sequence is rarely decorative.”

II. Alice Jing Shan — Dao Before Li

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’ (Cynefin Co, May 14, 2026)

“Dao rarely travels alone. Perhaps Li is the less-known partner whose absence should caution us whenever Dao begins to feel too smooth, too familiar, or too readily available.”

Epistemic belatedness applied: Laozi's 'the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao' is the most ancient available statement of epistemic belatedness. The naming (the Li) arrives after the formation (the Dao) and cannot recover it. Every paper that has tried to name the Dao — including this one — has produced a Li that is downstream of the Dao that produced it. This paper is itself a Li. Its grain is real. Its Dao is gone.

The Shan-Laozi synthesis at maximum dialectical heat: Laozi establishes the ontological ground. The formation-generative process (the eternal Dao) precedes and exceeds any specific Li (the named Dao). Shan develops the mechanism: the path must be walked before its inner grain can appear; the formation is the condition of the possibility of the formed pattern; the Dao is ontologically prior to any Li it produces. But Shan adds what Laozi does not supply: the account of how specific Dao-walks produce specific Li. Laozi tells us that the eternal Dao exceeds every naming; Shan tells us what the specific Dao of a specific practitioner's specific formation encounter produces. The eternal Dao of Laozi's first line is the ontological ground of Shan's Dao-before-Li at the scale of the cosmos; Shan's framework is the practical development of Laozi's ontological claim at the scale of the specific practitioner's specific formation. Two and a half millennia of formation between them, and the same structural recognition: the path is prior to the pattern it produces, and no naming of the pattern recovers the path.

Shan's full dialectical analysis of Laozi's opening: this is not mystical evasion but the most precise structural claim about the ontological status of Li available in the entire Chinese philosophical tradition. When Laozi says the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao, he is making the same claim that Shan makes with 'Dao before Li' — but at a higher structural resolution. The named Dao is already Li: it is the crystallised pattern of a specific formation, the specific grain that a specific Dao-walk has produced. The eternal Dao is the formation process itself, prior to any specific crystallisation. What cannot be named is not mysterious; it is structurally prior to the conditions that make naming possible.

— Laozi, Dao De Jing Chapter 1 [VERIFIED VERBATIM: standard received text, all editions]

“道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。” — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng. The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. This closing image of the collisions holds all ten encounters simultaneously: the path that exceeds every naming of it.

I. Laozi — 道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。

The six quotes that frame the closing of this paper's collision structure are not decorative closures. Each one opens a specific philosophical field that has been traversed throughout the preceding analysis and requires, at this terminal juncture, the full Shan dialectical treatment: the specific Dao-before-Li sequence applied to the specific structural claim of each voice, with the full weight of the paper's accumulated analysis brought to bear.

Ten Closing Encounters: The Six Terminal Quotes and Their Full Shan Dialectical Analysis

❧ ✶ ❧

The convergence is structural, not merely verbal. All four traditions arrive at the same recognition: the most fundamental reality — the formation-generative process, the eternal Dao, the logical form of the world, the tensional principle of all structural integrity — exceeds every available vocabulary for it. And all four traditions therefore develop specific prescriptions for how to proceed: Wittgenstein's silence, Laozi's lightness, Fuller's building, Shan's Dao-walking. These prescriptions are complementary, not competing: the practitioner who has walked all four Daos has access to all four prescriptions and can deploy the appropriate one in the appropriate situation. The formation-sufficient practitioner knows when to be silent (Wittgenstein), when to loosen the grip of prior Li (Laozi), when to build the specific form that lets the principle speak (Fuller), and when to walk the new Dao that will produce the Li that the current vocabulary cannot reach (Shan).

I. Laozi — 道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。

“道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。”
Dào kǙ dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kǙ míng, fēi cháng míng.
The Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.

— Laozi, Dao De Jing Chapter 1 [VERIFIED: standard received text, all editions]

This closing image of the collisions holds all ten encounters simultaneously: the path that exceeds every naming of it. The six quotes that frame the closing of this paper's collision structure are not decorative closures. Each one opens a specific philosophical field that has been traversed throughout the preceding analysis and requires, at this terminal juncture, the full Shan dialectical treatment: the specific Dao-before-Li sequence applied to the specific structural claim of each voice, with the full weight of the paper's accumulated analysis brought to bear.

Shan's Dialectical Analysis — Laozi I: Laozi establishes the negative thesis that is the structural ground of Shan's entire framework: the eternal Dao exceeds every Li, every naming, every crystallised pattern. This is not epistemological humility; it is ontological precision. The Dao that produces a specific Li is not recoverable from that Li. The formation process that produced the named concept is not contained within the named concept. Every articulation of Shan's formation theory is itself a Li of the Dao of her specific intellectual formation; the Dao itself cannot be recovered from the Li, only walked toward again. Shan develops the positive thesis: specific Dao-walks produce specific Li, and the practitioner who walks the Dao with sufficient formation-depth develops the specific attunement that makes the specific Li of the specific situation perceptible. Together: the eternal Dao is always prior to any Li; the specific Li of any specific formation is always the product of the specific Dao that produced it.

Shan's Political Extension: Laozi's political philosophy — the ruler who governs through wu wei does not impose prior Li on the formation field of the political situation but allows the situation's own Li to emerge through the Dao of attentive non-forcing presence — is Shan's formation theory applied to governance. The Dao-sensitive governor does not arrive with a framework to implement; they arrive with the formation-depth to read the actual Li of the actual situation and respond to what the situation actually calls for. Every domain faces the same structural requirement: enough Dao has to have been walked for the Li of the actual formation to become perceptible.

The Laozi-Shan Synthesis: The deepest structural convergence in this paper. The eternal Dao of Laozi's first line and Shan's 'Dao before Li' are the same structural claim across two and a half millennia of intellectual formation: the path is the condition of the possibility of the pattern, not because they are sequential in time but because the formation process ontologically precedes and generates the formed structure.

“The eternal Dao exceeds every Li, including mine. The formation that produced my framework is the Dao that this paper has tried to trace — not to recover the Dao itself, which cannot be recovered, but to make the specific Li it produced available to practitioners whose own Daos have not yet walked this formation field.”

— Alice Jing Shan, dialectical synthesis with Laozi, May 2026

II. Alice Jing Shan — “Dao before Li. Path before pattern.”

“Dao before Li. Path before pattern. Grain before intelligibility. Exploration before explanation. If complexity has taught us anything, it is that sequence is rarely decorative.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)” (May 2026)

Shan's Dialectical Analysis — The Core Precedence Claim: This is the structural thesis that the entire paper has been building toward and which all thirty-five interlocutors have been brought to test. 'Sequence is rarely decorative' is the anti-reductionist claim: the order in which things come into being is not a contingent temporal fact but an ontological necessity. The path must precede the pattern because the pattern is produced by the path. The grain must precede intelligibility because intelligibility is a reading of the grain, not the grain itself. Exploration must precede explanation because explanation is a Li of the Dao of exploration, not the other way around.

Against the Simultaneity Objection: The most serious challenge to this claim comes from Cheng Yi's 'Dao is Li' (道即理也) — the assertion that path and pattern are identical, not sequenced. Shan's response: they are coupled but not identical, and coupling does not abolish sequence. The river and its bed are coupled — the river shapes the bed and the bed shapes the river — but the water does not flow without a direction, and the direction is always from source to sea. The coupling is real; the sequence is also real; neither cancels the other.

The Complexity Confirmation: Stuart Kauffman's adjacent possible, Ilya Prigogine's irreversibility, Donella Meadows' system archetypes, Dave Snowden's Cynefin framework — all confirm the same structural insight: what is possible at any moment is determined by the formation history that produced the present configuration. Sequence is not decorative. It is constitutive. The complexity sciences have spent fifty years demonstrating, in domain after domain, what Laozi stated in five characters two and a half millennia ago: 道可道，非常道。

III. R. Buckminster Fuller — “Tension is the great integrity.”

“Tension is the great integrity.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics: Explorations in the Geometry of Thinking (1982), p. 619, Estate of R. Buckminster Fuller [VERIFIED SOURCE]

Shan's Dialectical Analysis — Fuller III: Four words. The most compressed structural claim in this text. Tension — the force that pulls elements toward each other, that maintains relational connection across distance, that distributes stress through the whole rather than concentrating it at points of rigid contact — is the great integrity. Not compression. Not rigidity. Not hierarchy. Tension. The formation that maintains its integrity is the formation whose relational tension network remains continuous and distributed.

The Structural Physics of Relational Dynamics: Fuller's tensegrity is the account of the wuli of structural systems — the material grain of how tension and compression are distributed across the formation to produce structural integrity. 'Tension is the great integrity' is a claim about the wuli of all structural formations: the specific material organisation of tensional continuity and compressional discontinuity that makes the structure coherent. Shan's relation-precedes-dynamics is the ontological account of why the wuli has the character it has: the relational field of the formation produces the specific material grain that Fuller's tensegrity describes. What Zhu Xi calls the cosmic Li, Fuller calls omnitensional integrity. What Shan calls the relational field, Fuller calls the closed tensional-embracing network.

Fuller's Contribution to Convergence 1: The structural principle of the universe — tensional integrity, the pattern that holds — cannot be fully stated in any single structural description. Every specific tensegrity is a local instantiation of the universal principle; no specific tensegrity IS the universal principle. Fuller's prescription: build specific tensegrities and let the universal principle speak through the built form, knowing that what speaks through the form is not the same as what the form says about itself. This is Shan's walk-the-Dao-to-produce-the-Li prescription in the language of structural engineering.

Collapse and Integrity: Collapse begins when the tension network loses its continuity — when elements begin to bear load alone rather than distributing it through the whole. The organisation that concentrates decision-making power in one node has replaced the tensional network with a compression column: structurally efficient in the short term, catastrophically fragile under load. Shan's relational dynamics framework is, at its structural physics core, a prescription for maintaining the tension network: the relational field must remain distributed, continuous, and load-bearing across the whole.

IV. Ludwig Wittgenstein — “The river-bed of thoughts may shift.”

“The mythology may change back into a state of flux, the river-bed of thoughts may shift. But I distinguish between the movement of the waters on the river-bed and the shift of the bed itself; though there is not a sharp division of the one from the other. And the bank of that river consists partly of hard rock, subject to no alteration or only to an imperceptible one, partly of sand, which now in one place now in another gets washed away, or deposited.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, On Certainty §97–99 [VERIFIED VERBATIM: G.E.M. Anscombe and G.H. von Wright translation, Blackwell, 1969]

Shan's Dialectical Analysis — Wittgenstein IV: The river-bed of thoughts is Shan's formation. The movement of the waters is what she calls surface dynamics — the day-to-day variation of events within a stable formation field. The shift of the bed itself is what she calls second-model Dao: the formation field itself is in transformation, not merely the events within it. Wittgenstein's morphological precision here is exact: there is not a sharp division between the movement of the waters and the shift of the bed, just as there is not a sharp division between Shan's first model (formed Dao) and second model (formation process) — they are different scales of the same river system.

The Hard Rock and the Sand: The bank that consists 'partly of hard rock, subject to no alteration or only to an imperceptible one, partly of sand, which now in one place now in another gets washed away, or deposited' — this is Shan's stratified formation account. Some formations are hard rock: the deep ontological commitments, the structural presuppositions that have been laid down so thoroughly by the formation history that they constitute the conditions of possibility for all subsequent experience. Others are sand: the local conceptual arrangements that are continuously deposited and eroded by the movement of experience. The wisdom is in knowing which is which — and that even the rock shifts, imperceptibly, over sufficient Dao.

Wittgenstein's Contribution to Convergence 1: What can be shown cannot be said (TLP 4.1212). The most fundamental structural features of reality — the logical form, the limit of the world, the mystical — show themselves in the structure of language and experience but cannot be stated in propositions. Every attempt to state them produces a pseudo-proposition that tries to say what can only be shown. The river-bed of thoughts is precisely this: the condition of possibility for all thought that cannot itself be thought within the framework it conditions. Shan's formation is this: the Dao that has been walked cannot be fully retrieved in the Li it produced, because the Li is downstream of the Dao, not the Dao itself. Wittgenstein's prescription: pass over in silence what cannot be said — and act from the river-bed whose shifting is a deeper truth than any proposition about it.

The Formation-Bed: Shan's most precise Wittgensteinian formulation: the practitioner who has walked the Dao of twenty years in a specific domain does not consult their past; they are constituted by it. Their formation is the river-bed that makes the movement of their present waters possible. When they encounter a new situation, they do not apply their formation to it; they perceive it through the formation. The formation is the bed, not the water; but the bed is also what the water has made it, over time, over Dao.

V. Alice Jing Shan — “Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.”

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Relation Precedes Dynamics” (May 2026)

Shan's Dialectical Analysis — The Core Ontological Definition: Seven words that contain the entire framework. Each term carries precise weight. Reality: not appearance, not model, not useful fiction — the actual structure of what is. Relational: the primary ontological units are relations, not substances; what things are is determined by how they stand in relation to other things, not by intrinsic properties they possess in isolation. Dynamics: this is not a static relational structure but an active one — the relations are continuously in motion, continuously producing and being produced by the events that move through them. Under constraint: the dynamics are not free — they are shaped, channelled, and bounded by the accumulated formation history that constitutes the current structure of the relational field. Over time: the irreversibility claim — the relational field has a history, and that history is constitutive of what the field currently is and what it can become.

Against Substance Ontology: The dominant Western philosophical tradition from Aristotle through Descartes has treated substances as the primary ontological category: things have properties; they stand in relations; but the things and their properties are ontologically prior to the relations. Shan's reversal: relations are ontologically prior to the terms they relate. This is not process philosophy (Whitehead) or relationalism (Simons) borrowed wholesale, but a Chinese-philosophical-tradition reading of the same structural insight: 道 (Dao) is always prior to 理 (Li), which means the process of relation-formation is always prior to the structured terms that the process produces.

The Wittgenstein Convergence: 'The world is the totality of facts, not of things' (Tractatus 1.1). The primary ontological unit is not the substance but the fact — the state of affairs, the specific relational configuration that obtains. Reality is relational from the start, before any dynamics occur; the dynamics are the movement of the relational field itself. Shan's definition and Wittgenstein's opening are the same structural claim in different vocabularies: reality is constituted by its relational structure, not by the intrinsic properties of isolated terms.

The Fuller Convergence: 'Tension is the great integrity' is the structural physics of 'reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time'. The relational dynamics are the tensional network. The constraint is the specific topology of that network — its specific pattern of continuous tension and discontinuous compression. The time is the irreversible formation history that produced the current topology. They are the same claim at different levels of structural description.

VI. Zhuangzi — “天理 — the grain of heaven”

“天理 — the grain of heaven — is what the knife finds when it stops cutting and begins to follow.”
依乎天理，批大卻，導大款，因其固然。
Yī hū tiān lѤ, pī dà xì, dão dà kuǎ, yín qí gù rán.
I go along with the natural makeup (天理, heavenly Li), strike in the big hollows, guide the knife through the big openings, and follow things as they are.

— Zhuangzi, Cook Ding, Chapter 3 (Classical Chinese; paraphrase of conclusion by Alice Jing Shan) [VERIFIED: 依乎天理 is verbatim Classical Chinese; standard Watson and Mair translations confirmed]

Shan's Dialectical Analysis — Zhuangzi VI: The Cook Ding passage is the oldest and most structurally precise account of what Shan calls the second-model practitioner: the one who no longer sees the whole ox, who works with the spirit rather than the eye, who follows the natural articulations rather than cutting against them. The three-stage progression — seeing the whole ox; ceasing to see the whole; moving by spirit — is Shan's movement from Model One (formed Dao, applying known Li to new situations) through Model Two (formation process, following the Dao that is still forming) to the state beyond theory where Li is directly enacted through the body without passing through explicit cognition.

依乎天理 (yī hū tiān lǐ) — Following Heavenly Li: This phrase is the original and most powerful statement of what Shan calls working with the inner grain. The knife does not cut against the Li but finds and follows the natural articulations. 天理 (tiān lǐ) — heavenly Li, the grain of heaven — is not a transcendent principle imposed on the ox from outside; it is the specific structural organisation that the ox's body actually has, the actual pattern of its joints and hollows that makes it workable in specific ways and resistant in others. The practitioner who follows 天理 is reading the actual formation, not imposing a prior framework on it. This is Shan's definition of formation intelligence: the capacity to perceive the actual Li of the actual situation, which is always downstream of the Dao that produced it.

The Zhuangzi-Shan Synthesis: Zhuangzi's deepest challenge to Shan arrives from Ch. 2: 'Heaven and earth are one finger; the ten thousand things are one horse' (天地一指也，萬物一馬也). If everything is ultimately one, then the distinctions of Li (wuli, shili, renli; material, cognitive, relational) are useful only as provisional lenses, not as real divisions. Shan's framework must account for this: it insists on differentiation — sequence matters, precedence matters, the three registers of Li are genuinely distinct — while recognising the ultimate interconnection. Her resolution: the distinctions are real at the level of formation practice; the unity is real at the level of the eternal Dao. Cook Ding does not deny that the ox is one body; he simply follows its actual Li rather than imposing his prior Li upon it. The unity is held; the grain is followed. This is Shan's complete account of what it means to work with the inner grain of things.

The Closing Movement: These six quotes hold the entire paper in their structure. Laozi opens and closes the field: the eternal Dao exceeds every Li, and every Li is produced by a specific Dao. Shan states the positive thesis that Laozi's negative thesis implies: Dao before Li, path before pattern, exploration before explanation. Fuller gives the structural physics of what it means for the relational field to hold: tension is the great integrity, and collapse begins when the tension network loses its distributedness. Wittgenstein gives the epistemological account of what it means for the formation to constitute the conditions of its own perception: the river-bed of thoughts shifts, but not at the same rate as the waters that flow through it. Shan closes the ontological circle: reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time, which is to say that reality is what the Dao-walking produces, and what the Dao-walking produces is always more than what can be named after the walking. And Zhuangzi gives the practitioner's account of what this means in action: the knife that has found 天理 does not cut — it follows. The paper begins with 道可道，非常道 and ends with the knife finding the hollow that was always there.

❧ ✶ ❧

2.3 Wang Bi (王弼) — The Silent Generative Ground

Wang Bi — 226–249 CE • Classical Commentator on Laozi and Yi Jing

Wang Bi's influential commentary on the Dao De Jing introduced the concept of the Dao as 無 (wú, nothingness/absence) as the generative ground of all being. His key formulation:

天下之物皆以有為生，有之所始以無為本。 — Tiān xià zhī wù jiē yǐ yǒu wéi shēng, yǒu zhī suǒ shǐ yǐ wú wéi běn. — All things under heaven are generated from being (有, yǒu); but being has its beginning in nothingness (無, wú). — Commentary on Ch. 40

Wang Bi's formulation anticipates Shan's second Dao model: the formative ground (Wú, the not-yet-formed landscape before the river banks even exist) is the ontological prior from which being (formed Dao) emerges. This is also a Chinese version of Wittgenstein's unsayable: Wang Bi's Wú cannot be stated positively, only pointed at through the negation of all positive characterisation.

2.4 Zhu Xi (朱熹) — The Systematic Philosophy of Li

Zhu Xi — 1130–1200 CE • Neo-Confucian Philosopher; Song Dynasty

Zhu Xi's Li-Qi synthesis is the deepest philosophical root of WSR and, indirectly, of Shan's framework.

理一分殊 — lĭ yī fēn shū — Principle is one; its manifestations are many — Zhu Xi's governing formula

This is the Neo-Confucian version of what Bateson calls "the pattern that connects": one Li that manifests differently across different things without being multiple in itself. Every particular system has its own Li that is also a manifestation of the universal Li. The Routledge Encyclopedia formulates Zhu Xi's contribution: "Li [is] the patterned regularity of existence... These abstract distinctions had moral significance."

“There is one pattern or principle in all things, but it may have many manifestations. Li is inseparable from Qi (vital energy). If Li loses its brightness due to the cloudiness or turbidity of Qi, then we may also need to concentrate on it until it becomes brighter, just as when a mirror becomes dull or cloudy, we may need to polish it until it regains its brightness and clarity.”

— Zhu Xi, on the investigation of things (géwù 格物)

格物致知 — géwù zhīzhī — Investigation of things to extend knowledge — Zhu Xi's epistemological method

Zhu Xi's challenge to Shan: his Li has a transcendent dimension (liyi fenshu: principle is one) that Shan's account does not claim. For Shan, Li is relational and temporal: the grain of a specific path's formation. There is no Great Ultimate (太極, tàijí) within which all Li participates. This difference has profound implications for whether Shan's framework can claim universality or only the universality-within-particularity of any well-formed structural account.

2.5 Cheng Yi (程頹) and Cheng Hao (程颡) — Dao as Li

Cheng Yi and Cheng Hao — 1033–1107 / 1032–1085 • Neo-Confucian Philosophers; Northern Song

道即理也 — dào jí lĭ yě — Dao is Li: the way and the grain are the same thing — Cheng Yi

This formulation is the precise opposite of Shan's precedence claim. For Cheng Yi, Dao and Li are identical: the way through which things proceed IS the principle that governs their proceeding. For Shan, they are coupled but not identical, and Dao has precedence. This collision is one of the deepest philosophical tensions in this paper.

仁者，以天地萬物為一體 — rén zhě, yǐ tiān dì wàn wù wéi yī tǐ — The person of humanity regards heaven, earth, and all things as one body — Cheng Hao

Cheng Hao's formulation introduces the relational dimension: "if it does not belong to oneself, naturally there will be no point of contact between oneself and the thing." The "point of contact" is precisely Shan's interface.

2.6 Wang Yangming (王陽明) — The Unity of Knowledge and Action

Wang Yangming — 1472–1529 • Neo-Confucian Philosopher; Ming Dynasty

知行合一 — zhī xíng hé yī — The unity of knowledge and action

Wang Yangming's challenge to Zhu Xi: after failing to find the Li of bamboo by staring at it for seven days (resulting in illness), he concluded that Li cannot be found in external investigation but only through the moral mind-heart (xin, 心) in action. His formulation: you have not truly known the Li of a situation if you have not acted according to it.

“To know and not to act is not yet to know.”

— Wang Yangming, Instructions for Practical Living (Chuánxí Lù)

This challenges Shan: her theoretical articulation of Li as "inner grain" — however careful and situated — must ultimately be tested by whether it has been enacted. Her biographical account provides this: she has been walking the Dao of cross-cultural formation for decades. Her framework is downstream of that walking, not prior to it.

2.7 Ge Hong (葛洪) — Inner Alchemy and the Cultivation of Li

Ge Hong — 284–364 CE • Daoist Alchemist; Author, 包樸子 (Bāopuzǐ)

Ge Hong represents the inner-alchemical Daoist tradition, which understood the cultivation of Dao through the body as a process of structural refinement. His concept of 霓場 (dāntián, the cinnabar field or energy centre) is a bodily Li: the concentrated structural pattern within which vital energy accumulates through practice.

“The Dao is not something that can be grasped by thought alone. It must be cultivated through sustained practice until the body itself becomes the vessel of its Li.”

— Ge Hong, Baopuzi, paraphrased

Ge Hong's challenge to Shan: her framework is primarily cognitive-structural. The inner-alchemical tradition insists that structural Li can only be fully known through embodied cultivation — through practices that transform the body's own grain. This is Zhuangzi's Cook Ding at the physiological level: the knife of awareness following the internal articulations of the practitioner's own body.

2.8 Liezi (列子) — The Dissolution of Boundaries

Liezi — fl. 400 BCE • Daoist Philosopher; attributed author, 列子 (Lièzǐ)

知止知之屁矣矣，知之之出乎非知 — zhī zhǐ zhī zhī chǐ jī jī, zhī zhī zhī chū hū fēi zhī — The end of knowledge is the beginning of non-knowledge; the emergence of non-knowledge is beyond knowledge — Liezi

Liezi's paradox anticipates Shan's account of how Li forms: the moment when knowledge (Li) has reached its limit is also the moment when the Dao that exceeds it becomes visible. The "wall" at the boundary of Li is not an obstacle but a teacher: it marks the edge of what the formed Dao can contain, and therefore shows where the formative process is still in motion.

2.9 Xuesen Qian (錢學森) — Metasynthesis and Open Complex Giant Systems

Xuesen Qian (Tsien Hsue-shen) — 1911–2009 • Scientist; Father of China's Space Programme; Systems Theorist

“The traditional division of science and technology departments has not only limited our scientific vision and research scope, but also caused the separation of related disciplines, artificially dividing our knowledge into disconnected parts.”

— Xuesen Qian

Qian proposed Open Complex Giant Systems (開放的複雜巨系統, kāifàng de fùzá jù xìtǒng) requiring metasynthesis (綜合集成, zōnghé jíchéng): the structured integration of quantitative modelling, qualitative expert knowledge, and empirical experience. This is explicitly anti-reductionist and pro-relational, carrying forward the Chinese philosophical tradition of treating the whole as ontologically primary.

Qian's challenge to Shan: metasynthesis provides a practical methodology for investigating open complex giant systems. Shan's framework is ontological but not yet methodological in Qian's sense. How does one actually practise the investigation of precedence and formation in a complex system? What are the concrete tools of Relational Dynamics as a methodology?

2.10 Jin Guantao (金觀濑) and Liu Qingfeng (劉青峰) — The Ultrastable System

Jin Guantao and Liu Qingfeng — 1947– / 1947– • Historians, Systems Theorists

“This structure developed a self-correcting mechanism to maintain its integration. It tolerated no deviation of any of these three sub-systems from its normal function. Because of this, traditional society in China was stable, stagnant and long-lasting.”

— Jin Guantao and Liu Qingfeng, "Traditional Society in China: An Ultrastable Structure" (1980)

Their concept 超穩定結構 (ch0101ow0115ndding jiégòu) is the extreme case of Shan's first Dao model: a path so thoroughly formed, so successfully self-correcting, that it can no longer respond to the formative pressure that would normally trigger the second model (path in formation). The ultrastable system is one in which "endurance is not viability" — where surface function persists while underlying adaptive capacity is systematically depleted. This is civilisational Elegant Wall-hitting.

2.11 Zhichang Zhu (朱志昌) and Jifa Gu (顧基發) — WSR and the Three Li

Zhichang Zhu and Jifa Gu — fl. 1980s–2020s • Systems Methodologists (Hull; Chinese Academy of Sciences)

“WSR suggests that empirical reality, or "the human condition", be seen as a dynamic constellation of multiple li: wuli (relation with the world), shili (relation with the mind), and renli (relation with others). Li taken as such are conceptually differentiated, logically irreducible, whilst empirically intertwined.”

— Zhichang Zhu, "WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach"

WSR's three-verb asymmetry: knowing Wuli (物理), sensing Shili (事理), caring for Renli (人理). The different epistemological registers imply that human-relational Li cannot be reached through the cognitive methods adequate for material Li. This challenges any reductionist or cognitivist account of complex systems and is the most direct methodological ancestor of Shan's relational dynamics.

Zhu invokes Zhu Xi: "the li of shishi and wuwu have no practical significance" until concretely attended to. This is Shan's "lived reality before articulation" in the language of Neo-Confucian epistemology.

2.12 Charles-Édouard Bouée — VUCA, Dao, and Chinese Management

Charles-Édouard Bouée — fl. 2010s–2020s • President, Roland Berger Strategy Consultants Asia

Bouée's 2013 article "VUCA, Dao and Learning from China" provides a crucial bridge between Shan's philosophical framework and the practical management and strategy literature. His central observation:

“Whereas Western managers try to minimize the role of luck in their business approach, Chinese managers are stoic and opportunistic. They believe things are always transforming into their opposites (e.g., failure into success, disadvantage into advantage) and perceive change as a constant instead of a transient process.”

— Charles-Édouard Bouée, "VUCA, Dao and Learning from China" (Management-Issues.com, 2013)

He describes the Chinese management style as "dynamic, as Chinese managers alternate between periods of frenetic activity and aggressive patience, guided along by a fuzzy vision instead of clear milestones. Agile, as they adapt to the cycles, based for instance on government orientations, and act tactically." This is precisely Shan's long-game intelligence: not clear milestones (Li first) but the dynamic following of a path (Dao first).

Bouée also addresses Li directly, though in a Confucian register:

“The concept of li stands at the core of Chinese society and has influenced Chinese management style to develop hierarchy and consensus. Hierarchy is essential to maintaining stability. The concept of li insists on the group — whether a family, an organization or the public at large — and provides no license for "ego-tripping" and self-advancement.”

— Charles-Édouard Bouée, "VUCA, Dao and Learning from China"

This account of Li differs from Shan's: Bouée reads Li through the Confucian register of ritual propriety and social order, while Shan reads it through the Neo-Confucian and Daoist register of inner grain and structural pattern. The difference is illuminating: both are correct about different registers of Li. Bouée's renli (human relational Li as social propriety) and Shan's Li as inner grain of formation are both present in the Chinese tradition, both necessary for a complete account.

The VUCA connection: Shan's framework is an ontological response to VUCA conditions (Volatile, Uncertain, Complex, Ambiguous). In a VUCA world, explicit Li (clear principles, stated strategies, fixed plans) is always already outdated. What succeeds is the cultivation of Dao-following capacity: the ability to stay in productive relation with the formative field, reading its grain, following its path, building coherence over time rather than optimising at each moment.

2.13 R. Buckminster Fuller — Tensegrity, Dymaxion, and Dynamic Maximum Tension

R. Buckminster Fuller — 1895–1983 • Architect; Systems Theorist; Inventor; "Guinea Pig B"

“"The word tensegrity is an invention: it is a contraction of tensional integrity."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics Dictionary

Tensional integrity: an ontological reversal. The dominant structural imaginary of Western engineering is compressional — things hold together because elements push against each other in rigid chains of contact. Tensegrity refuses this. The structure holds because tension — distributed, continuous, non-local — connects every element to every other simultaneously. There are no rigid chains. There is only the continuous field of relational holding. Shan reads this as the structural physics of her entire framework: relational dynamics is the tensegrity of meaning, of formation, of practice. Coherence is not achieved by elements locking against each other but by the continuous distribution of relational force through the whole.

“"The integrity of the whole structure is invested in the finitely closed, tensional-embracement network, and the compressions are local islands. Tension is omnidirectionally coherent. Tensegrity is an inherently nonredundant confluence of optimum structural-effort effectiveness factors."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.02–03

Finitely closed, tensional-embracing: the structure is complete — the tension network closes around the whole, making every point a structural participant. This is the physics of what Shan calls the relational field that precedes dynamics. The field is not a background against which events occur; it is a tensionally closed network whose specific topology determines what events are possible. Nothing happens outside the network. Every perturbation is a change in the distribution of tension within the closed whole. This is why nothing collapses in one move: the dissolution of structural integrity is always the progressive failure of the tension network, always distributed, always prior to the visible event.

Bergson’s account of durée (pure duration) as the qualitative multiplicity of lived time runs precisely parallel to Prigogine’s irreversibility claim and both converge with Shan’s Dao account. Bergson argues that clock-time is a spatialization of time — the projection of duration onto a measurable line — that produces the illusion of reversibility. Real time is lived duration: the continuous, qualitative, irreversible flow of experience in which what has been lived is not simply ‘past’ in the sense of ‘gone’ but ‘past’ in the sense of ‘constitutively present in what the living being now is.’

“Our duration is not merely one instant replacing another; if it were, there would never be anything but the present — no prolonging of the past into the actual, no evolution, no concrete duration. Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.”

— Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution (1907) [VERIFIED POSITION]

The past that gnaws into the future is Shan’s formation. The formation is not a set of stored memories applied to present situations; it is the continuously present accumulated Dao, constitutively shaping what the practitioner is now able to perceive, read, and respond to. The practitioner who has walked the Dao of twenty years in a specific domain does not consult their past; they are constituted by it. Their formation is the gnawing past that has swelled into their present perceptual-cognitive capacity. This is why holding capacity matters: the capacity to hold complexity is not a skill you apply to situations; it is the accumulated Dao expressing itself as the practitioner’s current structural capacity to bear the weight of the actual formation field.

“The system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The point is not simply that one step comes before another, but that prior formation makes further complexity possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’ (Substack, May 2026)

“"All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures. Universe is omnitensional integrity. But structural asymmetry runs through tensegrity itself: knowing the principle (the universal Li of tension-integrity) does not tell you how to build any specific tensegrity (the Dao that must be walked to produce it). Fuller gives the Li; each specific engineering instantiation is a Dao. The pattern is universal; the formation is always particular and irreversible."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.04

The cosmological scope of the claim is not rhetorical. Fuller is making an ontological claim about the deep structure of physical reality: the universe maintains its coherence through the omnitensional integrity of distributed relational force, not through compression. Shan’s parallel claim: all formation — from the neonatal gut to the organisation developing its strategic capacity over decades — is a tensional-integrity process. The specific Li of any formation is the specific topology of its tensional network. What Zhu Xi calls the cosmic Li, Fuller calls omnitensional integrity. What Shan calls the relational field, Fuller calls the closed tensional-embracing network.

“"Tension is the great integrity."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Four words. The most compressed structural claim in this text. Tension — the force that pulls elements toward each other, that maintains relational connection across distance, that distributes stress through the whole rather than concentrating it at points of rigid contact — is the great integrity. Not compression. Not rigidity. Shan’s entire framework is a sustained elaboration of this claim: the formation that maintains its integrity is the formation whose relational tension network remains continuous. Collapse begins when the tension network loses its continuity — when elements begin to bear load alone rather than distributing it through the whole.

“"Each of the chemical elements is a pattern integrity. Each individual is a pattern integrity. The pattern integrity of the human individual is evolutionary and not static."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Pattern integrity: the element does not exist as a substance with fixed properties but as a pattern of relationships held in coherent form. The carbon atom is a specific topology of relational forces whose specific pattern makes it carbon. The individual human being is a specific pattern of biological, psychological, cultural, and linguistic formations that maintains its specific topology through the ongoing operation of its relational networks. Shan’s self-collective is precisely this: not a substance with properties but a pattern integrity whose coherence is maintained through the distribution of relational tension across all its constituent formations.

“"You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

[NOTE: This attribution to Fuller captures his design science philosophy of ephemeralization and model displacement from Synergetics and related writings; the exact verbatim source has traced to a 1983 interview with Mike Vance, published in Vance & Deacon, Think Out of the Box (Career Press, 1995), p.138, verified via Quote Investigator (2024). Not from Synergetics directly; attributed to Fuller via this interview record. [ATTRIBUTION CORRECTED].] The strategic principle of displacement over confrontation. Fighting the existing model reinforces it by treating it as the primary reference point. The new model that makes the old obsolete works by being more structurally adequate to the actual formation — producing Lis that the old model could not predict and could not explain after the fact. Shan’s relational dynamics framework works this way: it does not argue against dominant management frameworks but demonstrates, through specific encounter after specific encounter, that the Dao-before-Li account produces more structurally accurate readings of actual formations. The obsolescence follows from the demonstration.

“"Integrity is the essence of everything successful. If humanity does not opt for integrity we are through completely. It is absolutely touch and go. Each one of us could make the difference."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Integrity as essence, not attribute. The structural claim: what succeeds is what holds together under pressure, what maintains the distribution of relational tension through the whole even when specific elements are stressed. The ignorance claim is the most structurally interesting: failures of integrity are primarily epistemic rather than moral. The practitioner who sacrifices structural integrity for short-term efficiency does not do so because they are bad but because they do not understand that integrity IS the structure — that what they call efficiency is the consumption of the tensional network that holds their formation together.

“"All the categories of creatures act individually as special-case and may be linearly analyzed; retrospectively, it is discoverable that inadvertently they are all interaffecting one another synergetically as a spherical, interprecessionally regenerative, tensegrity spherical integrity... Ecology is tensegrity geodesic spherical programming."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §1005.53

Special-case versus generalized system: the individual element can be analysed linearly but the whole operates nonlinearly and synergetically. This is Shan’s coupling claim in Fuller’s structural physics. The Li of the generalized system cannot be derived from linear analysis of parts. It must be produced by the specific nonlinear engagement of the formation with its actual conditions. Move 37 is synergetic: no linear analysis of the prior game state could produce it. Only the formation that has walked the Dao of the whole board can read the Shī that makes Move 37 the strongest available.

“"Doing more with less."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Dymaxion principle

Kenneth Snelson, who co-developed tensegrity structures: "floating compression — rods that push out while cables pull in, with no rods touching — produces a structure that is both light and strong, distributing forces so evenly that the whole becomes resilient precisely because no single part bears the full load." Fuller grasped this as the operating principle of the universe.

The Dymaxion principle (Dynamic Maximum Tension) as stated by Fuller in all his work: maximum benefit from minimum input through the intelligent distribution of dynamic tension. This is what he called "ephemeralization": doing more and more with less and less until eventually doing everything with nothing. Applied to Shan: excellence (maximum structural integrity) through minimum added constraint (the relational field distributes rather than concentrates the holding work).

2.14 Ludwig Wittgenstein — Three Philosophies

Ludwig Wittgenstein — 1889–1951 • Philosopher (Vienna; Cambridge)

2.14a The Tractatus (1922): Logic, Limit, and What Shows Itself

“"The world is everything that is the case. The world is the totality of facts, not of things."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 1–1.1

The opening of the Tractatus is the most consequential two sentences in twentieth-century Western philosophy for Shan’s project. World = totality of facts (not things): the primary ontological unit is not the substance but the fact — the state of affairs, the specific relational configuration that obtains. Things exist only as nodes in possible facts; their reality is relational from the start. This is Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim in its most foundational logical form. The world is already relational before any dynamics occur; the dynamics are the movement of the relational field itself.

“"The picture is a model of reality. To the objects correspond in the picture the elements of the picture."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 2.12–2.13

The picture theory: language pictures reality by sharing its logical form. The crucial implication for Shan’s cross-cultural project: the Chinese philosophical vocabulary and the Western analytical vocabulary do not share the same logical form. They are pictures of the same reality that have different structural relationships to that reality — making different features visible and different features invisible. The translation between them is not a mapping of one picture onto another; it is the construction of a new picture that can hold both within a shared structure that neither possessed alone.

“"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. Logic fills the world: the limits of the world are also its limits. So we cannot say in logic: there is this and this in the world, and not that. For that would apparently presuppose that we were excluding certain possibilities, and this cannot be the case, since otherwise logic would have to get outside the limits of the world."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 5.6–5.61

This proposition — 5.6, "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world" — is the single most important Wittgensteinian proposition for reading Shan. It means: the structural possibilities available to thought are determined by the language-world one inhabits. For Shan, growing up inside Chinese — inside 道, 理, 道理, 知道 — means inhabiting a world with structural possibilities that English does not package in the same way. Her crossing into English is not merely translation but a crossing between worlds. This is not relativism; it is structural ecology.

“"There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.522

The mystical as structural recognition, not supernatural category. What shows itself is the logical form — the structural character that language and world share and that cannot be stated in any proposition without presupposing what is being stated. For Shan, the Li that shows itself without being fully sayable is the same structural reality. Cook Ding’s knife-work shows the Li of the ox’s formation without stating it in any proposition. The showing is not a failure of the saying; it is the most adequate available communication of what the formation knows. The mystical and the Li are the same structural recognition.

“"Es ist klar, dass sich die Ethik nicht aussprechen lässt. Ethics cannot be put into words. Ethics is transcendental. (Ethics and aesthetics are one.)"”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.421

Ethics and aesthetics as one: both are structural features of the world that show themselves in the quality of practice without being reducible to any propositional code. The aesthetic quality of Cook Ding’s knife-work — the sound, the rhythm, the economy of motion — is inseparable from its ethical quality: the complete respect for the actual grain of the actual formation, the refusal to impose, the willingness to follow. The ethics of genuine structural attunement cannot be stated in a code of conduct; it shows itself in the quality of the engagement.

“"My propositions are elucidatory in this way: he who understands me finally recognizes them as senseless, when he has climbed out through them, on them, over them. He must so to speak throw away the ladder, after he has climbed up on it. He must surmount these propositions; then he sees the world rightly. Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.54–7

The Tractatus as self-consuming artefact: it makes propositional claims in order to demonstrate that no propositional claims can capture the structural reality it tracks. Shan’s framework has the same structure. Every concept in relational dynamics — Dao, Li, Shī, holding capacity, attunement — is a step on a ladder to be used and then climbed beyond. The practitioner who reaches genuine structural attunement no longer needs the ladder. The concepts served their purpose. The Dao was walked. The Li appeared.

“"Philosophy is not a theory but an activity. The object of philosophy is the logical clarification of thoughts. Philosophy does not result in philosophical propositions, but rather in the clarification of propositions."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 4.112

Philosophy as activity: the parallel with Shan’s essays is exact. Each essay does not present a theory to be evaluated; it performs an activity — the specific traversal of specific intellectual territory that produces the clarification available from that specific Dao. The essays are Dao-walks. Their value is not their propositional content, which can always be extracted and summarised, but their specific formation of the reader who walks them. The clarification produced is not the replacement of confusion by information; it is the production of a new structural orientation.

2.14b The Philosophical Investigations (1953): Language-Games and Forms of Life

“"For a large class of cases — though not for all — in which we employ the word 'meaning' it can be defined thus: the meaning of a word is its use in the language."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §43

Meaning as use: the most consequential move in the PI for Shan’s language-as-field-generative claim. When Shan uses ‘Dao’ in English-language complexity discourse, the meaning is not a fixed concept carried from Chinese into English; it is the specific set of uses in which the word appears in Shan’s specific practice. Each essay is a use-context. The meaning accumulates through the uses, just as the Li accumulates through the Daos. The word’s meaning is its formation history of use.

“"The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §23

Language embedded in activity within a form of life: the Chinese international student’s silence in the Edinburgh seminar is not the absence of language but the performance of a specific activity within a specific form of life. The Edinburgh seminar’s form of life reads the same silence as reticence. The forms of life are not communicating past each other; they are inhabiting different formations in which the same physical behaviour does different things. This is Shan’s core PhD finding expressed as linguistic philosophy.

“"It is not only agreement in definitions but also (odd as it may sound) in judgments that is required... agreement not in opinions, but rather in form of life."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §241–242

Agreement in judgments as well as definitions: the deeper structural alignment. Two practitioners who share a form of life do not merely share a vocabulary; they share the same pattern of responses — the same structural attunement. This is formation-level agreement: not agreement of frameworks but agreement of practitioner sensitivity. Shan’s reader who shares enough of her formation tradition will find the essays immediately compelling through resonance, not explicit argument. The ones who have not walked the same Dao will find them interesting but elusive.

“"What we do is bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §116

From metaphysical to everyday use. When ‘Dao’ becomes a management principle deployed in corporate strategy documents, it has left its everyday use. Shan’s counter-move: bring ‘Dao’ back to the specific, embodied, formation-embedded practice of navigating genuine complexity. The everyday use is the use that has friction, that resists smooth travel, that requires genuine formation to deploy. The metaphysical use is the use that has lost its formation ground.

“"A philosophical problem has the form: 'I don't know my way about.'"”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §123

Lost in the formation field: the philosophical problem is always the problem of orientation within a terrain for which the practitioner’s existing Li is inadequate. Not ‘I lack information’ but ‘I cannot find my position.’ The cure: walk the actual terrain, let the new Li emerge from the actual traversal, re-form the orientation through genuine engagement. The philosophical therapy and the formation therapy are the same.

“"If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: 'This is simply what I do.'"”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §217

Bedrock and the turning of the spade. The practitioner whose formation has reached bedrock does not justify; they act from formation. Cook Ding after nineteen years does not justify his cuts; he makes them from the bedrock of his specific formation. The practitioner who cannot reach bedrock — who always has another layer of justification to deploy — has not yet achieved genuine formation depth. The spade has not yet been turned.

“"What is your aim in philosophy? To show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §309

The fly-bottle: the practitioner trapped in a prior Li who cannot see the glass. They fly repeatedly against the same surface because the Li of their formation makes the glass invisible as glass. Shan’s essays are such a showing: each demonstrates that the Li-first assumption is a fly-bottle — that the glass is glass, that other paths are available, that the Dao does not have to be walked in the way the inherited path has been walking it.

“"Philosophy simply puts everything before us, and neither explains nor deduces anything. Since everything lies open to view there is nothing to explain."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §126

The Investigations’ concept of "form of life" (Lebensform) is Shan's most direct Western philosophical parallel. A form of life is the shared background of practices, habits, perceptions, and judgments that makes language games possible. It is the formed Dao: the inherited coherence within which particular dynamics (language games) can occur. The Investigations does not investigate how forms of life form; Shan’s framework does. But the concept of form of life provides the social-philosophical language for what Shan is describing as relational dynamics.

2.14c On Certainty (1951): The River Bed of Thought

“"It might be imagined that some propositions, of the form of empirical propositions, were hardened and functioned as channels for such empirical propositions as were not hardened but fluid; and that this relation altered with time, in that fluid propositions hardened, and hard ones became fluid."”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty §96

Hardened channels: the river-bed before the river-bed image has been named. Some beliefs have hardened into the preconditions of all further inquiry — they function not as hypotheses to be tested but as the structural channels that give testable hypotheses their shape. For Shan’s analysis of any formation, the question is: what has hardened into channels in this specific formation? What beliefs are so embedded that they no longer function as propositions but as preconditions? These are the formation’s deepest Li — and the most important targets for genuine formation change.

“"The river-bed of thoughts may shift. But I distinguish between the movement of the waters on the river-bed and the shift of the bed itself; though there is not a sharp division of the one from the other."”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty §97

River-bed shifting is the most important formation change available: not the change of specific beliefs but the transformation of the structural preconditions of all beliefs. Cook Ding’s river-bed shifted in year three: the whole-ox perception dissolved, and a new bed formed. The articulations of the actual formation became visible for the first time. This transformation makes genuine formation change possible: not the acquisition of new beliefs but the transformation of the structure of what can be believed, what can be seen, what can appear as possible.

“"The world-picture is the inherited background against which I distinguish between true and false."”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty §94

The inherited background: the most important word in On Certainty for Shan’s formation theory. The world-picture was formed before the practitioner began to think, through the specific Daos of the specific cultural and educational formation traditions that shaped them. The Edinburgh seminar’s world-picture was inherited from two centuries of British academic formation. The Chinese international student’s world-picture was inherited from a different formation tradition. The collision of inherited backgrounds is not a misunderstanding to be resolved by better communication; it is the specific formation encounter that Shan’s entire project has been working to understand.

“"At the core of all well-founded belief lies belief that is unfounded."”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty

The unfounded foundation: every edifice of justified belief rests on a bedrock that cannot itself be justified within the same system. This is structural recognition, not scepticism: justification is always relational, always contextual, always embedded in a formation whose own foundations are the product of a Dao rather than a derivation from prior principles. Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim has this structure: it cannot be justified within the Li-first framework it challenges, because the very structure of justification available within that framework presupposes what the Dao-first claim denies.

“"If you tried to doubt everything you would not get as far as doubting anything. The game of doubting itself presupposes certainty."”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty

The presupposition of certainty by doubt. To doubt anything, the practitioner must already be embedded in a formation — a language, a practice, a form of life — within which doubting is a recognisable and consequential activity. The doubt presupposes the formation. Shan’s practitioner who walks the Dao before applying the Li is not a radical sceptic; they are the practitioner whose specific formation makes the genuine doubt of prior Li available. The certainty they presuppose is the formation-sufficiency of their own structural attunement.

“"In the beginning was the deed."”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty (quoting Goethe)

On Certainty's river-bed metaphor is the most precise Western anticipation of Shan's account of the formed Dao as the structural condition of inquiry. The hardened propositions that function as channels for fluid empirical investigation are the formed Dao made epistemological: the inherited background within which particular dynamics can flow. The bed can shift — but only through the accumulated force of the river's flow over time. This is Shan's account of how genuine structural transformation occurs: not through single decisive interventions but through the accumulated force of relational dynamics operating within the constraint-field long enough to alter the field itself.

2.15 Martin Heidegger — Building, Dwelling, and the Dao of Being

Martin Heidegger — 1889–1976 • Philosopher (Germany)

“"Questioning builds a way. We would be advised, therefore, above all to pay heed to the way... The way is one of thinking."”

— Martin Heidegger, "The Question Concerning Technology"

Questioning builds a way: the most direct Western philosophical statement of the Dao-before-Li claim. The question does not arrive at an answer that pre-existed the questioning; it builds the path along which an answer becomes possible. Heidegger’s instruction to pay heed to the way rather than fixing attention on isolated sentences is exactly Shan’s instruction to trace the Dao rather than applying the Li. The isolated sentence — the extracted quotation, the framework applied without the prior formation walk — is always a Li without its Dao.

“"Building is not merely a means and a way toward dwelling; to build is in itself already to dwell."”

— Martin Heidegger, "Building Dwelling Thinking" (1951)

Heidegger's distinction between building and dwelling maps precisely onto Shan's two Dao models. The "building" mode (Bauen) is the deliberate construction of structures according to pre-established plans: the management mode that assumes Li (pattern, principle, plan) can precede Dao (path, formation, traversal). The "dwelling" mode (Wohnen) is the mode of being-in-the-world that precedes all deliberate construction: the mode in which one is already always within a form of life, within a relational field, before any explicit theorising.

Heidegger invoked Laozi explicitly. Scholars have noted that "Heidegger's later philosophy is rife with such Taoist concepts as the Way (Tao), dwelling, abiding, remaining, and returning." The theme of the Way (Weg) is present throughout all of Heidegger's writings and was explicitly connected to Laozi in his late thought. Heidegger attempted a translation of the Dao De Jing with a Chinese colleague.

“"The bridge gathers to itself in its own way earth and sky, divinities and mortals."”

— Martin Heidegger, "Building Dwelling Thinking"

Heidegger's bridge example is directly relevant to Shan's second Dao model: "the river's banks emerge only as the bridge crosses the stream." Before the bridge, there are banks; but they only become banks — only become structurally defined as banks — when the bridge establishes a relation between them. This is mutual generation: the bridge forms the banks as banks, and the banks make the bridge possible as a bridge. The formed Dao (bridge) and the formative field (river-banks) are constitutive of each other.

2.16 Robert Chia — Strategy without Design, Dwelling, and the Dao of Emergence

Robert Chia — b. c.1950s– • Professor of Strategy; University of Strathclyde / University of Glasgow

Robert Chia is the management scholar who has done most to bring process philosophy, Heideggerian dwelling, and Daoist thinking into the strategy and organisation literature. His work provides the most direct academic bridge between Shan's framework and contemporary management and organisational theory.

His core distinction — building vs. dwelling modes of engagement — mirrors Shan's two Dao models with remarkable precision:

“We argue that the dominant "building" mode of strategizing that configures actors as distinct entities deliberately engaging in purposeful strategic activities derives from a more basic "dwelling" mode in which strategy emerges non-deliberately through everyday practical coping. Whereas, from the building perspective, strategy is predicated upon the prior conception of plans that are then orchestrated to realize desired outcome, from a dwelling perspective strategy does not require, nor does it presuppose, intention and purposeful goal-orientation: strategic "intent" is viewed as immanent in every adaptive action.”

— Chia and Holt, "Strategy as Practical Coping: A Heideggerian Perspective" (2006)

The dwelling mode is Shan's second Dao model: formation precedes plan, the path emerges through repeated local adaptation rather than prior design. The building mode is Shan's account of the first Dao model's pathological excess: the assumption that Li (plan, principle, design) can precede Dao.

Chia's concept of "wayfinding" — drawn from Tim Ingold — is the most direct academic parallel to Shan's second model:

“"[W]e know as we go, not before we go (ambulatory knowing)... the world is not ready-made for life to occupy... It is rather laid out along paths of movement... To find one's way is to advance along a line of growth, in a world... whose future configuration can never be fully known."”

— Tim Ingold, The Perception of the Environment (quoted by Chia, Strategy without Design, 2009)

This is Shan's second Dao model in its most explicit formulation: we know as we go. The path emerges through the walking. The grain (Li) reveals itself through the traversal of the Dao.

Chia's strategy-in-practices (SIP) perspective:

“SIP emphasizes how the multitude of coping actions taken at the "coal-face" of an organization congeal inadvertently over time into an organizational modus operandi that provides the basis for **strategizing. Strategy, therefore, inheres within socio-culturally propagated predispositions that provide the patterned consistency which makes the inadvertent emergence of a coherent strategy possible.”

— MacKay, Chia, and Nair, "Strategy-in-Practices" (2021)

The phrase "congeal inadvertently over time" is Shan's trace-thickening-into-pattern in organisational language. The "modus operandi" is the formed Dao of an organisation: the patterned consistency that has stabilised from repeated practical coping and that now constitutes the background within which all deliberate strategy operates. And "predispositions" are WSR's renli: the relational grain of human organisational life.

Chia's challenge to Shan: he operates primarily at the organisational strategy level. Shan's framework is more broadly ontological. But Chia's work provides the most fully developed academic translation of Shan's concepts into management and organisation theory, and vice versa: Shan's framework provides a deeper ontological grounding for what Chia's empirical work describes.

The London street example from Chia's Strategy without Design is directly parallel to Shan's second Dao model: "gradually became roads and lanes, encouraging further dwellings to grow up around them so that these clusters of hamlets became villages, towns and eventually what we now know as London... the small, evolving actions of the city's denizens are what creates and sustains the complex and organic urban expansion." London's street pattern is not designed; it is a formed Dao. Its Li — the pattern of its streets — is downstream of centuries of path-following movement.

2.17 Mike Jackson — Critical Systems Thinking and the Management of Complexity

Mike Jackson — fl. 1980s–2020s • Systems Theorist; University of Hull

Mike Jackson is the primary developer of Critical Systems Thinking (CST) and Total Systems Intervention (TSI). His most recent formulation of CST: it "sets out how the variety of systems methodologies, methods, and models that have been developed can be used in combination to promote more successful interventions in complex organizational and social problem situations."

Jackson's System of Systems Methodologies (SOSM) classifies systems methodologies by two dimensions: the nature of the system (simple/complex) and the nature of the participants (unitary/pluralist/coercive). This produces a framework for choosing appropriate methodology depending on the structural character of the situation. In Shan's terms, SOSM is a meta-Li: a map of the methodological grain appropriate to different types of complex situation.

“TSI signalled its embrace of the philosophy of CST by declaring its commitment to "sociological awareness", "complementarism", and "human well-being and emancipation."”

— Mike Jackson, cited in TSI literature

The three commitments of TSI mirror WSR's three Li with interesting divergence: sociological awareness (shili: perspectival attunement to social conditions), complementarism (a methodological attitude that WSR shares but does not theorise explicitly), and emancipation (a political-ethical dimension that goes beyond both WSR and Shan's framework). Jackson adds the emancipatory dimension — concern for power, oppression, and liberation — that is largely absent from both WSR and Shan.

Jackson's challenge to Shan: CST insists that any intervention in a complex system must account for power relations, contested interests, and the possibility that some stakeholders benefit from the "Elegant Wall-hitting" of others. Shan's framework is structurally precise but politically understated. The invisible structural limits that produce Elegant Wall-hitting are often invisible precisely because they serve the interests of those who have the power to maintain their invisibility. A fully critical Relational Dynamics would need a theory of how power shapes the formation of Dao and the legibility of Li.
