The specific structural challenge Jackson poses — that any account of formation must address power relations, contested interests, and the possibility that some practitioners benefit from the ‘Elegant Wall-hitting’ of others — is the most important challenge in this paper that Shan’s framework has not yet fully answered. The specific case: if the Li of the Edinburgh seminar room was structured to make Chinese postgraduate students’ participation invisible, and if this invisibility served specific interests (the maintenance of British academic culture’s self-perception as meritocratic and open), then the structural analysis of why the wall-hitting occurred is simultaneously a political-critical analysis of who benefits from the wall. Shan’s formation theory explains the mechanism; it does not automatically reveal the beneficiary.

“Critical systems thinking insists that any intervention in a complex system must attend to power relations: who benefits from the current configuration, whose interests are served by the existing Li, and whose formations are systematically marginalised.”

— Mike Jackson, Critical Systems Thinking and the Management of Complexity (2019) [VERIFIED POSITION]

Shan’s response: the power critique is correct and necessary, but it presupposes the structural analysis it criticises. Jackson’s emancipatory commitment requires knowing what the formation actually is — which formations are invisible, which Li is dominant, which Daos have been foreclosed. Without the structural analysis of formation — Dao-before-Li, the holding capacity framework, the mutual generation account — the power critique floats free of the specific mechanisms that produce the power differentials it rightly opposes. The critical Li requires the structural Dao. Jackson challenges Shan to add the power dimension; Shan challenges Jackson to add the formation dimension. The synthesis: a Dao-sensitive critical systems thinking that can identify both how formations are structured and whose interests are served by specific Li-configurations.

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. The constraint is not ethically neutral. It is always worth asking: whose constraint? In whose interest? And what is the holding capacity of the formation that sustains it?”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics™ (2026)

2.18 Ilya Prigogine — Dissipative Structures and the Arrow of Formation

Ilya Prigogine — 1917–2003 • Nobel Laureate Chemistry 1977

“"The irreversibility of time is the mechanism that brings order out of chaos."”

— Ilya Prigogine

Irreversibility as mechanism: not a limitation to be overcome but the productive force that makes order possible. In Shan’s terms, irreversibility is the ontological ground of both ontological precedence and structural asymmetry: because Dao-walking is irreversible, its products (Li) cannot be used to reverse-engineer the Dao. The Li of a formed system tells you what Dao produced it, but it cannot reproduce that Dao for you. The asymmetry is written into time itself: the formation can produce the pattern, but the pattern cannot re-produce the formation. A reversible universe is a universe in which formation of structure is impossible. Shan’s Dao is irreversible: the path walked cannot be unwalked. The Li produced is genuinely new — it was not there before the Dao produced it. This is why the formation matters, why the specific Dao matters, why the order of events matters. Coupling does not abolish sequence. Irreversibility is the ontological ground of that claim.

“"Only when a system behaves in a sufficiently random way may the difference between past and future, and therefore irreversibility, enter its description. The arrow of time is the manifestation of the fact that the future is not given, that, as the French poet Paul Valéry emphasized, 'time is a construction'."”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

Sufficient randomness as the condition of irreversibility: only in genuinely complex systems does the arrow of time play an essential role. Shan’s formation field is such a system: not a closed mechanical system whose future state follows deterministically from its current state, but a genuinely complex, far-from-equilibrium formation whose Li emerges from the specific, historically irreversible Dao of its specific engagement with its specific conditions. The Dao’s irreversibility is the Li’s guarantee of novelty.

“"Entropy is the price of structure."”

— Ilya Prigogine

The price of structure: every formed Li requires the dissipation of energy to maintain itself against the entropic tendency toward disorder. The organisation that has developed genuine holding capacity is continuously paying the entropic price of maintaining that structure. When the paying stops — when the maintenance of structural integrity is sacrificed to short-term efficiency — the entropy that structure was holding at bay begins to reclaim its domain. Nothing collapses in one move; but collapse accelerates when the entropic price is no longer being paid.

“"The main character of any living system is openness."”

— Ilya Prigogine

Openness as the main character of living systems: continuous exchange with the formation field that sustains the living system’s far-from-equilibrium organisation. Shan’s Dao is the specific mode of openness of the formation: the direction and character of the exchange between practitioner and formation field. A closed formation — one that confirms only what its existing Li predicts — has ceased to be genuinely living in Prigogine’s sense. It is drifting toward equilibrium. Toward structural death.

“"The real is only one realization of the possible."”

— Ilya Prigogine

One realisation of the possible: the adjacent possible stated as ontology. The actual Li is one specific crystallisation from the field of all possible Lis that the formation conditions made available. The bifurcation point is the moment when the greatest range of possible Lis is available. Move 37 was one realisation of the possible — the practitioners who could not see it were accessing a different set of realisable possibles. AlphaGo’s different formation produced a different adjacent possible.

“"Classical science, the mythical science of a simple, passive world, belongs to the past, killed not by philosophical criticism or empiricist resignation but by the internal development of science itself."”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

The simple, passive world belongs to the past as a description of physical reality. But as a model of organisational formation, it persists with remarkable tenacity in management theory. Shan’s framework is the equivalent of Prigogine’s revolution applied to human and organisational formation: the formation field is not simple, not passive, not predictable from its current state. The Dao must be walked. The Li will appear in the walking.

2.19 Stuart Kauffman — Order for Free and the Adjacent Possible

Stuart Kauffman — b. 1939 • Theoretical Biologist; Santa Fe Institute

“"Much of the order found in nature is spontaneously present... Evolution is not just 'chance caught on the wing.' It is not just a tinkering of the ad hoc, of bricolage, of contraption. It is emergent order honored and honed by natural selection."”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1996)

Order for free: the universe has a spontaneous tendency toward the production of order that precedes and exceeds any selection pressure. The formation field has a spontaneous tendency toward the production of Li. The Dao does not need to be forced; it tends toward pattern. The practitioner who walks with the grain of the formation rather than against it is working with the order-for-free tendency of the field — leveraging the Shī of the situation rather than fighting it.

“"The complex whole may exhibit properties that are not readily explained by understanding the parts. The complex whole, in a completely nonmystical sense, can often exhibit collective properties, 'emergent' features that are lawful in their own right."”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe

Properties not explained by the parts: the Li of the generalized system cannot be reconstructed from analysis of its components because it is a property of the whole configuration — of the specific nonlinear interaction of all elements simultaneously. This is why the Dao-walk is irreplaceable: the Li must be produced by the specific nonlinear engagement of the formation with its actual conditions. The whole is not the sum of parts. The Li is not the summary of the Dao’s individual steps.

“"This web of life, the most complex system we know of in the universe, breaks no law of physics, yet is partially lawless, ceaselessly creative."”

— Stuart Kauffman

Not derivable from physics: even though life obeys every physical law, the specific forms it takes are not derivable from the underlying physics. The higher-level organisation has genuine causal efficacy not reducible to its substrate. Shan’s framework applies this to human formation: the Li of a specific organisational formation is not derivable from the biology of its members, even though it is constrained by them. The formation is genuinely emergent. The Dao that produces it is genuinely creative. The Li that appears is genuinely new.

2.20 John Holland — Building Blocks and Tags

John Holland — 1929–2015 • Computer Scientist; Father of Genetic Algorithms; Santa Fe Institute

“"Emergence is the notion that the whole is more than the sum of its parts."”

— John Holland, Emergence: From Chaos to Order

More than the sum of parts: when specific formation elements interact under specific constraints in a specific Dao, what emerges is not predictable from any prior analysis of those elements. Holland’s building blocks: complex systems build themselves from simple rules applied locally, and the complexity that emerges exceeds any prior specification of it. Move 37 is a building-block emergence: the local interaction of board positions and strategic principles produced a specific configuration whose global significance — whose Shī — was invisible to human formation but visible to a system formed through a different Dao.

“"We gain experience through repeated use of the building blocks, even though they may never twice appear in exactly the same combination."”

— John Holland, Hidden Order

Holland's building blocks and tags provide the computational equivalent of Shan's trace-accumulation: repeated traversal of paths builds structural intelligence (experienced building blocks) that enables new configurations without rebuilding from scratch. Tags function as Li at the micro level: the pattern in each agent that makes it recognisable by others, enabling the coupling that produces emergence.

2.21 David Snowden — Cynefin, Enabling Constraints, and Coherent Emergence

David Snowden — b. 1954 • Founder, Cynefin Co; Complexity Practitioner

“"We manage the emergence of beneficial coherence within attractors within boundaries. And that allows locally valid solutions to emerge."”

— David Snowden

Managing emergence rather than managing outcomes: Shan’s holding-capacity argument stated as complexity practice. The practitioner does not specify the Li in advance and then implement it; they cultivate the formation conditions — the attractors, the boundaries — within which beneficial coherence can emerge from the formation field’s own Dao. Small probes: not large interventions premised on prior knowledge of the Li that should appear, but minimal perturbations that allow the formation field to reveal its own grain. Walk the Dao before naming the Li.

“"An ordered system is like the external skeleton of an insect — it has a rigid shell that is not going to change but within it things may change. An endoskeleton is like our spine — it gives coherence but doesn't contain completely, so you get huge amounts of variation around it. How do you create enabling constraints that effectively allow locally valid solutions to emerge?"”

— David Snowden, "How Leaders Change Culture Through Small Actions"

Snowden's enabling vs. governing constraints maps directly onto Shan's distinction between constraint-that-shapes and constraint-that-collapses. The endoskeleton is tensegrity: it gives coherence without containing completely. The exoskeleton is the ultrastable system: a rigid shell that maintains surface structure while preventing adaptive transformation. Cynefin is itself the product of Snowden's Dao: 15+ years of practical engagement with complex organisational situations, from which a framework gradually congealed. Its Li (the five domains) is downstream of that formation history.

2.22 Maturana and Varela — Autopoiesis and Structural Coupling

Humberto Maturana / Francisco Varela — 1928– / 1946–2001 • Biologists (Chile)

“"Living systems are cognitive systems, and living as a process is a process of cognition."”

— Maturana and Varela, Autopoiesis and Cognition (1980)

Autopoiesis — the self-producing, self-maintaining character of living systems — is Shan's mutual generation at the biological level: what is formed is still in formation, because the formed state is the condition for ongoing forming. Structural coupling — organism and environment shape each other through repeated interaction without direct causation — is Shan's relational dynamics at the biological level.

2.23 Gregory Bateson — The Pattern That Connects

Gregory Bateson — 1904–1980 • Anthropologist; Systems Thinker

“"What is the pattern which connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all four of them to me? And me to you? And all six of us to the amoeba in one direction and to the back-ward schizophrenic in another?"”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature (1979)

The question that drives an entire intellectual life: what connects radically different formations into recognisable kinship? For Shan, the metapattern is Li at its most general: the structural principle that diverse formations share despite their surface differences. But the metapattern is discovered through ecological observation, through the patient watching of formation diversity that allows the underlying structural commonality to reveal itself. This IS the Dao-before-Li method applied to the natural world. Bateson walked the Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient attention to biological diversity, and the Li of the metapattern appeared.

“"Information is any difference that makes a difference."” In Shan’s ontology of precedence, this defines Li: which differences make a difference is downstream of formation. Epistemic belatedness means the practitioner without adequate formation cannot yet perceive which differences are Li-constitutive. Signal and noise are not fixed properties of the environment; they are relational achievements of formation-adequate engagement.

— Gregory Bateson

Information as difference that makes a difference: the most precise definition of what Shan means by the formation field’s salience structure. Not all differences make differences; only those the formation is structured to respond to register as information. What registers depends entirely on the specific Li of the specific formation — on the specific attunement that the specific Dao has produced. The practitioner who cannot see Move 37 is not receiving less information; they are receiving the same signals with a different formation that makes different differences make differences. Salience is relational, not intrinsic.

2.24 Edgar Morin — Complex Thought and the Dialogic Principle

Edgar Morin — b. 1921 • Sociologist; France

“"Complexity is not a recipe for the knowledge of the world. It is a challenge and a motivation to think."”

— Edgar Morin, Introduction à la pensée complexe

Morin's dialogic principle — holding antagonistic principles in productive tension — is an operational methodology for epistemic belatedness: the dialogic practitioner refuses premature synthesis (premature Li) because the Li that sustained tension generates is richer than what premature resolution produces. The tolerance for not-yet-knowing is its operating condition — a formation achievement that cannot be adopted but must be walked. It is structurally analogous to Shan's mutual generation, Fuller's tension-compression dialectic, and the Yin-Yang dynamic.

2.25 Niklas Luhmann — Social Systems as Self-Reference

Niklas Luhmann — 1927–1998 • Social Theorist (Germany)

“"Society is a self-organizing system that produces its own elements by means of its own elements."”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1995)

Autopoietic social systems: the organisation produces the communications that constitute it, which in turn produce the communications that sustain the organisation. For Shan, the practical implication is decisive: the organisation cannot be changed by introducing foreign elements — new frameworks, new language, new structures — without accounting for how the system will metabolise them. The system will incorporate the new element into its own self-production, potentially transforming the intended change into something entirely different. The Li-before-Dao error in organisational change: introducing the new Li before understanding the Dao through which the organisation produces itself.

2.26 Donella Meadows — Leverage Points

Donella Meadows — 1941–2001 • Systems Ecologist

“"The world is a complex, interconnected, finite, ecological-social-psychological-economic system. We treat it as if it were not, as if it were divisible, separable, simple, and infinite. Our persistent, intractable, global problems arise directly from this mismatch."”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)

The four false assumptions that dominate management practice: divisible (the formation can be analysed through its separate components), separable (the formation can be cleanly bounded), simple (the formation has a fixed Li that prior analysis can reveal), infinite (the system’s capacity to absorb interventions has no limit). Each assumption is a version of the Li-before-Dao error. Shan’s holding-capacity concept is the correction to the infinite assumption. The Dao-before-Li claim is the correction to all four simultaneously.

2.27 Henri Bergson — Duration and Creative Evolution

Henri Bergson — 1859–1941 • Philosopher (France)

“"The present moment... is the invisible progress of the past gnawing into the future."”

— Henri Bergson, Matter and Memory (1896)

Bergson's durée (duration) is the temporal medium within which Shan's mutual generation occurs. Time is not a sequence of discrete instants but a continuous flow in which past and present are mutually interpenetrating. The formed path carries the history of its formation within it; the formation history is constitutive of the current structure. This is the temporal structure that makes Shan's ontological precedence claim non-trivial: it is not about temporal sequence but about the living presence of formation in the formed.

2.28 Alfred North Whitehead — Process and Becoming

Alfred North Whitehead — 1861–1947 • Mathematician; Process Philosopher

“"Process is fundamental."”

— Whitehead, Process and Reality

Three words. The most compressed process-ontology claim in Western philosophy. If process is fundamental, then the formation is prior to the formed. The Dao is prior to the Li. The actual occasion is the primary unit of reality; the formed Li is the record of that process, not the substance that preceded it. Whitehead’s process ontology and Shan’s relational dynamics share the same ontological structure: both refuse the primacy of static substance, both insist on the primacy of the formation process, both locate genuine creativity in the specific, irreversible process of actual formation.

“"The notion of 'substance' is transformed into the notion of 'actual entity'. Actual entities — also termed 'actual occasions' — are the final real things of which the world is made up."”

— Whitehead, Process and Reality

Whitehead's process philosophy is the most systematic Western philosophical account of a universe constituted by becoming rather than being. His "actual occasions" are events of becoming that perish as they achieve definiteness (formation) and become data for subsequent becomings. This is Shan's mutual generation at the metaphysical level: each formed Dao (each actual occasion that has achieved definiteness) becomes the data within which the next formation occurs.

2.29 Sun Tzu (孫子) and Sun Bin (孫臼) — The Art of Strategic Formation

Sun Tzu / Sun Bin — fl. 5th–4th century BCE • Military Strategists

知彼知己，百戰不毜 — zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài — Know the other and know yourself, and you will not be imperilled in a hundred battles — Sun Tzu, Art of War Ch. 3

上兵伐謀，其次伐交，其次伐兵 — shàng bīng fᴇ móu, qí cì fᴇ jiāo, qí cì fᴇ bīng — The highest form of strategy is to attack the enemy's plans; next best is to disrupt alliances; next is to attack armies — Sun Tzu Ch. 3

兵者，詭道也 — bīng zhě, guǐ dào yě — The art of war is the art of deception — Sun Tzu Ch. 1

Sun Tzu and Sun Bin operate at the intersection of Li (strategic pattern, situational assessment) and Dao (the way of movement, the path of engagement). Their insistence on following the grain of the situation rather than imposing a fixed plan resonates directly with Shan's second Dao model. The highest strategy (fᴇ móu) attacks the enemy's Li — disrupts their formation pattern before it can become a formed Dao. This is field-shaping intelligence: Move 37 as military strategy.

VI

Part III: The Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計) and Alice Jing Shan

The Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計, Sānshíliù Jì) is an ancient Chinese text compiled between the 5th and 7th centuries CE, encoding thirty-six strategic principles drawn from the Chinese military tradition. It is organised in six chapters of six stratagems each: the first three chapters describe tactics for advantageous situations; the last three for disadvantageous situations. The text draws from the Yi Jing (I Ching): six is the number of yin, shared with the shadows of military strategy; thirty-six (6×6) denotes "numerous" or "all possible" strategies.

The Stratagems are not merely military tactics. They are structural principles for how to navigate asymmetric situations, how to use existing conditions to create new possibilities, how to follow the grain of a situation rather than forcing it. In this sense, every one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems is a specific application of Shan's relational dynamics — a particular way of working with the Li of a complex situation under constraint over time.

Each stratagem is presented in Traditional Chinese, with pinyin, English translation, and an extended analysis connecting it to Shan's concepts and to the other voices in this paper.

Chapter I: 勝戰計 (Shèng Zhàn Jì) — Stratagems for Situations of Superiority

◆ Stratagem 1: Cross the Sea by Deceiving the Sky

1. 瞑天遡海 / 瞒天过海 (mán tiān guò hǎi) Cross the Sea by Deceiving the Sky

Original text: 備周則意怠，常見則不疏，陰在陽中，不疑就局。 "Preparations for extreme caution make for negligence; what is commonplace will not arouse suspicion; the yin is hidden in the yang, and the unexpected lies within the expected."

Connection to Shan: The most powerful structural moves are not the dramatic ones but the ones that quietly reshape the field while appearing ordinary. Move 37 "deceives the sky": it looks like a peripheral move but crosses the entire strategic sea. In Shan's terms, the Li of this stratagem is that the formative Dao often operates under the surface of what the observer expects. The path forms while the formed path holds attention.

Wittgenstein parallel: "Philosophy simply puts everything before us, and neither explains nor deduces anything. Since everything lies open to view there is nothing to explain" (PI §126). The deception is not in hiding but in making the significant look ordinary — which is exactly how the river-bed of thought operates. The hinge propositions that constitute our world-picture are hidden in plain sight: so familiar they are invisible.

◆ Stratagem 2: Besiege Wei to Rescue Zhao

2. 圍魏救趙 / 围魏救赵 (wéi Wèi jiù Zhào) Besiege Wei to Rescue Zhao

When the enemy concentrates force at one point, attack their vulnerable rear or flank. When Zhao was besieged by Wei's army, the strategist Sun Bin attacked Wei's capital Daliang rather than rushing to Zhao’s relief — forcing Wei's army to withdraw.

Connection to Shan: Collapse rarely begins where it becomes visible. The move that finally loses the game is not the move that truly lost it. The correct strategic response in Shan's framework is to address the formation conditions, not the visible symptom. This is the same logic: do not attack where the enemy is strong (address the symptom of collapse) but where they are vulnerable (address the formation conditions that produced the collapse trajectory).

Fuller parallel: "You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete." This is precisely Stratagem 2: don't besiege what is besieging you; build the tensegrity of the alternative that makes the existing structure obsolete.

◆ Stratagem 3: Kill with a Borrowed Knife

3. 借刀殺人 / 借刀杀人 (jiè dāo shā rén) Kill with a Borrowed Knife

Attack the enemy using the strength of a third party. This stratagem operates through relational dynamics: rather than direct confrontation, it works through the existing relational field.

Connection to Shan: This is WSR's renli at the strategic level — the pattern of human relations as strategic resource. The borrowed knife is the relational field already in place. This stratagem recognises that dynamics (the attack) are most effective when working through the grain of existing relations rather than against it. Relation precedes dynamics: use the relational field (borrowed knife) to generate the dynamic (the kill), rather than generating the dynamic from scratch.

◆ Stratagem 4: Wait at Leisure While the Enemy Labours

4. 以逸待勞 / 以逸待劳 (yǐ yì dài láo) Wait at Leisure While the Enemy Labours

Conserve strength while the opponent exhausts themselves. This stratagem directly instantiates Shan's account of excellence as "capacity held in coherence under constraint over time." The player who preserves capacity under constraint (waiting at leisure) while the opponent depletes theirs (labouring) is building the tensional integrity that will hold when force is finally applied.

Fuller parallel: Dymaxion — maximum benefit from minimum input. The player who waits at leisure achieves maximum strategic benefit from minimum energy expenditure.

◆ Stratagem 5: Loot a Burning House

5. 趣火打劫 / 趣火打劫 (chèn huǒ dǎ jié) Loot a Burning House

When the enemy is in trouble (a fire), exploit the chaos. This is the stratagem of recognising when a system's corrective capacity has thinned to the point where intervention becomes possible. In Shan's terms: the moment when surface function and underlying viability have separated sufficiently that external actors can read the collapse trajectory and act before it becomes visible to those inside the system.

◆ Stratagem 6: Make a Sound in the East; Attack in the West

6. 聲東擊西 / 声东击西 (shēng dōng jī xī) Make a Sound in the East; Attack in the West

Create a diversion where the enemy expects attack; strike where they do not. This is field-shaping intelligence: the real move is not where attention is directed. AlphaGo's Move 37 makes a sound in the east (the opponents focus on conventional moves) while attacking in the west (reshaping the entire positional field).

Chapter II: 敵戰計 (Dí Zhàn Jì) — Stratagems for Confrontation

◆ Stratagem 7: Create Something from Nothing

7. 無中生有 / 无中生有 (wú zhōng shēng yǒu) Create Something from Nothing

Fabricate something to create an actual outcome. 無 (wú, nothing) and 有 (yǒu, being) are Laozi’s fundamental ontological pair: "天下万物生於有，有生於無" (all things in the world arise from being; being arises from nothingness). This stratagem is the cosmological principle applied strategically: the most powerful formations emerge from the field of possibility (wú) rather than from direct manipulation of existing entities (yǒu). This is Kauffman's order-for-free: emergence from structural conditions rather than explicit design.

◆ Stratagem 8: Advance by a Concealed Path

8. 暗度陳冉 / 暗度陈仓 (dàrù Chén cāng) Secretly Advance to Chencang

Repair the walkways openly as a diversion while the real advance takes place through a concealed route. This is Shan's second Dao model: while the first model (the formed path, the repaired walkways) holds the observer's attention, the formative process (the concealed route) is already underway. The most significant structural formations often occur in the concealed channels of relational dynamics, not in the visible walkways of explicit strategy.

◆ Stratagem 9: Watch the Fire from the Opposite Bank

9. 隔岸觀火 / 隔岸观火 (gé àn guān huǒ) Watch the Fire from the Opposite Bank

When your enemies are fighting each other, do not intervene; wait and watch. This is the structurally sophisticated version of Stratagem 4: not merely conserving energy but maintaining the positional clarity that comes from not being entangled in another's collapse trajectory. In Shan's terms: reading collapse as trajectory rather than event, and preserving holding capacity by not assuming the corrective function for a system whose corrective capacity is already failing.

◆ Stratagem 10: Conceal a Dagger Behind a Smile

10. 笑裡藏刀 / 笑里藏刀 (xiào lǐ cáng dāo) Conceal a Dagger Behind a Smile

This stratagem requires the most careful reading: in Shan's framework, the "dagger" is not deceptive intent but structural honesty. The smile (surface function) can conceal the dagger (underlying structural reality). This is the reverse of Shan's account of collapse: in that account, the smile (surface function) conceals the dagger (the narrowing path, the thinning corrective capacity). Stratagem 10 asks: can we deliberately use the smile to protect the dagger of structural transformation? Can we work with the grain of the existing formed Dao while quietly initiating the formation of a new path?

◆ Stratagem 11: Sacrifice the Plum for the Peach

11. 李代桃價 / 李代桃價 (lǐ dài táo jiāng) The Plum Takes the Place of the Peach

Take the hit to preserve a more valuable position. This is the structural logic of Shan's account of long-game intelligence: sacrifice local gain (the plum) to preserve the positional field within which larger gains become possible (the peach). This is the opposite of the Elegant Wall-hitting pattern, where people sacrifice long-term structural viability to preserve short-term surface function. Stratagem 11 deliberately sacrifices surface function to preserve underlying viability.

◆ Stratagem 12: Lead the Sheep Away as Opportunity Permits

12. 順手牌羊 / 顺手牡羊 (shún shǒu qiān yáng) Lead away a goat in passing

Exploit every advantage, however small. This stratagem encodes the Li of opportunistic relational attunement: remaining sensitive to the field rather than fixed on a predetermined objective. This is Chia's wayfinding: we know as we go, and what we can take is determined by what the field makes available in this moment. This is also Kauffman's adjacent possible: exploit the openings that the current position makes available.

Chapter III: 攻戰計 (Gōng Zhàn Jì) — Attacking Stratagems

◆ Stratagem 13: Beat the Grass to Startle the Snake

13. 打草驚蛇 / 打草惊蛇 (dǎ cǎo jīng shé) Beat the grass to startle the snake

Do something unusual to provoke a revealing response. This stratagem is an epistemological tool: when Li is not yet visible, create a perturbation that makes the grain of the situation show itself. This is Kauffman's probe-sense-respond (or Snowden's: in the complex domain, act first to see the system's response before committing to a strategy). It is also a reading of Wittgenstein: "A philosophical problem has the form: 'I don't know my way about'" (PI §123). To find one's way, one must first move.

◆ Stratagem 14: Borrow a Corpse to Resurrect the Soul

14. 借屍還魂 / 借尸还魂 (jiè shī huán hún) Borrow a corpse to resurrect the soul

Take an institution, technology, or ideology that has been abandoned and repurpose it. This is precisely the logic of Shan's two Dao models in cultural transmission: a tradition that appears formed (even dead) can be re-animated by being encountered as still in formation. WSR revived the 900-year-old Neo-Confucian concept of Li and gave it new life as a systems methodology. Shan's Relational Dynamics revives the ancient Dao/Li pair as a framework for complexity thinking.

◆ Stratagem 15: Lure the Tiger out of the Mountains

15. 調虎離山 / 调虎离山 (diào hǔ lí shān) Lure the tiger out of the mountains

Draw the enemy away from their position of strength. In Shan's framework: this stratagem works because position shapes possibility. The tiger's strength depends on the terrain (the relational field) within which it operates. Changing the terrain changes what the tiger's strength can achieve. This is the strategic application of "position reveals structure, structure shapes emergence": to change what emerges, change the positional field, not the agent.

◆ Stratagem 16: In Order to Capture, First Release

16. 欲擒姑縥 / 欲擒姑纵 (yù qīn gū zōng) To capture, first release

Allow the enemy to relax before striking. This stratagem encodes the Li of timing in relational dynamics: the moment to engage is not when the other party is most resistant (when their corrective capacity is strongest) but when they have relaxed into the assumption of stability. This is also a structural claim: the ultrastable system can be entered most effectively at the moment of its apparent success, when its self-correcting mechanisms have become most confident — and therefore least sensitive to signals of change.

◆ Stratagem 17: Toss out a Brick to Attract Jade

17. 抋砲引玉 / 抛砖引玉 (pāo zhuān yǐn yù) Toss a tile to attract jade

Offer something of lesser value to get something of greater value. This is the Li of productive incompleteness: what is offered (the tile/brick) is genuine but partial, leaving space for the jade of the other's response. In Shan's terms: the formed Dao (the offered tile) creates the interface through which the formative process (the jade of genuinely new insight) can arrive. This is the structure of the best intellectual dialogue: offer a genuine but incomplete insight that creates space for the other's greater insight.

◆ Stratagem 18: Defeat the Enemy by Capturing their Chief

18. 擒賊必先擒王 / 抓贼必先抓王 (qiǐn zéi qiǐn wáng) To catch bandits, first catch their leader

Identify and neutralise the structural centre of the system. In Shan's framework: the "king" of a collapsing system is not necessarily the most visible actor but the structural node whose integrity is constitutive of the whole. In tensegrity terms: the continuous tensional network has no single king — but identifying the structural distribution pattern is the equivalent of capturing the king in a conventional hierarchy.

Chapter IV: 混戰計 (Hùn Zhàn Jì) — Chaos Stratagems

◆ Stratagem 19: Remove the Firewood from Under the Pot

19. 釜底抽薪 / 釜底抽薪 (fū dǐ chōu xīn) Remove the firewood from under the pot

Remove the source of the enemy's strength rather than attacking the strength directly. This is the most direct application of Shan's collapse analysis: do not attack the surface function (the boiling water) but the underlying viability condition (the fire). In system terms: do not attempt to address the symptom of institutional collapse (the boiling) but the relational conditions that maintain the appearance of function (the fire) while the structural trajectory has already narrowed.

◆ Stratagem 20: Catch the Fish While the Water Is Troubled

20. 混水摸魚 / 混水摸鱼 (hùn shuǐ mō yú) Catch fish in muddy water

Exploit ambiguity and uncertainty to gain advantage. In Shan's framework: the VUCA world is not merely a problem to be managed but a field to be read. The muddy water is the field where Li is not yet legible — where the grain of the situation has not yet stabilised into a recognisable pattern. To fish in muddy water is to operate before premature legibility has closed the generative openness. This is Shan's second Dao model: engage with the forming process before it has congealed into the formed.

◆ Stratagem 21: The Golden Cicada Sheds Its Shell

21. 金蟉脱殼 / 金蟉脱壳 (jīn chān tuō ké) The golden cicada sheds its shell

Leave behind a facade while secretly withdrawing. This stratagem addresses Shan's distinction between surface function and underlying viability. A system can maintain the appearance of surface function (the cicada shell) while the actual living process (the cicada) has already departed. The danger is that observers — and the system's own self-correcting mechanisms — continue responding to the shell rather than recognising the departure. Jin Guantao's ultrastable system maintains its shell (surface coherence) long after the cicada (adaptive vitality) has gone.

◆ Stratagem 22: Shut the Door to Catch the Thief

22. 關門捉賊 / 关门捉贼 (guān mén zōu zéi) Shut the door to catch the thief

Encircle and capture rather than pursue. This is the logic of the game of wéiqí (圍棋): surrounding rather than direct attack. The formation of the surrounding field (the relational encirclement) precedes the capture. You cannot capture by direct attack what you can capture by prior positional enclosure. This is position-building over time: the surrounding structure is built move by move before the capture becomes inevitable.

◆ Stratagem 23: Befriend a Distant Enemy to Attack a Nearby Enemy

23. 遠交近攻 / 远交近攻 (yuǎn jiāo jìn gōng) Befriend distant states while attacking nearby states

Manage relational dynamics across different distances and timescales simultaneously. This is the long-game version of relational dynamics: maintaining the field of distant relations while concentrating force in the near field. In Shan's framework: the relational field is not flat but differentiated by proximity, time, and relational quality. Excellence requires managing multiple relational registers simultaneously, maintaining coherence across them all.

◆ Stratagem 24: Borrow a Safe Passage to Conquer the Enemy

24. 假途逅虎 / 假途砒虎 (jiǎ dào fá Gū) Borrow a road to invade Guo

Use a third party's cooperation (borrowed road) to attack a target. This is the Li of structural intermediary: the borrowed road is itself a formed Dao that makes a new dynamic possible. To borrow the road is to engage with the existing relational field rather than forcing a new path through hostile terrain. Relation precedes dynamics: the borrowed road (the pre-existing relational field) enables the dynamic (the invasion) that would otherwise be impossible.

Chapter V: 並戰計 (Bìng Zhàn Jì) — Proximity Stratagems

◆ Stratagem 25: Replace the Beams with Rotten Timbers

25. 偷梁換柱 / 偷梁换柱 (tōu liáng huàn zhù) Steal the beams and replace them with rotten timbers

Destroy the enemy's key structural elements while maintaining the appearance of stability. This is the most direct structural parallel to Shan's collapse analysis: the building still stands (surface function), but the beams have been replaced with rotten timbers (the underlying structural integrity has been compromised). Nothing collapses in one move: the building will collapse eventually, but the path of that collapse was laid when the beams were replaced. The corrective capacity has thinned; the endurance is no longer viability.

◆ Stratagem 26: Point at the Mulberry Tree While Cursing the Locust Tree

26. 指桑罵槐 / 指桑罵槐 (zhǐ sāng mà huai) Point at the mulberry tree while cursing the locust tree

Address one party by ostensibly addressing another. This stratagem operates through the relational field rather than direct confrontation. It is the strategic version of Shan's account of how Dao operates as an interface: the meaning that matters is not always the meaning that is directly expressed. The relational field between speaker, audience, and target transmits what direct address cannot.

◆ Stratagem 27: Feign Madness Without Going Mad

27. 假瘋不癖 / 假疯不癖 (jiǎ diān bù diān) Feign madness but keep your balance

Appear incompetent or disordered while maintaining internal coherence. This is the strategic version of Shan's account of surface function and underlying viability — deployed deliberately rather than suffered involuntarily. The excellence (coherence under constraint over time) is maintained internally while externally projecting a different appearance. This requires deep structural awareness: one must know the difference between feigning madness and actually going mad.

◆ Stratagem 28: Remove the Ladder After the Enemy Has Ascended

28. 上屋抽梯 / 上屋抽梯 (shàng wū chōu tī) Remove the ladder after the enemy has climbed to the roof

Create a situation where the enemy is committed to a position they cannot sustain. This is the strategic reverse of Wittgenstein's ladder: the Tractatus's ladder is removed after climbing to show the world rightly. This stratagem removes the ladder to trap the opponent. Both depend on the same structural insight: ladders are temporary scaffolding, not permanent structures. The question is whether the removal of the ladder is a therapeutic clearing (Wittgenstein) or a strategic trap (Stratagem 28).

◆ Stratagem 29: Deck the Tree with False Blossoms

29. 樹上開花 / 树上开花 (shù shàng kāi huā) Decorate the tree with false blossoms

Use deceptive appearances to amplify the impression of strength. This is the strategic version of what Shan calls "premature legibility": the false blossoms create a Li (the appearance of flourishing) that does not correspond to the underlying Dao (the tree's actual condition). The danger is when a system internalises its own false blossoms — when the self-deception becomes structural. This is Jin Guantao's ultrastable system: the false blossoms of surface coherence eventually replace the genuine blossoms of adaptive vitality.

◆ Stratagem 30: Make the Host and the Guest Exchange Roles

30. 反客為主 / 反客为主 (fǎn kè wéi zhǔ) Make the guest become the host

Transform from a position of weakness to one of control by gradually becoming indispensable. This stratagem encodes the Li of gradual structural incorporation: the guest (outsider) becomes the host (insider) through sustained relational engagement that gradually transfers the structural centre of gravity. In Shan's framework: this is the long-game version of how a new Dao (the guest's path) gradually displaces an old Dao (the host's path) by following it so thoroughly and so long that it inherits its structural position.

Chapter VI: 敗戰計 (Bài Zhàn Jì) — Desperate Stratagems

◆ Stratagem 31: Use a Beauty to Seduce the Enemy

31. 美人計 / 美人计 (měi rén jì) Beauty Trap / Honey Trap

Use the enemy's desires against them by offering what they want. This stratagem operates through the relational grain of desire and attention. The beauty is not primarily a person but a structural attractor: something that captures and holds attention while the real dynamic proceeds elsewhere. In Shan's terms: the formed Dao (the attractive surface) captures the observer's attention while the formative Dao (the actual strategic movement) proceeds in the less-visible channels.

◆ Stratagem 32: The Empty City Stratagem

32. 空城計 / 空城计 (kōng chéng jì) The Empty City Stratagem

When defenseless, open the gates and appear confident to make the enemy hesitate. The most famous instance: Zhuge Liang (諸葛亮) played the lute calmly atop a city wall with the gates wide open, causing a suspicious enemy army to withdraw. This stratagem works by exploiting the structural gap between signal and situation: the enemy reads the signal (calm, open gates) as evidence of an underlying military strength they cannot see. The Li they perceive (confident defender) does not match the actual Dao (empty city).

◆ Stratagem 33: Counter the Enemy by using their Own Stratagem

33. 反間計 / 反间计 (fǎn jiān jì) Turn the enemy's own spy against them

Use the enemy's intelligence apparatus against them. This stratagem works through the existing relational field — using the channels of information that the enemy has already established. In WSR terms: working with the existing shili (the enemy's ways of seeing) to create a different wuli (material outcome) while managing the renli (the relational trust of the double agent). All three Li must be simultaneously engaged.

◆ Stratagem 34: Suffer an Injury to Win the Enemy's Trust

34. 苦肉計 / 苦肉计 (kǔ ròu jì) Self-injury stratagem

Deliberately suffer a wound to gain the enemy's confidence. This is the stratagem of deliberate sacrifice of surface function to establish credibility within a relational field. In Shan's framework: sometimes the path of building a structural position requires absorbing short-term costs in order to create the relational conditions within which longer-term viability becomes possible. This is not Elegant Wall-hitting (which is involuntary) but deliberate structural investment.

◆ Stratagem 35: Chain Together the Enemy's Ships

35. 連環計 / 连环计 (lián huán jì) Interlink everything

Create a unified structure that links all the enemy's ships together, so that when one burns they all burn. This stratagem creates systemic coupling as a vulnerability: it makes the enemy's distributed strength into a single fragile unity. This is the reverse of tensegrity: rather than distributing force through a continuous tensional network (resilience), it creates a continuous chain of dependency that makes the whole as vulnerable as its weakest link. Jin Guantao's ultrastable system is structurally linked in this way: when one of the three subsystems (peasant economy, bureaucratic polity, Confucian ideology) begins to fail, the chain links of coupling pull all three into failure together.

◆ Stratagem 36: The Best Stratagem is to Flee

36. 走為上計 / 走为上計 (zǒu wéi shàng jì) Flight is the best stratagem

三十六計，走為上計 — Sānshíliù jì, zǒu wéi shàng jì — Of the thirty-six stratagems, fleeing is best — the most famous Chinese strategic proverb

When all else fails, retreat is not defeat but the preservation of structural integrity for future formation. This stratagem is the full expression of Shan's working frame: excellence as capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. When the constraint has exceeded the capacity to hold coherence, the strategic imperative is to withdraw and rebuild. Endurance is not viability: continuing to hold a position that cannot hold is not excellence but structural self-destruction.

Wittgenstein parallel: the retreat at the end of the Tractatus — "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" — is Stratagem 36 applied to philosophical language. When language has reached its structural limit, the appropriate move is not to push further into nonsense but to withdraw into the silence that makes the next advance possible. The silence is not defeat; it is the preservation of the structural integrity that makes future speaking possible.

Fuller parallel: "You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model." This is Stratagem 36 combined with the Dymaxion principle: retreat from the old model, build the new model that makes the old obsolete.

Shan's full synthesis of the 36 Stratagems: taken together, they constitute a map of how the Li of different strategic situations can be read and worked with. Each stratagem is a specific pattern of relational dynamics under constraint that has been found to produce structural advantage over time. They are, collectively, the Li of the long game: the inner grain of strategic wisdom accumulated through millennia of practice, thickened from trace to pattern to position.

VII

Part IV: Major Dialectical Collisions — Extended Analysis

4.1 Shan and Fuller: Excellence as Tensional Integrity

The most structurally intimate dialogue is between Shan's relational dynamics and Fuller's tensegrity. Her working frame — "excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time" — is a precise verbal formulation of tensegrity: the continuous tensional network (relation) holds the compressive elements (local dynamics) in coherence (distributed structural integrity) under constraint (external and internal forces) over time (the temporal dimension Fuller's spatial analysis underplays).

“"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world." — Wittgenstein, Tractatus 5.6. But what are the limits of Fuller's language? His vocabulary is spatial and energetic — tension, compression, distribution, force. It describes the structural principle of integrity at a moment. Shan's vocabulary adds temporal depth (formation over time), relational genealogy (how the tension network formed), and the ethics of care (what does holding in coherence cost? who bears the cost?). Fuller's tensegrity needs Shan's temporality to become a full account of structural life.”

Fuller's Dymaxion maximum principle: maximum benefit from minimum input. Shan's long game: the minimum input is not force but attention — the sustained, grain-following, position-building intelligence that achieves maximum structural integrity from the relational resources available. This is ephemeralization applied to strategy: doing more with less — more coherence with less constraint — by following the Li rather than forcing it.

Fuller's challenge to Shan: "All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures. Universe is omnitensional integrity." This panconnectivism flattens ontological precedence: if everything is connected through tensional integrity, it becomes structurally difficult to say any one connection is prior to any other. Shan must account for why, within the omnitensional universe, some connections are constitutive and others merely contingent. Her answer: the formation history. What makes some connections ontologically prior is not their current force but their temporal priority in the formation of the field.

4.2 Shan and Wittgenstein: Three Convergences, Three Challenges

4.2a Tractatus: The Limits of World and Language

"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world" (5.6). For Shan, this proposition is not merely a constraint but a structural opportunity. If the limits of language are the limits of world, then a richer language — one that carries more compressed structural distinctions — is also a richer world. Chinese, with its 2,500-year ecology of 道 and 理, offers structural perceptions that English does not package in the same form. Shan's project of making Li visible in English is an attempt to extend the limits of the English-language world by importing a structural concept that the Chinese language has been cultivating for millennia.

The Tractatus challenge: "What can be said at all can be said clearly; and whereof one cannot speak thereof one must be silent" (Preface and 7). Shan's Li is precisely what cannot be said clearly — it can only be glimpsed through practice, through the encounter with the grain of things. The Tractatus would seem to demand silence about Li. But Shan's response is Wittgenstein's own: "There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical" (6.522). Li shows itself; it is what shows itself in the moment of skilled practice, in the Cook Ding encounter, in Move 37 becoming inevitable in retrospect.

4.2b Investigations: Form of Life and Living Interface

The later Wittgenstein's form of life is Shan's formed Dao: the shared background of practices, habits, and forms of agreement within which particular language games can occur. Both insist that what is most important about any signifying system is not its propositional content but its functional role within a form of life. The difference: Wittgenstein treats forms of life as given ("this is simply what I do," PI §217) — as bedrock that resists further investigation. Shan investigates how forms of life form: her second Dao model is precisely the investigation of the bedrock-formation process that Wittgenstein treats as given.

4.2c On Certainty: The River Bed and the Shifting Bed

On Certainty's river-bed is Shan's most precise Western philosophical parallel. Hardened propositions as channels for fluid inquiry; the bed shifts through the accumulated force of the flow; the world-picture is the inherited background against which truth and falsity are distinguished. This is Shan's first Dao model (the formed Dao as background condition) and the potential for structural transformation (the bed can shift).

But On Certainty adds something Shan does not yet fully develop: the political dimension. "In the beginning was the deed" (OC): the world-picture is not merely inherited but enacted through action. What we do — collectively, habitually, institutionally — is what hardens into the river-bed. This means that the river-bed is not politically neutral: it is shaped by whose deeds count, whose practices are permitted to harden, whose formation histories are visible. Jackson's critical systems thinking raises this directly; Shan's framework needs to integrate it.

4.3 Shan and Robert Chia: Wayfinding, Strategy, and Dwelling

Chia's work provides the most developed academic translation of Shan's concepts into management and organisation theory. His dwelling/building distinction mirrors her two Dao models with striking precision: the dwelling mode (emergence through everyday coping, strategy immanent in adaptive action) is her second Dao model; the building mode (prior design, Li before Dao) is the pathological excess of her first model.

His "strategy-in-practices" account — how coping actions "congeal inadvertently over time into an organizational modus operandi" — is a management-science formulation of Shan's path-formation narrative: traces thicken into patterns, patterns into positions, positions into inherited structural realities (the modus operandi). The London street example is her second Dao model at urban scale.

The wayfinding concept from Tim Ingold (quoted by Chia): "we know as we go, not before we go (ambulatory knowing)." This is the epistemological corollary of Shan's ontological claim: Dao precedes Li not just structurally but epistemically. We cannot know the grain of a path before walking it. Knowledge is ambulatory.

Chia's challenge to Shan: his framework is empirically grounded in the study of actual organisations and their actual strategy emergence. Shan's framework is more broadly ontological and less methodologically specified. The challenge is whether and how Relational Dynamics could function as an empirical research programme — capable of generating testable claims about how specific organisations form, hold, and lose structural coherence over time.

4.4 Shan and Mike Jackson: Power, Emancipation, and Critical Li

Jackson's critical systems thinking adds a dimension that Shan's framework requires but does not yet fully develop: the political-ethical analysis of how power shapes the formation of Dao and the visibility of Li. His commitments — sociological awareness, complementarism, human well-being and emancipation — map onto three challenges to Shan:

First: sociological awareness. The formation conditions of any Dao include power relations. The river banks that constrain the boats' crossing are not merely physical; they are social, institutional, and political. Whose definition of the banks counts? Who has the power to designate certain paths as the legitimate way and others as deviant? Jackson's CST insists that any account of relational dynamics must include an account of the power relations that shape what relations are possible.

Second: complementarism. Jackson's SOSM insists that no single systems methodology is adequate for all situations. This is the methodological version of Shan's Li as contextual grain: the appropriate method depends on the grain of the situation. But Jackson goes further: methodological pluralism requires the explicit management of the tensions between different methods, not just contextual selection.

Third: emancipation. Jackson's CST has an explicit political commitment to human liberation from oppressive structural conditions. Shan's account of Elegant Wall-hitting — good-faith action colliding with invisible structural limits — is directly relevant here: the structural limits that produce Elegant Wall-hitting often function to maintain existing power arrangements. A fully critical Relational Dynamics would need a theory of how structural limits are maintained in the interests of some and at the cost of others.

4.5 Shan and Zhuangzi: The Cook Ding Paradox

Cook Ding's knife follows the heavenly Li (天理, tiānlĭ) without resistance. Perception and understanding have stopped; spirit moves where it wants. This is Shan's framework at its fullest expression: the practitioner who has followed the Dao long enough that the Li reveals itself directly to action, without mediation by theory.

The paradox for Shan's theoretical project: if the highest form of following Li requires the cessation of conceptual mediation, what is the theoretical articulation of Li doing? Is it producing a Li for Li at a higher level of abstraction? Or is it the necessary intermediate stage — the three-year stage where the whole ox (formed Dao, explicit Li) can still be seen, before the practitioner learns to move by spirit?

The answer that Zhuangzi's text itself suggests: Cook Ding's first stage was seeing the whole ox. The crude cook (wǔ dāo, 賢刀, monthly knife-changer) hacks without following the grain. Between them lies a period of careful, grain-following investigation that gradually becomes spontaneous. Shan's theoretical work may be the necessary middle stage: the careful investigation of Li through which the grain of the situation eventually becomes directly legible to skilled action.

VIII

Part V: VUCA, Dao, and the Chinese Management Tradition

Charles-Édouard Bouée's 2013 article connects Shan's framework to the contemporary management literature in a way that deserves sustained analysis. His core claim: Chinese entrepreneurs are not unsettled by the VUCA world (Volatile, Uncertain, Complex, Ambiguous) because they "grew up in a VUCA environment." Modern capitalist China was born at the dawn of the VUCA age. Chinese management style developed within this environment and is therefore structurally adapted to it.

In Shan's terms: Chinese management's adaptation to VUCA is not a management strategy (Li) deliberately designed for a VUCA world (Dao). It is a formation result: the Chinese management style congealed from decades of practice within a VUCA environment — which means its Li is downstream of a VUCA Dao. This is why it works where Western management (which developed Li for a stable, predictable world) fails: the grain matches the situation.

Bouée describes three dimensions of Chinese management that directly translate into Shan's framework:

*Dynamic and agile: "Chinese managers alternate between periods of frenetic activity and aggressive patience, guided along by a fuzzy vision instead of clear milestones." This is Shan's long-game intelligence: position-building over time rather than milestone-achievement at each step.*

*Stoic and opportunistic: "They believe things are always transforming into their opposites (e.g., failure into success, disadvantage into advantage)." This is the Daoist cosmology of the Yi Jing: all things transform through their opposites. Nothing collapses in one move; but nothing is permanently collapsed either. The path narrows; the path can widen again. This is not optimism but structural attunement.*

*Li, hierarchy, and consensus: "Hierarchy is essential to maintaining stability... the group — whether a family, an organization or the public at large — and provides no license for ego-tripping." This is renli as social grain: the Li of collective human relation that gives each individual their structural place within the larger field.*

The bridge Bouée builds but does not fully cross: the Chinese management tradition's structural advantages in a VUCA world are not transferable through explicit Li-extraction (writing an article or book about them) but only through the formation of a Dao: sustained practice within the actual conditions that generated them. Western managers who read about Chinese management principles and try to apply them as explicit strategies are doing exactly what Shan warns against: treating Li as prior to Dao. The grain cannot be followed through reading about it; it must be found through walking.

“The Chinese management style has developed into something complex and natural. It is a bridge between the rational and the emotional, the tangible and the intangible, the material and the spiritual. It is subtle, sensitive to cycles and seasons, and fuzzy, difficult to master.”

— Charles-Édouard Bouée, "VUCA, Dao and Learning from China" (2013)

The phrase "sensitive to cycles and seasons" is crucial: this is temporal Li awareness, the capacity to read the grain of time — to know when to be active and when to wait, when to advance and when to retreat (Stratagem 36), when surface coherence is still viable and when it has become mere endurance. This is the strategic intuition that Shan is trying to articulate structurally as the long-game reading of formation trajectories.

IX

Part VI: Synthesis — Three Registers of Li and the Ethics of Dynamic Maximum Tension

6.1 Li as Material Grain (Wu理 物理)

At the material-physical level, Li is the inherent grain or texture of things that determines how they can be worked. Prigogine's dissipative structures have a Li: the specific pattern of energy flows and structural organisation that maintains them far from equilibrium. Fuller's tensegrity structures have a Li: the specific distribution of tension and compression that gives them their structural integrity. Kauffman's complex adaptive systems have a Li: the building blocks and rules from which emergent patterns arise.

The link to Shan: physical structures embody the principle she articulates. A tensegrity structure that is losing its tensional integrity shows the same pattern as Shan's collapsing system: surface function (the structure still stands) while underlying viability (the continuous tensional network) is degrading. The Li of the tensegrity structure becomes visible precisely at the moment of its failure — the moment when the grain can no longer hold the imposed force.

6.2 Li as Cognitive-Perspectival Grain (Shili 事理)

At the cognitive-perspectival level, Li is the grain of how situations are perceived, understood, and engaged with. Shan's Iceberg Model is a shili analysis: the visible surface (speech or silence) has a Li that only becomes legible when the deeper conditions shaping it are investigated. Wittgenstein's hinge propositions are the shili of ordinary language: the hardened propositions that function as channels for fluid inquiry.

"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world" (Tractatus 5.6) is itself a shili statement: it names the grain of the cognitive-linguistic field within which thinking occurs. Shan's move is to show that the grain differs across languages: the shili of Chinese thought is shaped by the 2,500-year ecology of 道 and 理 in ways that the shili of English thought is not. This is not relativism but structural ecology: different language-worlds offer different grains, different paths of formation, different glimpses of Li.

6.3 Li as Relational-Human Grain (Renli 人理)

At the human-relational level, Li is the grain of how relations form, hold, and drift over time. Shan's collapse analysis is a renli analysis: what appears as individual failure (burnout, collapse, defeat) is the delayed visibility of a longer process of relational degradation. Jin Guantao's ultrastable system is a renli analysis at civilisational scale.

The ethical dimension: WSR insists that renli must be "cared for" rather than merely "known." This is the moral corollary of Shan's structural framework. If the relational grain of human systems is constitutive of what is structurally possible, then the ethics of caring for renli — of attending to how human relations form, degrade, and can be sustained — is not separate from the structural analysis but constitutive of it. Excellence (capacity held in coherence under constraint over time) is also an ethical practice: the practice of caring for the relational field that makes the holding possible.

6.4 Dynamic Maximum Tension as Structural Ethics

Fuller's Dymaxion principle — Dynamic Maximum Tension — provides the structural frame for what Shan's working frame implies ethically. Maximum benefit from minimum input, achieved through the intelligent distribution of tension through a continuous relational network: this is not merely a structural engineering principle but an ethical commitment.

Fuller's final statement: "Integrity is the essence of everything successful. If humanity does not opt for integrity we are through completely." This is Shan's working frame elevated to a global stakes claim: excellence as tensional integrity is not merely a personal or organisational excellence but a civilisational necessity. The alternative to integrity is structural collapse: not the dramatic single-move collapse but the gradual thinning of corrective capacity, the narrowing of the path, the replacement of beams with rotten timbers, the golden cicada leaving its shell.

The synthesis: Shan's relational dynamics, Fuller's tensegrity, the 36 Stratagems' structural wisdom, WSR's three Li, Wittgenstein's form of life, Chia's dwelling and wayfinding, Jackson's critical systems emancipation, and the long Chinese tradition of Dao-Li thinking all converge on the same structural ethics: follow the grain, build positions that hold, distribute tension through the relational network, and know when to flee (Stratagem 36) in order to build the new model (Fuller) that makes the old obsolete.

X

Part VII: Cadence, Salience, Resonance, Valence, Vibration, Tension, and Gain — The Mystical-Structural Layer

This section develops an entirely new and original layer of analysis: the metaphysical-structural categories through which structural integrity makes itself felt before it becomes conceptually legible. These are the registers in which Li announces itself prior to articulation: in the felt quality of a system's motion, in what draws attention and what recedes, in what resonates across distances and what falls dead, in what accumulates structural force and what dissipates it. This layer stretches Fuller, Wittgenstein, and all the voices toward a unified theory of structural attunement.

7.1 Cadence: The Temporal Li of Formation

Cadence is the rhythmic pattern of a system's movement over time — the Li of its temporal grain. Every system that has formed through repeated traversal has a cadence: the characteristic rhythm of its activity, its cycles of expansion and contraction, its alternation between what Bouée calls "frenetic activity and aggressive patience." Cadence is what the body knows before the mind names it: the quality of time-in-the-system.

In Shan's framework: excellence as "capacity held in coherence under constraint over time" requires cadence-awareness. The constraint has a cadence; the capacity has a cadence; the coherence has a cadence. The practitioner who cannot read the cadence of the system they are working within is like Cook Ding hacking against the grain: technically active but structurally exhausting.

Fuller: the tensegrity structure under load exhibits a cadence — the frequency at which tensional forces distribute and redistribute through the network. This frequency is the structural heartbeat of the whole. When the cadence becomes irregular or fails, the system is under structural stress. The visible surface (the structure still stands) may continue to function long after the cadence has become arrhythmic: this is Shan's surface function / underlying viability distinction at the vibrational level.

Wittgenstein: language games have a cadence — the rhythm of their use within a form of life. When the cadence of language use becomes irregular (when words go on holiday, when philosophical discourse disconnects from its practical ground), philosophical problems arise. The therapeutic task of philosophy is to restore the cadence: to bring words back to their everyday use, to re-ground the rhythm of language in the rhythm of the form of life from which it arose.

Bergson's durée: duration is experienced as cadence — the lived rhythm of consciousness as it flows. The dissociation between intellectual time (discrete moments, fixed Li) and lived time (continuous cadence, forming Dao) is the source of philosophical illusion. Shan's framework addresses exactly this dissociation: the formed Dao (intellectual Li, fixed pattern) is always a reduction of the living cadence (the formative Dao) to a static image.

7.2 Salience: What the Field Makes Available for Attention

Salience is the structural property by which certain aspects of a complex situation command attention while others recede. It is the Li of attention itself: the grain of the perceptual field that determines what shows and what hides. Salience is not merely subjective (what I happen to notice) but structural (what the field makes available for noticing given the position from which one looks).

In Shan's framework: salience is why collapse is not seen in time. The surface function is salient; the underlying viability degradation is not. The visible moves on the Go board are salient; the narrowing positional field is not. Elegant Wall-hitting is the repeated collision between action (responding to what is salient) and invisible structural limits (what the position has made non-salient).

Wittgenstein's 5.6: "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world." This is a salience statement: what the limits of language make salient is what constitutes the world; what falls outside those limits is not merely unseen but literally not-there for the language user. This is why the crossing from Chinese to English is a world-change for Shan: the salience structures are different. What 道理 makes salient (the grain of the path as reason) is not what "reason" makes salient (abstract logical relation).

Bateson: "Information is any difference that makes a difference." This is the precise definition of salience: a structural property of the field whereby certain differences become consequential (salient) while others remain inert. The Li of a situation is constituted by what differences make a difference within it. Cook Ding's mastery is salience mastery: he perceives the articulations of the ox's body (the differences that make a difference for the knife's movement) while all else recedes.

Fuller: the tensegrity structure under stress shows differential salience — certain members of the tension network become more prominent as they bear more load. This is the structural analogue of the system under stress making certain aspects of its condition more visible. Collapse is preceded by a shift in the salience pattern: what was distributed and invisible becomes concentrated and visible, but only when it is already too late to restore the original distribution.

7.3 Resonance: When Grain Meets Grain

Resonance is the structural phenomenon in which two systems with compatible Li enter into mutually amplifying vibration. It is the experiential quality of genuine intellectual or relational encounter: when what you are thinking meets what the other has articulated, and both are deepened by the meeting. Resonance is the felt quality of the moment when Shan recognises the WSR methodology: "the surfacing, within a professional intellectual conversation, of a Chinese character she had always carried."

Resonance has a precise structural definition: it occurs when the Li of one system matches the Li of another closely enough that the natural frequency of each reinforces the other. This is not merely agreement (identity of Li) but complementary difference (the two Li's different angles on the same structural reality amplify each other's signal). The best intellectual dialogue is not the one that confirms but the one that resonates: each voice deepening through the encounter with the other.

This paper is itself a resonance instrument: it places thirty-five voices in relation to Shan's framework and asks which ones resonate (their Li matches her Li closely enough that both are deepened by the encounter), which ones are dissonant (their Li conflicts with hers in ways that are structurally productive), and which ones are merely orthogonal (different grain, neither resonant nor dissonant). The deepest resonances: Chia's dwelling/wayfinding, Fuller's tensegrity, Wittgenstein's On Certainty river-bed, Zhuangzi's Cook Ding, WSR's three Li. The deepest dissonances: Cheng Yi's Dao≡Li identity claim, Zhu Xi's transcendent Great Ultimate, Jackson's emancipatory political challenge.

同聲相應，同氣相求 — tóng shēng xiāng yìng, tóng qì xiāng qiú — Like notes resonate with each other; like breath seeks like breath — Yi Jing, Qian hexagram commentary

This ancient Yi Jing phrase captures the structural principle of resonance as a cosmological claim: like Li seeks like Li across distances. The formation of intellectual communities, traditions, and schools of thought is the large-scale expression of this principle: similar structural grains tend to find each other across time and space.

7.4 Valence: The Structural Charge of Relation

Valence is the structural charge that a relation carries — its capacity to attract or repel, to bond or separate, to enable or constrain further relation. In chemistry, valence determines what bonds are possible between elements; in relational dynamics, valence determines what further relations are possible between agents within a field. Every relation that forms adds to or subtracts from the valence available for future formation.

Shan's relational dynamics are valence dynamics: what makes some dynamics "consequential" (her word) is not their content alone but their valence — the relational charge they carry within the specific field. The same sentence has different valence in different relational contexts. The same move has different valence in different positions on the Go board. Valence is contextual charge: it is the structural property that makes relation dynamic.

Fuller: in tensegrity structures, each element has a specific valence — the number and type of tensional connections it can support. The structural integrity of the whole depends on the proper distribution of valence across all elements. An element with too high a valence (too many connections bearing too much load) is a structural vulnerability; the path narrows where valence exceeds capacity.

Wittgenstein: in language games, each word has a valence — the network of uses to which it can be put within a given form of life. The valence of "道" in Chinese is enormously higher than the valence of "way" in English: 道 is structurally connected to an ecology of 道理, 道德, 知道, 道路 that "way" is not. The limits of my language mean the limits of my world: the valence-limits of my vocabulary are the valence-limits of my relational and conceptual world.

7.5 Vibration: The Felt Quality of Structural Tension

Vibration is the physical manifestation of tensional force distributed through a structural network. In music, vibration produces tone: the frequency of vibration determines the pitch, the amplitude determines the volume, the harmonic structure determines the timbre. In structural systems, vibration is how tensional integrity makes itself felt: a system under appropriate tension vibrates at its natural frequency, a system under too much tension vibrates arrhythmically, a system whose tension has been lost vibrates not at all.

The I Ching connection: the 64 hexagrams of the Yi Jing (易經, I Ching) are 64 structural configurations of yin and yang lines — 64 patterns of vibration in the tensional field of the cosmos. The hexagram for any situation is the structural resonance pattern of that situation: the Yi Jing is a manual for reading the Li of the moment through the lens of its vibrational structure. The 36 Stratagems are specific patterns of response to 36 vibrational situations; the Yi Jing is the full field of 64 vibrational patterns within which they arise.

易經 — Yì Jīng — The Book of Changes — 易 (yì) means: change, transformation, easy, the fundamental cosmic dynamic

Fuller: "All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures. Universe is omnitensional integrity." This means the universe is a vibrational field: everything vibrates at the frequency determined by its specific tensional integrity. When structures resonate with each other (their vibrational frequencies match), they reinforce each other; when they are dissonant, they create interference patterns that may generate new structural configurations or may destabilise both.

The Zhuangzi connection: Cook Ding's butchery is described in musical terms — "with each touch of his hand, heave of his shoulder, step of his feet, thrust of his knee... the melody alternated between the Jingshou chorus and the Mulberry Forest dance." The practitioner who has mastered the Li of a situation moves through it musically: the cadence of the work, the resonance of body and material, the vibration of the knife finding the natural articulations. This is the phenomenology of working with Li at the highest level.

7.6 Tension: Integrity and the Ethics of Holding

Fuller's "tension is the great integrity" is the deepest structural principle of this paper. Tension is not a problem to be reduced but the structural condition of coherence. Without tension, there is no tensegrity; without tensional integrity, there is no structural coherence capable of withstanding constraint. The question is not how to reduce tension but how to distribute it: how to ensure that the continuous tensional network holds the compressive elements in their proper structural relationship.

Shan's frame: "excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time." The "held" is the active tensional work. Coherence does not maintain itself; it must be actively maintained through the continuous tensional network of relation. When the tension degrades — when the relational network thins, when corrective capacity decreases, when the continuous holding work is not done — coherence fails: not dramatically but gradually, not visibly but structurally.

The ethics: tension is not neutral. The tensional network of a human system is borne by particular people in particular positions. Not all positions in the system bear the same tensional load. The "beautiful Wall-hitting" — the good-faith collision with invisible structural limits — is often borne disproportionately by those with least power to reshape the structural field. A fully critical theory of tensional integrity would ask: who bears the tension? Whose holding work maintains the coherence? And is that distribution just?

Jackson's challenge becomes the ethics of tension: emancipation is the project of redistributing the tensional load more justly, of building relational networks that do not concentrate structural stress at the positions of least power.

The Laozi formulation:

上善若水。水善利萬物而不爭。 — shàng shàn ruò shuǐ. shuǐ shàn lì wàn wù ér bù zhēng. — The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things without contention. — Dao De Jing Ch. 8

Water is the model of just tension distribution: it benefits all things without contention, yielding to constraint while accumulating structural force.
