ChatGPT’s fluency in Chinese does not extend to the limits of Chinese phonetic structure; its world lacks the tonal registration layer. Every management consultant fluent in "complexity" without having walked the Dao of genuine complex systems engagement: fluency as hallucination, naming as a substitute for understanding. Laozi (道可道，非常道): the smoothly circulating Dao is the one most at risk of having lost its structural depth. Smoothness is the sign that too much has been lost. Zhuangzi: the crude cook moves the knife with fluency; Cook Ding moves it with registration. The difference is not speed but structural contact.

Proposition 5: "Endurance Is Not Always Viability"

“Endurance is not always viability. Sometimes what looks like resilience is only delayed collapse.”

— Shan

This is the most counterintuitive and most structurally important claim in Shan’s failure theory. Confucius (岁寒然後知松柏): but equally, some things that appear to endure are pines; some are not. The discernment is structural: the difference between genuine viability and delayed collapse is not visible in the surface endurance. It is visible in the formation trajectory. Prigogine (dissipative structures): the system that appears to maintain its structure while its energy gradient is collapsing is enduring without viability. Jin Guantao (ultrastable system): two thousand years of dynastic endurance that never resolved the structural conditions of collapse. The 金蟉脱殼 stratagem (the cicada sheds its shell): the shell endures; the cicada has gone. The educational institution that maintains its surface metrics (graduation rates, research outputs) while its structural capacity for genuine learning collapses: endurance without viability. And crucially — the practitioner who continues to work heroically within a position that has structurally narrowed beyond the point of genuine correction: endurance that is consuming the very holding capacity it appears to be maintaining.

Proposition 6: "Relation Precedes Dynamics"

“Relation precedes dynamics. Not because there is first a static relation and only later movement. Not because of a crude timeline. Dynamics become dynamics only within a relation-bearing field.”

— Shan

Guanzi (天下不一志则不交, without unified will there is no communication): the relational condition (unified will) precedes the dynamic (communication). Zhang Zai (天地之塞，吾其體): we are born into a relational field that precedes our existence; our dynamics arise within the given of cosmic relation. Maturana and Varela (structural coupling): the organism’s relational history with the environment shapes what any perturbation can produce; the structural coupling (the relational field) precedes the specific dynamic. Chia (dwelling mode): strategy emerges non-deliberately through everyday practical coping within the relational field; the field precedes the strategic act. Heidegger (the bridge gathers the banks): the bridge (the relational structure) calls the banks into being as banks; the dynamic (crossing) is enabled by the relational gathering that precedes it. Luhmann: the autopoietic system’s self-reference (the relational closure) is the condition of any specific communication; the system precedes the operations that maintain it. The verdict: from cosmological to biological to social to strategic — relation precedes dynamics at every scale.

Proposition 7: "Dao before Li. Path before Pattern. Grain before Intelligibility."

This is Shan’s most compressed structural proposition: a cascade of ontological precedence claims, each more specific than the last.

DAO BEFORE LI: established at length. PATH BEFORE PATTERN: Dong Zhongshu (同類相動，和氣相感, things of the same kind move each other; harmonised Qi responds to Qi) — the pattern of resonance is downstream of the formation path that produced the kind-similarity in the first place. GRAIN BEFORE INTELLIGIBILITY: Wang Fuzhi (氣就萀而後成象, Qi first condenses and then form-pattern emerges) — the intelligible form (the grain that can be described) is downstream of the condensation process that produced it. Fang Dongmei (生生流行，永不停歇, continuous generativity, never ceasing) — the generative process (Dao) precedes and exceeds any specific form (Li) it produces.

Wittgenstein: "In the beginning was the deed" (On Certainty, quoting Goethe). The deed (the path, the formation, the Dao) is prior to the proposition (the pattern, the grain, the Li). This is the most compressed statement of Shan’s structural claim in Western philosophical vocabulary: in the beginning was not the word (Li, intelligibility) but the deed (Dao, formation, path-walking).

Fuller: "doing more with less" — the Dymaxion principle is itself the practical application of the Dao-before-Li principle: don’t start with the theory (Li) and then find the structure (Dao); start with the structural problem (the need for shelter, efficiency, elegance) and let the form (Li) emerge from the formation process. The geodesic dome is not a theory applied; it is a Dao that produced a Li. The doing came before the knowing.

Proposition 8: "What Is Formed Is Still in Formation"

“What is formed is still in formation. What is forming already carries the possibility of form.”

— Shan

This is the most ontologically dense statement in the entire body of work and the one that most directly challenges the static account of complexity — the idea that a formed system is a finished system. Fang Dongmei: continuous generativity, never ceasing. Whitehead: actual occasions perish as they achieve definiteness and become data for subsequent becomings. Bergson: the present moment is "the invisible progress of the past gnawing into the future." Prigogine: the dissipative structure is maintained only through continuous energy dissipation — it is always forming. Maturana and Varela (autopoiesis): the living system continuously produces the components that produce it; it is its own ongoing formation.

The doctoral thesis is still in formation: every reading of it, every application of its insights to new contexts (AI interface failure, Go strategy, neonatal medicine), is a continued formation of what the thesis is. The thesis does not stop being formed at the moment of submission; it continues to form through every encounter with it. This paper is one such encounter. The thesis is still in formation, in every reader who walks its arguments far enough to see where they point.

This is the final structural claim of this paper: the inquiry does not end because the formation does not end. The analysis of Shan’s work is itself a formation — a path walked through her texts and through the texts of thirty-five-plus other voices that has produced a specific Li: this paper. And this paper is still in formation: in your reading of it, in what it makes possible in your thinking, in what you do next. The path continues. The grain reveals itself to those who follow it. And the following is itself the finding.

14.6 The Beauty of Structural Thought: What Shan Does with Form

In the spirit of Lin Yutang’s claim that life should be like poetry, not prose, and in the spirit of the request that this paper be aesthetically beautiful — not merely correct but alive, textured, energetic — one final observation about Shan’s style that the analytical register has not yet captured.

The most beautiful sentence in Shan’s body of work is also the most structurally precise: "Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first." The beauty is in the economy. Two sentences, eleven words, a complete structural theory. The gap between them is the gap between the theory (first sentence) and the mechanism (second sentence). The first sentence disturbs the assumption (things collapse dramatically); the second sentence replaces it with a structural account (the path was already narrowing). The period after "one move" is the silence of the iceberg. Everything between the last stone standing and the collapse is in that silence.

The poem is beautiful because it enacts what it describes: "We do not step onto a path. We inherit one." The line break after "path" is the inheritance — the white space of all the formation history that preceded the step. You did not make that space; you arrived in it. The poem makes that arrival visible by making you experience the line break as something you did not choose but that was given to you by the poem’s form. This is the poem as a Dao model: it creates the experience of inheritance in the act of reading it.

These are not illustrations of structural theory. They are structural theory. The particular carries the universal in its full particularity, not as an example stripped of its peculiarity but as an instance that is structurally significant precisely because of its peculiar specificity. This is what Zhang Dainian means when he says that Li is first the grain of jade: before it is a universal principle, it is the specific, physical, tactile grain of a specific piece of material, workable in these directions and resistant in these others. The theory of Li begins in the particular grain, not in the universal principle. And Shan’s essays begin there too: in the particular seminar room, the particular Go board, the particular feeding tube, the particular tone mark that became a wing.

“The surface was never the whole story. This is true of speech, as it is of ideas.”

— Alice Jing Shan — the last word, as it was the first concern

This formulation engages the central tension that runs through the entire dialectical inquiry: between the named pattern and the formation process that produces it, between the Li that can be stated and the Dao that must be walked, between the framework that explains and the encounter that constitutes. Every voice in this text approaches this same structural reality from a different formation history, and the collision between them produces insights that none could have generated alone.

The path continues. The grain was always there. The inquiry is still in formation.

道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。

Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng.

— Laozi, Dao De Jing Ch. 1

Additional Analyses: Shan Essays — Second Pass

This paper constitutes one of the most sustained analytical engagements yet attempted with the thought of Dr Alice Jing Shan (PhD, Edinburgh), whose Substack series Dao: The Art of the Long Game (2025–2026) and her concurrent Cynefin Co article on Li (理) represent a distinctive and underexamined contribution to complexity ontology, systems philosophy, and the epistemology of structural formation. The paper does not merely describe Shan's work; it interrogates, extends, and pressure-tests it by placing it in genuine dialectical collision with thirty or more intellectual traditions and individual voices.

The central questions are: What does Shan mean by precedence — and is her claim that Dao precedes Li, and relation precedes dynamics, a genuinely defensible ontological claim or a metaphysical preference dressed in systems language? What does she mean by emergence, and how does her account of mutual generation as path-formation relate to the canonical accounts of emergence in Western complexity science (Kauffman, Prigogine, Holland, Snowden) and in Chinese systems philosophy (Qian, Gu, Zhu)? How does her working frame — "excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time" — relate to Fuller's Dynamic Maximum Tension and tensegrity? When and where does Wittgenstein's three-phase philosophical development — from the Tractatus through the Investigations to On Certainty — shed specific and illuminating light on Shan's problematic, and where does it fall short? And what is the full depth of the Chinese philosophical genealogy of Li (理) that Shan is drawing on, and how does it relate to the contemporary Chinese systems tradition?

The paper proceeds in six Parts: Part I presents a complete and analytical account of Shan's published work to date, drawing on every available Substack essay. Part II portrays the thirty-plus interlocutors in sufficient depth that each can genuinely challenge her. Part III presents ten major dialectical collisions in analytical detail. Part IV develops the synthesis: what emerges from the collision. Part V is an original analysis of the three registers of Li as a structural concept. Part VI presents open questions that this dialectical inquiry cannot resolve but must name.

The paper contains extensive Chinese-language citation (characters, pinyin, and English), extensive primary quotation from all major figures, and analytical sections of sufficient rigour to constitute an original contribution to the interdisciplinary study of precedence, emergence, coherence, and the ethics of structural formation.

In late 2025 or early 2026, a comment appeared on David Snowden's LinkedIn thread about his blog post "A Game of Encirclement." Mike Jackson mentioned the Wuli-Shili-Renli (WSR) approach of Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu. For most readers, this was a technical citation — one systems methodology among many. For Alice Jing Shan, it was something more intimate: the surfacing, within a professional intellectual conversation, of a Chinese character she had known since childhood.

That character is 理 (lĭ). It lives in the fabric of everyday Chinese: 物理 (wùlĭ, physics: the Li of material things), 事理 (shìlĭ, the Li of affairs), 人理 (rénlĭ, the Li of human relations), 道理 (dàolĭ, the Li of the Way: reason, principle, underlying logic). It was already operating in her language before she encountered any formal system theory. When WSR surfaced in that LinkedIn thread, what it surfaced for Shan was not a new concept but an old companion: the patterned grain that had always been travelling alongside the path, the less-known partner of Dao.

This is, formally, a very small occasion: a thread, a citation, a recognition. But Shan writes out of a deep commitment to the idea that large structural truths arrive through small occasions, that the path forms through repeated movement rather than grand declaration, and that what is most structurally significant about a concept is often most visible at the moment it resurfaces in an unexpected context. The occasion of WSR surfacing in that thread is itself a little model of her theory: the Li of the conversation became visible when someone followed the Dao of a long-running intellectual tradition far enough that its grain could be recognised.

This paper takes that occasion as its starting point and asks: what happens when we follow Shan's own structural logic — Dao before Li, path before pattern, formation before formed coherence — all the way through a conversation with thirty interlocutors who are, each in their own way, trying to think the same thing?

Too smooth, too familiar, too readily available: the warning signs that the Dao has become a Li. When a concept begins to circulate without friction, when ‘Dao’ sounds like something anyone can deploy without formation, when the term travels easily through management workshops — the smoothness is the signal of trouble. Li has detached from Dao. The pattern has separated from the path that produced it. Wittgenstein: bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use. The less-known partner must be sought. The Li must show itself against the specific resistance of the specific formation.

Alice Jing Shan holds a PhD in Education from the University of Edinburgh, where her doctoral research focused on Chinese postgraduate students' oral participation in English during their experience of a UK university. This biographical fact is not incidental to her intellectual framework — it is constitutive of it. Shan is a Chinese speaker who grew up inside the Chinese language, crossed into British higher education, completed a doctoral research programme in a language not her first, and has lived for many years in Scotland while raising a bilingual child. She describes her intellectual trajectory as shaped by "multilingual, intercultural, and institutional crossings" — by the repeated experience of moving meaning from one world to another.

In her own words, this experience produced a kind of cross-domain structural sensitivity:

What is analytically important here is Shan's claim that her cross-domain thinking is not abstraction but follows the same dynamic as it appears in different systems. She is not jumping from one domain to another; she is following a structural pattern as it manifests in different registers. This is already a claim about Li: that beneath the surface variation of different domains, a common grain is recognisable to someone trained to see it.

Her doctoral work produced the Iceberg Model of Oral Participation and the concept of Willingness for Oral Participation (WFOP). These are her first formal structural contributions and deserve sustained analytical attention, because they already contain in compressed form what later expands into the Relational Dynamics framework.

She coins Willingness for Oral Participation (WFOP) to differentiate from the established concept of Willingness to Communicate (WTC):

Her Iceberg Model distinguished visible participation (speech or silence) from the less-visible conditions shaping it: linguistic, cognitive, psychological, social-contextual, and wider external factors. These were not independent variables but interacting and mutually conditioning. The key structural move:

Revisiting this model in 2026, Shan sees it as already containing what she later calls Relational Dynamics: "not as overlapping semi-transparent circles, but as nested fields in motion. (system → field → field of fields)." The model was "grounded more deeply" rather than superseded. What was named "external factors" was not a residual category but "the edge of a larger problem": the constitutive role of relational conditions in shaping what appears as individual behaviour.

This is the first appearance in her work of the claim she will later generalise as "relation precedes dynamics": what appears as an individual communicative act (silence or speech) is already downstream of a relational field that shapes what is possible. The visible is always a "later formation." The key terms are already present: visibility/formation, surface/depth, coupling, nested fields.

The iceberg model and the foundational claim of Shan’s entire project. What appears in the seminar room — who speaks, when, how — is never the primary phenomenon. It is the crystallised surface of a formation field shaped before anyone entered the room. Bateson: the map is a phenomenon in the territory — the visible participation is the map, but the relational field is the territory. The practitioner who sees only the visible surface and intervenes at the level of participation norms is working on the Li without walking the Dao.

Shan's sustained engagement with Dao begins, by her account, with a poem — a very short poem that "travelled further than I had expected" — and then develops through a series of structural essays constituting what she calls the "Dao: The Art of the Long Game" series. The first theoretical claim, which anchors everything that follows, is that Dao is not primarily a philosophical concept but a living linguistic interface:

The concept of interface is philosophically precise. An interface is neither a mirror nor a window; it is an active structural relay that transforms what passes through it. A living interface is one that continues to do this work in the present tense, not as historical artefact but as functional structure. Shan's claim is that 道 (Dao) is exactly this: a character that, after 2,500 years of continuous use across philosophy, ordinary speech, ethics, governance, and embodied practice, still functions as a living relay between different registers of meaning and experience.

She demonstrates this through her personal word list, which maps how 道 appears across Chinese vocabulary:

道路 — dào lù — road, route, path — spatial Dao

知道 — zhī dào — to know — epistemic Dao

道歉 — dào qiàn — to apologise — moral Dao

道理 — dào lĭ — reason, underlying logic — the Dao–Li compound

道德 — dào dé — morality, virtue — ethical Dao

世道 — shì dào — the state of the world, way of the times — social Dao

味道 — wèi dào — taste, flavour, atmosphere — sensory Dao

说道 — shuō dào — to speak of, to mention — communicative Dao

道听途说 — dào tīng tú shuō — hearsay — things heard on the road and repeated

小道 — xiǎo dào — a small path; minor or unofficial route

大道 — dà dào — the great way, broad path, larger principle

康庄大道 — kāng zhuāng dà dào — a broad and flourishing road; a grand open way

悟道 — wù dào — to awaken to the Way

传道 — chuán dào — to transmit a teaching; to pass on a way of understanding

无间道 — wú jiān dào — infernal path / path without interval; also the film

大道之行，天下为公 — dà dào zhī xíng, tiān xià wéi gōng — When the Great Way prevails, all under Heaven is held in common

What this list demonstrates is not merely that Dao is polysemous. Polysemy is common. What it demonstrates is that Dao maintains structural coherence across all these registers: in each case, there is a "way" that has been made through movement, a pattern of passage that emerges through repetition, a logic that is followed rather than imposed. This functional coherence across registers is what makes Dao a living interface rather than a dead metaphor.

Shan notes that Dao has "travelled remarkably far while largely retaining its pinyin form," preserving "a certain continuity in how it moves across languages." This is contrasted with, for example, wéiqí (围棋), the board game known in Japanese as igo and in English as Go — a word that lost its Chinese form entirely as it crossed into English. Dao's relative retention of form across translation is itself evidence of its structural robustness as an interface.

Shan's most formally original contribution is her development of two interlocking Dao models through the act of drawing. The genesis is described with notable precision:

This description is philosophically significant: the structural insight arrives through the act of drawing, not through abstract reasoning. The body knows first. The image precedes the concept. This is itself a demonstration of Shan's claim that formation precedes articulation.

Model One: A Dao Already Formed

The first model begins with a path that is already visible as a way. This corresponds to the normal human experience of encountering systems after they have stabilised:

The poem that condensed this insight, which Shan reports "travelled far further than I had expected," has already circulated across multiple platforms:

The analytical precision here is in the last two lines: "We inherit one." The formed Dao does not merely exist as background context; it arrives with the force of the self-evident, as inherited coherence. Its long formation has already disappeared into legibility. This is what phenomenologists call "sedimentation" (Husserl, Merleau-Ponty) — the process by which prior acts of meaning-constitution become the taken-for-granted foundation of subsequent acts. Shan reaches this insight through systems thinking rather than phenomenology, but the structural convergence is striking.

Model Two: How a Path Comes into Being

The second model excavates what the first model conceals: the process of formation itself.

This is Shan's account of emergence: not the sudden appearance of novelty, but the gradual thickening of traces into patterns, patterns into routes, routes into ways. The river banks are constraint. The repeated movement is dynamics. The stable route is the formed Dao. And crucially: the route does not pre-exist the movement. The movement does not pre-exist the field (river banks, landscape). Constraint comes first; dynamics happen within constraint; formation accumulates over time.

Mutual Generation and the Reflexivity of Formation

The two models are not sequential (first formation, then formed) but mutually generative:

“The path of recognition is itself part of the pattern. The observer is not standing nowhere. The path by which something becomes visible is itself shaped within the field being observed.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

This reflexivity is analytically precise. Shan is not making a simple hermeneutic circle claim (we understand parts through wholes and wholes through parts). She is making a stronger ontological claim: the act of recognition is itself constitutive of the recognisable. The formed Dao becomes more fully formed — more legible, more inheritable, more useful as a way — precisely through being encountered and recognised as such. Formation does not stop when the path stabilises; it continues through the acts of traversal, inheritance, and recognition.

见道之路，亦在道中 — jiàn dào zhī lù, yì zài dào zhōng — The path of seeing the Dao is itself within the Dao

The article that most directly occasions this paper — "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" — is the conceptual centrepiece of Shan's published work to date, and the piece that most requires extended analytical treatment.

Shan introduces Li through its linguistic companionship with Dao in the compound 道理 (dàolĭ):

The translation of Li as "inner grain" is precise and important. "Grain" in English has a material meaning (the grain of wood or stone, the direction in which fibres run) and a textural meaning (the grain of a photograph, the granularity of a surface). Both are relevant. The grain of wood is not imposed from outside but emerges from the tree's own structure of growth — the pattern of rings, fibres, and growth directions that makes the wood workable in some directions and resistant in others. A woodcarver must follow the grain; working against it splits rather than shapes.

Li, for Shan, is this: the inner direction of workability in any system. It is not a rule imposed from outside but the structural texture that makes things "thinkable, workable, and manageable" from within.

理论 — lĭ lùn — theory — the patterned account of things; Li made explicit

理性 — lĭ xìng — rationality — the Li-nature of mind; reason as grain of thought

理科 — lĭ kē — science subjects — fields concerned with the Li of the world

整理 — zhěng lĭ — to organise — to bring into alignment with grain

治理 — zhì lĭ — to govern — to follow the Li of social order

管理 — guǎn lĭ — to manage — to oversee in accordance with pattern

纹理 — wén lĭ — texture — the visible grain of a surface

天理 — tiān lĭ — the pattern of heaven; natural order; cosmic grain

事理 — shì lĭ — the pattern of affairs; how things properly proceed

人理 — rén lĭ — the pattern of human relations; social grain

物理 — wù lĭ — the Li of material things; physics

内在逻辑 — nèi zài lúójí — internal logic — a modern phrase that carries the spirit of Li

Shan notes that across all these compounds, "what persists is not simply 'logic' in the narrow sense, but a concern with grain, pattern, intelligibility, and the ordering through which something becomes thinkable, workable, and manageable."

The philosophical weight of Shan's claim about Li rests on what she calls "ontological precedence." This is the conceptual move that requires the most analytical care:

What does "ontological precedence" mean here? Shan is not claiming that Dao is temporally prior to Li in a simple sequential sense — that would be too crude. She is claiming something more structurally precise: Li cannot be the condition of its own possibility. There must be something that makes Li possible — some prior formation, some path already being traversed — before the inner grain of that path can become recognisable as Li. Intelligibility requires something to be intelligible about; pattern requires something to be patterned; grain requires a material to be grained. The Dao — the path, the formation in progress — is the prior something.

“In complex systems, sequence is never merely a matter of order. It is often a matter of viability. A child plays in the mud. You tell them to wash their hands before eating. In surgery, anaesthesia comes before the first incision. A pilot checks the runway, instruments, and controls before take-off, not after the aircraft is already in the air. A checklist in a complex system is rarely just a list of items. The sequence is often doing the real work.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

And:

This last point is the most epistemologically consequential: the danger that Li — the intelligible pattern that makes the path recognisable — is mistaken for the generative source of the path itself. When this happens, explanation displaces formation, naming displaces understanding, and the map is mistaken for the territory. In Shan's language, this is "premature legibility": the closure of generative openness through the false assumption that because something has been named, it has been grasped.

The four-part sequence approaches the same structural recognition from four registers: Dao/Li (formation process/named pattern), path/pattern (traversal/map), grain/intelligibility (structural reality/conceptual grasp), exploration/explanation (genuine encounter/framework explanation). All four pairs are descriptions of the same ontological sequence. Each word in each pair is doing structural work. Together they constitute the most compressed possible statement of what the relational dynamics framework claims about the structure of formation.

Shan's treatment of coupling in complex systems is one of the most analytically precise contributions in her published work. She begins from the etymology of "complex":

牵一发而动全身 — qiān yī fà ér dòng quán shēn — Pull one hair and the whole body moves

But coupling, Shan insists, transforms without equalising. The dialectical precision of this claim is in its resistance to what she identifies as a common error in complexity discourse: the assumption that mutual interaction abolishes precedence. Her counter-example is marriage:

“That is why we do not describe such a relationship as an addition. We call them a couple. The word matters. A couple is not two separate units placed next to each other. It is a coupling: a relation within which each term is changed through sustained interaction with the other. And yet, even here, coupling does not abolish sequence. Mutual transformation is real, but it still depends on prior conditions: what was already in place, what shaped the opening of the relation, and what made later dynamics possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

The DNA example is analytically precise:

“DNA, too, belongs to one whole, yet its sequence remains structurally constitutive. Wholeness does not erase internal ordering. This matters even more in complex systems, where what we call "a system" is often nested within other systems and fields, all moving over time. A system may be tightly coupled and still asymmetrically generated. Coupling changes what can happen, but it does not necessarily change what had to be there first for any later happening to become possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

The holding capacity analysis is one of Shan's most original systemic contributions:

This principle — that holding capacity must precede what it holds — applies across domains: medicine (treatment sequencing), learning (ZPD and scaffolding), technology (operating systems before applications), and organisations (cultural infrastructure before strategic innovation). In each case, what is prior is not merely earlier in time but ontologically enabling: it is the structural condition that makes the next level of complexity viable rather than destabilising.

Harder to see: the coupling’s dominance in complex-systems discourse has produced a systematic blindness to the sequence. When everything is connected to everything else, the sequence seems to dissolve. Shan restores it: beneath the coupling, the sequence is always operating. The formation history is causally efficacious. Remove the sequence from the analysis and you have a map of the present without a trace of the Dao that produced it — and therefore without the capacity to understand why this specific present and not another.

Shan's most philosophically dense single essay is "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 16, 2026), which presents the ontological core of Relational Dynamics. It begins with the question provoked by the Dao/Li sequence argument:

“If coupling does not abolish sequence, then the next question is unavoidable: what, exactly, is prior within relational dynamics?”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

The answer is given as a formal ontological claim:

She identifies the most common conceptual error in complexity discourse:

Two vocabularies, one structural claim. The Chinese philosophical vocabulary and the Western complexity vocabulary are two different formation traditions that have independently arrived at the same structural recognition. The bilingual formation that makes this convergence visible is not incidental biography but the structural condition of Shan’s contribution. Only a practitioner formed simultaneously in both traditions can see what their specific convergence demonstrates.

Shan's analysis of structural failure is among her most original contributions and deserves sustained treatment. Her starting point is the game of Go (围棋, wéiqí):

Shan identifies "Elegant Wall-hitting" as the specific systemic condition of collapse-in-progress: the repeated collision between good-faith effort and an invisible structural limit. This is distinct from failure of competence or intention. Those inside the collapsing system are often acting rationally:

The distinction between surface function and underlying viability:

And the conclusion that brings failure analysis back to Dao:

Shan's analysis of AlphaGo's Move 37 is her most formally elegant structural essay and the place where her core concepts — position, pattern, emergence, long-game intelligence — come together in a single concrete case.

When AlphaGo played Move 37 in Game 2 of the 2016 match against Lee Sedol, DeepMind described it as having roughly a 1-in-10,000 probability of being played by a human and as having "upended centuries of traditional wisdom." Shan disagrees with this description:

The language analysis embedded in this essay is characteristically precise. Shan notes the transmission path of the word itself: 围棋 (wéiqí, Chinese) → 囲碁 (igo, Japanese) → "Go" (English) → AlphaGo → 阿尔法狗 (alpha dog, back in Chinese). This is not a digression but an illustration: what began as a 2,500-year-old Chinese game strategy concept travelled through three languages, was compressed into one syllable, fused with an AI brand name, and returned to Chinese as a literal dog. The structural insight about transmission failure is instantiated in the very name of the system whose move 37 exemplifies transmission success.

The cross-cultural journey of a game: this passage is Shan at her most distinctively bilingual and structurally precise simultaneously. The game that was 围棋 — surrounding, territory, positional field-shaping — became Go in English, losing its spatial ontology. Then AlphaGo: English fused with Chinese name, returning to China as the name of a dog. The Li of the game — its specific formation intelligence about position, territory, and the long game — survived its linguistic journey. The Li of the name was lost and transformed at every border crossing. This is the structure of all cross-cultural formation.

Shan's shortest structural essay — "Path, Pattern, Position" — articulates what has become the governing triad of her framework in compressed, almost aphoristic form:

The sequence Dao → Li → Position → Possibility names the causal-generative chain of her framework. Formation (Dao) accumulates into pattern (Li); pattern consolidates into positional advantage; positional advantage shapes what future dynamics become possible. This is the strategic logic of the long game: not local optimisation at each step, but the building of a field within which later optimisation becomes easier, more efficient, or structurally inevitable.

From a relational dynamics perspective, this means: long-run excellence depends not only on action but on whether the position being built can actually hold. This is the tensegrity insight expressed in strategic terms: a position holds not through the strength of any single move but through the distribution of structural advantage across the whole field.

Shan's recurring working frame deserves formal philosophical analysis, not just quotation:

This is a structurally complex definition containing five analytically distinct terms:

Excellence: not maximum output or maximal performance, but structural integrity under realistic conditions. It is quality in the sense of held coherence, not achievement in the sense of peak output.

Capacity: the structural potential to act, receive, process, or respond. Capacity is not fixed; it is built through formation and can be depleted through overextension, or degraded through the thinning of corrective capacity.

Held: the active, ongoing work of maintenance. This is not achieved once and possessed; it must be actively sustained. It points to the role of relation: what holds capacity in coherence is the continuous tensional network of relational connection.

Coherence: internal relational order, the condition in which the parts of a system are structured such that they support rather than undermine each other. Coherence is the Li of the system: its inner grain, its workability.

Constraint over time: the temporal and environmental pressures that test and shape the system. Constraint is not the enemy of excellence but its condition: without constraint, there is no test of coherence, and therefore no excellence in the structural sense.

Taken together, the frame is a dynamic structural definition: excellence is not a state but a trajectory. It is the ongoing project of maintaining relational coherence under the pressure of constraint across time. This is why it is a long game.

Additional Analyses: Interlocutors — Second Pass

Each voice below is presented in sufficient depth to function as a genuine intellectual challenger, not a walk-on character. The analytical question for each: where does this thinker’s framework converge with, extend, challenge, or expose the limits of Shan’s?

The Dao De Jing opens with the most famous problem-statement in Chinese philosophy, and perhaps the most analytically precise statement of what Shan calls the paradox of Li:

道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng. — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.

为学日益，为道日损，损之又损，以至于无为。 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi dào rì sǔn — In pursuit of learning, something is acquired every day; in pursuit of the Dao, something is relinquished every day. — Dao De Jing Ch. 48

知常容，容乃公，公乃王，王乃天，天乃道，道乃久。 — zhī cháng róng, róng nǎi gōng — Knowing the enduring is receptiveness; receptiveness is impartial; impartial is kingly; kingly is heavenly; heavenly is the Dao; the Dao is lasting. — Ch. 16

为学日益，为道日损 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi dào rì sǔn — Learning adds daily; the Dao subtracts daily — pointing to the paradox that articulation (Li-production) and Dao-following work in opposite directions.

Most relevantly for Shan’s framework, Laozi articulates the water metaphor that underpins her second Dao model (how a path forms through constraint and repetition):

天下莫柔弱于水，而攻坏强者无以易之。 — Tiān xià mò róu ruò yú shuĭ, ér gōng jiān qiáng zhě mò yǐshèng zhī. — Nothing under heaven is softer and more yielding than water; yet nothing is better at overcoming what is hard and strong. — Ch. 78

The river banks in Shan’s second Dao model are the structural constraints within which movement (water) accumulates into formation (the way across). Water’s "yielding" is not weakness but what Shan calls "working with the grain": the Dymaxion approach, maximum effect from minimum force, following rather than imposing.

Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding passage (Chapter 3) is the single most powerful illustration in Chinese literature of Li as embodied working intelligence — the grain followed by the practitioner who has moved beyond technique into direct contact with the structural reality of the thing itself.

臣之所好者道也，进乎技矣。 — chén zhī suǒ hào zhě dào yě, jìn hū jì yǐ. — What your servant cares about is the Dao, which goes beyond skill.

方今之时，臣以神遇，而不以目视，官知止而神欲行。 — fāng jīn zhī shí, chén yǐ shén yù, ér bù yǐ mù shì. — Now I work with my spirit and not with my eye. My mind works along without the control of the senses.

依乎天理，批大郤，导大稾，因其固然。 — yī hū tiān lĭ, pī dà xiì, dǎo dà kuǎn, yīn qí gù rán. — I go along with the natural makeup (天理 tiānlĭ, heaven's Li), strike in the big hollows, guide the knife through the big openings, and follow things as they are.

The phrase 依乎天理 (yī hū tiān lĭ) is pivotal: Cook Ding follows the 天理 (heavenly Li, natural grain) of the ox. The knife does not cut against the grain but finds and follows the natural articulations. This is the embodied equivalent of Shan’s second Dao model: the practitioner who has learned the forming field well enough to move within it without resistance. Cook Ding’s knife never dulls because it never cuts where it does not belong.

The temporal dimension: "When I first began cutting up oxen, all I could see was the ox itself. After three years I no longer saw the whole ox." This is the movement from formed Dao (the ox as a unified object) to the generative ground of formation (the articulations, hollows, and natural pathways within). This is precisely Shan’s movement from Model One to Model Two: from the path already visible to the field within which the path forms.

Zhuangzi’s challenge to Shan: the Cook Ding passage suggests that the highest form of following Li is not intellectual or theoretical but somatic — a matter of training the body to move without the interference of conceptual knowledge. "Perception and understanding have come to a stop and spirit moves where it wants." This challenges Shan’s project of articulating Li theoretically: is there a risk that the very attempt to make Li legible (to produce a Li for Li, so to speak) reproduces the error of premature legibility at a higher level?

Zhu Xi is the philosopher who gave Li its most fully developed systematic account in Chinese intellectual history. His synthesis of Li and Qi (气, vital force/material energy) constitutes the philosophical framework within which WSR, and indirectly Shan’s work, operates.

For Zhu Xi, Li is the patterned principle immanent in all things — a claim of ontological and generative precedence in the inverse direction: Li is prior to Dao in the order of being, and Li is the generative source that the Dao expresses rather than its product. Shan’s counter: Zhu Xi has mistaken retrospective intelligibility for ontological priority. The Li of a well-formed thing looks eternal precisely because the Dao that produced it has been concealed by its own success:

理一分殊 — lĭ yī fēn shū — Principle is one; its manifestations are many

This is the Neo-Confucian version of what Bateson calls "the pattern that connects": a single Li that manifests differently across all things without being multiple in itself. The Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy formulates Zhu Xi’s contribution: "Li [is] the patterned regularity of existence... These abstract distinctions had moral significance."

Zhu Xi’s method of gewu (格物, investigation of things) is particularly relevant:

格物致知 — géwù zhīzhī — Investigation of things to extend knowledge — the epistemological method for uncovering Li

For Zhu Xi, the extension of knowledge (zhizhi) is "a gradual process of investigating the principles of one thing after another until a great breakthrough takes place and the perfection of knowledge is attained." This is structurally analogous to Shan’s first Dao model moving into the second: we begin with the formed path (the thing as we encounter it) and gradually, through sustained attention, come to see the process of formation (its Li).

Zhu Xi’s challenge to Shan comes from the direction of his Li-Qi dualism. For Zhu Xi, Li has a kind of normative priority: it is the principle that things ought to manifest, against which actual manifestations (always partly shaped by the turbidity of Qi) can be more or less adequate. Shan’s account of Li is more radically immanent: Li is not a normative standard against which formation is assessed but the actual grain of a particular path's formation. There is no transcendent Li against which actual Dao–formations can be judged; there are only more or less legible grains of particular paths.

The Cheng brothers are the immediate philosophical predecessors of Zhu Xi and the thinkers who first gave Li its central philosophical role in Neo-Confucian thought. Cheng Yi’s formulation is the most directly relevant to Shan:

道即理也 — dào jí lĭ yě — Dao is Li: the way and the grain are the same thing

This formulation is the precise opposite of Shan’s claim. For Cheng Yi, Dao and Li are identical: the way through which things proceed IS the principle that governs their proceeding. There is no temporal or ontological gap between them. For Shan, they are coupled but not identical, and Dao has precedence. The collision between Cheng Yi’s identity claim and Shan’s precedence claim is one of the deepest philosophical tensions in this paper.

Cheng Hao’s formulation introduces the relational dimension:

“The person of humanity regards heaven, earth, and all things as one body. There is nothing that is not oneself. Recognizing this as the self, what is there that cannot be reached? If it does not belong to oneself, naturally there will be no point of contact between oneself and the thing.”

— Cheng Hao, "Knowing What is Benevolent"

The "point of contact" in Cheng Hao’s formulation is precisely Shan’s interface: the place where thing and self become available to each other. Li, on this account, is what makes contact possible — the shared grain of the cosmos that allows different beings to touch and know one another.

Wang Yangming challenged Zhu Xi’s method of gewu after his famous failed attempt to "investigate the Li" of bamboo through sustained external observation. The attempt produced illness but no insight. His conclusion: Li cannot be found by investigating things from outside. It must be discovered through the moral mind-heart (xin, 心) from within.

知行合一 — zhī xíng hé yī — The unity of knowledge and action

For Wang Yangming, knowing Li and acting according to Li are not two separate steps but one unified process. You have not truly known Li if you have not acted according to it. This is a performative account of knowledge that resonates with Shan’s claim that "the body knows first" and that formation precedes articulation.

Wang Yangming’s challenge to Shan: if knowledge and action are unified, then the Dao/Li distinction partially collapses. The path and its grain are not sequential but simultaneous: you discover the grain of a path by walking it, and you walk it by following its grain. This is the Cook Ding insight elevated to an epistemological principle. Wang Yangming’s "investigation of things" happens in action, not in observation.

But Shan’s response is available: even if knowledge and action are unified in the moment of genuine practice, this does not collapse the ontological precedence of Dao over Li. The formation still precedes the intelligibility of the formation, even if they are experienced as simultaneous in skilled practice.

The WSR methodology has a specific historical genealogy that the Cynefin Co discussion surfaced. In 1978, Qian Xuesen and Xu Guozhi (pioneer of Systems Engineering and Operations Research in China) promoted research on shili (事理, ways of engaging the world). Li Yaozi, an American-Chinese scientist, subsequently proposed attention to renli (人理, human motivations). Then, in 1988, Gu Jifa brought the wuli (物理), shili (事理), and renli (人理) concepts together into training programs for official-managers. The formal WSR as a systems methodology emerged from the Beijing-Ishikawa-Hull cooperation in the 1990s with Zhichang Zhu.

What this genealogy reveals: WSR is not a single intellectual act but itself a path of formation. The three Li-compounds were arrived at sequentially, through the pressure of real historical failure (Mao-era management disasters) and through sustained international encounter. WSR is, in Shan’s terms, a formed Dao: a path that hardened through repeated traversal across multiple institutional and cultural contexts. Its Li is now legible — but its formation history matters for understanding why it takes the specific shape it does.

Gu Jifa’s methodological contribution: WSR is described not as a theory but as "an approach" — a way of proceeding through complex situations rather than a framework for describing them. This approach-nature of WSR resonates with Shan’s claim that Dao is not a doctrine but a living encounter: both resist the reduction of method to theorem.

Zhu’s philosophical development of WSR is the most sustained attempt to ground systems methodology in the Neo-Confucian philosophical tradition of Li. His central claim:

“Based on the reconstruction of the Neo-Confucianist concept of Li and relevant teachings, and drawing on experiences in the Oriental context, we have consolidated a systems methodology so to improve and popularise systems research and practice.”

— Zhichang Zhu, "Dealing with Wuli Shili Renli" (ISSS Primer)

Zhu invokes Zhu Xi directly in one of the most analytically significant passages in WSR literature: "the Song scholar Zhu Xi (1130–1200) instructed, ‘the li of shishi and wuwu have no practical significance.’" This means: the Li of affairs and the Li of things are practically empty until they are attended to concretely. You cannot know Li in the abstract; you must investigate it in the specific. This is Shan’s "lived reality before articulation" expressed in the language of Neo-Confucian epistemology.

The three-verb asymmetry of WSR is philosophically crucial: knowing (knowing wuli), sensing (sensing shili), caring for (caring for renli). The epistemological registers differ: wuli can be known propositionally; shili must be sensed through perspectival engagement; renli cannot be merely known or even sensed — it must be cared for ethically. This asymmetry implies that human-relational Li cannot be reached through the cognitive methods adequate for material Li. This challenges any reductionist or cognitivist account of complex systems.

Zhu’s challenge to Shan: WSR is a methodology — it begins from the assumption of a "systems project" and provides a structured approach to uncovering the three dimensions of Li within that project. Shan’s framework asks the antecedent question: what made the systems project possible in the first place? This is her Dao-before-Li argument applied to methodology itself: the methodological structure (WSR’s process) is downstream of the formation (the relational field that made the methodology necessary and possible). WSR assumes the Dao; Shan investigates it.

Qian’s intellectual legacy is divided: in the West he is known as the rocket scientist who contributed to the Manhattan Project; in China he is the father of the space and missile programme and a foundational figure in systems science. His critique of reductionism:

Qian’s "open complex giant systems" (OCGS, 开放的复杂巨系统, kāifàng de fùzá jù xìtǒng) are systems in which:

(1) The system has open boundaries (it interacts with its environment); (2) its components are themselves complex systems (hierarchy); (3) it involves human beings and is therefore irreducibly value-laden; (4) it cannot be adequately modelled by any single scientific method. The appropriate method is metasynthesis (zonghe jicheng, 综合集成): the integration of quantitative methods, qualitative expert knowledge, and empirical experience in structured dialogue.

The relevance to Shan: Qian’s metasynthesis explicitly resists the premature closure of complex systems into formal models. The practitioner of metasynthesis must hold the quantitative and qualitative in productive tension — must maintain the "forming" alongside the "formed." This is Shan’s mutual generation expressed in methodological terms: the model and the system it models must remain in living contact.

In 1980, Jin Guantao and Liu Qingfeng published "Traditional Society in China: An Ultrastable Structure," applying cybernetics and systems theory to Chinese historical analysis. Their central concept: 超稳定结构 (chāowending jiégòu, ultrastable structure).

Their analysis: the peasant economy, bureaucratic polity, and Confucian ideology were integrated into a tripartite self-correcting system. When any one of the three deviated from normal function, the other two combined to restore it. This produced remarkable surface stability across two thousand years of dynastic succession — but also deep structural rigidity that precluded genuine transformation.

The convergence with Shan: Jin and Liu’s ultrastable system is, in Shan’s terms, the extreme case of a system in which corrective capacity has become the enemy of adaptive capacity. The self-correction that maintains surface coherence also narrows the path of genuine structural change. The ultrastable system is one in which "endurance is not viability" — where surface function persists while underlying adaptive capacity is systematically depleted. The collapse of dynasties in Chinese history is, from this perspective, the delayed visibility of a process that had been structurally determined for generations.

Jin and Liu’s challenge to Shan: they show that ultrastability is not simply a failure of intelligence or vision but a structural property of tightly coupled self-correcting systems. Individuals within such a system cannot see the narrowing path not because they are unintelligent but because the system’s own corrective mechanisms suppress the signals that would make the narrowing visible. This is systemic Elegant Wall-hitting at civilisational scale.

Zhang Dainian’s systematic analysis of the key categories of Chinese philosophy (Key Concepts in Chinese Philosophy, 1989/2002) provides the most comprehensive scholarly account of how Li functions across the Chinese philosophical tradition. His analysis confirms and deepens Shan’s intuition that Li is not a single philosophical term but a structural operator that appears across multiple registers:

Zhang identifies three primary meanings of Li in classical Chinese: (1) Li as the natural veins or grain of jade or wood; (2) Li as the order or pattern of natural phenomena; (3) Li as the principle or norm of human conduct. All three meanings are present in Shan’s account, and their convergence in a single character is precisely what makes Li structurally powerful as an interface.

Fuller’s structural philosophy is the most directly applicable Western framework to Shan’s working frame. His central claim about tensegrity:

The structural principle: in tensegrity, compression members (struts) are discontinuous — they do not touch each other — while tension members (cables, wires) form a continuous network. The integrity of the whole resides in the continuous tensional embrace, not in any single compressive element. When you push on a tensegrity structure, the force distributes through the entire tensional network; there is no local collapse because the whole absorbs and redistributes the stress.

Four words. The most compressed structural claim in this text. Tension — not compression, not rigidity — is the great integrity. The formation that maintains its integrity is the formation whose relational tension network remains continuous. Collapse begins when the network loses its continuity. Fuller’s physics and Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim converge here: the specific topology of the tensional network IS the specific Li of the formation.

Pattern integrity: not substance with properties but specific configuration of relational force. The individual is a specific pattern of biological, psychological, cultural, and linguistic formations that maintains its specific topology through the ongoing operation of its relational networks. Shan’s self-collective is precisely this: a pattern integrity whose coherence is maintained through the distribution of relational tension across all its constituent formations.

The Dymaxion principle (Dynamic Maximum Tension): Fuller designed his geodesic domes, teardrop cars, and hexagonal houses on the principle of achieving maximum structural benefit from minimum material input. The word "Dymaxion" itself is the portmanteau of "dynamic maximum tension." His commentator:

“"DYMAXION, which is a compound of dynamic maximum tension... in Fuller’s universe... described a much less traumatic concept: maximum benefit derived from minimal input of energy."”

— John Hodgman, "Dynamic Maximum Tension," Secret Society (2024)

Fuller on synergetics and ecology:

Kenneth Snelson, who developed the physical structures that Fuller named tensegrity, provides a structural artist’s account: "The discovery of the tensegrity structure was a matter of finding a new principle of structure... it is a structure where the entire system is in tension while the compression members float free, each one isolated within a prestressed network of tension members." Fuller’s insight was to recognise this as not merely an architectural novelty but the operating principle of the universe.

Wittgenstein’s thought underwent three distinct phases, each of which illuminates a different dimension of Shan’s framework.

The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921): Logic, Limit, Silence

“"Es ist klar, dass sich die Ethik nicht aussprechen lässt. It is clear that ethics cannot be put into words."”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.421

The ladder must be thrown away:

Philosophy as activity: each of Shan’s essays is an activity — the specific traversal of specific intellectual territory that produces the clarification available from that specific Dao. The essays are Dao-walks. Their value is not their propositional content but their specific formation of the reader who walks them.

The Philosophical Investigations (1953): Language-Games and Forms of Life

Wittgenstein abandons the Tractatus picture theory and enters language from within its living practices. The meaning of a word is its use:

“"For a large class of cases — though not for all — in which we employ the word ‘meaning’ it can be defined thus: the meaning of a word is its use in the language."”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §43

Language games are embedded in forms of life:

Meaning requires agreement in form of life, not agreement in opinion:

Philosophy aims to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle:

“"If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: ‘This is simply what I do.’"”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §217

Bring words back from metaphysics to everyday use:

“"A philosophical problem has the form: ‘I don’t know my way about.’"”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §123

Family resemblance: concepts do not share a common essence but overlap in a network of similarities, like different games all called "games" without any single feature common to all.

On Certainty (1951): The River Bed and Hinge Propositions

Wittgenstein’s final work is his most directly relevant to Shan’s account of how formation precedes articulation. His central metaphor:

“"The propositions describing this world-picture might be part of a kind of mythology. And their role is like that of rules of a game; and the game can be learned purely practically, without learning any explicit rules."”

The mythology claim in On Certainty: the hardened propositions that constitute the world-picture are not truths held for good reasons but the mythological structure that makes any reason-giving possible. For Shan, every formation tradition has its mythology: the inherited background of taken-for-granted assumptions about what counts as contribution, what counts as intelligence, what counts as the right relationship between Dao and Li. The mythology cannot be argued against; it can only be walked away from, through the specific Dao-traversal that produces a new world-picture.

The relevance to Shan: On Certainty’s "river bed" is precisely Shan’s first Dao model: the hardened, inherited propositions that function as the stable channel within which fluid empirical inquiry can flow. The hardened propositions are not themselves subject to normal epistemic scrutiny; they are the background against which scrutiny becomes possible. They are the formed Dao, the inherited coherence, the Li that has solidified into taken-for-granted reality. And crucially: Wittgenstein notes that the bed can shift — hard propositions can become fluid, and fluid ones can harden. This is the temporal, dynamic version of Shan’s mutual generation.

Prigogine’s work on non-equilibrium thermodynamics establishes the physical basis for irreversibility — the claim that time has a direction in complex systems, that formation is not reversible, and that order arises precisely from the dissipation of entropy in far-from-equilibrium conditions.

“"Only when a system behaves in a sufficiently random way may the difference between past and future, and therefore irreversibility, enter its description. The arrow of time is the manifestation of the fact that the future is not given, that, as the French poet Paul Valéry emphasized, ‘time is a construction’."”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

— Ilya Prigogine

Openness as the main character: continuous exchange with the formation field that sustains the living system’s far-from-equilibrium organisation. A closed formation — one that confirms only what its existing Li predicts — has ceased to be genuinely living in Prigogine’s sense. It is drifting toward equilibrium. Toward structural death.

One realisation of the possible: the actual Li is one specific crystallisation from the field of all possible Lis. Move 37 was one realisation of the possible. The practitioners who could not see it were accessing a different set of realisable possibles. AlphaGo’s different formation produced a different adjacent possible.

The relevance to Shan: Prigogine’s "arrow of time" provides the physical grounding for her ontological precedence argument. The reason formation precedes formed coherence is not a logical preference but a physical fact about how order forms in time. Dissipative structures — from convection cells to living organisms — do not exist outside time; they exist through time, maintained by the continuous dissipation of energy through them. The structure is the history of the dissipation. You cannot have the structure without the history; you cannot have the Li without the Dao.

Prigogine also challenges Shan: his account of order-through-fluctuations suggests that the path of formation is not smooth gradual accumulation (traces thickening into patterns) but discontinuous, involving bifurcation points where the system’s future trajectory is genuinely underdetermined. At a bifurcation, a small fluctuation can drive the system into one of several possible stable states. This suggests that Shan’s second Dao model — where the boat crossing the river eventually creates a stable route — may underestimate the role of contingency and fluctuation in actual path formation.

“"Much of the order found in nature is spontaneously present... Evolution is not just ‘chance caught on the wing.’ It is not just a tinkering of the ad hoc, of bricolage, of contraption. It is emergent order honored and honed by natural selection."”

Order for free: the universe has a spontaneous tendency toward the production of order. The formation field has a spontaneous tendency toward the production of Li. The Dao does not need to be forced; it tends toward pattern. The practitioner who walks with the grain of the formation is working with the order-for-free tendency of the field.

“"The past three centuries of science have been predominantly reductionist... The deep difficulty here lies in the fact that the complex whole may exhibit properties that are not readily explained by understanding the parts. The complex whole, in a completely nonmystical sense, can often exhibit collective properties, ‘emergent’ features that are lawful in their own right."”

The reductionist tradition has produced genuine knowledge about ordered domains. But the knowledge comes at a cost: it systematically misrepresents the complex domain by treating it as though it were ordered. The boundary between the ordered and the complex regimes of the Ashby Space is the boundary between where reductionism works and where it fails. Shan’s work is positioned in the complex domain: the domain where Dao must precede Li, where the formation must be encountered before it can be mapped.

Kauffman’s adjacent possible: from any given state of a complex system, only certain next states are accessible — the system’s future is constrained by its present configuration. As the system evolves, new adjacent possibles open up that were not previously available. This is Shan’s positional analysis at the evolutionary level: position shapes possibility, and the field of the possible expands and contracts as the system moves.

Kauffman’s "order for free": complex systems spontaneously generate order without external instruction, as a consequence of their own internal structure. This challenges Shan’s implicit assumption that formation requires repeated movement under constraint: some order is "free" in Kauffman’s sense, emerging without traversal. However, even "free" order still requires a field: the system must be in the right parameter range for self-organisation to occur. The constraint (the field within which emergence is possible) is prior, even in spontaneous emergence.

Holland’s account of emergence is the most formally precise in complexity science: emergence arises when a small number of rules (or laws) generates systems of surprising complexity. His key mechanism: building blocks. Complex adaptive systems accumulate experience through building blocks — tested sub-assemblies that recombine in new configurations to produce novel emergent properties.

"We gain experience through repeated use of the building blocks, even though they may never twice appear in exactly the same combination." This is Shan’s account of path formation compressed into evolutionary language: repeated traversal of paths (the building blocks of experience) accumulates structural intelligence that enables new configurations without requiring each new configuration to be built from scratch.

Holland’s concept of "tags" is also relevant: tags enable selective interaction among agents, allowing the formation of aggregates without central coordination. Tags function as what Shan would call "Li at the micro level" — the pattern in each agent that makes it recognisable by others, enabling the coupling that produces emergence.

Holland’s challenge to Shan: his formal account of emergence is mathematical and rule-based. The building blocks, rules, and generating constraints of a complex adaptive system can in principle be specified. This challenges Shan’s more holistic and phenomenological account of Li: is the grain of a system ultimately reducible to a finite set of building blocks and rules, or does it genuinely exceed any such formal specification?

Managing emergence: the practitioner does not specify the Li in advance and then implement it; they cultivate the formation conditions within which beneficial coherence can emerge. Small probes: not large interventions premised on prior knowledge of the Li, but minimal perturbations that allow the formation field to reveal its own grain. Walk the Dao before naming the Li.

“"An ordered system is like the external skeleton of an insect — it has a rigid shell that is not going to change but within it things may change. An endoskeleton is like our spine — it gives coherence but doesn’t contain completely, so you get huge amounts of variation around it. How do you create enabling constraints that effectively allow locally valid solutions to emerge within the governance framework?"”

— David Snowden, "How Leaders Change Culture Through Small Actions"

Snowden’s Cynefin framework distinguishes five domains (Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, Confused) based on the relationship between cause and effect and the appropriate type of constraint. In the Complex domain, enabling constraints replace governing constraints: rather than specifying outcomes, enabling constraints create the conditions within which good outcomes can emerge.

This is structurally isomorphic with Shan’s account of relational dynamics: relation (the enabling constraint field) precedes dynamics (what emerges within it). The difference is that Cynefin is primarily a decision-making framework — it tells practitioners how to act in different domains. Shan’s framework is ontological — it describes the structure of reality as relational-dynamic. They complement rather than compete.

Snowden on Shan’s specific contribution: as the Cynefin Co platform hosting Shan’s Li article, Snowden is an implicit interlocutor. His own blog post referenced by Shan — "The Way Is Not a Map" — is the direct intellectual occasion for her Dao models of mutual generation, where she notes: "A point in the trajectory: David Snowden, The Way Is Not a Map." This establishes a living dialogue within the Cynefin intellectual community.

“"Living systems are cognitive systems, and living as a process is a process of cognition. This statement is valid for all organisms, with and without a nervous system."”

— Maturana and Varela, Autopoiesis and Cognition (1980)

Autopoiesis: living systems continuously produce the components that produce them. The formed state is the condition for ongoing formation. This is Shan’s mutual generation at the biological level: what is formed is still in formation, because the formed state is the condition for the ongoing forming process.

Structural coupling: organism and environment shape each other through repeated interaction, without direct causation. The organism does not passively register environmental inputs but actively maintains its own organisation through selective coupling with environmental perturbations. This is Shan’s relational dynamics at the biological level: the relational field (structural coupling history) precedes and shapes what any given dynamic (environmental perturbation) can produce.

Bateson’s metapattern question is the question Shan’s framework answers from the inside. The pattern that connects is Li at the most general level. But the metapattern is discovered through the patient watching of formation diversity that allows the underlying structural commonality to reveal itself. Bateson walked the Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient attention to biological diversity. The Li of the metapattern appeared as the grain of that specific Dao.

Bateson’s "pattern that connects" is the most evocative precedent in Western thought for Shan’s Li. Both are attempts to name the meta-pattern — the structural regularity that manifests differently across different systems without being reducible to any single manifestation. Both resist the reduction of the pattern to a formal rule or propositional statement. Both insist on the relational nature of the pattern: it exists between things, not in them individually.

Morin’s "dialogic principle" holds that complex reality must be thought through the holding of antagonistic principles in productive tension rather than their collapse into synthesis. Order and disorder, unity and diversity, subject and object, the one and the many — these must be held together without resolution. This is structurally analogous to Shan’s mutual generation: the formed and the forming, Dao and Li, are not resolved into synthesis but maintained in ongoing productive tension.

Luhmann’s systems theory is the most formally rigorous account of social complexity in the Western tradition. His central insight: modern society consists of functionally differentiated autopoietic subsystems (economy, law, science, education, etc.) that each operate according to their own binary code and cannot be directly steered from outside. Communication is the basic element of social systems, not action. This challenges Shan’s account of relation as primary: for Luhmann, it is not relation per se but communication (the processing of information through binary codes) that is the generating operation of social systems.

Luhmann’s challenge to Shan: her concept of "relation" is underspecified. What kind of relation? Communication? Structural coupling? Power? Trust? Different theoretical traditions give different answers, and the choice of answer has major consequences for the analysis of social complexity.

“"The world is a complex, interconnected, finite, ecological–social–psychological–economic system. We treat it as if it were not, as if it were divisible, separable, simple, and infinite. Our persistent, intractable, global problems arise directly from this mismatch."”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)

Meadows’ leverage points — places in a system where a small shift can produce large changes — are placed in a hierarchy. At the highest level of leverage: the goals and paradigms of the system. This resonates with Shan’s positional analysis: the highest leverage in a complex system is not intervention in individual dynamics but reshaping of the relational field (the goal, paradigm, or structural position) within which all dynamics occur. Move 37 is a leverage-point move: it shifts the paradigm of the game rather than optimising within the existing paradigm.

Bergson’s concept of durée (duration) is one of the most important precedents for Shan’s temporal ontology. For Bergson, time is not a sequence of discrete instants (as in spatial or mathematical time) but a continuous flow in which past and present are mutually interpenetrating. Memory is not the retrieval of stored information but the living presence of the past in the present.

This is the temporal structure of Shan’s Dao: the formed path carries the history of its formation within it. The path does not merely reference its past; it is constituted by it. The river banks and the history of boats crossing are still present in the route that has formed, even if that formation is no longer visible as such. Bergson’s durée is the temporal medium within which Shan’s mutual generation occurs.

“"Life is not a mechanism, but a creative evolution."”

Bergson’s élan vital as the formation’s own creative force: the specific energy that the Dao generates as it walks, the formation pressure that makes new Li available by actively resisting the tendency toward equilibrium. The practitioner who aligns with the élan vital — who walks with the formation’s own creative force rather than against it — is the practitioner who produces the most formation with the least imposition.

“"Process is fundamental."”

Three words. If process is fundamental, then the formation is prior to the formed. The Dao is prior to the Li. The actual occasion is the primary unit of reality; the formed Li is the record of that process. Whitehead’s process ontology and Shan’s relational dynamics share the same ontological structure: both refuse the primacy of static substance, both insist on the primacy of the formation process.

“"The notion of ‘substance’ is transformed into the notion of ‘actual entity’."”

— Whitehead, Process and Reality

Whitehead’s process philosophy holds that "actual entities" (the ultimate constituents of reality) are not static substances but processes of becoming. Each actual entity perishes as it achieves definiteness (formation) and becomes data for subsequent becomings. This is the metaphysical version of Shan’s mutual generation: each formed Dao becomes the data within which the next formation occurs.

Whitehead’s "eternal objects" (potential forms that can be realised in actual entities) are analogous to Shan’s Li: they are the structural patterns that can be instantiated in particular formations, but only when the right actual occasions (path formations) provide the ground for their ingression.

Kuhn’s paradigm shifts and Lakatos’s research programmes both illuminate the macro-structure of formation in scientific knowledge. For Kuhn, a paradigm is precisely a formed Dao: a set of inherited assumptions, exemplary solutions, and instrumental practices that constitute the background within which normal science proceeds. The paradigm functions as Wittgenstein’s riverbed: it is what makes inquiry possible by providing the stable channel within which fluid empirical investigation can flow.

The paradigm shift is the moment when the riverbed shifts: when the accumulated anomalies of normal science force a structural reorganisation of the background assumptions themselves. This is Shan’s account of collapse at the epistemic level: "Nothing collapses in one anomaly. The path narrows first." The crisis of a paradigm is preceded by the invisible accumulation of anomalies that cannot be absorbed without threatening the structural integrity of the whole.

Lakatos’s "hard core" of a research programme (the foundational assumptions protected from falsification by a "protective belt" of auxiliary hypotheses) is structurally analogous to Wittgenstein’s hinge propositions and Shan’s formed Dao: the hardened propositions that must remain stable for the fluid inquiry to proceed.

“"Systems thinking is the discipline for seeing wholes. It is a framework for seeing interrelationships rather than things, for seeing patterns of change rather than static ‘snapshots’."”

— Fritjof Capra, The Web of Life (1996)

Capra explicitly connects Western systems thinking to Eastern philosophical traditions, arguing that the network view of life that complexity science has arrived at was already present in Daoist, Buddhist, and Hindu traditions. His account positions Shan at the intersection of these traditions: a thinker who has grown up inside the Chinese language that carries these traditions and is now engaged with the Western complexity discourse that has partially rediscovered them.

Additional Analyses: Collisions — Second Pass

Each collision below is presented with analytical rigour: the deepest convergence, the strongest challenge in each direction, and what the collision produces that neither tradition could reach alone. These are not "comparisons" but genuine dialectical encounters: each tradition is permitted to genuinely challenge the others.

The Convergence: Tension as the Condition of Integrity

The most structurally intimate dialogue in this paper is between Fuller’s tensegrity and Shan’s relational dynamics. Both are accounts of how integrity is maintained under constraint. Both resist the assumption that stability requires a dominant compressive core or a central authority. Both locate structural integrity not in any single element but in the distribution of relation through the whole.

Fuller’s claim that "tension is the great integrity" translates directly into Shan’s framework: excellence is held not by avoiding constraint but by distributing it. In tensegrity, the compressive elements are local, discontinuous islands; the tensional network is continuous, omnidirectional, coherent.
