In Shan’s framework, the relational field is continuous; particular dynamics are local. Both frameworks resist reductionism: you cannot understand the whole by analysing the parts, because the integrity of the whole resides in the distribution of relation, not in any individual element.

The Dymaxion principle maps precisely onto Shan’s working frame: maximum benefit from minimum input — maximum capacity from minimum material — is exactly what "excellence as capacity held in coherence" means in structural engineering terms. AlphaGo’s Move 37 is a Dymaxion move: it achieves maximum positional advantage from minimum local investment, redistributing force through the entire field rather than concentrating it at a single point of attack.

Fuller’s account of "pattern integrity" as "evolutionary and not static" maps onto Shan’s mutual generation: a pattern integrity (like a human individual) is always in the process of formation, even while it presents as a stable structure.

Where Shan Challenges Fuller

Fuller’s tensegrity is primarily spatial and synchronic: it describes the distribution of forces within an already-existing structure at a moment in time. Shan’s framework is temporal and diachronic: it asks how the structural integrity forms over time, how it degrades invisibly, and how its trajectory can be read before collapse becomes visible. Shan adds to Fuller’s architecture the dimension of formation history.

More critically: Fuller’s universe is continuous tensional integrity — everything is connected through tension, all the way from atoms to solar systems. Shan’s universe is not uniformly connected: it is differentially coupled, with some relations being constitutive and others merely contingent, some prior and others derived. Fuller’s panconnectivism tends to flatten ontological precedence — if everything is connected to everything, it becomes harder to say that any one connection is prior to any other. Shan insists on priority within the coupled system.

Where Fuller Challenges Shan

Fuller demands structural specificity. What, in a relational dynamic system, are the tension members and the compression islands? Shan’s "relation" is rich and evocative but underspecified structurally. What kind of relation? Communication? Trust? Power? Dependence? Attention? Fuller’s vocabulary — tension, compression, struts, cables, distribution of force — invites Shan to develop a structural topology of relational dynamics: to map which kinds of relation function as continuous tensional networks and which function as local compression elements.

Fuller’s most direct challenge: "Integrity is the essence of everything successful." If this is true, then the analysis of any system’s failure (Shan’s collapse analysis) must ultimately be an analysis of where and how tensional integrity was lost. Was it a failure of the continuous tensional network (the relational field failed to distribute strain adequately)? Or a failure of the local compression elements (the acting agents became structurally overloaded)? Or a failure at the interface between compression and tension (the coupling mechanism between agents and field broke down)? Fuller’s framework provides the vocabulary for a much more structurally precise account of collapse than Shan has yet offered.

The Deep Convergence

The early Wittgenstein and Shan share a central concern: the boundary between what can be articulated and what exceeds articulation. Wittgenstein draws this boundary at the limits of logical language: what can be said is within; what cannot be said shows itself in the logical form shared by language and world. Shan draws an analogous boundary at the level of formation: what can be articulated (Li) is within; what gave rise to the possibility of articulation (Dao, the path, the formation) is prior and cannot be recovered from articulation alone.

Both thinkers identify premature legibility as the central intellectual danger. Wittgenstein: "The book deals with the problems of philosophy and shows, as I believe, that the method of formulating these problems rests on the misunderstanding of the logic of our language." Shan: "There is a temptation, especially when concepts travel well, to let familiarity stand in for depth." Both are concerned with what is lost when conceptual smoothness replaces structural fidelity.

Wittgenstein’s ladder metaphor and Shan’s naturalisation of the formed path are structural equivalents: both describe how the scaffolding through which one climbs becomes invisible once it has served its purpose, appearing as the thing itself rather than as the means of its emergence. The ladder is thrown away; the path disappears into its own coherence. Recovery requires structural archaeology in both cases.

Shan’s Challenge to the Tractatus

The Tractatus assumes that language is, at its core, a relatively uniform logical medium within which propositions picture facts. But Shan’s analysis of Dao shows that language is not uniform: different languages carry different compressed structures of perception, inheritance, and relational possibility. The Chinese character 道, with its 2,500-year history of structural work across multiple registers, is not simply a word for "way." It is a living interface that carries compressed relational history in its very form. This challenges the Tractatus’s assumption that the logical form of language is transposed across languages in the same way: the transmission of Dao into English is not merely translation but interface change.

Shan’s more fundamental challenge: the Tractatus concludes with enforced silence — "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent." But Shan’s framework suggests that the appropriate response to what cannot be said is not silence but what she calls "the living encounter": an active engagement with the interface between the expressible and what exceeds it, refusing both the closure of silence and the hubris of complete articulation. The Daoist tradition, unlike the Tractatus, does not conclude with silence but with continued practice. Laozi’s opening paradox (道可道，非常道) does not command silence; it invites continued engagement with the tension between the sayable Dao and the unsayable Dao.

The Tractatus Challenges Shan

The Tractatus’s most pointed challenge: is Shan’s theory of Li itself subject to the sequentiality she describes? If Li is always downstream of Dao, if articulation is always downstream of formation, then her articulation of Li as "inner grain, pattern, texture, and intelligibility" is itself a Li that is downstream of some Dao — some path of formation that preceded and enabled this particular conceptualisation. What is the Dao of Shan’s theory of Li? This is the reflexive challenge: can Shan apply her own framework to her framework?

Her implicit answer — given in the account of her own intellectual biography — is yes: her theory of Li is downstream of a long path of formation that includes Chinese-language childhood, Edinburgh doctoral research, years of multilingual crossings, and the specific occasion of a LinkedIn thread. The Dao of her theory is her life. The Li of her theory is what became legible from that life when she began writing about it. But this answer raises a further question: if her theory is a particular Li formed from a particular Dao, how much can it claim to be a general account of Li as such?

The Intimate Convergence

The later Wittgenstein is Shan’s closest philosophical ally in the Western tradition. His insistence that meaning is use, that language games are forms of life, and that philosophy should be therapeutic rather than theoretical maps almost perfectly onto Shan’s claim that Dao is not a doctrine but a living encounter.

The specific convergence on the concept of form of life: for Wittgenstein, a form of life is the shared background of practices, judgments, and ways of being that makes language games possible. For Shan, Dao is a living interface that functions as exactly this: the shared structural background that enables different registers of meaning to remain in contact. Both thinkers resist the reduction of their subject matter to propositional content; both locate what is most important in the practices that precede and sustain any explicit theory.

Wittgenstein’s river bed (On Certainty) is the most precise anticipation of Shan’s account of Li: the hardened propositions that function as the stable channel within which fluid empirical inquiry can flow. The river bed is the formed Dao that makes particular intellectual movements possible. And Wittgenstein notes that the bed can shift: what was once hardened can become fluid again. This is Shan’s account of how positions lose their viability — when the formed Dao is no longer adequate to the field, it must be reformed.

The Productive Tension

The later Wittgenstein’s forms of life are relatively stable and largely unanalysed — they are the "given" from which inquiry starts, not what inquiry investigates. Shan’s framework asks precisely the question Wittgenstein does not pursue: how do forms of life form? What is the Dao of a form of life — the formation process that preceded and enabled the shared practices we inherit? This is the temporal dimension that Wittgenstein’s Investigations does not develop, and where Shan’s contribution is most distinctive.

Wittgenstein’s challenge: if "this is simply what I do" is bedrock — if at some point the justifications run out and practice is all that remains — then Shan’s framework, in seeking to articulate the formation conditions of practices, risks producing theories that are not grounded in the practices themselves. The therapeutic imperative of the Investigations — to bring words back from metaphysics to their everyday use — applies to "relational dynamics," "ontological precedence," and "mutual generation" as much as to any other philosophical term.

The Shared Commitment

Shan and Zhu Xi share a commitment to Li as the inner grain of things — the structural texture that makes them knowable, workable, and morally significant. Both resist the reduction of Li to a purely formal or logical category; both insist on its immanence (Li is in things, not merely a concept about things); both see the investigation of Li as a moral and practical project, not merely an intellectual one.

The deepest convergence: Zhu Xi’s principle liyi fenshu (理一分殊, "principle is one; manifestations are many") and Shan’s account of Li as a functional category that appears across multiple linguistic registers — both are saying that the same structural principle can manifest differently across different instances without being multiple in itself. This is Bateson’s pattern that connects, Shan’s inner grain, and Zhu Xi’s Li, all pointing at the same structural reality.

The Fundamental Disagreement

Zhu Xi gives Li a transcendent dimension that Shan’s account does not claim. For Zhu Xi, all Li participates in the Great Ultimate (taiji, 太极) — the ultimate principle from which all particular Li derive their character. Li is not merely contextual or historical; it has a normative character that transcends any particular formation. For Shan, by contrast, Li is radically relational and temporal: it is the grain of a particular path’s formation, shaped by the specific constraint-field within which the path developed. There is no transcendent Li against which particular formations can be evaluated; there are only more or less legible grains of particular paths.

This disagreement has practical consequences. For Zhu Xi, the investigation of Li (gewu) leads ultimately to a moral breakthrough: the recognition of the one principle underlying all things and the moral imperative that follows from it. For Shan, the investigation of Li leads to structural understanding: the recognition of how a particular path formed under particular constraints, and what this means for how it can be worked with, extended, or transformed. Shan’s Li is descriptive and practical; Zhu Xi’s Li is normative and metaphysical.

The Challenge from Wang Yangming

Wang Yangming’s challenge to both Zhu Xi and Shan: the Li of a situation cannot be found by investigating it from outside but only by living within it and acting according to what the moral mind-heart (xin) reveals. The unity of knowledge and action (zhixing heyi, 知行合一) means that you have not truly known the Li of a situation if you have not acted according to it. For Shan, this challenge has particular force: can you know the Li of Dao’s formation without yourself being on the path? Her answer — implicit in her biographical account — is that she has been on the path (the path of multilingual crossings, of doctoral formation, of living within Chinese language and British institutional culture) and that her structural account of Li is downstream of that embodied path-following.

The Physical Grounding of Ontological Precedence

Prigogine’s arrow of time provides the strongest physical argument for Shan’s ontological precedence claim. The reason Dao precedes Li is not a logical preference or a cultural-philosophical inheritance but a structural fact about how order forms in time. In dissipative systems, the formation history is constitutive of the current structure — you cannot recover the path of formation from inspection of the formed structure alone, and you cannot reverse the formation process without destroying the structure.

"Entropy is the price of structure." Every structure that forms through time does so at a cost — the cost of irreversible dissipation. This means that all formed structures carry within them the "price" of their formation: the history of constraint, movement, and dissipation that made them possible. Li (the inner grain of a formed path) is this "paid price" made visible as structural texture.

Prigogine’s dissipative structures also illuminate Shan’s distinction between endurance and viability. A dissipative structure maintains its form only as long as it is continuously supplied with energy (far from equilibrium). If the energy input is cut off, the structure dissipates. This is Shan’s account of collapse: surface function (the maintained structure) persists while the underlying energy supply (the relational field, the corrective capacity) degrades. The structure looks intact; its viability is already gone.

Prigogine’s Challenge to Shan

Prigogine’s bifurcation theory challenges the gradualism of Shan’s second Dao model. In her account, a path forms through the gradual accumulation of traces — a trace thickens, a pattern holds, a route stabilises. But Prigogine shows that near bifurcation points, the trajectory of a complex system is genuinely underdetermined: a small fluctuation can drive it into one of several qualitatively different stable states. The path of formation is not smooth accumulation but punctuated by moments of genuine indetermination. At these moments, the "choice" of which path forms is not merely a function of prior constraint but of contingent fluctuation.

Shan’s response: she does not deny contingency. Her account of the second Dao model includes the constraint of the river banks (the structural conditions that shape what paths are possible) but does not claim that within those constraints the specific path is determined. The boats crossing the river could have established many different routes; the one that formed was contingent. But once established — once the traces thickened into a pattern — it carried the force of a formed Dao: inheritable, legible, structurally prior to the next level of formation.

The Body That Knows First

Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding passage is the most illuminating classical Chinese illustration of what Shan means by Li as inner grain — and simultaneously the most challenging to her project of theoretical articulation. Cook Ding has learned the grain of the ox so thoroughly that he no longer cuts at all in the conventional sense: he finds the natural articulations (天理, tiānlĭ, the heavenly Li) and guides the knife through them without resistance. "Perception and understanding have come to a stop and spirit moves where it wants."

This is Shan’s claim that "the body knows first" given its fullest and most demanding expression: Cook Ding’s body knows the Li of the ox not through prior analysis or theoretical understanding but through years of practice that have made the grain directly available to skilled movement. The Li is not first known and then followed; it is followed first and then, perhaps, articulated retrospectively as something like understanding. This is Wang Yangming’s unity of knowledge and action at the somatic level.

Cook Ding’s Challenge to Shan’s Theoretical Project

Zhuangzi’s challenge runs deep: if the highest form of following Li is the cessation of conceptual mediation ("perception and understanding have come to a stop"), then what is Shan’s project of articulating Li theoretically doing? Is it producing a Li for Li at a higher level of abstraction? Or is it falling into the very trap of premature legibility that she identifies as the central intellectual danger?

The answer that Zhuangzi’s text itself suggests: Cook Ding’s skill required years of practice before the conceptual stage could be left behind. He began by seeing the whole ox (formed Dao, the named thing); then ceased to see the whole (beginning of structural investigation); then moved by spirit without conceptual interference (embodied Li). The theoretical articulation of Li may be a necessary stage in the path toward the embodied Li that no longer needs theory. Shan’s theoretical work may be the stage between the crude cook (who cuts against the grain) and Cook Ding (who no longer needs theory because the theory has become flesh).

Convergence on Structural Failure

Jin Guantao and Shan are the two thinkers in this paper who most directly address the systemic conditions of long-term structural failure. Their convergence is striking: both argue that surface function can persist long after underlying structural viability has been compromised; both identify self-correcting mechanisms as potentially self-undermining at the long timescale; both insist that what appears as collapse (dynastic crisis; organisational or personal burnout) is the delayed visibility of a much longer structural degradation.

Jin and Liu’s ultrastable system is, in Shan’s terms, the extreme case of a system in which the formed Dao (the established three-subsystem structure of peasant economy, bureaucratic polity, Confucian ideology) has become so coherent, so self-reinforcing, and so successfully self-correcting that it cannot undergo the kind of structural reformation that genuine adaptation would require. The path has not merely narrowed; it has hardened into a channel that can absorb surface turbulence while remaining structurally immovable. The corrective capacity maintains surface coherence but precisely at the cost of adaptive capacity.

Jin’s Challenge to Shan

Jin Guantao’s challenge to Shan: his analysis shows that ultrastability is not a failure of individual intelligence or vision but a structural property of tightly coupled, multiply self-correcting systems. The individuals within the Chinese dynastic system were not systematically less intelligent or less virtuous than individuals in other civilisations; they were operating within a structural field that suppressed the very signals that would have made the narrowing path visible. Shan’s "Elegant Wall-hitting" — good-faith action colliding with invisible structural limits — may be not merely a condition of individual actors but a structural feature of all highly coherent systems.

This suggests that Shan’s framework needs a more developed account of how the corrective capacity of a system is itself shaped by the system’s structural field. Not all systems have equal corrective capacity. Systems that are highly coherent (high Li, formed Dao) may be precisely the ones whose corrective capacity is most systematically obscured, because the very mechanisms that maintain coherence are also the ones that suppress the signals of its degradation.

Positional Analysis at Different Scales

Kauffman’s adjacent possible and Shan’s positional analysis are, at different scales of resolution, the same structural insight: from any given state, only certain next states are accessible, and the capacity of a system to move into more and better states depends on the structural quality of the position it currently occupies.

Move 37 in Go is an adjacent-possible move: it does not capture stones (local gain) but restructures the field (expands AlphaGo’s adjacent possible while contracting Lee Sedol’s). This is exactly what Kauffman describes when he says that the biosphere cannot, in principle, be predicted from any fixed specification because the adjacent possible keeps expanding through the very process of evolution. The game cannot be predicted move by move, but the structural logic of position-building can be discerned.

The Challenge Kauffman Poses

Kauffman’s order-for-free challenges the implicit gradualism of Shan’s path-formation model. Some order emerges "for free" — without the patient accumulation of traces into patterns. Catalytic closure (the moment when a chemical system crosses the threshold for self-replication) is not a matter of gradual accumulation but of a phase transition: below the threshold, nothing self-replicates; above it, self-replication is inevitable. If this is true at the chemical level, might it also be true at the social and cognitive levels that Shan is analysing? Are there threshold effects in path-formation — moments when a certain density of traversal suddenly produces a stable route, rather than the gradual process Shan’s second Dao model implies?

The Intimate Relation and Its Limits

WSR and Shan’s Relational Dynamics are the two most direct expressions of the Chinese philosophical tradition of Li in contemporary systems discourse. WSR is the most developed practical methodology built on Li; Shan’s framework is the most developed ontological account of why Li works the way it does.

The convergence: WSR’s three-fold structure (wuli, shili, renli) maps precisely onto three registers of what Shan calls Li: the Li of material things (wuli), the Li of how situations are perceived and engaged (shili), and the Li of human relational patterns (renli). WSR’s asymmetric epistemology (knowing wuli, sensing shili, caring for renli) is an implicit recognition of Shan’s ontological claim that different registers of Li require different modes of engagement: cognition for material patterns, attunement for perspectival patterns, ethical care for relational patterns.

Shan’s Challenge to WSR

WSR is a methodology: it begins from the assumption that one already has a "systems project" within which the three dimensions of Li are to be investigated. But Shan asks: what is the Li of the project itself? What is the Dao that made this particular project necessary, possible, and intelligible? The methodological structure of WSR (understanding desires, investigating conditions, formulating objectives, creating models, coordinating relations, implementing proposals) is itself a formed Dao — a path that was established through years of practice, international encounter, and historical pressure. Its Li is now legible as "WSR." But Shan’s framework insists that the legibility of the methodology is downstream of the formation history that produced it. To practise WSR without understanding its formation history is to use the map without knowing the territory.

WSR’s Challenge to Shan

WSR’s challenge to Shan: her framework is powerful at the level of structural diagnosis but less developed at the level of practical methodology. How does one investigate the Li of a complex situation? How does one distinguish between wuli, shili, and renli in practice? How does one care for renli without knowledge of wuli compromising the caring? Shan’s ontological claims about sequence and precedence need to be translated into practical methodological guidance before they can serve as a working tool. WSR has this translation; Shan does not yet.

The Deepest Convergence

Wittgenstein’s On Certainty is the closest Western philosophical text to Shan’s account of how formed Dao operates as the background condition of inquiry and action. The river bed metaphor is the precise equivalent of Shan’s first Dao model: the hardened propositions function as the stable channel within which fluid empirical investigation can flow, just as the formed path functions as the stable structure within which new movement can occur.

Wittgenstein’s key insight about the world-picture: "It is not only agreement in opinions but also (odd as it may sound) in judgments that is required, and this is agreement not in opinions, but rather in form of life." The world-picture (the inherited background of hinge propositions) is not a set of beliefs that can be individually scrutinised and accepted or rejected. It is the background against which any such scrutiny becomes possible. This is Shan’s formed Dao: not a set of propositions but a structural inheritance that shapes what questions can be meaningfully asked.

And Wittgenstein’s claim that fluid propositions can harden and hard ones become fluid directly parallels Shan’s account of how paths form and can be reformed: the river bed shifts, but not arbitrarily. The shift is shaped by the accumulated force of the river’s movement — by the dynamics that have been operating within the constraint-field for long enough to alter the constraint-field itself. This is Shan’s account of genuine adaptation: not surface-level change within the existing structural field but the gradual reformation of the structural field itself.

The Productive Divergence

Wittgenstein’s On Certainty does not offer a theory of how the river bed shifts: it merely notes that it can. Shan’s framework is precisely this theory: the bed shifts when the accumulated dynamics exceed the holding capacity of the existing channel, when corrective capacity thins to the point where surface function can no longer be maintained, when the path has narrowed so far that collapse becomes structurally necessary. Shan provides the dynamics that Wittgenstein gestures at.

The most important contribution to emerge from this dialectical inquiry is the articulation of ontological precedence as a complexity principle — one that current complexity science has underanalysed. Complexity science has been very good at describing coupling, feedback, emergence, and self-organisation. It has been less attentive to the question of what must already be in place for these dynamics to unfold.

Shan’s framework provides the most precise statement of this principle across all the traditions surveyed: relation precedes dynamics, Dao precedes Li, formation precedes formed coherence. This is not temporal priority in a simple chronological sense but ontological enabling: the prior term is the condition of possibility for the subsequent term, even when both are simultaneously present in the coupled system.

The physical grounding is provided by Prigogine: irreversibility means that formation histories cannot be recovered from current structures, which means that the sequence of formation is not merely chronological but constitutive. The cultural-philosophical grounding is provided by the Chinese tradition: Laozi’s 道可道，非常道, Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding, Zhu Xi’s gewu, WSR’s three-fold Li investigation, Jin Guantao’s ultrastable system — all express, in different registers, the same structural insight that formation is prior to articulation, that path is prior to pattern, that the grain reveals itself only to those who follow the way rather than those who merely name it.

The structural engineering grounding is provided by Fuller: the continuous tensional network is the condition of the compressive elements’ function, not vice versa. The relational field is prior to the local dynamics it enables.

Fuller’s Dymaxion principle — Dynamic Maximum Tension — provides a structural frame for Shan’s working frame that is more precise than she has yet articulated. Excellence as "capacity held in coherence under constraint over time" is tensegrity applied to life: the achievement of maximum structural integrity from the available relational resources, by distributing the holding work across the continuous tensional network of relation rather than concentrating it at a single compressive node.

The ethical dimension: Dymaxion is not merely an engineering efficiency but an ethical imperative. Fuller’s last public statement was "only integrity is going to count." The achievement of structural integrity through the intelligent distribution of tension is not merely a strategic advantage but a moral commitment — the commitment to doing more with less, to holding more with the minimum necessary constraint, to building positions that remain viable for others rather than collapsing under the weight of local excess.

Shan’s working frame can be read as a Dymaxion ethics: excellence is not the maximisation of local output but the maintenance of structural integrity across time, under the pressure of constraint, through the distribution of capacity across a continuous relational field. This is the long game of tensegrity: not one strong move but the continuous adjustment of an entire field.

The most analytically original contribution of this paper is its development of Li as a structural concept operating simultaneously in three registers — an account that goes beyond both Shan’s published work and the WSR methodology.

Register One: Li as Material Grain (Wuli 物理)

Register Two: Li as Cognitive Grain (Shili 事理)

At the cognitive-perspectival level, Li is the grain of how a situation is perceived, understood, and engaged with. Shan’s "iceberg model" is a shili analysis: the visible surface of oral participation (speech or silence) has a Li that only becomes legible when the deeper conditions shaping it are investigated. Kuhn’s paradigms are the shili of scientific practice: the background assumptions and exemplary solutions that shape what scientists see and how they engage with anomalies. Wittgenstein’s hinge propositions are the shili of ordinary language: the hardened propositions that function as the channel for fluid inquiry. At this register, Li is closest to what epistemology and philosophy of science investigate: the structural patterns of knowing and understanding that shape what can be seen and thought.

Register Three: Li as Relational Grain (Renli 人理)

Shan’s working frame — "excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time" — operates across all three registers: at the material level (a physical structure’s integrity), the cognitive level (a field of knowledge’s coherence), and the relational level (a community’s or individual’s capacity under pressure). The power of her framework is precisely this cross-register operation: the same structural principle — grain before intelligibility, formation before formed coherence, relation before dynamics — operates at every scale and level of Li.

The paper’s title names an epistemological condition that the dialectical inquiry has repeatedly produced: glimpses. Li cannot be directly stated; it can only be glimpsed — caught in the act of becoming recognisable, in the moment when a collision of frameworks makes visible what neither could see alone.

The glimpse is not a failure of adequate articulation. It is the correct epistemological response to what Li is: an inner grain that is always downstream of the Dao that produced it, always partially obscured by the very coherence it makes possible, always threatening to close into premature legibility if held too firmly. Li is best approached obliquely, through dialectical encounter, through the collision of multiple traditions that each hold a part of its surface without any holding the whole.

What this paper has produced are glimpses: the tensegrity-relational dynamics convergence (a glimpse of Li as the continuous tensional network of relation); the Tractarian silence and Shan’s living encounter (a glimpse of Li as what shows itself at the boundary of the sayable); Cook Ding’s embodied intelligence and Shan’s long-game analysis (a glimpse of Li as the grain that skilled practice follows without concept); the ultrastable system and Shan’s collapse analysis (a glimpse of Li as the grain that self-correcting systems mistake for permanent reality); the adjacent possible and Shan’s positional analysis (a glimpse of Li as the field of structural possibility that each position opens or closes).

Each glimpse is partial. Each is genuine. Together they constitute something more than any tradition alone produced: a dialectical approximation to the inner grain that all of them were circling.

If Li is always downstream of Dao, and if articulation is always downstream of formation, then Shan’s own theory of Li is itself a Li that is downstream of her particular Dao of formation. This means her framework cannot claim universality — only the universality-within-particularity that any well-formed structural account can claim. The question is: what is lost in the particularity? What Dao of formation is Shan’s framework not downstream of — what structural conditions has it not been shaped by — and what does this mean for its applicability?

Shan’s concept of "relation" remains underspecified. Fuller demands to know: what are the tension members and what are the compression islands? Luhmann demands to know: what kind of operation generates the relational field? Holland demands to know: what are the building blocks from which relational dynamics emerge? WSR partially answers by specifying three kinds of Li (wuli, shili, renli) — but Shan’s ontological account needs a more developed structural vocabulary for the different kinds and qualities of relation that constitute the relational field.

Prigogine’s bifurcation theory suggests that the specific path of formation (which particular route the boats established across the river) is contingent: at bifurcation points, small fluctuations determine which of several possible stable states the system enters. This means that the Li of any formed Dao is partly contingent — it reflects not just the constraint-field and the dynamics but also the specific fluctuation history. How much of a system’s Li is necessary (determined by the constraint-field) and how much is contingent (determined by specific historical fluctuations)? Shan’s framework does not yet address this.

WSR’s insistence that renli must be "cared for" rather than merely "known" introduces an ethical dimension that Shan’s framework has not fully developed. If Li is the inner grain of human relational systems, and if this grain can be worked with skillfully (like Cook Ding) or worked against destructively (like the crude cook), then the question of which ways of working with Li are ethically permissible is urgent. Zhu Xi’s Li was explicitly normative — it told you not just how things are but how they ought to be. Shan’s Li is more purely descriptive. The question of how to move from structural understanding to ethical action is one that her framework has opened but not answered.

Shan argues that Dao is a living interface partly because it has "travelled remarkably far while largely retaining its pinyin form." But Li has not travelled in the same way. The concept of Li is largely unknown outside Chinese-language intellectual traditions and the specialist literature on Neo-Confucianism and WSR. If Shan’s framework is to contribute to global complexity discourse, the translation of Li into terms accessible across multiple intellectual traditions is the central challenge. This paper has attempted one version of that translation — across Fuller’s tensegrity, Wittgenstein’s river bed, Prigogine’s dissipative structures, Bateson’s pattern that connects, and many others. But translation is always also transformation; the question of what is lost in the translation is always present.

The paper began with a LinkedIn thread. It ends with the recognition that all the traditions surveyed in this paper have been circling the same structural reality from different directions: a reality that is prior to any single articulation of it, that exceeds any single tradition’s vocabulary for it, and that shows itself most clearly in the collision of multiple frameworks each trying, from its own angle, to bring it into view.

Laozi named it as what the naming cannot capture: 道可道，非常道. Zhuangzi showed it in Cook Ding’s knife following the 天理 without resistance. Zhu Xi systematised it as the one principle in all things that is never fully present in any single manifestation. Wittgenstein drew its boundary in the Tractatus, brought it back to earth in the Investigations, and found its geological structure in On Certainty. Fuller made it the structural principle of the universe: tension is the great integrity. Prigogine showed it as the irreversible arrow of time that makes structure possible. Kauffman showed it as the adjacent possible that opens before the path that has been walked.

And Alice Jing Shan arrived at it from within the Chinese language, where it was already present in the word she had used since childhood to know something (知道), to apologise (道歉), to taste the world (味道), and to understand the reason of things (道理). The grain was always there. The glimpses come and go. The path continues.

“天理 — the grain of heaven — is what the knife finds when it stops cutting and begins to follow.”

The grain of heaven is not the universal cosmic principle of Zhu Xi’s metaphysics; it is the specific structural grain of this specific ox’s specific body — what heaven has produced through the specific formation of this specific living creature. The knife does not find the heavenly grain by applying a prior taxonomy of anatomical structures; it finds the heavenly grain by achieving the formation-sufficiency that makes the actual grain visible as the knife approaches the actual articulation. 天理 is Li at its most specific: the grain of the actual, encountered through the Dao of the actual encounter, visible only to the formation that is adequate to it.

Additional Analyses: Extended Build

This paper is a sustained, exhaustive, and analytically rigorous inquiry into the thought of Alice Jing Shan (b. 1980s, China; PhD Edinburgh), whose Substack series Dao: The Art of the Long Game and her article on Li (2026) constitute the productive centre of investigation. It places her framework of Relational Dynamics in dialectical collision with more than twenty-five intellectual voices spanning systems theory, complexity science, Chinese philosophy, structural engineering, phenomenology, and analytical philosophy. The paper is structured not as a survey but as a genuine dialectical encounter: each tradition is given its strongest voice before being challenged, pressed, and enriched by the others.

The central questions organising the inquiry are: What does Alice Jing Shan mean by precedence, emergence, and formation? How does her concept of Dao as a living interface and Li as inner grain hold up under the pressure of Western and Chinese systems science? What happens when her relational dynamics ontology meets Buckminster Fuller's tensegrity and Dymaxion principle of dynamic maximum tension? When it meets Wittgenstein's two philosophies — the early silence of the Tractatus and the later language-games of the Investigations? When it meets Prigogine's dissipative structures and the arrow of time? Kauffman's adjacent possible? Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian account of Li as the grain of the universe? Jin Guantao and Liu Qingfeng's ultrastable system? Snowden's Cynefin and enabling constraints? Maturana and Varela's autopoiesis? Morin's complex thought? Luhmann's systems theory? Meadows's leverage points?

The paper argues for the following propositions: (1) Shan's framework of precedence — Dao before Li, relation before dynamics, path before pattern — constitutes a genuine and underexamined contribution to complexity ontology; (2) her working frame — excellence as capacity held in coherence under constraint over time — is structurally isomorphic with tensegrity but exceeds it by adding temporality, relation, and the ethics of care; (3) the Chinese systems tradition supplies not a parallel but a deeper root for what Shan is articulating, in that Li has a philosophical genealogy of 900 years preceding the emergence of Western systems science; (4) Wittgenstein's two philosophies offer a stereo-image of Shan's problematic: the Tractatus maps the limits of the expressible, while the Investigations shows how meaning lives in use, practice, and form of life — exactly where Shan locates Dao; and (5) the dialectical collision of all twenty-five-plus voices produces a set of open questions that current complexity science has not yet adequately addressed.

In a LinkedIn comment thread discussing David Snowden's blog post "A Game of Encirclement," Mike Jackson mentioned the Wuli-Shili-Renli (WSR) approach of Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu. For most readers, this was a technical citation in a conversation about systems methodology. For Alice Jing Shan, it was something else: the surfacing of a character she already knew from childhood.

That character is 理 (Lĭ). It lives in 物理 (wùlĭ, physics), 事理 (shìlĭ, the pattern of affairs), and 人理 (rénlĭ, the pattern of human relations). It also lives in 道理 (dàolĭ) — the word that pairs Dao and Li: reason, underlying logic, the sense a thing makes from within its own grain. It was already in her language before she encountered systems theory. When WSR surfaced in that thread, what surfaced for Shan was not a new concept but a long-standing structural companion: the pattern that was always travelling alongside the path.

“"Dao rarely travels alone. Perhaps Li is the less-known partner whose absence should caution us whenever Dao begins to feel too smooth, too familiar, or too readily available."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (Cynefin Co, May 2026)

This paper will test that claim against twenty-five voices who are, each in their own way, trying to think the same thing.

“"Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Dao: The Art of the Long Game (recurring frame, 2026)

This is not an aphorism. It is a structural definition. Every term does work: capacity (potential that has been built), coherence (internal relational order), constraint (the external and internal pressures that test and shape integrity), and time (the dimension within which all of these are assessed). Remove any term and the definition collapses. This is already a tensegrity-like structure: it holds precisely because all four elements are in continuous mutual tension.

Her intellectual biography is itself a data set for her theory. She grew up in China inside the Chinese language, where Dao (a path, a road, a way, a reason, a method, a moral order) was not a philosophical concept but a word — a word encountered daily in compounds, ordinary speech, and the texture of cultural life. Her doctoral work at Edinburgh produced the Iceberg Model of Oral Participation, which attempted to decode silence — the meeting point of cognition, motivation, language, power, and context — in educational settings. This was already a systems move: the visible surface (silence or speech) is downstream of the structural conditions that produce it.

“"What appeared as silence was rarely a lack of ability. It was often the meeting point of cognition, motivation, language, power, and context."”

Wittgenstein’s claim generates immediate structural resonance with Shan’s formation framework. The philosophical precision of this formulation — refusing both naïve realism (the world as it is, fully accessible to cognition) and naïve idealism (the world as pure construction) — is the same precision that characterises Shan’s navigation between the Dao that exceeds naming and the Li that emerges from the Dao. Each tradition has arrived at the same structural recognition through a different formation history: Wittgenstein through logical analysis, Shan through cross-cultural formation phenomenology.

The concept of Dao as interface is the architectural centrepiece of Shan's framework. An interface, for Shan, is not a neutral conduit but a structural relay:

“"By interface, I mean the place where one thing becomes available to another: where it can be encountered, perceived, transmitted, and made to matter. It is where contact, translation, selection, distortion, amplification, and blockage become possible."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine, but a Living Encounter" (April 2026)

The claim that Dao "continues to function in this way" is an empirical claim about living language, not a historical claim about classical philosophy. Shan is tracing the ongoing structural work that Dao does in Chinese discourse — a work that is not metaphorical but systemic. The word carries compressed distinctions, patterned orientations, and perceptual orientations that operate at a level below explicit theory.

Her personal word list around Dao (which she explicitly frames as suggestive rather than exhaustive) traces this function across multiple registers:

What Shan demonstrates through this list is that Dao is not a static philosophical term but a living functional category. It operates at every level of ordinary life: bodily (the digestive tract, 消化道), epistemic (to know, 知道), moral (morality, 道德), spatial (road, 道路), and even comedic (the path without interval, 无间道, also the title of a famous film). The same character does structural work across all these registers because it encodes something irreducible: the idea of a way that has been made through movement over time under constraint.

One of Shan's most structurally original contributions is her articulation of two interlocking models of Dao, which she calls "models of mutual generation." The occasion was drawing:

“"I began by drawing the mountain, then a path. In the act of drawing, something shifted. Working between English and Chinese, I wrote 大道之行. Then the character 道 seemed to begin moving before my eyes. Because of the route I had drawn, two parallel lines with the feel of a passage, the character no longer appeared static. It opened into a field."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

The first model shows a Dao already formed: a path stabilised enough to be encountered as a way. This corresponds to the everyday human experience of entering systems after they have already taken shape:

“"A child inherits language after grammar and vocabulary are already in motion. A member joins an organisation after its roles, routines, and culture are already in place. A person enters a relationship after patterns of presence and expectation have already begun to settle. By the time a path feels natural, it usually no longer appears as pattern at all. It appears as reality."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

This insight has a precise phenomenological name: sedimentation. What was once a path, a choice, a contingent formation, sediments into the taken-for-granted. The second model excavates that sedimentation by asking: how did the path form at all?

“"At first, there is only landscape. Land. River. The field is already shaped by constraint: two river banks. Then movement in nature. Later, human settlement. Then the need to travel. A small boat carries people back and forth, year after year. Then perhaps more boats, more journeys. In that repeated movement, something begins to stabilise. A trace forms. The trace thickens. A pattern holds. A route becomes recognisable."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

The two models are not sequential but mutually generative:

“"What is formed is still in formation. What is forming already carries the possibility of form."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

And:

“"A formed Dao calls forth the question of formation. Formation, once seen, changes the meaning of what appears formed."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Dao Models of Mutual Generation" (April 2026)

This mutual generation is Shan's primary structural category. It resists both static structuralism (which takes the formed as given) and naive process philosophy (which dissolves structure into pure flow). For Shan, the formed and the forming are in permanent dialectical relationship: neither is prior in a simple chronological sense, but within that mutual relationship, ontological precedence — Dao before Li, formation before formed coherence — still matters.

The most philosophically dense of Shan's concepts is Li (理). She introduces it through its linguistic companionship with Dao:

“"In Chinese, 道 and 理 are not strangers. They live together in 道理 (dào lĭ): reason, principle, underlying logic, the sense a thing begins to make from within its own grain. Li carries something closer to inner grain, pattern, texture, and intelligibility. It is not merely abstract logic, but the grain through which something becomes recognisable."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

The words that carry Li are instructive as a system:

The crucial philosophical point Shan makes about Li is its ontological position: Li is real but secondary. It is the inner grain that becomes visible once a path has formed, not the source from which the path issues:

“"Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. This is not a semantic preference. It is a question of ontological precedence. The path must open before its inner grain can appear. Intelligibility does not come first. The path does."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

This claim has direct implications for complexity science. In many accounts of complex adaptive systems, the assumption is that patterns (Li) are what complexity generates, and that the task of the analyst is to detect and name these patterns. Shan's framework challenges this: pattern-naming is always downstream of path-formation. What we detect as patterns are always traces of prior movement under constraint. The detection comes after; the naming comes after even that. To mistake the name for the origin is what Shan calls "premature legibility":

Shan's treatment of sequence is one of the most philosophically careful aspects of her work. She is at pains to distinguish ontological precedence from simple temporal priority. The sequence argument is not: "first X happens, then Y happens." It is: "Y cannot be the condition of its own possibility. There must be something prior to it that makes it possible, even if the two now appear simultaneously coupled."

“"Mutual generation does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)" (May 2026)

She develops this through the concept of coupling. The word "complex" comes from the Latin complexus (entwined, encircled), and complex systems are defined by the fact that their elements are coupled: movement in one part propagates through the whole. The Chinese formulation is:

“"Chinese has a vivid saying for this: 牵一发而动全身. Literally, it means: pull one hair and the whole body moves."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

But coupling, Shan insists, transforms without equalising. The analogy she uses is marriage: two people become a couple through sustained interaction, each changed by the other. But even within that coupling, precedence remains. Prior conditions shape what later dynamics become possible. The DNA example is precise:

“"DNA, too, belongs to one whole, yet its sequence remains structurally constitutive. Wholeness does not erase internal ordering."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

This leads to one of her most important systemic insights: that holding capacity is itself sequential. A system must be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more:

“"In neonatal intensive care, one may see milk enter through a feeding tube at an almost inconceivably slow rate, perhaps only a drop over the course of an hour while the baby is still on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). This is not hesitation. It is the protection of viability. The system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence" (May 2026)

The same logic applies to learning (Zone of Proximal Development), to organisations (culture must hold new strategy), to software (operating systems before applications), and to any system where prior formation determines what can be received next.

Shan's analysis of collapse and failure is one of her most intellectually original contributions to complexity science. Trained through her doctoral work on corrective capacity degradation, she argues that failure is always a trajectory, never a single event:

“"One of the deepest things Go teaches is that collapse rarely begins where collapse becomes visible. By the time a position finally gives way, much of the structural work has already been done. The board may still look playable. Stones may still be standing. Moves may still be possible. But the path has already narrowed."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

And, more precisely:

“"Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

The concept she introduces is "Elegant Wall-hitting": the repeated collision between good-faith effort and an invisible structural limit. This is a systems-theoretic concept. People inside a collapsing system do not become irrational. They continue to act rationally within the portion of the system they can see, even while the wider position has already narrowed beyond recovery.

“"Surface function and underlying viability do not always decline together. A system may still look coherent, still compensate, still perform, while deeper conditions are already changing underneath it."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Nothing Collapses in One Move" (April 2026)

This introduces a critical distinction between endurance and viability:

Shan's analysis of AlphaGo's famous Move 37 in Game 2 against Lee Sedol constitutes one of her most elegant structural essays. The move, which DeepMind described as having roughly a 1-in-10,000 chance of being played, is often cited as evidence that AI overturned human Go wisdom. Shan disagrees:

“"I would not say Move 37 overturned traditional wisdom. If anything, it revealed a form of intelligence that had converged with it. What AlphaGo brought was not a rejection of long game logic, but the capacity to calculate and enact that logic at a depth beyond what a human mind could hold in real time."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "AlphaGo's Move 37" (April 2026)

The structural insight is about the nature of intelligence itself:

“"What if intelligence is not only the ability to maximise immediate gain? What if a deeper form of intelligence lies in building a position that remains viable across time? That would mean intelligence is not only about solving the problem in front of you. It is also about shaping the conditions under which future problems become easier, harder, or even unnecessary."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "AlphaGo's Move 37" (April 2026)

This reformulation of intelligence — from local optimisation to field-shaping over time — is directly continuous with her core frame: excellence as capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. The question is not which move wins this exchange but which move builds the field within which future exchanges become possible.

Shan's most recent Substack essay (May 16, 2026) — the day before this paper was written — states the core ontological claim of Relational Dynamics with maximum precision:

“"Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

But even within this coupling, sequence matters. Relation is ontologically prior to dynamics, not because there is first a static relation and only later movement, but because dynamics become dynamics only within a relation-bearing field:

“"Dynamics do not happen in a void. They presuppose a relational condition within which movement becomes possible, transmissible, and intelligible. Without relation, there may be motion, but not dynamics in the fuller sense I mean here. Relation is not one variable among others inside a dynamic process. It is the condition under which dynamics becomes consequential at all."**”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

She illustrates this with a communicative example: the same sentence lands differently in different relational contexts. Not because of a surface variation, but because relation is constitutive of what the dynamic is. The information may be identical; the relational conditions of uptake are not.

“"We notice dynamics first because dynamics are what move. They are visible, measurable, dramatic. But relation is what allows movement to matter across time, scale, and position. Relation is what makes movement consequential."”

— Alice Jing Shan, "Relation Precedes Dynamics" (May 2026)

And, in a formulation that completes the Dao/Li series:

Richard Buckminster Fuller was an American systems theorist who spent fifty-six years documenting what one individual could accomplish for the benefit of humanity. He called himself "Guinea Pig B." He held 28 patents, authored 28 books, and coined "Spaceship Earth," "ephemeralization," "synergetics," and "tensegrity." Robert Anton Wilson called him the man with "better claim to the title of polymath than any man since Leonardo."

His structural philosophy rests on two foundational concepts. The first is tensegrity:

Tensegrity describes structural systems where compression members (struts) are discontinuous and suspended within a continuous tensional network (cables). The integrity of the whole does not reside in any single element but in the distribution of tension through the whole:

Fuller's most cosmic claim extends tensegrity to the universe itself:

The second concept is Dymaxion — Dynamic Maximum Tension. Coined as a portmanteau for Fuller's housing designs and vehicles, it names the design ideal of achieving maximum benefit from minimum input. Not maximum force, but maximum efficiency through the intelligent distribution of dynamic tension. It is what Fuller also called "ephemeralization" — doing more with less:

“"If humanity does not opt for integrity we are through completely. It is absolutely touch and go. Each one of us could make the difference."”

— Buckminster Fuller

Fuller's synergetics extends the insight to ecosystems and knowledge:

Fuller's account of pattern integrity directly resonates with Shan's Li:

Kenneth Snelson, who co-developed tensegrity, describes the underlying principle: "Snelson's insight was that floating compression — rods that push out while cables pull in, with no rods touching — produces a structure that is both light and strong, distributing forces so evenly that the whole becomes resilient precisely because no single part bears the full load." Fuller grasped this as universal: the universe holds itself together not by rigid compression but by continuous tensional embrace.

Wittgenstein's two philosophies represent the two poles of the language-structure problem that Shan is navigating. The early Tractatus (completed 1918, published 1921) attempts to draw the limits of the expressible. The later Philosophical Investigations (published posthumously 1953) abandons that project and enters language from within its living use.

The Tractatus: Logic, Limit, and the Inexpressible

The Tractatus opens with three propositions that establish the ontological framework:

Language, for the early Wittgenstein, is a logical picture of reality:

“"The picture is a model of reality."”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 2.12

Language and world share a logical form that makes representation possible — but this shared form cannot itself be stated. It shows itself:

“"What can be said at all can be said clearly; and whereof one cannot speak thereof one must be silent."”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus, Preface and Proposition 7

This famous conclusion is not a positivist elimination of the unsayable. Wittgenstein is precise:

“"The book deals with the problems of philosophy and shows, as I believe, that the method of formulating these problems rests on the misunderstanding of the logic of our language."”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus, Preface

The Tractatus concludes with the famous ladder metaphor:

The Philosophical Investigations: Language as Form of Life

The later Wittgenstein abandons the picture theory and the project of drawing the limits of language from outside. Instead, he enters language from within its living practices:

Meaning is not reference to objects or facts. Meaning is use:

“"For a large class of cases — though not for all — in which we employ the word 'meaning' it can be defined thus: the meaning of a word is its use in the language."”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §43

Philosophical problems arise from language idling — from language going on holiday:

“"A philosophical problem has the form: 'I don't know my way about.'"”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §123

We accept forms of life as given — there is no deeper justification:

The Wuli-Shili-Renli (WSR) methodology, developed in the context of an international research exchange between Beijing, Ishikawa (Japan), and Hull (UK) over fifteen-plus years, is the most direct intellectual predecessor to Shan's work on Li. Its name encodes the three dimensions of Li:

“"WSR suggests that empirical reality, or 'the human condition', be seen as a dynamic constellation of multiple li: wuli (relation with the world), shili (relation with the mind), and renli (relation with others). Li taken as such are conceptually differentiated, logically irreducible, whilst empirically intertwined."”

— Zhichang Zhu, "WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach"

The philosophical grounding is explicitly in Neo-Confucian thought:

“"Based on the reconstruction of the Neo-Confucianist concept of Li and relevant teachings, and drawing on experiences in the Oriental context, we have consolidated a systems methodology so to improve and popularise systems research and practice. We call it the Wuli Shili Renli approach (WSR)."”

— Zhichang Zhu, "Dealing with Wuli Shili Renli" (ISSS Primer)

Zhu also invokes Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian instruction directly: "the li of shishi and wuwu have no practical significance" if not attended to in their concrete differentiation. The three verbs of the WSR methodology are philosophically asymmetric: knowing Wuli (objective cognition), sensing Shili (perspectival attunement), and caring for Renli (ethical engagement). This asymmetry is crucial: the relational-human dimension cannot be merely known; it must be cared for.

The historical genealogy of WSR is itself a systems story. Three key sources: (1) Chinese management experience since Mao's time, recognising the limits of science-technology-alone systems approaches; (2) Qian Xuesen's 1978 promotion of research on shili; (3) Li Yaozi's attention to renli; and (4) Gu Jifa's 1988 synthesis bringing all three together. This was then shaped by sustained international encounter — Checkland, Ackoff, Midgley, Flood, Jackson — producing the formal WSR as it now exists.

Qian Xuesen is one of the great figures of twentieth-century Chinese science and systems thinking. Known in the West as the rocket scientist who contributed to the Manhattan Project before being deported from the USA in 1950, he went on to develop China's missile and space programme. What is less known is his extensive work on systems philosophy and the concept of metasynthesis (zonghe jicheng, 综合集成).

“"The traditional division of science and technology departments has not only limited our scientific vision and research scope, but also caused the separation of related disciplines, artificially dividing our knowledge into disconnected parts."”

— Xuesen Qian, cited in "The Foundation of Chinese Systems Thinking"

Qian proposed that for "open complex giant systems" — systems too large, complex, and value-laden for reductionist analysis — the appropriate method is metasynthesis: the integration of quantitative modelling, qualitative expert knowledge, and empirical data in a structured dialogue. This is explicitly anti-reductionist and pro-relational, and it carries forward the Chinese philosophical tradition of treating the whole as primary.

Zhu Xi is the greatest synthesiser of Neo-Confucian thought and the philosopher who gave Li its richest philosophical formulation. His account is the deepest historical root of what Shan is working with, and the ground from which WSR grew.

For Zhu Xi, Li is the patterned principle immanent in all things. It is not transcendent to the world but constitutive of it:

“"There is one pattern or principle in all things, but it may have many manifestations. Li is inseparable from qi (vital energy)."”

— Zhu Xi, on the investigation of things (gewu 格物)

The Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy formulates it:

“"Li [is] the patterned regularity of existence... giving precedence to the former [li over qi] as identical with the grounding principle of Zhou Dunyi's cosmology, the Great Ultimate (taiji). Hence, Zhu Xi's wing of neo-Confucianism is often referred to as 'li learning'. These abstract distinctions had moral significance."”

— Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Chinese Philosophy"

The famous principle: liyi fenshu (理一分殊) — "principle is one; its manifestations are many." This is the Neo-Confucian account of how the same Li appears differently across different things, events, and relations without being multiple in itself. It directly parallels Shan's account of Dao as a living interface that appears across many compounds without being reducible to any single meaning.

Zhu Xi's method of gewu (格物, investigation of things) is a structured approach to uncovering Li through careful attention to the concrete. It is not deductive but inductive and attentional: to follow the grain of a thing until its pattern becomes clear. This is the intellectual ancestor of WSR's "sensing shili."

Zhu Xi's great Song-dynasty predecessor Cheng Yi articulates the dynamic relationship of Li and Dao:

Jin Guantao and Liu Qingfeng are the pioneers of applying cybernetics and systems theory to Chinese history. Their concept of the "ultrastable system" (chaowending jiegou, 超稳定结构), developed in the 1980s, applied systems engineering and feedback theory to explain why Chinese dynastic civilisation was both remarkably resilient and remarkably resistant to structural transformation.

Their analysis: in feudal China, the peasant economy, bureaucratic polity, and Confucian ideology were closely integrated into a self-correcting structure:

“"This structure developed a self-correcting mechanism to maintain its integration. It tolerated no deviation of any of these three sub-systems from its normal function. Because of this, traditional society in China was stable, stagnate and long-lasting."”

— Jin Guantao and Liu Qingfeng, "Traditional Society in China: An Ultrastable Structure" (1980)

This concept is directly relevant to Shan's analysis of collapse and corrective capacity. Jin and Liu's "ultrastable system" is a system that maintains surface coherence while its structural capacity for genuine change narrows. This is precisely what Shan describes as the condition where "endurance is not viability" and "what looks like resilience is only delayed collapse." The ultrastable system is, in Shan's terms, a system in which the path has narrowed so far that collapse is already structurally determined — even while the surface continues to function.

Prigogine's work on dissipative structures and irreversibility is one of the foundational contributions to modern complexity science. His central insight: far from equilibrium, physical and chemical systems spontaneously generate order through the continuous dissipation of energy. This order is irreversible — it requires the arrow of time.

“"Only when a system behaves in a sufficiently random way may the difference between past and future, and therefore irreversibility, enter its description. The arrow of time is the manifestation of the fact that the future is not given, that, as the French poet Paul Valery emphasized, 'time is a construction'."”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

Prigogine's concept of entropy as "the price of structure" is directly relevant to Shan's framework:

Prigogine also articulates the temporal asymmetry of complex systems:

“"The understanding of complexity and the use of the creativity of nature, the continuation of the work of nature are the grand challenges for the scientists of the 21st century."”

— Ilya Prigogine, Is Future Given?

For Shan, Prigogine's arrow of time provides a physical grounding for her claim that sequence matters. The reason Dao precedes Li is not arbitrary: it reflects the irreversibility of how order forms. You cannot reverse the process by which a path was made and still arrive at the same path. The directionality of formation is not a contingent feature but a structural one.

Kauffman's work on self-organisation and emergence provides one of the most important bridges between biology and complexity theory. His key insight: complex systems spontaneously generate order without external instruction, at the "edge of chaos" between rigid order and pure randomness:

“"The past three centuries of science have been predominantly reductionist... The reductionist program has been spectacularly successful, and will continue to be so. But it has often left a vacuum: How do we use the information gleaned about the parts to build up a theory of the whole? The deep difficulty here lies in the fact that the complex whole may exhibit properties that are not readily explained by understanding the parts. The complex whole, in a completely nonmystical sense, can often exhibit collective properties, 'emergent' features that are lawful in their own right."”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1996)

Kauffman's concept of the "adjacent possible" — the set of possibilities that become available from any given state — resonates directly with Shan's account of how paths shape the possibility space for future paths. What is adjacent from one position is not adjacent from another. The field of the possible is itself a product of formation history.

David Snowden's Cynefin framework provides one of the most widely used practical tools for navigating complexity. His distinction between enabling and governing constraints is directly relevant to Shan's analysis of how systems hold capacity under pressure:

“"An ordered system is like the external skeleton of an insect — it has a rigid shell that is not going to change but within it things may change. An endoskeleton is like our spine — it gives coherence but doesn't contain completely, so you get huge amounts of variation around it. How do you create enabling constraints that effectively allow locally valid solutions to emerge within the governance framework?"”

— David Snowden, "How Leaders Change Culture Through Small Actions"

The Cynefin distinction between enabling and governing constraints maps directly onto Shan's distinction between constraint-that-shapes and constraint-that-collapses: the former maintains holding capacity; the latter narrows the path to the point of structural failure.

Maturana and Varela's concept of autopoiesis — the self-producing, self-maintaining character of living systems — provides an important biological grounding for Shan's relational ontology. Their key insight: living systems do not merely respond to the environment but maintain their organisation through structural coupling with it.

“"Living systems are cognitive systems, and living as a process is a process of cognition. This statement is valid for all organisms, with and without a nervous system."”

— Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, Autopoiesis and Cognition (1980)

Their concept of "structural coupling" — where organism and environment reciprocally shape each other through repeated interaction — is a biological version of Shan's mutual generation. What appears as a formed path is the sedimentation of a long history of structural coupling between a living system and its environment.

Edgar Morin's "method of complexity" — "la pensée complexe" — argues that adequate thinking about complex phenomena must hold together what analytical thought separates: order and disorder, the one and the many, the universal and the particular. His dialogic principle holds that opposites must be held in productive tension rather than collapsed into synthesis:

Morin's dialogic principle — the holding of antagonistic principles together without resolving them — is structurally analogous to Shan's mutual generation, Fuller's tension-compression dialectic, and the Yin-Yang dynamic of Chinese philosophy.

Luhmann's systems theory is the most formally rigorous account of social complexity in the Western tradition. His central claim: modern society is functionally differentiated into autopoietic subsystems (economy, law, science, education) that each operate according to their own binary code and cannot be directly steered from outside.

Luhmann's concept of "structural coupling" between systems — the selective connection between autopoietic systems that allows influence without direct control — is a formal parallel to Shan's coupling that transforms without equalising.

Meadows' work on leverage points — places in a system where a small change can produce large effects — provides a practical framework that resonates with Shan's account of how path-shaping moves work. Her famous hierarchy places "the goal of the system" above "the rules of the system" above "the flows," suggesting that the highest leverage lies in the structural goals that shape the whole trajectory, not in individual interventions.

Bateson's "the pattern that connects" — his name for the meta-pattern that links mind, nature, and the living world — is one of the most compelling precedents for Shan's Li. His question "What is the pattern which connects all living creatures?" is precisely the question that Li, as inner grain, is designed to address.

Capra's "web of life" framework explicitly connects Western systems thinking to Eastern philosophical traditions, arguing that the pattern of life itself is relational rather than reductionist. His account of the "systems view of life" — where mind, life, and matter are understood as nested patterns of organisation — provides a bridge between Shan's relational dynamics and Western complexity science.

The Dao De Jing is the first sustained philosophical engagement with Dao, and it establishes several of the themes Shan is working with. Most crucially:

“"道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。"”

(Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng.)

"The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name." — Dao De Jing, Chapter 1

This is Laozi's version of the inexpressibility problem — the problem that Wittgenstein will approach from the side of logic and Shan from the side of grain. What can be said always falls short of what can be shown. The eternal Dao exceeds any naming, which is why Dao must precede Li: the path exceeds its own intelligibility.

“"为学日益，为道日损，损之又损，以至于无为。"”

(Wèi xué rì yì, wèi dào rì sǔn.) "In pursuit of learning, something is acquired every day; in pursuit of the Dao, something is relinquished every day." — Dao De Jing, Chapter 48

“"My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in pursuit of the limitless is fatal."”

— Zhuangzi, Cook Ding

Zhuangzi's story of Cook Ding — whose knife follows the natural articulations of the ox's body without effort because he has learned the Li of the animal — is one of the most luminous illustrations of what Li means as working intelligence. The cook does not cut against the grain; he follows the grain. This is what Shan means when she says Li is the condition under which something becomes "workable and manageable."

Wang Yangming challenged Zhu Xi's method of gewu by arguing that Li cannot be found by investigating things externally. It must be discovered by turning inward to the moral mind-heart (xin). His famous failed attempt to "investigate the Li" of bamboo outside his window led him to conclude that Li is not in things but in the mind's encounter with things.

This is a second dialectical position on Li that Shan's framework must navigate: is Li in the grain of things themselves, or in the mind's encounter with them? Shan's answer — that Li is the grain through which things "become recognisable" — leans toward Wang Yangming's position without fully embracing it: recognition is relational, happening at the interface of mind and thing, observer and system.

The Deep Convergence

The most structurally intimate dialogue in this paper is between Shan's relational dynamics and Fuller's tensegrity. Both are structural accounts of how integrity is maintained not by rigidity but by the distribution of tension through continuous relational networks. Both resist the assumption that stability requires a dominant compressive core. Both locate the condition of structural integrity in the continuous tensional embrace of the whole.

Fuller's claim that "tension is the great integrity" translates directly into Shan's framework: excellence is maintained not by avoiding constraint but by distributing it. The constraint in a tensegrity structure is not a problem to be solved; it is the condition of structural coherence. The tension members are not a weakness; they are the source of the whole's integrity. Similarly, in Shan's framework, constraint over time is not what undermines excellence but what tests and maintains it.

Fuller's Dymaxion principle — maximum benefit from minimum input — maps precisely onto Shan's account of what long-game intelligence looks like. AlphaGo's Move 37 is Dymaxion intelligence: the move that achieves maximum positional benefit from minimum local investment. It does not seek immediate material gain; it restructures the field within which future gains become possible. This is tensegrity applied to strategy: not the single strong compression member that bears all the load, but the continuous tensional network that distributes force so efficiently that each element does less while the whole holds more.

Where Shan Challenges Fuller

Fuller's tensegrity is primarily spatial and energetic. It describes how structural integrity is maintained at a moment in time. Shan's framework is temporal and relational: it asks how structural integrity forms over time, how it drifts, and how it can be read when it is beginning to fail. Shan's insight that "nothing collapses in one move" and that "surface function and underlying viability do not always decline together" adds a temporal and phenomenological dimension that Fuller's structural philosophy does not include.
