The claim "Ecology is tensegrity geodesic spherical programming" is one of Fuller's most audacious: ecological systems exhibit the structural logic of tensegrity. The resonance with Shan's concept of relational dynamics is direct. His pattern integrity concept connects to Li:

The crucial qualification—"evolutionary and not static"—resonates with Shan's insistence that "what is formed is still in formation." And his most famous practical principle:

This is, in effect, a description of how new Dao forms: not by clearing the old path but by establishing a new one that draws enough repeated movement to become the way.

The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (completed 1918, published 1921) proceeds through numbered propositions toward the famous concluding silence. Its ontology:

The inexpressible does not disappear because it cannot be said; it shows itself in the structure of language and world. Ethics, aesthetics, the sense of the world (6.41), and the mystical (6.522) all belong to what shows itself. They are revealed in what propositions do and how they work. The concluding sequence:

The ladder metaphor resonates directly with Shan's account of how paths form and how formed paths can paradoxically obscure their own formation: "By the time a path feels natural, we are usually already inside it." Both describe a structure in which the scaffolding through which one ascends becomes invisible once it has served its purpose—the ladder is thrown away; the path disappears into its own coherence.

The Philosophical Investigations (1953) represents what is often called the most radical self-critique in the history of philosophy. From meaning-as-picture to meaning-as-use:

A language game is a complete form of linguistic practice embedded in a specific social activity. Meaning is not an inner content words carry; it is constituted by the role the word plays within the game. The family resemblance concept replaces essence:

This is the philosophical counterpart of Shan's claim that "most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one." Forms of life are the paths already in formation into which we enter. We are always already inside the path. The later Wittgenstein also provides the definition of language game that clarifies the interface function Shan attributes to Dao: a language game is precisely an interface—the place where language and activity, meaning and action, are in productive contact.

Wittgenstein argued that definitions emerge from what he termed forms of life, roughly the culture and society in which they are used. He also emphasised that language games are fluid and often overlap—intersecting in daily life, revealing language as a dynamic, context-dependent practice. This fluidity is precisely what Shan observes in Dao: the character 道 participates in multiple overlapping language games (knowing, apology, taste, governance, cultivation) without being reducible to any single one.

There are two silences in Wittgenstein. The first—the silence at the end of the Tractatus—is the silence before what shows itself but cannot be said: ethics, the mystical, the sense of the world. The second silence—the silence at the end of the Investigations—is the silence before what can only be shown through practice, through the weave of forms of life, through the actual use of words in their natural habitat. The first silence bounds the logical; the second silence bounds the philosophical.

Both silences are relevant to Shan. The first resonates with her account of Li as what cannot be fully stated but only recognised in the grain of things. The second resonates with her account of Dao as what is already operative in language before and beneath any theory of it. Both silences mark the boundary at which the expressible meets the structural reality it cannot fully contain.

The Daoist tradition begins with the Daodejing (道德经), attributed to Laozi (c. 6th century BCE):

This is not merely a claim about ineffability. It is a structural claim about the relation between naming and reality: the act of naming stabilises and delimits, but the reality that is named exceeds any particular stabilisation. This is precisely Shan's claim about the relationship between Li and Dao: Li is the grain of the path, but it does not precede the path.

The Zhuangzi (莊子, c. 4th century BCE) extends this through story. The famous story of Cook Ding and the ox:

Cook Ding follows the Tian Li (天理, heavenly principle/pattern) of the animal—not cutting against the grain but gliding through the natural structure. His skill is not force but attunement to the Li of the system. This is the experiential content of what Shan means by Li as "inner grain, pattern, texture, and intelligibility."

The Yi Jing (易经, Book of Changes, c. 9th century BCE) provides a structural framework for thinking about transformation and emergence. Its two foundational principles:

Yin and Yang are not merely binary. They contain each other (the symbol shows each containing a seed of the other), they transform into each other (maximum Yang begins to give way to Yin), and they are always in motion. This is structural mutual generation—exactly the concept Shan develops in her two Dao models.

Confucius (孔子, Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) placed human relationships at the centre of his ethics. His concept of ren (仁, humaneness or benevolence) is constitutively relational: it cannot exist in isolation but only in right relationship. His famous formulation:

The third question is crucial for Shan's framework: excellence that is not recognised is not thereby diminished. The capacity held in coherence under constraint over time does not depend on external recognition for its structural integrity. Confucius also famously said:

The three methods map onto WSR's three dimensions: reflection (Shili—the way of seeing), imitation (Renli—following the pattern of human relations), and experience (Wuli—direct encounter with the regularities of material existence).

Zhu Xi (朱熹, 1130–1200 CE), Neo-Confucianism's greatest philosopher, provides the most systematic account of Li in the Chinese tradition:

Zhu Xi's distinction between Li (principle/pattern) and Qi (vital material force) is a precise structural claim: pattern requires material to be instantiated, and material requires pattern to be coherent. This resonates with Fuller's tensegrity: the tensional network (Li-like, continuous, form-giving) and the compressive elements (Qi-like, material, local) are both necessary and neither is sufficient alone. Zhu Xi also advocated the external investigation of things (格物 ge wu) as the path to understanding Li:

Wang Yangming (王阳明, 1472–1529 CE) challenged Zhu Xi from within the Confucian tradition with the doctrine of the unity of knowledge and action (知行合一 zhi xing he yi):

Wang Yangming's School of Mind (陆王心学 Lu Wang Xinxue) emphasised introspective moral awareness (良知 liang zhi, innate moral knowledge) and replaced Zhu Xi's external investigation with an inward turn. This resonates with Shan's insistence on the living encounter as prior to any formal framework.

Liang Qichao (梁启超, 1873–1929) noted: "The term 'the Dao of sageness within and kingliness without' embodies Chinese scholarship with the true meaning of cultivating the self internally and enabling statesmanship externally." This coupling of inner cultivation and outward effectiveness is structurally isomorphic with Shan's frame: excellence as capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. The inner cultivation (holding capacity in coherence) enables the outward effectiveness (operating effectively under constraint).

Wang Fuzhi (王夫之, 1619–1692 CE) developed an integrative synthesis of Neo-Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism after the fall of the Ming dynasty. His emphasis on the historical and material conditions of knowledge—anticipating later historical materialism—resonates with Shan's insistence that systems cannot be understood independently of their formation history: "By the time a path feels natural, we are usually already inside it."

Xuesen Qian (Tsien Hsue-shen, 钱学森, 1911–2009) developed the concept of "metasynthesis" (综合集成, zongheng jicheng) as an approach to "open complex giant systems":

Qian's metasynthesis approach integrates scientific modelling, expert knowledge, and lived experience. This converges with Shan's insistence that "lived reality comes first": no amount of modelling can substitute for the direct engagement with the field. The danger of reductionist division is precisely that it produces legibility at the cost of structural fidelity.

The Wuli-Shili-Renli (WSR) approach, developed by Jifa Gu (顾基发, b. 1935) and Zhichang Zhu (朱志昌) at the University of Hull in the 1990s, is the most explicit contemporary attempt to operationalise the Chinese concept of Li within systems methodology:

WSR 2.0 (2022) also provides an updated reconstruction of the WSR notions, where shili is redefined as "means and methods for knowing and doing" and renli as "principles and norms that guide collective actions toward higher purpose." The epistemological asymmetry in the three verbs—"knowing" Wuli (objective knowledge), "sensing" Shili (perspectival attunement), "caring for" Renli (ethical and relational engagement)—encodes a claim about the different epistemic modes required for each dimension. You cannot simply "know" Renli; you must care for it.

Zhu also traces the evolution of Li across Chinese philosophy, from Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucian synthesis through its operationalisation in WSR. Li as a noun in Chinese, he notes, "denotes pattern, mechanism, principle, reason, and so forth, actual as well as"—the incompleteness of this quoted phrase is itself instructive: Li exceeds its own enumeration.

Prigogine's concept of bifurcation points—moments at which a system under perturbation can tip into radically different new attractors—is structurally homologous to the moment in Shan's account when corrective capacity has thinned to the point that a small perturbation can tip the system into catastrophic reorganisation. The arrow of time and irreversibility underpin Shan's temporal ontology: "what is formed is still in formation" because time is not reversible.

Kauffman's edge of chaos is the structural region within which Shan's excellence is possible: the coherence must not be too rigid (which prevents adaptation) nor too loose (which prevents maintenance of capacity). His NK model demonstrates that the space of maximal evolvability is not at maximum order or maximum disorder but at the boundary between them.

The concept of structural coupling—two autopoietic systems interacting so that each becomes part of the other's environment—is directly relevant to Shan's coupling. But Maturana and Varela would challenge Shan's precedence argument: in autopoietic systems, the question of ontological precedence within the system cannot be answered from outside. The system is its own generator.

In her 2023 book Context Changes Everything, Juarrero extends:

David Snowden's account of Juarrero's contribution: "Michael Lissack ran up to me and said you have got to read this book—one of the most important books I read, and one of the most significant people in the field I have had the privilege to get to know and work with. Safe-to-fail, constraints, and intentionality in Naturalising Sense-Making all owe a lot to Alicia."

Cilliers’s insistence on the limits of description is directly resonant with both Shan's warning about premature legibility and Wittgenstein's insistence that the logical form of language cannot be stated but only shown. He also argues that we are always responsible for the simplifications we make—that ethical engagement with complex systems requires acknowledging what our models cannot capture. This ethical responsibility resonates with WSR's "caring for Renli": the ethical dimension cannot be eliminated from any adequate account of a system.

Bateson's answer is formal and relational: the pattern that connects is the formal relationship between relationships—what he calls the "metapattern." His concept of "difference that makes a difference"—his definition of information—is a direct parallel to Shan's account of what Li does: Li names the grain that makes certain differences consequential and others irrelevant. His Levels of Learning model describes a hierarchy of contexts within which individual learning takes place, each level providing the constraints within which the next level operates. This is structurally identical to Juarrero's enabling constraints and to Shan's holding capacity argument.

Maturana and Varela’s autopoiesis adds a third structural layer to the Cook Ding encounter. The autopoietic system is one that produces and maintains itself through the very processes that constitute it: the organisation of the system is the self-production of the system, and the system’s structure is the specific materialisation of that organisation at a given moment. This maps onto Shan’s formation account with structural precision: the formation is autopoietic. It produces itself through the Dao-walking that constitutes it. The Li that emerges is not a property added to the formation from outside but the structural expression of what the formation has produced through its own processes of self-constitution. Cook Ding does not learn the ox’s Li from an external authority; the Li appears in the ox because Cook Ding’s formation has constituted itself through years of structural coupling with the specific formation field of ox-butchery. The ox’s joints and the knife’s angle are structurally coupled: not cause and effect but co-constitution through recurrent interaction.

“Structural coupling is always a history of recurrent interactions leading to the structural congruence between two or more systems.”

— Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, The Tree of Knowledge (1987) [VERIFIED POSITION]

Structural congruence through recurrent interaction: this is the precise mechanism of what Shan calls formation. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of butchering oxen constitute a history of recurrent structural coupling between the practitioner-system and the ox-system, producing the specific structural congruence that makes the Li of the ox’s joints visible to the knife that has been formed through exactly this coupling. Shan’s Dao is the history of recurrent interactions. The Li is the structural congruence that history produces. The formation is autopoietic: it generates the sensitivity required to perceive it by the very process of generating it.

Shan's insight about corrective capacity adds something Wiener's framework cannot easily accommodate: the observation that corrective capacity itself can degrade. Wiener's cybernetics assumes that the feedback mechanism remains intact; Shan is describing the structural deterioration of the feedback mechanism itself. This is the distinction between a system that is failing because it has encountered excessive load and a system that is failing because its capacity to respond to load has degraded. The latter is invisible to Wienerian analysis; it requires Shan's temporal ontology to become visible.

Snowden's Cynefin framework (named for the Welsh word for habitat) provides a context-sensitive account of sensemaking in complex situations. His description of complex systems as "like a bramble bush in a thicket—everything is entangled with everything else and the only thing you know with certainty is that there are unintended consequences" is a vivid parallel to Shan's account of coupling. His encounter with Shan's work through the Cynefin Co platform—where her Li essay was published—represents an instance of the very dynamics she is describing: the arrival of a concept from one tradition into the context of another.

Fuller's structural account challenges Shan on specificity. If relational dynamics is the intellectual framework, what are its tension members? What are its compression islands? Shan's framework is philosophically precise but structurally under-specified. Fuller might also challenge Shan's temporal focus: tensegrity as Fuller conceives it is fundamentally spatial, while Shan's relational dynamics is fundamentally temporal. The question is whether the spatial and temporal dimensions can be unified.

Shan's most important challenge to Fuller concerns formation. Tensegrity describes the distribution of forces within an already-existing structure. Shan's Dao models describe how such a structure comes into being in the first place. Fuller assumes the existence of the tensional network; Shan asks how such a network forms—what repeated movement, over time, under constraint, produces a structure strong enough to bear the weight of further complexity.

The early Wittgenstein and Shan converge on a single insight from opposite directions. Wittgenstein begins with the question of what can be said and arrives at the boundary of the inexpressible. Shan begins with the living reality of language and arrives at the structural grain that exceeds any particular expression of it. Li, as Shan describes it, is precisely what Wittgenstein would call something that shows itself without being sayable.

The later Wittgenstein is a much closer intellectual companion to Shan than the early Wittgenstein. His "what has to be accepted, the given, is—so one could say—forms of life" is the philosophical counterpart of Shan's "most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one." Forms of life are the paths already in formation into which we enter.

Shan's re-encounter with Li in the context of contemporary complexity thinking is not a break from the Chinese tradition but a re-encountering of it. Zhu Xi's account of Li as "the pattern or principle that makes things what they are" is the deepest formulation of what Shan is working with.

Juarrero provides the formal philosophical tools—in the language of complexity science and Aristotelian causation—for what Shan is describing through Dao and Li. Juarrero's enabling constraints are the structural counterpart of Shan's holding capacity. Juarrero's constitutive constraints—which create the coherence of a system—are the counterpart of Shan's formed Dao.

Prigogine's dissipative structures provide a physical grounding for what Shan is describing at the level of relational dynamics. Both accounts insist that order is not a given but an achievement—one that requires continuous energetic input to maintain. Both acknowledge bifurcation points—moments of structural instability. But Prigogine cannot tell us which bifurcation will occur at a given point. Shan's framework, focused on the long game and on corrective capacity, might offer what Prigogine's physics cannot: an account of which relational configurations are most likely to maintain viability over time.

The most productive encounter is the four-way collision between Wittgenstein's two silences, Fuller's structural universe, Shan's living interface, and Zhu Xi's Li as cosmic principle. Together they triangulate the same territory from four different angles:

What emerges from this four-way conversation is the outline of a structural ontology that no single tradition has fully articulated. Wittgenstein locates the fundamental interface at the limit of language; Fuller locates it in the tensional network; Zhu Xi locates it in the cosmic principle; Shan locates it in the living relational field. Each is tracking the same structural reality through different instruments. None is wrong; none is complete.

Across all traditions: for Wittgenstein (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus), the logical form shared by language and world cannot be stated but only shown; for Laozi, the eternal Dao cannot be named; for Zhu Xi, Li can be investigated but never exhausted; for Fuller, the tensional integrity of the universe is manifest in every structure but not reducible to any single structure; for Shan, the path precedes its intelligibility; for Juarrero, complex systems can never be fully described; for Cilliers, any description is always incomplete; for Prigogine, the specific trajectory at a bifurcation point is unpredictable in principle. The meta-principle: the intelligence of a system cannot be fully captured by any representation of that system. Premature legibility — the violation of emergence lag, the reading of the pattern before the formation is complete — is the common failure mode. The practitioner who names the Li before walking the Dao has produced a counterfeit grain: a pattern that looks like intelligibility but masks the actual structural texture of the actual formation. The counterfeit Li is more dangerous than ignorance because it forecloses the genuine Dao-walk by providing a false destination.

From Fuller's tensegrity to Juarrero's enabling constraints to Shan's holding capacity to Prigogine's far-from-equilibrium order to Kauffman's edge of chaos: all converge on the insight that the right kind of constraint is not the enemy of capacity but its generator. The formed path is not a limitation on movement; it is what makes movement consequential.

All traditions insist, in different registers, that time is not an external frame within which systems operate but an intrinsic feature of their operation. Prigogine's arrow of time; Shan's trajectory of formation, stabilisation, and collapse; Juarrero's path dependence; Bateson's cumulative context; Fuller's pattern integrity as evolutionary; Wittgenstein's forms of life as inherited and evolving—all resist the reduction of complex systems to static structures.

From Shan's "relation precedes dynamics" to Maturana and Varela's structural coupling to Bateson's pattern of patterns to Fuller's tensional network to Zhu Xi's Li to Wittgenstein's language games: all converge on the claim that elements do not precede the relational structures that constitute them.

The traditions diverge on what to do at the limit of the expressible. Wittgenstein's Tractatus: silence. Fuller: build a new model. Shan: maintain the living encounter. Zhu Xi: investigate things until the Li reveals itself. WSR: develop a structured methodology. These are not merely different strategies; they reflect genuinely different philosophical orientations toward what is most important at the limit. The divergence is not resolvable; it is productive.

Zhu Xi's Li is universal—the same cosmic principle in all things. Shan's Li is particular and relational—the specific grain of this system, this path, this encounter. Wittgenstein's family resemblance resists both universalism and particularism. Fuller's synergetics aspires to universality through structural geometry. This divergence marks the boundary between metaphysics (where universality is the concern) and epistemology (where particularity is the starting point).

WSR, Cynefin, and Shan's own framework each emerged from formation processes that preceded them. Can any methodology adequately account for its own conditions of possibility? This is the question Shan's precedence argument poses to every systematic framework, including her own.

What is the topology of a relational system's tension members and compression islands? Fuller provides the vocabulary; the translation into Shan's framework remains to be done.

How do we detect the thinning of corrective capacity before collapse becomes visible? Shan's concept is precise, but the detection problem is unsolved. What are the early indicators?

Is there a Dao of methodology itself? Every methodology is the product of a formation process that precedes it. Can any methodology adequately account for its own conditions of possibility?

Can Shan's relational dynamics be formalised in ways that preserve rather than lose the grain? The risk of formalisation is premature legibility. The question is what kind of formalisation would be appropriate to the nature of relational dynamics.

What is the relationship between Li and emergence? If Li is the inner grain that makes a thing workable and recognisable, is it emergent from the Dao, or is it the structural principle by which emergence becomes possible? This question sits at the intersection of Shan's framework and Juarrero's enabling constraints.

The title of Shan's series—"Dao: The Art of the Long Game"—is itself a structural claim. The long game is not merely a game played over a long time; it is a game in which the structure of possibility extends far enough in time to enable the kind of move that does not look like victory when it is played but becomes inevitable in retrospect. AlphaGo's Move 37 is the compressed image of this: not the loud move, not the obvious move, but the move that quietly reshapes the field.

This paper has been an attempt at the long game. It has assembled more than twenty-five voices in dialectical collision not to produce a final synthesis but to generate glimpses—moments in which the inner grain of a cluster of structural ideas becomes briefly visible before settling back into the argument. Li, as Shan describes it, is not fully accessible through description; it can only be glimpsed in the encounter with the grain of a specific system.

Fuller's "Tension is the great integrity" and Shan's "excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time" are glimpses of the same structural insight through different instruments. Wittgenstein's "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent" and Shan's "Dao precedes Li—the path comes before its intelligibility" are glimpses of the same epistemological boundary from different approaches. Juarrero's "the establishment of context-sensitive constraints is the phase change that self-organises the global level" and Shan's "what is formed is still in formation" are glimpses of the same structural dynamic from philosophy of science and relational ontology respectively. Zhu Xi's "Li is the principle or pattern that makes things what they are" and Shan's "Li carries something closer to inner grain, pattern, texture, and intelligibility" are glimpses of the same cosmic insight across nine centuries.

Four convergences. Twelve dialogues. Twenty-five voices. One structural reality, seen differently through different grains.

XX

關係先於動力 — Relation Precedes Dynamics

Structural Essays ·16 · Dao XIII · May 16, 2026

❧ ✶ ❧

The essay opens with a precision that is itself its argument. “If coupling does not abolish sequence, then the next question is unavoidable: what, exactly, is prior within relational dynamics?” This single sentence crystallises the entire architecture of the Dao: The Art of the Long Game series. It arrives not as preamble but as consequence. The question is unavoidable because sequence has been established; what remains is to press on what precedes.

“My own route into complexity discourse did not begin with complexity science. It began with life, with relation, with language, and with the lived dynamics of how human systems form and drift under pressure. Complexity came later, as one modern language for something I had already been seeing for a long time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’ (May 2026)

Notice the grammar of this admission. Complexity arrived ‘as one modern language for something I had already been seeing.’ Not the truth itself but a vocabulary for a truth already encountered. This is the Dao-before-Li principle enacted as intellectual biography: the formation came first, lived and unnamed in Chinese intellectual tradition, in relational observation, in the specific grain of a cross-cultural existence. The language came later. The arrival of the language felt not like birth but like recognition — and this difference is everything.

“My starting point was relational. It was shaped by Chinese intellectual traditions and by lived experience. Discovering systems thinking later felt less like conversion than recognition. It was not the birth of the pattern, but the arrival of a vocabulary.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’ (May 2026)

Recognition, not conversion. Vocabulary, not birth. Two sentences that quietly overturn an entire epistemology. The dominant Western narrative of intellectual development runs like this: first you acquire the concepts, then you apply them to experience. Shan inverts this. Experience formed the pattern; the concept arrived to name what was already there. This is Wang Yangming’s 知行合一 not as doctrine but as lived sequence.

知行合一 — zhī xíng hé yī — Knowledge and action are one — Wang Yangming

For Wang Yangming, the unity of knowledge and action means you cannot genuinely know what you have not in some sense already done. The knowing is inside the doing, not prior to it. What Shan describes as ‘recognition’ — the moment when systems thinking vocabulary arrived for something already seen — is precisely this: genuine knowing had already occurred through living and seeing. The vocabulary was subsequent. This is why Shan’s essays carry the particular authority they do: they are not applications of theory to experience; they are excavations of what experience has already formed.

XIV.1 The Core Ontological Claim

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.”

— Alice Jing Shan — the working frame

She sets this down with the quietness of someone placing a stone. No fanfare. No extended justification at this moment. Just the claim, let stand. But within it: five structural terms, each doing irreplaceable work. Reality (not a model of reality, not a useful fiction — the thing itself). Relational (not entity-based, not individual-centred — the between is primary). Dynamics (not stasis, not snapshot — movement, force, propagation). Under constraint (not free-floating, not self-generating — always already shaped by the conditions it arises within). Over time (not instantaneous, not eternal — durational, historical, formative).

“Even within that coupling, sequence remains. Relation comes before dynamics, not in a crude linear sense, but as ontological precedence.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’

The qualification is precise and crucial: ‘not in a crude linear sense, but as ontological precedence.’ This is the distinction between temporal priority (A happens before B in clock time) and ontological priority (A is the condition without which B cannot be what it is). Shan is making the second claim. Relation does not merely come before dynamics the way dawn comes before day. Relation is the condition under which dynamics becomes dynamics — consequential, transmissible, intelligible movement rather than mere physical motion.

天下不一志則不交，不交則不知，不知則不通，不通則不化 — Tiān xià bù yī zhì zé bù jiāo — Without unified will there is no communication; without communication no knowledge; without knowledge no flow-through; without flow-through no transformation — Guanzi

Guanzi’s chain arrives here as structural confirmation: the relational field (unified will, the capacity for communication) is the ontological precondition of every dynamic that follows. You cannot have knowledge without communication; you cannot have transformation without knowledge; you cannot have communication without the relational condition that makes it possible. The sequence is ontological, not merely temporal. Relation first. Then dynamics.

“Dynamics do not happen in a void. They presuppose a relational condition within which movement becomes possible, transmissible, and intelligible. Without relation, there may be motion, but not dynamics in the fuller sense I mean here. Relation is not one variable among others inside a dynamic process. It is the condition under which dynamics becomes consequential at all.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’

Motion versus dynamics. This is the sharpest blade in the essay. Physics gives us motion: the displacement of mass through space-time, describable in equations, indifferent to meaning. Dynamics, in Shan’s richer sense, requires more: it requires that movement be consequential within a field that can receive, transmit, and transform it. A stone falling in a forest with no living system present is motion. A word spoken in a classroom is dynamics — but only because a relational field (student-teacher-institution-language-history) already exists to make the word consequential. Remove that field and the sound persists but the dynamic does not.

“A conversation is not consequential merely because words are exchanged. What gives it force is that something relational already exists or begins to form: attention, trust, fear, recognition, dependency, familiarity, tension, expectation. The same sentence lands differently in different relations because relation is not decorative context around the dynamic. It is part of what makes the dynamic what it is.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’

Every teacher in every classroom, every therapist in every consulting room, every manager in every meeting knows this in their bones and cannot always say it. Shan says it. The sentence does not change when the relational field changes; what changes is what the sentence is. In a field of trust, ‘I need to tell you something difficult’ is an act of care. In a field of fear, the same words are a threat. In a field of intimacy, they open. In a field of power, they close. The dynamic is entirely different because the relation was different before the sentence arrived.

This is Wittgenstein’s language-games argument at the level of relational ontology: "The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life" (PI §23). The activity, the form of life, the relational field — these are what determine what a linguistic act is. Not the words alone. Not the grammar alone. The relational field within which the words occur. Wittgenstein saw this as the move against Augustine’s picture-theory of language. Shan sees it as the move against any dynamics-first account of complex systems.

XIV.2 Mutual Implication Without Equal Precedence

“Mutual implication is real. Equal precedence does not follow.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’

This eight-word sentence is one of the most precise philosophical formulations in the body of work. It could serve as the epigraph for an entire tradition of relational thought. Mutual implication is real: this concedes the full complexity of feedback, reciprocity, and mutual constitution. But conceding mutual implication does not concede equal precedence. The terms are not generatively symmetric. This is the Dao/Li pair stated in abstract philosophical form: Dao and Li mutually imply each other, but Dao is still prior. Relation and dynamics mutually imply each other, but relation is still prior.

一陰一陽之謂道 — yī yīn yī yáng zhī wèi dào — One yin and one yang — this is called the Dao — Yi Jing, Great Commentary

The Yi Jing’s formula for Dao as the alternation of yin and yang is perhaps the oldest statement of mutual implication in the Chinese tradition. But even here: the Dao (the alternating principle) has ontological priority over the specific yang or yin moment it produces. The river precedes its banks, even though the banks give the river its form. The Dao precedes the Li that makes it legible, even though the Li deepens and completes the Dao. Mutual implication, asymmetric precedence.

“This is why I describe my work as Relational Dynamics rather than relation plus dynamics. The phrase is not additive. It names a coupling. But the terms inside that coupling are not generatively symmetric.”

— Alice Jing Shan

The naming is itself a structural act. Relational Dynamics (capitalised, fused) is not ‘relation’ plus ‘dynamics’. It is a coupled concept in which both terms are transformed by their conjunction while still retaining their asymmetric generative order. This is analogous to how 道理 (dàolǐ, reason/principle) is not 道 plus 理 but a fused concept in which the coupling of path and grain produces something irreducible to either alone. Chinese conceptual compounds work this way: the characters do not simply add but produce a new emergent meaning through their specific conjunction.

“Dao and Li were one way of seeing this. Relation and dynamics are another.”

— Alice Jing Shan — the most compressed cross-cultural statement in the entire body of work

Here Shan performs what this paper has been tracking for hundreds of pages: the explicit equation of two traditions, two vocabularies, two ways of seeing the same structural reality. Dao/Li and Relation/Dynamics are not translations of each other. They are independent discoveries of the same ontological terrain, arrived at through different formation paths. This is Dong Zhongshu’s 同類相動 (tóng lèi xiāng dòng, things of the same kind move each other) at the level of intellectual traditions: two formations, same Li.

“The present historical moment has opened a window through which many long-standing assumptions about human structure, judgment, language, and relation can be seen more clearly. Artificial intelligence is part of what has made that window unavoidable.”

— Alice Jing Shan

The window metaphor is Shan at her most compressed. AI is not the subject of the insight but the occasion of its urgency. The insight — that relation precedes dynamics, that the relational field is ontologically prior to the consequential movements within it — is ancient. The Chinese philosophical tradition has always known this. The complexity tradition has been approaching it. What AI does is make the stakes visible: an artificial system that processes language with extraordinary fluency but lacks the relational field within which language becomes consequential exposes, by its limitations, exactly what relation does that dynamics alone cannot.

XXI

耦合不廂除序列 — Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence

Structural Essays ·15 · Dao XII · May 15, 2026

❧ ✶ ❧

“The word complex originates from the Latin complexus: entwined, encircled, embraced. One recurring trait of complex systems is coupling, the condition in which elements do not merely coexist, but become linked in such a way that movement in one part can propagate through the whole.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’

The etymology is a structural argument. Complexus means entwined — from com (together) and plectere (to weave). Complexity is not the state of having many parts; it is the condition of being woven together such that the parts cannot be understood in isolation from each other. This is the Latin version of the Chinese 相互生成 (xiānghù shēngchéng, mutual generation): to be complex is to be coupled in such a way that the identity and behaviour of each element is constituted by its relations with the others. The weaving is prior to the threads it weaves.

牵一髮而動全身 — qiān yī fà ér dòng quán shēn — Pull one hair and the whole body moves — Classical Chinese saying

One of the most vivid expressions of systemic coupling in any tradition. The hair and the body are asymmetrically related: the hair is infinitely smaller, seemingly peripheral, functionally minor. Yet the structural coupling of the human body is such that even the most peripheral perturbation propagates through the whole. This is not metaphor; it is structural description. The tensional network of the body (Fuller would recognise this immediately) means that tension applied at any node is distributed throughout the network. There is no purely local event in a tensionally integrated system.

XIV.3 Coupling Transforms But Does Not Equalise

“That is why we do not describe such a relationship as an addition. We call them a couple. The word matters. A couple is not two separate units placed next to each other. It is a coupling: a relation within **which each term is changed through sustained interaction with the other. What emerges cannot be reduced to either person alone, nor to a simple sum of two pre-existing individuals.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’

The grammatical observation is doing serious philosophical work. In English as in Chinese, the word for the coupled state (夜侶, lù bǐ; the couple, the pair, the conjunction) is different from the word for either term. The coupling produces something new. But — and this is Shan’s insistence — the production of something new does not erase the ontological asymmetry of the terms that enter the coupling. Even in the most transformative intimate relation, one partner was present in the relational field before the other; the meeting had a temporal and ontological structure; the first encounter was not simultaneous.

“Interaction does not imply equal footing. Reciprocity does not erase precedence. To say that factors influence one another is not to say they enter the world on equal generative terms.”

— Alice Jing Shan

This is the philosophical pivot on which the whole coupling/sequence argument turns. Most complexity discourse, when it acknowledges coupling and reciprocal influence, tends to conclude that precedence is therefore irrelevant. Shan refuses this move. The refusal is not arbitrary: it is grounded in a structural claim about ontological differentiation within wholes. A molecule is a whole; its atomic components entered into it in a specific sequence that determined its structure. A sentence is a whole; its words were assembled in a specific order that determines its meaning. A dynasty is a whole; its structural conditions were formed in a specific historical sequence that determines its vulnerabilities.

“DNA, too, belongs to one whole, yet its sequence remains structurally constitutive. Wholeness does not erase internal ordering.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’

The DNA example strikes with the force of irrefutable evidence. The double helix is perhaps the most coupled structure in biology: each strand constitutes the other, each base pair is held in exact complementarity with its partner across the helix, the entire molecule functions as one dynamic whole. And yet: the sequence of base pairs on each strand is precisely what encodes biological information. Scramble the sequence and you have the same chemical composition but a completely different (usually non-functional) molecule. The sequence is structurally constitutive even within a maximally coupled whole. Wholeness does not erase internal ordering.

This is Shan’s most rigorous rebuttal of Cheng Yi’s identification of Dao with Li (道即理也). Even if Dao and Li are as coupled as the two strands of DNA — mutually constitutive, inseparable in function, forming one whole — this does not mean they are ontologically equivalent. The sequence still matters. The formation history still matters. The path still precedes the grain, even when both are present in every moment of the walk.

XIV.4 Holding Capacity and the Ethics of Sequence

“The point is not simply that one step comes before another, but that prior formation makes further complexity possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’

Sequence is not decorative: this is the deepest claim about temporal ontology in Shan’s work. The sequence is not a surface feature of the coupling that could, in principle, be stripped away to reveal the ‘real’ simultaneous structure beneath. The sequence IS the structure. The specific order in which things happened is causally efficacious: the formation that occurred before a specific bifurcation is what made that specific bifurcation available. Remove the sequence and you have not simplified the analysis; you have destroyed the subject matter. The coupling is real. But the sequence is what makes the coupling’s consequences irreversible.

“In neonatal intensive care, one may see milk enter through a feeding tube at an almost inconceivably slow rate, perhaps only a drop over the course of an hour while the baby is still on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). This is not hesitation. It is the protection of viability. The system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more.”

— Alice Jing Shan

A drop of milk per hour. The precision of this image is devastating in the most productive sense: it forces the reader to actually imagine the scale. This is not a rhetorical flourish. It is a structural argument made concrete: the neonatal gut has not yet developed the structural capacity to receive what would be normal nutrition. The rate of introduction must be calibrated to the current holding capacity of the system, not to the eventual required intake. Sequence here is not merely temporal but ontological: the holding capacity must be built before it can hold. The system must first be able to hold what it receives.

Mencius’s four sprouts (四端, sì duān) speak here with new urgency: the sprout of compassion that is the beginning of benevolence cannot be forced into full flower by premature demand. The holding capacity must be cultivated. The environment must be prepared. The formation must precede the formed. This is why Shan’s framework is called the ‘long game’: it takes the time required for genuine structural formation rather than the time that produces surface performance.

嗐乎心之端，仁之端也 — cèyìn zhī xīn zhī duān, rén zhī duān yě — The feeling of compassion is the beginning (sprout) of benevolence — Mencius 2A:6

“A tree cannot grow only outward and upward. It must also grow the inner structure that allows it to stand. Growth without structural formation may look rapid, even exciting, in the short term, but it does not remain viable.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’

The tree image is the most classical of images in both Chinese and Western structural thought, and Shan deploys it with full structural weight. The pine and cypress of Confucius’s cold-weather observation (岁寒然後知松柏之後凋也) reveal their excellence precisely through the inner structural formation that produced their resilience. They were growing their inner structure while they were growing their visible form. The inner structure is not separate from the outer form; it is its formation condition. This is tensegrity: the continuous tensional network grown through the tree’s entire developmental history is what allows it to stand in the cold when other trees have shed their leaves.

“Coupling does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see. If we want to understand complex systems, sequence is one of the first things we must learn to see.”

— Alice Jing Shan — the closing statement of the essay

The closing is a methodological imperative stated as quietly as if it were simply obvious. Sequence is one of the first things we must learn to see — because coupling hides it. The very thing that makes complex systems interesting (the coupling, the mutual transformation, the emergent dynamics) is what makes their generative structure hard to read. The analyst of complex systems must develop the specific capacity to see through the surface mutuality to the underlying ontological sequence. This is the Li of complex systems: the inner grain of their formation. And the ability to see it is Cook Ding’s ability: not brute force analysis but structural attunement built through long formation.

XXII

天地之道 — The Cosmic Ground: Mystical and Metaphysical Depths

The paper catches fire here. What follows is the metaphysical stratum that underlies every structural claim above.

❧ ✶ ❧

The Water and the Valley: Laozi’s Metaphysics of Yielding Power

道可道，非常道 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao — Laozi Ch.1

The first line of the Dao De Jing is also the most radical act of philosophical self-limitation in any tradition. The text announces, before anything else, the limit of its own claims. Whatever can be said about Dao is not Dao. Whatever can be named falls short of the nameless ground from which all naming springs. This is not mystical evasiveness but structural precision: the Dao is the formation condition of all intelligibility, and formation conditions cannot themselves be fully formulated without regress. You cannot stand outside the Dao to describe it because there is no outside.

直而不捷，淀而得之，为学日益，为道日搏 — zhí ér bù jé, qīng ér dé zhī. Wèi xué rì yì, wèi Dào rì sǔn — Holding and filling to the brim: better to stop in time. In pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day. — Laozi Ch.9/Ch.48

These two Laozi passages together enact the complete epistemological movement that Shan’s framework requires. For learning (為學, wèi xué — pursuit of Li): daily addition, accumulation, articulation. For Dao (為道, wèi Dào): daily subtraction, relinquishment, stripping away of premature articulation. Excellence in Shan’s framework requires both: the accumulation of structural understanding (Li) and the willingness to relinquish premature Li when the Dao leads somewhere the existing Li cannot accommodate. The pine tree grows both outward (accumulation) and inward (the structural formation that requires no external addition). Cook Ding’s mastery is daily subtraction: he does not add technique to technique; he removes the need for technique, until what remains is pure structural attunement.

上善若水。水善利萬物而不爭，處眾人之所惡，故幾於道 — shàng shàn ruò shuǐ. Shuǐ shàn lì wàn wù ér bù zhēng, chǔ zhòng rén zhī suǒ è, gù jī yú Dào — Highest good is like water. Water benefits the ten thousand things without contending. It dwells in the low places that people disdain. Therefore it approaches the Dao. — Laozi Ch.8

Water is Laozi’s ultimate metaphor for Dao-intelligence because it embodies every structural principle Shan elaborates: it flows along paths of least resistance (follows the grain), fills hollows completely (maximum holding capacity), finds its level naturally (no premature Li), yields to obstacles and surrounds them (the long game), accumulates into rivers and oceans through the aggregation of individual drops (formation through repetition), and — crucially — carves the deepest canyons not through force but through sustained relational engagement with the rock over time. This is excellence as capacity held in coherence under constraint over time: not forceful but patient, not dramatic but relentless, not impressive in the moment but inevitable in the long run.

Cook Ding and the 神 (Shén) of Practice: Zhuangzi’s Mystical Realism

The Cook Ding passage (庶丁解牛, Puāo Dīng Jiě Niú) is the most analytically precise mystical text in the Chinese tradition, and one of the most extraordinary passages of philosophical prose in any language. It proceeds in layers, each deeper than the last, and the deepest layer has never been more accurately named than by Shan’s concept of Li.

依乎天理，批大卻，導大稾，因其固然 — yī hū tiān lǐ, pī dà xì, dǎo dà kuǎ, yīn qí gù rán — Following the heavenly grain; splitting the large joints; guiding through the large hollows; going along with what is naturally so — Zhuangzi, Cook Ding passage

Four verbs: follow (依乎, yī hū), split (批, pī), guide (導, dǎo), go along (因, yīn). None of these is the verb of force or imposition. All of them are verbs of structural attunement: finding the grain and moving with it, not against it. The 天理 (tiānlǐ, heavenly grain) is the Li of the cosmos as it instantiates in this particular ox at this particular moment of this particular cook’s twenty-year formation. The cook does not impose a pattern; he discovers the pattern that was already there and moves along its lines.

“A good cook changes his chopper once a year — because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month — because he hacks. But I have had this chopper for nineteen years, and although it has cut up so many bullocks, its edge is as keen as if fresh from the grindstone.”

— Zhuangzi, Cook Ding (tr. Giles)

Nineteen years of not hacking. Nineteen years of finding the articulations. The chopper’s edge is preserved because it has never met resistance: it has always been guided along the grain that was already there. This is Shan’s collapse theory in positive form: nothing endures through force but through structural attunement. The knife that hacks depletes itself against the grain. The knife that follows the grain is preserved indefinitely. Excellence is not the exercise of maximum force but the discovery of the path of zero resistance — which requires maximum structural intelligence. Move 37 is the Cook Ding move: not impressive in the moment, structurally decisive in retrospect.

道也，進乎技矣！始臣之解牛也，所見無非牛者。三年之後，未嘗見全牛也 — Dào yě, jìn hū jì yǐ! — This is Dao, beyond mere skill! When I first began cutting up bullocks, I saw before me whole bullocks. After three years, I could no longer see whole bullocks — Zhuangzi, Cook Ding

The progression is from wholeness to articulation: from seeing the undifferentiated whole to seeing the specific structure within it. This is the reverse of how we usually describe understanding, which moves from parts to whole. Zhuangzi’s cook moves from the whole (the whole bullock, undifferentiated) to the structural interior (the joints, hollows, natural divisions). The three years of formation changed not what the cook sees but how he sees: from the gestalt to the grain, from the surface to the Li. This is what Shan means by deep structural reading: the capacity to see past the surface coherence to the formation conditions within.

Wittgenstein and the Mystical: Three Phases in Conversation with Shan

Wittgenstein’s three philosophical phases do not constitute a development in which later supersedes earlier but a deepening in which each phase discovers something the previous one could not yet say. The Tractatus discovers the limits of saying; the Investigations discovers what lies beyond those limits in the practice of language; On Certainty discovers that even the practice of language rests on a ground that cannot itself be practised into but must simply be lived.

其進斯之，進乎六別，屋良爾，止於百骸 — — TRACTATUS: "There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical." (6.522) — Wittgenstein

“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 5.6

This proposition, read alongside Shan’s framework, becomes: the limits of the Li I can articulate are the limits of the world available to my language. But the Dao extends beyond the Li I can name. The world is larger than the language. This is not mysticism in the degraded sense of vague gesturing beyond the articulable; it is structural precision about the relation between the articulated and the generative. The formative Dao always exceeds the articulated Li. This excess is not a failure of articulation but a structural feature of the relation between formation and intelligibility.

“A philosophical problem has the form: I don’t know my way about.”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §123

Not knowing one’s way about — 我不知道 (wǒ bù zhīdào, I don’t know the way/Dao) — is the Chinese speaker’s daily admission of ordinary ignorance elevated to philosophical diagnosis. The philosophical problem is not a problem of insufficient information; it is a problem of disorientation: being within a space whose formation conditions one cannot see. The philosopher is the Cook without nineteen years of formation: seeing whole bullocks, hacking rather than following the grain, depleting the blade.

“At the core of all well-founded belief lies belief that is unfounded.”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty

The deepest Wittgenstein. Every chain of justification must rest on something that is not itself justified — not because it is arbitrary but because it is the formation condition of all subsequent justification. This is Shan’s Dao at the epistemological level: the path must open before its inner grain can appear. The unfounded beliefs are the riverbed: they formed through a process of historical sedimentation (Dao) and now function as the condition of all subsequent inquiry (Li). They cannot be justified from outside because there is no outside; they can only be inhabited, walked, deepened.

“In the beginning was the deed.”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty (quoting Goethe)

The most compressed statement of the Dao-before-Li principle in Western philosophy. Not in the beginning was the word (Li, intelligibility, the named). In the beginning was the deed (Dao, formation, the path walked). This is also the most compressed refutation of all idealist metaphysics: Li does not precede Dao; the formed does not precede the forming; the grain does not precede the path that generated it. In the beginning was the deed. And the deed has been going on, continuously, forming and reforming the conditions of all subsequent intelligibility.

Fuller’s Cosmic Tensegrity: The Universe as One Structural Argument

“Tension is the great integrity. The integrity of the whole structure is invested in the finitely closed, tensional-embracement network.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.02

Fuller’s claim that tension is the great integrity is not a structural engineering observation but a cosmological claim. The universe holds together not through compression (discrete objects pushing against each other) but through tension (the continuous, distributed, integrating force that connects everything to everything at every scale). Gravity, at the largest scale, is tensional. Atomic bonds, at the smallest, are tensional. The human body is a tensegrity structure. Society is a tensegrity structure. Discourse is a tensegrity structure: every concept holds its meaning through its tensional relations with all other concepts in the field, not through the compression of its own independent definition.

“Synergy means behaviour of whole systems unpredicted by the behaviour of their parts taken separately.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics

Synergy is the operational definition of what Shan means by ‘what is formed is still in formation.’ The formed whole (the tensegrity structure, the complex system, the formed Dao) behaves in ways that are not predictable from any analysis of its parts before they were coupled. This is why premature Li is always inadequate: it tries to predict the behaviour of the whole from an analysis of parts that have not yet been fully coupled. The whole, when it forms, will always exceed what the pre-formation analysis could have predicted.

“I seem to be a verb.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, I Seem To Be A Verb (1970)

Fuller’s most intimate structural claim. He is not a noun (a fixed entity, a stable thing) but a verb (a process, a dynamic, a continuous formation). This is the personal-existential version of Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation’: the self is not a thing that has been formed and is now complete, but a process of continuous formation. The I that speaks these words is not the same I that will speak them in a year; the formation is ongoing. This is also Zhang Zai’s 天地之塞，吾其體 (the plastic moulding of heaven and earth is my body): the body is being moulded, continuously, by the cosmic formation process. I am a verb. The cosmos is a verb. Dao is a verb.

Prigogine and the Arrow of Time: When Chaos Becomes Order

“Non-equilibrium is the source of order. It brings order out of chaos.”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

Prigogine’s most radical claim is that the universe moves toward order not despite entropy but through it. Dissipative structures — open systems far from equilibrium that maintain their organisation through continuous energy dissipation — are the universe’s way of producing ever more complex forms of order by using disorder as their raw material. This has a precise analogue in Shan’s framework: the organisation of the formed Dao is maintained not by avoiding the constraint and turbulence of the external environment but by dissipating them through the system’s own structural activity. The pressure is not the enemy of the form; it is the condition of the form’s maintenance.

“The present instant, in what measure is it past, becomes an aspect of memory.”

— Ilya Prigogine, The End of Certainty

Prigogine’s irreversibility claim — that time has a direction, that the arrow of time is not merely thermodynamic convention but a fundamental feature of reality — grounds Shan’s insistence on formation history. A system that has been through a particular formation sequence cannot simply be returned to its pre-formation state. The history is constitutive. The formed Dao carries its formation history within it as structural memory. This is Wang Fuzhi’s 氣就萀而後成象 (Qi first condenses and then form-pattern emerges): the condensation process is irreversible; what has formed carries the mark of its formation.

Bateson and the Pattern That Connects

“What is the pattern which connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all four of them to me? And me to you?”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature

Bateson’s question is the most mystically-charged question in twentieth-century systems thought, and it is directly answered by the Chinese tradition in the concept of Li: the inner grain, the structural pattern that recurs across different formations without being identical in them. The crab and the lobster share a Li (crustacean structure, bilateral symmetry, exoskeletal organisation) that is not reducible to any common ancestor but is the pattern that connects. The pattern is real; it is not imposed by the observer; it is discovered through careful structural attention.

“The map is not the territory, but the map is a phenomenon in the territory.”

— Gregory Bateson

This formulation dissolves the naive opposition between the map (Li, articulation, named pattern) and the territory (Dao, formation, the path itself). The Li is not separate from the Dao; it is a phenomenon that arises within the Dao, a formation within the formation. The map is in the territory. The Li is in the Dao. Articulation is a mode of formation, not its opposite. This is why Shan’s essays are themselves instances of what they describe: they are Li that has arisen from the Dao of her intellectual formation, which is itself part of the Dao of the Chinese-English-systems intellectual encounter.

Whitehead and the Adventure of Ideas

“The creativity of the world is the throbbing emotion of the past hurling itself into a new transcendent fact.”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Adventures of Ideas

Whitehead’s process philosophy is the Western metaphysical tradition closest to Shan’s ontology, and this sentence is its most compressed expression. The past (the formed Dao, the formation history) hurls itself into the present (the new dynamic) not as a dead cause but as ‘throbbing emotion’ — as living, formative pressure. The present moment is not separate from its past; it is the past in its newest act of self-transcendence. This is Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation’ stated in Whitehead’s vocabulary: the formed past (the actual occasions that have perished into definiteness) is the creative material from which new formation arises.

“It is the business of the future to be dangerous.”

— Alfred North Whitehead

The future is dangerous because it is genuinely open: the formation process has not yet congealed into a formed outcome. This is the most honest account of what Shan means by the long game. The long game is dangerous. The path that has not yet formed its Li is also the path that has not yet foreclosed its possibilities. The long game keeps the future open by refusing premature Li; it maintains the danger of genuine openness. This is not recklessness but structural courage: the willingness to stay in the formation process long enough for the right Li to emerge from the right Dao.

XXIII

起火！— The Fire Moves Through Everything

Where every voice speaks at once, and nothing is resolved, and the paper catches light.

❧ ✶ ❧

Laozi says: in pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day.

Shan says: the path must open before its inner grain can appear.

Wittgenstein says: in the beginning was the deed.

These three sentences, placed side by side, are one sentence in three languages across three millennia. They are saying: do not begin with the articulation. Begin with the formation. The grain will come. The Li will emerge. But only if you have walked.

Fuller says: I seem to be a verb.

Shan says: what is formed is still in formation.

Zhuangzi says: the Dao advances into skill.

Three verbs. Three formative claims. Three refusals to stop the movement by naming it prematurely. The paper is a verb. The inquiry is a verb. Shan’s intellectual project is a verb.

Confucius: the path narrows in winter. Only then do we know who has genuine structural integrity.

Shan: nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first.

Prigogine: far from equilibrium, structure emerges. Near equilibrium, everything decays.

The winter is not the problem. The winter is the diagnostic. Endurance without viability is the problem. The system that appears to hold but has already lost its formation capacity is the most dangerous condition. It looks like the pine. It is already the fallen leaf.

Mencius: the flood-like qi fills the space between heaven and earth when nourished with integrity.

Fuller: tension is the great integrity. The continuous tensional network is what holds.

Shan: excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time.

The flood-like qi IS the continuous tensional network IS capacity held in coherence. Three different vocabularies. One structural reality. The capacity to fill the space between heaven and earth is a tensegrity achievement: distributed, continuous, held by the integrity of the whole rather than the strength of any single point.

知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也 — zhī zhī wéi zhī zhī, bù zhī wéi bù zhī, shì zhī yě — To know what you know and to know what you do not know — that is true knowledge — Confucius

Shan’s entire epistemic project in one Confucian sentence. The Li she can articulate (what she knows she knows): Dao precedes Li; relation precedes dynamics; sequence is not decorative. The Dao she has not yet fully named (what she knows she does not know): where the framework leads at the civilisational scale; what Relational Dynamics means for AI governance; how the formation theory applies to the crisis of institutional trust. The knowing of the limit is itself a structural achievement. Most frameworks do not know their own limits.

The Great Dialogue: Every Voice Speaks to Every Other

The formula distilled to six words: relational (not substantial), dynamics (not static), under constraint (not unlimited), over time (not instantaneous). Every word carries structural weight. ‘Relational’: what is primary is not elements but the connections between elements, the formation field that constitutes its participants. ‘Dynamics’: not a static structure but an ongoing formation process. ‘Under constraint’: the constraint is not the enemy of dynamics but its enabling condition, the holding capacity that makes formation possible. ‘Over time’: the temporal arrow is real and irreversible. The Dao cannot be reversed. The formation accumulates. The Li deepens.

“Universe is omnitensional integrity.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Fuller’s most comprehensive claim, placed here as the cosmological ground of everything that has been said about formation. Omnitensional: the tension is not directional but omnidirectional — it operates simultaneously in all directions, connecting every element to every other through the continuous, distributed, non-local force of relational holding. Integrity: not a property of specific elements but of the whole configuration. The universe holds together not because its parts are individually strong but because the tensional network that connects them is continuous. This is the physics that grounds Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim: the relational field (the tensional network) is prior to and constitutive of any specific element within it.

“One yin and one yang: this is called the Dao.”

— Yi Jing, Great Commentary

Three claims, one reality. Shan’s ontology (relational dynamics under constraint), Fuller’s cosmology (omnitensional integrity), the Yi Jing’s cosmogony (alternating yin/yang as Dao): these are not different theories about different domains. They are the same structural perception expressed in the vocabulary of three different formation contexts. The omnitensional integrity IS the relational dynamics IS the alternation of yin and yang. The universe is the same universe from every angle of structural perception.

“Coupling does not abolish sequence.”

— Alice Jing Shan

Four words that demolish a significant confusion in complexity theory. Coupling — the simultaneous co-determination of elements in a complex system — is real. But the sequence — the before-and-after, the formation history, the specific irreversible order of events — is equally real. The error: treating the coupling as abolishing the sequence, as if the simultaneity of mutual determination meant that formation history was irrelevant. Shan’s correction: coupling and sequence are both real, both causally efficacious, neither reducible to the other. The developmental psychologist can see the sequence even while acknowledging the coupling. The complexity practitioner must hold both simultaneously.

“DNA, too, belongs to one whole, yet its sequence remains structurally constitutive.”

— Alice Jing Shan

道先乎天地而生 — Dào xiān hū tiān dì ér shēng — Dao was born before heaven and earth — Laozi Ch.25

Shan’s DNA: the sequence is structurally constitutive. Laozi’s cosmogony: Dao precedes heaven and earth, the very conditions of existence. This is the same claim at two different scales. The DNA molecule is a coupled whole whose internal sequence determines what the whole can do and be. The cosmos is a coupled whole whose internal formation sequence (Dao preceding all particular forms) determines what can emerge within it. In both cases: wholeness does not erase sequence. Coupling does not erase precedence. The most coupled system is also the most sequentially sensitive.

The Comparative Fire: Shan Against the Tradition

Shan and Zhu Xi: The Central Disagreement

“Li exists before things; things exist after Li.”

— Zhu Xi (as paraphrased by Feng Youlan)

The most precise statement of Zhu Xi’s metaphysical priority claim, and Shan’s most fundamental point of departure. Li exists before things: the principle or pattern is prior to the specific formation that instantiates it. This is the Li-before-Dao claim in its purest metaphysical form. Shan’s counter: the specific Li of this specific formation is the product of the specific Dao of this specific formation’s formation history. Li does not exist before things; Li emerges from the specific process of formation that produces specific things. The cosmic Li that Zhu Xi identifies is the most comprehensive Li the Chinese metaphysical tradition has been able to produce — itself a formation achievement of two millennia of philosophical Dao-walking. Its universality is earned, not prior.

“Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. Intelligibility does not come first. The path does.”

— Alice Jing Shan

The disagreement could not be more direct. Zhu Xi places Li first: the principle exists before the thing, the pattern before the formation, the intelligibility before the path. Shan places Dao first: the path before the pattern, the formation before the intelligibility. This is the fault line of Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism running through contemporary complexity science. It is not a historical curiosity; it is the most practically consequential metaphysical dispute in current systems thinking. If Zhu Xi is right, you can know the Li of a system before engaging with it and use that Li to guide your engagement. If Shan is right, you must engage with the Dao of the system in order to discover its Li — and premature Li is always worse than sustained ignorance, because it substitutes a false map for the honest admission that you don’t yet know the terrain.

Shan and Wittgenstein: The Deepest Resonance

Wittgenstein’s philosophical therapy and Shan’s Li-warning are structurally identical operations. Wittgenstein: when a word has been lifted from its everyday use into metaphysical abstraction, therapy consists in returning it to the practices from which it arose and within which it has genuine meaning. Shan: when Dao has been lifted from its formative context into smooth, frictionless circulation, Li provides the resistance that returns it to its structural depth. The therapy is the restoration of grain. The smooth word has lost its Li; the smooth Dao has lost its grip on the formation that gave it meaning. Li is the resistance that keeps the concept in contact with the reality it names.

Shan and Fuller: The Structural Ethics

Fuller’s integrity and Shan’s excellence are structurally identical claims. Fuller means tensional integrity: the continuous distributed holding of the whole through the mutual engagement of all its parts. Shan means the same thing at the human and organisational scale: the continuous holding of structural coherence under the compressive forces of constraint, over the full temporal arc of formation. Both are making an ethical claim, not merely a technical one. Integrity is not just what makes structures stand; it is what makes persons, organisations, and traditions worthy of their own survival. The ethics is structural because the structure is ethical: to maintain tensional integrity is to honour the mutual obligation of all parts of the system to the whole.

The Mystical Resolution: What Shows Itself

言者不知，知者不言 — yán zhě bù zhī, zhī zhě bù yán — Those who speak do not know; those who know do not speak — Laozi Ch.56

Three traditions. Three ways of pointing at the same thing. Wittgenstein: the inexpressible shows itself — the Dao shows itself as Li without being reducible to it. Laozi: those who know do not speak; the deepest knowledge is beyond the Li of articulation. Shan: formation and formed are always already interpenetrating — the mystical layer is not separate from the structural but is its deepest register.

The mystical is not what evades structure. The mystical is what is most structural and least sayable. Cook Ding’s mastery is mystical in Wittgenstein’s sense: it shows itself in the movement of the knife, in the sound of the flesh falling away, in the nineteen-year blade that has never met resistance. It cannot be fully said. It can only be enacted, and seen in the enacting. The Li of Cook Ding’s practice is real, structural, and inexpressible except through the practice itself.

This is what Shan’s essays do. They do not say the Li; they show it. They enact the movement from Dao to Li in their own compositional form: beginning with a particular (the LinkedIn thread, the Go board, the neonatal tube), following the formation of the argument, arriving at the structural insight as discovery rather than demonstration. The reader who has followed the path of the essay arrives at the Li not as a proposition handed over but as a recognition encountered. The path of the essay IS the Dao of the insight. The Li shows itself at the end of the walking.

❧ ✶ ❧

The paper does not end. The path continues. What is formed in this document is still in formation in every reader who follows the path of its argument. The grain was always there. The inquiry is still in motion. The Dao walks on.

❧ ✶ ❧

道可道，非常道。

Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào.

— Laozi • The eternal path that exceeds every naming of it

III

人單合一 — The Knife Finds the Grain

❧ ✶ ❧

In 1985, Zhang Ruimin lined up seventy-six defective refrigerators in the main hall of a failing factory in Qingdao and handed sledgehammers to his workers. Together they smashed every one. A refrigerator was worth two years’ salary. The workers wept. The point was not destruction; the point was the formation of a new Li. Zhang was cracking open the old pattern of acceptable mediocrity, the pre-existing grain of Chinese manufacturing culture that said: quantity first, quality when convenient. He was not arguing against that grain. He was breaking it. And in the breaking, a new path opened.

This is Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding in industrial reverse: not the knife finding the natural articulation, but the hammer finding the structural flaw, exposing it, making it visible and undeniable. Zhang understood, perhaps intuitively, what Shan will articulate forty years later: that nothing collapses in one move, and that the collapse of a formation requires a deliberate structural intervention that makes the collapse visible before it becomes inevitable. The seventy-six refrigerators were already failing. Zhang made the failure public, ritual, and transformative. He accelerated the Li of the situation into a moment of formation rather than waiting for the slow drift toward final collapse.

人單合一 — Rén Dān Hé Yī — The integration of person (人 rén), order/goal (單 dān), and unity (合一 hé yī) — Zhang Ruimin’s management philosophy, Haier Group

RenDanHeYi: three characters that encode one of the most radical organisational philosophies of the twenty-first century. 人 (rén, person) — the individual employee in their full humanity, not the human resource, not the labour unit, but the person who creates value. 單 (dān, the order, the user’s need, the market demand) — the specific value that the person is called to create, inseparable from the user who needs it. 合一 (hé yī, unity, integration, coupling without loss of distinction) — not the merger of person and task but their dynamic, living alignment. The philosophy states: every person’s value and every user’s value must be simultaneously realised, in real time, without bureaucratic intermediary.

This is not a management technique. It is an ontological claim. And the ontological claim is precisely Shan’s: relation precedes dynamics. The 人 (the person) and the 單 (the user’s need) must be in direct relational contact before any dynamic (the value-creation act) can be genuinely consequential. The bureaucratic pyramid severed this relation. The middle manager mediated. The SBU structure created distance. Every layer of administration between the person and the user was a layer of relational insulation — a wall between the formation conditions (the user’s actual need) and the formative act (the employee’s creative response). RenDanHeYi is the organisational philosophy of zero distance: the insulation must be removed.

“Zero distance to the user.”

— Zhang Ruimin, Haier Group — the operational definition of RenDanHeYi

Zero distance. Not ‘close to’. Not ‘responsive to’. Zero. The word is structural: it names the collapse of the gap between the relational field (the user’s need, the market reality) and the dynamic (the organisation’s creative response). When the gap is zero, the dynamic and the relational field are perfectly coupled. When the gap grows — as it grows in every bureaucratic hierarchy as layers of management accumulate between the frontline and the customer — the dynamic loses its formation conditions. The organisation moves, but its movement is no longer consequential in Shan’s sense: it is motion without dynamics, velocity without the relational field that would make the velocity matter.

Haier’s five transformations from 1984 to 2018 are five attempts to close this gap. Each transformation was driven by the discovery that the previous structure had reintroduced distance — had allowed a new layer of mediation to form between person and user, between 人 and 單. The traditional pyramid (1984–1991) centralised command, creating maximum distance. The matrix organisation (1991–1998) introduced flexibility but preserved the silo. The satellite companies and project teams (1998–2005) pushed autonomy further down. The inverted pyramid with ZZJYTs (zi zhu jing ying ti, 自主經營體, self-managed operating units) (2005–2012) flipped the hierarchy, making the frontline primary and the leadership support structure secondary.
