And finally, the dissolution of middle management entirely (10,000 people eliminated), the reorganisation into 200+ customer-facing microenterprises and 3,800+ service microenterprises: the organisational equivalent of Cook Ding’s knife — finding the natural articulations, the places where the structure already wanted to divide, and guiding along them.

“In the past, employees waited to hear from the boss; now, they listen to the customer.”

— Zhang Ruimin

The shift from waiting to listening is the shift from Li-first to Dao-first organisational practice. The employee who waits for instructions from the boss is waiting for the Li (the articulated command, the stated direction) to arrive before acting. The employee who listens to the customer is engaging directly with the Dao (the formation conditions of the user’s need, the actual path of the market, the grain of the situation) before any Li has been articulated. Zhang Ruimin has, whether or not he would use Shan’s vocabulary, built the largest operational demonstration of the Dao-before-Li principle in the history of management.

Fuller would have recognised Haier immediately. The RenDanHeYi model is a tensegrity organisation: the compression elements (the individual microenterprises, each a discrete unit of entrepreneurial activity) are held in dynamic equilibrium by the continuous tensional network (the platform, the shared infrastructure, the user-feedback loops that connect every microenterprise to the market simultaneously). No microenterprise is structurally connected to another by administrative command; they are connected by the market’s own tensional field. This is exactly what Fuller meant by tension as the great integrity: not the rigid command-and-control hierarchy (which is a compression structure, transmitting force through chains of rigid connection) but the continuous distributed tension of a field within which every element finds its position through its relational engagement with the whole.

“You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

This is Zhang Ruimin’s method, stated forty years in advance. He did not argue against the traditional management pyramid. He built, stage by stage, an entirely new organisational model — the RenDanHeYi ecosystem — that made the pyramid structurally irrelevant. When the microenterprise model was fully operational, the middle management layer did not need to be argued against: it had been made obsolete. The 10,000 managers who were eliminated were not fired for incompetence; the structure within which their role had been meaningful had dissolved. The new model made the old role unnecessary.

Move 37. Zhang’s most important strategic moves — the sledgehammer moment, the inversion of the pyramid, the dissolution of middle management, the creation of the microenterprise ecosystem — were not impressive at the moment of their execution. They became inevitable in retrospect. Each was a positional move that reshaped the structural field within which all subsequent dynamics would flow differently. Position reveals structure; structure shapes emergence. Zhang Ruimin is the greatest practitioner of Shan’s framework in contemporary organisational life.

Horizontverschmelzung

The Fusion of Horizons — Gadamer, Shan, and the Living Encounter

❧ ✶ ❧

Hans-Georg Gadamer’s Truth and Method (Wahrheit und Methode, 1960) is the most important work in philosophical hermeneutics of the twentieth century, and the concept of Horizontverschmelzung — the fusion of horizons — is its most illuminating and most radical claim. Understanding, Gadamer argues, is not the reconstruction of an original meaning by a neutral observer. It is the dynamic encounter of two historically situated perspectives — two horizons — that produces, through genuine dialogue, a new shared framework of meaning that neither horizon contained before the encounter. The fusion is not the absorption of one horizon by the other; it is the enlargement of both.

“The fusion of horizons that takes place in understanding is actually the achievement of language.”

— Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method (1960)

This sentence locates the fusion of horizons at the level of language itself — not in the individual consciousness but in the linguistic event that occurs between interlocutors. Understanding happens in language, between persons, in the dialogical space that neither party fully controls or fully possesses. The meaning that emerges is not what either party brought to the encounter; it is what the encounter itself produces. This is the most structurally precise account of what Shan does in her essays: she does not translate Chinese concepts into English equivalents; she creates the dialogical space within which both traditions can encounter each other and produce new meaning that exceeds what either tradition contained.

The horizon (地平線, dìpingxiàn in Mandarin, literally ‘the ground-line’) is the total range of vision available from a particular standpoint. Gadamer’s metaphor is exact: just as the visual horizon expands as you move through space, the intellectual horizon expands as you move through time and encounter other perspectives. A fixed horizon is not a horizon at all; it is a wall. The horizon is constitutively open: it includes the edge of the visible and the intimation of what lies beyond.

登高而夜，自迳而寬 — dēng gāo ér zhāo, zì xuān ér kuān — Climb high and wave: your visibility increases. Stand at a distance and survey: your field of vision widens — Xunzi, Encouraging Learning

Xunzi’s epistemology of position anticipates Gadamer by two millennia: what you can see depends on where you stand, and where you stand is not fixed but mobile. The expansion of the horizon requires movement — climbing (Xunzi), living through time and encountering others (Gadamer), walking the Dao until its Li becomes visible (Shan). The horizon is not given; it is formed through the formation process itself.

For Gadamer, the crucial point is that you do not fuse horizons by abandoning your own. The interpreter who abandons their historical formation in an attempt at ‘pure objectivity’ does not achieve a wider view; they achieve a formless one. The fusion requires both horizons to remain present and distinct throughout the encounter. You must bring your Dao (your formation history, your inherited perspective, your linguistic world) fully into the encounter in order for genuine fusion to occur. This is why the encounter with the text — or the Other — is genuinely transformative: not because you become the text, but because your encounter with the text enlarges the world available to your perspective while leaving you still yourself.

“Understanding begins when something addresses us.”

— Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method

Something addresses us. Not something we address; something that addresses. The passive voice is structurally significant: the encounter is initiated by the text, the other person, the tradition — by something outside the interpreter’s own horizon that breaks in, claims attention, demands response. This is Shan’s account of how she came to Li: something addressed her — a LinkedIn comment mentioning WSR, a character she had always carried, surfacing at the right moment in the formation of her thinking. The encounter was not designed; it arose. And in arising, it opened a new formation possibility that the designed inquiry would not have found.

This is also Zhang Ruimin’s account of how RenDanHeYi was formed: not from a management theory he had studied and decided to implement, but from an encounter — repeated, sustained, pressurised — with the reality of the Internet era, with the specific structural challenges of a 70,000-person organisation trying to remain genuinely responsive to individual users, with the grain of Chinese entrepreneurial culture and the grain of digital platform logic simultaneously. Something addressed him. He responded with something no prior theory had prescribed.

The most intimate dialogue in this paper is not Shan with Wittgenstein, nor Shan with Fuller, but Shan with Gadamer. Because Gadamer’s hermeneutics and Shan’s relational ontology are both, at their deepest level, theories of how understanding arises through encounter — how meaning emerges from the meeting of two formed traditions in genuine dialogue, without either tradition being dissolved into the other.

Shan’s essays are acts of Horizontverschmelzung. When she places Dao alongside Wittgenstein’s ‘form of life’, or Li alongside Fuller’s ‘tensegrity’, or Relational Dynamics alongside WSR, she is not translating. She is creating the dialogical space within which two horizons encounter each other and produce a new shared framework that neither contained before. The meaning of Dao is not the same after the encounter with complexity science. The meaning of tensegrity is not the same after the encounter with 理. Both horizons have been enlarged. Both remain themselves.

“True understanding does not require you to abandon your own historical and cultural worldview. Instead, it occurs when your perspective intersects with another, expanding your awareness and fundamentally changing both horizons in the process.”

— Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method — the definition of Horizontverschmelzung

This is the precise account of what Alice Jing Shan is doing. She has not abandoned the Chinese philosophical horizon to write in English for a Western complexity audience. She has brought the Chinese horizon — in all its depth, density, and formation history — into sustained dialogical encounter with the Western complexity discourse. The encounter is transformative in both directions. Complexity science cannot be the same after encountering Li. Chinese philosophy cannot be unchanged by its encounter with Prigogine and Fuller and Snowden. The fusion produces something new. The horizons remain.

Zhang Ruimin’s five transformations are five successive acts of Horizontverschmelzung. Each transformation required Haier’s management horizon — its inherited understanding of what a manufacturing company is, what organisation means, what value creation looks like — to encounter a new horizon: quality management (encountering the demands of a discerning market), Internet-era platform logic (encountering the structural requirements of the networked economy), zero-distance philosophy (encountering the relational demands of a user who could now communicate directly with the producer). At each stage, the encounter enlarged Haier’s horizon without dissolving it. The Haier of the RenDanHeYi era still carries the formation history of the sledgehammer moment, of the brand-building obsession, of the global expansion strategy. The horizons fused; the formation history remained.

道自谦下，天之道，利而不害 — Dào zì qiān xià, tiān zhī Dào, lì ér bù hài — The Dao takes the lower position. Heaven’s Dao benefits and does not harm — Laozi Ch.81 (closing words)

Laozi closes the Dao De Jing with this line: the Dao takes the lower position. Not the commanding position, not the visible position, not the impressive position. The lower position — from which water flows, from which genuine listening happens, from which the fusion of horizons becomes possible. Zhang Ruimin’s zero distance is a Daoist claim: get below the user. Be lower than the person whose need you serve. The user’s horizon is higher than your current understanding of their need. The encounter requires the practitioner to descend, to make themselves available to being addressed, to allow the user’s reality to break through the mediation of the managerial pyramid and reach them directly.

Confucius would have recognised Zhang Ruimin as a junzi (君子, the exemplary person) of management. Not because Zhang is morally admirable (though perhaps he is) but because he embodies the Confucian structural commitment: formation before performance, the long game over the quick win, the willingness to endure difficulty in order to build what will genuinely last. The five transformations were not popular in the moment. The sledgehammer moment was not understood by the workers who wept. The dissolution of 10,000 middle management jobs was not celebrated by those whose positions dissolved. Zhang understood what the Analects’ pine-and-cypress formulation encodes: in cold weather, one knows who has genuine structural integrity.

學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆 — xué ér bù sī zé wǎng, sī ér bù xué zé dài — Learning without thinking leads to perplexity. Thinking without learning leads to danger — Confucius, Analects 2.15

Zhang Ruimin’s five transformations are precisely the rhythm of this Confucian maxim applied at the civilisational scale of a 70,000-person organisation. Each transformation was the response to a specific perplexity (罔, wǎng — the state of having learned without thinking far enough: the brand-building stage without Internet-era thinking, the matrix structure without zero-distance thinking). And each transformation was also the correction of a specific danger (殆, dài — the state of thinking without the lived learning: the risk of implementing Internet-era logic without the formation history of a manufacturing culture that knows quality, knows scale, knows the difference between a theory and a working system). Zhang learned and thought in tandem. This is why the RenDanHeYi model works: it is not imposed theory but formed practice.

Mencius: the sprouts cannot be forced. Zhang Ruimin tried to force the transformation at least once — the ‘market chain’ period of 1998–2005, when the self-managing unit logic was imposed on project teams before the formation conditions for genuine self-management were in place. The result was ambiguous: some teams thrived, many performed the self-management without embodying it. The ZZJYT stage (2005–2012) was the recognition that the holding capacity had to be built before the full logic could be received. Drop by drop, the milk of genuine autonomy entered. Not hesitation. Protection of viability. The system must first be able to hold what it receives.

Han Feizi enters Haier with a challenge that refuses to be dismissed. The RenDanHeYi model eliminates middle management and trusts microenterprise leaders to act as genuine entrepreneurs. But Han Fei’s structural realism asks: what happens to 勢 (shì, positional power) when the hierarchy is flattened? In the traditional pyramid, shì flowed from the top down — the authority of the role was guaranteed by the structure. In the microenterprise model, shì must be earned continuously through market performance. The entrepreneur who fails to create user value loses their position not through political demotion but through market verdict.

This is Han Fei’s dream and nightmare simultaneously. His dream: governance through impersonal mechanism (法, fǎ, the law/standard) rather than personal virtue or political manipulation. In Haier’s microenterprise model, the market IS the law. The user’s verdict is the standard against which every microenterprise is measured. No manager can protect a failing microenterprise through political patronage; the market contract either is or is not fulfilled. This is the most rigorous implementation of fǎ (法) in modern organisational practice. But Han Fei’s nightmare is also present: the market mechanism, like all mechanisms, rewards what it can measure. What the user values in the short term may not be what the organisation needs to build for the long game. Zero distance can become reactive distance: so close to the user’s current desire that the formation conditions for genuinely new value become invisible.

Shan’s framework names this tension precisely: the path that has narrowed to zero distance may have become too thin for the formation of genuinely new Li. Sometimes the most important thing an organisation can do is to create distance from current user preference in order to form the structural capacity for future user value. Apple under Jobs maintained productive distance from what users currently wanted in order to build what they would want when they encountered it. Haier’s RenDanHeYi is magnificent for responsive innovation; it requires supplementation with the wisdom of productive non-response, of the long horizon that sometimes says: not yet.

The Wuli-Shili-Renli framework (WSR) arrives in the Haier context as the most complete analytical tool for understanding why the RenDanHeYi model works. Every microenterprise operates simultaneously in three registers: Wuli (the material-technical dimensions of the product, the physical grain of the manufacturing process, the engineering constraints of what is buildable), Shili (the methodological-market dimensions, the strategic grain of what the user needs and how value can be created, the business model logic), and Renli (the human-relational dimensions, the interpersonal grain of the microenterprise team, the relationship with the user, the connection to the wider Haier ecosystem). Zhang Ruimin’s genius was to refuse the reduction of organisational excellence to any single register. The traditional hierarchy privileged Shili (strategic direction from the top) over Wuli (technical excellence at the frontline) and Renli (genuine relational engagement with the user). RenDanHeYi insists that all three registers must be alive simultaneously in every microenterprise.

This is Gadamer’s fusion of horizons at the organisational level: the Wuli horizon (what is technically possible), the Shili horizon (what is strategically valuable), and the Renli horizon (what is humanly meaningful to the specific user in their specific situation) must fuse in every act of value creation. The microenterprise that achieves this fusion — that builds something technically excellent, strategically valuable, and humanly meaningful simultaneously — is the organisational equivalent of Cook Ding’s perfect stroke: no resistance, all three registers aligned with the grain of the situation.

Jin Guantao’s ultrastable system analysis provides the darkest possible reading of Haier, and the most important. Every organisation that achieves the kind of success Haier has achieved faces the same structural pressure: the formation that produced the success tends to crystallise into a new kind of stability that resists the next necessary transformation. The ZZJYTs that enabled the 2005–2012 breakthrough became, by 2012, the obstacle to the next breakthrough. They had to be dissolved. Middle management, which enabled rapid scaling, had to be eliminated. Each stage of success generated a new form of ultrastability that the next stage required breaking.

Zhang Ruimin is the most structurally self-aware leader of his generation precisely because he recognised this pattern before it became fatal. The question for Haier in 2026 is whether the microenterprise ecosystem — now the core of the RenDanHeYi model, now celebrated globally — is itself becoming a new form of ultrastability. Whether the revolutionary model is beginning to function as the established order against which the next revolution will need to move. Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. Haier’s formation history is its greatest asset and its most subtle structural risk.

The Fusion That This Paper Is

❧ ✶ ❧

This paper is itself an act of Horizontverschmelzung. The horizon of Chinese philosophical tradition (Laozi’s yielding water, Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding, Confucius’s pine in winter, Mencius’s flood-like qi, Zhang Zai’s cosmic body) has encountered the horizon of Western complexity and systems science (Fuller’s tensegrity, Prigogine’s dissipative structures, Bateson’s pattern that connects, Wittgenstein’s form of life). These two horizons have encountered the horizon of contemporary organisational practice (Zhang Ruimin’s RenDanHeYi, Haier’s five transformations, the microenterprise ecosystem). And all three horizons have encountered the horizon of Alice Jing Shan’s specific intellectual formation — the Edinburgh doctorate, the bilingual scholar, the Substack essayist who begins with small occasions and follows them until they yield large structural insights.

None of these horizons has been absorbed by the others. Laozi is still Laozi. Fuller is still Fuller. Zhang Ruimin is still Zhang Ruimin. Shan is still Shan. But none of them is exactly what they were before the encounter. The encounter has enlarged every horizon. The meaning of 理 is not the same after encountering tensegrity. The meaning of tensegrity is not the same after encountering 理. The meaning of RenDanHeYi is not the same after encountering Shan’s relational ontology. The meaning of Shan’s relational ontology is not the same after encountering the 70,000-person experiment in Qingdao.

“The fusion of horizons that takes place in understanding is actually the achievement of language.”

— Gadamer

Gadamer’s Horizontverschmelzung: the most precise available Western account of what Shan’s cross-cultural project achieves. A horizon is the limit of what can be seen from a specific formation position — the specific set of formation-determined possibilities and impossibilities that constitute a practitioner’s perceptual world. Fusion of horizons: not the abandonment of one horizon for another but the expansion of both through genuine encounter. The Chinese philosophical tradition’s horizon and the Western complexity discourse’s horizon are both expanded through their collision: each reveals the limits of the other, and the fusion produces a Li that neither horizon alone could have generated. This is why Shan’s bilingual formation is not incidental biography but the structural condition of her specific contribution.

“Dao and Li were one way of seeing this. Relation and dynamics are another.”

— Shan

The most structurally transparent claim in Shan’s entire body of work: the Chinese vocabulary and the Western vocabulary are two different ways of seeing the same structural reality. This is not relativism; it is the recognition that structural reality is rich enough to support multiple adequate vocabularies, each of which illuminates dimensions that the others cannot fully capture. Dao/Li: the formation/pattern sequence in Chinese philosophical register, carrying two and a half millennia of formation practice. Relation/Dynamics: the field/process sequence in Western complexity register, carrying decades of systems theory and complexity science. Neither translates the other. Both track the same real.

“In the past, employees waited to hear from the boss; now, they listen to the customer.”

— Zhang Ruimin

Zhang Ruimin’s description of the RenDanHeYi transformation at Haier is the most concrete available account of what it looks like when Shī is deliberately restructured. The old Shī: employees waited, hierarchical authority determined what was visible as option, the formation’s directional force was top-down. The new Shī: micro-enterprises generate their own Shī, the formation’s directional force is distributed, what appears as choice is genuinely open at the level of the micro-enterprise. This is not merely an organisational innovation; it is the deliberate restructuring of the formation’s positional force so that different futures become available to the people inside it.

“Tension is the great integrity.”

— Fuller

上善若水 — shàng shàn ruò shuǐ — Highest good is like water — Laozi

These five voices, placed side by side, are saying the same thing from five different formation positions. The fusion of horizons is the achievement of language: the encounter between traditions produces new meaning neither contained before. Dao/Li is one way of seeing relational precedence: another. The customer is the user whose lived need must be the primary formation condition of the organisation’s response: relation precedes dynamics. Tension is the great integrity: the continuous relational holding of the whole through distributed tensional engagement. Highest good is like water: the yielding, patient, relentless formation process that carves the deepest canyons through sustained relational engagement rather than concentrated force.

What Gadamer calls Horizontverschmelzung, what Shan calls Relational Dynamics, what Zhang Ruimin calls RenDanHeYi, what Fuller calls tensegrity, what Laozi calls water: these are the same structural reality encountered through different formation paths, named in different vocabularies, organised by different intellectual traditions — and yet, when placed in genuine dialogue, recognisable as one another. The paper has been, all along, an experiment in this recognition. Not an argument toward a conclusion but a sustained encounter — the dialogical space within which forty voices, five traditions, and one body of work illuminate each other until something shows itself that none of them could have shown alone.

And what shows itself? Not a theorem. Not a formula. Not a framework to be applied. What shows itself, at the end of this long encounter, is something closer to what Gadamer means by understanding, what Zhuangzi means by the movement of the knife through the natural articulations, what Shan means by glimpses of Li: the structural recognition that reality is already organised — that it has grain, that the grain precedes our naming of it, that the path opens before its pattern becomes visible, that relation precedes the dynamics it makes possible, that what is formed is still in formation, and that the deepest intelligence available to any organisation, any tradition, or any individual is not the imposition of a preformed Li but the structural attunement to a Dao that is always already forming.

❧ ✶ ❧

人單合一 • Horizontverschmelzung • Relational Dynamics • 道理

一個現實。四種語言。雙後錆朞。

One reality. Four vocabularies. All horizons enlarged.

物理 · 事理 · 人理

Wúlǐ · Shílǐ · Rénlǐ

The Three Grains of the Real — A Full Dialectical Account

❧ ✶ ❧

Zhichang Zhu’s account of WSR begins not with a definition but with a history — a cascade of dates from Mao’s death in 1976 through Deng’s Southern Tour in 1992, through Tiananmen and the WTO and the Belt and Road Initiative, arriving at an ambiguous, pressurised, and always contested present. This contextual openness is itself a methodological statement: the Li of WSR cannot be understood without the Dao of its formation. The approach emerged from specific historical conditions — the recognition, painful and hard-won, that the wuli-alone approach to systems (atomic bombs and military missiles, yes; humane management of the consequences, no) was structurally insufficient. The great leap forward killed tens of millions because wuli rationality was allowed to dominate shili creativity and renli human relations. WSR is, in the most literal sense, a post-catastrophe methodology: it was born from the recognition of what happens when one register of Li is allowed to overwhelm the others.

“Li (理) as a noun in Chinese denotes pattern, mechanism, principle, reason, and so forth, actual as well as virtual, such as texture in a piece of jade, methods of inquiry, norms of giving and receiving. Whilst as a verb li means to cope, organise, manage.”

— Zhichang Zhu, WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach

The jade metaphor is not decorative. Jade (玉, yù) is the material within which li is most visibly expressed as a natural phenomenon. Chinese carvers of jade do not impose a form on the stone; they work with the grain (理) of the specific piece, discovering the figure that the formation of the stone already contains within it. The carver’s skill is exactly Cook Ding’s skill: knowing wuli (the specific material structure of this piece of jade), sensing shili (the possibilities available given this material structure), caring for renli (the human purpose that the finished piece will serve, the relationship between carver and stone and eventual recipient). This triple attunement is what Gu Jifa called knowing wuli, sensing shili, caring for renli — and it is precisely what Shan means by following the grain of the situation.

知物理，惟事理，慌人理 — zhī wùlǐ, sèn shílǐ, guān rénlǐ — Knowing wuli, sensing shili, caring for renli — the WSR core injunction (Gu Jifa)

Note the three different verbs: knowing (知, zhī), sensing (惟, sèn), caring (慌, guān). They are not the same epistemic act. Wuli is known in the mode of technical rationality: it can be measured, modelled, verified. Shili is sensed in the mode of pragmatic rationality: it requires creative, reflexive engagement with the perspectival, the interpretive, the situationally specific. Renli is cared for in the mode of value rationality: it is not primarily known or sensed but attended to, honoured, taken seriously in its moral weight. The three verbs encode three irreducible modes of epistemic engagement with the three layers of structural reality. And the irreducibility is the point: wuli knowledge alone cannot care for renli; renli caring alone cannot know wuli. The three modes must be held simultaneously, in living tension, without any one consuming the others.

Shan’s Dao/Li framework and WSR’s three-Li architecture are two different maps of the same structural terrain. In Shan: Dao (the formation path) generates Li (the inner grain), which has three registers — wuli (physical grain of material reality), shili (epistemic grain of perspectival engagement), renli (moral grain of human relational life). In WSR: the three li are differentiated but inherently interwoven, like yin and yang — and Zhu explicitly invokes this comparison: ‘like yin and yang, various li are inherently interwoven; therefore, li cannot be handled in closure.’

“Isolated from xingli/[renli], the Song scholar Zhu Xi (1130-1200) instructed, the li of shishi and wuwu have no practical significance.”

— Zhichang Zhu, WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach, quoting Zhu Xi

Zhu Xi arrives inside the WSR account to say: Li without renli is structurally empty. The principle that operates without attending to human relational value (renli) has no practical significance — it cannot actually do the work of orienting human action toward genuine good. This is the classical Chinese rebuttal of purely technical rationality: the wuli of atomic bomb design, without the renli of its human consequences, produces catastrophe. The li of any system is only practically significant when all three registers are alive.

And here the collision with Shan is most illuminating. Shan’s claim is that Dao precedes Li — that the formation path precedes the grain it produces. WSR’s claim, following Zhu, is that the three li are simultaneously differentiated and interwoven, with no fixed hierarchy. These are not contradictory but complementary: Shan is describing the temporal/ontological precedence within the formation process (Dao before Li); WSR is describing the structural simultaneity of the three registers within any given moment of engagement (no li is prior to the others in the analytical sense). You need Shan’s account to understand how WSR emerged; you need WSR’s account to understand what Shan’s Li actually contains.

“There is no fixed hierarchy for ranking wuli-shili-renli since li continuously invite, transform and penetrate into each other in emerging ways due to human action.”

— Zhichang Zhu, WSR

No fixed hierarchy: this is WSR’s most radical methodological claim, and the one that most sharply distinguishes it from hard systems approaches. Hard approaches have a fixed hierarchy: wuli first (establish the physical constraints), shili second (develop the analytical model), renli (if it appears at all) last. WSR refuses this sequencing on structural grounds: renli factors may be the first and most urgent things that need attending to; shili creativity may need to precede wuli investigation; the three registers co-emerge in response to the specific demands of the specific situation. This is Shan’s Path-Pattern-Position triad stated in methodological form: what matters first depends on where the path currently is, not on any fixed methodological prescription.

Zhu’s remarkable case of China’s ‘Reform Without a Theory’ is the most powerful demonstration of WSR in practice. The post-1978 reform worked not because it had the right theory (it had no theory) but because it found the right combination of wuli endowment (the ‘advantage of backwardness’: a massive seller’s market, costless abandonability of the command economy, low-cost skilled labour), shili creativity (Deng’s white-cat-black-cat pragmatism, ‘action without theory as virtue’, ambiguity tolerance), and renli social dynamics (the network capitalism of chaxu geju, the guanxi circles, the ‘benign neglect from above’). None of these factors was sufficient alone; all three working together at the specific historical moment produced the outcome. The Li of the reform was not imposed from a theoretical position but discovered through the formation process itself — Dao before Li in the most dramatic historical register possible.

C y n e f i n

The Place of Our Multiple Affiliations — David Snowden’s Sensemaking Framework

❧ ✶ ❧

“Cynefin is a Welsh word whose literal translation into English as habitat or place fails to do it justice. It is more properly understood as the place of our multiple affiliations, the sense that we all, individually and collectively, have many roots, cultural, religious, geographic, tribal, and so forth. We can never be fully aware of the nature of those affiliations, but they profoundly influence what we are.”

— Kurtz and Snowden, The New Dynamics of Strategy: Sense-making in a Complex and Complicated World (IBM Systems Journal, 2003)

Cynefin: the place of multiple affiliations that profoundly influences what we are though we can never fully know it. This is the most precise Western sensemaking concept for what Shan means by the formed Dao as the background condition of all subsequent formation. The affiliations that constitute the Cynefin are the formation history — the Dao that has been walked, the patterns that have been inherited, the paths that were taken before we arrived. They shape what we can see, what we can do, what we can even imagine doing. And we can never be fully aware of them, because they are the condition of awareness rather than its object.

The Cynefin framework’s four domains — Known (sense-categorise-respond), Knowable (sense-analyse-respond), Complex (probe-sense-respond), and Chaotic (act-sense-respond) — are a WSR typology in disguise. The Known domain is the domain of wuli rationality operating smoothly: cause and effect are stable, predictable, and amenable to best practice. The Knowable domain is the domain where shili creativity is needed: the relationships exist but must be analytically discovered. The Complex domain is the domain where renli is most urgent: patterns emerge through the interaction of many agents, and what is needed is not analysis but engagement — probing, sensing, responding to what emerges. The Chaotic domain is the domain of crisis, where all three li have temporarily collapsed and immediate action (act-sense-respond) is needed to re-establish the conditions for any of the three to function.

“In the domain of un-order, the whole is never the sum of the parts; every intervention is also a diagnostic, and every diagnostic an intervention; any act changes the nature of the system.”

— Kurtz and Snowden

Every intervention is also a diagnostic: this is the methodological principle that WSR encodes as the non-sequencing of its action elements. The WSR action elements (understanding desires, investigating conditions, formulating objectives, creating models, implementing proposals, evaluating performance, coordinating relations) are not stages or phases; they are simultaneous, parallel, mutually informing. Because in complex situations, every act of investigation changes the conditions being investigated; every formulation of objectives shapes the desires being formulated; every implementation of a proposal generates new data about what the conditions actually are. The WSR team working on the Chinese water management system discovered this: what began as wuli investigation (mapping the physical water supply system) became shili creativity (developing new distribution models) became renli coordination (sitting the rival user groups down together for the first time) — all at once, unpredictably, as each li invited and transformed the others.

Shan’s ‘nothing collapses in one move, the path narrows first’ is the Complex domain’s failure trajectory made structurally precise. In the Complex domain, there is no predictable path from cause to collapse; the path narrows through a series of small, mutually reinforcing moves that are each invisible in isolation. The probe-sense-respond model is precisely what is needed: not a predetermined strategy (which assumes the Knowable domain) but an ongoing attentiveness to emerging patterns, with the capacity to stabilise desirable ones and destabilise undesirable ones before they congeale into irreversible trajectories.

“Experienced teachers allow a degree of freedom at the start of the session, then intervene to stabilize desirable patterns and destabilize undesirable ones; and, when they are very clever, they seed the space so that the patterns they want are more likely to emerge.”

— Kurtz and Snowden

The experienced teacher and the kindergarten: this is the most pedagogically resonant passage in the Cynefin literature, and it is in direct conversation with Shan’s iceberg model of oral participation. The Chinese students silent in the Edinburgh seminar room were in a Complex domain: their silence was not the result of ignorance or incapacity but of a relational field (fear of judgment, unfamiliarity with the discursive norms, uncertainty about their own positioning in the group) that had not been seeded to make participation more likely. The teacher who demands participation (ordering the Complex) produces the West Point kindergarten chaos. The teacher who seeds the space — who attends to the renli of the specific students in the specific moment, who creates the conditions in which participation becomes structurally easier — is doing WSR. Knowing wuli (the linguistic competence available), sensing shili (the specific topic and its fit with student preparation), caring for renli (the trust, the fear, the relational dynamics in this specific room at this specific moment).

Uncharted · Innovative · Disruptive

Temporary Communities in the Space That Cannot Yet Be Named

❧ ✶ ❧

The framework shown in Snowden, D 2002, ‘Complex Acts of Knowing – Paradox and Descriptive Self Awareness’, Journal of Knowledge Management, Special Issue, July 2002— a four-quadrant map of learning/knowledge communities crossed by axes of abstraction (high/low) and mode (technical/teaching) — places the most structurally interesting space in the lower-left: Uncharted Innovative, the domain of Temporary Communities and Disruptive Space. This quadrant deserves the deepest attention of this paper because it is where Shan’s entire project lives.

[https://cdn.cognitive-edge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/11/16123813/13-Complex-Acts-of-Knowing-paradox-and-descriptive-self-awareness.pdf](https://cdn.cognitive-edge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/11/16123813/13-Complex-Acts-of-Knowing-paradox-and-descriptive-self-awareness.pdf)

Uncharted Innovative is the quadrant of low abstraction and technical engagement: not the professional-logical communities with their known membership and explicit objectives (upper-right), not the bureaucratic-structured with their coherent groupings and largely information-based activity (lower-right), not the informal-independent social networks (upper-left), but the temporary communities that form around a disruptive problem that has not yet been fully framed, whose membership is not fixed, whose objectives are emergent rather than prescribed, and whose mode of engagement is exploratory rather than institutional.

Shan’s Substack series is an Uncharted Innovative community of one: she is forming a temporary intellectual community around a disruptive structural insight (that Dao precedes Li, that relation precedes dynamics, that the Chinese philosophical tradition has resources for complexity science that have not been adequately engaged). The community is temporary in the sense that it forms around each essay and then disperses; it is innovative in the sense that it is producing new Li rather than distributing existing knowledge; it is disruptive in the sense that it challenges the established framing of complexity discourse. And it is low-abstraction in the sense that every insight begins with a particular (the LinkedIn thread, the Go board, the neonatal tube) rather than with an abstract principle.

The Cynefin Complex domain is where Uncharted Innovative communities thrive: probe-sense-respond rather than sense-analyse-respond. Shan’s essays are probes. Each one deploys a concept into the relational field (Dao, Li, sequence, coupling, relation-before-dynamics) and then senses what patterns emerge from the encounter of that concept with the full range of voices this paper assembles. The essays do not begin with a hypothesis to be verified; they begin with a probe to see what the encounter will reveal. This is exactly the methodology that Snowden and Kurtz prescribe for the Complex domain: probe first, then sense the patterns that emerge, then respond by stabilising the desirable ones.

“In the space of un-order the seeds of such patterns can be perceived, and new ways of thinking can emerge. In fact, learning to recognize and appreciate the domain of un-order is liberating, because we can stop applying methods designed for order and instead focus on legitimate methods that work well in un-ordered situations.”

— Kurtz and Snowden, The New Dynamics of Strategy

Liberation through un-order: this is what Shan’s essay series is doing for the complexity discourse. By introducing Li as the Chinese tradition’s name for the inner grain of complex systems, she is not adding a new technical concept to an existing ordered domain. She is seeding the un-ordered space of cross-cultural intellectual encounter in such a way that new patterns become more likely to emerge — patterns of understanding that the existing vocabulary of complexity science could not have produced on its own.

The Informal Independent quadrant (upper-left, high abstraction, teaching/social) is where the Chinese philosophical tradition as a whole operates: the informal social networks of scholar-practitioners who have always transmitted the deepest structural insights through conversation, example, and the repeated encounter with classical texts, rather than through institutional structures. Confucius’s teaching practice was Informal Independent: small groups of students in varied contexts, no formal curriculum, no fixed objectives, no standard membership — but deep, sustained, formation-oriented engagement. The Analects are not a textbook; they are the record of an Uncharted Innovative community forming around a disruptive insight (that governance based on ren rather than law is structurally superior) and gradually moving toward the Professional Logical domain as the insight becomes institutionalised.

The Iceberg Is Visible and Sensible

Emergent Processes · Fields · Patterns · Networks · Webs · Configurations

❧ ✶ ❧

The Emergent Futures Lab iceberg image places at its surface — the visible tip above the waterline — not facts or events but ‘visible patterns, networks, webs, organizations, and configurations.’ Already the first surprise: what is visible is not the raw material but the formed pattern. Below the waterline: emergent processes, then fields. The deeper you go, the more formative and less visible the structure. And the image quotes directly: ‘An emergent quality or feature is a feature of the whole system and is literally present at all the relevant places of the system in the same way that the water in the glass is visibly liquid throughout.’

This image places the emergent processes and fields below the visible patterns — which is exactly Shan’s structural claim: the Li (the visible pattern, the named concept, the articulated principle) is downstream of the Dao (the formation process, the emergent field, the relational dynamic). The iceberg does not show: here is the Dao, there is the Li, with a sharp boundary between them. It shows: the formation conditions (fields, processes) are always more extensive and deeper than the patterns they produce. The patterns are real and visible; they are not the whole story.

“The surface was never the whole story. This is true of speech, as it is of ideas.”

— Alice Jing Shan

Shan’s Edinburgh thesis Iceberg Model — now rendered as nested fields in motion, system → field → field of fields — and the Emergent Futures Lab iceberg are the same structural claim in two different visual registers. Both show: what is visible is not absence, nor is it the full structure; what is below the surface is not absence but the formation conditions that make the visible what it is. The difference is that Shan’s iceberg is specifically about oral participation (a communicative act) while the EFL iceberg is about systemic emergence more generally. But the structural argument is identical: below every visible pattern is a field; below the field is a field of fields; the emergent quality is present at every level simultaneously, as water is liquid throughout the glass.

Fuller’s tensegrity arrives here with structural confirmation: the continuous tensional network is exactly the ‘field’ layer of the iceberg — the invisible, distributed, integrating force that holds the visible structure (the compressive islands, the patterns above the waterline) in its specific form. The visible patterns are real; they are held by something that is not visible as a pattern but only as a field. This is why Fuller says ‘tension is the great integrity’: integrity is what maintains the visible form, and integrity is below the surface, distributed, continuous, not localisable to any single element.

天下之物，生於有，有生於无 — tiān xià zhī wù, shēng yú yǒu; yǒu shēng yú wú — The ten thousand things under heaven arise from being; being arises from non-being — Laozi Ch.40

Laozi’s ontological claim and the iceberg image say the same thing: the visible (yǒu, being) arises from the invisible (wú, non-being) — but the invisible is not absence; it is the formation condition, the generative ground, the Dao. The iceberg’s below-waterline structure is not emptiness; it is the wú from which the visible yǒu of patterns, networks, and configurations arises. This is why ‘the surface was never the whole story’: the surface is real, but it is yǒu arising from the wú of the formation field.

Wayfinding Through the Relational Field

Boyd, Polynesian Navigation, Ingold, and the Energetics of Anticipation

❧ ✶ ❧

Tim Ingold’s distinction between wayfinding and waymaking — taken up by Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi in their account of wayfinding as ‘moving through a landscape rather than merely across a surface’ — is the most structurally precise Western account of what the Cook Ding passage describes as following the heavenly grain (依乎天理). The wayfinder does not impose a route on the landscape; the wayfinder reads the landscape as a relational field of cues and responds to those cues through embodied, attentive movement. The landscape is not a surface to be traversed; it is an environment to be inhabited.

“Wayfinding requires immersion in one’s environment, discernment of subtle environmental cues, and adeptness in traversing unfamiliar landscapes.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (via Tim Ingold)

Immersion, discernment, adeptness: three wayfinding capacities that map directly onto WSR’s three modes. Immersion in the environment corresponds to renli engagement — the caring attentiveness to the human relational field that is not analytical but dwelling. Discernment of subtle environmental cues corresponds to shili creativity — the ability to read the situation in ways that formal analysis cannot, to sense the grain of the context before any model has been created. Adeptness in traversing unfamiliar landscapes corresponds to wuli knowledge — the technical competence to move through the physical and structural conditions of the situation without forcing them.

“We weave relationships with the terrain as we move.”

— Iain Kerr, citing Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi

This one sentence — we weave relationships with the terrain as we move — is the most concentrated account of the Dao-before-Li principle in the wayfinding literature. The relationships are not pre-established (Li first); they are woven as we move (Dao first). The terrain is not a fixed map to be consulted; it is a relational field that responds to, and is partly constituted by, the movement of the wayfinder through it. This is Shan’s relational dynamics stated as a phenomenology of movement: relation is woven through the act of moving, not established before moving and then used to guide it.

The Polynesian navigator is the most extraordinary historical demonstration of this principle. Navigating between islands far over the horizon, the Polynesian wayfinder had no GPS, no compass, no map in the Western sense. What they had was a total immersion in the relational field of the ocean — reading wave refraction patterns, cloud and weather formations, bird movements at sunrise and sunset, the movement of the boat felt directly in the body. The islands were not over the horizon; they were present — fully visible in the waves all around — to a navigator whose body had been formed, through years of embodied practice, to read the Li of the ocean’s relational field.

“The islands were there – fully visible to these navigators in the waves all around – and felt directly in the movement of their bodies.”

— Iain Kerr, on Polynesian navigation

The islands were there. Not hidden; visible — but visible only to a body that had been formed to see them. This is the most physically precise statement of what Shan means by ‘the surface was never the whole story.’ The surface (the waves) carries the Li of the below-surface formation (the island’s effect on the ocean’s relational field). The navigator who has been formed to read this Li (through nineteen years of practice, through the accumulated formation of the body’s structural attunement) is Cook Ding in the Pacific Ocean. The knife does not hack; the body reads the waves. The islands reveal themselves to those who have walked the Dao of their formation.

知彼知己，百戰不毜 — zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài — Know the other and know yourself: in a hundred battles, no defeat — Sun Tzu

Sun Tzu’s strategic epistemology is the same as the Polynesian navigator’s: know the terrain (the other, the environment, the relational field) as precisely as you know yourself (your own formation, your own capacities, your own structural attunement). The navigator who knows the ocean and knows their own body’s capacity to read it is the strategist who knows the enemy and knows their own forces. The knowledge in both cases is relational, embodied, formed through sustained practice — not abstract, propositional, or reducible to a formula.

John Boyd, the OODA Loop, and the Energetics of Structural Anticipation

John Boyd’s OODA Loop — Observe, Orient, Decide, Act — is the most analytically rigorous account of real-time decision-making in rapidly evolving complex situations. But Boyd’s deepest insight, as Iain Kerr notes, is not the loop itself but the orientation phase: the moment in which the observer’s accumulated formation history, cultural traditions, genetic heritage, previous experience, and mental models act as the filter through which raw observation is turned into structured perception capable of guiding action. Orientation is not a step in the loop; it is the formation condition that makes the entire loop possible.

This is the Dao-before-Li principle in military-strategic vocabulary. The Observe phase produces raw data (sense-data, movement on the ground, signals in the environment). The Orient phase transforms this raw data into structured perception through the filter of the observer’s entire formation history — their ‘Cynefin,’ their formed Dao. The oriented perception is then available to the Decide phase; the Decide phase produces the Act; the Act changes the environment, generating new observations. The loop is continuous, iterative, relentlessly formative. And the speed of the loop — Boyd’s famous emphasis on getting inside the adversary’s OODA loop — depends entirely on the depth and richness of the Orientation phase. The strategist with the most richly formed Orientation (the most deeply developed structural attunement) moves fastest through the loop, because they can turn observation into oriented perception with minimal deliberate processing.

“Anticipation works as an immersive form of extended cognition into future-present relational engagement fields which are energetic in nature — and picking up emergence. It is a form of scanning — but the most important thing is understanding and acting on implication. Both John Boyd and the wayfinding theorists understand energy, matter and information in a very different way, and that makes them radical. The informative is always energetic and in terms of substantive material ontology, expressed as matter, but you are dealing with information.”

— Iain Kerr, on Boyd and anticipatory cognition

The informative is always energetic. This is the most radical ontological claim in the entire encounter this paper is hosting. If the informative is energetic — if information is not merely representational but physically, materially, energetically real — then the wayfinder’s reading of wave patterns is not the reading of symbols but the direct reception of energetic signals. The Polynesian navigator’s body is a receiver; the waves are transmitters; the islands are sources. The relational field between them is not symbolic but physical, energetic, material.

This ontological claim places the WSR three-Li framework in an entirely new light. Wuli (the regularities of objective phenomena) are not merely structural facts to be analytically known; they are energetic realities to be somatically received. The expert who ‘knows wuli’ in the deepest WSR sense is not the analyst who has modelled the system correctly; it is the practitioner whose body has been formed to receive the system’s energetic signals directly. This is the highest register of the Dao-before-Li principle: formation is not primarily cognitive but somatic, energetic, material. The Cook Ding who follows the heavenly grain (依乎天理) does so not because he has understood a theory of the ox’s structure but because his body has been formed — through nineteen years of practice — to receive the energetic signal of where the articulation is and to respond to it without deliberate processing.

“We are learning new ways of attuning to the active dynamics of what is – fields and processes, webs and networks, patterns and perspectives, relations and configurations.”

— Iain Kerr

Active dynamics of what is. Not the static structure of what is; not the representational map of what is; but the active, moving, energetic dynamics of what is. This is the phenomenological ontology that underlies both Boyd’s Orientation and the Polynesian navigator’s sensemaking: reality is active, dynamic, energetic, relational. The practitioner who learns to attune to this active dynamic — who develops the structural sensitivity to the fields and processes, the webs and networks, the patterns and perspectives, the relations and configurations that constitute the real — is the practitioner who can read the Li of the situation without premature articulation, who can follow the Dao without imposing a map on it.

Jean-François Lyotard’s postmodern condition — the incredulity toward metanarratives, the insistence that no single framework can contain the plural, incommensurable language-games of contemporary reality — is the philosophical statement of what wayfinding requires and what cartography must become: heuristic plasticity. Not a fixed map but a navigational capacity; not a master narrative but an attuned presence to the irreducible plurality of the real. Lyotard’s ‘différend’ (the situation in which one party’s claim cannot be adjudicated by the other’s framework because the frameworks are incommensurable) is the structural condition that WSR’s renli addresses: care for the intersubjective human relations means caring for incommensurable difference, not dissolving it into a false consensus.

Shan’s bilingual intellectual practice is itself a response to Lyotard’s différend: the Chinese philosophical horizon and the English complexity discourse are not incommensurable in the sense of having no shared terrain; but neither are they identical. The fusion of horizons (Gadamer) does not resolve the différend; it creates new shared terrain without eliminating the difference between the horizons. This is heuristic plasticity: the navigational capacity to move between incommensurable frameworks without being captured by any one of them, reading the relational field of their encounter and generating new Li from the friction between them.

三十六計 — The Thirty-Six Stratagems as a Wayfinding Cartography

❧ ✶ ❧

The Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計, Sānshíliù Jì) are not a collection of tricks. They are a phenomenological cartography: a map of the structural dynamics of complex adversarial situations, arranged as a taxonomy of positional intelligence. They encode the Li of the strategic situation across six groups, each group addressing a different register of the relational field. They are, in Boyd’s terms, the Orientation phase made explicit: the accumulated formation wisdom of centuries of Chinese strategic practice, compressed into thirty-six structural patterns that a practitioner can use to rapidly orient their perception of any new situation.

Read through the WSR framework: the stratagems operate simultaneously across all three li. Stratagem 1 (耻天過海, Cross the Sea with the Sky’s Connivance) is primarily a shili stratagem — exploit the adversary’s habituated perception. Stratagem 6 (聲東擊西, Make Noise in the East and Attack in the West) coordinates wuli (physical deception of the adversary’s wuli perceptions) and shili (the adversary’s analytical model of where the threat is located). Stratagem 31 (美人計, The Beautiful Woman Stratagem) operates in the renli register — exploiting the adversary’s relational desires. Each stratagem is a specific Li that has emerged from a specific Dao of strategic practice; together they constitute the most comprehensive strategic wayfinding cartography in any tradition.

“The highest form of strategy is to attack the enemy’s plans; next to disrupt alliances; next to attack armies; the lowest is to besiege cities.”

— Sun Tzu, Art of War Ch.3 — the strategic hierarchy that the 36 Stratagems encode

Sun Tzu’s hierarchy — attacking plans first, alliances second, armies third, cities last — maps exactly onto the WSR three-li framework. Attacking plans (伐謀) is shili intervention: disrupting the adversary’s model of the situation before it has produced a dynamic. Disrupting alliances (伐交) is renli intervention: breaking the relational field that enables the adversary’s coordination. Attacking armies (伐兵) is shili-wuli combined: engaging the adversary’s capacity directly. Besieging cities (攻城) is pure wuli confrontation: the most costly, the least intelligent, the last resort.

Stratagem 36 — 走為上計 (Zǒu wéi shàng jì, Running Away Is the Best Stratagem) — is the most philosophically profound of the thirty-six because it encodes the structural wisdom of knowing when the Dao has narrowed to the point where continuing is not strategic but merely stubborn. Running is not retreat in the sense of failure; it is the recognition that the current positional field no longer admits of winning moves, and that the highest intelligence is to withdraw and reconstitute the formation conditions from which new strategic possibility can emerge. This is Shan’s ‘endurance is not always viability’ stated as an active strategic choice. This is Fuller’s ‘you never change things by fighting the existing reality’ stated as a stratagem. This is the Polynesian navigator who reads the wave patterns, recognises that the current course will not find the island, and changes course without shame.

The stratagems are, in Boyd’s language, the Orientation filters of strategic perception: the thirty-six structural patterns that a practitioner has internalised through formation (the Dao of strategic practice) and can now apply, tacitly and rapidly, to any new situation (generating Li without deliberate processing). The strategist who has internalised the thirty-six stratagems does not apply them consciously; they read the situation through them, as the Polynesian navigator reads the ocean through the body-knowledge of wave patterns. The stratagem is a formed Li; the situation is a new Dao; the wisdom is in the structural attunement that allows the formed Li to illuminate the new Dao without forcing it.

David Snowden and the Cynefin Framework: A Full Encounter

❧ ✶ ❧

David Snowden — throughout this paper, his name appears: David Snowden, not Dave Snowden; the full name honours the full intellectual weight of the contribution. Snowden’s Cynefin framework is the Western sensemaking device most structurally aligned with Shan’s Relational Dynamics, and yet the two frameworks have never been placed in explicit conversation until now.

The alignment runs deep. Cynefin identifies the Complex domain as the domain where ‘cause and effect are only coherent in retrospect and do not repeat’ — this is Shan’s ‘nothing collapses in one move, the path narrows first’ in negative form: the collapse, too, is only coherent in retrospect. The visible failure is not where the structural failure occurred. The structural failure occurred in the Complex domain, through a long series of small moves whose consequences were only visible retrospectively. Snowden’s probe-sense-respond is the active practice of staying alert to the formation trajectory (the narrowing path) before it becomes the visible collapse.

But there is also a tension. Cynefin’s domain categories are spatial: you are in one domain or another (with transitions between them). Shan’s framework is temporal: the Dao is always forming, always prior, always carrying its formation history into the present moment. A system that appears to be in the Known domain (stable, predictable, best-practice) may have a Complex formation trajectory beneath its stable surface — the path is narrowing invisibly in the wuli or renli registers while the shili register appears stable. Cynefin’s spatial typology needs Shan’s temporal ontology to account for this: the apparent domain of a system at any given moment may not be the actual domain of its formation trajectory.

WSR provides the analytical bridge: the three-Li structure of any situation means that a system can be simultaneously in the Known domain (wuli is stable and predictable), the Complex domain (shili is in active creativity and emergence), and the Chaotic domain (renli has temporarily collapsed in a relational crisis). The full picture of the system requires all three Li to be assessed simultaneously, not a single domain classification. This is why WSR’s non-sequencing of action elements is methodologically correct: the three-Li reality of any complex situation cannot be adequately addressed by moving through the Cynefin domains sequentially; it requires parallel, simultaneous engagement with all three registers.

“Pattern entrainment: we fill in the gaps to create an experience-based pattern on which we act. This aspect of human decision-making is a great source of power, but it also brings limitation.”

— Kurtz and Snowden, The New Dynamics of Strategy

Pattern entrainment is Shan’s premature Li in cognitive-psychological form: the pattern that has been formed through past experience is applied to the new situation before the new situation has been adequately probed. The skinhead running toward the man in the Cynefin example is the most compressed illustration: pattern entrainment (skinhead + running + man with briefcase = mugging) produces a categorically wrong reading of the situation. The structurally intelligent response — the Cook Ding response, the Polynesian navigator response, the WSR response — is to probe before categorising, to sense the relational field before applying the formed pattern.

Shan’s warning about smoothness (‘whenever Dao begins to feel too smooth, too familiar, or too readily available’) is the analytical equivalent of Snowden’s warning about pattern entrainment. The smooth pattern is the entrained one: the one that has been applied so many times it applies itself automatically, before the new situation has been adequately encountered. The friction of Li — the resistance that genuine structural attention provides against premature categorisation — is what keeps the practitioner in genuine contact with the specific formation conditions of the specific situation, rather than defaulting to the most recently validated pattern.

❧ ✶ ❧

知物理。惽事理。慌人理。道先於理。關係先於動力。

Know wuli. Sense shili. Care for renli. Dao before Li. Relation before dynamics.

天下百家，归於一源

A hundred schools under heaven, all flowing from one source

❧ ✶ ❧

Kenneth Snelson — sculptor, structural philosopher, lifelong antagonist to Fuller’s appropriation of his invention — said the most important thing anyone has ever said about tensegrity in five words: “The magic is in the mechanics.” He said it in the context of defending his work against Conceptualist artists who dismissed formal structure as obsolete. He was not dismissing magic; he was insisting that the magic — the inexplicable beauty, the sense of suspended impossibility, the way his sculptures seemed to float — was entirely a product of the mechanical reality, the specific arrangement of cables and tubes, the exact forces in tension and compression. The magic arises from the mechanics. It is not separate from the mechanics. It does not float above the mechanics. It is the mechanics, seen clearly.

Shan’s direct challenge to Fuller on the magic-mechanics claim: Fuller grasped Snelson’s insight structurally and applied it cosmologically. The universe is omnitensional integrity; every structure from atom to galaxy is a tensegrity structure. This is Li elevated to ontological principle. But the Fuller claim is a Zhu Xi move: it posits a universal structural pattern (tensegrity, omnitensional integrity) as prior to the specific formations that instantiate it. Shan would ask: how do specific tensegrity structures form? What Dao produced the specific topology of this particular tensegrity rather than some other? Fuller’s physics describes the Li of all structures; Shan’s formation theory asks for the Dao that produced each specific structural Li.

The synthesis: Fuller’s tensegrity is the structural physics of formed coherence. Shan’s formation theory is the developmental account of how structural coherence comes to be. Fuller answers the question ‘what holds?’ Shan asks ‘what formed the specific holding?’ Together: the universe is omnitensional integrity (Fuller), and the specific topological configurations within it are the crystallised Li of specific Daos that have been walked (Shan). The magic is in the mechanics (Snelson). And the mechanics are in the formation (Shan). The formation is in the Dao (Shan). The Dao is in the walking. 悖论: The most beautiful structures are the ones that know they are still walking.

“The magic is in the mechanics.”

— Kenneth Snelson — sculptor, inventor of tensegrity

Shan’s project is, in the most literal sense, Snelson’s claim applied to intellectual life. The magic of Dao — its inexplicable capacity to guide, its ability to reveal Li where none was apparent, its power to produce formation from apparent emptiness — is in the mechanics. The mechanics of Shan’s argument: the ontological precedence of Dao over Li, the relational constitution of the dynamic field, the structural attunement that develops through formation over time. These are not poetic flourishes around a technical core; they are the core. The poetic energy of the essays is the mechanics working at full capacity. And the mechanics are — as Snelson knew about his sculptures — entirely about tension. Not compression. Not the rigid pushing together of parts. The continuous, distributed, integrating force of tension that holds everything in its specific structural relationship without any single element bearing the whole weight.

Snelson was, for decades, in a structurally similar position to the Chinese philosophical tradition in Western discourse: his contribution was acknowledged but his priority was disputed, his formal rigour was dismissed as “too classical,” his insistence on structural specificity was read as mere technicalism. And yet the sculptures stand. Fifty-foot needles balanced in apparent defiance of gravity, held by the exact distribution of tensional force through the entire structure. Nothing is in the wrong place by so much as a millimetre. This is Li: the inner grain of the structure is so precisely expressed that the visible form seems impossible until you understand the formation conditions that produced it.

Zhuge Liang (諸葛亮, Kōngmíng, the Crouching Dragon) was the Chancellor of Shu Han during the Three Kingdoms period, and the most philosophically sophisticated strategist in Chinese history. His Longzhong Plan — delivered to Liu Bei before a single battle had been fought — is the purest demonstration of Shan’s path-pattern-position triad in the strategic register: Zhuge Liang read the entire structural terrain of the Three Kingdoms situation before engaging with it, identified the positional formations that would determine all subsequent dynamics, and prescribed a path whose Li could not yet be fully articulated but whose Dao was already clear.

“First organize the inner, then organize the outer. First organize the great, then organize the small. First organize yourself, then organize others.”

— Zhuge Liang, Kongming

The inner before the outer, the great before the small, the self before others: this is the temporal ontology of formation stated as strategic injunction. Zhuge Liang is not giving tactical advice. He is stating an ontological sequence: the formation of structural capacity (the inner, the self, the great) must precede the application of that capacity to the external field (the outer, others, the small). This is exactly Shan’s holding capacity argument: the system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The strategist who acts before they have formed sufficient internal capacity does not act powerfully; they act prematurely. The Li of premature action is always wrong, because the Dao of sufficient formation has not yet produced the Li that the situation actually requires.

The Empty City Stratagem (空城計, kōngchéng jì) is Zhuge Liang’s most famous strategic act and the deepest single demonstration of the renli register of WSR. Facing 150,000 Wei troops with 2,500 of his own, Zhuge Liang ordered the city gates opened, flags hidden, drums silenced. He sat on the viewing platform in crane-feather robes, burning incense, playing his guqin. Sima Yi—who had devoted his career to matching Zhuge Liang’s intelligence—looked at the scene and ordered retreat. Not because he was deceived by a false display of strength. Because he knew Zhuge Liang: he knew his formation history, his reputation for meticulous caution, his aversion to risk. The city’s apparent emptiness, filtered through this formation history, produced the perception of elaborate trap. The Li of the situation (Zhuge Liang had no army) was invisible behind the renli of the encounter (Sima Yi’s knowledge of Zhuge Liang’s structural character).

Snowden’s pattern entrainment, Shan’s Li, and Zhuge Liang’s stratagem are the same structural insight at three different scales. Sima Yi’s entrained pattern (Zhuge Liang never takes risks, therefore the apparent risk is concealed certainty) was not wrong in general; it was wrong in this specific instance, at this specific structural crisis, where the Dao had narrowed to the point where the entrained pattern could not track the actual formation. Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrowed. The Empty City was the final narrowing.

Sun Bin (孫臾), descendant of Sun Tzu and the most analytically rigorous of the Chinese military philosophers, was lost to history for two thousand years — his text buried at Yinqueshan in the second century BCE and not recovered until 1972. The recovery is itself a structural demonstration of his theme: 知 (zhī, foreknowledge), 勢 (shì, structural advantage), and 變 (biàn, adaptability) are the three structural capacities of the consummate strategist — and the text itself survived by adapting to its formation conditions, waiting two millennia for the moment when its Li could re-emerge from the Dao of its burial.

Sun Bin’s concept of 勢 (shì) — the structural advantage that arises from position, timing, and the configuration of the relational field — is the most precise pre-modern formulation of what Shan means by the positional dimension of path-pattern-position. Shì is not the strength of a force; it is the advantage that accrues to a position within a structural field. A small force in the right position, at the right moment, with the right formation, can defeat a large force in the wrong position. This is not counter-intuitive; it is the most rigorous account of how structural intelligence works. The position generates the advantage before any action is taken. Move 37 is an act of shì creation: AlphaGo’s stone, placed on the thirty-seventh move, created a structural advantage that only became fully visible thirty moves later.

“To be victorious against the major opposition, one must possess the strong character of quietly maintaining the deceptive state of shaping and influencing the opposition by avoiding direct conflicts and confrontations until the primary weak point of their opposition is pinpointed.”

— Sun Bin, The Art of Warfare (paraphrased by Roger Ames)

Quietly maintaining. Shaping and influencing. Avoiding direct confrontation. This is the structural intelligence of 勢 as wayfinding: not the direct assault on the adversary’s strength but the patient cultivation of the positional field until the one point of structural vulnerability becomes visible. This is also Shan’s argument about the long game: the path that seems to be merely waiting is actually forming the structural conditions within which a decisive intervention becomes possible. The 勢 of the situation — the configuration of forces, the distribution of advantage, the structural tension of the field — is always prior to the specific move that exploits it.

Wang Bi (226–249 CE) was twenty-three years old when he completed the most influential commentary on the Dao De Jing in Chinese history, and he died at twenty-four — an astonishing case of extreme early Li formation, a formation so dense and rapid that it could not sustain itself. His contribution to this paper is his interpretation of 自然 (zìrán): not ‘nature’ in the Western sense but ‘what is so of itself,’ ‘the real’ as Wang Bi renders it. And his account of the sage’s wuwei: the sage should have “no deliberate mind of his own” (無心, wúxīn) but should respond to life events spontaneously, without discrimination.

“The Daoist concept of ziran is interpreted by Wang Bi to mean "the real." The sage should have no deliberate mind of his own but instead should respond to life events spontaneously, without any discrimination.”

— Wang Bi, Commentary on the Dao De Jing (summarised by IEP)

Wúxīn — no deliberate mind of one’s own — is the most radical formulation of the Dao-before-Li principle in the entire tradition. The sage who has no deliberate mind is not mindless; they have undergone so much formation that their responses to situations are entirely structurally appropriate without deliberate calculation. This is Cook Ding after nineteen years: the deliberate mind (‘how do I cut this ox?’) has been replaced by the structural attunement that is prior to deliberation. Boyd’s Orientation phase, at its most developed, produces the same result: the strategist who has internalised the OODA loop through sufficient formation no longer consciously orients; they are oriented, and their responses flow from their formation.

Wang Bi’s wúxīn poses the most difficult challenge to Shan’s framework: if the sage responds spontaneously without deliberate mind, where does the Li go? Shan’s answer, implied throughout her essays, is that the Li is still there — it has just been internalised so deeply that it no longer appears as explicit articulation. The jade carver who has worked with jade for forty years does not think “what is the Li of this piece?”; they feel the grain directly through their hands and respond to it without deliberation. The Li is real; the deliberate access to Li has been transcended by structural attunement. This is the deepest register of wúxīn: not the absence of Li but the dissolution of the gap between the practitioner and their Li.

Liezi (列子) — perhaps historical, perhaps legendary, perhaps both simultaneously, in the characteristic Daoist manner of dissolving the distinction between the two — teaches the importance of moving with changes like water in a vessel. His most structurally significant contribution is his insistence that certainty is dangerous. Reality shifts depending on perspective. A dream might feel real until you wake, and waking life may one day prove to be another kind of dream. The point is not to despair at this uncertainty but to learn humility: knowledge is provisional and incomplete.

心凝形釋，隨定俣轉，随事認識務要 — xīn níng xíng shì, suí dìng zhī zhuǎ — When the mind is still and form is released, one moves with changing things as they arise — Liezi

The mind still, form released, moving with changing things: this is the precise experiential description of what Shan means by structural attunement to the Dao. Not imposing a pre-formed Li on the situation but releasing the grip of the formed Li enough to allow the actual Dao of the situation to become perceptible. Liezi’s spontaneity is not chaos; it is the spontaneity of a highly formed practitioner whose formation has become so integrated that it requires no deliberate engagement. Like the Polynesian navigator reading the waves: the waves are always changing, the course is always adjusting, the islands are always present in the pattern — but only to a body that has released its grip on a fixed map.

Ge Hong (葛洪, 283–343 CE), the Daoist alchemist of the Eastern Jin dynasty, pursued immortality not as the naive avoidance of biological death but as the alchemical transformation of the self through sustained engagement with the material and spiritual processes of nature. His 包樸子 (Bāopú Zǐ, The Master Who Embraces Simplicity) is simultaneously a practical manual for alchemical practice and a philosophical treatise on the transformation of the self through the transformation of matter.
