Ge Hong’s alchemy is WSR at the level of self-transformation: knowing wuli (the material processes of cinnabar and gold, the physical transformations of matter under heat and pressure), sensing shili (the patterns of transformation, the way specific materials respond to specific processes), and caring for renli (the spiritual and relational dimensions of the practitioner’s own transformation through the practice). The alchemist who fails in any one of these three registers fails entirely: the wuli alone produces dangerous chemistry without spiritual transformation; the renli alone produces spiritual aspiration without material grounding; the shili alone produces technical competence without structural wisdom.

Prigogine’s dissipative structures arrive here as the modern scientific description of what Ge Hong was pursuing: far from equilibrium, under sustained energy dissipation, matter spontaneously organises into higher and more complex forms. The alchemist’s furnace is a dissipative structure. The practitioner’s self, subjected to the sustained formation process of alchemical practice, is a dissipative structure. Order arises through the disciplined engagement with disorder, not despite it. The immortality Ge Hong sought is the immortality of structural integrity — the capacity to maintain coherent organisation through the maximum possible range of perturbation.

He Shanggong (河上公, the Old Man by the River) — tradition attributes to him one of the earliest commentaries on the Dao De Jing, though his historical identity is as uncertain as Liezi’s — reads Laozi’s text as a guide to self-cultivation and governance simultaneously, on the principle that the structural dynamics of the individual organism and the political body are the same dynamics at different scales. This is the most ancient Chinese statement of what complexity theorists call self-similarity across scales: the same structural patterns recur at different levels of organisation, and the practitioner who understands the Li of one scale understands the Li of all scales.

修身、治國、同道耳 — xiū shēn, zhì guó, tóng Dào ěr — Cultivating the self and governing the state proceed by the same Dao — He Shanggong, Commentary on the Dao De Jing

The same Dao: self-cultivation and governance as structurally isomorphic processes. He Shanggong is making Bateson’s claim in classical Chinese form: the pattern that connects the individual and the political community is the same pattern at different scales. Shan’s framework honours this isomorphism without reducing it: Relational Dynamics describes a structural reality that manifests differently at the individual, organisational, civilisational, and cosmic scales, but whose formation logic is the same at each. The Li of a conversation and the Li of a dynasty share the same ontological structure — not because they are identical but because they are instances of the same Dao.

Yang Zhu (楊朱), perhaps the most controversial figure in classical Chinese philosophy, developed a philosophy of self-preservation so radical that Mencius accused him of not caring even for the king. His principle: do not sacrifice a single hair for the entire world. This is not selfishness in the conventional sense; it is a structural claim about the ontological priority of the individual life-form as the unit of genuine flourishing. Yang Zhu’s challenge to Shan’s framework is the sharpest possible: if relation precedes dynamics, and relational fields are the formation conditions of all consequential action, what is the structural basis for the individual’s claim against the field? At what point does the demand of the relational field become the dissolution of the individual life that the field was supposed to sustain?

“Preserve life in its wholeness. Do not maim life. Do not sacrifice the life of even one person for the whole world.”

— Yang Zhu (as recorded in the Liezi)

Preserve life in its wholeness: this is the most structurally serious challenge to the renli register of WSR. Caring for renli — the human relational field, the intersubjective network of value and purpose — can, in pathological cases, demand the sacrifice of individual integrity for the maintenance of the relational field. Yang Zhu refuses this demand. And Shan’s framework, at its most sophisticated, agrees: the Excellence framework she describes is ‘capacity held in coherence’ — coherence, not dissolution. The individual who sacrifices all their structural integrity for the relational field does not strengthen the field; they weaken it, because the field requires structurally integral individuals to remain structurally vital.

Martin Heidegger’s ‘Building, Dwelling, Thinking’ (1951) contains the most structurally precise account of what it means for a relational field to be genuinely constitutive of its elements — as opposed to merely containing them. The bridge, he argues, does not connect banks that already exist; the banks come into existence as banks only when the bridge crosses the stream. The locale does not pre-exist the bridge; it comes into existence only by virtue of the bridge.

“The bridge does not just connect banks that are already there. The banks emerge as banks only as the bridge crosses the stream. The locale comes into existence only by virtue of the bridge.”

— Martin Heidegger, Building, Dwelling, Thinking (1951)

The banks emerge as banks only as the bridge crosses: this is Shan’s relation-precedes-dynamics principle stated as a phenomenology of place. The elements of the relational field (the banks) do not pre-exist the relational act (the bridge crossing); they emerge as what they are only within and through the relational act. Before the bridge, there were two stretches of riverbank. After the bridge, there are two banks that face each other, call to each other, constitute each other as the two terminals of a crossing. The relation is prior; the terms that the relation connects emerge as what they are through the relation.

Heidegger’s fourfold (earth, sky, divinities, mortals) — the four dimensions of the world as encountered in genuine dwelling — maps precisely onto WSR’s three-Li framework with the addition of the cosmic register. Earth is wuli: the material-technical dimension of objective existence. Sky is shili: the perspectival, interpretive, mentally-projected dimension of engagement with the world. Divinities are renli extended to the cosmic: the normative, sacred, purposive dimension of human life that cannot be reduced to either material fact or perspectival model. And mortals are the human practitioners who must hold all four dimensions in simultaneous, non-reductive engagement. Dwelling is the achievement of this holding. Heidegger: true building is not the production of structures but the creation of places of dwelling. Zhang Ruimin: building Haier was not the production of a company but the creation of conditions within which human flourishing could occur.

Robert Chia and Robin Holt’s Strategy Without Design (2009) is the management theory text most deeply aligned with Shan’s framework, and it does its work through a structural argument that is almost identical to Shan’s Dao-before-Li principle: success in strategy may inadvertently emerge from the everyday coping actions of a multitude of individuals, none of whom intended to contribute to any preconceived design. Strategy Without Design argues that the Western strategic tradition’s commitment to deliberate design (Li first, then Dao) is precisely what makes it so often self-defeating.

“The more single-mindedly a strategic goal is sought, the more likely such calculated instrumental action eventually works to undermine its own initial success.”

— Robert Chia and Robin Holt, Strategy Without Design (2009)

The single-minded pursuit of the goal undermines itself: this is the most precise Western management theory formulation of what Laozi describes as ‘holding and filling to the brim: better to stop in time.’ The strategic goal, pursued with maximum deliberate force, creates the very resistance that prevents it from being achieved. The path that hacks through the grain depletes the blade. The strategy that imposes its Li on the situation without following the Dao of the situation’s formation produces a result that is formally correct (the goal was stated, the action was taken) and structurally catastrophic (the action destroyed the formation conditions that would have allowed the goal to be genuinely achieved).

“Success may inadvertently emerge from the everyday coping actions of a multitude of individuals, none of whom intended to contribute to any preconceived design.”

— Chia and Holt

The medieval city analogy that runs through Chia and Holt’s book: London did not emerge from a plan. Tracks and footpaths wound their way between dwellings; these gradually became roads and lanes; clusters of hamlets became villages, then towns, then the city. The pattern is extraordinarily complex, dense, and habitable. No planner conceived it. It grew from the Dao of ten thousand individual coping acts, each responding to the formation conditions of the specific moment, each adding its small increment to the Li of the emerging whole. This is not an argument against planning; it is an argument that planning cannot substitute for the formation intelligence that is distributed across the whole system. The Li of London emerged from the Dao of its walking. The Li of a strategy emerges from the Dao of its implementation.

Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela’s theory of autopoiesis (1972) is the biological account of the formation principle that Shan articulates at the philosophical level. An autopoietic system is one that produces and maintains itself through its own operations: the system’s structure determines what changes of state are possible, what perturbations from the environment can be absorbed, what the system can become. The environment does not determine the system’s response; it triggers changes of state whose specific form is determined by the system’s own structure.

“Evolution has no purpose; it simply drifts with the only constraint of maintaining structural coupling.”

— Francisco Varela, The Tree of Knowledge (1987)

Structural coupling without purpose: this is the most biologically precise account of Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation.’ The autopoietic system drifts — it changes continuously, it adapts continuously, it responds continuously to perturbations from its environment — but it drifts in a specific structural direction determined by the coherence of its own organisation. The drift is not random; it is structurally constrained by the system’s own formation history. This is the Dao of an organism: the path the organism has walked, the perturbations it has absorbed and transformed, the structural adaptations it has made — all of this constitutes the formation history that constrains and enables its future drift.

Shan’s coupling-does-not-abolish-sequence argument finds its most rigorous biological grounding in Maturana’s structural determinism: the perturbation from the environment does not determine the response; the system’s own structure does. Two structurally different organisms may receive identical environmental perturbations and respond in completely different ways, because their formation histories (their accumulated structural adaptations) are different. Sequence is structurally constitutive. The order in which perturbations were absorbed, the specific adaptations that were made at each stage, the formation path that the organism has walked — all of these are internal to the organism’s current structure and determine what it can do next. Coupling does not abolish this sequence. It makes it harder to see.

Donella Meadows’ hierarchy of leverage points — from parameter adjustments (weakest) through feedback loops and information flows through goals and paradigms to the power to transcend paradigms (strongest) — is the most practically useful account of where structural change actually happens in complex systems. But this leverage point operates through emergence lag: genuine paradigm transcendence cannot be effected by deciding to transcend paradigms. The formation capacity required is produced by walking Daos that loosen the grip of any single Li, and the emergence lag between beginning those Daos and achieving genuine transcendence may span decades. You cannot shortcut emergence lag through intention. Her most important claim: the higher the leverage point, the more the system will resist changing it. And the highest leverage point: the ability to transcend paradigms — not to shift from one paradigm to another, but to step outside the system of paradigms entirely and recognise that no single worldview is absolute truth.

“There is yet one leverage point that is even higher than changing a paradigm. That is to keep oneself unattached in the arena of paradigms, to stay flexible, to realize that no paradigm is "true," that every one, including the one that sweetly shapes your own worldview, is a tremendously limited understanding of an immense and amazing universe.”

— Donella Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

Meadows’ hierarchy of leverage points culminates in three insights that Shan’s framework makes structurally precise. The highest leverage: the power to transcend paradigms. Meadows says this means keeping oneself unattached to any particular paradigm — using all of them as lenses rather than any of them as truth. Shan’s structural account: the practitioner who has walked diverse Daos has accumulated diverse Li, and diverse Li loosens the grip of any single Li’s claim to be the whole. The bilingual practitioner who has walked the Dao of Chinese and the Dao of English does not simply have two vocabularies; they have two structurally different worlds, and the gap between them is the source of their capacity to transcend either. Shan’s biographical formation is itself the highest Meadows leverage point enacted: the Dao of migration, translation, and cross-cultural formation has produced the specific formation sensitivity that makes the Dao-Li framework possible.

“My everyday life has involved translation, childcare, migration, social, educational, and organisational systems, cultural negotiation, and the constant work of moving meaning from one world into another. None of these conditions alone was extraordinary. But none of them was absent either. Over time, they coupled.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘When Dao Leads to a New Way’ (Substack, May 2026)

The coupling is the key word. The formation was not produced by any single condition; it was produced by the specific coupling of all of them over time under constraint. This is Meadows’ systems thinking translated into biographical formation theory: the leverage is not in any single variable but in the pattern of relationships among all variables — the Li that the coupled system produces through its specific, irreversible, formation-constituting Dao.

Unattached in the arena of paradigms: this is Meadows’ formulation of what Shan means by following the Dao before any Li has been named. The practitioner who is attached to a specific paradigm (a specific Li, a specific named pattern) cannot follow the Dao when it leads somewhere the paradigm cannot accommodate. The practitioner who can hold multiple paradigms simultaneously, who can move between them without being captured by any one of them, who can recognise that every named pattern is a partial articulation of a formation process that exceeds it — this practitioner has achieved the highest leverage point Meadows identifies. This is also Wittgenstein’s therapeutic goal: not to impose a new theory but to free the philosopher from their captivity to the grammar of a single language-game.

“The future can’t be predicted, but it can be envisioned and brought lovingly into being. Systems can’t be controlled, but they can be designed and redesigned. We can listen to what the system tells us, and discover how its properties and our values can work together to bring forth something much better than can ever be produced by our will alone.”

— Donella Meadows

Listen to what the system tells us: this is the WSR practitioner’s injunction (know wuli, sense shili, care for renli) stated as a relationship between human will and systemic formation. The will alone, imposing its Li on a system whose Dao it has not followed, cannot produce what the system and human values together can bring forth. Meadows’ ‘brought lovingly into being’ is one of the most important phrases in the literature: it introduces the renli register into systems thinking explicitly, insisting that the relationship between the designer and the system is not merely technical but caring. This is also Fuller’s tensegrity ethics: the structure that holds is the structure that was built with structural love, with attention to the Li of every connection, with care for the integrity of the whole.

Niklas Luhmann’s social systems theory is the most structurally ambitious attempt in Western sociology to describe how complex social formations produce and reproduce themselves through their own operations. His central claim: there are no social systems without communication. The communication communicates. Social systems are not composed of human beings; they are composed of communications that refer to other communications, in an autopoietic loop of self-referential meaning-production. Human beings are in the environment of social systems, not constitutive of them.

“There are no social systems without communication. The communication communicates.”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems

The communication communicates: a sentence that is simultaneously tautological and radically revealing. The communication is not the channel through which human intentions pass; it is the operative element of the social system itself. This places Luhmann in direct and productive tension with Shan’s relational ontology. For Shan, relation is primary; for Luhmann, communication is the operative unit of social reality. But these are not incompatible: communication is, in Shan’s terms, a specific form of relational dynamic — one in which the relational field is constituted through the very act of communication. The relational field (relation precedes dynamics) is what makes communication consequential; communication is the specific dynamic through which the social relational field reproduces itself.

Luhmann’s concept of meaning (‘Sinn’) as the horizon of all possible experience — following Husserl, meaning is the ‘horizon’ within which any specific communication takes place, the background of all possible references that give a specific communication its significance — is structurally identical to Gadamer’s Cynefin (the place of multiple affiliations that we can never fully know but that profoundly determine what we are). Both are saying: every specific act of communication or understanding occurs within a formation field that is larger than the act, that preceded the act, and that the act cannot fully articulate. This is the Dao within which every Li occurs.

Thomas Kuhn’s Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) introduced the concept of the paradigm shift into intellectual culture so thoroughly that the phrase has become a cliché — which is itself a demonstration of Shan’s Li-smoothness warning: the concept has become so smoothly circulating that its structural depth has been lost. What Kuhn actually argued was this: scientific progress is not cumulative but revolutionary; normal science (puzzle-solving within an established paradigm) is periodically interrupted by revolutionary science (the abandonment of the old paradigm for a new, incommensurable one); the two paradigms cannot be adjudicated by appeal to common criteria because they use different concepts, ask different questions, speak different languages.

“The normal-scientific tradition that emerges from a scientific revolution is not only incompatible but often actually incommensurable with that which has gone before.”

— Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)

Incommensurable: the paradigms cannot be directly compared because they are asking different questions. This is Lyotard’s différend at the level of scientific discourse, and it is Gadamer’s Horizontverschmelzung in negative: the horizons that must be fused are so different that no direct comparison is possible. Only the fusion itself — the dialogical encounter that produces new shared terrain — can bridge the incommensurability. Shan’s essays are precisely this fusion: Chinese philosophical discourse and Western complexity science are not simply talking about different things in different languages. They are, in Kuhn’s sense, incommensurable — and Shan’s project is to create the Horizontverschmelzung that makes productive dialogue possible despite the incommensurability.

Imre Lakatos refined Kuhn by replacing the single paradigm with the ‘research programme’: a structural complex consisting of a hard core of irrefutable assumptions (protected by a belt of auxiliary hypotheses that absorb anomalies) and a positive heuristic (a programme for future research). Research programmes do not simply shift; they progress or degenerate. A progressive research programme generates new predictions, opens new research questions, expands the domain of inquiry. A degenerating programme protects its hard core from disconfirmation at the cost of theoretical vitality, producing increasingly ‘monster-barring’ ad hoc adjustments that save the core while explaining nothing new.

Shan’s project is a new research programme in Lakatos’s sense: it has a hard core (Dao precedes Li; relation precedes dynamics; coupling does not abolish sequence), a protective belt (the specific philosophical, organisational, and strategic arguments that show how the core applies in specific domains), and a positive heuristic (the programme of connecting Chinese intellectual tradition with complexity science, WSR, Cynefin, and organisational practice in ways that generate new insights across all domains). The question Lakatos would ask: is this programme progressive or degenerating? The evidence of the essays so far is that it is powerfully progressive: each new essay opens new research questions, connects new domains, generates new structural insights that could not have been produced by any of the contributing traditions alone.

Fritjof Capra’s Web of Life (1996) — and its structural sequel, Systems View of Life (2014) — provides the most accessible account of the shift from the parts-based, linear-causal worldview of classical science to the relationship-based, emergent, networked worldview of complexity science. Capra’s key structural claim: the fundamental pattern of organisation of living systems is the network; the properties of the network arise from the relations between the nodes, not from the nodes themselves; understanding life requires understanding relationships, patterns, and context.

“The web of relationships is the pattern that connects. The network is prior to its nodes.”

— Fritjof Capra, The Web of Life (paraphrasing the central thesis)

The network is prior to its nodes: this is Shan’s relation-precedes-dynamics in the language of network theory. The nodes of a network — the specific entities that participate in the relational field — are not prior to the network; they emerge as what they are through their participation in the network. This is Heidegger’s bridge: the banks emerge as banks only as the bridge crosses. This is Shan’s relational dynamics: the elements of a complex system are constituted by their relations, not prior to them. And it is the WSR principle: wuli, shili, and renli are not separate layers added together; they are differentiated but inherently interwoven aspects of a single relational field.

Edgar Morin’s Method (six volumes, 1977–2004) is the most ambitious attempt in Continental philosophy to develop a genuine epistemology of complexity — one that can hold the whole without reducing it to its parts, while still thinking rigorously. His core concept: dialogic — the capacity to hold two apparently contradictory principles simultaneously, neither dissolving in the other, both necessary for understanding the whole. Order and disorder are not opposites to be resolved; they are dialogically necessary for the emergence of organisation.

“Complex thought is not thought that avoids or suppresses uncertainty; it is thought that traverses and lives with uncertainty.”

— Edgar Morin, Introduction à la pensée complexe

Traverses and lives with uncertainty: this is Shan’s ‘endurance is not always viability’ stated as an epistemological principle. The complex thinker who avoids uncertainty by premature Li (by imposing a known pattern on an unknown situation) does not achieve clarity; they achieve false certainty that prevents genuine structural engagement. The complex thinker who traverses uncertainty — who stays with the formation process long enough for the actual Li to emerge from the actual Dao — achieves a genuinely structural understanding that premature Li could never have reached. Morin’s dialogic is the epistemological equivalent of WSR’s no-fixed-hierarchy: you cannot resolve the tension between wuli and renli by declaring one prior; you must hold both in the tension of the dialogic encounter.

Henri Bergson’s philosophy of duration (élan vital, durée) is the most sustained attack in Western philosophy on the spatialization of time — the tendency to represent time as a series of points on a line rather than as the continuous, indivisible flow that is lived experience. Bergson insists: real time is duration; duration is the continuous movement of formation, the living present that is always already becoming past while anticipating future. No two moments of duration are identical; the formation process is irreversible and constitutive.

“Élan vital: the original impetus of life, the creative energy that drives the evolution of life and consciousness upward against the tendency of matter to fall into inertia.”

— Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution (1907)

The élan vital — the vital impetus — is Bergson’s name for the Dao as it manifests in the biological register: the creative energy that drives formation against the tendency of matter toward equilibrium and inertia. This is precisely Prigogine’s non-equilibrium thermodynamics stated as metaphysics: life is what happens far from equilibrium, where the continuous energy dissipation maintains organisation against entropy. And it is Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation’: the élan vital is never finished, never finally formed, always pressing forward into new formation. The tree grows its inner structure while growing its outer form. The Dao does not arrive at Li and stop; it continues forming.

Stuart Kauffman’s concept of the adjacent possible — developed in At Home in the Universe (1995) and expanded in Reinventing the Sacred (2008) — is the complexity science formulation of the structural constraint on formation that Shan’s holding-capacity argument describes. The adjacent possible is the set of all possible states a system can move into from its current state: the immediate neighbourhood of transformation that is structurally accessible given the system’s current formation. You cannot leap from the current state to any imaginable state; you can only move into states that are adjacent to your current structural configuration.

“The biosphere is always doing something for the first time. We live in a universe of ceaseless creativity, not a universe that is forever returning to the same configurations.”

— Stuart Kauffman, Reinventing the Sacred (2008)

Ceaseless creativity: the universe is always doing something for the first time. This is the cosmological version of Shan’s anti-determinism: the formation process is genuinely creative, not merely the unfolding of a pre-specified programme. The Li that emerges from a Dao is not predictable from the Dao alone; it is the creative achievement of a specific formation process under specific constraints, producing something that could not have been predicted but that, in retrospect, appears entirely fitting. Move 37 was not in the game-tree before AlphaGo played it; it was in the adjacent possible of the specific board configuration at that specific moment. The adjacent possible is the structural horizon of what is genuinely next.

John Holland’s work on complex adaptive systems — from Hidden Order (1995) to Emergence (1998) — provides the computational and formal underpinning for the emergence claims that run through the Chinese philosophical tradition. Holland’s most important structural insight: emergence is the systematic production of macro-level patterns from micro-level interactions, where the macro-level patterns have properties that none of the micro-level agents possess individually. Emergence is the name for the structural reality that makes the whole irreducible to its parts.

“The behaviour of the whole system cannot be predicted from even the most complete knowledge of the components and their interactions taken individually. Emergence is everywhere we look.”

— John Holland, Emergence: From Chaos to Order (1998)

Emergence everywhere: Holland’s empirical generalisation and Shan’s ontological claim are perfectly aligned. The reason ‘nothing collapses in one move’ is that the collapse is an emergent phenomenon: it arises from the interaction of many small moves, none of which is itself the collapse. The reason ‘the path reveals its pattern retrospectively’ is that the pattern is an emergent product of the path — it was not fully present at any single stage of the walking, but it arises as a recognisable structure from the interaction of all the stages together. Fuller’s synergy is Holland’s emergence in the vocabulary of structural engineering. Shan’s Li is the name for the emergent pattern that the Dao produces.

Zhang Dainian (1909–2004), the philosopher who worked across the entire twentieth century of Chinese intellectual transformation, developed what he called the Comprehensive Harmony (綜合和谐, zōnghé héxié) as the core structural principle of Chinese philosophy: not the synthesis of opposites (which would dissolve their distinctness) but the harmonious integration of irreducibly distinct elements in a structured whole where each contributes its specific character to the vitality of the whole.

和而不同 — hé ér bù tóng — Harmonious without being identical — Confucius, Analects 13.23

Harmonious without being identical: the most compressed account of what Gadamer means by Horizontverschmelzung, what Shan means by the encounter of Chinese and Western intellectual traditions, what Haier’s RenDanHeYi means by the coupling of person and user without the dissolution of either, what Snelson’s tensegrity means by the continuous tensional integrity of a structure whose elements remain distinct and discontinuous. Harmony is not identity. The fusion of horizons does not produce a single merged horizon; it produces a new, richer horizon within which both original horizons remain present and active. The whole is more than the sum of its parts without any part being lost in the summation.

The River Receives All Tributaries Without Ceasing to Be Itself

❧ ✶ ❧

Laozi says: the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. Snelson says: the magic is in the mechanics. Shan says: what is formed is still in formation. Heidegger says: the locale comes into existence only by virtue of the bridge. Maturana says: the system drifts with the only constraint of maintaining structural coupling. Meadows says: listen to what the system tells us. Luhmann says: the communication communicates. Kauffman says: emergence is everywhere we look. Holland says: the behaviour of the whole cannot be predicted from the parts. Morin says: complex thought traverses and lives with uncertainty.

Zhuangzi says: follow the heavenly grain. Wang Bi says: the sage has no deliberate mind. Liezi says: move with changing things as they arise. Ge Hong says: transformation is achieved through sustained engagement with the formation process. He Shanggong says: cultivating the self and governing the state proceed by the same Dao. Yang Zhu says: preserve life in its wholeness. Zhuge Liang says: first organise the inner, then the outer. Sun Bin says: quietly shape the positional field until the primary weak point becomes visible. Snelson says: the magic is in the mechanics.

Bateson asks: what is the pattern that connects? Capra answers: the web of relationships is the pattern that connects. Bergson insists: real time is duration, always forming. Whitehead says: creativity is the throbbing emotion of the past hurling itself into new transcendent fact. Prigogine says: non-equilibrium is the source of order. Varela says: wisdom consists in being open to the groundlessness of experience. Kuhn says: paradigms are incommensurable but must be fused. Lakatos says: progressive programmes generate new predictions, open new questions, expand the domain. Chia and Holt say: success may inadvertently emerge from everyday coping actions of a multitude, none of whom intended to contribute to any preconceived design.

And Shan says, across thirteen essays and a doctoral thesis that cuts open all of this with the precision of Cook Ding’s knife: Dao precedes Li. Relation precedes dynamics. Coupling does not abolish sequence. The surface was never the whole story. What is formed is still in formation.

One hundred voices, one structure. Not the same doctrine. Not the same vocabulary. Not even commensurable in Kuhn’s strict sense. But the same structural recognition, arrived at through different formation paths, named in different languages, organised by different intellectual traditions, illuminating the same formation field from different positions within it. This is what Bateson meant by the pattern that connects. This is what Gadamer meant by the fusion of horizons. This is what Dong Zhongshu meant by 同類相動 (things of the same kind move each other). The Li of these one hundred voices is the same Li. The Dao that produced them was the same Dao, walked by different people in different times and places.

The paper does not end. The path continues. The Dao walks on.

❧ ✶ ❧

道可道，非常道。

Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào.

— Laozi ·1 • The path that can be named is not the eternal path

Ήâme et Corps — The Metaphysics of Duration and Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

The exact verified words of Henri Bergson, from Creative Evolution, Chapter 1 (1907, tr. Arthur Mitchell, 1911), the most important sentence he ever wrote:

“For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.”

— Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, Ch. 1 (1907) — verified exact quotation

To go on creating oneself endlessly: this is not a comfortable thought. It abolishes the idea of a fixed self that has been formed and is now complete. There is no completed self; there is only the ongoing process of self-creation. Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation’ is this Bergsonian claim applied to every structured whole: the person, the organisation, the intellectual project, the tradition. Nothing is complete; everything is continuously becoming what it is next. The formation process is not something that happens to a pre-existing entity; it is what the entity ‘is’ in the deepest sense. The élan vital is the name for this ceaseless self-creative movement — the Dao as Bergson names it in French.

The élan vital traverses all the branching diversity of evolution, following no preconceived plan, but always drawn towards more freedom. This is Laozi’s water: it follows no predetermined course but always finds the lowest path, always carves through the rock, always arrives at the sea. The élan vital is not a directing intelligence imposing a plan (Li first) but a creative impetus following the grain of the situation (Dao first). The most striking confirmation: Bergson explicitly rejects both mechanism (pure wuli determinism: the future is entirely contained in the present configuration) and teleological finalism (pure shili pre-determination: the end is given before the beginning). His third way — the élan vital — is the Dao: formation that is genuinely creative, neither mechanically determined nor teleologically pre-ordained.

And the deepest mystical register of Bergson’s thought: in The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1932), the élan vital returns as the élan d’amour, the impetus of love that Bergson, without embarrassment, calls God. The Dao that drives the universe toward complexity and freedom is, in Bergson’s final metaphysics, love. Not a personal deity who commands; a creative force that draws all things toward greater freedom, more complex organisation, more subtle and differentiated flourishing. This is Wang Bi’s 自然 (zìrán, what is so of itself, the real) named as love: the real is what loves — what reaches toward, connects, and creates.

天地之始 — The Origin of Heaven and Earth

The Metaphysical Ground of Relational Dynamics

❧ ✶ ❧

This paper has been, up to this point, primarily structural: it has argued that Dao precedes Li, that relation precedes dynamics, that coupling does not abolish sequence, that the formation process is irreversible and constitutive. These are structural claims. They are true as far as they go. But they stop short of what is most important about Shan’s project: the metaphysical dimension that lies beneath the structural one. The structure of reality (relational dynamics under constraint over time) is grounded in a metaphysical claim about what reality ultimately is. Not what it is made of (that is the wuli question). Not what its patterns mean (that is the shili question). What it ultimately is, in the deepest register of renli-extended-to-cosmos.

無名天地之始，有名萬物之母 — wú míng tiān dì zhī shǐ, yǒu míng wàn wù zhī mǔ — The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things — Laozi Ch.1

Two states of the Dao. The nameless: the formation condition prior to all articulation, the generative emptiness from which all things arise, the wú (無) that is prior to all yǒu (有). The named: the emergence of specific form from the nameless ground, the mù (母, mother) that nurses the ten thousand things into existence. This is not mysticism in the degraded sense of vague gesturing beyond the expressible. It is a precise ontological structure: there is a formation condition (the nameless, the Dao as generative ground) from which all specific formations (the named, the ten thousand Li) arise. The nameless does not precede the named in clock-time; it is ontologically prior, the condition within which all naming becomes possible.

Whitehead’s ‘creativity’ is the Western metaphysical name for this nameless ground. In Process and Reality (1929), Whitehead identifies creativity as the ultimate ground of all existence: not God, not Nature, not Being, but the creative process itself — the fundamental restlessness of reality, its ontological incapacity for stasis. This is not a property of things; it is the condition that makes thingness possible. Every actual entity (every specific formation, every achieved Li) arises from the creative advance into novelty (the Dao of its formation) and perishes into definiteness, making itself available as the creative material for the next actual entity. The universe is not a collection of things; it is a process of perpetual self-creation.

“It is as true to say that God creates the World, as that the World creates God.”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (1929)

Whitehead’s most radical theological claim, and the one most structurally aligned with the deepest Chinese metaphysical tradition. God is not the unmoved mover who creates from outside; God and the world are mutually constitutive aspects of a single creative process. The world creates God by providing the material of the divine experience; God creates the world by providing the initial aim toward which each actual entity develops. This is the philosophical theology of mutual generation (相互生成) at the cosmic scale: Dao and Li, God and World, Creativity and Created — all in the process of mutual constitution, with no term prior to the other in the sense of one existing without the other, but with asymmetric roles in the process.

Zhang Zai and the Western Inscription: The Cosmic Body

天地之塞，吾其體；天地之帥，吾其性 — tiān dì zhī sè, wú qí tǐ; tiān dì zhī sō i, wú qí xìng — The plastic moulding of heaven and earth is my body; the commanding thereof is my nature — Zhang Zai, Western Inscription

Zhang Zai’s Western Inscription (西銘, Xī Míng) opens with this sentence and it is possibly the most metaphysically ambitious claim in the Chinese philosophical tradition. My body is not a biological organism enclosed within a skin boundary; my body is the plastic moulding of heaven and earth. The universe is literally my extended body; the creative process of cosmic formation is the formation of what I am. This is not pantheism (God is everything) or panentheism (everything is in God); it is a specific ontological claim about the constitution of the self through the cosmic formation process.

The cosmic body of Zhang Zai is what Fuller means when he says ‘I seem to be a verb.’ The self is not a noun (a bounded, static entity) but a verb (a process, a formation, a continuous act of self-creation within the larger formation of the cosmos). Fuller is a verb in the cosmic context of the universe’s ongoing synergetic self-organisation. Zhang Zai is a body constituted by the plastic moulding of heaven and earth. Bergson goes on creating oneself endlessly within the élan vital that drives all of life. Shan says what is formed is still in formation. The metaphysical ground is the same: the self is a formation process within a larger formation process, not a completed entity navigating an external world.

民，吾同胞；物，吾與也 — mín, wú tóng pào; wù, wú yǔ yě — The people are my companions in the same womb; all things are my companions — Zhang Zai, Western Inscription

Companions in the same womb: the metaphysical foundation of renli as cosmic relational obligation. If the cosmic formation process is what constitutes the self, and the cosmic formation process constitutes all people and all things simultaneously, then the relation between self and other is not contingent (merely social, merely conventional) but ontological: the other is constituted by the same formation process that constitutes me. We are companions in the same cosmic womb. This is the deepest possible grounding for Shan’s relational ontology: relation is prior not merely structurally (the relational field precedes the dynamics within it) but cosmically (the formation process that constitutes all things is prior to the things it forms, and this constitutive process is itself a relational process — Dao as cosmic relation).

The Yi Jing: Change as the Deep Grammar of Reality

天行健，君子以自強不息 — tiān xíng jiàn, jūnzǐ yǐ zìqiáng bù xī — Heaven moves with strength; the junzi thereby strengthens himself without ceasing — Yi Jing, Qian Hexagram

The Yi Jing’s first hexagram (乾, Qián, Heaven/Creative) carries the structural injunction that runs through everything this paper has been saying: heaven moves with strength, and the exemplary person therefore self-strengthens without ceasing. Not strengthening in the sense of accumulating power or building defensive walls; strengthening in the sense of maintaining the ceaseless creative movement of heaven at the level of the individual formation process. The junzi does not rest in achieved Li; they continue walking the Dao of their formation without cessation. Self-strengthening without ceasing is Bergson’s ‘going on creating oneself endlessly’ in classical Chinese cosmological form.

地勢坤，君子以厚德載物 — dì shì kŭn, jūnzǐ yǐ hòu dé zǎi wù — Earth’s force is receptive; the junzi thereby cultivates thick virtue to bear all things — Yi Jing, Kun Hexagram

Heaven is creative and ceaseless; Earth is receptive and bearing. The junzi must cultivate both: the ceaseless creative movement of heaven (the Dao as formation) and the thick virtue of earth that can bear all things (the relational holding capacity that makes formation sustainable). This is the cosmological version of Shan’s Excellence framework: capacity held in coherence under constraint over time is the human enactment of the earth’s thick virtue — the holding, the bearing, the sustained receptivity that allows the creative force of heaven to produce genuine formation rather than mere turbulence.

潛龍勿用：陽氣潛藏 — qián lóng wù yòng: yáng qí qián cáng — The dragon submerged: do not use — the yang force is still hidden — Yi Jing, Qian first line

The submerged dragon: the yang force (the creative power, the Dao-in-motion) that has not yet risen to the surface. The first line’s injunction is “do not use” — not because the force is absent or weak but because it has not yet reached the stage of formation at which its deployment would be structurally appropriate. The dragon is submerged but real; the power is latent but genuine; the time for deployment has not yet come. This is Shan’s ‘path narrows first’ in the cosmological register: the creative force that will eventually produce the decisive structural move (Move 37, the Longzhong Plan, the sledgehammer moment) is already present and forming before it becomes visible. The submerged dragon is the Dao in its pre-Li stage: real, forming, not yet manifest.

Wang Yangming: The Unity of Knowledge and Action as Mystical Experience

知行合一 — zhī xíng hé yī — The unity of knowledge and action — Wang Yangming’s central doctrine

Wang Yangming’s 知行合一 (the unity of knowledge and action) is not an epistemological claim about how we learn. It is a metaphysical claim about the structure of genuine knowing. Genuine knowledge of a thing and genuine action in relation to it are not sequential (first know, then act) but simultaneous and inseparable. To genuinely know fire is to feel its heat; one who can describe fire without feeling heat does not genuinely know fire. To genuinely know what is right is to act rightly; one who knows what is right but does not act rightly does not genuinely know rightness — they have an idea of it, a shili model of it, but not the renli knowledge that can only arise through embodied formation.

This is the most radical version of the Dao-before-Li principle as an account of genuine knowing: the Dao (the lived formation, the embodied action) is not subsequent to the Li (the knowledge, the understanding) but simultaneous with it. You do not first understand and then act; you act-understand as a single formation process. Cook Ding after nineteen years is not someone who first came to understand ox anatomy and then acted in accordance with that understanding; he is someone whose understanding and acting have become one movement, one process, one structural attunement. This is Wang Yangming’s 良知 (liángzhī, innate moral knowledge) at the level of somatic practice.

良知良能，人之本老 — liáng zhī liáng néng, rén zhī běn lǎo — Innate moral knowledge and innate moral capacity are the original nature of humanity — Wang Yangming

Innate moral knowledge and capacity: Wang Yangming’s challenge to all purely procedural or analytical accounts of virtue. The capacity to know and do what is right is not acquired through study or argument; it is the original nature of humanity, the formation condition of all subsequent moral development. This has a precise structural parallel in Shan’s framework: the relational attunement that makes genuine structural understanding possible is not acquired through abstract analysis; it is already present as a capacity in every human being, requiring formation (not creation) to manifest. The Cook Ding-capacity is everyone’s original nature; what differs is the formation that has been undergone to let it manifest.

Zhu Xi and Cheng Yi: The Most Important Wrong Answer in Chinese Philosophy

道即理也 — Dào jí lǐ yě — Dao just is Li — Cheng Yi

Cheng Yi’s identification of Dao with Li is the most important wrong answer in Chinese philosophy, and it is wrong in an instructive way. Not wrong as a statement about the intimate relationship between Dao and Li (they are, in Shan’s framework, mutually implicating; coupling is real); wrong as a statement about their ontological equivalence (they are not equivalent; coupling does not abolish sequence; the mutual implication is asymmetric). Cheng Yi reaches 道即理也 because he has seen, profoundly and correctly, that the Dao is always already intelligible, that the path always already has grain, that Dao and Li are inseparable in any actual moment of formation. What he has not seen is that the inseparability in any actual moment does not imply ontological equivalence: the banks are inseparable from the bridge in any moment when the bridge exists, but the locale still came into existence only by virtue of the bridge.

天地之間，一理而已 — tiān dì zhī jiān, yī lǐ ér yǐ — Between heaven and earth there is one Li and nothing else — Zhu Xi

Zhu Xi’s one Li that pervades all things is the most ambitious unification project in Chinese intellectual history, and it is magnificent in its scope. Every thing, every person, every situation, every pattern — all instantiations of one cosmic Li. This is Capra’s web of life, Holland’s emergence, Bateson’s pattern that connects — all in classical Chinese Neo-Confucian form. The structural insight is real and profound: there is a pervasive structural principle (Li) that makes all things what they are, that connects the grain of jade with the grain of history with the grain of a person’s character. The problem is not the insight but the direction: Zhu Xi makes Li primary, the Dao secondary, the understanding of the pattern prior to the formation that produces it. Shan’s entire project is the correction of this direction without losing the insight.

The correction: yes, there is one Li between heaven and earth. But that one Li is produced by the Dao of cosmic formation, not prior to it. The pattern that connects (Bateson) is real; it is the product of the formation process (the élan vital, the creative advance, the self-strengthening of heaven) that has always been and continues to be. Li is not the starting point of cosmic reality; it is the always-already-forming achievement of the Dao. Shan’s relational dynamics: reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time. The one Li of Zhu Xi is the structural signature of the one Dao that has been forming under the constraint of heaven and earth over all of time.

Cheng Hao: The Person of Ren Feels the Universe as One Body

仁者，以天地萬物為一體 — rén zhě, yǐ tiān dì wàn wù wéi yī tǐ — The person of humaneness takes heaven and earth and the ten thousand things as one body — Cheng Hao

Cheng Hao’s account of ren (humaneness) as the experience of the universe as one body is the most mystically powerful formulation in the Neo-Confucian tradition, and the one that most directly grounds Shan’s relational ontology in genuine moral-metaphysical experience. To feel the universe as one body is not a doctrine to be held; it is an experiential achievement to be cultivated. The person who has achieved this form of structural attunement does not reason from the fact that others are part of one cosmic formation process to the conclusion that they should care for others; they feel the suffering of others as directly as they feel their own pain, because the boundary between self and other has become, at the deepest level, permeable.

Cheng Hao’s analogy: a numb limb does not feel pain. The person who is closed to others, who has not achieved the relational attunement that is ren, does not feel the suffering of others not because they have decided not to care but because the structural connection is blocked. Numbness is the failure of the relational field to conduct the signal. And the cultivation of ren is the restoration of conductivity — the re-opening of the structural connection between self and cosmos, self and other, self and the formation process that constitutes all things.

This is Fuller’s tensegrity as moral philosophy: the continuous tensional network that holds the cosmos together is also the network of care and attention and response that constitutes genuine humaneness. The person of ren is the node in the cosmic tensegrity that maintains its connections with full conductivity, that transmits and receives the tension of the whole without blocking or distorting. Integrity (Fuller) is humaneness (Cheng Hao). The structure that holds is the structure that cares.

Where Structure Becomes Experience: The Mystical Stratum

❧ ✶ ❧

The structural arguments of this paper — Dao precedes Li, relation precedes dynamics, coupling does not abolish sequence — are not, at their deepest level, structural arguments. They are phenomenological descriptions of what genuine experience feels like to a practitioner who has undergone sufficient formation. Cook Ding’s knowledge of the ox’s articulations is not primarily structural (though it is structurally exact); it is primarily experiential: the blade finds the hollow before the mind names it, the hands know the joint before the knowledge arrives. The structure is the articulation of the experience; the experience is the reality that the structure describes.

Every mystical tradition in every culture has attempted to describe this register of experience: the experience of structural attunement so deep that the distinction between the practitioner and what they are attuned to becomes, in specific moments of practice, temporarily transparent. The Christian mystic’s ‘dark night of the soul’ is the dissolution of the premature Li that had been mistaken for the experience of God, making room for the genuine Dao of divine encounter. The Zen practitioner’s satori is the moment when the koan’s apparent paradox (the false Li that the mind has been trying to solve) dissolves, and the structural reality that was always present (the Dao beneath the surface of the question) becomes directly perceptible. The Daoist sage’s wuwei is the state in which the practitioner’s action is so perfectly attuned to the Dao of the situation that no gap remains between intention and action, between knowing and doing, between the self and the grain of what is.

“The Dao is too great to be named. But words are all we have. And words, wielded with structural precision and genuine formation, can show what cannot be said.”

— Paraphrase of the encounter between Laozi and Wittgenstein across two and a half millennia

This is the meeting point of all the traditions this paper has assembled: not the meeting point of their doctrines (which diverge massively) but the meeting point of their gestures, their pointing at what exceeds every pointing. Laozi says: the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. Wittgenstein says: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. But the silence at the end of the Tractatus is not empty; it is ‘what shows itself,’ what cannot be said but can be enacted in the movement of genuine inquiry. Bergson says: genuine knowledge requires intuition, the plunging into the flow of duration itself, not the spatial snapshot. Wang Yangming says: genuine knowledge is action; the knowledge that does not act is not genuine knowledge. Cook Ding says nothing; he moves the knife.

Shan’s essays move the knife. They begin with a particular (the LinkedIn thread, the Go board, the neonatal tube, the waving of a letter that turns into chicken wings, the coupling that does not abolish sequence) and follow the formation of the structural insight through the specific texture of the specific starting point. The essay does not demonstrate a thesis; it enacts a formation. The reader who follows the path of the essay arrives at the Li not as a proposition that has been handed over but as a recognition that has occurred — the specific form of knowing that Wang Yangming calls genuine knowing, that Bergson calls intuition, that the Yi Jing calls 得乎心應手 (dé hū xīn yìng shǒu, gaining it in the heart and responding with the hand).

Five Cosmological Registers of One Recognition

The Dao that Laozi cannot name and Wittgenstein cannot say. The élan vital that Bergson cannot capture in a formula. The creativity that Whitehead makes the ultimate ground. The structural attunement that Wang Yangming says is the original nature of humanity. The universe-as-one-body that Cheng Hao says is the experience of genuine humaneness. The submerged dragon of the Yi Jing that is real but not yet manifest. The Polynesian navigator’s islands that are fully visible in the waves. Boyd’s Orientation that has become so deep it no longer appears as orientation.

These are five cosmological registers of the same recognition: that the deepest intelligence available to any practitioner is not the application of a pre-formed Li to an encountered situation but the structural attunement to the formation process that is always already happening, always already producing the Li that will be needed, always already walking the Dao that will arrive at the right position at the right moment. This is not mysticism in opposition to structure. This is structure understood at its deepest level, where the structural and the mystical are not two things but two names for the same formation reality — seen from above (the structural view: how it works) and from below (the mystical view: what it is like to be inside it, moving with it, becoming it).

Snelson: the magic is in the mechanics. Not despite the mechanics. Not above the mechanics. In the mechanics. The magic and the mechanics are one. The Dao and the Li are one — not in the sense that Cheng Yi meant (they are ontologically identical) but in the sense that the deepest practitioner cannot feel the difference between following the grain and being the grain, between reading the Li and being the Li, between walking the Dao and being the Dao. This is the experience that all the mystical traditions in all the traditions assembled in this paper are pointing at. And it is the experience that Alice Jing Shan’s essays are, at their deepest level, teaching.

❧ ✶ ❧

No text has been removed from any previous version of this document. The document grows by accumulation and by the deepening of what was already present; nothing is lost. The formation process of the document is itself a demonstration of its argument: the path is still in formation, the grain is still being discovered, the Dao walks on.

❧ ✶ ❧

天行健，君子以自強不息。

Tiān xíng jiàn, jūnzǐ yǐ zìqiáng bù xī.

— Yi Jing, Qian Hexagram • Heaven moves with strength; the exemplary person thereby strengthens without ceasing

VII — Twelve Dialectical Dialogues

Every Encounter Written Out in Full — Every Voice Speaking at Its Sharpest

❧ ✶ ❧

Dialogue 1: Fuller and Shan — Tension, Coherence, and the Integral Network

The most immediate and productive dialogue is between Fuller’s tensegrity and Shan’s relational dynamics. Both are structural accounts of how integrity is maintained in complex wholes. Both refuse reduction to parts. Both insist on the primacy of the relational field over the elements it connects. And both locate the source of structural integrity not in compression (the parts pushing against each other) but in tension (the continuous distributed holding that connects everything to everything). The encounter is immediately productive precisely because the two frameworks are genuinely analogous without being identical.

“Tension is omnidirectionally coherent. Tensegrity is an inherently nonredundant confluence of optimum structural efficiency.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.03

Fuller is saying: the structural integrity of a tensegrity system is not located in any single element but distributed continuously through the tensional network. No element bears the whole weight; every element contributes to the whole’s coherence. This is the structural principle of omnitransformation: change at any node propagates through the entire network, because the network is one continuous thing, not a collection of discrete parts.

Shan’s definition of excellence maps perfectly onto Fuller’s tensegrity: ‘capacity held in coherence’ is tensional integrity — the continuous distributed holding of structural coherence; ‘under constraint’ is the compressive islands of tensegrity — the specific structural challenges that the tensional network must hold; ‘over time’ is the temporal dimension that tensegrity engineering understands as fatigue and creep — the sustained performance of the system under repeated loading.

Fuller’s structural account challenges Shan on specificity. If relational dynamics is the intellectual tensegrity that holds the paper’s argument in coherence, then what are the specific tension members? What are the compression islands? Fuller would demand: show me the geometry. Show me the specific structural relationships. Shan’s framework is powerful as a structural analogy; what would it mean to make it as geometrically specific as a tensegrity structure? The challenge is productive: it pushes toward the formalisation that Shan explicitly avoids as premature Li.

Shan’s most important challenge to Fuller concerns formation. Tensegrity describes the distribution of tension and compression in an achieved structure. But how does the structure achieve its form? Fuller’s geodesic domes were assembled — their Li was imposed by the architect. Shan’s framework insists that the most important structural formations are not assembled but formed: they emerge from a Dao that precedes any explicit design. The tensional integrity of a living system is not engineered; it forms. And the question of how it forms — what formation process produces the tensional integrity — is precisely what tensegrity engineering cannot answer but Shan’s framework can.

“All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures. Universe is omnitensional integrity.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.04

The universe as tensegrity: Fuller’s most metaphysically ambitious claim. If correct, it means that Shan’s relational dynamics — her account of how coherence is maintained in complex relational fields — is not a social or intellectual theory but a cosmological one. The formation of relational integrity at every scale (the intimate relationship, the organisational ecosystem, the intellectual tradition, the universe itself) follows the same structural logic: continuous tension distributed through the whole, holding discrete elements in their specific structural positions without any single element bearing the full compressive load. The magic is in the mechanics. And the mechanics, at every scale, is tensegrity.

Dialogue 2: Wittgenstein (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus) and Shan — The Sayable and the Grain

The inexpressible that shows itself: both Wittgenstein and Shan are tracking a structural reality that exceeds every propositional statement about it. The mystical is not supernatural; it is the natural structure of the limit of language, the point at which the formation field’s depth exceeds the Li of any available vocabulary. The dialogue does not resolve this. It demonstrates it: through the collision of two formation traditions that each track the same inexpressible structural reality from different directions.

Wittgenstein’s mystical is precisely what shows itself at the limit of the sayable: the logical form shared by language and world, which cannot itself be stated in language because it is the condition of any statement. Li, for Shan, is precisely the inner grain that shows itself in the specific texture of the formed thing: the specific resistance of jade to the carver’s hand, the specific structural signature of a system’s formation history, the specific way this Dao has produced this pattern and no other. Neither can be fully said, because both are the condition of the saying rather than its object.

The challenge Wittgenstein poses to Shan: if Li shows itself rather than being said, what does Shan’s project of articulating Li actually accomplish? The Tractatus ends in silence. Shan’s essays do not end in silence; they reach for the articulation of what cannot quite be articulated. Wittgenstein would say: this is the attempt to say what can only be shown; it produces nonsense elevated to clarity by rhetorical force. Shan would respond: yes, and this is the only way a living tradition can transmit what it knows. The articulation is not the Li; it is the path that points toward the Li. The essay is a Dao that enables the reader to encounter the Li for themselves.

“Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 7 — the last line

The last line: Wittgenstein ends the Tractatus and stops. Shan begins her essays the next morning and writes again. Both are right. The silence is the recognition of the limit. The writing is the Dao of approaching the limit from a different direction. The tension between them — between falling silent and continuing to write — is itself the finest attunement that Heraclitus identifies: things bearing in opposite directions, the opposition that generates the structural reality neither can reach alone.

Wittgenstein’s silence and Shan’s surface: two ways of pointing at the same structural reality. The surface (the said, the spoken, the explicit Li) is never the whole story. Something shows itself beneath the surface that the surface cannot contain. Wittgenstein responds to this with silence: stop speaking at the limit. Shan responds with the essay form: speak carefully up to the limit, and let what cannot be said show itself in the speaking. Both are right. The silence is necessary. The careful speaking is also necessary. The tradition requires both.

Dialogue 3: Wittgenstein (Philosophical Investigations) and Shan — Forms of Life and the Inherited Path

“What has to be accepted, the given, is — so one could say — forms of life.” Forms of life are the fullest expression of retrospective intelligibility in Wittgenstein’s philosophy: they appear as unquestionable givens precisely because the Daos that produced them have been so thoroughly walked that their formative nature is entirely concealed. The form of life does not appear as a formation; it appears as ‘how things simply are.’ Wittgenstein’s philosophical therapy is, in Shan’s terms, the recovery of retrospective intelligibility — asking what Daos produced the Li that now presents itself as the unquestionable given.

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations p. 226

The given that must be accepted: forms of life are the inherited Daos — the accumulated, sedimented, largely pre-reflective formation patterns that practitioners enter rather than create. The Edinburgh seminar’s form of life was given before any Chinese international student arrived. The Chinese educational tradition’s form of life was given before any of those students began to speak. The collision of given forms of life is the Dao that produced Shan’s specific Li. The acceptance is the precondition of genuine transformation.

The form of life, for Wittgenstein, is not chosen; it is the pre-reflective background against which all choosing occurs. The child who grows up in a language community does not choose the language-game; they enter a form of life that is already in formation. This is Shan’s inherited path: the Dao that was already being walked before we arrived, the Li that was already forming before we could name it. Both Wittgenstein and Shan insist: the given is not a problem to be overcome but a formation condition to be inhabited.

“The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a life-form.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §23

Language as activity within a life-form: when Shan writes in English about Dao and Li, the speaking is part of a specific activity — cross-cultural complexity scholarship — and part of a life-form — the bilingual intellectual practice that is her specific formation. The same Chinese characters, deployed in a different activity and life-form, would produce different meaning through different use. This is why translation is always formation-transformation rather than meaning-transfer.

“For me, Dao functions as an accessible interface. By interface, I mean the place where one thing becomes available to another: where it gains access and finds traction.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine, but a Living Encounter’ (April 2026)

The form of life as interface: Wittgenstein sees language as embedded in activity; Shan sees the Dao as the interface between what is and what can be formed from it. Both are describing the same structural level: not the explicit statement (Li, proposition, rule) but the living practice within which statements occur and rules are followed. The language-game is the Dao of a specific linguistic practice; the Li of the language-game is the grammatical structure that emerges from the practice and makes it intelligible.

Wittgenstein challenges Shan on the question of private language. Can there be a purely individual Dao, a formation process that belongs entirely to one practitioner? Wittgenstein’s private language argument suggests not: all genuine formation is embedded in a shared form of life, a community of practice, a tradition of use. Shan’s framework is compatible with this: the individual formation process always occurs within and through the relational field, which is always already shared. But Shan adds something Wittgenstein cannot: the account of how the shared form of life itself was formed, how the Dao of a tradition came to produce the Li that now constitutes it.

Dialogue 4: Zhu Xi and Shan — Li and the Neo-Confucian Inheritance

Shan’s re-encounter with Li in the context of contemporary complexity thinking is not a break from the Chinese tradition but a re-encountering of it. Zhu Xi’s account of Li as “the pattern or principle that makes things what they are” is the deepest formulation of what Shan is working with. But the encounter is also a point of productive tension: Shan’s Dao-before-Li challenges Zhu Xi’s Li-first metaphysics at its foundations.

“Li is the principle or pattern that makes things what they are. Human nature is the Li that is universally present in all people.”

— Zhu Xi, as summarised in Britannica, Chinese Philosophy

The structural ambiguity: is Li prior to the things it makes, or is Li the product of the formation process that produced those things? Zhu Xi: Li is prior, qi is posterior. Shan: the Dao that produces the specific thing also produces the specific Li — they are co-emergent. The collision: if Li is prior, the investigator reveals a pre-existing pattern. If Li is co-emergent, the investigator must walk the Dao that produces the Li while remaining genuinely open to what the specific formation will produce. The stakes for practice are total.

The central agreement: Li is real. It is not a subjective projection; it is the actual structural grain of things. The jade’s texture, the organism’s developmental pattern, the tradition’s formation logic — all of these are instantiations of Li, not mental constructions imposed on a structureless material world. Zhu Xi and Shan share this structural realism completely.

The central disagreement: which comes first? Zhu Xi’s cosmic principle (天地之間，一理而已, between heaven and earth there is one Li and nothing else) is ontologically prior: the Li exists before the things it patterns. Shan’s Dao-before-Li inverts this: the formation process (Dao) precedes the grain it produces (Li). Intelligibility does not come before the path that gives rise to it.

“Between heaven and earth there is one Li and nothing else.”

— Zhu Xi

The most totalising claim in Neo-Confucian metaphysics, and Shan’s most significant challenge. One Li: the cosmic principle is single, unified, prior to all specific manifestations. Shan does not deny the coherence; she relocates its source. The unity is a formation achievement rather than a metaphysical foundation. The one Li that Zhu Xi identifies is the most comprehensive Li that two millennia of Chinese metaphysical formation has been able to articulate. Its universality is genuine; but it is earned, not given. 悖论: the most universal Li is the one that took the longest Dao to produce.

“Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. Intelligibility does not come first. The path does.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’ (May 2026)

The stakes of the disagreement: if Zhu Xi is right, you can know the Li of a situation before engaging with it and use that prior Li to guide your engagement. This is the Zhu Xi research programme: study the Li of all things until you understand the one cosmic Li that pervades them all. If Shan is right, you must walk the Dao of engagement with the specific situation in order to discover its specific Li. You cannot approach the situation with a pre-formed Li and expect structural attunement; you will impose the wrong pattern on the wrong grain. The practical stakes are enormous: Zhu Xi’s programme justifies encyclopedic learning; Shan’s insists on formation through lived engagement.

Dialogue 5: Juarrero and Shan — Enabling Constraints and Holding Capacity

Juarrero provides the formal philosophical tools — in the language of complexity science and Aristotelian causation — for what Shan is describing through Dao and Li. Juarrero’s enabling constraints are the structural counterpart of Shan’s holding capacity. Juarrero’s constitutive constraints — which create the coherence of a system — are the counterpart of Shan’s formed Dao.

“Far from representing messy, noisy complications that can be safely ignored, time and context are as much constituents of behavior as the behavior itself.”

— Alicia Juarrero, Dynamics in Action (1999)

Juarrero’s demolition of the standard analytical move: treat time and context as external conditions that can be abstracted away. Time and context are constitutive of behaviour, not noise. The behaviour cannot be understood as the output of a timeless algorithm because the behaviour IS its temporal unfolding in its specific context. Shan’s coupling-does-not-abolish-sequence claim is this argument applied to the Dao: the sequence is not a complication of the coupling; it is constitutive of what the formation IS.

“The path must open before its pattern can appear. The formation must precede the formed.”

— Alice Jing Shan — the ontological claim that underlies every essay

Juarrero’s enabling constraints are constraints that open the possibility space rather than closing it. A grammar is an enabling constraint: it does not determine what sentence you will say, but it enables the enormous space of possible sentences that are grammatical. The holding capacity that Shan describes — the structural capacity that must be built before greater complexity can be received — is precisely an enabling constraint in Juarrero’s sense: it opens the space within which further formation is possible, without determining what that formation will be.

“The establishment of context-sensitive constraints is the phase change that self-organizes the global dynamics of the whole system.”

— Alicia Juarrero, as summarised by Chris Corrigan

The formation threshold that separates a collection of interacting elements from a genuinely complex adaptive system. After the phase change, the constraints that emerge from the interactions become sensitive to the context that the interactions have created — the system begins to structure its own possibilities. This is Shan’s holding-capacity threshold: the formation achieves holding capacity when its constraints become context-sensitive, when the Li begins to actively shape the Dao that produces further Li.

“Relation is not one variable among others inside a dynamic process. It is the condition under which dynamics becomes consequential at all.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’ (May 2026)

The phase change: Juarrero’s most important concept for understanding Shan. A phase change is not a gradual increase in some parameter; it is a discontinuous structural transformation in which the whole system reorganises. The formation of the holding capacity is a phase change: before it, certain kinds of complexity cannot be received; after it, they can. The neonatal gut that has received enough milk (drop by drop) to begin developing reaches a phase transition: the system can now receive more. This is not a linear accumulation; it is a structural reorganisation. The Dao of gradual formation produces, at the right moment, a Li of transformed capacity.

“Coherence is induced by meaningful constraints, not forceful causes, and is then maintained by constraint propagation through the system.”

— Alicia Juarrero, Context Changes Everything (MIT Press, 2023)

Meaningful constraints, not forceful causes: this is the most precise Western complexity science formulation of the wuwei principle. The formation process that produces genuine structural coherence does not force; it constrains meaningfully — it shapes the possibility space without determining the specific outcomes. The Dao moves spontaneously and accomplishes its tasks without forceful intervention. Juarrero gives this the language of complexity science: coherence propagates through the system via constraint, not via linear causation. The grain forms through the walking of the path, not through the imposition of a predetermined pattern.

Dialogue 6: Zhu (WSR) and Shan — The Grammar of Li in Practice

Zhichang Zhu’s WSR framework and Shan’s relational dynamics are sister projects in a shared intellectual enterprise: both attempt to honour the full complexity of the Chinese philosophical tradition’s account of structural reality while connecting it to the contemporary discourse of complexity and systems science. The encounter between them is the most intimate in this paper, and therefore the most productive.

“The basic theme of WSR contends that wuli (regularities in objective existence), shili (ways of seeing and doing) and renli (human relationships) are ontologically differentiated yet methodologically inseparable.”

— Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu, ‘Knowing Wuli, Sensing Shili, Caring for Renli’ (2000)

Three irreducible registers of Li: wuli (the physical grain of things), shili (the situational grain of how things relate), renli (the human grain of how people should act). Each register requires a different formation to read: knowing wuli, sensing shili, caring for renli. The practitioner who reads all situations as wuli problems — or all as renli problems — is missing two-thirds of the Li of every actual situation.

WSR’s three-Li structure and Shan’s relational dynamics are complementary, not competing. WSR asks: how do practitioners engage with the multiple registers of structural reality (wuli, shili, renli) in specific problem situations? Shan asks: what is the fundamental ontological structure of reality that makes these registers necessary? WSR is primarily methodological; Shan is primarily ontological. Together they are complete: Shan provides the philosophical ground for what WSR practices; WSR provides the concrete methodological form for what Shan describes.

“Complementarity (yin-yang opposites), complex emergence (yi – perpetuated changes), spontaneous creativity (wu-wei – non-forced doing), and the unity of knowledge and action (zhi-xing heyi).”
