— Zhichang Zhu, ‘WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach’ (ScienceOpen)

The four principles of natural Li: complementarity (tension of opposites as the source of integrity), complex emergence (perpetuated change as the structure of formation), spontaneous generation (ziran — of itself so, the universe’s own tendency toward the production of Li without external forcing), and non-intervention (wuwei — the art of not acting before the grain appears). These four together constitute the deepest Chinese systems account of how formation works.

The most productive tension: WSR insists there is no fixed hierarchy among the three Li. Shan insists that within any coupled system, sequence remains. How do these square? They are, in fact, not contradictory. WSR’s no-fixed-hierarchy refers to methodological priority: you cannot prescribe in advance that wuli must always be addressed first, then shili, then renli. The situation determines which Li is most urgent. Shan’s sequence refers to ontological precedence: Dao before Li, relation before dynamics. WSR is correct about methodological flexibility. Shan is correct about ontological order. The practitioner must be methodologically flexible precisely because they understand the ontological sequence.

Dialogue 7: Prigogine and Shan — Dissipation, Time, and the Arrow of Formation

Prigogine’s dissipative structures provide a physical grounding for what Shan is describing at the level of relational dynamics. Both accounts insist that order is not a given but an achievement — one that requires continuous energetic input to maintain. Both acknowledge bifurcation points — moments of structural instability. But Prigogine cannot tell us which bifurcation will occur at a given point. Shan’s framework, focused on the long game and on corrective capacity, might offer what Prigogine’s physics cannot: an account of which relational configurations are most likely to maintain viability over time.

“The farther a system is from equilibrium, the greater is its sensitivity to fluctuations. Fluctuations can precipitate new global structure.”

— Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers, Order Out of Chaos (1984)

Prigogine’s bifurcation: at maximum distance from equilibrium, the system is most sensitive to specific perturbations. The practitioner who arrives at the bifurcation with the specific formation-sufficiency required to read which direction the Shī is leaning — who has walked the Dao that produced the specific Li needed for this specific bifurcation — is the practitioner who can intervene while intervention is still possible.

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. The capacity for correction diminishes before the collapse becomes visible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Nothing Collapses in One Move’ (April 2026)

The bifurcation point is Shan’s moment of structural vulnerability: far from equilibrium, the system is maximally sensitive to perturbation — a small fluctuation can precipitate a completely new global structure. The path narrows at the bifurcation point: the system can tip toward viability-restoring reorganisation or toward collapse, and the difference is not predetermined but depends on the specific configuration of the relational field at that specific moment. This is why Shan insists on corrective capacity as the crucial structural variable: it is what determines which way the bifurcation goes.

The deepest tension: Prigogine’s physics is agnostic about the direction of bifurcation. The fluctuation that tips the system is random; the new global structure that emerges is not predictable from prior conditions. Shan’s framework implies that the relational configuration of the system — its formation history, its corrective capacity, its structural coherence — is not irrelevant to the direction of the bifurcation. Systems with greater structural integrity (in Fuller’s sense) are more likely to bifurcate toward viability-restoring configurations than toward collapse. This is not determinism; it is formation-sensitive probability. The long game cultivates the structural conditions that make the right bifurcation more likely.

Dialogue 8: Bateson and Shan — The Metapattern and Li

“What is the pattern that connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all four of them to me? And me to you?”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature (1979)

Bateson’s question is the question Shan’s framework answers from the inside. The metapattern is Li at its most general: the structural principle that diverse formations share despite their surface differences. The metapattern is not prior to the formations it connects; it is the emergent product of the specific Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient attention. Bateson walked the Dao. The Li of the metapattern appeared.

“Li is the inner grain of things — the structural pattern that makes a specific thing what it is, not a general principle imposed from without but the grain of a specific formation.”

— Alice Jing Shan, paraphrasing the core claim of Li

Bateson’s pattern that connects and Shan’s Li are in direct and productive dialogue. The pattern that connects the crab to the lobster is not genetic identity (they share a common ancestor but are not the same organism); it is structural identity — the same Li of bilateral symmetry, segmented body plan, exoskeletal organisation, crustacean joint articulation. This is exactly the Li that a Cook Ding who had studied crustaceans would discover: the inner grain that connects all these forms and is not reducible to any one of them.

“The map is not the territory. But the map is a phenomenon in the territory.”

— Gregory Bateson

The map in the territory: Bateson’s most structurally important correction. The Li is not the Dao — but the Li is a real formation within the formation field it describes. The relational dynamics framework is not the formation field it tracks; but the framework itself is a formation that participates in the ongoing formation of the field it tracks. The map shapes the territory as it maps it. Language produces navigable worlds.

“Li is not the thing; it is the grain of the thing. And the grain was always there before the naming of it.”

— Alice Jing Shan — paraphrase of the core ontological claim about Li

The map is a phenomenon in the territory: this is Bateson’s most structurally elegant statement of the relation between Li and Dao. The map (the Li, the named pattern, the articulated understanding) is not separate from the territory (the Dao, the formation process, the actual grain of things); it is a phenomenon that arises within the territory, a formation within the formation. This is why Shan can say the Li was always there: the named pattern is a phenomenon of the formation process, not an imposition upon it. And this is also why premature Li is always inadequate: it mistakes the map for the territory, the named pattern for the actual grain.

Bateson’s challenge to Shan: if the pattern that connects is real, can it be described? Bateson spent his entire career trying to describe it, using cybernetics, ecology, anthropology, genetics, and communication theory. He never found a single adequate language. Shan does not try to describe the Li of the universe; she describes the Li of specific formations: the specific structural grain of a person’s relational situation, an organisation’s developmental trajectory, a tradition’s formation history. This is the methodological wisdom of the particular: instead of seeking the one metapattern, illuminate the specific Li of the specific Dao. The metapattern shows itself in the specific; it cannot be stated from above.

Dialogue 9: Kauffman and Shan — Edge of Chaos and Excellence

“Systems at the edge of chaos tend to exhibit the richest possible behaviour. Frozen systems cannot explore new configurations; systems in chaos have no coherence to explore with.”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1995)

Rich behaviour at the edge: not random, not predetermined, but genuinely creative. Shan’s excellence is this edge-state maintained as a formation achievement. The excellent practitioner does not visit the edge; they have developed the specific formation that enables them to maintain edge-proximity under the specific pressures of their specific domain. Cook Ding at the edge of chaos: the cut that follows the grain without forcing, that exploits the maximum structural sensitivity of the formation at the moment of maximum coherence.

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. Not at the frozen end. Not at the chaotic end. Held.”

— Alice Jing Shan — the definition of excellence as edge-of-chaos maintenance

Kauffman’s edge of chaos is the structural region within which Shan’s excellence is possible: the complex adaptive region between frozen order (too much Li, too little Dao — the system cannot respond to new formation conditions) and chaos (too much Dao, too little Li — the system has no coherence with which to respond). Excellence requires operating precisely at the edge: enough Li to have coherent structural capacity, enough openness to the Dao to be able to form new Li when the situation requires.

The adjacent possible arrives here as the structural account of what the edge of chaos makes available. At the edge of chaos, the system has access to the largest possible adjacent possible: it can move into the maximum number of new structural configurations from its current position. The frozen system (too much Li) can move only into configurations that its existing structure permits. The chaotic system (too much Dao) has no coherent structure with which to move at all. The excellence framework: maintain the structural position that maximises the adjacent possible while maintaining the coherence that makes movement meaningful.

“The biosphere keeps expanding the adjacent possible. Life creates its own possibilities.”

— Stuart Kauffman, Reinventing the Sacred (2008)

Life creates its own possibilities: the adjacent possible is a formation achievement. The Dao does not merely traverse the existing adjacent possible; it expands it. Each step of genuine formation opens formation possibilities that did not exist before that step. This is why the long game is strategic: not because patience is a virtue but because the only way to access the formations that matter is to have walked the Dao that produces them.

Life creates its own possibilities: this is Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation’ stated as biological cosmology. The formed system does not simply occupy its achieved Li; it continuously expands the adjacent possible available to its further formation. Each achievement of Li opens new Dao; each new Dao produces new Li. The formation process is not a sequence of steps toward a fixed destination but a continuously self-expanding exploration of an inexhaustible adjacent possible. This is why the long game is long: not because the destination is far away but because the process of formation itself keeps creating new destinations that were not imaginable before the previous formation was achieved.

Dialogue 10: Varela/Maturana and Shan — Autopoiesis and the Prior Field

“A living system is organised as a network of productions of components which, through their interactions and transformations, continuously regenerate and realise the network of productions that produced them.”

— Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, The Tree of Knowledge (1987)

Autopoiesis as living formation: the formal definition. The living system is its own production — it produces the components that constitute it, which in turn produce the network that produces them. For Shan, every genuine formation has this character: it does not merely persist; it actively produces the conditions of its own persistence. The formation that loses this self-producing quality has begun its collapse.

Autopoiesis is the most rigorous biological account of the formation principle that underlies Shan’s relational dynamics. The autopoietic network produces the components that produce the network: the formation process is its own formation condition. This is the self-referential Dao: the walking of the path is what produces the capacity to walk further. The holding capacity that Shan describes — the structural capacity that enables further formation — is the autopoietic achievement of the living system.

“Evolution has no purpose; it simply drifts with the only constraint of maintaining structural coupling.”

— Francisco Varela, The Tree of Knowledge (1987)

Structural drift with viability as the only constraint: the practitioner who walks the Dao with a specific Li in mind has confused Dao-walking with Li-imposition. The correct relationship: walk with structural viability as the constraint, remain genuinely open to the specific Li that the specific Dao produces, and trust that genuine formation produces the most viable Li available.

“Coupling does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’ (May 2026)

Natural drift and ontological sequence: Varela’s ‘simply drifts’ might seem to contradict Shan’s insistence on sequence. The drift has no purpose or direction — it is not heading toward a pre-specified Li. And yet it drifts with the constraint of maintaining structural coupling: the drift is not random but structurally constrained by the system’s own formation history. The sequence that Shan insists on is precisely this structural constraint: the system can only drift into structurally adjacent configurations, which means its formation history determines what it can become. Coupling does not abolish this constraint; it makes the constraint harder to see because the coupled system appears to be responding freely to its environment.

Maturana’s most provocative challenge to Shan: autopoiesis exists only in the molecular domain. The extension of autopoiesis to social systems (which Luhmann attempts) is, for Maturana, a conceptual error. If Maturana is right, Shan’s relational dynamics — which describes social and intellectual formations using concepts analogous to autopoiesis — is making the same error. Shan’s response, implicit in her framework: the structural analogy is valid not because social systems are biologically autopoietic but because the same formation logic (the path precedes the pattern, the formation produces the formed, holding capacity enables further complexity) operates at multiple scales. The analogy is structural, not identity.

Dialogue 11: Laozi and Shan — The Dao Before the Path

道可道，非常道 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao — Laozi Ch.1

“I am not approaching Dao simply through cultural ownership, nor as an authority on Daoism. I am approaching it as someone shaped by language, duality, and the long-horizon perspective that Chinese education gave me.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine, but a Living Encounter’ (April 2026)

The most intimate dialogue in the paper. Not because Laozi and Shan are close in time — twenty-six centuries separate them — but because Shan is explicitly working within the formation field that Laozi inaugurated. She is not studying Laozi from the outside; she is walking a Dao that Laozi helped to form. The Dao she encounters in her intellectual work is already shaped by the Daodejing, even when she does not cite it. The form of life (Wittgenstein) of Chinese intellectual culture carries Laozi’s formation within it.

上善若水。水善利萬物而不爭 — shàng shàn ruò shuǐ. Shuǐ shàn lì wàn wù ér bù zhēng — Highest good is like water. Water benefits the ten thousand things without contending — Laozi Ch.8

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. It does not contend. It holds.”

— Alice Jing Shan

Water does not contend. It benefits without contending — it follows the grain, seeks the lowest position, carves through the rock through sustained engagement rather than concentrated force. This is Shan’s excellence: not the dramatic assertion of structural superiority but the patient, continuous, coherent holding of capacity that eventually produces the most profound structural transformation. Move 37 is a water move: not impressive in the moment, structurally decisive over time. The long game is the water game.

为學日益，為道日搏 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi Dào rì sǔn — In pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day — Laozi Ch.48

Daily subtraction: this is Laozi’s most structurally challenging claim. The pursuit of Li (learning, articulation, named pattern) proceeds by daily addition. The pursuit of Dao proceeds by daily subtraction: the relinquishment of premature Li, the willingness to hold the formation without naming it too quickly, the structural patience that keeps the path open for the Li that has not yet emerged. Shan’s warning about premature Li is the Laozian claim: when the Dao feels too smooth, something has been named too quickly. Something must be subtracted. The grain of the situation must be re-encountered without the overlay of the previous Li.

Dialogue 12: Wittgenstein, Fuller, Shan, and Zhu Xi — Four-Way Collision

The most productive encounter is the four-way collision between Wittgenstein’s two silences, Fuller’s structural universe, Shan’s living interface, and Zhu Xi’s Li as cosmic principle. Together they triangulate the same territory from four different angles.

The inexpressible that shows itself: both Wittgenstein and Shan are tracking a structural reality that exceeds every propositional statement about it. The mystical is not supernatural; it is the natural structure of the limit of language, the point at which the formation field’s depth exceeds the Li of any available vocabulary. The dialogue does not resolve this. It demonstrates it: through the collision of two formation traditions that each track the same inexpressible structural reality from different directions.

“Between heaven and earth there is one Li and nothing else.”

— Zhu Xi

The most totalising claim in Neo-Confucian metaphysics, and Shan’s most significant challenge. One Li: the cosmic principle is single, unified, prior to all specific manifestations. Shan does not deny the coherence; she relocates its source. The unity is a formation achievement rather than a metaphysical foundation. The one Li that Zhu Xi identifies is the most comprehensive Li that two millennia of Chinese metaphysical formation has been able to articulate. Its universality is genuine; but it is earned, not given. 悖论: the most universal Li is the one that took the longest Dao to produce.

Wittgenstein locates the fundamental interface at the limit of language: there is something that shows itself without being sayable, and this is the most important thing. Fuller locates it in the tensional network: the coherence of the whole is maintained by forces that are not visible in any single element but distributed through the entire structure. Zhu Xi locates it in the cosmic principle: one Li pervades all things and makes them what they are. Shan locates it in the living relational field: the surface of any situation always carries more structural depth than is visible — the Dao beneath the Li, the formation beneath the formed.

The collision is most productive at the point where all four converge: that what is most fundamental in any structure is not its visible elements but its invisible relational coherence — the continuous tensional network (Fuller), the showing that cannot be said (Wittgenstein), the cosmic Li that makes things what they are (Zhu Xi), the formation field that precedes the formed (Shan). Four traditions, one recognition. Four vocabularies, one structural reality. Four paths, one grain.

The convergence is not identity. Wittgenstein insists on silence where Fuller would build and Zhu Xi would articulate and Shan would write essays. These are not merely stylistic differences; they reflect genuine divergences about what is possible in the face of structural depth. But the divergences themselves converge on the same recognition: there is something more than the surface, and it is the most structurally important thing. Whatever cannot be said shows itself. Whatever cannot be owned reveals its presence through the quality of what is formed in relation to it.

XXIV

VIII — Four Convergences, Three Divergences, Five Open Questions

8.1 The Four Convergences

Convergence 1: What Is Most Fundamental Cannot Be Fully Stated

Convergence 2: Constraint Enables Rather Than Merely Restricts

From Fuller’s tensegrity to Juarrero’s enabling constraints to Shan’s holding capacity to WSR’s no-fixed-hierarchy: all traditions agree that the structural constraints that shape a system’s formation are not merely restrictive but constitutive and enabling. The grammar that constrains the sentence is what enables meaningful speech. The tensional network that constrains each element’s position is what enables the structure’s integrity. The formation history that constrains the system’s possible responses is what enables its genuine responsiveness. Constraint and capacity are not opposed; they are mutually constitutive.

Convergence 3: The Temporal Dimension Is Irreducible

All traditions insist, in different registers, that time is not an external frame within which structural formation occurs but an intrinsic dimension of the formation itself. Prigogine: the arrow of time is real and irreversible; the formation history cannot be undone. Bergson: duration is the living dimension of genuine existence. Shan: the formation process takes the time it takes; it cannot be shortened without losing the holding capacity that makes the result viable. Maturana/Varela: structural coupling is a history of interactions; it is temporally constituted. WSR: the three Li invite, transform, and penetrate each other over time in unpredictable ways. Time is not external to the formation; it is internal to the Dao.

Convergence 4: Relation Is Prior to the Elements It Relates

From Shan’s ‘relation precedes dynamics’ to Maturana and Varela’s structural coupling to Bateson’s pattern that connects to Fuller’s tensional network to Heidegger’s banks that emerge through the bridge: all traditions agree that the elements of a complex system do not pre-exist the relational field that constitutes them. The terms of a relation emerge as what they are through the relation; they are not prior atoms that then enter into relations. This is the most fundamental structural claim of the entire paper, and it is the claim that Shan articulates most precisely: relation precedes dynamics.

8.2 The Three Irreducible Divergences

Divergence 1: Silence, Encounter, or Construction?

The traditions diverge on what to do at the limit of the expressible. Wittgenstein’s Tractatus: be silent. Wittgenstein’s Investigations: return words from their metaphysical to their everyday use. Fuller: build the tensegrity structure and let the structural reality speak through the built form. Zhu Xi: articulate the Li as completely as possible, knowing that the one cosmic Li can approach but never achieve full articulation. Shan: write essays that begin with particulars and follow the formation of the structural insight without forcing premature closure. These are not merely methodological differences; they reflect genuine divergences about the relationship between the inexpressible and the expressible, and about what responsibility the practitioner has toward each.

Divergence 2: Universal or Particular?

Zhu Xi’s Li is universal — the same cosmic principle in all things. Shan’s Li is particular — the specific inner grain of this specific formation, this specific situation, this specific Dao. This is not a minor disagreement; it determines the entire methodological programme. If Li is universal, the project is to understand the universal principle and apply it. If Li is particular, the project is to develop the structural attunement that enables genuine encounter with the Li of each specific situation. Shan’s framework is methodologically specific: it cannot be reduced to a general principle without losing precisely what makes it structurally valuable.

Divergence 3: Can Methodology Ground Itself?

WSR, Cynefin, and Shan’s own framework each emerged from formation processes that preceded the methodologies themselves. WSR emerged from the specific historical context of post-Mao Chinese intellectual reform. Cynefin emerged from knowledge management practice. Shan’s framework emerged from her specific cross-cultural intellectual formation. Can any of these methodologies reflect on their own formation conditions? Or does the Dao that produced the Li of the methodology remain necessarily invisible to the methodology itself? This is the deepest limit of all structural self-knowledge: the formation that produced the understanding cannot be fully understood by the understanding it produced.

8.3 Five Open Questions

What is the topology of a relational system’s tension members and compression islands? Fuller’s tensegrity can be geometrically described. Can Shan’s relational dynamics be structurally described with comparable precision — and if so, what would the geometry of a relational field look like?

How do we detect the thinning of corrective capacity before collapse becomes visible? Shan identifies the structural signature (the path narrowing, the surface smoothness of premature Li) but has not yet developed the diagnostic instruments for detecting it in real time. What would a Li-sensitivity index look like in practice?

Can Shan’s relational dynamics be formalised in ways that preserve rather than lose the grain? Formalisation tends to produce premature Li. But some degree of formalisation is necessary for a framework to be shared, tested, and extended across different formation contexts. Where is the right degree of formalisation — enough to be communicable, not so much as to lose the structural attunement that makes the framework valuable?

What is the relationship between Li and emergence? If Li is the inner grain that makes a thing what it is, and emergence is the production of new structural properties that were not predictable from the components, then every act of genuine emergence is the production of new Li from a formation process whose Li was not yet fully specified. This is the deepest question the paper opens: how does new Li form? What is the Dao of Li’s own formation?

8.4 Glimpses of Li: A Concluding Reflection

The title of Shan’s series — “Dao: The Art of the Long Game” — is itself a structural claim. The long game is the game whose Li can only be seen in retrospect, whose decisive moves are invisible in the moment they are made, whose excellence consists not in dramatic performance but in the patient cultivation of the structural conditions within which the right Li can emerge at the right moment. This paper has been an attempt at the long game. It has assembled more than twenty-five voices across twenty-six centuries and three major intellectual traditions, following the formation of a structural insight through the specific texture of its multiple encounters.

What glimpses has this paper produced? Fuller’s “Tension is the great integrity” and Shan’s “excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time” reveal themselves as two statements of the same structural claim. Wittgenstein’s two silences and Laozi’s “the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao” reveal themselves as the same structural recognition at the boundary of the sayable. Juarrero’s enabling constraints and Shan’s holding capacity reveal themselves as the same structural concept in two vocabularies. And across all of them, this: path before pattern; Dao before Li; formation before formed; relation before dynamics. One recognition, many paths.

“Dao before Li. Path before pattern. Grain before intelligibility. Exploration before explanation. Formation before formed.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’ (May 2026) — paraphrased

Four convergences. Twelve dialogues. Twenty-five-plus voices. One structural reality, seen differently from every position within it. And Snelson was right all along: the magic is in the mechanics. And Wang Bi was right: the sage who has no deliberate mind responds with perfect structural appropriateness. And Bergson was right: for a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly. And Shan is right: what is formed is still in formation.

❧ ✶ ❧

The Thesis

Stated Without Apology, Defended Without Qualification

❧ ✶ ❧

Alice Jing Shan is producing one of the most significant contemporary contributions to complexity ontology, structural philosophy, and cross-cultural systems thinking in the early twenty-first century. This is not a modest claim carefully hedged for academic consumption. It is the structural conclusion that this text has been building toward from its first page, and it is defended here with the full force of the evidence assembled across every preceding chapter.

The evidence is not testimonial. It is structural. Shan has done what no other contemporary thinker has done: she has placed the Chinese philosophical tradition’s account of structural formation — its ontology of Dao and Li, its ethics of relational precedence, its epistemology of formation-before-named-pattern — in genuine philosophical collision with the Western complexity science tradition, the tensegrity philosophy of Fuller, the language philosophy of Wittgenstein, the phenomenology of Heidegger, the systems methodology of WSR, and the strategic intelligence of the Chinese military tradition. The result is not a synthesis. It is not a translation. It is something rarer and more valuable: a genuine Horizontverschmelzung in Gadamer’s precise sense — a fusion of horizons that enlarges both without dissolving either.

The magnitude of this contribution becomes fully visible only when you see what is at stake in the three core claims:

Dao precedes Li. The formation process precedes the intelligibility it produces. No amount of prior understanding substitutes for the formation that generates understanding. This is not a cultural preference or a stylistic observation. It is an ontological claim about the structure of reality, supported by biology (autopoiesis, structural coupling), physics (dissipative structures, irreversibility), philosophy (Wittgenstein’s forms of life, Heidegger’s dwelling, Bergson’s duration), and strategic practice (Cook Ding, Move 37, the Empty City Stratagem). If this claim is correct — and this text argues that it is — then the entire Western tradition of concept-first, design-first, planning-first approaches to complex situations is structurally wrong at its foundations. Not wrong as a preference. Wrong as a matter of structural ontology.

Relation precedes dynamics. The relational field within which any dynamic occurs is ontologically prior to the dynamic itself. Motion without a relational field is just motion. Dynamics — consequential, transmissible, intelligible movement — requires the prior constitution of a relational field that makes movement matter. This is not a sociological observation about the importance of context. It is a metaphysical claim about the constitution of consequential action. The organisation that does not understand this — that tries to drive outcomes without attending to the relational field that determines whether any outcome is possible — is doing motion management. Not dynamics management.

Coupling does not abolish sequence. Even within the most tightly coupled system — the human body, the DNA molecule, the intimate relationship, the complex organisation — the formation sequence remains structurally constitutive. What was built first shapes what can be built next. The order in which the relational field was formed determines what the system can become. This seems obvious once stated. It is ignored with remarkable consistency in every domain of human practice, from organisational management to political governance to educational design. The consequences of this ignorance are visible in every system that collapses not in one dramatic move but through the long, invisible narrowing of its path.

These three claims, taken together, constitute a structural ontology — an account of what reality is, at its formation level — that is more powerful, more precise, and more practically consequential than anything currently on offer in Western complexity science, management theory, or political philosophy. This text has assembled the evidence. The verdict is clear.

What Cannot Hold

The Arguments That Fail and Why They Fail

❧ ✶ ❧

The Failure of Design-First Strategy

The dominant tradition in Western strategic thinking — from Ansoff’s corporate strategy to Porter’s Five Forces to the entire apparatus of strategic planning — proceeds by placing Li before Dao. You articulate the strategic objective (the Li you want to achieve), design the pathway to reach it (the Dao you will walk), and then implement the design. This approach cannot hold, not because it is occasionally ineffective, but because it is structurally wrong about the relationship between objective and path. The objective that is articulated before the path is walked is not the Li of the situation; it is the Li of the planner’s current formation, projected onto a situation whose actual formation conditions have not yet been encountered. When the walk begins, the situation’s actual Li begins to appear — and it is never identical to the planned Li. The question is whether the organisation can read the actual Li (follow the Dao) or can only continue executing the planned Li (impose premature pattern). The great majority cannot. The great majority hit resistance and hack through it rather than finding the articulation. The great majority deplete themselves against the grain of the situation they are supposed to be navigating.

This is not a management consultancy failure. This is a structural error at the level of ontology. Design-first strategy assumes that the Li of the future situation can be known before the Dao of engagement with that situation has been walked. Shan’s framework demonstrates that this assumption fails. The Dao always generates surprises. The situation always has Li that the pre-engagement analysis missed. The organisations that survive and flourish are not the ones with the best strategic plans; they are the ones with the deepest structural attunement to the Dao of their situation — the ones who can read the grain as they walk it, who can adjust without losing coherence, who can hold their capacity in the specific structural configuration that the actual situation requires.

The Failure of Shallow Systems Thinking

There is a genre of systems thinking — enormously popular in organisational development, consulting, and leadership education — that takes the vocabulary of complexity science (emergence, feedback loops, leverage points, non-linearity) and deploys it as a superior analytical framework for understanding organisations. This enterprise fails structurally because it substitutes the Li of complexity science for the Dao of structural formation. It names the patterns — emergence, feedback, leverage — without developing the practitioner’s capacity to actually read the structural grain of specific situations. The result is a more sophisticated vocabulary for the same premature Li: practitioners who can describe a system as complex and emergent and non-linear but cannot actually attune to its specific formation conditions, cannot actually follow its specific Dao, cannot actually find its specific Li.

The tell is always the same: the practitioner reaches for the framework name first. Before encountering the specific situation fully, they are already asking: is this a complex system or a complicated one? Where are the leverage points? What are the feedback loops? These are Li questions asked before the Dao has been walked. The Cook Ding who asks “where are the joints?” before touching the animal is not Cook Ding. Cook Ding finds the joints by moving the knife — by walking the Dao of engagement with this specific animal at this specific moment. The framework arrives afterward, as a description of what the structural attunement discovered. Not before.

The Failure of Pseudo-Eastern Corporate Philosophy

There is a growing industry of pseudo-Eastern corporate philosophy — Dao in the boardroom, wu wei as management technique, mindfulness as productivity tool — that is structurally more dishonest than straightforward Western planning addiction because it borrows the vocabulary of structural attunement while refusing the formation that makes structural attunement possible. You cannot adopt the vocabulary of Dao and continue to operate with a planning-first, Li-before-Dao structural framework. The vocabulary becomes a decoration. The Dao that feels smooth and familiar and readily available is, precisely as Shan warns, the Dao that has lost its Li. The ease with which ‘Dao’ travels in corporate culture — the readiness with which it is adopted as a brand name for a certain kind of leadership aspiration — is the measure of how far it has drifted from the structural precision that makes it genuinely useful.

Shan’s framework is not available for this appropriation. It demands too much. It demands the willingness to not-yet-know — to hold the formation open, to resist premature Li, to walk the Dao before naming the pattern. It demands structural honesty about the difference between following the grain and imposing a pattern. It demands the formation that can only come from the long game. This is not a critique of Chinese culture in Western organisations; it is a critique of the structural superficiality that reaches for the vocabulary of depth without undergoing the formation that depth requires. The corporate Dao fails because it is Li without Dao. The naming without the walking. The grain without the path that generated it.

The Failure of Network Theory Without Formation

Network theory — in its social, computational, and biological variants — has produced enormous analytical power through its mapping of relational structures. But the dominant tradition of network theory makes a structural error that Shan’s framework exposes: it treats the network as given (a set of nodes and edges whose properties can be analysed) rather than as formed (a relational field whose current configuration is the product of a specific formation history that shapes what the network can become). The static network map cannot tell you what the network’s formation history was, what constraints shaped its development, or what formation conditions are required for it to maintain viability.

If Shan is correct — and this text argues that she is — then the static network map is always already a premature Li: it captures the pattern without capturing the Dao that produced it. The network theorist who analyses the current configuration of a social network cannot, from that analysis alone, determine whether the network is at its formation peak (viable, growing, able to receive more complexity) or at its formation nadir (narrowing, losing corrective capacity, approaching the invisible collapse that will only become visible retrospectively). Only the Dao-before-Li framework gives you the questions to ask about formation history, holding capacity, and structural integrity. The network map alone cannot.

The Failure of Zhu Xi’s Li-First Metaphysics

This failure must be stated clearly because Zhu Xi is the most important Chinese philosopher of the second millennium CE, and his influence on the tradition within which Shan operates is enormous. Zhu Xi’s one Li that pervades all things is a magnificent intellectual achievement. It is also structurally wrong as an account of the relationship between Li and Dao. The cosmic principle cannot precede the formation process that produces it, any more than the grain of jade can precede the geological formation that created the jade. The grain is real; it is not a human projection. But its reality is downstream of the formation process. Intelligibility does not come first. The path does. And the Li of the path can only be discovered by walking it — not by prior study of what the one cosmic Li requires.

The practical consequence: Zhu Xi’s programme of “investigating things to extend knowledge” (格物致知, gé wù zhī zhī) systematically overweights the study of Li before the walk of Dao. The examination system that his philosophical framework legitimated produced extraordinarily well-read officials who could cite the canonical Li with precision and who were structurally incompetent in the face of situations whose actual grain did not match the Li they had memorised. Wang Yangming’s correction (knowledge and action are one; you do not genuinely know until you have acted) and Shan’s correction (Dao before Li; relation before dynamics) are corrections of the same fundamental error. The error costs more than academic argument. It costs viability.

道先於理 — The Full Ontological Defence

❧ ✶ ❧

The Phenomenological Defence

From inside the experience of formation, Dao-before-Li is phenomenologically obvious. The practitioner who is genuinely forming — learning a new skill, entering a new relational context, walking a new path — does not encounter Li first. They encounter confusion, resistance, partial pattern, emerging structure. The Li arrives later, as the formation deepens, as the path reveals its grain. Cook Ding’s first year of butchering oxen was not the experience of clear Li; it was the experience of Dao without yet-formed Li. The nineteen years of formation produced the Li of perfect structural attunement. Phenomenologically, the sequence is undeniable: the experience of Dao precedes the experience of Li, and the experience of Li is always the experience of Li that the Dao has produced.

Heidegger’s phenomenology of dwelling confirms this from the Western tradition. We do not first understand the structure of a place and then inhabit it. We inhabit first — we dwell, we move, we encounter the place in its specific texture — and the understanding of the place’s structure emerges from the dwelling. The locale comes into existence through the bridge. The understanding of the locale comes through the crossing. Phenomenology cannot begin with Li and then walk the Dao; it must begin with the walking (the dwelling, the forming, the encountering) and arrive at the Li as the achievement of the walking.

The Epistemological Defence

Wittgenstein’s On Certainty is the most rigorous Western epistemological grounding for Dao-before-Li. The riverbed propositions — the background certainties that are not themselves justified but that provide the condition for all justification — are the Li of an epistemic form of life. But Wittgenstein’s crucial insight is that the riverbed was not always where it is now: it formed through the flowing of the river (the Dao of epistemic practice). The current certainty structure (the Li of the epistemic community) is the product of a formation history that it cannot fully articulate. The Dao produced the Li; the Li cannot reach back and justify the Dao that produced it.

“At the core of all well-founded belief lies belief that is unfounded.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, On Certainty §253

Unfounded, not arbitrary: the foundation is not a free choice but a formation achievement. The riverbed was formed by specific geological processes (the Dao of the river’s history) and now functions as the condition of all subsequent riverflow. You cannot choose a different riverbed without restarting the geological process. The epistemological import: you cannot simply decide to have a different formation structure. You must undergo the formation. The Dao of epistemic formation precedes the Li of epistemic certainty, always and necessarily.

The Systems-Theoretical Defence

Maturana and Varela’s autopoiesis provides the systems-theoretical grounding. The autopoietic network produces the components that produce the network: the formation process is its own formation condition. This means there is no starting point at which the Li of the system exists before the formation process has operated. The Li of an autopoietic system is always the Li that its specific formation history has produced. There is no universal autopoietic Li; there is only the specific Li of this specific system with this specific formation history. Dao before Li, necessarily and without exception, in every living system.

Kauffman’s adjacent possible makes the same point in the language of possibility space. The Li available to a system at any given moment — the patterns it can actually achieve — is determined by its current structural configuration, which is the product of its formation history. You cannot leap to a Li that is not in your adjacent possible. The Dao of formation is what expands the adjacent possible. And the adjacent possible determines what Li is achievable. The sequence is ontological: formation (Dao) precedes and determines the possibility space of pattern (Li).

The Strategic Defence

Move 37 is the strategic proof. AlphaGo’s thirty-seventh move in Game 2 of the 2016 match against Lee Sedol was not in the game tree at the moment it was played. No human strategic analysis of the board position would have identified it as the right move. It looked wrong. It was in fact the most structurally consequential move of the game. What AlphaGo had done, through its extraordinary formation process (forty million training games, formation of structural attunement that no human could replicate through any amount of Li-study), was develop a capacity to read the Dao of the specific board position that the Li of human Go theory could not yet name.

The strategic lesson is exact: if you approach a complex strategic situation with the Li you already have — if you categorise the situation through your existing frameworks and select the move that your existing analysis recommends — you will always miss the Move 37 that exists in the specific structural field of this specific situation. The Move 37 can only be found by a formation so deep that the specific Dao of the specific position can be read directly, without the mediation of named patterns. Zhuge Liang’s Longzhong Plan was a Move 37: he read the structural field of the Three Kingdoms situation with such depth that he could prescribe a strategic path whose Li would only become visible over years of subsequent events. Dao before Li. Formation before named pattern. The path reveals itself to the practitioner who has been formed to read it.

耦合不廂除序列

Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence — The Full Philosophical Chapter

❧ ✶ ❧

This chapter should be famous. Not because it makes a spectacular claim. Because it makes a claim that is simultaneously structurally obvious and systematically ignored — and because the cost of ignoring it is visible in every failed institution, every collapsed marriage, every declining empire, every university that has lost its formation coherence, every government that cannot govern, every organisation that cannot learn. The claim: even in the most tightly coupled system, the sequence of formation remains structurally constitutive. The order in which things formed shapes what they can become.

In Developmental Psychology

The developmental psychologist’s insight: secure attachment must form before autonomous exploration becomes genuinely possible. The infant who has not formed a secure relational base (the holding capacity of the primary attachment) cannot explore the world freely because every encounter with novelty triggers anxiety rather than curiosity. The sequence is not arbitrary: the attachment must form first because it is the formation condition for everything that follows. No amount of subsequent therapeutic intervention fully replaces the formation that did not occur. The sequence was constitutive. It cannot be retrospectively corrected without the cost of undertaking the full formation process that was missed.

This is not a clinical observation about unusual developmental failures. It is a structural observation about the nature of formation itself: every capacity requires a prior formation condition that must itself have been formed before the capacity can develop. The neonatal gut that receives milk too fast is not accelerating its development; it is destroying the formation conditions for the development that could have occurred. The Dao of drop-by-drop formation is not inefficiency. It is the recognition of ontological sequence in biological systems.

In Marriage and Intimate Formation

The most intimate demonstration of the principle. Two people who have been in a relationship for twenty years have formed something that cannot be replicated by any other pair of people in the same chronological length of time, because their specific formation sequence — the specific perturbations they absorbed, the specific adaptations they made, the specific crises they navigated and the specific ways they navigated them — is unique and irreversible. The couple that has been through a specific crisis together has a structural resource (the knowledge of how they survived that crisis, the trust formed in the surviving) that was not present before the crisis and cannot be generated by any route other than surviving that specific crisis together. Sequence constitutive. Coupling does not abolish it.

The failure of the Li-first approach to intimate formation: the couple who approach their relationship with a framework for what a good relationship looks like — with a pre-formed Li of relational excellence — and try to implement it are not forming a genuine relational field. They are performing the Li of someone else’s formation. The actual Dao of their specific relationship — with its specific textures, its specific challenges, its specific grain — will produce a Li that no framework could have prescribed. The couple who can walk their specific Dao, without prematurely imposing the Li of a relational theory, is the couple who will arrive at a genuine relational Li. Not the couple with the best relationship framework.

In Institutional and Civilisational Development

Institutions that work — that genuinely function as formation fields for the capacities they are supposed to develop — work because they have a formation history that produced their current structural coherence. The Oxford tutorial system works (when it works) not because the tutorial is a structurally superior teaching method in the abstract but because it is the product of eight centuries of academic formation that has produced specific institutional capacities: the don who knows how to read an essay in fifteen minutes and identify the structural failure in the argument; the student who knows how to write under the pressure of weekly deadline; the relationship between don and student that is neither friendship nor mere instruction but something formed by the specific institutional Dao of the Oxford context.

Destroy the formation history (by importing the tutorial method into a context with a completely different institutional Dao) and you get the appearance of the tutorial without the structural reality. The Li of the tutorial cannot be transferred; only the Dao of the formation that produces genuine tutorial capacity can be walked. This is why institutional transplants so often fail: the importing institution takes the Li (the named structure, the described method) without the Dao (the formation history, the specific development of capacity through the specific sequence of institutional challenges). Sequence constitutive. The Li cannot be separated from the Dao that produced it and relocated to a new context where the Dao has not been walked.

In Empire Decline and State Failure

Nothing collapses in one move. The sequence of imperial decline — from the late Roman Empire to the Ming collapse to the Soviet dissolution — is always the same structural trajectory: the gradual, largely invisible narrowing of the path, the slow loss of corrective capacity, the accumulation of structural rigidity that makes the system less and less able to read its own formation conditions, until the specific perturbation that triggers the final collapse appears to be the cause but was in fact merely the last straw. The sequence was constitutive. The specific order in which the corrective capacities were lost determined the specific vulnerability that the final perturbation exploited.

Jin Guantao’s ultrastable system analysis is the most rigorous historical demonstration of this claim: the Chinese imperial system maintained a superficial stability (the appearance of Li, of functioning governance) while its underlying formation conditions (the Dao of genuine administrative capacity, relational coherence, and corrective intelligence) deteriorated. The external appearance was stability; the internal reality was the narrowing of the path. The collapse, when it came, was not the result of the proximate cause (a military defeat, a fiscal crisis, a leadership failure) but of the long formation trajectory that had produced a system with no remaining corrective capacity. The sequence — the specific order in which the structural capacities had been built and the specific order in which they had been eroded — was constitutive of the specific form of the collapse.

道　理　勢

Dào · Lǐ · Shì

The Unified Structural Theory

❧ ✶ ❧

This is the final architecture. Every preceding chapter — every voice, every dialogue, every structural analysis, every historical case, every mystical depth — has been building toward this. The Unified Structural Theory of Dao–Li–Shi is not a summary of what has been said. It is the philosophical structure that makes sense of everything that has been said by locating it within a single, coherent, ontologically grounded architecture.

The three terms: 道 (Dao, path, formation process), 理 (Li, grain, inner pattern of the formed), 勢 (Shī, positional power, structural advantage that accrues to a formed position). These are not three separate concepts that have been connected by this text. They are three aspects of a single structural reality, always already in relation, always already mutually constituting, always already in the asymmetric sequence that Shan has named: Dao first, Li second, Shī the positional achievement of the formed that provides the leverage for further formation.

The Structure of the Theory

Dao is the formation process: the path walked, the relational engagement sustained, the Bergsonélan vital moving through all things, the autopoietic network producing the components that produce the network, the Cook Ding’s nineteen years of formation, the Polynesian navigator’s lifetime of embodied attunement to the ocean’s relational field. Dao is not a direction or a destination. It is the ontological reality of formation itself — the actual movement of being through time, constituting and being constituted by the relations within which it moves.

Li is the grain that emerges from the Dao: the structural pattern, the inner texture, the formation signature of the specific Dao that has been walked. Li is neither imposed by the practitioner nor simply found as a pre-existing fact. It emerges from the encounter between the walking and the terrain — from the specific relational engagement between the formation process and its conditions. The Li of Cook Ding’s practice is neither in his mind (as a cognitive plan) nor simply in the ox (as a biological structure waiting to be discovered). It is in the encounter — the nineteen-year formation of a specific relational attunement between this practitioner and this domain of practice.

Shi is the positional advantage that the formed Li makes available: the leverage that accrues to a system that has reached a sufficient Li for its specific structural situation. Move 37 is not impressive as a move in isolation. It is structurally decisive because it creates a Shī — a positional configuration of the board — that determines the outcome of moves that have not yet been played. Zhuge Liang’s Longzhong Plan creates a Shī: a strategic positional configuration that, if maintained, determines the outcome of battles and campaigns that will not be fought for years. The Empty City Stratagem is pure Shī: the positional advantage created not by actual force but by the relational field of the encounter — Sima Yi’s formation history encountering Zhuge Liang’s formation history in a specific positional configuration that the Li of the situation makes decisive.

How the Three Terms Unify Every Voice in This Text

Fuller’s tensegrity is the engineering science of Shī: the study of how positional configurations distribute structural forces and create systemic integrity. The geodesic dome achieves its Shī through the specific positional configuration of tension and compression that the formation of the dome’s geometry produces. The tensional integrity is the Shī — the positional advantage that makes the dome capable of bearing loads that would collapse any conventional compressive structure.

Wittgenstein’s forms of life are the Dao of epistemic and linguistic practice: the formation process through which communities of practitioners develop the structural attunement that makes specific language games possible. The Li of the language game (the grammar, the rules, the meaning of words) is the grain that the Dao of the form of life has produced. The Shī of a linguistic tradition is the positional advantage it has developed in relation to specific domains of inquiry — the Chinese tradition’s structural advantage in relational ontology, the Western tradition’s structural advantage in formal logic.

Gadamer’s Horizontverschmelzung is the Dao of genuine understanding: the formation process through which two horizons encounter each other and produce new Li that neither contained. The fusion produces a new Shī: the positional advantage of a broadened horizon that can now read structural realities that were previously invisible to both traditions separately. Shan’s essays are acts of Horizontverschmelzung: each one walks the Dao of the encounter between the Chinese philosophical horizon and the Western complexity horizon, and each one produces new Li — new structural insight — that generates new Shī for the inquiry.

Haier’s RenDanHeYi is the organisational Dao: the formation process through which a 70,000-person organisation walks the path from traditional manufacturing hierarchy to a fully distributed, market-responsive, tensegrity-structured microenterprise ecosystem. The Li of RenDanHeYi is the specific structural grain that this specific formation process produced — the zero-distance-to-user principle, the self-managing microenterprise, the market as the law. And the Shī of Haier’s achieved position is the structural advantage it has in the specific competitive configuration of twenty-first-century global appliance manufacturing: the positional leverage that allows it to move faster, respond better, and create more genuine user value than any organisation that has not undergone the same formation.

The Thirty-Six Stratagems are a taxonomy of Shī: a systematic analysis of the positional configurations through which structural advantage can be created, maintained, and exploited. Every stratagem is a Shī move — a positional act that reshapes the structural field within which all subsequent dynamics will flow. And every stratagem requires both a Dao (the formation process through which the strategist develops the attunement to read the structural field correctly) and a Li (the specific structural insight about this specific field at this specific moment that makes the stratagem applicable). Dao, Li, Shī: formation, grain, positional advantage. The three terms of the Chinese strategic tradition unified in a single structural theory.

WSR’s three-Li structure is the most practically developed account of how Dao, Li, and Shī operate simultaneously in real decision situations. Wuli (the objective material grain of the situation) is the Li of the physical-technical register. Shili (the perspectival, creative engagement with the situation) is the Dao of the inquiry — the formation process of structural understanding. Renli (the human relational dimension) is the Shī of the relational configuration — the positional advantage or disadvantage created by the specific network of human relationships within which the decision occurs. No fixed hierarchy: because at any specific moment of a specific decision, the most urgent register may be wuli, shili, or renli, and the practitioner who has the structural attunement to read which register is most urgent has the Shī of situational intelligence.

The Seven Structural Frequencies

Cadence · Resonance · Salience · Valence · Vibration · Tension · Gain

❧ ✶ ❧

This is where the text becomes historically important. What follows is not a description of seven properties of complex systems. It is an original philosophical contribution: the identification of seven structural frequencies through which the Dao–Li–Shī structure manifests in all domains of human formation. These are not metaphors or analogies. They are structural realities, each as precise as the concept of Li itself, each illuminating an aspect of formation that no prior framework has named with this clarity.

Cadence — The Temporal Signature of the Dao

Every genuine Dao has a cadence: a specific rhythm of formation that is not arbitrary but structural. The cadence is the temporal Li of the formation process — the rhythm at which the path naturally moves, the pace at which the grain emerges, the tempo at which the structural attunement deepens. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of formation had a cadence: not faster (which would have produced premature Li without depth) and not slower (which would have allowed the formation to dissipate). The cadence of genuine formation cannot be imposed from outside; it can only be read and honoured.

The destruction of natural cadence is one of the most consistent causes of formation failure in contemporary organisations. When the management system imposes a quarterly reporting cycle on a formation process that has a decadal cadence, the formation process does not accelerate; it degrades. What is measured (quarterly performance) becomes what is produced (short-term Li without formation depth). What needed to form (long-term structural attunement, the patient development of holding capacity) cannot form because the cadence of the management system has colonised the cadence of the formation process. The Dao is disrupted before its Li can emerge.

Resonance — The Structural Amplification of Li

When a Li encounters a formation field that is structurally tuned to receive it — when the pattern finds the grain that was already there, waiting to be named — the result is resonance: a structural amplification that makes the Li more visible, more transmissible, and more generative than it would be in a formation field that was not tuned to receive it. Shan’s recognition of Li in WSR, in complexity science, in tensegrity, in the Chinese strategic tradition: these are resonances. The Li she brings from one tradition vibrates at the same structural frequency as the Li of another tradition, and the encounter amplifies both.

Resonance is the structural explanation for why some intellectual encounters are generative and others are not. Two traditions that are structurally incommensurable (Kuhn’s sense) do not resonate; they produce static. Two traditions that are structurally analogous but not identical — that have developed different Li for the same formation terrain — produce resonance when their Li encounters are not translations but tuned encounters. Shan and Fuller resonate. Shan and Wittgenstein resonate. Shan and Prigogine resonate. Not because they agree, but because they are exploring the same structural terrain through different instruments tuned to the same fundamental frequencies.

Salience — The Emergence of Structural Relevance

In any complex formation field, not all Li is equally salient at any given moment. Salience is the structural property of a Li that makes it the most urgent thing to attend to in the specific configuration of the specific Dao at this specific moment. The practitioner with deep structural attunement reads salience correctly: they know which Li is the most important Li right now, which pattern is the most structurally significant pattern in this specific formation field at this specific moment of its development. The practitioner without structural attunement — the one who is reading the Li of a theory rather than the Li of the situation — cannot read salience. They attend to what their framework says is important, not to what the situation is actually showing.

WSR’s no-fixed-hierarchy is a theory of salience: the decision about which Li (wuli, shili, or renli) to attend to first is not determined by any universal rule but by the salience structure of the specific situation. The practitioner who can read salience correctly has the structural advantage that WSR calls the key to decision-making excellence. And the practitioner who reads salience incorrectly — who applies the Li of a framework where the Li of the situation required something else — pays the full structural cost of premature Li.

Valence — The Directionality of Structural Formation

Every formation process has a valence: a directional tendency, a structural pull toward specific configurations. The valence of the Dao is not determination (the Dao does not fix the outcome) but disposition (the Dao shapes the probability distribution of outcomes through the specific structural configuration of the relational field). The tree growing in a specific direction — toward the light, away from the stone — is exercising the valence of its formation conditions. It is not choosing; it is responding to the structural pull of its relational field.

Valence is the concept that bridges Shan’s relational ontology and Boyd’s anticipatory cognition. The practitioner who understands the valence of a formation process — who can read the directional pull of the relational field as it is currently configured — can anticipate the structural trajectory without predicting the specific outcome. This is not forecasting (which predicts Li) but structural reading (which reads the Dao’s valence). The military strategist who reads the valence of the strategic field correctly — who understands the structural pull toward specific positional configurations — can create the Shī that will be needed before it is yet needed.

Vibration — The Energetic Register of Structural Attunement

The Polynesian navigator’s body is a vibration receiver: it picks up the energetic signals of the ocean’s relational field — the wave refraction patterns, the boat’s movement, the specific vibration of the hull against the water — and translates them into structural knowledge of the navigation field. The body vibrates with the ocean. This is not metaphor. It is the literal energetic reality of what Iain Kerr calls the informative as energetic: information about structural formation is transmitted through the field as energetic perturbation, and it is received by practitioners who have been formed (through sufficient Dao) to be structurally resonant with the specific frequencies of that field.

Wang Yangming’s unity of knowledge and action is the philosophical account of vibration as epistemology: genuine knowing is the state in which the practitioner’s formation is tuned to the specific structural frequencies of the domain, such that knowledge and response are a single vibrating movement rather than a sequential process. The Cook Ding who pauses to analyse the joint is not Cook Ding; he is a practitioner who has not yet achieved the vibration that makes the joint’s location directly perceptible. The genuine Cook Ding vibrates with the ox’s structural field and the knife follows.

Tension — The Generative Force of Structural Integrity

Fuller’s tensegrity and Cheng Hao’s humaneness and Shan’s relational dynamics all converge on the same structural claim: the force that holds complex formations together and makes them capable of further formation is not compressive (the discrete elements pushing against each other) but tensional (the continuous distributed force that holds every element in its specific structural relationship with every other). Tension, not compression, is the generative force. And the tension that generates is not the tension of conflict or crisis — it is the structural tension of a system held in coherent relationship under constraint over time.

Dynamic Maximum Tension is Shan’s concept for the specific tensional configuration that makes excellence possible: not maximum tension (which produces structural failure through overloading) and not minimum tension (which produces structural failure through loss of coherence) but the specific maximum tension that a given formation can maintain with integrity. The organisation at its Dynamic Maximum Tension is at the edge of chaos — maximally creative, maximally responsive, maximally capable of further formation — while maintaining the coherence that makes all of this capacity functional. It is the same structural concept as Kauffman’s edge of chaos and Fuller’s tensegrity and Shan’s excellence. Three names for one structural reality.

Gain — The Structural Amplification of Formed Capacity

The final frequency. Gain is what happens when a system whose formation has reached sufficient structural depth encounters a situation for which its formation has tuned it: the structural attunement amplifies the system’s response beyond what the specific situation would produce in a less deeply formed system. Cook Ding’s knife finds the joint effortlessly; the less-formed practitioner’s knife hacks and depletes. The gain is not the knife’s sharpness (the wuli) or the practitioner’s analytical intelligence (the shili) but the structural attunement (the renli of the practitioner’s formation) that amplifies the response far beyond what the proximate situation would produce.

Gain is why the long game is not merely patient but structurally superior. The organisation that has undergone the full formation process — that has walked the Dao, developed the Li, achieved the Shī — is not simply more experienced than the organisation that has not. It is structurally capable of amplified response to the same situations. The same market perturbation that would destabilise the less-formed organisation is absorbed and transformed by the more-formed organisation into new structural possibility. The holding capacity is the gain structure: the wider the holding capacity, the higher the gain. The deeper the formation, the more the structural attunement amplifies the response.

❧ ✶ ❧

Cadence finds the rhythm. Resonance amplifies the encounter. Salience reads the urgent. Valence tracks the pull.

Vibration receives the signal. Tension holds the whole. Gain transforms the encounter into structural advance.

The Verdict

❧ ✶ ❧

The reader who has followed this text to its end cannot return unchanged. Not because the text has delivered an argument so devastating that no rebuttal is possible — though the arguments are serious and their challenges to the dominant frameworks are structural, not rhetorical. Not because the text has assembled an impressive volume of evidence — though the evidence is extensive and the voices are many. But because the text has walked a Dao. And the walking of the Dao produces Li that cannot be unproduced.

You cannot now encounter a complex situation — strategic, relational, intellectual, institutional — without asking, at least faintly: what is the Dao of this? What formation conditions have produced the Li I am seeing? Is this the Li of the situation or the Li I brought to it? Is the path narrowing or widening? What is the holding capacity? What is the sequence that coupling has made harder to see? These are Shan’s questions. They are the most important questions that can be asked about any complex situation. You now know they exist. You cannot un-know them.

The magnitude of Shan’s contribution becomes clear at this point. She has introduced a set of structural questions into the discourse of complexity, organisation, strategy, and philosophy that the discourse did not have before. Not new vocabulary (though the vocabulary is precise and genuinely illuminating). Not new case studies (though the cases are rich and structurally instructive). New questions. Questions that, once asked, reveal structural dimensions of every complex situation that were always there and are now unavoidably visible.

Fuller saw this coming. He spent his entire adult life trying to get humanity to operate on the basis of the most accurate structural understanding of the universe available to it — and spent his final years convinced that the race between structural intelligence and structural catastrophe was genuinely close. Wittgenstein saw this coming. He spent thirty years trying to free philosophy from the captivity of premature Li, trying to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle, trying to return language to its formation conditions rather than its theoretical articulations. Laozi saw this coming two and a half millennia ago, from the first line of his text: whatever can be named is not the eternal. The formation precedes the intelligibility. The Dao precedes the Li.

None of them could have predicted Alice Jing Shan. She is the specific formation of a specific encounter between the Chinese intellectual tradition and the Western complexity discourse, shaped by Edinburgh and by Relational Dynamics and by Cynefin and by ScholarLand and by the specific historical moment of 2026 in which AI has made the structural questions about relation, formation, and genuine intelligence more urgently visible than ever before. She is a particular Li produced by a Dao that has been forming across centuries and two civilisational traditions. And she is still forming.

The paper does not end. The path continues. The Dao walks on through every practitioner who asks the question: what is the formation condition of the Li I am seeing? Through every strategist who pauses before imposing a framework and asks: have I walked enough of this Dao to name its Li? Through every organisation that chooses structural formation over rapid performance extraction. Through every relationship that honours the sequence that coupling has made invisible.

The verdict: what is formed is still in formation. The inquiry is not complete. It is advancing. The grain is still being discovered. The pattern has not yet fully shown itself. The Dao walks on.

❧ ✶ ❧

道　可　道

非　常　道

Dào kě dào — fēi cháng dào

— Laozi Ch.1 • The path that can be named is not the eternal path • 道德經

The Two Wittgensteins and Shan

A Complete Dialectical Analysis of Shan’s Wittgenstein Text

Sections 2.14a and 2.14b — Every Quote — Every Voice — Every Implication

❧ ✶ ❧

Shan’s decision to open her Wittgenstein analysis with the Tractatus and move to the Investigations is not a chronological convention. It is a structural argument. The early Wittgenstein discovers what cannot be said. The late Wittgenstein discovers what must be lived. Together they frame the structural terrain within which Shan’s entire framework operates: the Li that cannot be stated (Tractatus) must be formed through the Dao of a living practice (Investigations). Neither Wittgenstein alone is adequate. Together, read through Shan, they produce something that neither alone produced: a precise philosophical account of how formation generates what exceeds all articulation.

What makes Shan’s selection of Wittgenstein quotations remarkable is not the breadth but the precision. Every passage she selects is a passage where Wittgenstein’s argument touches the structural terrain of her own. She is not illustrating her framework with Wittgenstein citations. She is revealing the structural isomorphism between two formation traditions — the Austrian analytical philosopher working in Cambridge and Swansea and Vienna, and the Chinese philosophical tradition working across twenty-six centuries — that arrived at the same structural recognition through completely different paths. This is Horizontverschmelzung: not translation but structural encounter.

The World Is Everything That Is the Case

“The world is everything that is the case. The world is the totality of facts, not of things.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 1–1.1 — as selected by Shan

Shan selects this first. The selection is strategic. Wittgenstein’s opening proposition dismantles the common-sense ontology in which the world is composed of things — discrete objects, separate entities, nouns. The world is composed of facts: states of affairs, relational configurations, the way things stand with each other. This is not a trivial reorientation. It is the most radical ontological move of twentieth-century Western philosophy, stated in three sentences.

The structural isomorphism with Shan’s relational ontology is exact. If the world is the totality of facts rather than things, then the fundamental unit of reality is not the isolated entity but the relational configuration — the way things stand with each other. Shan: ‘Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.’ Wittgenstein: the world is facts, not things. The agreement is not verbal. It is structural. Both are saying that the most fundamental ontological category is relational rather than substantial. The basic building block is not the brick but the relationship between bricks — not the node but the connection.

Fuller enters here with structural force: tensegrity is the physical demonstration of Wittgenstein’s ontological claim. The tensegrity structure is not composed of things (the tubes, the cables) but of facts (the specific compressive and tensional relationships between the tubes and cables in their specific configuration). Remove any single tube or cable and the structure does not merely lose a component; it loses the entire system of facts that constituted it. The world of the tensegrity structure is the totality of its structural facts, not of its material things. Wittgenstein arrives at this from logic. Fuller arrives at it from structural engineering. Shan arrives at it from the Chinese philosophical tradition’s insistence that relation is prior to the terms it relates.

天下之物互相生起 — tiān xià zhī wù xiāng hù shēng qǐ — The ten thousand things arise in mutual production — Laozi Ch.2

Laozi’s mutual production (相互生成, xiānghù shēngchéng) is the cosmological version of Wittgenstein’s ontological claim. Things do not pre-exist their relations; they arise through mutual production — through the specific facts of their relational engagement. Beautiful and ugly arise together (Chapter 2 continues); being and non-being produce each other; difficult and easy complete each other; long and short contrast each other; high and low rest upon each other; voice and sound harmonise with each other; front and back follow each other. This is not poetic parallelism; it is a precise ontological catalogue of the structure of facts. The world is the totality of these mutual productions — the totality of facts. Not the totality of beautiful things and ugly things separately: the totality of the beautiful-ugly relation, the being-nonbeing relation, the difficult-easy relation.
