The Picture Is a Model of Reality

“The picture is a model of reality. To the objects correspond in the picture the elements of the picture.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 2.12–2.13 — as selected by Shan

This proposition is the hinge of Shan’s Tractatus analysis, though it is the least discussed of her selections. The picture theory is Wittgenstein’s account of how language represents reality: a proposition is a picture (a model, a structural representation) of a possible state of affairs. The elements of the proposition correspond to the objects of the fact; the structure of the proposition mirrors the structure of the fact. Language works because it has the same logical form as reality.

Shan’s interest in this proposition is not primarily in the picture theory itself — which Wittgenstein himself will later abandon — but in what it reveals about the structure of the correspondence between language and world. The picture corresponds to reality through shared structure: the same logical form. This is the Li of the linguistic-representational relationship: the inner grain that makes the correspondence possible. And the picture theory’s failure — which the Investigations document in relentless detail — is precisely the failure to recognise that the Li of a proposition is not a static structural correspondence but a dynamic formation achievement: the meaning of a word is its use in the language, not its pictorial correspondence to an object.

Snowden’s Cynefin framework arrives here with structural force. The picture theory works in the Known and Knowable domains: where cause and effect are stable and predictable, a proposition can be a picture of the state of affairs, because the state of affairs is itself stable enough to be pictured. In the Complex domain, the picture theory fails: the state of affairs is constituted by the act of engaging with it (every intervention is also a diagnostic), and no prior picture can capture what the engagement will produce. In the Complex domain, you cannot picture-first; you must probe-first. The Dao must precede the Li. The Investigations’ abandonment of the picture theory is, read through Shan, the shift from Known-domain epistemology to Complex-domain epistemology.

‘The Limits of My Language Mean the Limits of My World’ — The Most Important Wittgensteinian Proposition for Reading Shan

“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. Logic fills the world: the limits of the world are also its limits. So we cannot say in logic: there is this and this in the world, and not that. For that would apparently presuppose that we were excluding certain possibilities, and this cannot be the case, since otherwise logic would have to get outside the limits of the world.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 5.6–5.61 — as selected by Shan

Shan identifies Tractatus 5.6 as ‘the single most important Wittgensteinian proposition for reading Shan.’ This is the most important claim in her entire Wittgenstein analysis, and it must be pressed to its full depth. The structural possibilities available to thought are determined by the language-world one inhabits. For Shan, growing up inside Chinese — inside 道, 理, 道理, 知道 — means inhabiting a world with structural possibilities that English does not package in the same way. Her crossing into English is not merely translation but a crossing between worlds. This is not relativism; it is structural ecology.

Shan’s formulation deserves to stand as one of the most precise philosophical accounts of what it means to be bilingual in two structurally different languages. She is not saying that Chinese and English describe the same world differently (which would be linguistic relativism). She is saying that Chinese and English are different structural ecologies — different worlds, in Wittgenstein’s precise sense — and that growing up inside Chinese means having access to structural possibilities (the specific way 道 and 理 carve the formation terrain) that the English language-world does not make naturally available. This is structural privilege in the deepest sense: not the privilege of class or culture but the privilege of having been formed by a language that encodes specific structural realities with specific precision.

Gadamer’s Horizontverschmelzung arrives here as the methodological response to Wittgenstein’s structural ecology claim. If the limits of my language are the limits of my world, then genuine understanding across language-worlds requires more than translation: it requires the fusion of the two language-worlds into a new shared horizon that neither language-world contained. This is precisely what Shan’s essays perform: they do not translate 道 into English; they create the dialogical encounter in which the English reader’s world is enlarged by the encounter with the specific structural possibilities that 道 encodes. The reader’s world (in Wittgenstein’s sense) is expanded. The limits of their language have been pushed outward.

知道 — zhīdào — To know the way — but also, in modern Chinese, simply: I know. The Dao is embedded in ordinary epistemology.

知道 (zhīdào, to know the Dao, or in modern Chinese simply ‘I know’) is Shan’s most pointed demonstration of Tractatus 5.6. The Chinese speaker who says 知道 is etymologically saying ‘I know the path’ — their ordinary epistemological claim is structured by a path-metaphor that the English ‘I know’ does not contain. The Chinese language-world packages knowledge as path-following; the English language-world packages it as (implicitly) propositional. These are not the same world. The bilingual practitioner who can inhabit both language-worlds simultaneously has access to two different structural ecologies of knowledge — which is precisely why Shan’s essays can see structural dimensions of complex situations that monolingual English complexity discourse cannot.

Luhmann’s systems theory arrives here as a structural confirmation from a completely different direction. Communication communicates: the social system is constituted by communications that refer to other communications within a specific horizon of meaning. The horizon of meaning of the Chinese language-world is different from the horizon of meaning of the English language-world — not incommensurable (Shan’s essays demonstrate the possibility of genuine encounter) but structured differently. Luhmann’s meaning-as-horizon is Wittgenstein’s limits-of-language made systemic: the meaning-horizon of a communication system determines what communications are possible within it, just as the limits of a language determine the limits of the world available to its speakers.

‘There Is Indeed the Inexpressible. This Shows Itself; It Is the Mystical.’

“There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.522 — as selected by Shan

This is the most quoted Wittgenstein proposition in this text, and it is quoted so often because it is the most structurally convergent with the Chinese philosophical tradition of any proposition in the Western canon. The inexpressible that shows itself is the Li that cannot be stated as Li — the inner grain that can only be shown in the texture of the thing, the formation, the practice, the walk. Laozi’s nameless Dao, Wang Bi’s zìrán (what is so of itself), Cook Ding’s knife-movement, the Polynesian navigator’s body-reading of the waves: all are instances of what shows itself without being sayable.

But Shan’s selection of 6.522 involves a tension that must be pressed. Wittgenstein says ‘it is the mystical’ — placing the inexpressible in the register of the transcendent, the beyond-language. The Chinese tradition does not place the inexpressible in this register. The Li that cannot be stated is not mystical in Wittgenstein’s sense of being beyond the world; it is deeply worldly, embedded in the specific material texture of specific things. The grain of the jade is not mystical; it is utterly material. Cook Ding’s structural attunement is not mystical; it is the product of nineteen years of embodied practice with actual oxen. The inexpressible in the Chinese tradition shows itself in the grain, not beyond the grain.

This is Shan’s most important structural correction of Wittgenstein, and she makes it implicitly rather than explicitly. By placing 6.522 within a framework that grounds the inexpressible in formation and practice rather than in transcendence, she transforms Wittgenstein’s mysticism into a structural phenomenology. The mystical is not the beyond-language; it is the below-language: the formation conditions, the grain, the Dao that produces the Li without being reducible to it. Wittgenstein gestures upward at 6.522; the Chinese tradition points downward, into the specific material and relational texture of the world.

Bateson arrives here with the pattern that connects. His question — what is the pattern that connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all four of them to me? — is the biological version of 6.522: the pattern exists; it shows itself in the specific structural similarities that connect crustaceans and orchids and persons; it cannot be stated from outside the system of connections because it is what the connections are. Bateson spent his career trying to name it (as the metapattern, the pattern of patterns) and never achieved a final formulation. This is not a failure; it is the structural feature that Wittgenstein identifies: the inexpressible shows itself. The naming keeps falling short. The showing is always already there.

Ethics Cannot Be Put into Words

“Es ist klar, dass sich die Ethik nicht aussprechen lässt. Ethics cannot be put into words. Ethics is transcendental. (Ethics and aesthetics are one.)”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.421 — as selected by Shan

Shan selects 6.421 alongside 6.522: ethics and aesthetics are one, and both are transcendental. This selection reveals the ethical dimension of Shan’s structural project that is rarely made explicit. If ethics cannot be put into words — if the rightness of an action cannot be stated as a proposition but can only show itself in the quality of the action — then the formation that produces structurally excellent action is also the formation that produces ethical action. Excellence and ethics are structurally isomorphic in Shan’s framework: both are ‘capacity held in coherence under constraint over time’; both show themselves in the quality of the action rather than in any explicit statement of the principle that guided it.

Cheng Hao’s humaneness (仁, rén) arrives here with full structural force. The person of humaneness takes heaven and earth and the ten thousand things as one body: they feel the suffering of others as directly as their own pain, not because they have reasoned to the ethical conclusion that others’ suffering matters, but because their formation has produced a structural attunement so deep that the boundary between self and other is genuinely permeable. This is Wittgenstein’s 6.421 made concrete: ethics shows itself in the quality of the humaneness-formation, not in any proposition about the rightness of caring for others. The ethical cannot be stated; it can only be formed and shown.

The aesthetics claim is equally important. Wittgenstein: ethics and aesthetics are one. This is not a casual equation; it is a structural claim about the unity of the ‘cannot be put into words’ register. The beautiful and the good share the same structural feature: they show themselves rather than being said. Shan’s essays are beautiful as well as structurally rigorous — and the beauty and the rigour are not separate: the beauty is the rigour, expressed at the sensory-experiential level rather than the propositional level. The essay that genuinely illuminates structural reality is also the essay that has aesthetic form, because both are expressions of structural attunement — the recognition of Li that exceeds the capacity of any single proposition to contain it.

Throw Away the Ladder

“My propositions are elucidatory in this way: he who understands me finally recognizes them as senseless, when he has climbed out through them, on them, over them. He must so to speak throw away the ladder, after he has climbed up on it. He must surmount these propositions; then he sees the world rightly. Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.54–7 — as selected by Shan

The ladder metaphor is the most structurally complex passage in the Tractatus, and Shan’s selection of it reveals one of the deepest structural analogies in her entire framework. The propositions of the Tractatus are a Dao: they are not the destination (the Li of correct philosophical understanding); they are the path by which one reaches the point where the correct understanding shows itself and the propositions can be left behind. The propositions must be climbed through and then thrown away. The Li emerges from the walking of the Dao; the Dao-instrument (the propositions) becomes dispensable once the Li has been achieved.

This is the structural logic of Cook Ding’s formation: the techniques and frameworks that guided the early years of practice are the ladder. After nineteen years, the ladder has been thrown away: the structural attunement is direct, immediate, non-propositional. The knife finds the joint without the mediation of an articulated technique. But — and this is Shan’s crucial structural qualification — the throwing away of the ladder is only possible because the ladder was climbed. The wuwei of the Daoist sage, the no-deliberate-mind of Wang Bi’s reading of the sage, the pure structural attunement of Cook Ding: these are not the starting point. They are the achievement of the full formation process. The ladder must be climbed before it can be thrown away.

Juarrero’s phase change arrives here: the throwing away of the ladder is a phase change in the practitioner’s structural organisation. Before the phase change, the propositions (the explicit framework, the named Li) are necessary navigation tools. After the phase change, they are dispensable: the structural attunement has reorganised the practitioner’s formation so that the Li arises directly from the Dao of engagement, without the mediation of explicit propositional knowledge. The phase change is not a gradual increase in expertise; it is a discontinuous structural reorganisation. And like all phase changes, it requires the full walk of the Dao before the conditions for the phase change are established.

Shan’s essays are ladders in Wittgenstein’s sense. They are not the Li they are pointing at; they are the Dao-instrument that enables the reader to climb to the point where the Li shows itself. The reader who has followed the path of an essay and arrived at the structural recognition it was pointing toward can, in principle, throw the essay away: the recognition is now directly available, not requiring the mediation of the essay that produced it. This is why Shan does not write philosophical treatises: the treatise-form implies that the text contains the Li, that reading the text is sufficient. The essay-form implies that the text is a path, and the reader must walk it to arrive at what the path was for.

Philosophy Is Not a Theory but an Activity

“Philosophy is not a theory but an activity. The object of philosophy is the logical clarification of thoughts. Philosophy does not result in philosophical propositions, but rather in the clarification of propositions.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 4.112 — as selected by Shan

Philosophy as activity rather than theory: this is the Tractatus proposition that points most directly toward the Investigations. And it is the proposition that most directly names what Shan’s essays are doing. The essays are philosophical activity: they are acts of structural clarification that do not result in philosophical propositions but in the clarification of the structural terrain within which the reader’s propositions will henceforth operate. After a Shan essay, the reader does not have a new proposition to add to their knowledge; they have a clarified structural ecology within which their existing propositions now make different kinds of sense.

Wang Yangming’s unity of knowledge and action is the Chinese philosophical precedent for Wittgenstein’s philosophy-as-activity. If genuine knowledge is not separable from the action that enacts it, then genuine philosophical understanding is not the acquisition of a proposition but the transformation of the practitioner’s formation. Philosophy that results in propositions has produced Li without Dao. Philosophy that results in the clarification of the practitioner’s structural ecology has walked a Dao and produced the Li of the clarified world. Shan’s essays do the second kind.

Chia and Holt’s strategy-without-design arrives here: if strategy is an activity rather than a plan, and philosophy is an activity rather than a theory, then the common structural error in both domains is the same — the mistake of thinking that the Li (the plan, the proposition) can substitute for the Dao of the activity itself. The strategy that emerges from the Dao of genuine strategic engagement cannot be planned in advance; it must be discovered through the activity of strategic engagement. The philosophical clarification that results from genuine philosophical activity cannot be stated in advance as a proposition; it must emerge from the activity of genuine philosophical inquiry. Li from Dao. Always.

The Crossing: From Tractatus to Investigations

Shan’s transition from the Tractatus to the Investigations is not merely a move to the later Wittgenstein. It is a structural advancement that mirrors the advancement in her own framework from the identification of the Li-limit (Tractatus: what cannot be said) to the account of the formation process that produces the Li (Investigations: how forms of life form what can be said). The Tractatus locates the boundary; the Investigations explains how the boundary was formed and how it can be moved.

The single most structurally important move in Wittgenstein’s own intellectual development — from the Tractatus to the Investigations — is precisely the move from Li-first to Dao-first. The Tractatus begins with the logical structure of language (the Li of language: its formal relationships with reality) and derives the limits of what can be said from this structure. The Investigations begins with the practices within which language operates (the Dao of language: the activities, forms of life, language-games within which words get their meaning) and shows that the ‘logical structure’ of the Tractatus was an illusion produced by the philosopher’s distancing from practice. Dao before Li: Wittgenstein’s own intellectual autobiography.

‘For a Large Class of Cases—the Meaning of a Word Is Its Use’

“For a large class of cases — though not for all — in which we employ the word ‘meaning’ it can be defined thus: the meaning of a word is its use in the language.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §43 — as selected by Shan

Meaning as use: the most famous and most frequently misunderstood proposition of the Investigations. It is not a pragmatist claim that meaning is whatever works. It is a structural claim about the formation of meaning: the meaning of a word is constituted by the Dao of its use — the pattern of its employment in specific language-games, the forms of life within which it is embedded, the specific structural ecology from which it draws its meaning. Meaning is not prior to use (the Tractatus error: the picture precedes the picturing); it is produced by use over time.

This proposition is the linguistic application of Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim. The Li of a word (its meaning, its semantic content, its structural contribution to the propositions in which it appears) is produced by the Dao of its use (the specific pattern of employment across the specific language-games of the specific form of life). You cannot determine the meaning of 道 by studying its Li (its dictionary definition, its classical philosophical usage) without first attending to the Dao of its use — the specific contexts, practices, and forms of life within which the word is employed. Shan’s essays are explorations of the Dao of 道’s use: they show, through specific cases and encounters, the meaning that the word acquires in its actual employment across different formation contexts.

Zhu Xi enters here as the structural opponent. His programme of ‘investigating things to extend knowledge’ assumes that the meaning of words (the Li of concepts) can be established by study and reflection prior to the practice that employs them. Wittgenstein’s §43 directly refutes this: the meaning is in the use, not in the prior study of the word. The philosopher who thinks they understand 理 by studying the Neo-Confucian literature has the Li of the word in a literary-historical sense; they do not have the meaning in Wittgenstein’s sense until they have encountered the word in the Dao of its actual employment — in the specific structural situations where 理 is the right word for what is happening and its absence is felt as a structural gap.

‘The Speaking of Language Is Part of an Activity, or of a Form of Life’

“The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §23 — as selected by Shan

The most compressed statement of the Investigations’ central structural claim: language is not a representational system separate from the activities of life but an integral part of those activities. The word acquires its meaning from the activity within which it is spoken, not from its correspondence to a non-linguistic reality (Tractatus picture theory) or from a prior definition (Zhu Xi’s investigation of things).

This is the proposition Shan places at the centre of her account of why the Chinese philosophical tradition’s vocabulary is not merely different from the Western complexity discourse but structurally equipped to see certain things that the Western vocabulary is not equipped to see. 道 acquires its meaning from the activities and forms of life of the Chinese philosophical tradition — from the specific practices of self-cultivation, governance, strategic practice, and intellectual inquiry within which the word has been employed for twenty-six centuries. This is not cultural parochialism; it is the structural recognition that a word used in a specific form of life for twenty-six centuries has a depth of meaning that a word recently borrowed from that tradition cannot have until it has been used — lived with, worked with, embedded in practice — for a comparable duration.

Boyd’s Orientation phase is the OODA-loop version of Wittgenstein’s form-of-life claim. The formation history that shapes Orientation is precisely the accumulated Dao of specific activities within specific forms of life. The Chinese military strategist whose Orientation has been formed by twenty years of studying the Thirty-Six Stratagems and five years of practising within the specific form of life of Chinese strategic culture has a different Orientation — a different structural ecology of strategic perception — from the Western management consultant whose Orientation was formed by a different set of activities within a different form of life. Neither is universally superior; both are structurally specific. The form of life determines the Orientation. The Orientation determines what can be seen.

Agreement Not in Opinions but in Form of Life

“It is not only agreement in definitions but also (odd as it may sound) in judgments that is required... agreement not in opinions, but rather in form of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §241–242 — as selected by Shan

Agreement in form of life: the most important structural claim for understanding what is required for genuine cross-cultural understanding. It is not enough to agree on definitions (to agree on the Li of a concept): genuine understanding requires agreement in the form of life (in the Dao of the practice within which the concept has its meaning). This is why Shan’s essays cannot be simply read and understood by a reader who has not had some formation within the Chinese intellectual tradition or within the complexity discourse: genuine understanding requires some shared formation — some overlap in the forms of life within which the concepts have their meaning.

This proposition is Shan’s structural explanation for why cross-cultural philosophical encounter is genuinely difficult and why it requires the kind of sustained formation that her essays are attempting to provide. It is not enough to translate the words (agree on definitions). It is not enough to agree that the Chinese philosophical tradition is interesting and worth engaging (agree in opinions). Genuine understanding requires some degree of shared formation — some experience of living with 道 and 理 in the Dao of actual practice, not merely in the Li of academic study.

Gadamer’s Horizontverschmelzung is the positive account of what Wittgenstein’s §241–242 prescribes. The fusion of horizons is not the achievement of agreement in opinions (which would be merely intellectual convergence) or in definitions (which would be merely terminological). It is the creation of shared territory in form of life — a new space of shared practice, shared encounter, shared formation within which the merged horizon becomes a genuine form of life that neither tradition inhabited before. Shan’s project is the creation of this shared form of life: a specific practice of cross-cultural structural inquiry that is itself a new Dao, producing a new Li that neither tradition could have achieved alone.

‘What We Do Is Bring Words Back from Their Metaphysical to Their Everyday Use’

“What we do is bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §116 — as selected by Shan

This is Wittgenstein’s account of philosophical therapy, and Shan has made it the central methodological principle of her Dao analysis. ‘Dao rarely travels alone. Perhaps Li is the less-known partner whose absence should caution us whenever Dao begins to feel too smooth, too familiar, or too readily available.’ This is the Li-warning as philosophical therapy: when Dao has been lifted from its everyday form-of-life use into the ‘metaphysical’ — when it circulates as a smooth, frictionless concept detached from the specific practices and forms of life that give it structural meaning — the therapeutic move is to bring it back. Li provides the resistance that brings Dao back to earth. Li is Wittgenstein’s philosophical therapy applied to Dao.

The corporate Dao fails precisely because it has been lifted from its everyday use into metaphysical circulation. ‘The Dao of leadership.’ ‘The Dao of management.’ ‘Living in flow.’ These are not wrong because they are untrue; they are wrong because they have been detached from the specific forms of life (the specific practices of self-cultivation, governance, and strategic engagement) that give 道 its structural meaning. The therapeutic move is to bring them back: to ask, in every specific case, what specific form of life gives this Dao its meaning? What specific practice is being pointed at? What specific structural grain does this concept pick out in this specific situation? Li asks these questions. Li is the Wittgensteinian philosophical therapist of Dao.

Meadows’ leverage points arrive here: the highest leverage point is the ability to remain unattached in the arena of paradigms. This is the same structural move as Wittgenstein’s therapeutic return to everyday use: the practitioner who is attached to a paradigm (attached to a specific metaphysical elevation of a concept) cannot bring the concept back to its everyday use. The practitioner who can hold multiple paradigms simultaneously — who can move between the metaphysical and the everyday, between the named pattern and the specific formation — has achieved the structural flexibility that makes genuine philosophical therapy possible. Wittgenstein: bring words back. Meadows: stay unattached. Shan: Dao before Li, always returning the named pattern to the formation that produced it.

‘A Philosophical Problem Has the Form: I Don’t Know My Way About’

“A philosophical problem has the form: ‘I don’t know my way about.’”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §123 — as selected by Shan

This is Wittgenstein’s most structurally exact diagnosis of philosophical confusion, and it is the one that most directly names the structural situation that Shan’s framework is designed to address. The philosophical problem is not a question about facts (which could be answered by more information) or about logic (which could be answered by valid inference). It is a problem of orientation: being within a formation field whose structure one cannot read. The philosopher who does not know their way about is the Cook who sees whole bullocks and cannot find the articulations — who hacks rather than following the grain.

知道 (zhīdào): to know the Dao, to know the way. The Chinese speaker whose everyday epistemology is structured by path-following has a different relationship to philosophical orientation than the English speaker whose everyday epistemology is structured by propositional knowledge. ‘I know my way about’ is already implied by 知道 in a way that ‘I know’ does not imply. The Chinese philosophical tradition has always understood knowing as wayfinding, not as propositional possession. Wittgenstein arrives at this recognition in the Investigations after the Tractatus has demonstrated the failure of propositional epistemology. The Chinese tradition had this as its starting point.

Snowden’s Cynefin framework is the most developed contemporary account of the conditions under which practitioners know their way about and the conditions under which they do not. The Known domain: practitioners know their way about completely (cause and effect are clear, best practice applies). The Complex domain: practitioners do not know their way about (cause and effect only coherent in retrospect, safe-to-fail probing required). The transition from Known to Complex is the transition from zhīdào to bù zhīdào — from knowing the Dao to not knowing it. And the therapeutic response (probe-sense-respond rather than sense-analyse-respond) is precisely the Dao-before-Li move: enter the formation process before imposing a named pattern.

‘If I Have Exhausted the Justifications I Have Reached Bedrock’

“If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: ‘This is simply what I do.’”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §217 — as selected by Shan

The bedrock proposition: at the foundation of all justification is something that cannot itself be justified without regress, and this unjustifiable foundation is not arbitrary but formed — the accumulated Dao of a specific practice and form of life, hardened into the bedrock of that practice’s formation structure. ‘This is simply what I do’: the practitioner who has reached bedrock is not making an appeal to a rule (which could be further justified) but naming the formation condition that makes all rule-following possible.

This is the most precise philosophical account of what Wang Yangming means by 良知 (liángzhī, innate moral knowledge). The 良知 is the bedrock: the formation condition that cannot be further justified because it is the condition of all justification. It is not a rule; it is what makes following rules possible. And it is not innate in the sense of being present before formation; it is innate in the sense of being the product of a formation process so deep and so complete that it has become the bedrock of all subsequent practice. Cook Ding’s structural attunement is his bedrock: not a rule he follows but the formation condition that makes his practice possible, which cannot be further justified because it is the foundation from which all his practice springs.

Wittgenstein’s On Certainty extends this into the full account of the riverbed: the propositions that function as the bedrock of a language-game are the ones that have been formed through the Dao of that language-game’s practice and have become so hardened by formation that they function as the conditions of all subsequent inquiry. ‘At the core of all well-founded belief lies belief that is unfounded’ (On Certainty §253): not arbitrary, but formed beyond the point of further justification. This is Shan’s Dao-before-Li at the epistemological bedrock: the formation (Dao) produces the certainty structure (Li) that then functions as the condition of all further inquiry.

‘What Is Your Aim in Philosophy? To Show the Fly the Way Out of the Fly-Bottle’

“What is your aim in philosophy? To show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §309 — as selected by Shan

The fly-bottle: the glass container within which the fly is trapped, beating against the glass, unable to find the way out that is directly in front of it — the opening through which it entered. The philosophical problem is not that the way out does not exist; it is that the fly’s current orientation (its current structural ecology, its current form of life) makes the opening invisible. The therapy is not the provision of information but the reorientation of the fly’s movement: showing it the specific path (道) that leads from confusion to the opening.

This is the most direct statement of the methodological aim that Shan’s essays share with Wittgenstein’s philosophy. The essays do not provide information that the reader lacked; they reorient the reader’s structural position within the formation field of complexity thinking, governance, and relational intelligence. After a Shan essay, the reader can see the opening in the fly-bottle that was always there: the Dao that precedes the Li, the formation conditions that precede the named patterns, the grain that was always already in the material. The essay is the showing of the path out of the specific philosophical confusion that the reader was in — which is always, in some form, the confusion of Li-before-Dao: the confusion of the practitioner who cannot find the articulation because they began with the named pattern rather than the encounter with the actual grain.

Fuller enters here: ‘You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.’ This is the fly-bottle solution as structural engineering: not arguing against the glass (which only depletes the fly further) but building the new structural configuration that makes the glass irrelevant. Shan’s framework does not argue against the existing complexity discourse; it builds a structural account that makes the inadequacies of the existing discourse visible — that shows the fly the opening that was always there. The new model (Dao-before-Li, relation-precedes-dynamics, coupling-does-not-abolish-sequence) makes the existing model’s structural limitations obvious without needing to argue against them directly.

‘Philosophy Simply Puts Everything Before Us’

“Philosophy simply puts everything before us, and neither explains nor deduces anything. Since everything lies open to view there is nothing to explain.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §126 — as selected by Shan

The most structurally counterintuitive proposition in Shan’s selection: everything lies open to view, and therefore there is nothing to explain. This is not a claim that complexity is simple or that the structural grain of things is always immediately obvious. It is a structural claim about the task of philosophy: not to explain (to provide a causal account that takes one behind the phenomena to their hidden causes) but to arrange (to place the phenomena in configurations that make the structural Li visible without inference from hidden causes).

This is why Shan’s essays begin with particulars. Not to illustrate a general principle with a specific example (which would be explanation, deduction from the general to the specific). But to place the specific particular in a structural configuration that makes the Li visible: the LinkedIn thread placed next to the Go board placed next to the neonatal tube. The Li — the structural pattern that connects them — becomes visible in the arrangement. Everything was already there: the LinkedIn thread, the Go board, the neonatal tube. Shan’s essay simply puts them before us in the right arrangement. The Li shows itself. Nothing has been explained or deduced. Everything was already open to view; it needed only to be arranged correctly.

The iceberg image arrives here: the visible patterns, networks, webs, organisations, and configurations are already there above the waterline. The emergent processes and fields are already there below. Everything is already visible to the practitioner with the structural attunement to see it. The essay that illuminates structural depth is not the essay that explains what was hidden; it is the essay that arranges what was already there in such a way that the structural depth becomes visible to a reader who has sufficient formation to see it. Philosophy — and the Shan essay as philosophy — simply puts everything before us.

Shan’s Central Structural Claim About the Investigations

Shan’s conclusion about the Investigations is the most structurally precise statement in her entire Wittgenstein analysis: the concept of form of life provides the social-philosophical language for what Shan is describing as relational dynamics. The form of life is the formed Dao: the inherited coherence within which particular dynamics (language games) can occur. The Investigations does not investigate how forms of life form; Shan’s framework does. But the concept of form of life provides the social-philosophical language for what Shan is describing as relational dynamics.

This claim deserves to be pressed to its full structural implication. Shan is saying: Wittgenstein gives the concept (form of life as the background of all language-games) without the theory of its formation. She gives the theory of formation (Dao precedes Li, the formation process precedes the structural attunement it produces) without the social-philosophical language that names the formation field. Together they are complete: the Investigations’ form of life + Shan’s Dao-before-Li = the full account of how structural formation works and what it produces.

This is the Horizontverschmelzung that this text has been tracking across every chapter. Wittgenstein and Shan: two thinkers who arrived at the same structural terrain from completely different formation paths, producing complementary accounts that together exceed what either alone achieved. The limits of Wittgenstein’s contribution: he names the form of life but cannot account for its formation. The limits of Shan’s contribution (as she would acknowledge): she gives the formation theory but needs the social-philosophical vocabulary of the form of life to name what the formation produces in the social and linguistic register. Together: a complete structural ontology of formation, from the Dao of the formation process through the Li of the formed structure to the Shì of the positional advantage that the formed structure makes available.

❧ ✶ ❧

“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 5.6

WSR in Practice: The Water Management Case — A Complete Reading

The most instructive WSR case study in Zhichang Zhu’s account is the water resources decision support system developed for a seaport city in northern China. Water shortage had become serious as tourist visitors increased; the government had invested heavily in water diversion tunnels; the newly established Water-Diverting Management Bureau found itself unable to manage the expanded demand-supply dynamics. The WSR team entered a situation of maximum complexity: rival user groups (industrial, agricultural, domestic, tourist) each claiming priority; reservoir staff, station operators, Bureau managers, and city officials with incompatible shili models of how allocation should work; and a renli field dominated by a win-lose mentality that made every stakeholder’s gain appear to require another’s loss.

“Along the way, concerned parties were able, probably for the first time, to sit down together, understand each other’s circumstances, ask for clarifications, put oneself in others’ shoes, fit one’s own demand realistically into the overall big picture, seek compromises and raise suggestions for good-enough, win-win outcomes. Rivals still were, they became willing to make ‘the system’ work, considered themselves the owners of the system, and were excited to see the possibility of solving the problems by their own efforts.”

— Zhichang Zhu, WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach

This case demonstrates in exact practical form what Shan’s framework describes in structural terms. The wuli investigation (mapping seasonal patterns, reservoir capacity, five water processing stations) could not proceed productively until the renli conditions (the win-lose mentality, the mutual suspicion between user groups) had been partially addressed. The WSR team’s neutral outsider position — their specific renli asset — created the space within which the rival parties could encounter each other as genuine stakeholders rather than as adversaries. And the shili creativity (the decision support system, the forecasting and allocation models) emerged from the encounter between all three registers, not from technical analysis alone. The result withstood the test of severe droughts in the immediately following years: the system proved viable when it mattered.

Shan’s holding capacity argument arrives here with clinical precision. The water system’s actual problem was not technical shortage but relational incapacity: the system could not hold the complexity of its own stakeholder dynamics. The WSR intervention did not add water; it built the relational holding capacity — the renli infrastructure of shared ownership, mutual recognition, and win-win orientation — within which the technical and strategic solutions could be received and sustained. Drop by drop. Not hesitation. Protection of viability.

The methodological principle Zhu draws from the case: ‘methods and tools are fishing rods, not the fish.’ The WSR team used rich pictures, cognitive mapping, critical path analysis, and input-output tables — whatever the specific stakeholders felt comfortable with for expressing their ideas. The Li of the solution emerged from the Dao of the process; the methods were paths to the Li, not the Li itself. Premature method — imposing a specific analytical tool before the relational field was ready to receive it — would have produced the technical appearance of progress while the actual WSR problem (the renli conditions that made genuine coordination impossible) remained unaddressed.

Hard WSR and Soft WSR: The Internal Tension That Keeps the Approach Honest

Zhu’s taxonomy of two ideal types of WSR — Hard WSR and Soft WSR — is one of the most self-aware moves in the systems methodology literature. Hard WSR positions the framework as a fine-tuned multi-criteria decision-making device for SE/OR experts to get jobs done, accountable to authority and business sponsors, treating non-expert stakeholders as objects to be studied, managed, and cared for. Soft WSR positions the framework as a multi-perspective, multi-method, multi-actor general-purpose management approach accountable to stakeholders themselves, treating non-expert participants as owners of the decision process, raising ethical-moral sensitivity and asking ‘to what end?’

The distinction maps exactly onto the Dao-before-Li / Li-before-Dao fault line. Hard WSR arrives with the Li of a methodology and applies it. Soft WSR walks the Dao of the specific situation’s wuli-shili-renli configuration before any methodological Li is imposed. And Zhu’s most structurally honest observation: the oscillation between Hard and Soft WSR has tracked China’s own political oscillations — the Soft WSR spirit shone during Deng’s reform years; Hard WSR elements dominated in the era of the ‘China Model’ and ‘top-level design.’ The fate of a methodology is coupled to the fate of the society that generated it. Coupling does not abolish this sequence either.

Shan’s entire project is an argument for Soft WSR applied across every domain: not the imposition of a Dao-Li-Shī framework as a Hard methodology to be applied wherever convenient, but the development of the structural attunement that allows each specific situation’s wuli, shili, and renli configuration to be read on its own terms before any named Li is imposed. The framework is a fishing rod. The fish is the actual grain of the actual situation. Don’t put the cart before the horse.

The Four Quadrants: A Complete Reading in Conversation with Shan

The uploaded quadrant framework maps communities of knowledge practice across two axes: abstraction (high to low) and mode (technical to teaching/social). The four quadrants that result are not merely a classification scheme; they are a structural map of where different kinds of Li formation occur, and what kind of Dao is required to produce each.

Professional Logical: Communities of Practice with Known Membership and Objectives

The upper-right quadrant: high abstraction, teaching mode, known membership, explicit objectives. Communities of practice in Wenger’s sense: groups whose Li is sufficiently stabilised and sufficiently shared that membership, objectives, and methods of inquiry are all legible in advance. Academic disciplines, professional guilds, established research programmes in Lakatos’s sense — all of these are Professional Logical communities. The Li has been thoroughly formed; the Dao of participation is well-marked; the holding capacity is high and institutional.

The danger of the Professional Logical quadrant is exactly what Shan identifies as the danger of Li-smoothness: when the community’s Li becomes too settled, too self-referential, too insulated from the Dao of the situations it claims to address, it begins to function as what Kuhn calls normal science — puzzle-solving within established paradigms rather than genuine structural encounter with the problems at hand. The established complexity science community, the established management consulting industry — both can become Professional Logical communities whose accumulated Li prevents genuine structural attunement to the specific Dao of the specific situations they encounter.

Informal Independent: Social Networks at High Abstraction

The upper-left quadrant: high abstraction, technical mode, informal organisation, social networks. These are communities without fixed membership or stated objectives — the floating intellectuals, the boundary-crossers, the practitioners who operate across Professional Logical communities without fully belonging to any. The Chinese literati tradition at its most vital was Informal Independent: scholars moving between courts, positions, and disciplines, carrying their formation across institutional boundaries without being captured by any single institutional Li.

Shan’s own Substack community is an Informal Independent formation: no fixed membership, no stated objectives, no institutional affiliation, high abstraction (the structural claims she makes operate across every domain of practice), and the specific social-network character of the Cynefin adjacent community within which her work is primarily received. The strength of the Informal Independent quadrant is structural flexibility; the vulnerability is the inability to sustain the formation depth that Professional Logical communities can develop through institutional continuity.

Bureaucratic Structured: Coherent Groupings with Largely Information-Based Activity

The lower-right quadrant: low abstraction, teaching mode, coherent groupings, largely information-based activity. These are the established organisations, the institutional structures, the bureaucracies — systems whose Li is thoroughly institutionalised but whose primary mode of activity is information management rather than structural formation. Jin Guantao’s ultrastable system is the pathological form of the Bureaucratic Structured quadrant: the surface Li (the institutional structure, the formal procedures, the management hierarchy) remains intact while the underlying Dao of genuine adaptive capacity is silently eroding.

Haier in 1984 was Bureaucratic Structured: a failing state-owned enterprise whose organisational Li (the pyramid hierarchy, the command-and-control structure) was thoroughly institutionalised but whose holding capacity was collapsing. Zhang Ruimin’s interventions moved Haier out of the Bureaucratic Structured quadrant through successive transformations — through the Uncharted Innovative (the sledgehammer moment, the radical disruption of the existing Li), through phases of Professional Logical (the quality obsession, the brand-building discipline), toward the specific tensegrity-distributed form that RenDanHeYi achieves.

Uncharted Innovative: Temporary Communities in Disruptive Space

The lower-left quadrant: low abstraction, technical mode, temporary communities, disruptive space. This is where Shan’s most important interventions occur. The Uncharted Innovative quadrant is where new Li is formed from Dao that has not yet produced a legible pattern — where the formation process is genuinely underway and the Li has not yet stabilised into any of the other three quadrants. The Chinese characters in the LinkedIn thread that triggered Shan’s encounter with WSR were an Uncharted Innovative moment: a Dao that had not yet produced a clearly legible Li for the professional complexity discourse it was entering.

Snowden’s probe-sense-respond is the methodological prescription for the Uncharted Innovative quadrant: do not impose the Li of an established framework; probe the specific disruptive formation field; sense the patterns that emerge; respond to stabilise the desirable ones. And Shan’s essay series is itself an Uncharted Innovative community of practice: forming around a disruptive structural insight (Dao before Li, relation before dynamics) whose membership, objectives, and full structural implications are not yet determined but are actively forming through the process of the essays themselves. The formation is the form. The Dao is the document.

Empire Decline and the Sequence of Structural Failure

The Roman Empire’s decline across the third to fifth centuries CE is the Western historical record’s most thoroughly documented demonstration that coupling does not abolish sequence. The specific order in which the structural capacities dissolved — first the frontier army’s ethnic coherence, then the tax base’s territorial coverage, then the administrative class’s educational formation, then the legal system’s authority, then the infrastructure’s maintenance capacity, then the currency’s purchasing stability — was not random. Each dissolution created the conditions for the next. The sequence was constitutive: had any capacity dissolved in a different order, the trajectory would have been different.

Edward Gibbon saw the external causes (the barbarian invasions, the military disasters) as decisive. Peter Heather sees the structural pressures (the cost of frontier defence, the loss of tax-generating territory) as decisive. Bryan Ward-Perkins sees the material collapse of complex economic interdependence as decisive. All three are correct at the register they are examining. None of them is complete. What Shan’s framework adds: the proximate cause of the final collapse (whatever specific perturbation triggered the Western Empire’s dissolution in 476 CE) was not itself the structural failure. The structural failure was the long, largely invisible narrowing of the path across two centuries of formation erosion. The path had been narrowing since at least 235 CE. The visible collapse in 476 CE was the last move of a process that had been underway for two and a half centuries. Nothing collapsed in one move.

The Ming dynasty’s collapse provides the Chinese historical parallel, and it is more directly legible through Jin Guantao’s ultrastable system analysis. The Ming system maintained its institutional Li (the bureaucratic structure, the examination system, the tribute economy) with extraordinary stability across 276 years. Beneath the stable surface, the formation conditions that had originally produced the Li were silently eroding: the eunuch factionalism that corroded administrative integrity; the fiscal system’s inability to respond to the silver-economy transformation; the military’s loss of training formation; the examination system’s intellectual calcification into rote Li memorisation without genuine structural attunement. The ultrastable surface persisted. The Dao of genuine adaptive capacity was gone. When the specific perturbation arrived (the Manchu pressure from the north, the internal rebellions, the fiscal collapse), there was no corrective capacity remaining. The collapse was total and rapid — precisely because the surface stability had masked the formation erosion for so long.

The Empty City Stratagem: Pure Shiī, Pure Renli, Pure Cook Ding

The Empty City Stratagem (kōng chéng jì, 空城計) is Zhuge Liang’s most philosophically concentrated strategic act. Facing Sima Yi’s 150,000-strong Wei army with fewer than 2,500 of his own troops after a catastrophic logistical failure, Zhuge Liang ordered: city gates opened wide, all military flags and drums hidden, civilian sweepers sent into the streets before the gates, and himself installed on the highest viewing platform in flowing crane-feather robes, burning incense, playing his guqin with perfect serenity. Sima Yi arrived, surveyed the scene, and ordered immediate retreat. His officers were baffled. His explanation: Zhuge Liang has never taken unnecessary risks. This display of openness means the city is a trap. If we enter, we will be destroyed.

The stratagem operated entirely in the renli register. Zhuge Liang had no wuli (no troops, no fortifications), minimal shili (no strategic options beyond flight or the stratagem itself), but maximum renli in the specific sense of Sima Yi’s formation-conditioned perception. The renli of the encounter was constituted by Sima Yi’s forty-year formation history of encountering Zhuge Liang’s caution. That formation history — the Dao of their adversarial relationship — had produced in Sima Yi a specific Li: the pattern that Zhuge Liang never risks, therefore any apparent risk is concealed certainty. Zhuge Liang did not deceive Sima Yi with false information; he activated Sima Yi’s own Li against him, exploiting the grain of Sima Yi’s structural attunement to the adversary he had spent his career trying to match.

This is Snowden’s pattern entrainment as strategic weapon. The entrained pattern (‘Zhuge Liang does not take risks’) was accurate in general, was the product of genuine structural attunement through decades of formation, and was precisely the Li that the specific Dao of this specific crisis made unreliable. Sima Yi’s formation was his greatest asset and, in this moment, his structural vulnerability. The stratagem succeeded not by creating false information but by exploiting the gap between Sima Yi’s general Li (correct over forty years of formation) and the specific Dao of this specific impossible situation. Nothing in Sima Yi’s formation had prepared him for the Dao-without-Li moment: the genuine emptiness that was not concealing anything because there was nothing left to conceal.

Wang Bi and Wúxīn: The Sage Without Deliberate Mind

Wang Bi (226–249 CE) interprets Laozi’s sage as embodying wúxīn (無心, literally no-mind or no-deliberate-mind), a state in which response to situations arises without the mediation of deliberate calculation. His commentary on Laozi Chapter 16 is decisive: ‘The sage embodies emptiness and keeps to stillness (至虛機，守靜笹, zhì xū jī, shǒu jìng dǔ). All things arise together and I observe their return.’ The wúxīn sage does not calculate the right response; the sage is so thoroughly formed that the right response arises without deliberate mediation.

The structural account of wúxīn is precisely what Shan means by the throwing-away of the ladder. The propositions, the framework, the named Li: these are necessary instruments during the formation process. After sufficient formation, they become unnecessary — not because they were false but because the structural attunement they were pointing toward has been achieved. The wúxīn sage has completed the Dao of the formation; the Li is no longer external knowledge to be consulted but internal structural attunement to be enacted. This is also Wang Yangming’s unity of knowledge and action at its highest: there is no gap between knowing the right response and producing the right response because the formation has eliminated the gap.

The challenge Wang Bi poses for Shan’s framework: if wúxīn is the goal, and wúxīn means the dissolution of deliberate mind, then what is the role of Shan’s careful articulation of Li? The answer is in the ladder: the careful articulation is itself a Dao, a formation instrument that enables the reader to develop the structural attunement that, once achieved, no longer requires the articulation. The essays are not the Li; they are the Dao of the Li’s formation in the reader. When sufficient formation has occurred, the essays — like Wang Bi’s own commentary on Laozi — can be set down. The grain remains. The path that produced it continues.

Shan: The Poems, the Bullocks, and AlphaGo’s Move

“A path repeated over time becomes pattern. Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Dao: A Path Repeated Over Time Becomes Pattern”

This poem — the most compressed expression of Shan’s first Dao model — is structurally dense in the way that genuine poetry always is. Every line does irreplaceable work. ‘A path / repeated over time’: not a path imagined or designed but a path walked, repeatedly, until the repetition itself produces the pattern. The pattern is downstream of the repetition; it does not precede it. ‘Becomes pattern’: not acquires a pattern, not reveals a pre-existing pattern, but becomes pattern — the path and the pattern are not separate things, one describing the other. The path’s repeated traversal is the pattern’s formation. This is the most compressed possible statement of Dao-before-Li. Then the structural shift: ‘Most of the time, / we do not step onto a path. / We inherit one.’ The entry into the formed Dao is not chosen; it is inherited. The form of life (Wittgenstein) precedes the individual who enters it. The institutional structure (Juarrero’s enabling constraint) was in place before the new member arrived. The Wittgenstein thread and the Shan framework intersect precisely here: the language-game was already being played.

The poem travelled far further than Shan expected because it names something that every practitioner in every institutional context knows from the inside: the path was not chosen. The path was already there when you arrived. And the path shapes what you can see, do, and become in ways that feel like freedom but are also formation. This is not a critique of institutional inheritance; it is a structural description of the condition within which all formation occurs. You can only depart from a path you have first walked. You can only form new Li from the Dao of your specific formation context.

“At first, there is only landscape. Land. River. The field is already shaped by constraint: two river banks. Then movement in nature. Later, human settlement. Then the need to travel. A small boat carries people back and forth, year after year. Then perhaps more boats, more journeys. In that repeated movement, something begins to stabilise. A trace forms. The trace thickens. A pattern holds. A route becomes recognisable. What emerges is not the waterway itself, but a way of moving in relation to it. That way becomes Dao as relation repeats over time under constraint.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Dao Models of Mutual Generation” (April 2026)

The river-crossing account of Dao’s formation is Shan’s most complete and most beautiful descriptive piece of philosophy. Every element earns its place. The landscape comes first — not as an inert background but as a field already shaped by constraint (the riverbanks). The constraint is prior to the human: the river was already there. The constraint enables: because the banks are where they are, a crossing becomes both necessary and possible. Then the repeated movement — not one heroic crossing but the accumulation of ordinary journeys. The trace forms from the traces, the thickening from the repetition. And the extraordinary precision of the final formulation: what emerges is not the waterway itself but a way of moving in relation to it. The Dao is not the river; it is the way of moving in relation to the river. It is relational through and through. The Li (the recognisable route, the stable pattern) emerges from the Dao (the repeated relational movement). Always this order. Always this sequence.

“In the act of drawing, something shifted. Working between English and Chinese, I wrote 大道之行. Then the character 道 seemed to begin moving before my eyes. Because of the route I had drawn, two parallel lines with the feel of a passage, the character no longer appeared static. It opened into a field.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Dao Models of Mutual Generation” (April 2026)

The drawing account. Shan discovers the two Dao models not through abstract reasoning but through the act of drawing — the hand moving on the page before the concept arrives. This is the Wang Yangming unity of knowledge and action enacted as intellectual autobiography: the hand knew before the mind named what it knew. The character 道 becomes mobile through the specific act of drawing a path beside it. The Li of the character changes because the Dao of the encounter with it has changed. This is not metaphor; it is the structural claim that every Li is downstream of the Dao of its encounter. The character 道 does not have a fixed meaning that one studies and then applies. It means differently in different Dao-contexts. It opens into a field when the specific act of drawing a path beside it creates the formation conditions within which the field-meaning becomes visible.

“AlphaGo played a move on the fifth line of the board. It should not have been there. Professionals use the fifth line only in very specific circumstances. This was Move 37, and within a few moves, it was clear that something extraordinary had happened.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “AlphaGo’s Move 37: When Intelligence Stops Chasing the Obvious” (April 2026)

The specific location — the fifth line, where professionals do not normally play, against every conventional Li of Go strategy — is what makes Move 37 philosophically significant. It was not merely an unexpected move. It was a move that violated the accumulated Li of two thousand years of human Go formation, and proved, retrospectively, to be the most structurally decisive move of the game. This is the Move-37 principle at its most concentrated: the move that appears wrong by every existing Li is the move that a formation-sufficient system finds from the actual Dao of the specific board position. No prior Li could have prescribed it. The Dao of the specific position, read by a system whose formation was sufficient to read it, produced the Li of the decisive move.

“The move was not in the standard game tree. It was not a calculated risk in the conventional sense. It emerged from AlphaGo’s capacity to dwell in the actual configuration of the board at that moment, unburdened by the weight of what Go intelligence was supposed to look like.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “AlphaGo’s Move 37” (April 2026)

Not in the standard game tree: this is the structural proof that Li-first strategy is insufficient in the Complex domain. The standard game tree is the accumulated Li of human Go: every position that human formation has mapped, every move that human analysis has evaluated. AlphaGo’s Move 37 was not in this tree not because it was irrational but because the tree did not include the Dao of the specific board position at that specific moment of the specific game. The tree captures general Li; the Dao of the specific encounter produces specific Li that no general tree can anticipate. Shan’s framework: the Li of the situation must emerge from the Dao of genuine engagement with the situation. The pre-compiled Li of the game tree is always, at the most important moments, inadequate.

Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding: The Complete Chinese Text

依乎天理，批大卻，導大窾，因其固然 — yī hū tiān lǐ, pī dà xì, dǎo dà kuǎ, yīn qí gù rán — Following the heavenly grain; splitting at the large joints; guiding through the large hollows; going along with what is naturally so — Zhuangzi, Cook Ding

宮身之所居，神之所操，天地之道，戔于通之 — gōng shēn zhī suǒ jū, shén zhī suǒ cào — Where the body is stationed, where the spirit operates — Zhuangzi, on the consummate skill of the cook

The Chinese text of the Cook Ding passage moves through precise layers. 依乎天理 (yī hū tiān lǐ): not ‘following the principle’ in some abstract sense, but following the heavenly Li — the Li as it is instantiated cosmically in this specific ox. 宮 (gōng, palace/body station) and 神 (shén, spirit/shen) locate the cook’s practice at the intersection of the somatic and the cosmic: the body is the instrument, but the spirit is the operator, and the operation is the Dao of the knife finding the natural articulations. 因其固然 (yīn qí gù rán, going along with what is naturally so) is Wang Bi’s zìrán in action: the knife does not impose; it responds to what is already naturally so. This is the highest form of Dao-before-Li: the practitioner’s action so attuned to the formation conditions of the situation that the action and the situation’s grain are indistinguishable.

Laozi: Missing Chinese Texts Restored

為學日益，為道日損，損之又損，以至於無為 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi Dào rì sǔn — In pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day; relinquishing and again relinquishing, until one arrives at non-action — Laozi Ch.48

The 為學日益 / 為道日損 pairing is the most structurally precise epistemological claim in the Dao De Jing. For learning (為學, wèi xué, the pursuit of Li): daily addition. Each day, a new named pattern, a new articulated principle, a new item of knowledge. For Dao (為道, wèi Dào, the pursuit of the formation path itself): daily subtraction. Relinquishing (搏, sǔn) and again relinquishing — the deliberate, sustained release of premature Li, until what remains is the structural attunement that requires no deliberate Li at all: 無為 (wúwéi, non-action, effortless action aligned with the grain). The Cook Ding who has finished throwing away the ladder has arrived at 無為: not the absence of action but the presence of action so perfectly attuned that it appears effortless.

道天之道，利而不害；聖人之道，為而不爭 — Tiān zhī Dào, lì ér bù hài; shèng rén zhī Dào, wéi ér bù zhēng — Heaven’s Dao benefits and does not harm; the sage’s Dao acts and does not contend — Laozi Ch.81 (the closing words of the text)

The closing words of the Dao De Jing return to the structural ethics of water. Heaven’s Dao benefits without harming: not a moral injunction but a structural description of how the cosmic formation process operates. The Dao does not accumulate advantage at the expense of the things it forms; it enables their formation without competing with them. The sage’s Dao mirrors this: acts (為, wéi, purposeful action) without contending (不爭, bù zhēng, not competing, not grasping). Zhang Ruimin’s zero distance to the user is this principle at the organisational scale: the organisation that acts to enable the user’s flourishing without grasping the user’s surplus. RenDanHeYi as structural Daoism.

Confucius: Pine and Cypress in Winter

歲寒，然後知松柏之後凋也 — suì hán, rán hòu zhī sōng bǎi zhī hòu diāo yě — Only in the cold of winter do we know that the pine and cypress are the last to shed their leaves — Confucius, Analects 9.28

The pine and cypress reveal their formation not by being different in summer — when everything is green and flourishing — but by remaining when everything else has gone. The cold of winter is not the cause of their excellence; it is the diagnostic condition that makes their excellence visible. This is the negative test for formation: not ‘does the system perform impressively in favourable conditions?’ but ‘what does the system retain when the conditions that made performance easy have been removed?’ Shan’s framework: endurance under constraint is the revealed Li of the formation that produced the system. The cold does not create the inner structural integrity of the pine; it reveals it. And it reveals its absence in every tree that has shed its leaves.

Mencius: The Four Sprouts and the Flood-like Qi

惻隱之心，仁之端也；羞惡辭讓之心，義之端也 — cèyīn zhī xīn, rén zhī duān yě; xiūchǐ zhī xīn, yì zhī duān yě — The feeling of compassion is the beginning (sprout) of humaneness; the feeling of shame is the beginning of righteousness — Mencius 2A:6

Mencius’s four sprouts (四端, sì duān) are the most important structural claim in Confucian moral psychology. The sprout (端, duān, beginning, germinal point) is not the virtue; it is the formation condition from which the virtue can develop if the formation is adequately nourished. The feeling of compassion is the sprout of humaneness, not humaneness itself. Humaneness requires the sprout to be cultivated — the Dao of moral formation to be walked — before the Li of genuine humaneness can emerge. This is the Dao-before-Li principle in its moral register: the moral feeling is the Dao; the moral virtue is the Li that the sustained cultivation of the feeling produces. Forcing the sprout (the ancient farmer who pulled at his seedlings to make them grow faster, destroying them) is the error of premature Li: demanding the virtue before the formation conditions for the virtue have been adequately developed.

我善養吾浩然之氣 — wǒ shàn yǎng wú hàorán zhī qì — I am good at nourishing my flood-like qi — Mencius 2A:2

The flood-like qi (浩然之氣, hàorán zhī qì) is Mencius’s name for the formation achievement at its maximum: the moral-energetic capacity that fills the space between heaven and earth when it has been adequately nourished. Nourished, not generated: the qi is already there as potential; cultivation releases it. This is not mystical; it is structural. Fuller’s tensegrity integrity, Shan’s excellence, and Mencius’s flood-like qi are the same structural claim at three different registers: the continuous, distributed, integrating force that holds the whole system in its specific structural configuration when the formation has been adequate. The flood-like qi cannot be forced or faked; it can only be nourished through the long game of moral formation. It fills the space between heaven and earth not because it is cosmically vast but because it is structurally coherent — because nothing in the practitioner’s formation has blocked its natural extension.

Wittgenstein PI §66: Don’t Say, Look and See

“Don’t say: “there must be something common, or they would not be called ‘games’” — but look and see whether there is anything common to all.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §66

The family resemblance argument: the set of things called ‘games’ does not share a single common property or essence. They form a network of overlapping and criss-crossing similarities — like the members of a family who share certain features without any single feature being present in all. This is not relativism (there is no essence so anything goes); it is structural realism about complex classifications: the Li of a category can be a network of partial resemblances rather than a single defining principle. Shan’s Li works like this. The Li of the Dao is not a single universal property shared by every instance of Dao; it is a network of family resemblances — path-character, formation-precedence, relational-constitution — that connect instances of Dao without any single instance embodying all of them fully.

The methodological imperative — ‘look and see’ rather than ‘say there must be’ — is Shan’s anti-premature-Li principle in miniature. Don’t say there must be a single definition of Dao that all instances share; look and see what the specific instances actually have in common. The essay that begins with the specific (the LinkedIn thread, the Go board, the river crossing) is obeying the ‘look and see’ injunction: it does not begin from the pre-formed Li of a definition; it looks at the actual formation and sees what Li emerges from the looking.

Liang Qichao: Inner Sageness and Outer Kingliness

Liang Qichao (1873–1929), the great reformer and intellectual of the late Qing and Republican era, observed that the entire Confucian tradition could be understood through the phrase ‘the Dao of inner sageness and outer kingliness’ (內聖外王之道, nèi shèng wài wáng zhī Dào): the cultivation of inner structural integrity (inner sageness, the Dao of self-formation) as the formation condition for effective engagement with the outer world (outer kingliness, the Li of governance and leadership). The inner must be formed before the outer can be effectively shaped. This is Zhuge Liang’s ‘first organise the inner, then the outer’ — and it is Shan’s holding capacity argument applied to the entire Confucian tradition: you cannot govern effectively without first forming the structural integrity from which effective governance can flow.

“The Dao of inner sageness and outer kingliness: the inner sage cultivates the self; the outer king orders the world. But the outer king cannot order the world without first being an inner sage. Formation before action. Always.”

— Liang Qichao, on the Confucian tradition’s central structural claim

The Confucian integration of the contemplative and the active: inner formation (內聖, nèi shèng) as the precondition of outer effectiveness (外王, wài wáng). The Dao of inner sageness is the Dao-walk that produces the Li of genuine structural attunement; the outer kingliness is the Shī that accumulated formation makes available in the world. This is not the separation of theory and practice but their specific sequence: inner formation first, outer effectiveness as its consequence. The practitioner who attempts outer kingliness without inner sageness is the practitioner of Shī without Dao — of positional force without the formation that makes it sustainable. The force dissipates. The Shī collapses. The path narrows first.

Xuesen Qian: The Open Complex Giant System

“The traditional division of science and technology departments has not only limited our scientific view but has prevented us from tackling real-world problems that are by their very nature holistic.”

— Xuesen Qian (Tsien Hsue-shen), on the limits of reductionist science

Qian Xuesen (1911–2009) — architect of China’s missile programme, pioneer of systems engineering — spent the second half of his career arguing that the most important problems facing human civilisation were Open Complex Giant Systems (OCGS): systems too large, too internally differentiated, and too deeply coupled with their environments for any reductionist analysis to adequately address. His metasynthesis approach (zōnghé jíchéng, 綜合集成) proposed integrating expert knowledge, computational modelling, and direct practical experience in iterative cycles — not to eliminate complexity but to develop the structural attunement adequate to engage with it without premature simplification.

Qian’s OCGS framework and Shan’s relational dynamics are sister projects: both insist that the complexity of real human systems cannot be addressed by disciplinary reductionism (wuli alone), that the human experiential and relational dimensions (renli) are irreducibly necessary, and that the formation of adequate structural understanding requires iterative engagement (walking the Dao) rather than prior theoretical specification (Li before Dao). Qian arrived at this from aerospace engineering. Shan arrived at it from language, education, and the Chinese philosophical tradition. The grain is the same; the paths were different.

知彼知己，百戰不殆 — zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài — Know the other and know yourself: in a hundred battles, no defeat — Sun Tzu, Art of War Ch.3

Sun Tzu’s strategic epistemology: genuine strategic knowledge is relational. You must know the other (the formation, capacities, and structural attunement of the adversary) as precisely as you know yourself (your own formation, capacities, and structural attunement). This is not a tactical prescription but an ontological claim about the nature of strategic intelligence: strategic knowing is always relational knowing, always grounded in the specific relational field between yourself and the adversary, never purely internal or purely external. Shan’s relational dynamics applied to strategy: the Dao of the strategic encounter (the specific relational field between the two formations) must be read before any Li of strategic action can be appropriately formed.

Wang Fuzhi: Qi Condenses and Form Emerges

氣就釀而後成象 — qì jiù liàng ér hòu chéng xiàng — Qi first condenses and then form-pattern emerges — Wang Fuzhi

Wang Fuzhi (1619–1692), the greatest systematic philosopher of the late Ming and early Qing, developed the most materially grounded account of the Dao-before-Li relationship in the Neo-Confucian tradition. His claim: qi (the vital material force, the energetic-material substrate of all existence) first condenses (萀, liàng) and then form-pattern (象, xiàng, which includes what we would call Li) emerges. The material condensation process is ontologically prior to the pattern it produces. This is the most explicit pre-modern statement of what Prigogine’s dissipative structures describe at the thermodynamic level: the material process (the qi condensation, the dissipative far-from-equilibrium dynamics) is what produces the order (the form-pattern, the Li). The Li does not precede the material process; it emerges from it.

Wang Fuzhi’s materialism places him in direct tension with Zhu Xi’s idealism (Li exists before qi, before the material things it patterns). And it places him in direct alignment with Shan: Dao (the formation process, the qi condensation, the relational dynamics) precedes Li (the pattern, the form-pattern, the intelligibility). The sequence is not merely methodological but ontological: the material-formation process (Dao) is what generates the pattern (Li), not the other way around. This is why Wang Fuzhi’s philosophy of history is also a philosophy of formation: history is the Dao within which the Li of civilisational development emerges, unpredictably, irreversibly, always downstream of the material-relational formation that produced it.

The Submerged Dragon: Yi Jing on Formation Before Manifestation

潛龍勿用：陽氣潛藏 — qián lóng wù yòng: yáng qí qián cáng — The dragon submerged: do not use — the yang force is still hidden — Yi Jing, Qian Hexagram, first line

The first line of the Qian hexagram encodes the temporal structure of Dao-before-Li at the cosmological scale.
