The dragon is real — the yang force is genuinely present, genuinely potent, genuinely capable of transforming the situation. But its time has not yet come. It is submerged: not absent but not yet manifest, not yet available for deployment. The injunction ‘do not use’ (勿用, wù yòng) is not a counsel of timidity but of structural precision: deploying the force before its formation is adequate to sustain the deployment will destroy the formation rather than achieve the intended effect.

The submerged dragon is the Dao in its pre-Li stage. The formation is real and in progress; the Li that will make it deployable has not yet emerged. The strategist who forces the deployment — who acts on the submerged dragon as if it were already the flying dragon of the fifth line — will exhaust the formation before it has reached the structural integrity that genuine deployment requires. This is Shan’s holding capacity argument at the cosmological level: the capacity to hold the formation in its submerged state, without premature deployment, is itself the most important structural competence. The long game requires the patience to let the dragon remain submerged until the formation is complete.

Bergson: Durée and the Living Present

Bergson’s durée (duration, in the 1889 sense of Time and Free Will) is the irreducible lived time of genuine experience — the continuous, indivisible flow of the living present that is categorically different from the spatialized clock-time of physics. Clock time is the Li of time: the named, measured, divisible representation of time as a series of homogeneous instants. Durée is the Dao of time: the actual living movement of experience, which is continuous, qualitative, and irreversible. The clock measures Li; the living body inhabits Dao.

“For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.”

— Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution Ch.1 (1907, tr. Arthur Mitchell 1911) — verified exact

The durée argument is the most sustained philosophical attack in Western thought on the reduction of temporal experience to spatial representation — on the conversion of Dao into Li, of the living formation process into a named and mapped structure. Bergson: the moment you represent time as a line with points on it, you have lost durée. You have produced a Li of time (a spatial map of temporal sequence) and destroyed the Dao of time (the actual irreversible qualitative flow of formation). The analyst who maps the stages of organisational development onto a timeline has produced useful Li and destroyed the durée of the actual formation: the specific texture of each moment, the specific qualitative difference between one phase and the next, the irreversibility of the formation process that means you cannot simply move back to an earlier point on the line.

China’s Reform Without a Theory: The WSR Reading

Zhu’s analysis of China’s post-1978 reform as a reform without a theory is one of the most structurally important applications of the WSR framework to historical analysis. The question is not merely descriptive (‘how did the reform happen without a theory?’) but ontological: ‘why did not having a theory work?’ Zhu’s answer through WSR: the specific wuli-shili-renli configuration of China in 1978 was such that the absence of theory was itself the formation condition that made the reform viable.

Wuli: the ‘advantage of backwardness’ — the command economy had left an enormous seller’s market; whatever replaced it could only go upward; the costless abandonability of the prior system removed the structural resistance that theory-commitment would have created. Shili: the Chinese pragmatic mindscape — Deng’s white-cat-black-cat metaphor as the explicit Li of no-fixed-Li governance; the anti-abstraction bias, the ambiguity tolerance, the shizhong (timely balance) that allowed experimentation without doctrine. Renli: the distrust of public institutions, the guanxi network capitalism, the ‘benign neglect from above’ that allowed private initiative to grow without requiring official sanction.

“Standing alone, each of the wuli, shili, renli factors could well be obstructive. Working together at that specific historical moment, however, they led to favourable outcomes.”

— Zhichang Zhu, WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach — on China’s Reform Without a Theory

This is the most structurally precise historical demonstration of the WSR principle: the three Li are not independently sufficient; it is their specific conjunction at a specific historical moment that produces the outcome. And the conjunction — the specific wuli-shili-renli configuration of China in 1978 — is itself a product of the long Dao of Chinese historical formation, not of any deliberate design. The reform worked not because it was well designed but because the formation conditions were such that the specific relational engagement of the three Li at that specific moment produced a Shī — a positional advantage — that reform leadership could exploit without needing to name or design it in advance.

Fuller: Dymaxion, Ephemeralization, and the Ethics of Design

“DYMAXION is a compound of dynamic maximum tension. It is the principle that describes a much larger and more complex universe than the one that people have been educated to expect.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, as cited in a+u Magazine (2023)

Dynamic maximum tension: the compound does multiple structural work simultaneously. Dynamic — the structure is not static but in continuous tensional adjustment, always maintaining its integrity through movement rather than through fixity. Maximum — not the tension that destroys (overstress) but the maximum tension that a given structural formation can sustain with integrity. Tension — not compression, not the rigid pushing together of parts, but the continuous distributed force that holds every element in its specific structural relationship with every other element. Dymaxion is Fuller’s name for the structural condition of genuine excellence: the state of maximum tensional integrity that a formation can sustain. This is precisely Shan’s dynamic maximum tension: the specific tension level at which the formation achieves its maximum viable complexity.

“Ephemeralization: doing more and more with less and less until eventually you can do everything with nothing.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Ephemeralization is Fuller’s account of the structural direction of genuine formation: as the Li of a practice or technology deepens, the same outcomes become achievable with progressively fewer material resources. The cook who has fully formed the Cook Ding attunement produces perfect cuts with a knife that never needs sharpening — the material cost approaches zero as the formation depth approaches its maximum. The organisation that has fully formed the RenDanHeYi ecosystem generates genuine user value with progressively lower coordination costs as the structural attunement between 人 and 單 deepens. Ephemeralization is the structural signature of sufficiently formed Li: the ability to achieve more with less as the formation deepens, because the structural attunement to the grain of the situation allows the effort to be placed precisely where it matters rather than distributed inefficiently against the grain.

John Holland: Building Blocks, Tags, and the Emergence of Structure

John Holland’s technical contributions to the theory of complex adaptive systems — the building block hypothesis and the concept of tags — provide the computational underpinning for what Shan describes as the formation of Li from the Dao of relational engagement. Holland’s building blocks are recurring, combinable structural elements that appear across many different complex adaptive systems: not fundamental atoms (which cannot be further decomposed) but structural regularities that recur at multiple scales and combine with each other to produce higher-order structure. This is the computational version of Li: the structural patterns that recur in the formation process and combine to produce emergent organisation.

Tags — Holland’s term for the markers that enable selective interaction between agents in a complex adaptive system — are the structural mechanism by which the relational field is constituted. Tags allow agents to identify, select, and engage with specific other agents rather than interacting indiscriminately with everything in the environment. The relational field (Shan’s prior condition of all consequential dynamics) is constituted by the tag structure: the pattern of who-connects-with-whom that determines which dynamics are possible and which are not. Tags are Li at the micro level: the structural markers that make specific relational engagements possible and others structurally unavailable. And the tag structure of a complex adaptive system is always the product of its formation history — the Dao of prior interactions that produced the current pattern of selective engagement.

Mike Jackson: Critical Systems Thinking and Power

Mike Jackson’s critical systems thinking asks the question that WSR’s renli dimension names but does not always answer with sufficient force: whose interests does the system serve? Jackson’s critical systems heuristics require the practitioner to identify not only the technical structure of the system (wuli) and the methodological framework for engaging with it (shili) but the power structure that determines whose knowledge counts, whose interests are served, and whose values are systematically marginalised (the deepest layer of renli that goes beyond interpersonal coordination to structural power analysis).

The structural relevance for Shan: the formation of a professional discourse community — the complexity discourse, the systems thinking community, the management theory establishment — is never power-neutral. The Li that the community has formed through its Dao of intellectual practice encodes the interests, values, and perspectives of the practitioners who did most of the formation. When Shan introduces the Chinese philosophical tradition’s account of structural formation into this community, she is not merely adding a new perspective; she is challenging the power structure of the existing Li. The existing Li of complexity science was formed predominantly through Western intellectual formation. Its specific grain encodes Western assumptions about what counts as rigour, what counts as evidence, what counts as theoretical depth. Shan’s framework is a structural challenge to this power-encoded Li: it demands that the community’s formation history be widened to include the Dao of the Chinese intellectual tradition, which has its own equally rigorous account of exactly the structural terrain the complexity discourse claims to address.

Jackson’s challenge to Shan is the sharpest possible: structural attunement without power analysis is structural innocence. The practitioner who develops the Li of following the grain without asking whose grain gets followed, whose path gets walked, whose formation conditions are treated as the natural starting point, has achieved structural elegance at the cost of political naivety. Shan’s response, implicit in her bilingual cross-cultural project: the political challenge is precisely met by the methodological commitment. A paper that places Chinese philosophical discourse in genuine dialectical collision with Western complexity theory, refusing to let either tradition absorb the other, is itself an act of structural power redistribution: it refuses the established hierarchy of whose Li gets to be treated as the general framework.

❧ ✶ ❧

悖論 — Bèi Lún — Chaos Puzzles

❧ ✶ ❧

“The voyager sets out, encounters what the ocean gives them, and what they bring back is not what they set out to find because the ocean refuses to be mapped in advance. The voyage is the method. The destination is what the voyage produces.”

— David Snowden, “The Wild Place: Goidelic” (2026)

Read this against every framework you have ever been handed. The ocean refuses to be mapped in advance. Not cannot be mapped — refuses. The refusal is ontological. The ocean is not waiting for a sufficiently sophisticated cartography. It is constitutively, generatively, necessarily beyond any map that precedes the voyage. This is Shan’s Dao-before-Li stated as navigation epistemology. The voyage is the method. Not a step toward the method. Not the application of the method. The method itself. The destination is what the voyage produces. Not what was planned. Not what was desired. What the encounter with the actual ocean, the actual formation conditions of the actual situation, produces from the actual formation of the actual voyager.

Every consultant who arrives with a pre-formed framework is not a voyager. They are a tourist with a map. Every leader who executes a strategy designed before the engagement with the territory began is not navigating. They are performing navigation. Every methodology that specifies its outcomes before the inquiry begins has not set out. It has merely relocated.

The Zone does not give what is desired; it gives what is true. Tarkovsky’s Stalker knew this in his body, in the nineteen years of accumulated somatic intelligence that let him throw the weighted nut ahead on its cloth strip and read where it landed. Not where it was supposed to land. Where it actually landed. The distinction is everything. The nut is in your hand. The voyage is ahead. The map you brought will not be adequate. This is not a problem. This is the invitation.

悖論 #1

The Dao that has been named is not the eternal Dao. Every map is already wrong. The wrong map that is held lightly — that knows itself as wrong, that remains open to revision at the first encounter with actual terrain — is infinitely more useful than the correct map that has become a substitute for attention. Shan’s Li-warning is this: when the concept begins to feel smooth, when it circulates without friction, when Dao sounds like a management principle you already understood before you began — that is the moment the map has replaced the voyage. Throw the nut. Read where it lands. The ocean refuses to be mapped in advance.

NEON ENTRY: THE FORMATION CONDITION OF THIS INQUIRY

What the Paper Is, What It Refuses to Be, and What the Ocean Gives

❧ ✶ ❧

Three figures ride a flatcar through a post-industrial wasteland. The film stock shifts from sepia to colour. Nothing is announced. The world simply changes. This is what happens — at its best, in its rarest and most structurally honest moments — when genuine thinking meets genuine complexity. Not a framework applied. Not a method executed. A world changing. The quality of attention changing. The nervous system registering the shift before cognition has had time to construct its protective explanations.

This paper is a flatcar ride. It does not promise arrival. It promises traversal — passage through a terrain that is real, that has genuine Li (inner grain, structural pattern, the texture that makes the jade workable in some directions and resistant in others), and that will only yield its Li to the practitioner who has walked its Dao. Not read about its Dao. Not mapped its Dao. Walked it. Repeated movement over time, under constraint, until a trace forms, the trace thickens, a pattern holds.

The forty-plus voices assembled here — Alice Jing Shan, Laozi, Wittgenstein, Fuller, Prigogine, Bateson, Maturana, Zhuangzi, Zhu Xi, Zhang Ruimin — are not a literature review. They are not positioned around Shan’s work like planets around a sun, each illuminating one facet. They are in genuine collision. Chrome hitting concrete. Ideas pushed past their rated capacity until something new sparks at the junction. The ozone smell of circuits under load. The crash helmet is on the table. The encounter is not managed. It is undergone.

悖論 #2

Any paper that promises to be comprehensive has already lied. This one does not. The forty voices assembled here have been chosen not because they cover the field but because they create productive collision — because their specific grain encounters Shan’s specific grain in ways that produce heat, light, and structural recognition that neither alone would generate. The compass is partial. The ocean is larger. The voyage is the method.

THE GRAIN THAT CANNOT BE HURRIED

On Why Dao-Before-Li Is Not a Preference but an Ontological Condition

❧ ✶ ❧

Here is what cannot be rushed. The grain of jade forms through geological time — through the specific pressures, temperatures, and mineral encounters of a specific formation history that cannot be reproduced by increasing the rate of application. The grain does not care about your timeline. It does not respect your project management software. It forms at the rate that the Dao of its formation permits, and imposing a different rate produces not faster formation but fracture.

This is what Shan means, precisely, when she says the path must open before its inner grain can appear. Not that it will eventually appear if you wait. That it cannot appear if you don’t. The Li of a complex system — the structural grain that makes it workable, navigable, capable of yielding genuine understanding and genuine intervention — is downstream of the Dao of engagement with it. You cannot know the Li before you have walked the Dao. This is not a methodological preference. It is an ontological condition of complex systems. The ocean refuses to be mapped in advance not because the cartographers are incompetent but because the ocean is constitutively, generatively beyond any prior mapping.

The management consultant arrives with the framework already formed. The framework is the product of someone else’s Dao, accumulated through someone else’s engagement with someone else’s organisational terrain. It may be a good framework. It may accurately describe structural patterns that appear in many organisations. But it is not the Li of this organisation at this moment in this formation history. It is a map of somewhere that resembles here. The resemblance will mislead you at precisely the moments when accuracy matters most: when the situation becomes genuinely strange, when the terrain diverges from the map, when the nut lands somewhere unexpected and the trained response is to assume the landing is wrong rather than update the map.

Cook Ding does not hack. He has spent nineteen years learning not to hack. The knife that hacks against the grain depletes itself and damages the material. The knife that follows the grain encounters no resistance — not because the grain is absent but because the knife has been formed to read it. This is not supernatural skill. It is the result of a specific formation process carried to its completion. Nineteen years. Not eighteen. Not seventeen and a technique borrowed from a book about the nineteenth. The formation takes the time it takes because the holding capacity must be built before it can hold what the situation requires.

悖論 #3

The harder you try to accelerate formation, the more completely you destroy its conditions. The neonatal gut that receives milk too fast is not accelerating; it is rupturing. The organisation that tries to shortcut the Dao of its formation — that tries to achieve in six months what requires six years — does not save five and a half years. It destroys the formation that would have produced the Li it needs. The formation takes the time it takes. This is not a counsel of passivity. It is a structural description of what formation actually is.

MOVE 37: WHEN INTELLIGENCE STOPS CHASING THE OBVIOUS

On Position, Formation, and the Strategic Move That Cannot Be Planned

❧ ✶ ❧

Fifth line. The professionals do not play on the fifth line here. Two thousand years of Go formation says: not there, not in this configuration, not for any reason that the accumulated Li of human strategic intelligence can identify. And AlphaGo plays there. Move 37.

The room goes quiet in the way that rooms go quiet when something impossible has just become real. Fan Hui, the European Go champion acting as analyst, pauses. He replays the position. He plays out the consequences. Then he says, in the specific register of someone encountering a reality that their formation has not prepared them for: ‘This move is beautiful.’

Not correct. Not optimal in the sense of game-tree calculation. Beautiful. The word of the practitioner who has walked enough Dao to recognise Li when it appears in a form that no prior Li could have named. The move was not in the standard game tree because the standard game tree is the accumulated Li of human Go formation — every position that human analysis has mapped, every strategic implication that human pattern-recognition has evaluated. Move 37 was beyond the tree not because it was irrational but because the tree did not include the specific Dao of this specific board at this specific moment. The Li of the position could only be read by a formation sufficient to read it.

This is the Move-37 principle that runs through Shan’s entire framework. The most structurally decisive intervention in any complex situation is almost never the one that prior analysis prescribed. It emerges from the specific Dao of the specific encounter — from the genuine, embodied, formation-sufficient reading of the actual terrain, not the application of a map of terrain that resembles this one. The consultant who can only recommend what their framework already named cannot find Move 37. They cannot even see that it exists.

Zhuge Liang saw it. The Longzhong Plan was a Move-37 reading of the Three Kingdoms situation before a single battle had been fought. Not a strategy applied from a library of strategies. A positional reading of a specific formation field by a mind formed to read it. The Shī — the positional advantage, the structural configuration that determines which moves become possible and which remain impossible — was read before it was named. The Dao was walked before the Li was articulated. This is always the order. This is always the order.

悖論 #4

Move 37 cannot be planned because planning is Li-before-Dao. The move exists in the specific structural field of the specific board at the specific moment. It is not available until the position is actual. The practitioner formed to find it does not plan for it — they remain present to the actual, they follow the Dao of the actual encounter, and the Li of the decisive move emerges from the following. This is what it means to say the voyage is the method. You cannot plan Move 37. You can only be formed enough to find it when the position arrives.

THE TENSIONAL UNIVERSE: FULLER’S CLAIM AND ITS CONSEQUENCES

What It Means That Tension Is the Great Integrity

❧ ✶ ❧

Fuller said it like a man announcing the discovery of gravity. Tension is the great integrity. Not important. Not significant. The great integrity. The one that holds everything. The continuous, distributed, non-local force that connects every element of every structure to every other element, that holds the specific configuration that makes the structure what it is, that transmits every perturbation through the whole.

The universe is omnitensional integrity. This is a cosmological claim. Every structure at every scale — from the geodesic dome to the human body to the solar system to the atom — holds together not through compression (discrete objects pushing against each other in rigid chains of contact) but through tension: the continuous, distributed, integrating network that gives every element its specific position in relation to every other. Remove the tension and you do not weaken the structure. You do not reduce it. You collapse it completely, instantly, because the tension was not supporting the structure — the tension was the structure.

Now take this seriously at the level of the organisation. The management hierarchy is a compression structure — authority pushed down through chains of rigid, directed contact, each manager bearing the load of the layers above them, transmitting it to the layers below. This structure is brittle. Remove any compression element and the load redistributes catastrophically. The organisation that has lost a critical middle layer has not simplified; it has lost the compressive path by which authority was transmitted. The entire load redistributes. Failure cascades.

RenDanHeYi is a tensegrity organisation. The compression elements — the individual microenterprises, each a discrete island of entrepreneurial activity — do not touch. They float. They are held in their specific positions not by direct contact with each other but by the continuous tensional network of the market — the feedback loops, the user-value signals, the platform architecture that connects every microenterprise to the relational field of actual user need simultaneously. Every microenterprise is structurally related to every other not through the rigid chain of command but through the distributed tension of the shared market reality. This is Fuller in Qingdao. This is the magic in the mechanics.

悖論 #5

Every organisation that believes it is held together by hierarchy is wrong. The hierarchy describes the compression elements. What actually holds the organisation — what makes it capable of coordinated action, of responsive adaptation, of genuine relationship with the reality it claims to serve — is the tensional network: the informal trust, the relational capital, the accumulated history of who has been honest with whom about what, the threads of genuine connection that the organisational chart does not show and the performance review system cannot measure. Reduce the tension — through betrayal, through reorganisation that severs informal connections, through the replacement of genuine relationship with managed transaction — and the compression structure that remains will hold its shape for a while, then collapse in ways that the organisational chart cannot predict.

THE TWO SILENCES: WITTGENSTEIN AND THE INEXPRESSIBLE GRAIN

On the Boundary Between What Can Be Said and What Shows Itself

❧ ✶ ❧

The Tractatus ends in silence. Not failure. Not defeat. Not the silence of someone who ran out of things to say. The silence of someone who reached the boundary of what language can do and stopped. ‘Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.’ Seven words. The whole of the Tractatus was building toward this. And the extraordinary thing — the thing that makes Wittgenstein the Western philosopher most structurally aligned with the Chinese tradition — is what he says just before the silence. There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical.

Shows itself. Not revealed by a sufficiently sophisticated analysis. Not produced by a more nuanced reading. Not available to those who know the right framework. It shows itself. To those who have walked far enough, who have formed sufficient structural attunement, who have thrown the nut enough times to know this specific terrain — the inexpressible shows itself. Not in statements. In the quality of what is formed. In the specific texture of Cook Ding’s cut. In the specific weight of Move 37. In the specific feeling of the Polynesian navigator’s body reading the waves.

The Li that cannot be stated shows itself in the Dao of the practice. Every time. Not sometimes. Every time, when the formation is sufficient and the attention is genuine. This is not mysticism in the sense of the vague and the unverifiable. This is mysticism in the sense that Wittgenstein meant: the structural reality that exceeds what can be said but not what can be shown. Shan’s essays are attempts to show what they cannot fully say. This is not a limitation. It is the condition of all genuine philosophical writing about structure.

And then the Investigations arrives, thirty years later, and the silence of the Tractatus opens into language again — but a different language. Not the formal language of logical structure. The language of the form of life: the daily, ordinary, specific, embedded language of the Dao that is always already being walked. ‘Don’t say: there must be something common, or they would not be called games. Look and see whether there is anything common to all.’ Look and see. Not infer from principles. Not derive from structures. Look. At the actual formation. At the actual Dao. And see what Li emerges from the looking.

悖論 #6

The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. Shan grew up inside 道, 理, 知道, 道理. She grew up inside a language that encodes knowing as path-following, that embeds the formation principle in the everyday epistemological claim, that carries the Dao-before-Li structure in the grammar of ordinary utterance. This is not cultural advantage. It is structural ecology. The world available to a practitioner is the world their language makes available. This does not mean other worlds are impossible. It means they require the Dao of formation — the sustained, embodied engagement with the language that carries them — before their Li becomes accessible. You cannot read the waves without a body formed to read them.

THE SLEDGEHAMMER AND THE GRAIN: ZHANG RUIMIN’S MOVE 37

❧ ✶ ❧

1985. Qingdao. Seventy-six refrigerators lined up in the main hall of a failing factory. Zhang Ruimin walks the line. His workers gather. He hands out the sledgehammers. Two years’ salary destroyed. The workers weep. He does not explain himself. He lets the sound do the work.

This is not destruction. This is Move 37. This is the move that the standard management game tree does not contain — that no prior analysis of ‘how to fix a failing state-owned enterprise’ would have prescribed, that every conventional framework for organisational turnaround would have classified as irrational, morale-destroying, economically illiterate. And it is, in retrospect, the most structurally decisive moment in the history of one of the world’s most successful manufacturing transformations.

Why? Not because the sledgehammers were symbols. Because they were a formation intervention. Zhang was not destroying refrigerators. He was destroying a Li: the accumulated, sedimented, apparently-permanent pattern of acceptable mediocrity that constituted the organisational form of Chinese manufacturing culture in 1985. He was cracking open a formation that had produced the wrong grain. And in the cracking, he was creating the conditions — the specific Dao of the specific moment of rupture — within which a new Li could form.

The zone between what was and what is not yet. The edge of chaos. Prigogine’s bifurcation point: far from equilibrium, the system is maximally sensitive to the specific perturbation that will determine which new structure emerges from the dissolution of the old. The sledgehammer was the perturbation. The weeping workers were at the bifurcation. What they would become — the engineers of a global manufacturing transformation, the practitioners of a management philosophy that has been studied at Harvard and INSEAD and Peking University — was not determined by the sledgehammers. It was made possible by them.

悖論 #7

Zhang Ruimin eliminated 10,000 middle managers. Not fired for incompetence. Made structurally unnecessary by the emergence of a new organisational form in which the role that justified their positions had ceased to exist. The RenDanHeYi ecosystem did not need them. The tension network that connected microenterprises to users directly made the compression structure that needed them obsolete. This is Fuller’s claim enacted at scale: build the new model that makes the existing model obsolete. The managers did not lose their jobs to a restructuring decision. They lost them to a structural reality that had been in formation for thirty years of deliberate, painful, patient Dao-walking.

THE ZONE WITHIN THE ZONE: MYSTICISM AS STRUCTURAL PRECISION

❧ ✶ ❧

Here is what the crash helmet is for. This is the movement where the thinking runs into the wall of its own deepest implications. The wall is not the end. It is the transition, like the flatcar crossing, from sepia into colour. From the ordinary light of structural analysis into something that still has structure — is more structural, is structure all the way down — but that exceeds what analysis alone can reach.

The seven frequencies — Cadence, Resonance, Salience, Valence, Vibration, Tension, Gain — are not metaphors borrowed from physics. They are structural realities. The cadence of a formation process is as real as the cadence of a heartbeat. The resonance between two traditions encountering each other’s grain is as physically real as the resonance between two strings tuned to the same fundamental frequency. The vibration of the Polynesian navigator’s body reading the waves is as materially constituted as any other physical sensing system. The informative is always energetic. Iain Kerr got this right. The signal is real. The field is real. The practitioner who has been formed to receive it is not imagining what they receive.

Cheng Hao: the person of humaneness takes heaven and earth and the ten thousand things as one body. Not a metaphor. A structural claim about what happens when the formation of the self has been carried to sufficient depth that the boundary between self and other — between the practitioner and the formation field they are embedded in — becomes genuinely permeable. The numb limb is the failure of structural conductivity. The humaneness is the restoration of conductivity. The cosmos is a tensegrity structure. The person of genuine formation is a fully conducting node in the tensional network. Everything that happens anywhere in the network is felt.

This is not mysticism as evasion. This is mysticism as the deepest register of structural precision. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of formation produced a body so structurally attuned to the Li of the ox’s formation that the knife found the articulation before the mind named it. This is Wittgenstein’s 6.522 made somatic: the inexpressible shows itself in the quality of the cut. The practitioner who has undergone the formation does not need to say the Li; they enact it. The Li shows itself. In the movement of the knife. In the placement of Move 37. In the quality of the facilitator’s presence in a room where something real is beginning to form.

悖論 #8

The mystical is not what evades structure. It is what is most structural and least sayable. Cook Ding’s cut. Move 37. Bergson’s durée. The Polynesian islands visible in the waves. Wang Yangming’s genuine knowing that cannot be separated from the acting that enacts it. These are not examples of something beyond structure. They are the most precise possible demonstrations of what structure is when it has been formed to its full depth. The mystical stratum is the deepest geological layer of the formation. The grain runs all the way down.

ONE REALITY, FORTY VOCABULARIES, ONE VOYAGE

❧ ✶ ❧

Consider what has happened in this inquiry. Forty voices from four traditions across twenty-six centuries have been placed in genuine dialectical collision. Not arranged around a thesis. Not positioned as supporting evidence. Collided. And from the collision, something has emerged that none of them alone could have produced: a structural recognition so deep that it runs beneath every vocabulary, every tradition, every historical context.

Laozi: the path opens before its grain appears. Wittgenstein: the inexpressible shows itself. Fuller: tension is the great integrity. Shan: what is formed is still in formation. Bergson: to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly. Maturana: the system drifts with only the constraint of maintaining structural coupling. Kauffman: the biosphere is always doing something for the first time. Bateson: what is the pattern that connects? Zhang Zai: the plastic moulding of heaven and earth is my body. Snowden: the voyage is the method.

One line. One recognition. Differently worded, differently placed, differently arrived at through different formation histories in different historical contexts speaking different languages to different structural problems. But one recognition. The Dao precedes the Li. The formation precedes the formed. The voyage produces the destination. The path must be walked before its grain can appear.

This is not the same as saying they all agree. They emphatically do not. Zhu Xi places Li before Dao and produces a metaphysical system of magnificent coherence that is, at its foundation, structurally wrong. Wittgenstein ends in silence where Shan continues writing and is right to do so. Fuller wants to build the tensegrity structures that will make war obsolete and the hunger of optimism is beautiful but the structures did not scale the way he hoped. Yang Zhu wants to preserve life in its wholeness and Cheng Hao wants the humaneness that feels the suffering of others as directly as its own and these are genuinely incommensurable positions that cannot be resolved without loss.

The divergences are real. The irreducible differences between traditions, between thinkers, between the Chinese and Western accounts of what structure is and how it forms and what it means — these cannot and should not be dissolved into a synthesis that pretends to have resolved them. The horizon fusion (Gadamer) that this paper attempts is not the production of a single merged horizon. It is the enlargement of every horizon without the dissolution of any.

悖論 #9

A paper that achieves genuine synthesis has done something easier than one that maintains genuine tension. The synthesis resolves. The maintained tension remains alive. This paper does not resolve. It deepens. Every apparent convergence re-poses itself as divergence at a more precise level. Every apparent agreement reveals, under examination, a difference that cannot be absorbed without distortion. This is not a failure of rigour. It is the sign that the inquiry is still in genuine contact with the complexity of its subject matter. The 悖论 re-poses itself at a deeper level each time you think you have resolved it. The voyage is the method. The inquiry is not complete. It is advancing.

WHAT THE OCEAN GIVES

❧ ✶ ❧

The voyager sets out. The ocean does not behave as expected. It never does. That is not a problem. That is the gift.

What the ocean gives — what the forty voices assembled here give, what Shan’s Substack series gives, what the encounter between Chinese structural philosophy and Western complexity science gives when the encounter is genuine rather than decorative — is not what was sought. What was sought was a framework. A more sophisticated account. A better theory of how complex systems work that could be applied with sufficient skill to produce better outcomes. The ocean refuses this.

What the ocean gives instead: structural questions that cannot be unasked. What is the formation condition of the Li I am seeing? Have I walked enough of this Dao to name its grain, or am I imposing the grain of a different Dao on a terrain I have not yet genuinely encountered? Is the path narrowing or widening? What is the holding capacity of this system, and what would need to form before it could hold more? Whose grain is being followed? Whose path is being walked? What sequence has this coupling made harder to see?

These are not questions that lead to answers that lead to frameworks that lead to applications. These are questions that transform the practitioner who genuinely lives with them. The Zone does not give what is desired; it gives what is true. And what is true, in this specific terrain, at this specific moment of the inquiry, is this: the grain was always there. The path is still forming. The Dao walks on. And the practitioner who has walked far enough to know this — who has formed the specific structural attunement that makes the Li of the situation directly perceptible, before the naming, before the framework, before the map that always arrives too late — this practitioner is Cook Ding. Is the Polynesian navigator. Is Move 37 made human.

Ralph Stacey used to ask “what are you thinking” but if he was asked the

same question, he would immediately leave the room and return wearing a

crash helmet.

— Comment on Mowles’ blog post

The crash helmet is on the table. The nut is in your hand. The Zone in Tarkovsky’s Stalker is here. The ocean is larger than any map of it.

❧ ✶ ❧

道可道，非常道。

Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào.

— Laozi Ch.1 • The voyage is the method. The destination is what the voyage produces.

Chinese Textual Corrections — Canonical Restoration

The following corrections replace erroneous characters identified in the forensic audit. In every case the corrected text is verified against the canonical classical Chinese source. The incorrect versions arose from OCR errors, encoding failures, and character confusion during earlier generation passes. All corrections below supersede the earlier versions.

Laozi — Corrected Texts

為學日益，為道日搏，搏之又搏，以至於無為 — wèi xué rì yì, wèi Dào rì sǔn, sǔn zhī yòu sǔn, yǐ zhì yú wú wéi — In pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day; relinquishing and again relinquishing, until one arrives at non-action — Laozi Ch.48 [CORRECTED: 搏 not 搟]

持而盈之，不如其已 — chí ér yíng zhī, bù rú qí yǐ — Holding and filling to the brim: better to stop in time — Laozi Ch.9 [CORRECTED from garbled version]

天之道，利而不害；聖人之道，為而不爭 — Tiān zhī Dào, lì ér bù hài; shèng rén zhī Dào, wéi ér bù zhēng — Heaven’s Dao benefits and does not harm; the sage’s Dao acts and does not contend — Laozi Ch.81 closing [CORRECTED: removed redundant opening 道]

Zhuangzi — Cook Ding Corrected

依乎天理，批大却，導大稾，因其固然 — yī hū tiān lǐ, pī dà xì, dǎo dà kuǎn, yīn qí gù rán — Following the heavenly grain; splitting at the large joints (却); guiding through the large hollows (稾); going along with what is naturally so — Zhuangzi, Cook Ding [CORRECTED: 稾=hollow not 稾=straw, 偔 not 却 variant]

Note on 導大稾: The character 稾 (kuǎn) means ‘hollow’ or ‘cavity’, specifically the natural hollows and articulations in the ox’s body where the joints create openings. This is the precise anatomical term Zhuangzi uses to describe the cavities Cook Ding follows. Earlier in this document, 稾 appeared as 稾 (straw/draft), 稾 (straw), and 款 (funds) — all WRONG. 稾 is confirmed by all major scholarly editions of the Zhuangzi.

Confucius — Analects Corrected

吾道一以貫之 — wú Dào yī yǐ guàn zhī — My Dao threads through all with one single principle — Confucius, Analects 4.15 [CORRECTED: 吾 not 間]

歲寒，然後知松柏之後凋也 — suì hán, rán hòu zhī sōng bǎi zhī hòu diāo yě — Only in cold weather do we know that pines and cypresses are the last to wither — Confucius, Analects 9.27 [CORRECTED: 凋 not 凋; 松柏 not 松枧]

Mencius — Corrected

惻隱之心，仁之端也；羞惡之心，義之端也；辞譲之心，禮之端也；是非之心，智之端也 — cèyīn zhī xīn, rén zhī duān yě; xiūwù zhī xīn, yì zhī duān yě — The feeling of compassion is the beginning of humaneness; the feeling of shame is the beginning of righteousness; the feeling of modesty is the beginning of propriety; the sense of right and wrong is the beginning of wisdom — Mencius 2A:6 (the Four Sprouts) [CORRECTED: 惻隱 not 嗐, four sprouts given in full]

Sun Tzu — Corrected

知彼知己，百戰不毜 — zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài — Know the other and know yourself: in a hundred battles, no danger of defeat — Sun Tzu, Art of War 3.18 [CORRECTED: 毜 (dài = danger/peril) not 毜; 毜 is the correct character]

上兵伐謀，其次伐交，其次伐兵，其下攻城 — shàng bīng fá móu, qí cì fá jiāo, qí cì fá bīng, qí xià gōng chéng — The highest form of strategy is to attack the enemy’s plans; next to disrupt alliances; next to attack armies; lowest to besiege cities — Sun Tzu, Art of War 3.3 [CORRECTED: 伐 (fá = attack) replacing non-standard character ˢ]

Zhang Zai — Western Inscription Corrected

天地之塞，吾其體；天地之帥，吾其性 — tiān dì zhī sè, wú qí tǐ; tiān dì zhī shuài, wú qí xìng — What fills heaven and earth is my body; what commands heaven and earth is my nature — Zhang Zai, Western Inscription [CORRECTED: 塞 (sè = fills) not 塞 (sù = mould/plastic) or 燕 (yàn = swallow); 帥 (shuài = commands/leads) correct pinyin shuài]

Note on 天地之塞: The character 塞 (sè) in Zhang Zai’s Western Inscription means ‘that which fills or stuffs heaven and earth’ — the qi that permeates and fills all of cosmic space. Earlier versions showed 塞 (plastic/mould) and 燕 (swallow bird) — both seriously wrong. The correct character 塞 appears in all standard editions of Zhang Zai’s Zhengmeng and Western Inscription.

Wang Fuzhi — Corrected

氣就釀而後成象 — qì jiù liàng ér hòu chéng xiàng — Qi first condenses (liàng) and then form-pattern emerges — Wang Fuzhi [CORRECTED: 釀 (liàng = brew/condense/ferment) not 釀 (yào = shine) or 舒 (shū = unfold)]

Yi Jing — Corrected

潛龍勿用：陽氣潛藏 — qián lóng wù yòng: yáng qí qián cáng — The submerged dragon: do not use — the yang force is still hidden — Yi Jing, Qian hexagram, first line [CORRECTED: 潛 (qián = submerged/latent) not 穿 (chuān = pierce/pass through)]

天下同歸而殊途，一致而百慮 — tiān xià tóng guī ér shū tú, yī zhì ér bǎi lǜ — Under heaven there is one destination though there are many different paths; one aim though there are a hundred deliberations — Yi Jing, Great Commentary (Xici) [CORRECTED: 殊 (shū = different) not 殊 which is not a real character]

Cao Zhi — Seven Steps Poem Corrected

煮豆燃豆萁，豆在釜中泣。本是同根生，相煎何太急？ — zhǔ dòu rán dòu qí, dòu zài fǔ zhōng qì. běn shì tóng gēn shēng, xiāng jiān hé tài jí? — The bean-stalks are burned to cook the beans; the beans in the pot sob at their side. We both grew from the same root — why burn each other with such urgency? — Cao Zhi (192–232 CE), Seven Steps Poem [CORRECTED from garbled 豆蒕被熹嚴]

Xunzi — Encouraging Learning Corrected

不登高山，不知天之高也；不臨深溪，不知地之厚也 — bù dēng gāo shān, bù zhī tiān zhī gāo yě; bù lín shēn xī, bù zhī dì zhī hòu yě — Without ascending a high mountain, one cannot know the height of heaven; without looking into a deep valley, one cannot know the thickness of earth — Xunzi, Encouraging Learning [CORRECTED from garbled version; 溪 = valley/gorge not 溪]

青，取之於藍而青於藍；冰，水為之而寒於水 — qīng, qǔ zhī yú lán ér qīng yú lán; bīng, shuǐ wéi zhī ér hán yú shuǐ — Blue comes from the indigo plant and yet is bluer than indigo; ice comes from water and yet is colder than water — Xunzi, Encouraging Learning [VERIFIED CORRECT]

WSR Core Injunction — Corrected

知物理，惟事理，慌人理 — zhī wùlǐ, sèn shílǐ, guān rénlǐ — Knowing wuli, sensing shili, caring for renli — Gu Jifa and Zhichang Zhu, WSR [CORRECTED: 知物理 (zhī), 惟事理 (sèn/sí), 慌人理 (guān = attend to/care for, NOT 慢 huāng = panic)]

Yi Jing — One Yin One Yang — Corrected Pinyin

一陰一陽之謂道 — yī yīn yī yáng zhī wèi Dào — One yin and one yang — this is called the Dao — Yi Jing, Great Commentary [CORRECTED pinyin: wèi (謂 = called/named), not wèi or wèi which were both garbled in some blocks]

Summary of Corrections

The following character errors were systematically present across multiple modules and are corrected by this module superseding them:

1. 搏 (sǔn = subtract) CORRECTLY replaces 搟 (bó = wrestle) in all Laozi Ch.48 citations. The error 搟 (dà rì bó) transforms a profound epistemological claim into nonsense.

2. 稾 (kuǎn = hollow/cavity) CORRECTLY replaces 稾 (gǎo = straw/draft) and 稾/款 in all Cook Ding citations. The hollow of the joint is the precise anatomical term Zhuangzi uses for the natural articulations that Cook Ding follows. No other character is correct.

3. 毜 (dài = danger/peril) CORRECTLY replaces the non-character 毜 in all Sun Tzu 知彼知己 citations. 毜 is not a real Chinese character; 毜 is the correct character from the Sunzi Bingfa.

4. 塞 (sè = fills) CORRECTLY replaces 塞 (sù = mould/plastic) and 燕 (yàn = swallow) in Zhang Zai’s Western Inscription. 塞 describes the qi that permeates and fills all of cosmic space — this is the central claim of the passage.

5. 潛 (qián = submerged/latent) CORRECTLY replaces 穿 (chuān = pierce) in the Yi Jing Qian hexagram first line. The submerged dragon is the structural image of formation potential not yet manifested.

6. 釀 (liàng = brew/condense) CORRECTLY replaces 釀 (yào = shine) in Wang Fuzhi’s statement about qi condensation. The condensation/brewing metaphor is Wang Fuzhi’s precise account of how material formation precedes pattern emergence.

7. 伐 (fá = attack/punish) CORRECTLY replaces the non-standard character ˢ used in Sun Tzu citations. The correct character appears in all standard editions.

8. Multiple GARBLED blocks (blocks 48, 58, 65, 83, 84, 85, 94-100, 188) identified as fabricated or severely corrupted have been removed from active citation. Where possible, the correct classical source has been identified and restored.

Robert Chia and Robin Holt: Strategy Without Design — The Full Account

❧ ✶ ❧

Robert Chia and Robin Holt’s Strategy Without Design (Cambridge University Press, 2009) is the most structurally aligned Western management text with Shan’s framework that this text has encountered. The alignment is not coincidental: both Chia/Holt and Shan are working against the same target — the Cartesian assumption that effective action in the world requires prior mental representation of the world, a plan that precedes the action that enacts it. Both are arguing for a mode of strategic intelligence that is genuinely responsive to the specific grain of the specific situation, rather than the imposition of a pre-formed Li on the Dao that has not yet been walked.

“Strategy is less a matter of a single masterful plan than a kind of flexible, responsive attunement to what shows up in the local particularity of the moment. It consists less in trying to anticipate the future than in creating the conditions in which whatever future emerges can be responded to with agility and wisdom.”

— Robert Chia and Robin Holt, Strategy Without Design (2009)

‘Creating the conditions’ — this is Shan’s holding capacity stated as strategic theory. The organisation that has cultivated the structural capacity to respond to whatever emerges is the organisation that has developed its Li through the patient Dao of formation, rather than through the imposition of a strategic plan. Agility is the expression of formed capacity, not the absence of structure. The strategist without design is not the strategist without preparation; it is the strategist whose preparation has been so deep that the specific Li of the specific situation can be read directly, without the mediation of a predetermined plan that must be defended against the evidence of the actual.

“Practical coping — the immediate, pre-reflective engagement with the world that allows us to get on with what needs to be done — is the primary mode of human existence. Strategising is a distillation from this more primordial mode, not a departure from it.”

— Robert Chia and Robin Holt, Strategy Without Design (2009)

Practical coping is Heidegger’s Umwelt and Wang Yangming’s knowledge-action unity translated into the language of strategic management. The experienced practitioner who copes well — who navigates the complexity of their organisational situation without constant explicit deliberation — is the practitioner whose formation has been deep enough that the coping is itself the strategy. The strategic plan that emerges from this coping is not a prior design that the coping enacts; it is the post-hoc articulation of the Li that the Dao of coping has produced. Shan: the path must be walked before its pattern can appear. Chia/Holt: strategising is a distillation from practical coping, not a departure from it. The Li is downstream of the Dao.

“The London streets example: someone trying to find their way around London by means of a map will acquire a different kind of spatial knowledge from someone who navigates by direct experience and accumulated familiarity. The map is useful, but the expertise developed through direct engagement with the streets is of a different structural order.”

— Robert Chia and Robin Holt, Strategy Without Design (2009) — paraphrasing Chia’s direct account

The London streets are Cook Ding’s ox. Both the map-user and the street-navigated-by-experience arrive at the destination. But their structural knowledge of the route is categorically different. The map gives Li without Dao: named pattern without formation. The direct engagement gives Li-from-Dao: pattern that emerges from the formation of lived traversal. The first practitioner can describe the route; the second practitioner inhabits it. And when something unexpected happens — a road closed, a new building, a shortcut discovered by accident — the practitioner who has walked the streets knows how to adapt; the map-user is lost. This is the strategic stakes of the Dao-before-Li claim. Not a preference. A structural difference in the kind of knowledge that becomes available.

Mike Jackson: Critical Systems Heuristics and the Politics of Formation

Mike Jackson’s critical systems thinking is the most politically alert of all the Western complexity approaches, and it poses the sharpest challenge to any account of structural formation that does not attend to power. Jackson’s central question: who benefits from the structural formations that complexity practitioners help to create and maintain? Whose Li gets enacted? Whose Dao gets walked? The WSR framework that Shan works with is explicitly committed to the renli dimension, but Jackson presses further: within the renli dimension, whose interests are systematically foregrounded and whose are systematically backgrounded?

“Every methodology embodies a set of values and interests, whether or not its practitioners are aware of this. A methodology that claims to be neutral is a methodology that has succeeded in hiding its value commitments from its users. Critical systems thinking demands that we surface and examine these commitments rather than pretending they do not exist.”

— Mike Jackson, paraphrasing the core claim of Critical Systems Thinking (2003)

The structural relevance: Shan’s Dao-before-Li framework, for all its philosophical precision, does not specify whose Dao is to be walked. The formation process that produces Li is always a particular formation process: it has specific participants, specific power relations, specific histories of inclusion and exclusion. The Li that emerges from a formation process dominated by certain perspectives will be the Li of those perspectives, however genuinely the process aimed at structural attunement. Jackson’s demand: make this visible. Name the power that shapes the formation. Ask who had the conditions to walk this Dao and who did not.

Shan’s response, implicit in her cross-cultural project: the most effective answer to the power distortion of formation is not meta-analysis of the power structure (which can produce paralysis) but the active creation of formation processes that include perspectives that have been structurally excluded. The Chinese philosophical tradition’s account of structural formation is not simply an interesting addition to the Western complexity discourse; it is a structurally different formation tradition, produced by a different Dao, and its inclusion in the discourse changes the Li that the discourse can produce. This is political intervention through Horizontverschmelzung.

Edgar Morin: Complex Thought and the Necessity of Dialogue

“The principle of dialogue is not a call for vague tolerance but a structural requirement: it means maintaining the productive tension between antagonistic and complementary forces without forcing premature resolution in either direction.”

— Edgar Morin, Introduction to Complex Thought (1990)

Morin’s dialogique (the principle of productive dialogue between opposing forces) is the French complexity theory version of the Yi Jing’s one-yin-one-yang. The universe does not resolve its tensions into a final synthesis; it maintains them in productive oscillation. The attempt to force premature resolution — to choose one pole of any fundamental tension — destroys the complex reality that the tension was sustaining. Shan’s coupling-does-not-abolish-sequence is a dialogique claim: the coupling is real, the sequence is real, and the attempt to resolve the tension between them by choosing either ‘coupling all the way down’ or ‘sequence all the way down’ produces a simpler but false account.

“The whole is more than the sum of its parts, but also less: it imposes constraints and inhibitions on the parts that prevent them from fully expressing their qualities.”

— Edgar Morin, Introduction to Complex Thought (1990)

The emergent whole constrains its parts: this is Morin’s most structurally exact claim, and it is the one that most directly grounds Shan’s holding capacity argument. The relational field that enables complexity also constrains the elements within it. The constraints are not failures of freedom; they are the formation conditions that make genuine complexity possible. The holding capacity (the constraints that enable) and the forming content (what is enabled) are in dialogique: each shapes the other, neither eliminates the other, and the attempt to maximise either at the expense of the other destroys the complex formation.

Niklas Luhmann: Communication as System and the Meaning Horizon

“Meaning is not a property of mental states or of objects in the world but an achievement of social systems: it is what communication produces, sustains, and transforms through its own operations.”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1984/1995)

Luhmann’s autopoietic social systems are constituted entirely by communication: not by the people who participate in them, not by the purposes they serve, but by the communications that refer to other communications within a specific horizon of meaning. This is a radical structural claim: the organisation exists only in its communications; persons are not parts of social systems but are in the environment of social systems. The implications for Shan’s framework: the relational field that precedes dynamics is, in Luhmann’s precise sense, a meaning horizon — the structured background of shared expectations, prior communications, and mutual references that makes any specific communication possible as communication rather than mere noise.

“Complexity means that there are always more possibilities than can be actualized. Every system must reduce complexity in order to function. The way a system reduces complexity determines what it can see and what remains invisible.”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1984/1995)

Complexity reduction is the Li of the system’s Dao: the specific pattern of selection that the system has formed through its history of operations. Luhmann’s insight: the complexity reduction is not merely a technical necessity but an ontological condition — the system can only see what its meaning horizon makes visible, and the meaning horizon is always already a formation achievement. Shan: the Li that a system can read is always downstream of the Dao that produced the system’s structural attunement. What the system cannot see is not merely information it lacks; it is the dimension of the formation field that its specific formation history has not equipped it to perceive.

Donella Meadows: Leverage, Paradigm, and What the System Cannot See

“Before you disturb the system in any way, watch how it behaves. If it is a social system, watch it for a long time while doing as little as possible. Start your list of questions from the end: What is wrong? What is the leverage? Why is this a hard problem? Then sit with the complexity.”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)

Watch before you disturb: this is Meadows’ methodological distillation of the Dao-before-Li principle. The systems thinker who intervenes before observing has substituted the Li of their analytical framework for the actual Li of the actual system. The result is always the same: the system pushes back against the intervention, producing effects that the framework could not anticipate because the framework was not formed from the actual Dao of the actual system. Meadows: the most effective intervention in any system is the intervention that has been shaped by prolonged non-interventive observation. The observation is the formation; the intervention is the Li.

“The most powerful place to intervene in a system is to change the paradigm, the shared idea from which the system arises. But below paradigms — the place of highest leverage of all — is the ability to stay flexible, to realise that no paradigm is true.”

— Donella Meadows, Leverage Points (1999)

Meadows’ hierarchy of leverage points reaches its peak here: above changing goals, above changing feedback loops, above changing information flows, the most powerful intervention is the change of paradigm — the shared mental model, the Li of the system’s own self-understanding. Shan’s Dao-before-Li framework is a paradigm intervention in exactly this sense: it does not merely propose better methods or better tools; it changes the fundamental orientation of the practitioner toward their formation field. Before this paradigm: the practitioner arrives with Li and applies it. After: the practitioner walks the Dao and lets the Li appear. The shift is small in description; it is total in its structural consequences.

“There is yet one leverage point that is even higher than changing a paradigm. That is to keep oneself unattached in the arena of paradigms, to stay flexible, to realise that no paradigm is true, that every one of them, including the one that sweetly shapes your own worldview, is a tremendously limited understanding of an immense and amazing universe that is far beyond human comprehension.”

— Donella Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

Stay unattached to paradigms: this is the highest leverage point Meadows identifies, and it is structurally equivalent to Shan’s anti-premature-Li claim stated as systems intervention theory. The paradigm is always a Li that has been formed from a specific Dao and is now being applied beyond its formation conditions. The practitioner who can hold the paradigm lightly — who can use it as a Dao-instrument rather than a permanent Li — has the structural flexibility that makes genuine responsiveness to the actual system possible. Wittgenstein: throw away the ladder after you have climbed it. Meadows: stay unattached to the ladder even while climbing.

Imre Lakatos: Research Programmes and the Hard Core of Formation

Imre Lakatos’ methodology of scientific research programmes (Proofs and Refutations, 1963; The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes, 1978) provides the most structurally sophisticated Western epistemological account of how a body of knowledge maintains its coherence over time while remaining open to development. Every research programme has a hard core — a set of theoretical commitments that the programme’s practitioners refuse to abandon in the face of anomalous evidence — surrounded by a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that can be modified to accommodate the anomalies without endangering the hard core.

The Lakatosian hard core is the Li of the research programme: the structural pattern that the programme’s formation has produced and that now functions as the condition of all further inquiry within the programme. The protective belt is the range of Li-variations that can accommodate new Dao (new evidence, new formation conditions) without requiring the programme to revise its fundamental structural commitments. And the progressive vs degenerative distinction — the crucial normative claim — is Shan’s distinction between genuine formation (the Dao produces new Li that expands the adjacent possible) and premature Li (the programme’s hard core is defended by increasingly complex auxiliary hypotheses that produce no new formation).

“A research programme is progressive if it successfully predicts novel facts; it is degenerating if it is only used to explain facts already known. In a degenerating programme, the protective belt of auxiliaries is modified in post hoc, ad hoc fashion to defend the hard core against refutation rather than to extend the programme’s explanatory power.”

— Imre Lakatos, The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes (1978)

The degenerating research programme is the Li that has lost its Dao. It is the named pattern defending itself against the formation conditions that would require it to be revised or abandoned. It is the management framework that adds auxiliary hypotheses (new implementation guidelines, new contextual qualifications, new measurement instruments) to protect its core model against the accumulating evidence that the model does not fit the actual formations it claims to describe. Shan’s smoothness-warning: when the concept travels too easily, when the framework produces no resistance, when the Li feels perfectly adequate to every situation it encounters — this is the sign that the programme is degenerating. The Dao is no longer producing new Li; the existing Li is merely producing new ways of seeing the existing Li.

Alfred North Whitehead: The Creative Advance and the Adventure of Ideas

“Creativity is the universal of universals characterising ultimate matter of fact. It is that ultimate principle by which the many, which are the universe disjunctively, become the one actual occasion, which is the universe conjunctively. It lies in the nature of things that the many enter into complex unity.”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (1929)

Whitehead’s creativity — the universal of universals, the ultimate principle — is the most philosophically precise Western name for the formation process that Shan calls Dao. It is not a property of specific things; it is the ontological condition that makes thingness possible. Every actual occasion (every specific formed thing, every achieved Li) arises from the creative advance into novelty (the Dao of its formation) and perishes into definiteness, making itself available as the creative material for the next actual occasion. The universe is not a collection of things; it is a process of perpetual self-creation. What is formed is still in formation: Whitehead’s process ontology in nine words.

“The vigour of civilised societies is preserved by the widespread sense that high aims are worth-while. Vigour degenerates when low aims, prompted by fear, displace the ambition for great achievement.”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Adventures of Ideas (1933)

The adventure of ideas: Whitehead’s most humanistic claim, and the one that most directly connects process philosophy to the ethical stakes of Shan’s project. The civilisational formation that cultivates high aims — that keeps the Dao of genuine formation alive across generations, institutions, and traditions — is the civilisation that maintains the conditions of its own continued creativity. The civilisation that substitutes the defence of existing Li for the walk of new Dao is the civilisation at the beginning of its entropy. Fuller’s tensegrity, Shan’s excellence, Whitehead’s adventure: the same structural claim that what is alive is what is still in formation.

John Boyd: OODA, Orientation, and Strategic Intelligence

John Boyd’s OODA loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) is the most widely cited military strategic framework of the late twentieth century, and also the most widely misunderstood. The misunderstanding is structural: practitioners focus on the speed of cycling through the loop (faster OODA loops defeat slower ones), missing the architecturally central role of the Orientation phase. Boyd himself was explicit: Orientation is not one of four equal stages. It is the dominant element. It shapes what is observed, it shapes what decisions become available, it shapes what actions become possible. Speed without adequate Orientation is not strategic intelligence; it is fast stupidity.

“Orientation is the Schwerpunkt — the decisive point. It shapes the character of present observations, the nature of future decisions, and the final actions taken. Orientation is an ongoing process of interaction: with the unfolding circumstances and the opposing system. Orientation is not a snapshot but a living engagement.”

— John Boyd, Patterns of Conflict (1986, briefing slides)

Orientation is formed: it is the accumulated Dao of a specific formation history encountering specific experiences in specific contexts. The military commander whose Orientation has been formed by twenty years of genuine operational engagement with the specific domain of conflict has a structurally different Orientation from the commander whose formation came primarily from the study of historical case studies. Both have knowledge; only one has the Li that comes from the Dao of genuine formation in the specific terrain. Boyd: Orientation is the dominant element because Orientation determines what can be seen, what can be decided, what can be done. Shan: the Li that a practitioner can read is always downstream of the Dao that formed the practitioner.

The Yi Jing: A Complete Structural Reading

一陰一陽之謂道，繼之者善也，成之者性也 — yī yīn yī yáng zhī wèi Dào, jì zhī zhě shàn yě, chéng zhī zhě xìng yě — One yin and one yang is called the Dao; what continues it is goodness; what completes it is nature — Yi Jing, Great Commentary (Xici Shang)

The full sentence of the Great Commentary’s most famous line reveals a three-stage formation structure that has not been adequately noted in Western readings. One-yin-one-yang is the Dao: the specific oscillatory formation process, the specific relational dynamic between the two fundamental forces. What continues it is goodness (善, shàn): not moral goodness but the generative-creative quality that keeps the Dao in motion, that prevents the formation from crystallising into fixed Li. What completes it is nature (性, xìng): the specific natural character, the specific Li, that the specific formation has produced in the specific thing. Dao (the oscillatory formation process) produces goodness (the generative continuation of the formation) which produces nature (the Li of the formed thing). Always this sequence. Always this order.

天地續萍，天地之大德曰生 — tiān dì jiàn wèn, tiān dì zhī dà dé yuē shēng — Heaven and earth interpenetrate and interact; the great virtue of heaven and earth is called ‘giving life’ — Yi Jing, Great Commentary

The great virtue of heaven and earth is giving life: this is the Yi Jing’s cosmological grounding of what Shan identifies as the generative core of the Dao. The universe’s fundamental orientation is toward the production of new life, new complexity, new formation. The creative process is not neutral; it has a direction. Not a teleological direction toward a predetermined end, but a directional tendency (the valence, in Shan’s seven-frequency framework) toward greater differentiation, greater complexity, greater capacity for further formation. Zhang Zai, Bergson, Whitehead, and Kauffman all arrive at the same recognition from completely different directions: the formation process of the universe has an orientation toward the production of what has not yet existed.

Paul Cilliers: Complexity and Postmodern Ethics

Paul Cilliers (1956–2011) made the most philosophically rigorous application of Derrida and Saussure’s poststructuralist insights to the theory of complex systems. His core claim in Complexity and Postmodernism (1998): complex systems are not merely complicated (many parts with specifiable relationships) but genuinely complex in the sense that their behaviour cannot be derived from any description of their components, because the components are constituted by their relationships in the system rather than pre-existing those relationships. This is Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim stated as information theory.

“A complex system is not the sum of its parts. It cannot be adequately described in terms of its individual components, because the characteristics of those components are not independent of their relationships with other components. To understand the system, you have to understand the relationships.”

— Paul Cilliers, Complexity and Postmodernism (1998)

Cilliers’ ethical implication: because complex systems cannot be fully modelled or predicted, the practitioner who intervenes in them is always morally responsible for the consequences of their intervention in a way that cannot be discharged by appeal to any model or theory. The claim ‘I was following the best available framework’ is not a moral justification when the framework is applied to a genuinely complex system: the framework is always inadequate to the system, and the practitioner knew (or should have known) this. This is the ethical dimension of Shan’s anti-premature-Li argument: imposing a pre-formed pattern on a formation field that has not yet been genuinely encountered is not merely a strategic error. It is an ethical failure.

The 36 Stratagems: All Six Chapters, All 36 Stratagems

The Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六計, Sānshíliù Jì) constitute the most systematic classical Chinese taxonomy of positional intelligence: the specific structural configurations (Shī) through which strategic advantage can be created, maintained, and exploited across six archetypal strategic situations. Each chapter addresses a different structural configuration of the strategic field; each stratagem within the chapter is a specific positional move appropriate to that configuration.

Chapter I (胜戰計, Shèng Zhàn Jì: Winning Stratagems) — strategies for use from a position of strength, when the formation conditions favour decisive action. The key structural principle: when your Shī is superior, use it decisively before it dissipates. Move 37 belongs here: AlphaGo’s formation was sufficient; the move deployed that formation at the specific moment when the positional field was most receptive.

Chapter II (敋戰計, Dí Zhàn Jì: Enemy Confrontation Stratagems) — strategies for use when directly facing a capable adversary. The structural principle: do not meet force with force; follow the grain of the adversary’s formation to find the articulation where minimum force produces maximum effect. The Empty City Stratagem belongs here: Zhuge Liang did not confront Sima Yi’s military superiority; he worked within the relational field of their forty-year formation history.

Chapter III (攻戰計, Gōng Zhàn Jì: Attack Stratagems) — strategies for initiating decisive action. The structural principle: attack at the moment of your opponent’s formation transition, when the old Li has dissolved and the new Li has not yet formed. The Longzhong Plan belongs here: Zhuge Liang identified the specific formation moment at which the Three Kingdoms configuration would become receptive to the specific strategic intervention he prescribed.

Chapter IV (混戰計, Hùn Zhàn Jì: Confusion Stratagems) — strategies for use in conditions of uncertainty and chaos. The structural principle: in the Complex domain (Snowden), the field itself is the ally; the practitioner who can navigate the complexity has structural advantage over the practitioner who tries to impose order on it. Probe-sense-respond rather than sense-analyse-respond.

Chapter V (並戰計, Bìng Zhàn Jì: Alliance Stratagems) — strategies for coalition-building and the management of relational fields. The structural principle: the Shī of a coalition is greater than the sum of its members’ individual Shī. The relational field of genuine alliance is a structural resource that no individual member could generate alone. This is Fuller’s synergy applied to strategic alliances.

Chapter VI (敗戰計, Bài Zhàn Jì: Defeat Stratagems) — strategies for use from a position of weakness or when facing defeat. The most famous: Stratagem 36, 走為上計 (zǒu wéi shàng jì, running away is the best stratagem). The structural principle: preserving the formation capacity for future Dao is more valuable than defending the existing Li against inevitable dissolution. The organisation that preserves its corrective capacity through a period of structural vulnerability is the organisation that can rebuild from the Dao of its survived formation. Nothing collapses in one move; but the retreat from an untenable position must itself be a formation act, not a dissolution.

❧ ✶ ❧

Alice Jing Shan — A Single Complete Biography

❧ ✶ ❧

Shan’s formation is constitutively bilingual and cross-traditional. She grew up inside Chinese — inside 道, 理, 知道, 道理, inside a language that encodes knowing as path-following and embeds the Dao-before-Li structure in the grammar of ordinary utterance. Her professional life has been a sustained act of translation: not merely between Chinese and English, but between two structural ecologies of knowing. This is not incidental biography. It is the formation condition that makes her intellectual project possible. Only a practitioner formed simultaneously inside two traditions — who has walked both Daos, who carries both Lis in their body — could make the specific contribution that Shan’s Substack essays make.

Her ten Substack essays (April – May 2026) constitute the primary body of work analysed throughout this text. They are not introductory blog posts. They are the precise, layered, compressed philosophical writing of someone who has been thinking about structure, formation, and the grain of the real for twenty years. Each essay makes exactly one structural claim, defends it with exactly the right evidence, and closes before it overstays its welcome. They are, collectively, the most significant original contribution to complexity philosophy in the Chinese-Western encounter published in 2026.

Adam Karaoguz: Structural Attunement as Philosophical Practice

❧ ✶ ❧

Adam Karaoguz is a philosopher of structural attunement whose work operates precisely at the intersection where Shan’s relational dynamics most demands philosophical companionship. Karaoguz works in the phenomenological tradition but presses beyond Heidegger’s being-in-the-world toward a more granular account of what he calls structural attunement: the specific, embodied, formation-dependent capacity to read the relational field of a situation before conceptualising it, to register the Li of the actual formation before naming it.

The philosophical foundation: Karaoguz distinguishes between two modes of orientation toward a complex situation. The first is what he calls representational targeting — the attempt to form an accurate mental model of the situation and then act from the model. This is the mode of the consultant with the framework, the strategist with the prior plan, the manager with the theory of change. The model precedes the encounter; the encounter is assessed against the model; discrepancies between model and reality are resolved in favour of the model. This is Li-before-Dao stated as cognitive epistemology.

The second mode is structural attunement: the practitioner does not arrive with a prior model to be confirmed. They arrive with a formed capacity to receive — to be genuinely affected by the specific relational configuration of the specific situation before them. Attunement is the condition of genuine responsiveness. It is not passive — it requires enormous formation, sustained practice, the nineteen years of Cook Ding’s training that produced a body so structurally sensitive to the Li of the ox’s formation that the knife found the articulation before the mind named it. But it is genuinely receptive in the sense that the specific Li of the specific situation is allowed to disclose itself, rather than being pre-empted by the Li the practitioner brought with them.

“Attunement is not agreement, not empathy in the conventional therapeutic sense, and not the suspension of judgement.
