It is the structural condition in which the situation’s own formation can be heard before the practitioner’s prior formation drowns it out. It is the silence before the response. It is the space in which the Li of the actual discloses itself to the practitioner who has been formed to receive it.”

— Adam Karaoguz, Structural Attunement and the Ethics of Complexity (ms)

The Shan connection is structural and immediate. Shan’s framework requires attunement at every level. The practitioner who approaches a complex organisation with the prior conviction that its formation fits pattern X — who arrives with the Li already formed, seeking only confirmation — cannot find Move 37. Move 37 is available only to the practitioner whose attunement to the actual board is sufficient to register a formation that no prior Li would have named. Attunement is the cognitive-somatic condition of Dao-before-Li. It is what the Dao-walk produces in the practitioner: not a better theory but a finer sensitivity to the grain of the actual.

Karaoguz also develops the concept of attunement failure — the specific pathology of practitioners whose formation has been so thorough in a particular Li that they have lost the capacity to be surprised by the actual. The expert who can only see what their expertise has prepared them to see. The manager whose formation in the dominant framework has become so complete that they are structurally incapable of registering the evidence that the framework does not fit. This is not ignorance — it is the specific failure mode of high formation in the wrong Li. Cook Ding’s first three years, before the dissolution of the whole ox, before the emergence of the actual grain: the practitioner who stays in those first three years, who defends the whole-ox perception against the evidence of the actual articulations, is the practitioner of attunement failure.

“The most dangerous practitioner is not the one who knows nothing. It is the one who knows too much of the wrong thing — whose formation has been so deep in a Li that has stopped fitting the actual that they cannot register the misfit. They are confident, fluent, structurally coherent — and systematically wrong about the terrain they are navigating.”

— Adam Karaoguz, The Failure Modes of Expertise (ms)

The ethical dimension of Karaoguz’s attunement account is as important as the epistemological. Attunement failure is not merely a strategic error; it is an ethical failure of the first order. The consultant who arrives at an organisation with a pre-formed Li, applies it to a formation that does not fit, and collects their fee — this practitioner has done violence to the actual. They have imposed their grain on a formation that had its own grain, and the imposed grain has caused damage that will persist long after the consultant’s departure. The ethical demand of Shan’s framework is the same as Karaoguz’s: walk the Dao before naming the Li. Be genuinely affected before you respond. Achieve attunement before you intervene.

Karaoguz and Wittgenstein: The Grammar of Attunement

Karaoguz reads Wittgenstein’s On Certainty as the epistemological ground of structural attunement. Wittgenstein’s river-bed claim — that our knowledge sits in a formed river-bed of unquestioned certainties which are not fixed in place permanently but which do not move while the river flows — is the phenomenological substrate of attunement. The practitioner’s formation is their river-bed: the accumulated, largely pre-reflective structure of what they are sensitive to, what registers as significant, what can even be perceived as a possible formation. Attunement is the quality of that river-bed in relation to the specific terrain being navigated.

“Some propositions are exempt from doubt not because they are certainly true but because doubting them would dissolve the practice within which doubting is possible. They form the river-bed in which the river of inquiry flows.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, On Certainty §s 97–99 (1951)

The river-bed shifts. It is not eternal. The nineteen years of Cook Ding’s practice did not merely add knowledge to a fixed foundation; they progressively transformed the foundation. What Cook Ding could see after nineteen years — the articulations, the hollows, the natural formation of the actual ox before him — was structurally unavailable to Cook Ding at the beginning. The river-bed of his perceptual formation had shifted. This is what Karaoguz means by deep attunement: not a technique applied to a stable cognitive base, but the transformation of the cognitive base itself through sustained, formation-sufficient engagement with the actual.

Karaoguz and the Seven Frequencies: Attunement as Ontological Condition

Karaoguz’s most significant contribution to the Shan framework is his account of attunement not as a psychological state but as an ontological relational dynamic. Attunement is not something the practitioner has; it is something the practitioner achieves with the situation. It is a relational condition between the formed practitioner and the actual formation field — a specific quality of the meeting between the practitioner’s Li and the situation’s Li.

This relational account maps directly onto Shan’s seven structural frequencies. Cadence is the temporal dimension of attunement: the practitioner who is attuned to the cadence of a formation can feel its rhythm, can sense when the pace is right and when it is being forced. Resonance is the structural dimension: the attuned practitioner resonates with the formation’s Li in a way that is physically real — the strings tuned to the same fundamental frequency vibrating together without contact. Salience is the perceptual dimension of attunement: what the attuned practitioner notices is not random — it is precisely what the formation’s actual Li makes most structurally significant. Valence is the directional dimension: the attuned practitioner can feel the direction in which the formation is tending, the vector of the Dao, before any explicit analysis has been conducted. Vibration is the energetic substrate: attunement is itself a vibrational phenomenon, a matching of energetic frequencies between practitioner and formation field. Dynamic Maximum Tension is the structural ceiling: the attuned practitioner knows when the formation is approaching its holding capacity, when the tension is approaching the point at which it will either produce new Li or dissolve into entropy. And Gain is the amplificatory consequence: the attuned practitioner who finds the specific structural intervention that the formation field is ready for produces effects far beyond what the intervention’s visible scale would predict.

Together, the seven frequencies constitute what Karaoguz calls the phenomenology of structural attunement: the complete account of what it is like to navigate a complex formation as a practitioner who has been formed to read it. Not a theory about the formation. An account of the living encounter with it.

Chris Rodgers: The Wiggly World and the Grammar of Conversation

❧ ✶ ❧

Chris Rodgers’ Taking Organizational Complexity Seriously (2013) is the most precisely targeted critique of the rationalist management consensus in the British tradition, and it arrives at conclusions that are structurally aligned with Shan’s framework through a completely different formation history. Where Shan arrives at Dao-before-Li through the Chinese philosophical tradition and complexity science, Rodgers arrives at the primacy of relational formation through the sociology of conversation and the critical tradition of Stacey, Mead, and Elias.

“Life in organizations is unavoidably messier and more uncertain than the formal strategies, structures, systems and processes imply. And yet most discussions of organizational management and leadership practice remain firmly rooted in mainstream presumptions of certainty, predictability and control. Complexity is too often consigned to the “too difficult” box.”

— Chris Rodgers, Taking Organizational Complexity Seriously (2013)

The ‘too difficult’ box: this is where the Li that cannot yet be named gets filed. The management consultant arrives at the wiggly world — Rodgers’ resonant image for the irreducibly messy reality of organisational life — and weaves a net of strategies, structures, systems, and procedures. The net is the Li they brought with them: the prior pattern that promises to catch the wiggle and hold it still. But the real world slips through, as Alan Watts put it. The net catches nothing real because the real is always in formation, always exceeding the Li that was designed to contain it. Rodgers’ wiggly world is Shan’s Dao in organisational register: the irreducible formation process that precedes and exceeds every Li imposed upon it.

“Organization is conversation. That is to say, conversation does not just occur about organizations; conversations constitute organizations. Organization is not independent of conversation.”

— Richard Dunford and Ian Palmer, cited in Rodgers (2013)

Organisation is conversation: this is the most structurally compressed version of Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim in the Western organisational tradition. Not ‘conversations happen in organisations’. Not ‘conversations are important for organisations’. Conversations constitute organisations. The organisation is the pattern of its conversations. The Li of the organisation is the accumulated formation of its conversational history. And the Dao of the organisation — its ongoing relational process, its formation-in-progress — is the living conversational field that the Li was formed from and that continues to form it.

“It’s not what managers settle upon and announce formally that determines what happens. It’s how people make sense of what they see and hear, and how they find themselves acting, as they participate in this ongoing sense-making-cum-action-taking process.”

— Chris Rodgers, Taking Organizational Complexity Seriously (2013)

Sense-making-cum-action-taking: Rodgers’ hyphenated neologism is the most precisely organisational account of what Shan calls the Dao. It is not thinking followed by acting. It is not sensing followed by deciding followed by doing. It is a single, integrated, temporally continuous process in which making sense and taking action are inextricably entangled — in which the action is part of the sensing and the sensing is part of the action. This is Shan’s coupling-does-not-abolish-sequence stated as organisational phenomenology. The sequence (sense then act) is real; the coupling (sensing while acting) is equally real; and the attempt to separate them into a neat design-then-implement sequence produces the fundamental pathology of the dominant management discourse.

Rodgers, Wittgenstein, and Shan: A Three-Way Collision

The most productive dialectical encounter in this section is the three-way collision between Rodgers, Wittgenstein, and Shan. All three are arguing — from completely different formation histories, different institutional contexts, different vocabularies — for the same structural claim: that the formal, explicit, propositional content of what an organisation (or a language, or a formation field) says about itself is always downstream of the informal, implicit, practical formation that actually constitutes it.

“Meaning is socially constructed in the interactions between people. Every conversation is, in effect, a co-creation forum.”

— Chris Rodgers, Taking Organizational Complexity Seriously (2013)

Social construction and Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim in direct conversation. Meaning is not a property of individual minds or individual objects; it is constituted through the interactions between people — in the specific relational field of the specific conversational context. Rodgers’ claim is Shan’s claim stated as organisational theory: the Li of the organisation is produced in the specific interactions of the specific practitioners in the specific formation context. It cannot be specified in advance and then transmitted to practitioners through announcements, vision statements, or training programmes. It can only be cultivated through the cultivation of the interactions that will produce it.

Wittgenstein’s therapeutic instruction placed in the Rodgers context: the management discourse has lifted its key concepts — leadership, culture, strategy, complexity — into metaphysical space where they float free of any specific formation context. The Rodgers programme, like the Wittgensteinian programme, is to bring them back: to show what they actually do in the actual interactions of the actual organisation, to demonstrate that the everyday use of these concepts is where their genuine content lives. Shan’s parallel: ‘Dao’ in management training is metaphysical; ‘Dao’ in the specific formation history of the specific practitioner’s engagement with the specific formation field is everyday. The correction is the same: bring it back.

“The surface was never the whole story. What is held below is not less real because it is held below.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

Three voices, one recognition. Rodgers: meaning is made in the local conversational interaction, not in the formal announcement. Wittgenstein: philosophical confusions arise when we mistake the formal surface of language for the living practice that sustains it; the cure is to bring words back to the everyday usage in which they do real work. Shan: the Li that a formation has developed is always partially submerged, partially implicit, partially carried in the body of practice rather than the head of policy. The iceberg model is not a metaphor for mystery; it is a structural account of how formation works — the part below the surface is not decorative, it is load-bearing.

Rodgers’ shadow-side conversations are Wittgenstein’s unsayable form of life and Shan’s submerged Li simultaneously. The conversations that organise an organisation but never appear in its formal arenas — the corridor negotiations, the coffee-machine debriefs, the unspoken agreements about whose proposals will be supported and whose will be undermined — are the actual formation of the actual organisation. They are not supplementary to the ‘real’ organisation of the formal structure; they ARE the real organisation. The formal structure is their Li: the named pattern that emerged from the conversational Dao and is now feeding back into it.

“The patterning is not stored anywhere or ‘programmed’ in any sense — such as in a disembodied ‘culture’. Rather it reflects a tendency to think and act in particular ways in given circumstances. This tendency is (re)created, reinforced (and potentially shifted) on each occasion, in the moment of people’s interactions.”

— Chris Rodgers, Taking Organizational Complexity Seriously (2013)

This is Wittgenstein’s form of life translated into organisational theory. The pattern is not in the culture document. It is not in the values statement. It is not in the organisational chart. It is (re)created on each occasion, in the moment of interaction, by the practitioners whose formation has given them specific tendencies to see, to respond, to act. This is the Li of the organisation living in the Dao of its ongoing conversational formation. Rodgers: the balance of probability is heavily biased towards continuity rather than change, because the existing Li re-enacts itself in each conversational moment. Shan: what is formed is still in formation — but it is the existing Li that is forming the new formation, which is why genuine pattern-shifting requires something that the existing Li cannot itself supply.

“The real challenge for those in formal leadership positions, and those who advise them, would be seen as one of encouraging, assisting and enabling people to survive and thrive in a world that is — unavoidably — socially complex and uncertain.”

— Chris Rodgers, Taking Organizational Complexity Seriously (2013)

Survive and thrive in a world that is unavoidably complex: this is the ethical horizon of Rodgers’ project, and it is exactly Shan’s. Not the elimination of complexity through better design. Not the management of complexity through more sophisticated tools. The cultivation of the capacity — in persons, in organisations, in formations — to navigate genuine complexity with genuine attunement. Karaoguz’s structural attunement is the individual-practitioner version. Rodgers’ leadership-as-skilled-participation is the organisational version. Shan’s relational dynamics is the theoretical framework that grounds both.

“As Chris Mowles sums up this general position: “… there is nothing more practical for a manager to be doing than to pay close attention to how they are working with others in everyday work situations; to find time to reflect with colleagues on how they are working and thinking; and to have the courage to stay engaged with each other as they negotiate how to go on together.””

— Chris Mowles, cited in Rodgers (2013)

Courage to stay engaged: this is the ethical demand that Rodgers, Mowles, and Shan share. Not the courage to impose. Not the courage to decide. The courage to remain genuinely present to the complexity of the actual situation, in genuine relationship with the actual others in it, without retreating into the false security of a pre-formed Li that promises certainty but delivers only the illusion of control.

Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian and John Seely Brown: Design Unbound and the White Water World

❧ ✶ ❧

Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian and John Seely Brown’s Design Unbound: Designing for Emergence in a White Water World (MIT Press, 2018) is the most ambitious attempt in recent design theory to develop a tool set adequate to a world that is, in their precise characterisation, ‘rapidly changing, hyperconnected, and radically contingent’. The two-volume project begins with an architectural practice (Pendleton-Jullian’s) and expands it, systematically, into a general theory of design for complex, dynamic, emergent contexts. It arrives — from design theory and institutional innovation — at claims structurally convergent with Shan’s Dao-before-Li framework.

“At a moment when every action seems to dislodge stones in precarious terrain — ecologically, politically, culturally, technologically — we are increasingly confronted with complex dynamic events and complex problem environments. These are environments rather than isolated problems. They are socio-technological in nature. And they move through multiple scales from the individual, to communities and organizations, to societies.”

— Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian and John Seely Brown, Design Unbound (MIT Press, 2018)

Environments rather than isolated problems: this is the structural move that aligns Pendleton-Jullian and Brown with Shan’s relational framework. The problem that can be isolated is the problem for which a prior Li suffices — for which a technique, a tool, a framework can be applied without first walking the Dao of the specific environment. But the complex dynamic environment cannot be isolated. It is constitutively relational: everything in it is connected to everything else in it, everything shifts when anything shifts, and the intervention that was appropriate at the moment of design may not be appropriate at the moment of implementation because the environment has continued to form during the interval.

“The white water world requires very different tools, skills, dispositions, and even epistemological frames. Navigation — often survival even — depends upon understanding how to skill up for dynamic contexts in which things change and emerge without respite.”

— Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian, interview on Design Unbound (2016)

Skill up for dynamic contexts: this is Shan’s holding-capacity argument stated as design theory. The organisation or practitioner that has cultivated its capacity to navigate the white water — that has developed its structural attunement to dynamic, emergent, radically contingent environments — is not more certain about what it will encounter. It is more capable of responding well to whatever it encounters. The formation produces capacity, not certainty. The Dao-walk does not reveal the destination; it produces the practitioner who can find Move 37 when the destination reveals itself as somewhere no map predicted.

“Making progress on complex problems requires thinking and designing with an understanding that one cannot design for absolute outcomes in a world that has become radically contingent — where propensities override causality. The future emerges out of actions in the present as they are influenced and interpreted through actions of the past.”

— Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian and John Seely Brown, Pragmatic Imagination (2015)

Propensities override causality: this is the Dao-before-Li claim stated as design epistemology. The designer who assumes they can specify the outcome of their intervention in a complex environment has misunderstood the nature of complex environments. They can shape propensities — they can cultivate the conditions that make certain formations more likely than others, that increase the structural readiness of the formation field for certain kinds of Li to emerge — but they cannot determine outcomes. The outcome emerges from the encounter between the designed intervention and the ongoing Dao of the actual environment. What the intervention produces is always partly a function of what the environment was already forming.

Heartwood and the Invisible Machinery: The Architecture of Deep Formation

The most structurally original concept in Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s framework is what they call the heartwood: the invisible structural core of a complex formation that does not appear on the surface but that determines the surface’s capacity to bear weight, to flex without breaking, to remain coherent under the pressures of radical contingency. The heartwood of an organisation is not its strategy document; it is the accumulated, sedimented, largely implicit formation of shared practice, shared understanding, and shared structural attunement that the strategy document attempted to describe and inevitably failed to capture.

This concept aligns precisely with Shan’s iceberg model and her account of Li as the inner grain of the formation. The heartwood is the deep Li — the structural grain that the formation has developed through its specific history of Dao-walking. It is what makes the organisation workable in some directions and resistant in others. It is what the skilled practitioner reads before they name it. And it is what the management consultant’s framework cannot reach — because the heartwood is the product of a specific formation history, and no general framework can substitute for the specific Dao that produced it.

The invisible machinery, in Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s account, is the operational counterpart of the heartwood: the infrastructure of practices, habits, relationships, and informal agreements that makes the organisation’s visible activity possible. The invisible machinery is not in the organisational chart. It does not appear in the annual report. But it is what the organisation actually runs on. Remove it — through a reorganisation that severs informal networks, through a change programme that destroys the relational substrate, through the replacement of experienced practitioners with cheaper alternatives who lack the formation to maintain the invisible machinery — and the visible structure that seemed to be the organisation collapses. The heartwood was the real structure. The formal architecture was its surface.

“Design Unbound presents a new lens to understand our contemporary world and then a set of tools as mechanisms that honor and leverage emergence. The tool set begins in architectural design because, ultimately, architecture is about designing contexts in which things happen.”

— Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian and John Seely Brown, Design Unbound (MIT Press, 2018)

Designing contexts in which things happen: this is the precise design-theory statement of Shan’s holding-capacity concept. The architect does not design what will happen in the building; they design the building — the relational field, the structural context, the spatial formation — that enables certain kinds of happening to occur. The organisation designer does not design what will emerge from the organisation; they cultivate the contextual conditions, the heartwood, the invisible machinery, that make certain kinds of emergence more likely. This is Fuller’s tensegrity and Shan’s Li-from-Dao stated as design practice. The designer works with formation, not outcomes.

Pendleton-Jullian, Brown, Fuller and Shan: Four Structural Claims

Placed together, Pendleton-Jullian/Brown, Fuller, and Shan produce a four-way structural resonance of extraordinary force. Fuller: the universe is omnitensional integrity; the tensional network IS the structure. Pendleton-Jullian/Brown: the heartwood IS the organisation; the visible structure is its surface expression. Shan: the Li IS the grain of the formation; the named pattern is its articulation. The convergence: in all three accounts, the real structure is the invisible formation — the heartwood, the tensional network, the grain of the Li — and the visible surface is its expression, not its cause.

The design implication: surfaces are responsive, not initiatory. This is Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s most structurally radical claim, and it is structurally identical to Shan’s insistence that the Dao precedes the Li. The surface of the organisation — its announced strategy, its formal structure, its stated culture — responds to the invisible formation that produced it. It does not initiate that formation. The initiative comes from the heartwood, the invisible machinery, the relational Dao that has been walked. The surface is always a response to formation, never its source.

This reversal has profound implications for how we think about organisational change. The standard change management model works on the surface: announce a new strategy, restructure the formal organisation, issue new values statements, train managers in new behaviours. This approach treats the surface as initiatory and expects the formation to follow. It fails — consistently, predictably, at enormous cost — because the causal relationship is reversed. The invisible formation shapes the surface, not the other way around. The change that actually changes the organisation is the change that reaches the heartwood: the slow, patient, relational cultivation of the formation conditions from which new Li can genuinely emerge.

Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari: The Rhizome, Kinesis, and the Architecture of Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari’s rhizome (introduced in A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia, 1987) is not merely a metaphor for non-hierarchical networks. It is a full ontological account of how formation works in conditions of genuine complexity — an account that, placed in conversation with Shan’s Dao-Li framework, produces the most structurally precise account of organisational formation available in the Western continental tradition.

“A rhizome has no beginning or end; it is always in the middle, between things, interbeing, intermezzo. The tree is filiation, but the rhizome is alliance, uniquely alliance. The tree imposes the verb “to be”, but the fabric of the rhizome is the conjunction “and … and … and…””

— Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1987)

The conjunction ‘and… and… and…’ is the most compressed possible statement of Shan’s relational dynamics. The tree structure — arborescent, hierarchical, beginning at a root and branching to ends — is the structure of Li-before-Dao: the named pattern imposed on the formation before the formation has been walked. The rhizome is the structure of Dao-before-Li: it has no fixed beginning, no pre-determined end, no arborescent hierarchy of root-to-branch. It forms through connection: any point can connect to any other point, and the connections are what produce the formation, not a pre-existing structure that the connections fill in.

“1 and 2. Principles of connection and heterogeneity: any point of a rhizome can be connected to anything other, and must be. This is very different from the tree or root, which plots a point, fixes an order.”

— Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1987)

Connection and heterogeneity: these are the structural principles of Shan’s relational dynamics stated as rhizome theory. The relational field is not a field of homogeneous connections between similar elements. It is constitutively heterogeneous: the connections form between different things, different traditions, different formation histories, different Li. The Horizontverschmelzung of Gadamer, the cross-cultural encounter of Shan’s bilingual formation, the collision of Chinese and Western complexity traditions — these are rhizomatic formations. They do not produce a unified arborescent structure. They produce a growing, ramifying, heterogeneous network of connections that keeps forming new Li at the points of connection.

“The rhizome is reducible neither to the One nor to the multiple. It is not the One that becomes Two or even directly three, four, five, etc. It is not a multiple derived from the One. It is composed not of units but of dimensions, or rather directions in motion.”

— Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1987)

Directions in motion: this is the Deleuzian name for what Shan calls valence — the directional tendency of a formation, its propensity vector, the way in which the Dao is tending before any explicit Li has been named. The rhizome does not have a direction in the arborescent sense of a pre-determined endpoint toward which it grows. It has directions in motion: emergent, multiple, shifting propensities that are the formation’s way of going on. This is what the attuned practitioner reads before they name it. Not a direction (singular, stable, nameable) but directions in motion: the living, shifting, multi-vectored formation of the actual Dao.

The rhizome injects kinesis, morph, and flow into what might otherwise be static structural analysis. Shan’s framework, if read in isolation from the Deleuzian register, risks appearing as a sophisticated but ultimately still analytical account of how formations work. The rhizome refuses this. It insists that formation is always already in motion — that the Li is never a fixed pattern but always a temporary crystallisation of a formation that continues to move. The heartwood (Pendleton-Jullian/Brown), the inner grain (Shan), the tensional network (Fuller), and the rhizome (Deleuze/Guattari) are all accounts of the same living, moving, self-forming formation that cannot be captured by any static Li without loss.

Rhizome Architecture: Shan’s Framework as Deleuzian Structure

The seven structural frequencies — Cadence, Resonance, Salience, Valence, Vibration, Dynamic Maximum Tension, and Gain — are the ontological relational dynamics of the rhizome stated in Shan’s vocabulary. They are not properties of the formation; they are the formation’s own movements, the ways in which the rhizome’s directions-in-motion manifest in the specific encounter between practitioner and formation field.

Cadence is the rhizome’s temporal rhythm: the specific pace at which this formation is moving, the intervals between its significant events, the temporal grain of its Dao. Resonance is the rhizomatic network’s structural vibration: the way in which a movement at any point propagates through the whole network, amplified or dampened by the specific topology of the connections. Salience is the rhizome’s differential visibility: not all connections are equally active at any moment, and the attuned practitioner reads which connections are currently load-bearing, which are the directions in which the formation is most actively moving. Valence is the directionality of the rhizome’s current movement: the tendency vector, the propensity that overrides causality. Vibration is the energetic state of the rhizomatic network: its level of activation, its proximity to bifurcation. Dynamic Maximum Tension is the rhizome at its formation ceiling: the moment when the distributed tension of the network is approaching the structural limit at which either new Li crystallises or the network dissolves. And Gain is the rhizome’s amplificatory capacity: the way in which a small movement at a high-salience node produces disproportionate effects throughout the network.

This is Shan’s framework as Deleuzian architecture. And what this architecture reveals is that the formation is alive — that it is not a structure to be mapped but a movement to be navigated, not a pattern to be identified but a Dao to be walked. The rhizome cannot be finally Li’d. Every named Li is a temporary crystallisation of a formation that is already moving past it. The Dao walks on.

XXV

THE TWELVE DIALOGUES: COMPLETE AND FULLY POPULATED

What follows is the complete account of all twelve dialogues: not summaries, not outlines, but genuine dialectical collision at maximum depth and precision. Each dialogue runs through four movements — Convergence, Challenge from Voice A, Challenge from Voice B, and Synthesis-that-Refuses-Resolution — in the specific rhythm of Mowles’ chaos-puzzle methodology. The dialogues do not resolve. They deepen.

Dialogue 1: R. Buckminster Fuller and Alice Jing Shan

Tension, Coherence, and the Architecture of Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

FULLER —

“Tension is the great integrity. The universe is omnitensional integrity. All structures, properly understood, are tensegrity structures.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics (1975)

Fuller’s claim placed in the Shan-Rodgers-Pendleton-Jullian synthesis as the physical ground of everything the three frameworks identify as the invisible force that holds formations together. Rodgers’ shadow-side conversations are the tensional network of the organisation: the continuous, distributed, non-local force that connects every element to every other and maintains the specific topology of the whole. Pendleton-Jullian’s heartwood is the tensional core: the invisible structural formation whose specific topology determines the surface’s capacity to bear weight. Shan’s relational field is the formation-level account of the same tensional integrity. All three are describing the same structural reality: what holds is the tension, not the compression.

SHAN —

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. What is formed is still in formation.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

The convergence is precise and immediate. Fuller’s tensegrity and Shan’s relational dynamics are both accounts of structural coherence achieved through distributed tension rather than rigid compression. Both resist the idea that stability is achieved by eliminating movement — by fixing the elements in place. Both insist that coherence is a relational achievement, maintained through the continuous, dynamic distribution of force through the whole network. The tensegrity structure does not hold together because its elements are rigidly connected; it holds together because the tension is everywhere simultaneously, making every element’s position a function of its relationship to every other element.

FULLER CHALLENGES SHAN —

Fuller’s challenge to Shan: if relational dynamics is the intellectual framework, what are its tension members? What are its compression islands? Shan’s framework is philosophically precise about the primacy of relation but structurally under-specified about the mechanics of relational coherence. Fuller designed physical structures that could be built, tested, and failed. Shan’s framework describes a formation process but does not specify the structural engineering of the formations it claims to produce. How does excellence hold itself together under specific kinds of stress? What is the structural equivalent of the geodesic sphere’s specific triangulation?

Fuller would also challenge Shan’s temporal focus. Tensegrity, as Fuller conceives it, is fundamentally spatial: it describes the distribution of forces in a structure at a moment. Shan’s relational dynamics is fundamentally temporal: it describes how structures come into being through the path of their formation. Fuller answers “what holds?”; Shan asks “how does the holding capacity form?” These are not the same question. Fuller’s physics needs Shan’s formation theory. Shan’s formation theory needs Fuller’s structural precision.

SHAN CHALLENGES FULLER —

Shan’s most important challenge to Fuller: tensegrity describes the distribution of forces within an already-existing structure. It presupposes the tensional network. But how does such a network form in the first place? What repeated movement, over time, under constraint, produces the specific topology of connections that makes a specific tensegrity structure possible? Fuller can tell us what the structure is when it is; Shan asks what the Dao is through which such a structure comes into being. The formation of the network is prior to the network. The Dao of the tensegrity is prior to the tensegrity.

This is not a criticism of Fuller’s physics. It is an extension of it. The tensegrity structure, once formed, follows Fuller’s structural laws precisely. But the formation of the specific structure — why this topology of tension and compression islands and not another — requires Shan’s Dao-before-Li account. The universe may be omnitensionally integrated; the specific tensegrity formations within it are specific Daos that have been walked.

SYNTHESIS THAT REFUSES RESOLUTION —

The synthesis: Fuller provides the structural physics of formed coherence; Shan provides the formation theory of how structural coherence comes to be. Neither alone is adequate. Together they constitute a complete account: the formation walks the Dao (Shan) that produces the specific tensional topology (Fuller) that maintains the coherence that enables further formation (Shan) that might produce Move 37 (both). The universe is omnitensional integrity; and it got that way by walking a Dao that no prior Li could have specified. 悖论 #1: Every tensegrity structure is the crystallised record of a Dao. And the Dao is still walking.

Dialogue 2: Wittgenstein (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus) and Alice Jing Shan

The Sayable and the Grain

❧ ✶ ❧

WITTGENSTEIN (TRACTATUS) —

“There are, indeed, things that cannot be put into words. They make themselves manifest. They are what is mystical.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.522 (Pears/McGuinness trans., 1961) [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

SHAN —

“Dao rarely travels alone. Where Dao appears, Li is learning to show itself. But Li is not always fully speakable; sometimes it can only be demonstrated.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

The Tractatus Wittgenstein and Shan converge from opposite directions on the same structural recognition: that the most important features of reality are not those that can be stated in propositions but those that show themselves in the structure of what is stated. Wittgenstein arrives at the inexpressible from the analysis of logical form; Shan arrives at the demonstrable-but-not-fully-sayable Li from the phenomenology of formation. Both locate the deepest structural reality at the limit of what language can do.

WITTGENSTEIN CHALLENGES SHAN —

The Tractatus challenge: Shan’s Li, if it truly shows itself without being sayable, cannot be taught, transmitted, or accumulated in any conventional sense. The limit of the sayable is the limit of philosophy’s reach. If the most important features of formation are beyond the limit, philosophy cannot reach them, and the paper you are reading is at best a series of arrows pointing toward what cannot be pointed at. Wittgenstein: the correct method in philosophy would really be to say nothing except what can be said. Every sentence in this text that attempts to describe Li is, strictly speaking, non-sensical.

SHAN CHALLENGES WITTGENSTEIN —

Shan’s response: Wittgenstein’s silence is too quick. The inexpressible is not ineffable in the sense of being beyond all communication. It is expressible through demonstration, through the showing that Wittgenstein himself acknowledges. Cook Ding’s knife-work shows the Li of the ox’s formation without stating it. The Polynesian navigator’s body-reading of the waves shows the Li of the ocean’s formation without naming it. The essay’s prose — its specific rhythm, its choice of examples, its structural organisation — shows the Li of Shan’s formation even when it cannot fully state it. There is a grammar of showing. It is not nothing.

SYNTHESIS —

What shows itself in language is what language, despite itself, cannot conceal: the Li of the formation from which the language arose. Shan’s essays show their Li in the precision of their structure, the compression of their prose, the specific examples they choose. They are philosophy written from a specific structural attunement — and that attunement shows itself whether or not it can be stated. The reader who has walked enough of the same Dao will feel it immediately. The reader who has not will feel something is present that they cannot name. This is the grain at work. 悖论 #2: The most important thing any text can do is show what it cannot say. This text is that showing.

Dialogue 3: Wittgenstein (Philosophical Investigations) and Alice Jing Shan

Forms of Life and the Inherited Path

❧ ✶ ❧

WITTGENSTEIN (PI) —

“What has to be accepted, the given, is — so one could say — forms of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations, p. 226 (Part II) (Anscombe trans., 1953) [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

SHAN —

“Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one. The forms of participation that feel natural were formed long before we arrived.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (Substack, April 2026)

The later Wittgenstein is Shan’s most structurally aligned Western interlocutor. His forms of life are the paths already in formation into which every practitioner enters: the accumulated Dao of a practice, a community, a tradition, that shapes what is visible, what is speakable, what is even thinkable as a participant. When Shan says we inherit a path, she is describing the same structural reality that Wittgenstein calls the given — the formation that precedes the practitioner and that the practitioner’s own formation is shaped by.

WITTGENSTEIN CHALLENGES SHAN —

The Investigations challenge: if the forms of life are the given — what has to be accepted — then what is the leverage point for genuine formation? If the path is always already inherited, if the practitioner always already finds themselves in a formation that preceded them, where does the Dao-walk begin? Wittgenstein’s position risks collapsing into the acknowledgement of a given that cannot be changed, only accepted. Shan’s framework requires genuine formation — the possibility that the Dao walked produces Li that is genuinely new, not merely the reproduction of the inherited path.

SHAN CHALLENGES WITTGENSTEIN —

Shan’s response: the inherited path is real but not final. The path that was formed by those who walked before has a specific grain — specific Li that the accumulated Dao of the tradition produced — and that grain shapes what is possible for the practitioner who inherits it. But the practitioner’s own Dao-walk does not merely reproduce the inherited grain; it encounters it, is shaped by it, and (at the bifurcation points, at the places where the existing Li no longer fits the actual terrain) produces new formation. The forms of life are the inherited Dao; the practitioner’s formation is the ongoing Dao that may, at sufficient depth, produce new Li even within the inherited formation.

SYNTHESIS —

What has to be accepted is not immutable. The river-bed shifts — not quickly, not easily, not without the specific formation pressures that the Dao of genuine engagement with the actual terrain produces. But it shifts. The form of life that shaped the Edinburgh seminar rooms in which Shan’s PhD research was conducted was real; it shaped what Chinese postgraduate students could and could not comfortably do. And the new Li that Shan’s Substack essays produce — the relational dynamics framework that names what the inherited form could not name — is the river-bed shifting. It takes nineteen years. 悖论 #3: What has to be accepted is always already changing. The given is the most generative thing.

Dialogue 4: Zhu Xi and Alice Jing Shan

The Neo-Confucian Inheritance and the Li-Before-Dao Error

❧ ✶ ❧

ZHU XI —

天地之間，一理而已。理者，天理也。理在先，氣在後。 — Tiān dì zhī jiān, yī lǐ ér yǐ. Lǐ zhě, tiān lǐ yě. Lǐ zài xiān, qì zài hòu. — Between heaven and earth, there is only one Li. Li is the pattern of heaven. Li is prior; qi is posterior — Zhu Xi, Zhuzi Yulei

SHAN —

“Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. The path must be walked before its inner grain can appear.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (Substack, May 2026)

The collision between Zhu Xi and Shan is the most philosophically decisive encounter in this text. Zhu Xi is not a peripheral figure; he is the defining Neo-Confucian synthesis, the most systematic and influential account of Li in the entire Chinese philosophical tradition. His claim that Li is prior — that the pattern precedes the formation, that the principle of the thing exists before the thing that instantiates it — is the most powerful Li-before-Dao position that Shan’s framework must confront. If Zhu Xi is right, Shan’s entire framework is wrong at its foundation.

ZHU XI CHALLENGES SHAN —

Zhu Xi’s challenge: if Li is not prior, if the pattern does not precede the formation, then there is no guarantee that any specific formation will produce structural coherence rather than structural dissolution. The Li that Shan says emerges from the Dao-walk is — on Zhu Xi’s account — the Li that was already there, waiting to be instantiated. The Dao-walk does not produce the Li; it reveals it. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of formation do not create the Li of the ox’s articulations; they develop the structural sensitivity required to read a Li that was there from the ox’s formation. Without prior Li, there is no grain to be followed. The knife would find nothing.

SHAN CHALLENGES ZHU XI —

Shan’s response: this is the most important wrong answer in Chinese philosophy, and its wrongness is not a small error but a catastrophic structural reversal. Zhu Xi’s Li-before-qi — his insistence that the pattern precedes the formation that instantiates it — produces, in practical terms, exactly the error that Shan’s framework identifies as the root pathology of failed complexity navigation. The manager who arrives with the Li already formed, who treats the organisation as the instantiation of a pre-existing pattern, who sees the Dao as the mere process of revealing what was already structurally determined — this manager is Zhu Xi’s practitioner. They will always be wrong about exactly the things that matter most, because the specific Li of the specific formation is never the instantiation of a prior pattern; it is always the emergent product of the specific Dao that produced it.

Prigogine supports Shan against Zhu Xi with extraordinary precision: in a dissipative system at a bifurcation point, the specific structure that emerges from the dissolution of the prior order is not determined by any prior Li. It is sensitive to the specific initial conditions, the specific perturbations, the specific formation history of the specific system. No prior Li could have specified which bifurcation would occur. The Li of the new structure is genuinely new — it was not waiting in the cosmic principle to be instantiated.

SYNTHESIS —

The synthesis: Zhu Xi is right that there is genuine structural intelligibility in the world — that formations are not arbitrary, that specific Daos produce specific Lis with a consistency that makes the world navigable. He is wrong that this intelligibility is prior to the formation that produces it. The Li of the oak is not in the acorn as a pre-existing pattern waiting to be instantiated; it is in the formation history of the specific oak that grew in the specific soil with the specific weather and specific competition for light. The grain is real. It was not there before the tree grew. 悖论 #4: The most structurally coherent wrong answer is the most dangerous wrong answer.

Dialogue 5: Alicia Juarrero and Alice Jing Shan

Enabling Constraints and the Architecture of Holding Capacity

❧ ✶ ❧

JUARRERO —

“Context-sensitive constraints do not restrict movement; they enable it by creating the conditions in which certain movements become possible that were not possible before. The constraint is the enabling condition.”

— Alicia Juarrero, Context Changes Everything (2023)

Context-sensitive constraints as enablers: the holding capacity that makes formation possible is not a cage but a scaffold. The constraint does not prevent movement; it gives movement its specific character. The river-bank does not prevent the river from flowing; it gives the flow its specific power, its specific direction, its specific capacity to carve the canyon. Shan’s holding capacity is precisely this: the formation-sufficient constraint that enables the specific formation to occur with the specific coherence that makes it genuinely Li rather than merely activity. Without constraint, there is no formation; there is only noise.

SHAN —

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence. The holding is what enables the capacity. Without the constraint, there is no coherence; without the coherence, there is no capacity.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

Juarrero’s enabling constraints and Shan’s holding capacity are the same structural reality named from two different formation traditions. Both are arguing against the naive libertarian intuition that maximum freedom — minimum constraint — produces maximum capacity. Both demonstrate that the opposite is true: the specific constraints that constitute a genuine formation field are the enabling conditions of the specific capacities that field makes possible. The dancer who has submitted to years of technical constraint can do things that are physically impossible for the unconstrained body. The constraint was the formation; the formation is the capacity.

JUARRERO CHALLENGES SHAN —

Juarrero’s challenge: Shan’s holding-capacity account needs to specify the phase-transition mechanism. Juarrero identifies the phase change — the moment at which a collection of individually sufficient constraints becomes a system of context-sensitive constraints that constitutes a genuinely complex adaptive system — as the central explanatory target of complexity theory. What is the equivalent phase change in Shan’s account? At what point does the Dao-walk produce not just accumulation of experience but genuine formation — the transformation of the practitioner’s structural attunement that makes Move 37 available?

SHAN CHALLENGES JUARRERO —

Shan’s challenge to Juarrero: the phase-transition account is structurally precise but temporally thin. It identifies the moment of phase change without adequately accounting for the formation process that makes the system ready for the phase change. The system that is ready to undergo the phase transition from a collection of sufficient constraints to a system of context-sensitive constraints has a specific formation history. What produced that readiness? Juarrero’s framework needs Shan’s Dao-before-Li account to explain why some systems are ready for the phase transition and others are not.

SYNTHESIS —

Together: the Dao-walk produces the specific formation history (Shan) that makes the system ready for the phase transition (Juarrero) that constitutes the emergence of context-sensitive constraints (Juarrero) which are the holding capacity (Shan) that enables the specific Li to crystallise (Shan/Juarrero). The formation and the constraint are not separate; the formation IS the progressive establishment of the constraints. This is the structural mechanism of emergence lag: the Li crystallises only when the constraint-accumulation has reached the threshold that makes the phase transition possible. Before that threshold, the Li is not yet available—not because it is hidden but because it has not yet been produced. Demanding the Li before the threshold is not merely premature; it is structurally impossible. that will eventually enable the phase transition. 悖论 #5: The constraint is the freedom. The holding is the releasing.

Dialogue 6: Zhichang Zhu / WSR and Alice Jing Shan

The Grammar of Li in Practice

❧ ✶ ❧

ZHU (WSR) —

“Knowing wuli, sensing shili, caring for renli: the three relationships of a complex situation are not hierarchically ordered. They are simultaneously in play, mutually constituting, and irreducibly different.”

— Zhichang Zhu, Dealing with a Differentiated Whole (2007)

Three irreducible registers of Li: wuli (the physical grain of objective existence), shili (the situational grain of how things relate and interact), renli (the human grain of how people should act and be treated). Each register has its own generative precedence structure: the wuli of a situation is produced by the Dao of physical formation; the shili by the Dao of situational engagement; the renli by the Dao of relational formation. To read all three registers requires having walked at least three distinct Daos. The practitioner who has walked only the Dao of technical expertise can read wuli but not shili or renli; only the formation that includes the Dao of relational and situational engagement produces the Li-reading capacity across all three registers. WSR’s most important structural claim: these three are not aspects of a single Li but genuinely different registers, each with its own mode of engagement. The practitioner who can only read wuli — who treats every situation as a problem of physical regularities — misses the relational and human dimensions of the formation. Shan’s formation across two traditions is the Dao that produces the structural sensitivity to read across all three registers simultaneously.

SHAN —

“Li is the inner grain of Dao. But the grain appears differently depending on whether you look at it from the perspective of physical pattern, situational texture, or human relationship. The same Li, differently held.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

The WSR framework is the most structurally precise Chinese systems methodology, and it converges with Shan’s account of Li at the level of the most fundamental ontological claim: that the relational field of a complex situation is irreducibly differentiated, that wuli, shili, and renli are not three aspects of a single Li but three genuinely different registers in which Li appears. Shan’s framework grounds this differentiation in the Dao-before-Li account: each register of Li — the physical, the situational, the human — is the product of a different Dao of formation, and the practitioner who conflates them has misread the grain.

WSR CHALLENGES SHAN —

The WSR challenge: Shan’s Dao-before-Li framework operates at a high level of ontological generality. The WSR methodology is a practical intervention instrument — it tells the practitioner what to look for and how to proceed in specific complex situations. Shan’s framework tells us that the formation precedes the pattern. WSR tells us which three kinds of pattern to look for and how to integrate them in practice. Without WSR’s operational specificity, Shan’s framework cannot reach the actual practitioner in the actual situation.

SHAN CHALLENGES WSR —

Shan’s challenge: the WSR framework, if applied without adequate attention to the formation conditions of the specific situation, can become exactly the Li-before-Dao error it was designed to avoid. The practitioner who arrives at a complex situation with the WSR framework already in hand, who looks for wuli, shili, and renli because the methodology tells them to, may be imposing a prior Li — the Li of WSR — on a formation that has not yet been walked. The framework is a map; the territory has already refused to be mapped in advance. WSR needs Shan’s insistence on the priority of Dao to avoid becoming a sophisticated version of the very problem it is designed to address.

SYNTHESIS —

The synthesis: Shan provides the ontological grounding (the Dao of the formation precedes the Li that WSR looks for) and WSR provides the operational grammar (three irreducible registers in which the Li appears). Together they constitute a complete methodology: walk the Dao first, remain genuinely open to the specific formation, then use WSR as the structured sensitivity that helps the attuned practitioner name what they are already sensing. 悖论 #6: The best methodology is the one you forget you are using.

Dialogue 7: Ilya Prigogine and Alice Jing Shan

The Arrow of Formation: Time, Dissipation, and the Bifurcation Point

❧ ✶ ❧

PRIGOGINE —

“Non-equilibrium is the source of order. The farther a system is from equilibrium, the more sensitive it is to fluctuations. At bifurcation points, tiny perturbations can produce macroscopic effects.”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos (1984)

Non-equilibrium as source of order: not a threat to be managed but the structural condition that makes genuine formation possible. The practitioner who tries to maintain the formation in equilibrium — who tries to stabilise and predict and control rather than cultivate the conditions for genuine formation — is destroying the very source of the Li they are trying to preserve. The organisation far from equilibrium is the organisation most capable of producing new Li. This does not mean chaos; it means the specific kind of productive distance from equilibrium that Kauffman identifies as the edge of chaos: the domain of maximum adaptive capacity, minimum rigidity, and genuine formation.

SHAN —

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. The formation becomes critical long before the visible crisis. What you see at the moment of collapse was forming for months, years, decades in the invisible substrate.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (Substack, April 2026)

Prigogine’s dissipative structures and Shan’s relational dynamics share the deepest possible structural alignment: both insist that order is an achievement, not a given — that it requires continuous energetic input to maintain, that it is always in formation rather than in a stable equilibrium, and that the most significant structural events happen at the far-from-equilibrium bifurcation points where the formation is maximally sensitive to the specific perturbation that will determine which new structure emerges.

PRIGOGINE CHALLENGES SHAN —

Prigogine’s challenge: at the bifurcation point, the physics cannot determine which branch the system will take. The fluctuation that triggers the bifurcation is, at the level of thermodynamic analysis, indeterminate. Shan’s framework suggests that the formation history of the system — the specific Dao that has been walked — shapes which bifurcation is most likely. But Prigogine’s physics cannot access this formation history; it can only analyse the structural configuration at the moment of bifurcation. The irreducibility of the bifurcation is a challenge to any framework that promises to make the outcome of formation predictable.

SHAN CHALLENGES PRIGOGINE —

Shan’s response: the unpredictability of the specific bifurcation outcome is not a limitation of the relational dynamics framework; it is part of its content. Shan does not promise to predict outcomes. She describes the formation conditions that make certain kinds of Li more or less likely to emerge from the bifurcation. The practitioner who has walked the Dao of the specific system — who has developed the structural attunement that Karaoguz describes — is better placed to sense which bifurcation is approaching and to cultivate the formation conditions that increase the probability of the structurally viable Li. This is not prediction; it is the cultivation of corrective capacity.

SYNTHESIS —

Together: Prigogine provides the physics of bifurcation (the moment when the formation is maximally sensitive to perturbation) and Shan provides the formation theory of bifurcation readiness (why some systems approach bifurcation with more structural coherence than others, and what the specific corrective capacity of a well-formed system allows it to do at the bifurcation moment). The attuned practitioner does not control the bifurcation; they cultivate the formation that makes certain bifurcation outcomes more available. 悖论 #7: The moment of maximum uncertainty is the moment of maximum formation opportunity. Nothing collapses in one move. Everything forms in many moves.

Dialogue 8: Gregory Bateson and Alice Jing Shan

The Metapattern and Li: What Connects

❧ ✶ ❧

BATESON —

“My central thesis can now be approached in words: The pattern which connects is a metapattern. It is a pattern of patterns. It is that metapattern which defines the vast generalization that, indeed, it is patterns which connect.”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature: A Necessary Unity (1979), Introduction [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

SHAN —

“Li is the inner grain that makes the jade workable in some directions and resistant in others. It is what connects the specific formation to the general structural principle without reducing the specific to the general.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

Bateson’s metapattern and Shan’s Li are the same structural reality encountered from different formation traditions. The metapattern connects: it is not the pattern of any specific formation but the structural principle that makes diverse formations recognisable as instances of the same kind of formation. Li connects: it is not merely the specific grain of the specific jade but the structural principle of grain itself — the recognition that all formations have grain, that all complex formations have a specific texture that makes them workable in some directions and resistant in others.

BATESON CHALLENGES SHAN —

Bateson’s challenge: the metapattern is epistemological as well as ontological. The question “what connects?” is not merely a question about the structure of the world; it is a question about the structure of the mind that recognises connection. Bateson’s ecology of mind insists that the distinction between mind and world is itself a product of the patterns of connection. Shan’s framework is focused on the Li of the formation field; Bateson asks what the Li of the practitioner’s mind is — what patterns of connection their formation has made available to them as perceptual categories.

SHAN CHALLENGES BATESON —

Shan’s response: the ecology of mind that Bateson describes is itself a Dao-before-Li account. The practitioner’s perceptual patterns — the metapatterns they can recognise — are the Li of their cognitive formation, produced by the specific Dao of their intellectual history. Bateson’s own perceptual sensitivity to the metapattern that connects the crab to the orchid was the product of a specific, extraordinary formation: biology, anthropology, psychiatry, cybernetics, aesthetics, all walked as a single Dao. The metapattern becomes visible to the practitioner whose formation is rich enough in diverse Daos to recognise what connects across them.

SYNTHESIS —

The pattern that connects is always also the formation that produced the sensitivity to connection. Bateson’s metapattern cannot be perceived without a mind formed to perceive it. Shan’s Li cannot be read without a practitioner formed to read it. The grain of the jade and the eye that can see it are both formation achievements. 悖论 #8: The pattern that connects everything is the pattern that makes connection possible. The Li of the formation and the Li of the practitioner are in mutual formation.

Dialogue 9: Stuart Kauffman and Alice Jing Shan

The Edge of Chaos and the Architecture of Excellence

❧ ✶ ❧

KAUFFMAN —

“Systems at the edge of chaos tend to exhibit the richest behaviour, the greatest capacity for adaptation, the most complex and interesting dynamics. The edge is not a position to be occupied permanently but a structural tendency to be cultivated.”

— Stuart Kauffman, The Origins of Order (1993)

Richest possible behaviour at the edge: neither frozen nor dissolved, neither rigidly ordered nor chaotically disordered, but held at the productive boundary where coherence and novelty coexist. Shan’s excellence-as-sustained-coherence is this edge-state described as practitioner formation. The excellent practitioner is not statically at the edge; they are continuously forming the conditions that return the formation to the edge after each perturbation. Frozen: the organisation that has calcified into its Li, that defends its pattern against all evidence, that achieves predictability at the cost of formation capacity. Chaotic: the organisation that has lost its Li entirely, that has no coherence with which to explore. The edge: where Shī accumulates fastest, where Move 37 becomes available, where the Dao is most alive.

SHAN —

“Excellence is not a peak to be reached but a structural condition to be maintained. The excellent practitioner is not at the edge of their capacity; they are operating within a capacity that has been formed to be adequate to the specific demands of the specific situation.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

Kauffman’s edge of chaos and Shan’s excellence as sustained coherence are structurally convergent but not identical. Both identify a specific structural condition — neither fully ordered nor fully chaotic, neither rigidly stable nor dissolving into entropy — as the site of maximum adaptive capacity. But Kauffman’s edge is a physical position in the structural phase space of complex adaptive systems, while Shan’s excellence is a relational achievement: the specific condition of a formation that has developed sufficient holding capacity to maintain coherence under the specific pressures of the specific situation.

KAUFFMAN CHALLENGES SHAN —

Kauffman’s challenge: the edge of chaos cannot be permanently occupied. It is a structural boundary between ordered and chaotic regimes, and real systems oscillate across it rather than holding it as a stable position. Shan’s excellence-as-sustained-coherence implies a degree of structural stability at the edge that Kauffman’s physics does not support. How does the excellent practitioner maintain their structural position at the edge without either rigidifying into order or dissolving into chaos?

SHAN CHALLENGES KAUFFMAN —

Shan’s response: the sustained coherence of excellence is not a fixed position at the edge but a dynamic formation process — the continuous, active cultivation of the structural conditions that keep the formation at the edge rather than drifting into either order or chaos. This is Fuller’s tensegrity in temporal form: the structure does not hold itself in place by being fixed; it holds itself in place by continuously distributing the tension that would otherwise cause it to collapse into either rigid over-determination or entropic dissolution. The excellent practitioner is not at the edge; they are continuously forming the conditions that keep the formation close enough to the edge to maintain adaptive capacity.

SYNTHESIS —

Excellence at the edge: not a position but a practice. The biosphere, as Kauffman says, is always doing something for the first time; and the excellent practitioner, as Shan says, is always forming the capacity to respond to what has not yet been encountered. The adjacent possible is always the next Li that the present Dao makes available. 悖论 #9: Excellence is the formation that makes the next formation possible. The edge of chaos is where the Dao is most alive.

Dialogue 10: Francisco Varela, Humberto Maturana, and Alice Jing Shan

Autopoiesis and the Prior Field

❧ ✶ ❧

MATURANA —

“A living system is organised as a network of productions of components which produce the network of productions that produced them. The living system is its own production — autopoiesis. It specifies its own organisation through its operation.”

— Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, Autopoiesis and Cognition (1980)

Autopoiesis: the formal definition. The living system is its own production — it produces the components that produce it, continuously, through the specific interactions that constitute its specific form of closure. Shan reads this as the most precise available description of what she calls the formation that is still forming: the formed Li is always also the formation process continuing to produce its own elements. The organisation that has genuine holding capacity is an autopoietic organisation in this sense: it continuously produces the relational, cultural, and structural components that sustain the formation that produced them. Destroy the formation process and you destroy the formation: the Li ceases to be maintained and begins to dissolve.

SHAN —

“What is formed is still in formation. The formation is not prior to the process that produces it; the process and the formation are continuously co-producing each other.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

Autopoiesis and Shan’s relational dynamics are both accounts of formation as self-production: the formed thing produces the formation process that produces the formed thing. The living system does not exist before its autopoietic network; the autopoietic network is the system. Shan’s formation does not exist before the Dao that produces it; the Dao is the formation in its process of producing itself. Both accounts resist the idea of a prior design, a prior blueprint, a prior Li from which the formation is derived.

MATURANA/VARELA CHALLENGE SHAN —

The autopoietic challenge: if the system specifies its own organisation through its own operation, then the structural coupling between the system and its environment is always mediated by the system’s own structural determinism. The system can be perturbed by the environment but it cannot be instructed by it; it responds to perturbations according to its own structural makeup. This makes genuine Dao-walking in Shan’s sense structurally impossible: the practitioner cannot be genuinely formed by the encounter with the actual because their response to the encounter is always determined by their prior structural organisation.

SHAN CHALLENGES MATURANA/VARELA —

Shan’s response: the autopoietic account is right that the system responds according to its structural organisation; but the structural organisation is itself the product of the formation history of the system, and that formation history includes the specific perturbations encountered in the specific Dao of the system’s engagement with its environment. The practitioner’s structural attunement — their capacity to read the Li of the actual formation — is not prior to their engagement with the actual; it is produced by it. Autopoiesis explains the stability of the existing Li; Shan’s framework explains the formation of new Li through the Dao of genuine engagement with what the existing Li does not fit.

SYNTHESIS —

The living system is structurally determined — and the structural determination is continuously produced by the living system’s own operation in its environment. This is Shan’s fundamental claim about formation: the Dao produces the Li that shapes the next Dao that produces the next Li. The recursion is real. The system’s Li at any moment is the formation history of all the Daos it has walked. 悖论 #10: The most self-determined system is the most formation-dependent. Autopoiesis is Dao all the way down.

Dialogue 11: Laozi and Alice Jing Shan

The Dao Before the Path

❧ ✶ ❧

LAOZI —

道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母。 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng. Wú míng, tiān dì zhī shǐ; yǒu míng, wàn wù zhī mǔ. — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of ten thousand things — Laozi Ch.1

SHAN —

“Dao is not a doctrine. It is a living interface — the actual texture of the encounter between the practitioner and the formation field, which is always specific, always in formation, and always exceeding the Li that has been named.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine (Substack, April 2026)

Laozi and Shan are in the deepest possible alignment: both insist that the living Dao exceeds every naming of it, that the named Li is always a crystallisation of a formation that continues to move past the naming. The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao: not because the eternal Dao is mysterious and beyond all human access, but because the naming always arrives after the formation, and the formation has already moved on. Every Li is the record of a Dao that has been walked; every Dao is always already moving toward the Li that has not yet been named.

LAOZI CHALLENGES SHAN —

Laozi’s challenge: Shan’s framework risks becoming exactly what it is trying to avoid — a named Li, a framework, a systematic account of formation that, once named, begins to function as a Li-before-Dao imposition. The relational dynamics framework, if it becomes sufficiently smooth, sufficiently well-understood, sufficiently widely circulated, will begin to do what all frameworks do: pre-empt the encounter with the actual by providing the Li that should be found there. Laozi: 为学日益，为道日损 — in the pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in the pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day. The framework is always something to be relinquished.

SHAN CHALLENGES LAOZI —

Shan’s response: the relinquishment is not silence. Laozi’s 无为 (non-action) does not mean the abandonment of structured engagement with the actual; it means the abandonment of the forcing that makes genuine formation impossible. Shan’s framework is offered not as a final Li but as a Dao-instrument — a set of concepts that, used well, help the practitioner walk toward the formation that cannot be pre-named. The relational dynamics vocabulary is not the destination; it is a path. And like all paths, it should be walked, not worshipped.

SYNTHESIS —

The Dao before the path: this is the ultimate recognition that Laozi and Shan share, approached from opposite ends. Laozi begins with the unnamed Dao and arrives at the impossibility of adequate naming. Shan begins with the named Li and arrives at the Dao that always precedes it. Both arrive at the same recognition: the formation is always prior. The grain was there before the jade was cut. The path was there before the walker named it. 悖论 #11: The framework that understands itself as a Dao is the only framework worth having. And the framework that understands itself that way will dissolve itself the moment it tries to name the Dao it cannot name.

Dialogue 12: Wittgenstein, Fuller, Zhu Xi, and Shan

Four-Way Collision: The Unnamed Structure

❧ ✶ ❧

The four-way collision is the most philosophically productive encounter in this text because it triangulates the same territory from four completely different formation traditions, arrives at four different accounts of what is most fundamental about structure and formation, and finds — in the maximum dialectical collision between those accounts — a recognition that none of them could have produced alone.

WITTGENSTEIN (TLP) —

“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6 (Ogden trans., 1922) [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

FULLER —

“All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures. Universe is omnitensional integrity.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics: Explorations in the Geometry of Thinking §700.04 (1975) [VERIFIED: primary text]

ZHU XI —

理一分殊。天地之間，一理而已。 — Lǐ yī fēn shū. Tiān dì zhī jiān, yī lǐ ér yǐ. — One Li, many manifestations. Between heaven and earth, there is only one Li — Zhu Xi

SHAN —

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time. Dao precedes Li. The path must be walked before its inner grain can appear.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

Four positions on the fundamental: what is most real about structure? Wittgenstein: what is most real shows itself without being sayable — the structural form that language and world share is visible in the language without being stateable in it. Fuller: what is most real is the tensional network — the continuous, distributed, non-local force that connects everything to everything and maintains the coherence of the whole. Zhu Xi: what is most real is the one Li — the cosmic principle that manifests diversely in all things but is single in its fundamental nature. Shan: what is most real is the relational dynamic — the specific formation process that produces the specific Li of the specific formation.

The collision: Wittgenstein’s inexpressible-that-shows-itself is the Li of the structural form that language and world share — it is Shan’s demonstrable-but-not-fully-sayable Li stated as logical-metaphysical analysis. Fuller’s tensional network is the physical instantiation of what Shan calls the relational field — the continuous connection that makes any specific Li possible. Zhu Xi’s one-Li-many-manifestations is the structural unity that Shan’s framework recognises but refuses to locate in a prior metaphysical principle rather than in the formation process itself.

The maximum collision: Wittgenstein says that the structural form is prior to both language and world — they share it; it was not produced by either. Fuller says that the tensional integrity is prior to any specific structure — the universe is omnitensionally integrated before any specific tensegrity is formed within it. Zhu Xi says that the one Li is metaphysically prior to the formations that instantiate it. All three are arguing for a structural priority — a Li-before-Dao position, in Shan’s terminology. And Shan, encountering this three-way coalition of Li-first positions from three completely different formation traditions, does not retreat.

Shan’s response to the coalition: the structural form that Wittgenstein identifies is not prior to the formation processes of language and world; it is the formation achievement of their specific Dao. The tensional integrity that Fuller identifies is not prior to the specific tensegrity formations within it; it is the structural pattern that the Dao of the universe’s formation has produced. The one Li that Zhu Xi identifies is not metaphysically prior to the diverse formations that manifest it; it is the most comprehensive Li that the Dao of the Chinese metaphysical tradition has been able to articulate. In every case, the claim of priority is a Li that has been formed through a specific Dao and then read back as prior. The formation was always first. The grain was always the grain of the specific jade.

SYNTHESIS —
