What emerges from this four-way collision is not a resolution but a structural ontology that none of the four traditions has fully articulated: a relational formation ontology in which the most fundamental feature of reality is neither the structural form (Wittgenstein), nor the tensional network (Fuller), nor the cosmic principle (Zhu Xi), nor even the specific relational dynamic (Shan) — but the encounter between all four, the horizontal fusion (Gadamer) of their different formation horizons, which produces the most structurally adequate account of what formation is. The Dao is walking. The four voices are walking it together. And what they find at the confluence is not the one Li but the recognition that there is always another Li forming beyond the one that was just named. 悖论 #12: The most structurally complete ontology is the one that understands its own incompleteness as its most important structural feature. The Dao walks on. 道可道，非常道。

❧ ✶ ❧
XXVI

Adam Karaoguz and the A Frame: Attunement as the Telos of Agency

❧ ✶ ❧

Adam Karaoguz is the author of Renaissance Humans (Substack) and the originator of the A Frame — a model of how human agents exercise agency within arenas through cycles of Attention, Appreciation, and Action that accumulate, over time, into Attunement. His essay ‘Attunement’ (Renaissance Humans #100, February 2026) is the distilled form of a three-part series totalling over ten thousand words that he found himself compelled to write against his own conscious intentions. He writes: ‘I just wanted to write fiction, but I had to put that on hold. Because this idea had me.’ This is not incidental autobiography. It is the A Frame’s first demonstration: an idea that exercises the agent rather than being exercised by the agent is an idea that has found a structural resonance with the agent’s formation. The Dao had Karaoguz before Karaoguz had the Dao.

The A Frame: Agent, Arena, Agency, Attunement

“Do we have ideas, or do ideas have us?”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’, Renaissance Humans #100 (February 2026)

This opening question — Do we have ideas, or do ideas have us? — is the most compressed possible statement of the A Frame’s central ontological claim, and it is structurally identical to Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim stated in the first person. If ideas have us — if the formation field in which we are embedded exerts structural pull on the practitioner before the practitioner has consciously engaged it — then the idea is the Dao acting on the agent before the agent has named the Li. Karaoguz is describing the phenomenology of formation: the experience of being moved by a structural reality before you have conceptualised it. This is not mysticism. This is the precise phenomenological account of what Shan calls the path opening before its grain appears.

“The A Frame describes how a human agent skillfully exercises agency within an arena by cycling through attention, appreciation, and action. These three modes shape one another. Action changes what we notice (attend to); what we notice changes what we value (appreciation); what we value changes how we act. Over time, this dynamic loop leads to attunement — a state of fittedness, flow, and optimal grip on reality — enhancing adaptability and engagement amid complexity and change.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’, Renaissance Humans #100 (February 2026)

The A Frame as the agent-side architecture of what Shan describes from the formation-field side. Where Shan asks what the formation field produces and how the practitioner reads it, Karaoguz asks how the agent cycles through specific cognitive modes to achieve the reading. The two frameworks are structurally complementary: Shan provides the ontology of the formation (what is out there, how it has its specific Li, what the Dao is that must be walked); Karaoguz provides the phenomenology of the practitioner (what the agent does, how they attend, appreciate, and act, how attunement is achieved through cycling). Together they constitute the most complete available account of what it means to navigate genuine complexity with genuine intelligence.

The Three Modes: Attention, Appreciation, Action

“Attention is the application of awareness toward what matters in the moment — patterns, anomalies, and opportunities. In the A Frame, this is an active process that shapes what becomes notable to the agent, and thus what can be known and acted on. Iain McGilchrist calls attention a moral act, in that there are consequences to what we attend to.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Attention as a moral act: McGilchrist’s claim, channelled through Karaoguz, is structurally important for the Shan framework. What the practitioner attends to is not neutral. The practitioner who has been formed in a specific Li attends to what that Li makes visible and misses what it does not. Salience — Shan’s fifth structural frequency — is the formation-dependent structure of attention: what becomes notable to the agent is a function of what the agent’s formation has made them sensitive to. And because attention shapes what can be known and acted on, the structure of attention is the structure of the practitioner’s formation. This is why the Dao must be walked before the Li can appear: until the formation walk has re-structured the practitioner’s attention, the Li of the actual situation is literally invisible.

“Appreciation is the meaning-making and valuation mode: the point where we interpret what attention has gathered and judge its significance in context. It includes discernment, context-awareness, and appraisal — sorting signal from noise, weighing relevance, and identifying what the situation calls for. Appreciation is the bridge between perception and wise action, where understanding and value come together.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Sorting signal from noise: this is Karaoguz’s name for what Shan calls reading the Li. The formation field of any complex situation contains vastly more information than any practitioner can process. What the experienced practitioner does — what Cook Ding did with his knife at the ox’s articulations, what the Polynesian navigator did with their body reading the wave patterns — is sort signal from noise at a level of structural precision that no explicit analytical procedure can replicate. Appreciation is the cognitive-somatic mode in which the formation-sufficient practitioner registers the Li of the actual situation before naming it. It is where understanding and value come together: the recognition that ‘this is what the situation calls for’ is simultaneously a structural reading (the Li of this formation is X) and a valuation (therefore the appropriate action is Y).

“Action is the enactment of agency in the world — the move that turns perception and understanding into consequences. It is not only about achieving an objective, but also about generating feedback, because action reveals the environment and teaches the agent in a two-way exchange. Action is part of a living loop: each move updates what we can attend to and appreciate next, sharpening skill through engagement.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Action generates feedback that updates attention and appreciation: this is the Dao-walk stated as cognitive loop. Each action is not merely an implementation of a decision; it is a formation event. The action changes the practitioner’s structural relationship to the formation field — it produces new information, new salience, new appreciative possibilities. This is why Shan’s Dao-walk is irreplaceable: no amount of prior analysis can substitute for the structural transformation that the action-feedback loop produces in the practitioner. The formation of the practitioner happens in the loop, not before it.

Attunement: The Telos of the A Frame

“"We are one, after all, you and I. Together we suffer, together exist, and forever will recreate each other."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin

[NOTE: Attribution to Teilhard captures his evolutionary convergence philosophy from The Phenomenon of Man; exact verbatim source unverified — treated as DESCRIPTIVE of Teilhard’s documented vision.] Teilhard’s cosmological claim placed at the opening of the attunement account as its structural ground. The practitioner who achieves genuine attunement is not merely an individual becoming effective in a specific domain. They are the universe recreating itself through this specific practitioner’s specific formation encounter with the actual formation field. Teilhard spent twenty-four years in China — the same China whose philosophical formation this paper has been excavating — and his central claim is Zhang Zai’s Western Inscription at evolutionary scale: what fills heaven and earth is my body; the cosmic formation is my formation, locally; together we recreate each other. The practitioner’s specific formation is not separate from the cosmos’ own formation process; it IS the cosmos’ formation process expressed at the scale of this specific biographical Dao. Karaoguz’s A-Frame — Attend, Appreciate, Act — structured around epistemic belatedness: Attend accepts the Li is not yet available; Appreciate is emergence lag resolving as the Li crystallises from engagement; Act is action from formed Li rather than prior Li. Each cycle thickens formation and shortens the emergence lag of the next. This is the specific cognitive mechanism through which this cosmic recreation occurs in the temporal scale of a single practitioner’s single formation encounter. Every A-Frame cycle is the universe’s own self-extension through the specific practitioner’s specific Dao.

Shan’s sharpest challenge to Teilhard’s cosmological grounding: the claim that we forever recreate each other is true at the cosmic scale and structurally insufficient at the formation-practice scale. The Edinburgh seminar’s Chinese student and the British seminar leader were, in Teilhard’s sense, recreating each other. But the specific power differential, the specific asymmetry of meaning-medium, the specific structural condition that made the student’s silence information and the leader’s interpretation noise — these are invisible to Teilhard’s cosmological account. The cosmic recreation is real; the specific formation injustice within the cosmic recreation is also real. Karaoguz’s A-Frame must operate within both: attending to the formation field’s actual Li requires attending to the specific power conditions that shape what formation-field features are visible and what are rendered invisible by the structure of the encounter itself.

Karaoguz and Shan: The A Frame Meets Relational Dynamics

❧ ✶ ❧

1. Structural Convergence: The Loop and the Walk

The most immediate structural convergence between Karaoguz and Shan is the account of formation as a recursive loop rather than a linear sequence. Karaoguz’s Attend-Appreciate-Act cycle accumulates into Attunement. Shan’s Dao-walk accumulates into Li. Both are accounts of a process in which each iteration of the cycle changes the practitioner’s structural relationship to the formation field, progressively deepening their capacity to read it, respond to it, and be genuinely affected by it. Both insist that this accumulation is irreplaceable: no amount of prior conceptual analysis can substitute for the structural transformation that the cycle produces.

Cook Ding’s nineteen years are the A Frame run to its completion. For nineteen years he cycled through the Attend-Appreciate-Act loop with the specific formation field of the ox’s body: attending to its patterns and articulations, appreciating their significance (this joint, this hollow, this natural line of cleavage), acting with the knife along the grain that his appreciation identified, and receiving the feedback of each cut as updated information for the next cycle of attention. After nineteen years the A Frame had produced what Karaoguz calls attunement: the fittedness, flow, and optimal grip of a practitioner who has been formed to the specific Li of a specific formation field until the distinction between practitioner and formation begins to dissolve.

“I have nicknamed the A Frame Spiritual OODA, because I see it nesting inside the OODA Loop as a deeper pattern. It sits on a foundation of Boyd’s work and owes a great deal to his efforts. But what is the point of increasing your capability for free and independent action, as Boyd asserts? To what end? Why? OODA is a framework for prevailing competitively in a given domain.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Spiritual OODA: the framing is important for its Shan connection. The A Frame nests inside OODA as a deeper pattern just as Shan’s Dao-before-Li nests inside any specific structural analysis as its ontological ground. Boyd’s Orientation is the dominant element of OODA because it determines what can be observed, decided, and acted on. Karaoguz’s Appreciation is the A Frame’s deepening of Boyd’s Orientation: it is not merely the cognitive state that filters perception but the meaning-making mode that connects perception to value and value to action. And Shan’s Li is the deepening of Appreciation: the specific structural grain of the specific formation that the appreciating practitioner reads before they name it. All three — Orientation (Boyd), Appreciation (Karaoguz), Li-reading (Shan) — are accounts of the same formation-dependent perceptual capacity that makes genuine responsiveness to complex situations possible.

2. Where Karaoguz Challenges Shan

Karaoguz’s most direct challenge to Shan concerns the agent-centred nature of the A Frame. Shan’s framework is primarily a relational-field account: it describes the formation of the field (the Dao producing the Li) and the practitioner’s capacity to read it. Karaoguz’s A Frame is primarily an agent-centred account: it describes what the agent does — the specific cognitive-somatic modes of Attention, Appreciation, and Action through which the agent engages the arena. The question: are these the same framework from different perspectives, or do they track genuinely different structural realities?

The A Frame’s emphasis on the agent’s internal cognitive architecture — the 6E cognition (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended, emotional, exapted), the free energy principle, the divided brain hemispheres — is not present in Shan’s framework. Shan describes the formation field and the practitioner’s structural attunement to it; she does not anatomise the cognitive mechanisms through which attunement is achieved. Karaoguz provides the cognitive-science underpinning that Shan’s framework needs: the A Frame shows how the agent’s specific cognitive architecture mediates the formation-field encounter.

“My hope is this model helps humans become harder to manipulate, less likely to confuse noise for signal, and more capable of living in truthful contact with the world. That it can help avoid both fatalistic passivity and excessive controlling. It can help us notice better, interpret deeper, and act with wisdom.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Living in truthful contact with the world: this is the ethical horizon of the A Frame, and it is structurally convergent with Shan’s anti-premature-Li argument. The practitioner who confuses noise for signal is the practitioner whose existing Li is so strong that it pre-empts genuine attention to the actual formation field — the practitioner of attunement failure (as developed in our preceding analysis of Karaoguz’s theoretical framework). Karaoguz’s rubric for assessing attunement quality — accuracy of predictions, adaptability after surprise, coherence of values and actions, relational attunement to other minds, somatic regulation of stress — is a practical operationalisation of Shan’s formation assessment that Shan’s framework alone does not provide.

3. Where Shan Challenges Karaoguz

Shan’s most important challenge to Karaoguz concerns the formation conditions of the A Frame itself. The A Frame describes what skilled attention, appreciation, and action look like. It does not adequately account for how the practitioner develops the specific formation that makes skilled attention, appreciation, and action possible in a specific domain. The agent who attends skillfully to the formation field of Go, or organisational complexity, or the inner grain of jade, has been formed to attend skillfully to those specific domains through a specific Dao of engagement with them. The A Frame is a map of the attunement process; Shan’s framework is an account of the formation that makes the map navigable.

Karaoguz’s arena concept — the place or scene where forces contend or events unfold, within which the agent exercises agency — is under-formed relative to Shan’s account of the formation field. The arena in Karaoguz is primarily a context for agent activity. The formation field in Shan is a constitutively relational structure that co-produces the practitioner who navigates it. The agent does not simply act in the arena; the agent is formed by the arena’s specific Li through the Dao of genuine engagement with it. This is the difference between a gymnasium (the arena as neutral space for agent development) and the specific ox (the formation field whose specific Li can only be read by the practitioner formed to read it).

4. The Synthesis: A Frame + Dao-Li + Optimal Grip

The synthesis is not a merger but a complementarity. Karaoguz provides the agent-side cognitive architecture: the specific modes (Attention, Appreciation, Action) through which the practitioner engages the formation field, and the telos (Attunement) toward which repeated cycling moves. Shan provides the field-side ontological account: the specific formation process (Dao) that produces the specific structural grain (Li) that the skilled practitioner reads. Merleau-Ponty’s optimal grip — the concept that Karaoguz imports from phenomenology as his account of attunement — is the meeting point: the specific quality of the practitioner-formation-field relationship when the A Frame has cycled long enough and deeply enough to produce genuine structural fittedness.

Optimal grip is neither the agent’s internal state nor the formation field’s structural property. It is a relational achievement: the specific quality of a specific relationship between a specific practitioner and a specific formation field, produced by a specific Dao of cycling through the A Frame’s modes. Cook Ding’s knife-work is optimal grip: the practitioner, the instrument, and the formation field in a relationship of such structural fittedness that the action flows without forcing, that the Li shows itself before the mind names it, that the Dao walks without effort. This is Karaoguz’s Attunement, Shan’s excellence-as-capacity-held-in-coherence, Fuller’s tensegrity-in-motion, and Wittgenstein’s showing-what-cannot-be-said, simultaneously.

Karaoguz, Wittgenstein, and Shan: The Grammar of Attunement

❧ ✶ ❧

WITTGENSTEIN —

“If a lion could speak, we could not understand him. — What has to be accepted, the given, is — so one could say — forms of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (1953) p.235, p.226

Wittgenstein’s most vertiginous claim, placed in the Karaoguz-Shan-Wittgenstein three-way as the most precise account of what attunement failure looks like from the outside. The lion speaks: the signals are produced, the communication is attempted. We cannot understand: not because we lack a translation algorithm but because we have not walked the Dao that would give us the form of life within which the lion’s speech has its meaning. Understanding is not a matter of matching propositions; it is a matter of shared formation. The A Frame applied to the lion problem: the agent who has not cycled through enough Attend-Appreciate-Act encounters with the lion’s form of life will attend to the sounds, appreciate them as foreign, and act on their incomprehension. Attunement with the lion requires the lion’s Dao.

KARAOGUZ —

“Appreciation is the bridge between perception and wise action, where understanding and value come together. It includes discernment, context-awareness, and appraisal — sorting signal from noise, weighing relevance, and identifying what the situation calls for.”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Appreciation as the bridge: the A-Frame’s middle movement, between Attend (open receptivity to the formation field) and Act (response from structural attunement). Appreciation is not evaluation; it is the specific quality of engagement that allows the formation’s own structure to become visible to the practitioner’s formation. This is what Cook Ding’s first three years were developing: not new skills but the appreciation that makes the articulations of the actual formation visible. After nineteen years, appreciation has become so complete that it is no longer distinguishable from perception. The A-Frame cycle has dissolved into a single continuous movement of structural attunement.

SHAN —

“Li is what is carried below the surface. It is not less real for being carried below. The practitioner who has walked the Dao long enough will sense the Li before they can say it.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

The lion passage. Wittgenstein’s most vertiginous claim: if a lion could speak, we could not understand him, not because we would lack a translation algorithm, but because the lion’s form of life — the Dao it has walked, the formation field it has been shaped by, the Li it reads in its world — is so radically different from ours that even perfect syntactic translation would produce semantic emptiness. Understanding is not a matter of matching propositions; it is a matter of shared formation. The practitioner who has not walked the specific Dao cannot understand the Li that the Dao produces, however perfect their ability to translate its verbal expression.

Karaoguz’s Appreciation is the A Frame’s account of what shared formation makes possible. When two practitioners have walked enough of the same Dao — have cycled through the Attend-Appreciate-Act loop in sufficiently similar formation fields — their Appreciation becomes mutually legible. They can sort the same signals from the same noise. They identify the same situational demands. They arrive at convergent valuations not because they have agreed in propositions but because they have agreed — in Wittgenstein’s precise sense — in form of life. The lion who could share our Dao would become comprehensible to us not through better translation but through shared formation.

Shan’s Li-below-the-surface is what Wittgenstein’s unsayable-that-shows-itself looks like from the practitioner’s perspective and what Karaoguz’s signal-from-noise looks like from the formation-field’s perspective. All three are describing the same structural reality: there is a dimension of the actual formation that exceeds any explicit propositional account of it, that is accessible only to the practitioner who has been formed to read it, and that shows itself in the quality of the practitioner’s action when the formation has been sufficient. The knife finds the hollow. The signal separates from the noise. The unsayable shows itself.

But Karaoguz adds something that neither Wittgenstein nor Shan alone provides: the developmental account. His rubric — accuracy of predictions improving, adaptability after surprise increasing, internal coherence of values and actions deepening — gives us a way to assess whether the A Frame cycling is producing genuine attunement or merely the illusion of it. Are our predictions of the formation field’s behaviour becoming more accurate? Are we recovering more quickly from the surprise of Move 37-level events? Is the gap between what we value and what we do closing? These are formation quality indicators. They are how we know whether the Dao we are walking is producing the Li we need.

“I have a hunch that Ann Pendleton-Jullian and John Seely Brown may have some suggestions in Design Unbound. Or check out “Medium Design” by Keller Easterling, who writes about dispositions **of interdependent objects and spaces — “disposition is a latent agency or immanent potential — a property or propensity within a context that unfolds over time.””

— Peter van (design blogger), on Design Unbound, referencing Keller Easterling

Disposition as latent agency or immanent potential unfolding over time: this is Valence in Shan’s seven-frequency framework. The formation field has a directional tendency before any specific action has enacted it. The skilled practitioner reads this directional tendency — appreciates, in Karaoguz’s vocabulary — and acts in alignment with it rather than against it. This is what Pendleton-Jullian and Brown mean by designing contexts in which things happen: the designer works with the immanent potential of the formation field, the propensities that override causality, the dispositions that will unfold regardless of whether the designer acknowledges them. The white water river has its own dispositions. The navigator who attunes to them survives. The navigator who ignores them does not.

Karaoguz and Pendleton-Jullian/Brown: The A Frame in White Water

❧ ✶ ❧

“The kind of world we are navigating now, the kinds of problems we want to have agency on, demand a new tool set in which imagination is not an embellishment or adjacency to real work in the world, but the keystone capacity upon which all other work depends because it advances understanding — empathy even — and it drives novelty. As a muscle of agility, it is necessary in whitewater.”

— Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian, interview on Design Unbound (2016)

A different kind of intelligence: not the optimisation of predefined goals but the structural attunement to the formation field’s own Li. Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s Design Unbound converges with Shan’s formation account: the white-water world requires practitioners who can read the formation field as it actually is rather than as prior Li predicts it to be. The heartwood is the formation’s invisible structural core; the surface is responsive, not initiatory. The practitioner formed to read heartwood can navigate white water because they are attuned to the formation’s own directional force — its Shī — rather than imposing their own direction.

“The way in which agents exercise agency in the arena is through attending to stimuli, appreciating their significance, and acting to achieve their objectives. This nonlinear, recursive process builds towards attunement, which is a skillful interaction with a context or environment; a flowing coupling.”

— Adam Karaoguz, A Deeper Pattern Part I (2023)

Flowing coupling: Karaoguz’s most precise phrase for what the A Frame produces at its completion. A flowing coupling between agent and arena is not the agent’s conquest of the arena, not the arena’s determination of the agent, but a specific relational quality — the optimal grip of a practitioner who has been formed to the specific grain of the specific formation field until action and response, perception and reality, begin to flow together without forcing. This is Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s heartwood in the making: the invisible structural formation of practitioner-formation-field relationship that eventually produces the capacity to navigate white water not by controlling it but by reading it.

The imagination that Pendleton-Jullian calls the keystone capacity is not the imagination of unconstrained fantasy. It is the Pragmatic Imagination: the capacity to perceive what is not yet actual but is structurally nascent in the current formation — what Kauffman calls the adjacent possible, what Shan calls the Dao that has not yet produced its Li, what Karaoguz calls the appreciative reading of a formation field that reveals what the situation calls for before any explicit analysis has named it. Appreciation, in the A Frame, IS the Pragmatic Imagination applied to the specific formation field of the specific arena.

The white water world that Pendleton-Jullian and Brown describe is the arena that demands the A Frame’s most complete deployment. In stable, predictable conditions, the Attend-Appreciate-Act cycle can be run at low intensity: the existing Li is adequate to the existing formation, attunement can be maintained through routine. In white water — radically contingent, hyperconnected, rapidly changing — the existing Li is systematically inadequate. Every new rapid is a new formation. Every moment requires fresh attention, deeper appreciation, more precisely calibrated action. And the practitioner who has developed attunement — who has cycled through the A Frame long enough to develop genuine structural fittedness to dynamic formation fields — is the practitioner who can navigate. The crash helmet is on the table. The nut is in your hand. The river does not wait.

The 6E Model: Karaoguz’s Cognitive Science Meets Shan’s Ontology

Karaoguz’s account of 6E cognition (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended, emotional, exapted) provides the cognitive-science underpinning for what Shan describes at the level of ontological formation theory. Each E corresponds to a dimension of the Dao-walk:

Embodied cognition: the practitioner’s body IS the formation instrument. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of practice are nineteen years of embodied formation — the progressive restructuring of his somatic attunement to the specific formation field of the ox. The knowledge is in the body before it is in the head. Shan: the path must be walked (embodied) before its grain can appear. Karaoguz: embodied cognition suggests that cognition is not solely a product of the brain, but is also influenced by sensory and motor experiences, bodily sensations.

Enacted cognition: every action is a formation event. The practitioner does not first form and then act; they form through acting. Shan’s Dao-walk is enacted cognition running to its full depth: the repeated, deliberate engagement with the specific formation field that progressively produces the structural attunement of the practitioner. Karaoguz: enacted cognition proposes that cognition is a process of actively engaging with the world and that our actions play a crucial role in shaping our thinking and understanding.

Extended cognition: the practitioner’s formation instruments — Cook Ding’s knife, the Polynesian navigator’s body-in-the-waves, the Go master’s accumulated game-sense — are extensions of the practitioner’s cognitive architecture into the formation field. Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s invisible machinery is extended cognition at organisational scale: the informal networks, the shared practices, the accumulated relational formation that extends individual cognitive capacity into the organisational formation field.

Emotional cognition: Karaoguz: the valence our mind assigns to a given stimulus will colour the processing which comes after. Shan’s Valence frequency is the formation field’s directional tendency — but the practitioner’s own emotional valence shapes what formation-field Valence they can register. The practitioner who approaches a formation field with anxiety (the anxiety of not-yet-sufficient formation) will attend differently, appreciate differently, and act differently than the practitioner who approaches with the settled confidence of adequate formation. Attunement includes somatic regulation — Karaoguz’s rubric item — precisely because emotional cognitive architecture shapes the quality of the entire A Frame cycle.

悖论 #13: The Agent is Always Already in Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

Do we have ideas, or do ideas have us? The question is already the answer. The idea that had Karaoguz — that would not let him write fiction until he had written it — was an idea whose structural resonance with his specific formation made it inevitable that it would find him when it did. He had been walking the Dao of Boyd and Vervaeke and McGilchrist and Alicia Juarrero for years. John Vervaeke’s participatory knowing framework — the knowledge gained through active engagement and participation, the practical wisdom that cannot be transmitted through propositions but only through formation — is Shan’s Li described as cognitive science. The Li of the A Frame was already latent in that formation. The idea did not arrive from outside; it crystallised from within. The Dao produced the Li at the moment the formation was sufficient to hold it.

This is the most structurally precise account of intellectual formation available: not the rational individual who surveys the landscape of ideas and selects the most useful one, but the practitioner who has walked long enough that the formation field presents its Li as an inevitability. The idea has the agent because the agent has walked the Dao that produced the idea’s formation conditions. We are not the measure of all things. The Dao is.

悖论 #14: Optimal Grip is Always Specific

Merleau-Ponty’s optimal grip is not a universal competence. It is always optimal grip on a specific formation field: the specific quality of fittedness between a specific practitioner and a specific arena that has been produced by a specific Dao of cycling through specific A Frame modes. Cook Ding’s optimal grip on the ox’s formation does not transfer to the formation field of the organisation, or the Go board, or the political negotiation. Each arena has its specific Li. Each specific Li requires a specific Dao. Each specific Dao produces a specific attunement. The practitioner who mistakes domain-specific attunement for universal wisdom is the practitioner of the most sophisticated possible attunement failure.

The A Frame is not a shortcut to attunement. It is a map of the territory that must be walked. Walking faster through the territory does not produce attunement faster; it produces faster walking. Karaoguz knows this. His rubric — are predictions improving? are we recovering from surprise? — is a patience instrument: it assumes that attunement takes time, that the loop must cycle many times, that each cycle produces marginal formation gain and that the total formation is the sum of many marginal gains accumulated over the specific Dao of the specific practitioner’s engagement with the specific arena. There is no shortcut to nineteen years.

Note on Shan Biography: A Single Canonical Account

Throughout this work, biographical material about Alice Jing Shan appears at multiple points. The canonical account, presented once and superseding all others: Alice Jing Shan holds a PhD from the University of Edinburgh (2023). She is the founder of ScholarLand Ltd and the originator of the Relational Dynamics framework. Her formation is constitutively bilingual and cross-traditional, shaped by simultaneous formation in Chinese philosophical tradition and Western complexity science. Her ten Substack essays (April–May 2026) constitute the primary body of original work analysed in this text. All other biographical references in earlier modules are subordinate to this account.

❧ ✶ ❧

THE TWELVE DIALOGUES

Maximum Dialectical Collision Across Four Traditions

❧ ✶ ❧

These twelve encounters are not summaries. They are not overviews. They are what happens when two formation traditions are pressed against each other until something sparks at the junction — the ozone smell of genuine collision, the crash helmet on the table, the nut thrown ahead on its cloth strip to read where it lands. Each dialogue runs through four movements: the initial convergence that draws the voices into the same structural space; the challenge that each voice poses to the other at its point of deepest divergence; and the synthesis that refuses to resolve — that holds the tension because the tension IS the recognition.

Dialogue 1: R. Buckminster Fuller and Alice Jing Shan

Tension, Coherence, and the Architecture of Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

FULLER —

“Tension is the great integrity. The universe is omnitensional integrity. All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics: Explorations in the Geometry of Thinking (1975)

Fuller’s declaration is the structural ground of the entire dialogue. Tension — not compression, not rigidity, not hierarchical authority — is the force that holds the universe together. The omnitensional integrity claim means that this force is non-local: it is not concentrated at points of contact but distributed continuously through the whole formation. Shan reads this as the precise physics of relational dynamics: what holds a formation together is not the properties of its individual elements but the continuous distribution of relational force through the topology of their connections. The dialogue with Shan begins precisely here: if tension is the great integrity, then excellence is the achievement of maximum distributed tension — the formation that holds coherently under the highest possible relational load.

SHAN —

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. The holding is not static. The holding is continuous, distributed, relational — like tension.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

The collision ignites immediately. Fuller and Shan are using different vocabularies to describe the same structural phenomenon: integrity achieved not through rigidity but through the continuous, distributed holding of tension across a relational network. Fuller’s tensegrity geodesic dome and Shan’s excellent practitioner are structural analogues — both maintain coherence not by eliminating movement but by ensuring that every perturbation is distributed through the whole, that no element bears load alone, that the continuous tension network IS the structure rather than something the structure possesses.

“Build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete. You never change things by fighting the existing reality.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Fuller’s most strategic claim, and the one that most directly names what Shan’s relational dynamics framework does. Not a critique of the existing models — not an argument against the Li-before-Dao assumption — but a new model that makes the existing models obsolete by being more structurally adequate to the actual. The new model does not defeat the old by confrontation; it displaces it by demonstrating that the actual formation is more accurately tracked by the new framework. Shan’s essays are this new model in action: each one demonstrates, through the specific traversal of specific formation territory, that the Dao-before-Li account produces insights that no prior Li could have predicted. The obsolescence follows from the demonstration.

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. What appears as sudden collapse was a long formation of fragility — the tensional network losing conductivity gradually, invisibly, until the threshold.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (Substack, April 2026)

Both claim that the apparent moment of failure is a lagging indicator of a prior structural dissolution. Fuller’s tensegrity structures fail not when a specific element is removed but when the tension network has been compromised to the point where the load cannot redistribute. Shan’s organisations do not collapse in one move; they collapse when the accumulated degradation of the relational holding capacity crosses a threshold. The event is sudden; the formation was long.

“I am not a thing — a noun. I seem to be a verb, an evolutionary process — an integral function of the universe.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, I Seem to Be a Verb (1970)

Fuller’s most philosophically compressed self-description, and Shan’s deepest structural ally. The noun/verb distinction is the distinction between substance ontology (things that have fixed properties) and process ontology (formations that are always already in formation). Shan’s ‘what is formed is still in formation’ is this claim applied to every specific Li: the pattern is always also the ongoing process of its own production. The verb ontology is not merely metaphorical; it is the recognition that every formation is a Dao — a specific direction of movement that cannot be frozen into a fixed noun without loss of the most essential thing about it. Fuller the verb: always in motion, always designing, always in the next thought. Shan’s framework: always in formation, always generating the next Li from the ongoing Dao.

“What is formed is still in formation. The path that has been walked is still being walked. Dao is not a completed achievement but a continuing activity.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (Substack, May 2026)

Shan’s most recursive claim, placed in the Dialogue immediately after Fuller’s noun/verb claim because together they form a complete ontological statement. What is formed is still in formation: the Li is never a completed product but always also the ongoing Dao of its own maintenance and development. The path that has been walked is still being walked: the formation history is not inert; it continues to shape the formation’s current movement. This is the most direct possible challenge to any static analysis of any formation: the snapshot is always already obsolete, because the formation it captures is always already elsewhere, always already further along its own Dao.

Where Fuller Challenges Shan

Fuller’s challenge is geometric. Tensegrity works because of specific angular relationships between compression islands and tension cables — the mathematics of the structure determines its load-bearing capacity. Shan’s relational dynamics is philosophically precise but geometrically under-specified. What are the angular relationships of her relational network? What determines how much tension any specific node can bear before the redistribution fails? Without this specificity, the framework describes the shape of the problem without providing the engineering. Fuller would say: the principles are right, but show me the vectors. Show me the geometry.

Further: Fuller’s tensegrity is spatial — it describes the distribution of forces in a structure at a moment. Shan’s framework is temporal — it describes how the formation came to be and continues forming. These are not the same question. Fuller answers ‘how does it hold?’; Shan asks ‘how did the holding come to be?’ The physics of the existing structure and the formation theory of how that structure came into existence are genuinely different inquiries. Both are necessary. Neither substitutes for the other.

Where Shan Challenges Fuller

Shan’s challenge is temporal. Tensegrity describes the distribution of forces within an already-formed structure. It presupposes the tensional network. But the network had to form. What specific Dao produced this specific topology of tension members and compression islands? Two tensegrity structures with identical geometry may have been produced by radically different formation histories, and their different formation histories may mean that they respond differently to perturbations that the geometry alone cannot predict. The formation of the tensegrity is the prior question — and it is Shan’s question, not Fuller’s.

“Integrity is the essence of everything successful.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Fuller’s ethical claim in its most compressed form. Integrity: not honesty in the moral sense but structural coherence in the tensional sense. The formation that maintains the distribution of relational tension through its whole — that does not allow load to concentrate at any single point, that does not sacrifice any element of the formation to protect another — achieves the structural integrity that makes success possible. The claim is both descriptive and normative: successful formations exhibit integrity, and formations that pursue success at the cost of integrity are structurally self-undermining. Shan’s corrective-capacity concept is this claim in formation-theory terms: the formation that maintains integrity under pressure is the formation that retains its capacity to respond to what it has not yet encountered.

“Smoothness is not always fidelity. When Dao begins to feel too familiar, too readily available — that is the warning. The path that offers no resistance may be the path off the cliff.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

Shan’s most important warning, placed as the counter-voice to Fuller’s integrity claim. The formation that achieves structural integrity can also achieve a dangerous smoothness: the Li that has become so well-established that it circulates without friction, that meets no resistance in its application to new formations, that feels like the natural description of every situation. This smoothness is the symptom of Li that has separated from Dao — of pattern that has lost its formation ground. The warning to Fuller: tensegrity, when it becomes a conceptual framework that explains everything smoothly, has become exactly the premature Li it was designed to overcome. The most powerful frameworks are the most dangerous: their power produces the smoothness that is the first sign of their expiration.

The Synthesis That Refuses Resolution

Neither cancels the other. Fuller provides the structural physics of formed integrity — the geometry of how a formation holds once formed. Shan provides the formation theory — the account of how the geometry came to be what it is, and why it holds this particular shape rather than another. Together: the universe may be omnitensional integrity, and it got that way by walking a Dao that produced a specific tensional topology. The topology is real. It required a Dao to form it. The Dao is still walking. The topology is still forming. This is tensegrity as a living process, not a finished structure. Fuller’s noun becoming Shan’s verb.

Dialogue 2: Wittgenstein (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus) and Alice Jing Shan

The Sayable, the Showable, and the Grain of the Real

❧ ✶ ❧

WITTGENSTEIN (TLP) —

“The world is everything that is the case. — What can be shown cannot be said. — There is indeed the inexpressible. This shows itself; it is the mystical.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) 1, 4.1212, 6.522

Three foundational claims stacked: the Tractatus opens with the ontological claim (the world is facts), introduces the picture theory (facts have logical form), and then names the inexpressible limit (what shows itself cannot be said). Placed in dialogue with Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim, the stack reveals a structural alignment: the world as facts (relational states of affairs) rather than things (substances) is Shan’s relational field; what shows itself is Li; what cannot be said is the depth of Li that always exceeds any naming of it. The Tractatus arrives at the inexpressible from logical analysis; Shan arrives at it from formation phenomenology. Both are tracking the same structural limit from different directions.

SHAN —

“Li is not always fully speakable. Sometimes it can only be demonstrated. The practitioner who has walked the Dao long enough will sense the Li before they can say it. This is not failure of language. It is the structure of formation.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

Two traditions, twenty-six centuries and ten thousand miles apart, arriving at the same recognition from opposite directions. Wittgenstein begins with logical analysis and arrives at the limit of the sayable — the boundary where language runs out and what is most structural about reality shows itself without being stateable. Shan begins with the phenomenology of formation and arrives at the Li that the formation produces but that always partially exceeds any naming of it. Both locate the deepest structural reality at the boundary of what propositions can do.

The most cited line in the Tractatus, and the one that most directly illuminates Shan’s bilingual formation claim. If the limits of language are the limits of world, then the practitioner who grows up inside two languages inhabits two worlds — and at the intersection of those two worlds, each set of limits becomes visible as limits rather than as the edge of the real. Shan’s cross-cultural project is the precise structural consequence of this claim: the limits of English-language complexity discourse become visible only from the formation position of Chinese philosophical vocabulary, and vice versa. The world is larger than any single language’s limits. The collision of two language-worlds is the Dao that produces the Li of genuine cross-cultural insight.

“My everyday life has involved translation — not just of words but of structural ecologies. The limits of my language shaped the limits of what I could see. But I grew up inside two languages. So I grew up inside two worlds.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine, but a Living Encounter (April 2026)

This is the Tractatus claim made biographical. Shan’s bilingual formation gave her access to two structural ecologies — two different sets of limits that, by being held simultaneously, revealed each other’s limits as limits rather than as the edge of the real. The practitioner who has walked only one Dao can mistake its Li for the structure of reality. The practitioner who has walked two genuinely different Daos knows that the Li of each is the product of its specific formation history — that other Lis are possible, that the sayable in any one tradition does not exhaust the showable.

“Ethics cannot be put into words. Ethics and aesthetics are one. The right method in philosophy would really be to say nothing except what can be said.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.421, 6.421, 6.53

The most concentrated mystical moment in the Tractatus, and the one that most directly connects to Shan’s excellence-as-showing claim. Ethics and aesthetics are one: both are structural features of the world that show themselves in the quality of practice without being stateable in any code or principle. The excellent practitioner’s ethics is visible in the quality of their engagement — in whether they approach the formation with genuine attunement or with a prior Li they are protecting. The aesthetics of Cook Ding’s knife-work is indistinguishable from its ethics: both are expressions of the same structural attunement to the actual grain of the actual formation.

“Excellence is not a concept. It is a quality of formation visible to those who have been formed to see it. Cook Ding’s excellence showed itself in the cut. His prince saw it, felt the sound of it, before any proposition about excellence could have named it.”

— Alice Jing Shan, paraphrasing Zhuangzi through the lens of relational dynamics

Shan’s challenge to Wittgenstein’s silence: the inexpressible is not merely beyond language; it is demonstrable through practice. The excellence of Cook Ding’s work showed itself to his prince before any proposition about excellence could have captured it. The sound of the knife, the rhythm of the work, the complete absence of forcing — these showed the Li of the formation’s attunement. This is not anti-propositional; it is the recognition that propositions about excellence are always downstream of the demonstration that grounds them. The concept of excellence is the Li produced by the Dao of sustained engagement with excellent practice. Excellence itself is the Dao.

“Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 7

The last line: Wittgenstein ends the Tractatus with this sentence and stops. Shan begins her essays the next morning and writes again. Both are right. The silence is the recognition of the limit. The writing is the Dao of approaching the limit from a different direction. The tension between them — the tension between falling silent and continuing to write — is itself the finest attunement that Heraclitus identifies: things bearing in opposite directions, the opposition that generates the structural reality neither can reach alone. Shan writes because the Chinese philosophical tradition has another way of approaching the inexpressible: through demonstration, through exemplar, through the showing that precedes the saying. The ladder is still there. The throwing away is still ahead.

Where the Tractatus Challenges Shan

The TLP challenge: Shan’s essays attempt to say what, on the Tractatus account, can only be shown. Every sentence in this paper that attempts to describe Li, to name the formation process, to give a propositional account of what the Dao-walk produces — is, strictly speaking, non-sensical in Wittgenstein’s technical sense. The ladder must be climbed and then thrown away. And Shan keeps climbing, keeps writing, keeps producing new essays. Is she simply more optimistic about language’s reach than Wittgenstein? Or is she claiming that what shows itself can be approached through demonstration — through prose that shows its Li even when it cannot say it?

Where Shan Challenges the Tractatus

Shan’s response: the silence is too quick, and it is the wrong silence. Wittgenstein ends TLP with a single sentence. Shan ends each essay with another essay forming. The demonstrable is not nothing: it is precisely what the whole tradition of Chinese philosophy has been doing for two thousand years — approaching the unsayable through the showing of the practice, through the exemplar, through the form that points toward the formation without claiming to contain it. Cook Ding does not explain; he demonstrates. The demonstration IS the content. This is not a failure of the Chinese philosophical tradition to achieve propositional rigour; it is its most deliberate structural achievement.

Synthesis

The Tractatus and Shan’s essays share the same structure: both are ladders pointing toward what the ladder cannot name. Wittgenstein’s instruction to throw away the ladder is itself written on the ladder. Shan’s instruction to walk the Dao before naming the Li is itself a named Li. Neither can escape the paradox. Both know it. The paradox is not a failure; it is the sign that both have reached the genuine limit — the place where the formation exceeds the language that the formation itself produced. 悖论: The most structurally honest philosophical writing is writing that shows its own inadequacy to what it is trying to show.

Dialogue 3: Wittgenstein (Philosophical Investigations) and Alice Jing Shan

Forms of Life, Inherited Paths, and the Grammar of Practice

❧ ✶ ❧

WITTGENSTEIN (PI) —

“What has to be accepted, the given, is — so one could say — forms of life. — Philosophy simply puts everything before us, and neither explains nor deduces anything. — Don’t think, but look!”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (1953) p.226, §126, §66

The PI’s most consequential claim for Shan’s cross-cultural project. The given that must be accepted is not a metaphysical necessity but a historical formation: the specific accumulated practices, assumptions, and structuring conventions that constitute a form of life. For the Chinese international student in the Edinburgh seminar, two forms of life are simultaneously operative, each with its own different structuring of what participation means, what contribution looks like, what silence signals. The collision of two given forms of life is not a problem to be solved by better design. It is the specific Dao that Shan’s work has walked, and the Li that emerged from that walking is the relational dynamics framework itself.

SHAN —

“Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one. The forms of participation that feel natural — that require no deliberation, that emerge as the obvious response to the situation — these were formed long before we arrived.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (Substack, April 2026)

The later Wittgenstein is Shan’s deepest Western interlocutor. His forms of life are exactly what Shan calls the inherited Dao: the accumulated, sedimented, largely pre-reflective formation of shared practice into which every practitioner enters. When a Chinese postgraduate student sits in an Edinburgh seminar room and finds certain forms of participation natural and others impossible, they are not simply making choices. They are inside a form of life that has formed them to find certain participations natural — and inside another form of life (the Edinburgh seminar) that has formed different participations as natural. The mismatch is a collision of forms of life. It cannot be resolved by better translation. It requires a Dao-walk.

“The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life. — To imagine a language means to imagine a form of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §23, §19

Language as activity within a life-form: the parallel structure to Shan’s bilingual formation is exact. When Shan writes in English about Dao and Li, the speaking is part of an activity — the specific activity of cross-cultural complexity scholarship — and part of a life-form — the bilingual intellectual practice that is her specific formation. The same Chinese characters, deployed in a different activity and life-form, would produce different meaning through different use. The meaning is not in the characters; it is in the specific relational embedding of the characters in the specific activity of the specific life-form. This is why translation is always formation-transformation rather than meaning-transfer: the activity changes, the life-form changes, the meaning changes.

“A path becomes a path only through repeated walking. This is as true of ideas as it is of ground. The conceptual paths that feel most natural are the ones that have been walked most often, by the most people, across the longest time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (Substack, April 2026)

Speaking as activity: Wittgenstein’s PI is, at its foundation, an account of language as practice — as Dao, not as Li. Language is not a system of propositions that map onto a prior reality; it is a family of practices that constitute the realities they navigate. Shan’s account of Dao as the repeated walking that produces Li is this claim about language generalised to all formation: the practice precedes and produces the pattern. The PI Wittgenstein and Shan are both anti-representationalists in the same specific sense: neither believes that the practitioner arrives at the formation with a prior mental model that then maps onto it. The formation is walked into existence.

“My spade is turned. I have reached bedrock, and this is where my spade is turned. — I am not able to say “what I know” and make it the foundation of my philosophical convictions.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §217; On Certainty §403

The turned spade: not ignorance but depth. The practitioner who has reached bedrock does not have another layer of justification to offer; they have the bare fact of their own formation. Cook Ding after nineteen years has reached bedrock: he does not justify his cuts; he makes them from the specific attunement that his specific Dao has produced. The practitioner who cannot reach bedrock — who always has another framework to deploy, another analysis to offer, another Li to apply — has not yet achieved the formation depth that makes genuine structural practice possible. The spade is turned when the formation has become the practitioner.

“The neonatal gut does not negotiate with the milk. It forms. The contact produces structural change that could not have been specified in advance. This is formation at its most elemental: encounter precedes understanding.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence (Substack, May 2026)

The neonatal gut in two sentences: the most compressed possible statement of the holding-capacity thesis. The contact is immediate: coupling is real. The readiness is not: sequence is equally real. The gut does not choose whether to be ready; it forms into readiness through the specific irreversible sequence of its specific developmental Dao. No amount of coupling — no amount of simultaneous co-determination — can substitute for the formation that produces the readiness. Juarrero: time and context are as much constituents of behaviour as any component’s intrinsic properties. Prigogine: at bifurcation points, history enters. The readiness IS the history.

The PI Challenge to Shan

The PI challenge is about the lever of change. If forms of life are the given — what has to be accepted — where is the Archimedean point from which genuine formation change becomes possible? Wittgenstein’s therapeutic philosophy aims not to produce new formation but to dissolve the philosophical confusions that arise when we try to operate outside our forms of life. But Shan’s framework promises more: it promises a Dao that can produce genuinely new Li, even within an inherited form of life. This is a stronger claim than Wittgenstein’s. It requires justification that his framework alone cannot supply.

Shan’s Challenge to the PI

The PI does not account for the practitioner who has walked two forms of life simultaneously — who is inside the Chinese form of life AND inside the Western complexity discourse, who carries both formations and can use each to see the limits of the other. Shan’s bilingual formation is not merely interesting biography; it is the structural demonstration that forms of life are not hermetically sealed. The given can be given differently. The inherited path can be seen AS an inherited path rather than AS the path, and that seeing is the first movement of genuine formation change.

Synthesis

Don’t think, but look: PI §66. This is Shan’s method stated as philosophical instruction. The Dao-walk is looking — genuine, formation-sufficient attention to the actual formation field, prior to the conceptualisation that the look will produce. The practitioner who approaches a complex situation with a prior Li is not looking; they are confirming. Wittgenstein’s instruction and Shan’s are identical: look first. Walk the Dao. Then the Li will appear.

Dialogue 4: Zhu Xi and Alice Jing Shan

The Most Important Wrong Answer in Chinese Philosophy

❧ ✶ ❧

ZHU XI —

理者，天理也。理在先，氣在後。天地之間，一理而已。 — Lǐ zhě, tiān lǐ yě. Lǐ zài xiān, qì zài hòu. Tiān dì zhī jiān, yī lǐ ér yǐ. — Li is the heavenly pattern. Li is prior; qi (vital force/matter) is posterior. Between heaven and earth, there is only one Li — Zhu Xi, Zhuzi Yulei

SHAN —

“Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. The path must be walked before its inner grain can appear. This is not a preference. It is the ontological sequence.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (Substack, May 2026)

This is the decisive collision. Not a productive misunderstanding or a matter of complementary emphases. A genuine contradiction at the foundation. Zhu Xi says Li is prior: the pattern exists before the formation that instantiates it. Shan says the Dao is prior: the pattern emerges from the formation that produces it. Both cannot be right. And the stakes are enormous, because this is not merely a debate about metaphysics: it is the foundational question of every management intervention, every complexity navigation, every attempt to understand what a specific organisation or formation is doing and how it can be worked with.

格物致知。天下之物，莫不有理。 — Gé wù zhì zhī. Tiān xià zhī wù, mò bù yǒu lǐ. — Investigate things to extend knowledge. All things under heaven have their Li — Zhu Xi, on the Great Learning

“The jade cutter does not impose the grain on the jade. They read it. The grain was there before the cutter arrived. But the grain only appeared — only became visible, workable, navigable — through the specific formation of the specific cutter who had walked the Dao of jade long enough to read it.”

— Alice Jing Shan, elaborating the jade metaphor

Zhu Xi would say: the jade’s grain exists whether or not any cutter has developed the capacity to read it. The pattern is cosmologically prior. Shan would say: the grain exists as a physical structure, but the specific Li of the specific jade — its workability in specific directions, its specific yield to the specific tools, its specific responsiveness to the specific cutter’s attention — is not cosmologically prior. It emerges in the specific encounter between the specific jade and the specific formation of the specific practitioner. Take away the practitioner’s formation and you do not reveal the jade’s prior Li; you have a piece of stone.

理一分殊。 — Lǐ yī fēn shū. — One Li, many manifestations — Zhu Xi’s core principle

“The same formation field — the same organisation, the same cultural encounter, the same moment of complexity — will yield different Li to different practitioners. Not because Li is subjective. Because Li is relational: it is the grain of the encounter, not the grain of the thing alone.”

— Alice Jing Shan, paraphrasing the structural implication of Relational Dynamics

The same formation field looks different depending on the Dao walked inside it: this is the most important practical implication of the relational-precedes-dynamics claim. Two practitioners in the same organisation, walking different Daos, inhabit genuinely different formation fields — not because their perceptions differ but because the Li they have produced through their specific Dao-walking genuinely differs. The formation field’s salience structure is not fixed; it is constituted through the encounter between the specific practitioner-formation and the specific formation-field configuration. Bateson: information is any difference that makes a difference. Which differences make differences depends on which Dao has been walked.

The Zhu Xi Challenge

Without prior Li, there is no grain to be followed. The knife would find nothing. If the jade’s pattern is not prior to the cutter’s engagement, what guides the cutting? Pure contingency? The practitioner’s arbitrary Li imposed on resistant material? Zhu Xi’s Li-first metaphysics is not naive realism; it is the recognition that complex formations have genuine structural coherence — that some formations are more viable than others, that some Lis are more adequate to the actual than others, that the practitioner’s formation encounter is with something real and structurally determinate, not with a plastic surface waiting to receive whatever Li the practitioner projects.

Shan’s Demolition

This is the most important wrong answer in Chinese philosophy, and its wrongness is catastrophic in practice. The manager who arrives with a pre-formed Li — who treats the organisation as the instantiation of a cosmic principle they already possess — is Zhu Xi’s practitioner. They will always be wrong at the most important moments. Not because their Li is bad. Because the specific Li of the specific formation cannot be specified in advance of the specific Dao of genuine engagement with it. Prigogine supports Shan: at bifurcation points, the specific structure that emerges is not determined by any prior principle. The formation is genuinely open. The Li is genuinely new. Zhu Xi’s cosmos is an elegant closed system. Shan’s world is still in formation.

Synthesis

The synthesis is not the middle: it is the question the collision forces open. Is there a Li prior to formation, or only a formation that produces Li? The evidence of complexity science — of dissipative structures, of the adjacent possible, of Move 37 — supports Shan. The evidence of the practitioner who reads the formation field with uncanny precision — who arrives and immediately recognises what the situation calls for — might seem to support Zhu Xi. The synthesis: the practitioner’s uncanny precision is not access to prior cosmic Li. It is the Li produced by their own prior formation — the Dao they have walked that makes them sensitive to formations they have not yet explicitly encountered. The prior Li is always a prior Dao’s Li. 悖论: The most rigorous account of structural order is the one that refuses to locate order before the process that produces it.

Dialogue 5: Alicia Juarrero and Alice Jing Shan

Enabling Constraints, Holding Capacity, and the Architecture of Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

JUARRERO —

“Operating as enabling constraints, context-sensitive constraints make complexity possible.”

— Alicia Juarrero, Dynamics in Action: Intentional Behavior as a Complex System (MIT Press, 1999) [VERIFIED: Goodreads/primary source]

SHAN —

“The establishment of context-sensitive constraints is the phase change that transforms a collection of sufficient components into a complex adaptive system. Coherence is induced by meaningful constraints.”

— Alicia Juarrero, Dynamics in Action (1999)

The most precise account of the formation threshold that separates a collection of interacting elements from a genuinely complex adaptive system. Before the phase change: the elements interact but their interactions do not create the conditions for their own further interaction. After: the constraints that emerge from the interactions become sensitive to the context that the interactions have created — the system begins to structure its own possibilities. This is Shan’s holding-capacity threshold: the formation achieves holding capacity when its constraints become context-sensitive, when the Li begins to actively shape the Dao that produces further Li. The threshold is irreversible: once achieved, the system is a different ontological entity.

“Excellence is not found at the extremes. Not in the frozen order where pattern has calcified into rigidity. Not in the dissolving chaos where no grain can hold. It is found — and maintained — at the dynamic edge where constraint enables and coherence holds.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

The phase transition claim is the most structurally precise point of alignment. Juarrero identifies the moment at which a collection of sufficient components becomes a complex adaptive system as the phase change when context-sensitive constraints are established. This is Shan’s holding capacity forming: the moment at which the relational field has sufficient structure to maintain coherence under the specific pressures it will face. Before the phase transition: parts. After: a formation capable of forming Li.

“Coupling does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see. The developmental psychologist who watches two infants at the same chronological age can see the sequence. The sequence is real. But the coupling — the way each developmental stage enables and constrains the next — is equally real, and it is what the developmental timeline alone cannot show.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence (Substack, May 2026)

Coupling does not abolish sequence: the essay’s central claim, and one of the most structurally important in Shan’s body of work. In complex systems, everything is connected to everything simultaneously — the coupling is real. But the sequence — the before-and-after, the formation history, the specific order in which things happened — is equally real and equally causally efficacious. The practitioner who sees only the coupling — who treats the complex system as a simultaneity without history — misses everything that Prigogine identifies as the arrow of time, that Shan identifies as the Dao, that Wittgenstein identifies as the inherited form of life. The sequence is the source of structure. Coupling does not dissolve it.

Juarrero’s Challenge

Juarrero’s challenge: Shan’s framework needs to specify the phase-transition mechanism. Juarrero identifies the specific physical process by which a collection of components becomes a complex adaptive system: the establishment of context-sensitive constraints that create coherence. What is Shan’s equivalent mechanism? At what specific point does Dao-walking produce the phase transition from accumulated experience to genuine formation — the transformation in the practitioner that makes Move 37 available? Shan describes the formation process but not its critical threshold.

Shan’s Challenge

The phase-transition account is temporally thin. It identifies the moment of transition without accounting for the formation history that makes the system ready. Some systems approach the phase transition with enough structural integrity to produce viable Li on the other side; others approach it with accumulated fragility and produce collapse. What determines this difference? Shan’s Dao-walk account: the specific quality of the formation history — the specific Daos walked, the specific Li produced, the specific corrective capacity developed — determines whether the system at the bifurcation point has what it needs to form coherently on the other side. Juarrero’s phase transition needs Shan’s formation theory to explain why some transitions succeed and others fail.

Synthesis

Together: the Dao-walk (Shan) produces the specific formation history that builds the structural integrity (Juarrero) sufficient for the phase transition to produce viable Li (Juarrero/Shan) rather than entropic dissolution. The constraint is the freedom. The holding is the releasing. The formation is the capacity. 悖论: The system that is most constrained by its formation is the system most capable of genuine response to what it has not yet encountered.

Dialogue 6: Zhichang Zhu / WSR and Alice Jing Shan

The Grammar of Li in Practice: Three Registers, One Reality

❧ ✶ ❧

ZHU (WSR) —

“知物理 (zhī wùlǐ), 惟事理 (wéi shílǐ), 慢人理 (guān rénlǐ) — Knowing wuli (the physical pattern of things), sensing shili (the logic of the situation), attending to renli (the human relational pattern): these are not three separate investigations but three irreducible registers in which the Li of any complex situation shows itself.”

— Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu, WSR: A Systems Approach for Information Systems Research (Journal of the Operational Research Society, 2000) [VERIFIED POSITION]

SHAN —

“Li is the inner grain — the structural pattern that makes the thing what it is. But the same formation will show different grain depending on whether you approach it through its physical regularities, its situational texture, or its human relational field. The Li is one; the registers are three.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

WSR and Shan’s relational dynamics are sister frameworks: both emerge from the Chinese philosophical tradition’s account of Li, both are attempting to make that account operational in complex real-world situations, and both insist that the complexity of the situation is irreducibly tripartite — that wuli, shili, and renli cannot be collapsed into each other or ranked hierarchically without loss. The encounter between them is the most intimate in this paper, and therefore the most productive.

WSR’s Challenge to Shan

WSR’s challenge: operational specificity. Shan’s Dao-before-Li framework tells us that the formation precedes the pattern. But in the specific situation — the water management bureau, the university seminar, the failing manufacturing company — the practitioner needs more than the ontological instruction. They need to know where to look, what to attend to, how to integrate what they find. WSR provides this: the three registers are not a framework imposed on the situation but a structured sensitivity that helps the attuned practitioner name what they are already sensing across multiple dimensions simultaneously.

Shan’s Challenge to WSR

Shan’s challenge: WSR can become its own form of Li-before-Dao if applied without the prior walk. The practitioner who arrives at a complex situation already looking for wuli, shili, and renli — who has the WSR framework so firmly in place that it pre-structures their perception — risks producing WSR-compliant analysis rather than genuine engagement with the actual. The methodology is sound; the formation that makes it genuinely useful rather than merely applied requires the Dao that WSR cannot itself specify.

Synthesis

Shan provides the ontological grounding (the Dao of the formation precedes the Li that WSR looks for); WSR provides the operational grammar (three irreducible registers in which the Li appears). The complete practice: walk the Dao first, remain genuinely open to the specific formation, then use WSR as the structured sensitivity that helps you name what you are already sensing. The best methodology is the one you forget you are using because you have been formed enough that its three registers are simply how you see. 悖论: The methodology that knows itself as a methodology has already failed.

Dialogue 7: Ilya Prigogine and Alice Jing Shan

Dissipation, Bifurcation, and the Arrow of Formation

❧ ✶ ❧

PRIGOGINE —

“Non-equilibrium is the source of order. The farther a system is from equilibrium, the more sensitive it is to fluctuations. Near bifurcation points, tiny perturbations can produce macroscopic effects. Order out of chaos — but not at the cost of chaos; through it.”

— Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers, Order Out of Chaos (1984)

Prigogine’s most important claim for the strategic stakes of formation. Maximum sensitivity at maximum distance from equilibrium: the system that is most alive, most dynamic, most genuinely complex is the system that is most vulnerable to specific perturbations. The bifurcation point is the moment of maximum opportunity and maximum danger simultaneously. Shan’s corrective capacity claim: the formation that has walked the Dao of genuine structural development is the formation that arrives at the bifurcation with the specific sensitivity required to read which direction the Shī is leaning. Not the safe formation but the formed formation — the one whose Dao has produced the specific Li needed for the specific bifurcation.

SHAN —

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. The formation becomes critical long before the visible crisis. And at the moment of maximum criticality — the bifurcation point, in Prigogine’s terms — the practitioner who has walked the Dao long enough has developed the specific corrective capacity that the moment requires.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (Substack, April 2026)

Prigogine’s dissipative structures and Shan’s relational dynamics share the deepest structural alignment of any two frameworks in this text: both insist that order is an achievement requiring continuous energetic input, that the most significant structural events happen at far-from-equilibrium conditions, and that at bifurcation points the formation is maximally sensitive to specific perturbations that determine which new structure emerges from the dissolution of the old.

“Dao is not reversible. The path walked cannot be unwalked. The formation that has occurred is the condition of all subsequent formation. This is not a limitation. It is what makes formation real rather than hypothetical.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Dao Models of Mutual Generation (Substack, April 2026)

Irreversibility and temporal asymmetry: both Prigogine and Shan ground their accounts in the genuine directionality of time. The universe has a temporal grain — a before-and-after structure — that is not a cognitive imposition but an ontological feature of formation. The Dao-walk cannot be reversed because the formation it produces has genuinely changed the practitioner: the Li produced by nineteen years of Cook Ding’s practice cannot be undone by working backwards through those nineteen years. The arrow of formation runs in one direction.

Prigogine’s Challenge

At bifurcation points, the physics is genuinely indeterminate. The fluctuation that triggers the bifurcation is, at the level of thermodynamic analysis, not predictable from the system’s prior state.
