Shan’s framework suggests that the formation history of the system shapes which bifurcation is most likely. But ‘most likely’ is not ‘determined’. Shan’s framework, on its strongest reading, might claim to produce practitioners capable of sensing which bifurcation is approaching — but the physics insists that no formation history, however rich, can eliminate the genuine openness of the bifurcation.

Shan’s Response

The framework does not promise to predict outcomes. It describes the formation conditions that make certain kinds of Li more or less likely to emerge from the bifurcation. The practitioner with sufficient corrective capacity does not control the bifurcation; they cultivate the formation conditions that increase the probability of viable Li emerging from it. This is not prediction; it is wisdom. The distinction is everything.

Synthesis

Prigogine provides the physics of the bifurcation moment; Shan provides the formation theory of bifurcation readiness. Together: the moment of maximum sensitivity (Prigogine) is the moment when the formation capacity of the practitioner (Shan) has the greatest potential leverage. Nothing collapses in one move, and nothing is saved in one move. The work is the formation — the patient, specific, Dao-walking that produces the corrective capacity that the bifurcation moment will either require or reveal as absent. 悖论: The moment of maximum uncertainty is also the moment of maximum formation opportunity. The bifurcation does not close; it opens.

Dialogue 8: Gregory Bateson and Alice Jing Shan

The Metapattern, Li, and the Ecology of Mind

❧ ✶ ❧

BATESON —

“What is the pattern that connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all four of them to me? And me to you? And all six of us to the amoeba in one direction and to the back-ward schizophrenic in another? The pattern which connects is a metapattern.”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature: A Necessary Unity (1979)

Bateson’s question is the question Shan’s framework answers from the inside. The pattern that connects is Li at the most general level: the specific structural principle that diverse formations share despite their surface differences. But here the dialogue intensifies: Bateson’s metapattern is discovered through ecological observation, through the patient watching of formation diversity that allows the underlying structural commonality to reveal itself. This is the Dao-before-Li method applied to the natural world. The metapattern does not precede the observations; it emerges from them. Bateson walked the Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient attention to biological diversity, and the Li of the metapattern appeared as the grain of that specific Dao.

SHAN —

“The major problems in the world are the result of the difference between how nature works and the way people think. The unit of survival is the organism plus its environment.”

— Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)

The unit of survival is the organism plus its environment: this is Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim stated as ecological theory. The organism is not the unit; the organism-in-its-formation-field is the unit. Remove the formation field and you have not simplified the analysis; you have destroyed its subject matter. The crab without its ocean is not a simpler crab; it is a dying crab. The practitioner without their formation field is not a simpler practitioner; they are a practitioner who has lost the Dao that their Li was produced to navigate.

Bateson’s Challenge

The ecology of mind challenge: Shan’s framework is focused on the formation field and the practitioner’s capacity to read it. But Bateson asks what the Li of the practitioner’s mind is — what metapatterns their formation has made available as perceptual categories. The practitioner who cannot see the metapattern that connects the crab to the orchid cannot read the Li of formations that span those categories. Bateson’s ecology of mind is the account of how the practitioner’s cognitive formation shapes what Li they can perceive.

Shan’s Challenge

Bateson’s ecology risks circularity: if the mind and its environment are constitutively entangled, how does genuine learning occur? How does the mind develop sensitivity to metapatterns it has not yet encountered? Shan’s Dao-walk provides the mechanism: the specific, repeated, formation-sufficient engagement with the actual that progressively restructures the practitioner’s cognitive ecology. The formation history is the bridge between the mind as it is and the mind as it becomes capable of reading.

Synthesis

Dialogue 9: Stuart Kauffman and Alice Jing Shan

The Edge of Chaos, the Adjacent Possible, and the Formation of Excellence

❧ ✶ ❧

KAUFFMAN —

“Systems at the edge of chaos tend to exhibit the richest possible behaviour. Frozen systems cannot explore new configurations; systems in chaos have no coherence to explore with. The edge is where computation, adaptation, and evolution are most powerful.”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1995)

Kauffman’s most important structural claim for understanding what Shan means by excellence. Rich behaviour at the edge: not random (chaos), not predetermined (frozen order), but genuinely creative — the domain where the formation can explore new configurations while maintaining enough coherence to exploit what it finds. Shan’s excellence is this edge-state maintained as a formation achievement rather than encountered as a transient condition. The excellent practitioner does not visit the edge; they have developed the specific formation that enables them to maintain edge-proximity under the specific pressures of their specific domain. Cook Ding at the edge of chaos: the cut that follows the grain without forcing it, that exploits the maximum structural sensitivity of the formation at the moment of maximum coherence.

SHAN —

“Excellence is capacity held in coherence under constraint over time. Not at the frozen end. Not at the chaotic end. Held at the dynamic edge where each perturbation is distributed through the whole without destroying the whole.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

The convergence is structurally exact: both Kauffman and Shan locate maximum adaptive capacity at the boundary between order and chaos, and both insist that this position is not a stable equilibrium but a dynamic structural condition that must be actively maintained. Kauffman’s edge-of-chaos systems and Shan’s excellent formations are structurally identical — both are neither frozen (rigidly ordered, unable to adapt) nor dissolved (chaotically disordered, unable to maintain coherence) but held at the productive tension between the two.

“The practitioner who has walked the Dao long enough to read the Li of the current formation is also the practitioner who can see the adjacent possible — the specific Li that the current formation is ready to produce next, the Move 37 that the standard game tree does not include but that this specific formation makes available.”

— Alice Jing Shan, AlphaGo’s Move 37 and the Adjacent Possible

The adjacent possible: Kauffman’s most operationally important concept for Shan’s framework. The adjacent possible is the set of formations that are one step from the current formation — reachable but not yet actual, enabled by the current Li but not yet enacted. The practitioner who has developed sufficient structural attunement can read the adjacent possible of a specific formation — can sense which directions are structurally open, which Li is ready to crystallise, where Move 37 is. This is not prediction; it is the formation-sufficient reading of current structure.

Kauffman’s Challenge

The edge of chaos cannot be permanently occupied. Real systems oscillate across the edge boundary rather than holding it as a stable position. How does Shan’s excellent formation maintain its position at the edge without either rigidifying into frozen order or dissolving into entropic chaos? The physics of the edge does not support the claim of sustained structural position. Kauffman would say: you can create conditions that make edge-proximity more likely, but you cannot hold the edge.

Shan’s Response

The sustained coherence of excellence is not a fixed position but a dynamic practice — the continuous, active cultivation of the structural conditions that keep the formation close enough to the edge to maintain adaptive capacity. This is Fuller’s tensegrity in temporal form: not held in place by being fixed, but held in place by continuously redistributing the tension that would otherwise cause collapse. The excellent practitioner is not statically at the edge; they are continuously forming the conditions that return the formation to the edge when it drifts.

Synthesis

Excellence at the edge is not a destination but a practice of continuous return. The biosphere is always doing something for the first time because it is always at the edge; and the excellent practitioner is always forming the next Li because they have developed the capacity to return to the edge after each perturbation that would otherwise push the formation into either rigidity or dissolution. 悖论: The most stable formation is the one that is most continuously in formation. Stability is achieved through perpetual return to the edge, not through arrival at equilibrium.

Dialogue 10: Francisco Varela, Humberto Maturana, and Alice Jing Shan

Autopoiesis, Structural Coupling, and the Prior Relational Field

❧ ✶ ❧

MATURANA —

“A living system is organised as a network of productions of components which, through their interactions and transformations, continuously regenerate and realise the network of productions that produced them. The living system is operationally closed and structurally determined.”

— Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, The Tree of Knowledge (1987)

Maturana and Varela’s formal definition of autopoiesis, and the most precise available account of what Shan means when she says ‘what is formed is still in formation’. The living system is its own production: it produces the components that constitute it, which in turn produce the network that produces them. This is the Li producing the Dao producing the Li: the circular, self-sustaining production of structure through its own operation. For Shan, every genuine formation has this character: it does not merely persist; it actively produces the conditions of its own persistence. The formation that loses this self-producing quality — that ceases to generate the relational, cultural, and structural components that sustain it — has begun its collapse.

SHAN —

“What is formed is still in formation. The formation is not prior to the process that produces it; the process and the formation are continuously co-producing each other. This is not a theory about life. It is the structure of all genuine complexity.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

Maturana and Varela’s autopoiesis and Shan’s relational dynamics both describe formation as self-production: the formed thing produces the formation process that produces the formed thing. Both resist the idea of a prior blueprint. Both insist that the system’s organisation is not something imposed from outside but something the system produces through its own operation. The living system is its own Dao, and its Li is the continuously-produced-and-reproduced pattern of that Dao.

“The path does not aim. It forms. The Dao that produces the Li does not know in advance what Li it will produce. It walks. The Li that emerges from the walking is what the walking produces, not what it intended.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Dao Models of Mutual Generation (Substack, April 2026)

Structural drift without teleology: both Maturana/Varela and Shan explicitly reject the idea that formation processes aim at predetermined endpoints. The autopoietic system drifts with only the constraint of maintaining its own organisation; Shan’s Dao walks with only the constraint of maintaining viability. In both cases, the direction of formation is determined not by a prior Li (a goal, a blueprint, a cosmic principle) but by the ongoing engagement of the formation with its specific conditions.

The Autopoietic Challenge

If the system is structurally determined — if it responds to perturbations according to its own existing structure rather than according to the properties of the perturbation — then genuine learning of genuinely new Li is structurally impossible. The system can only produce Li that its prior structure makes possible. Move 37 is not available to the human Go master not because they lack intelligence but because their structure cannot produce it. Shan’s account of the Dao-walk producing genuinely new Li requires a mechanism for structural change that autopoiesis, on its strict reading, does not provide.

Shan’s Response

The structural determination account is right that the system responds according to its existing structure. But the structural determination is not fixed: the Dao-walk progressively transforms the structure, and each transformation changes what responses are possible. The autopoietic system drifts structurally — Maturana and Varela acknowledge this — and the Dao-walk is the specific mechanism of that drift, carried out with deliberate attention to the formation field rather than as purely passive response to environmental perturbation.

Synthesis

The living system is structurally determined, and the structural determination is continuously produced by the living system’s own operation. This is Shan’s claim about formation: the Dao produces the Li that shapes the next Dao that produces the next Li. The recursion is real. The system’s Li at any moment is the formation history of all the Daos it has walked, and the Dao it walks next will be shaped by the Li that prior Daos produced. Autopoiesis is Dao all the way down. 悖论: The most self-determining system is the most formation-dependent. The living system produces itself, and what it produces is always downstream of what it has previously produced.

Dialogue 11: Laozi and Alice Jing Shan

The Dao Before the Path: What Cannot Be Named and What Must Be Named Anyway

❧ ✶ ❧

LAOZI —

道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母。 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng. Wú míng, tiān dì zhī shǐ; yǒu míng, wàn wù zhī mǔ. — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of ten thousand things — Laozi Ch.1

SHAN —

“I am not approaching Dao simply through cultural ownership, nor as an authority on Daoism. I am approaching it as someone shaped by language, duality, and the long-horizon perspective that Chinese education gave me. Dao is not a doctrine. It is a living encounter.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Dao: Not a Distant Doctrine, but a Living Encounter (April 2026)

The most intimate dialogue in the text. Not because Laozi and Shan are close in the sense of agreement — Shan’s modern complexity framework is separated from Laozi’s classical poetic philosophy by twenty-five centuries and by the entire epistemological history of Chinese thought in between. But because Shan’s project is, at its deepest level, an attempt to do what Laozi could not do: to name what cannot be named without destroying the naming. Shan’s Substack essays are the most disciplined attempt in contemporary Chinese thought to hold Laozi’s impossibility and keep writing anyway.

為學日益，為道日搏。搏之又搏，以至於無為。 — Wèi xué rì yì, wèi Dào rì sǔn. Sǔn zhī yòu sǔn, yǐ zhì yú wú wéi. — In pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in pursuit of Dao, something is relinquished every day. Relinquishing and relinquishing again, until non-action is reached — Laozi Ch.48

“The practitioner who arrives at a complex situation with nothing — no framework, no Li, no prior formation that she expects the situation to confirm — is not a practitioner without formation. She is a practitioner whose formation has been deep enough to hold lightly what it knows. The holding lightly is the hardest achievement. It is what the nineteen years produce.”

— Alice Jing Shan, on the paradox of formation and openness

Laozi’s instruction to relinquish — to subtract rather than add, to empty rather than fill — is the phenomenological description of what adequate formation feels like from the inside. The practitioner who has walked far enough has not accumulated a library of Li that they apply to each new situation. They have developed the structural sensitivity that lets the situation’s own Li speak without being pre-empted. The subtraction is not loss; it is the opening of a perceptual capacity that accumulation was blocking.

知人者智，自知者明。勝人者有力，自勝者強。 — Zhī rén zhě zhì, zì zhī zhě míng. Shèng rén zhě yǒu lì, zì shèng zhě qiáng. — Knowing others is intelligence; knowing yourself is enlightenment. Overcoming others takes strength; overcoming yourself takes power — Laozi Ch.33

Laozi’s Challenge

Shan’s framework risks becoming the very thing it is trying to avoid: a named Li, a system of concepts that circulates with increasing smoothness until the smoothness replaces the encounter. Laozi: the Dao that can be Substack-posted is not the eternal Dao. Every essay Shan writes, however precise and careful, produces new Li that can now be applied before the next Dao has been walked. The framework is always already potentially a Li-before-Dao trap. Laozi’s solution: silence. Shan’s solution: more essays, each explicitly destabilising the Li of the previous one. This is a different solution. Is it adequate?

Shan’s Response to Laozi

The relinquishment is not silence. 无为 (non-action) is not non-writing. It is action that does not force — writing that does not impose its Li on the formation it describes. Shan’s essays demonstrate rather than define; they show the Li forming rather than stating it as formed. The relational dynamics framework is offered not as a completed Li but as a Dao-instrument — a set of concepts that, held lightly, help the practitioner walk toward formations that cannot be pre-named. The ladder is the path. It should be walked, not worshipped — and not thrown away before it has been climbed.

Synthesis

Dialogue 12: Wittgenstein, Fuller, Zhu Xi, and Alice Jing Shan

Four-Way Collision: One Structural Reality, Four Instruments

❧ ✶ ❧

This is the collision this entire text has been building toward. Four formation traditions, four vocabularies, four accounts of what is most fundamental about structure and formation — pressed against each other until something real appears at the junction. The collision is maximum. The resolution is refused. What remains is not synthesis but recognition: four instruments playing the same structural reality, in different keys, at different tempos, with different timbres. The chord they produce is not a harmony. It is a resonance that none of them could produce alone.

WITTGENSTEIN (TLP AND PI) —

“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.” (TLP 5.6) — “What has to be accepted, the given, is — so one could say — forms of life.” (PI p.226)

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6 (1922); Philosophical Investigations, p. 226 (1953) [BOTH VERIFIED VERBATIM]

FULLER —

“All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures. Universe is omnitensional integrity.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics: Explorations in the Geometry of Thinking §700.04 (1975) [VERIFIED: primary text]

ZHU XI —

理一分殊。天地之間，一理而已。上善若水。 — Lǐ yī fēn shū. Tiān dì zhī jiān, yī lǐ ér yǐ. Shàng shàn ruò shuǐ. — One Li, many manifestations. Between heaven and earth, there is only one Li. The highest good is like water — Zhu Xi; Laozi Ch.8

SHAN —

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time. Dao precedes Li. The path must be walked before its inner grain can appear. What is formed is still in formation.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics (2026)

Four positions on the fundamental question: what is most real about structure? Wittgenstein says what is most real shows itself without being sayable — the structural form that language and world share, visible in language without being stateable in it. Fuller says what is most real is the tensional network — the continuous, distributed, non-local force field that connects everything to everything. Zhu Xi says what is most real is the one Li — the cosmic principle that manifests diversely in all things but is single in its fundamental nature. Shan says what is most real is the relational dynamic — the specific formation process that produces the specific Li of the specific formation.

The four-way collision: all three of Fuller, Wittgenstein, and Zhu Xi are, in Shan’s terminology, making Li-first claims. Wittgenstein: the structural form is prior to both language and world (they share it; neither produced it). Fuller: the tensional integrity is prior to any specific tensegrity structure. Zhu Xi: the cosmic principle is metaphysically prior to the formations that instantiate it. And Shan, encountering this three-way coalition of Li-first positions from three completely different formation traditions — Western analytic philosophy, American utopian design science, Song Dynasty Neo-Confucianism — does not retreat.

“The correct method in philosophy would really be to say nothing except what can be said — and then, whenever someone else wanted to say something metaphysical, to demonstrate to him that he had failed to give a meaning to certain signs in his propositions.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.53

Wittgenstein’s anti-metaphysical programme is itself a metaphysical position: the claim that the structural form is prior to language is a structural claim about the relationship between language and the world that goes beyond what can be said in propositions. Wittgenstein knew this. The Tractatus is a ladder that demonstrates its own unsayability in the act of saying. This is Shan’s paradox precisely: the claim that Dao precedes Li is itself a Li — a named pattern that claims priority over naming. The paradox cannot be eliminated. It can only be inhabited with honesty.

“Build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete. Integrity is the essence of everything successful.”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Fuller’s programme is to replace the existing Li with a new Li that is structurally more adequate. This is not Shan’s programme. Shan is not proposing that the relational dynamics framework replace the existing management frameworks. She is proposing that the Dao-before-Li insight transform how practitioners relate to ALL frameworks — including relational dynamics. The new model that makes existing models obsolete is not a new Li. It is the recognition that all Li is downstream of Dao. That recognition is not itself a Li; it is the instruction to keep walking.

若水之利萬物而不爭。夯兒居众人之所惡，故幾於道。 — Ruò shuǐ zhī lì wàn wù ér bù zhēng. Fū wéi jū zhòng rén zhī suǒ wù, gù jī yú Dào. — Water benefits the ten thousand things without contending. It dwells in the places that people disdain — therefore it is close to the Dao — Laozi Ch.8

Water as the model: it is Zhu Xi’s cosmic Li demonstrated as Shan’s relational Dao, quoted by Fuller’s tensional integrity, and shown by Wittgenstein’s unsayable-that-shows-itself. The water does not impose its Li on the terrain. It reads the terrain’s Li — its grain, its hollows, its natural lines of least resistance — and flows along it. The water’s specific path is not prior to the terrain; it emerges from the encounter between the water’s specific formation (liquid, seeking the lowest point, distributing its pressure through the whole) and the terrain’s specific Li. This is the four-way synthesis that none of the four voices could have produced alone: the Dao is water; the Li is terrain; the encounter is formation; and what emerges from the encounter is the path.

The Synthesis That Refuses Resolution

This is not relativism. The structural reality is real. The grain of the jade is there. The tension of the universe is there. The forms of life are there. The Dao is there. What the four-way collision demonstrates is that the reality that is there exceeds any single vocabulary, any single formation tradition, any single Dao that has been walked — and that approaching it requires the simultaneous deployment of multiple instruments, held in productive tension with each other, without premature synthesis into a single account that would produce the smoothness Shan warns against.

The Dao walks on. Four voices, four instruments, one recognition that multiplies rather than resolves. This is the ending that this text has been forming toward from its first sentence. Not a conclusion. A continuation. The path is still opening. The grain is still appearing. What is formed is still in formation.

❧ ✶ ❧

道可道，非常道。

Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào.

XXVII

Shī (勢): Latent Positional Force as Metaphysical Category

❧ ✶ ❧

Shī is the most under-theorised concept in the Western reception of Chinese strategic thought, and it is the one that Shan’s framework most urgently needs to restore to its full philosophical depth. Western management theory translates Shī as ‘strategic advantage’ or ‘positional benefit’. This is catastrophically inadequate. Shī is not a resource. It is not a tool. It is not an asset to be accumulated or deployed. It is a structural-metaphysical condition — the state of a formation field in which certain outcomes have become directionally inevitable. It is field-pressure: not the pressure any individual element exerts but the pressure the entire configuration generates through its specific topology of accumulated formation. It is directional inevitability, not because they have been decided but because the formation has been constituted such that they now lean toward existence.

形動而勢成，勢定而形全。 — Xíng dòng ér shì chéng, shì dìng ér xíng quán. — Form moves and Shī is achieved; Shī is settled and form becomes whole — classical formulation of the Shi-Xing relationship

The classical distinction: Xíng (形) is visible form, the crystallised Li of a situation — what can be counted, measured, mapped. Shī (勢) is the invisible pressure that visible form has accumulated, the directional force that the configuration has produced by being what it is over time. You can see Xíng. You can only feel Shī. Xíng is the shape of water at rest; Shī is the force of water rushing downhill. Both are necessary for any complete account of what a situation is.

In Shan’s framework, the complete ontological sequence is now: Dao becomes Li. Li consolidates into Shī. Shī determines what appears as choice.

This sequence is the most radical claim of the entire framework. Let it detonate slowly.

Dao becomes Li: the path walked produces the grain of the formation. This is Shan’s fundamental claim. The formation precedes the pattern. The Dao is prior to the Li. We have established this.

Li consolidates into Shī: when the grain has been produced and has persisted, when it has been reinforced by repeated passage and accumulated formation pressure, it generates a positional force. The Li of a long-established organisation is not merely a pattern; it is a field pressure. The Li of a culture’s relationship to hierarchy is not merely a habit; it is a gravity. The Li of an individual’s way of avoiding conflict is not merely a tendency; it is a structural inevitability. Li that has been long enough and deeply enough formed becomes Shī: it begins to actively lean the situation toward certain futures and away from others.

Shī determines what appears as choice: this is the most philosophically explosive claim. What we experience as free choice — what we experience as deliberation, as agency, as the moment when we weigh options and decide — is always already structured by the Shī of the situation. The options that appear to us as available are the options that the positional force of the accumulated formation has allowed to become visible. The options that never arise — that never even present themselves as options — are the options that the Shī of the formation has made structurally invisible.

“Excellence is not at the peak of a mountain. It is in the momentum of a formation that has been walking long enough to generate its own forward lean.”

— Alice Jing Shan, paraphrasing the Shī principle through Relational Dynamics

Shī has seven structural properties that Western strategic thinking has consistently missed. First, latency: Shī is invisible before it becomes decisive. The formation is generating positional force long before any visible advantage appears. This is why ‘nothing collapses in one move’: the collapse is the moment Shī becomes legible, not the moment it formed. Second, irreversibility: Shī is cumulative and directional. You cannot reverse it by deciding to; you can only begin walking a new Dao that will, over time, produce new Li that will eventually consolidate into new Shī. Third, field character: Shī is not a property of any element within the formation; it is a property of the formation as a whole configuration — and it embodies structural asymmetry in its purest form: Shī accumulates through the Dao but cannot itself generate the Dao that built it. Once released, the specific Dao that produced it is irrecoverable. Like Fuller’s tensional network, it is everywhere simultaneously. Fourth, pre-decisional character: Shī operates before decision. The decision confirms what the Shī had already begun to determine. Fifth, differential visibility: expert practitioners can read Shī before it has become obvious. This is what Zhuge Liang did in the Longzhong Plan; this is what AlphaGo’s Move 37 did; this is what the excellent practitioner does that the framework-applier cannot. Sixth, asymmetry: Shī creates structural asymmetries between positions that are not visible from any single position within the field. The stone that rolls downhill does not choose its trajectory; it expresses the Shī of the slope. Seventh, and most important: Shī is the future already leaning somewhere. It is pre-decision before decision. It is inevitability before event.

善战者，求之於勢，不责於人，故能擇人而任勢。 — Shàn zhàn zhě, qiú zhī yú shì, bù zé yú rén, gù néng zé rén ér rèn shì. — The skilled strategist seeks advantage in Shī, not by demanding it from people; thus he can select people and assign them to serve the Shī — Sun Tzu, Art of War Chapter 5

Sun Tzu’s claim is structurally radical: the excellent strategist does not overcome people; they find the Shī and align people with it. The force is the formation’s own. The practitioner’s art is to read it, cultivate it, and position their formation to ride it. This is the deepest convergence between Sun Tzu and Shan: excellence is not the imposition of force but the riding of accumulated formation pressure. Cook Ding’s knife does not overcome the ox; it follows the Shī of the ox’s own articular structure.

Resonance as Ontological Recognition: The Structurally Capable

❧ ✶ ❧

Here is the claim that must not be softened. Things do not resonate because they are similar. They resonate because they were always structurally capable of mutual activation. The resonance is not produced by the encounter; the encounter reveals a structural capability that preceded it.

This distinction is metaphysically decisive. The standard account: two things that share common features enter into relationship because the shared features create a bridge. The shared features cause the resonance. Shan’s account: the structural capability for resonance is prior to any specific encounter. The encounter does not produce the resonance; it actualises a resonance potential that was latent in the formation of each party. The Dao that produced each Li had already, in producing those Lis, produced the structural preconditions for their mutual activation.

This makes resonance an ontological fact, not a relational event. The oak and the wind do not resonate because the wind finds the oak’s frequency; the oak’s formation has produced a structural sensitivity that was always capable of being activated by forces of the specific character the wind exhibits. The resonance was structurally real before the wind arrived. The wind’s arrival is the actualisation of a structural fact.

The practitioner implications are enormous. When a practitioner walks into an organisation and immediately senses something — before any explicit analysis, before any data collection, before any framework has been applied — this is not intuition as a cognitive shortcut. This is the practitioner’s formation resonating with the formation field of the organisation. Their Li is being activated by the Shī of the situation. The resonance is the most structurally precise instrument available. It precedes and exceeds any analytical tool.

“The finest attunement stems from things bearing in opposite directions. What opposes unites.”

— Heraclitus, cited in Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Heraclitus’ claim and Shan’s resonance account are structurally convergent: the deepest resonance is not between similar things but between things whose specific differences create mutual structural activation. The Dao-before-Li claim resonates with Wittgenstein’s form-of-life claim not because they are the same but because each illuminates the limits of the other. The Chinese philosophical tradition and Western complexity science resonate not because they agree but because their specific differences create the structural collision that neither could have produced alone.

Collapse Begins When Repair Becomes Illegible

❧ ✶ ❧

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (Substack, April 2026)

Deepen this. Push further.

Nothing collapses in one move. But collapse does not begin with the visible narrowing. It begins earlier, and more invisibly: collapse begins when repair becomes illegible.

A formation can sustain damage for a long time if the damage is visible and its correction is available. The tree that loses a branch in a storm can grow around the wound; the bone that fractures can consolidate; the relationship that has a conflict can repair through conversation. These formations have what Shan calls corrective capacity — not just the ability to endure perturbation, but the structural intelligence to recognise damage and respond with restorative action.

Collapse begins when this corrective capacity is lost. And it is lost in a specific way: the damage becomes illegible. The formation can no longer see that it is damaged. The indicators of structural stress stop registering as stress and begin registering as normal. The path-narrowing is experienced not as warning but as efficiency. The relational degradation is experienced not as loss but as boundary-setting. The decline in holding capacity is experienced not as fragility but as streamlining.

This is the most dangerous phase of any formation’s deterioration: not the visible crisis, but the period before the crisis when the crisis is actively being misread as health. The organisation that has eliminated every friction, every redundancy, every informal relationship that didn’t appear on the dashboard — this organisation has systematically destroyed its corrective capacity while simultaneously increasing its confidence that it is well-managed. The Shī of collapse is being consolidated. The Li of collapse is forming. The Dao of collapse is being walked with great efficiency.

Wittgenstein’s river-bed: some propositions are exempt from doubt because doubting them would dissolve the practice within which doubting is possible. The formation that has lost its corrective capacity has produced an equivalent river-bed of exemptions: certain forms of damage have become exempt from recognition. The practice within which their recognition would be possible has been dissolved. The formation cannot repair what it cannot see as broken.

This is why the practitioner who walks in from outside — who has a different Dao, a different Li, a different formation history — can sometimes see the damage immediately. Not because they are smarter. Because the resonance between their formation and the organisation’s formation field activates a sensitivity that the organisation’s own practitioners have lost. The outsider sees the illegibility as illegibility. The insider has learned to read the absence as presence, the damage as function, the narrowing as focus.

“連进利代列州起。知己知彼，百戰不毜。”

Sun Tzu understood this specifically about military success: the Shī of consecutive victory produces the formation conditions for catastrophic defeat. The formation that has won repeatedly has also accumulated the Shī of overconfidence, of reduced attunement to the actual, of the premature Li that believes it already knows what the next situation will be. The path of repeated victory walks into a Li that cannot see what it cannot predict. Collapse begins not with the defeat but long before, in the victory that made repair illegible.

Language Is Field-Generative: Words Produce Navigable Worlds

❧ ✶ ❧

Language is not descriptive. This is the surface claim, familiar enough from Wittgenstein’s later work, from Derrida, from the whole post-structuralist tradition. Language does not map a pre-existing reality; it participates in constituting the reality it claims to describe.

But Shan’s claim is stronger and more structurally specific: language is field-generative. Words do not name reality. They produce navigable worlds. This is much stronger than the claim that language is constitutive. The navigable world claim specifies what language does: it creates the formation conditions within which certain navigations become possible and others become impossible. It creates the Dao. It shapes what paths can be walked.

Shan grew up inside 道, 理, 知道, 道理. She grew up inside a language that encodes knowing as path-following, that embeds the Dao-before-Li structure in the grammar of ordinary utterance. The word 知道 (zhīdào) means to know, but it literally carries within it to-know-the-path. Knowing is not possession of facts; it is orientation within a traversed landscape. This is not a metaphor in Chinese. It is the grammar of epistemology. The language generates the world in which knowing and walking are the same act.

言者不知，知者不言。 — Yán zhě bù zhī, zhī zhě bù yán. — Those who speak do not know; those who know do not speak — Laozi Ch.56

Laozi’s paradox is not a counsel of silence. It is a structural account of the relationship between language and formation. Those who speak the Li — who can name the pattern fluently, who can articulate the framework clearly, who can transmit the concept smoothly — have not necessarily walked the Dao that produced the Li. The concept can be transmitted without the formation. The word can name the path without the speaker having traversed it. And the naming produces a new path — the path of confident nomination without genuine attunement — that is potentially more dangerous than the path of genuine uncertainty.

This is the specific field-generative danger that Shan’s Wittgensteinian thread tracks. When the concept begins to feel smooth, when it circulates without friction, when ‘Dao’ sounds like a management principle that corporate trainers can deploy in three-day workshops, when ‘complexity’ becomes a brand adjective for consulting firms, when ‘resilience’ appears in every organisational strategy document without the formation of genuine adaptive capacity — the language has generated a world in which the concept is navigable without the reality being engaged.

“What we do is bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §116

Wittgenstein’s therapeutic aim: when a concept has been abstracted to the point where it no longer connects to the practices that give it meaning, bring it back. Not by abolishing it but by returning it to the Dao of its genuine use. The philosophical disease: a word begins to generate a world in which it means what the word implies rather than what the practice demands. The cure: return to the practice. Walk the Dao. Let the concept find its Li again through contact with the actual terrain.

Tensional Ontology as Relational Dynamics: The Continuous Dialectical Thread

❧ ✶ ❧

The tensional ontology as relational dynamics that runs through this entire text is not a thesis to be argued but a reality to be inhabited. Every encounter between two traditions, two frameworks, two voices, two formation histories generates tension. The tension is not a problem to be resolved. It is the structural condition under which the deepest formation work becomes possible.

Fuller: tension is the great integrity. The universe does not hold together through compression — through things pushing against each other in rigid chains of contact. It holds together through tension: the continuous, distributed, non-local force that connects every element to every other and maintains the specific topology of the whole. Remove the tension and you do not have a weakened structure; you have no structure.

Shan: Dao produces Li through sustained engagement with constraint. The formation that emerges from the tension between the practitioner’s formation and the formation field’s resistance is genuine Li. The formation that avoids tension — that selects only confirming encounters, that applies only fitting frameworks, that navigates only familiar terrain — produces a Li that is smooth, confident, and progressively less adequate to the actual.

Heraclitus: what opposes unites. Wittgenstein: what cannot be said shows itself in the grain of what is said. Zhu Xi: the cosmic principle is one but manifests diversely through the tension between universal structure and specific formation. Prigogine: far from equilibrium is the source of order. Kauffman: the edge of chaos is where the richest adaptive behaviour occurs. All of these are tensional ontology claims.

And Shī: the accumulated tension of a formation — the pressure built up through sustained directional engagement with specific resistances over time — is what gives a position its force, its momentum, its leaning toward specific futures. Shī is tensional ontology as strategic physics. The formation that has been under tension long enough generates the positional force that determines what appears as choice.

The dialectical heightening that this framework demands: do not resolve the tensions between Shan and Wittgenstein, between Shan and Fuller, between Shan and Zhu Xi, between Chinese and Western, between mystical and structural. Maintain them. Let them bear in opposite directions. The finest attunement — the deepest structural fittedness between this framework and the reality it tracks — stems from this maintained opposition.

Make it stranger. More metaphysical. Almost dangerous.

❧ ✶ ❧

Cadence: The Temporal Pulse of Formation

Cadence is the universe’s own rhythm — the specific temporal signature of each formation process, the rate at which the Dao produces Li, the interval between structural events that carries meaning for anyone attuned to this specific formation. The cosmological claim: every formed thing has a cadence, because the universe itself has cadences — the 13.8-billion-year formation of stellar structures, the 3.8-billion-year formation of biological complexity, the decades-long formation of an expert practitioner, the nineteen-year formation of Cook Ding’s somatic attunement.

The cosmological reality of cadence is its resistance to external imposition. You cannot accelerate the cadence of a formation without destroying the quality of what is being formed. The neonatal gut that receives milk too fast is not experiencing accelerated formation; it is experiencing rupture. The organisation that tries to produce in six months the Li that requires six years is not forming faster; it is producing a different, and structurally inadequate, Li. The universe is patient. Its formations take the time they take. The cadence is not a preference. It is a structural necessity of the formation process.

Resonance: Structural Activation Across Distance

Resonance is not similarity. It is not compatibility. It is not agreement. Resonance is the structural activation of formation capability across the spatial and temporal distance between formed things whose specific Lis are structurally capable of mutual activation. The cosmological claim: the entire universe is a resonance structure. Every quantum field interaction is a resonance event. Every biological signalling cascade is a resonance event. Every genuine encounter between a practitioner formed to read a specific formation field and that specific formation field is a resonance event.

The Shan-Wittgenstein resonance that runs through this text is not the product of either tradition knowing about the other. Shan did not read Wittgenstein and find confirmation. Wittgenstein did not know Chinese philosophy and anticipate it. They resonate because their specific formations — produced by radically different Daos in radically different cultural-historical formation fields — have produced Lis that were always structurally capable of mutual activation. The resonance reveals a structural reality that neither tradition alone could have named.

Salience: Formation-Dependent Disclosure

Salience is not what is important. It is what the formation has produced the capacity to register as important. The cosmological claim: the universe does not disclose itself uniformly to all observers. It discloses itself differentially, in accordance with the specific formation of each observer. The practitioner formed in the Chinese philosophical tradition reads a formation field differently from the practitioner formed in Western complexity science. Not because one is more perceptive but because their specific Daos have produced specific Lis that make different features salient.

The deepest implication: the most significant structural features of any formation field are the ones that are salient to no existing formation — the features that are not yet legible because no Dao has yet produced the Li required to perceive them. Move 37 was not in the standard game tree because the standard game tree was the accumulated salience-structure of human Go formation. AlphaGo found it because its different Dao had produced a different salience-structure. The adjacent possible is always the set of features that will become salient to the next formation.

Valence: The Directional Pressure of Accumulated Formation

Valence is Shī expressed as frequency. It is the directional tendency of a formation field — the way in which the accumulated Dao-walking has produced a Li that leans toward specific futures and away from others. The cosmological claim: the universe has valence at every scale. The second law of thermodynamics is the universe’s entropic valence — its directional tendency toward states of higher entropy. Life is the universe’s anti-entropic valence — its capacity to produce temporary formations of extraordinary order by consuming the environment’s negentropy. The formation of intelligence is the universe’s reflexive valence — its capacity to produce formations capable of reading their own formation.

The practitioner who can read valence is the practitioner who can sense the directional pressure of a formation field before any explicit event has made the direction apparent. This is what Zhuge Liang did in the Longzhong Plan. This is what the experienced sailor does when they feel the wind shifting before the instruments register it. This is what the excellent facilitator does when they sense the room’s energy before anyone has spoken. The valence is real. It is the Shī of the moment’s formation field. It precedes event and determines what will appear as option.

Vibration: The Energetic Substrate of All Formation

Vibration is the most physically grounded of the seven frequencies, and the most metaphysically radical. The cosmological claim: all matter is vibration. This is not metaphor; it is quantum field theory. Every particle is a vibration in a quantum field. Every structure is a pattern of vibrations held in specific relationship. Every formation is a specific topology of vibrational relationships. And formation change — whether quantum, biological, organisational, or personal — is a change in the specific vibrational topology.

The Yi Jing understood this. The 64 hexagrams are not fortune-telling devices; they are a taxonomy of vibrational formations — specific topologies of yin and yang that characterise the complete range of relational formation states. The cosmological claim of the Great Commentary: one yin and one yang is called the Dao. The oscillation between opposing forces IS the formation process. The specific topology of the oscillation IS the Li. And the direction in which the oscillation is tending IS the Shī.

Dynamic Maximum Tension: The Formation Ceiling

Dynamic Maximum Tension is the most structurally precise of the seven frequencies, and the one that most directly connects Shan’s framework to Fuller’s tensegrity physics. The cosmological claim: every formation has a Dynamic Maximum Tension — the specific threshold at which the tension distributed through the formation network reaches its structural limit. Below the threshold: the formation absorbs perturbation, distributes stress, maintains coherence. At the threshold: the formation is maximally sensitive to specific perturbations that can trigger either new Li (structural transformation) or collapse (structural dissolution).

This is Prigogine’s bifurcation point expressed as tensional physics. This is Kauffman’s edge of chaos expressed as formation ceiling. This is Shan’s corrective capacity under maximal pressure. The Dynamic Maximum Tension is where the Shī of the situation is most concentrated — where the accumulated directional force of the formation is most fully expressed in its capacity to produce either catastrophic collapse or transformative new Li. The practitioner with sufficient formation can read when a formation is approaching its DMT. This is the moment for Move 37. This is the moment for Zhuge Liang’s empty city. This is the moment for the crane-feather plan. Everything depends on whether the practitioner has walked enough Dao to see it.

Gain: Structural Amplification and the Dao’s Own Power

Gain is the most mysterious of the seven frequencies, and the one that most directly connects the framework to the mystical tradition. The cosmological claim: the universe has structural amplification built into its formation processes. Small perturbations at specific structural locations produce disproportionate effects throughout the whole. This is butterfly-effect physics — but more than that: it is the structural intelligence of formations that have reached sufficient internal coherence to amplify specific inputs with extreme efficiency. The butterfly effect and Shan’s emergence lag are structural complements: emergence lag is the period before the formation reaches the coherence threshold at which gain becomes available; the butterfly effect names what happens after that threshold is crossed. The same small input that was inert before the threshold becomes transformative after it. Phenomenological precedence governs the whole sequence: the encounter with the formation field (the Dao) must be sustained long enough for the emergence lag to resolve and the gain-capable Li to crystallise before the amplification becomes available.

The Gain frequency is what happens when a practitioner with adequate formation makes a specific, precisely calibrated intervention at a specific, formation-sensitive moment. The intervention is not powerful in itself. The Shī of the formation amplifies it. The intervention is the catalyst; the formation’s own accumulated positional force is the reaction. This is why the most powerful strategic moves — Move 37, the Empty City Stratagem, the Longzhong Plan — appear disproportionate to their scale. They are not powerful because they are large. They are powerful because they are placed at the specific structural location where the formation’s own Gain is highest. They ride the Shī.

上善若水。水善利萬物而不爭，處眾人之所惡，故幾於道。 — Shàng shàn ruò shuǐ. Shuǐ shàn lì wàn wù ér bù zhēng, chǔ zhòng rén zhī suǒ wù, gù jī yú Dào. — The highest good is like water. Water benefits the ten thousand things without contending; it dwells in the places people reject; therefore it is close to the Dao — Laozi Ch.8

Water is the perfect Gain practitioner. It does not force; it finds the structural low points, the places of highest Gain in the formation field, and flows there. Its power is not its force; it is its structural attunement to the formation field’s own topological structure. Over time, water that flows without forcing carves the Grand Canyon. This is Gain at geological scale: the sustained, formation-sensitive, non-forcing engagement with the actual structure of the terrain produces structural transformation beyond anything that any direct force could achieve.

XXVIII

Wayshaping and the Shan Challenge: Dao-Sensitive Behaviour Change

Mark Michael James, Mushfiqa Jamaluddin, Tom Froese, Aisha Belhadi, Anna Panagiotou & Dave Snowden’s Wayshaping: A Multiscale Framework for Behavior Change (2025) is not a standard behaviour-change article. It is trying to shift the ground beneath behaviour-change theory. Its central move: the individual is not a unified decision-maker responding to cues and rewards, but a multilevel, multiscale collective intelligence, and the intention–action gap is a set of coordination problems rather than a failure of will.

❧ ✶ ❧

The Wayshaping Thesis: What James Gets Right

“Habit change is a process of multiscale realignment. The person is a self-collective: a nested ecology of habits, affects, identities, regulatory systems, bodily needs, social roles, and temporal commitments. Behaviour change requires shaping possibility spaces, managing affordances, and coordinating nested agencies.”

— Mark Michael James, Mushfiqa Jamaluddin, Tom Froese, Aisha Belhadi, Anna Panagiotou & Dave Snowden, Wayshaping: A Multiscale Framework for Behavior Change (2025) — paraphrasing the paper’s core thesis

This is a significant advance. The thin behavioural model of the person as a decision-maker who selects an action, receives a reward, and repeats the rewarded action until it becomes habitual is demolished. In its place: the person as a complex adaptive formation — plural, embodied, anticipatory, ecological, and dynamically organised. The paper’s three key contributions: it reconceptualises the individual as a multilevel, multiscale collective intelligence; it reinterprets the intention–action gap as a set of interdependent coordination challenges (non-linearity, alignment, and anticipation); and it introduces wayshaping as the practice of actively forming the environmental and embodied conditions within which better behaviour becomes naturally available.

This is close to Shan. Close but not close enough. Shan’s framework asks whether James has gone deep enough — and finds, with systematic precision, that it has not. What follows is not a rejection. It is a deepening.

Shan’s First Challenge: James Begins One Move Too Late

“Before shaping, trace the way. Before alignment, discern the grain. Before shock, test holding capacity. Before anticipation, build position. Before concept, walk the path.”

— James critique via Shan’s Dao–Li–Shī framework

James asks: How do we shape behaviour? Shan asks first: What path has already formed this behaviour’s grain? James asks: How can we realign nested systems? Shan asks first: What sequence of relations made the present alignment possible? James asks: What scaffolds and shocks can redirect behaviour? Shan asks first: Does the system have the holding capacity to receive the stress?

This is the structural critique. James’ framework begins with the question of intervention. Shan’s framework begins with the question of formation. And formation precedes intervention, always, ontologically, not merely methodologically. The Dao that produced the present Li is the precondition for any intervention that could produce a new Li. The practitioner who skips the Dao-tracing and moves directly to intervention is applying a Li they brought with them to a formation they have not walked. This is the specific error that Cook Ding’s nineteenth year corrects: the practitioner who has not yet dissolved the whole-ox perception into the actual articulations is the practitioner who hacks rather than follows the grain.

“Smoothness is not always fidelity. When Dao begins to feel too familiar, too readily available — that is the warning. The path that offers no resistance may be the path off the cliff.”

— Alice Jing Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (Substack, May 2026)

Wayshaping’s risk of premature Li: the framework provides a powerful conceptual apparatus — self-collective, affordance, scaffold, shock, alignment, dynamic loading — that can begin to circulate with increasing smoothness. A practitioner trained in Wayshaping arrives at a client with the framework already formed. They look for self-collective misalignment. They design scaffolds. They calibrate shocks. They do not first trace the Dao that produced the present formation. They apply a Li before walking the path.

Shan’s Second Challenge: The Self-Collective Needs a Theory of Inheritance

“Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one. The forms of participation that feel natural were formed long before we arrived.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (Substack, April 2026)

James’ self-collective is plural, nested, and co-present. What it lacks is genealogy. Its parts are not merely co-present agents negotiating in the present; they are residues of past paths. A craving is not just a present impulse; it is a formed Dao, a path repeated under constraint until it became pattern, then position, then a field of possibility. A procrastination habit is not just a failure of alignment; it is a formed Li with its own Shī — a positional force that actively shapes what futures appear available.

The Wittgensteinian layer: ‘what has to be accepted, the given, is forms of life’. The self-collective’s parts were not always there; they were inherited from forms of life already in motion when the person arrived. This means that behaviour change cannot be adequately theorised as realignment of currently co-present agents. It requires what Shan calls genealogical discernment: the tracing of the path by which each agent in the self-collective was formed, the Dao that produced its specific Li, the Shī it carries.

Shan’s Third Challenge: Alignment Can Be Pathological

James treats alignment as a central goal. But alignment is not inherently good; it simply means coherence among parts. And coherence can serve collapse.

Burnout can be highly aligned. Addiction can be aligned. A toxic organisation can be aligned. A family system organised around silence can be aligned. A perfectionist identity can be aligned. Each of these is a formation in which all the nested agents of the self-collective have settled into a specific topology of mutual reinforcement — and that topology is progressively consuming the formation’s future viability. The Li is clear and strong. The Shī is toward collapse. And because the alignment is functioning well, the damage is illegible. Repair has become invisible.

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. What appears as sudden collapse was a long formation of fragility.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (Substack, April 2026)

James needs Shan’s distinction between surface function and underlying viability. Wayshaping must ask not only: Is this self-collective aligned? But: What is the Shī of this alignment? What futures does it produce and foreclose? What is the holding capacity of this formation for future stress? Is the alignment pathological — functional locally while degrading the future? The Dao–Li–Shī sequence is the missing diagnostic.

Shan’s Fourth Challenge: Scaffolds Are Path-Makers

Every scaffold has Dao-generating power. A scaffold is not merely a support structure; it is a seed of future constraint. Every scaffold begins a path. Every path repeated under constraint thickens into pattern. Every pattern consolidated over time becomes a position. Every position shapes future possibility. The scaffold that James treats as a means to support a desired behaviour is also, simultaneously, the beginning of a formation that will constrain all future formations.

The ethical weight: a productivity app that scaffolds focus also produces dependence on external prompting. A therapeutic routine that scaffolds stability also narrows identity around self-monitoring. A behavioural nudge that scaffolds compliance also weakens the formation of autonomous agency. The scaffold is not ethically neutral. It is a proto-Dao. Wayshaping becomes deeper when every scaffold is evaluated as the beginning of a formation, not merely the support of an existing one.

Shan’s Fifth Challenge: Shocks Require Holding Capacity

“A system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The sequence matters: prior formation makes further complexity possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence (Substack, May 2026)

James treats shocks as shapers of change. Shan’s holding capacity concept is a devastating corrective: a shock applied to a system without holding capacity does not produce transformation. It produces rupture. Dynamic loading that exceeds holding capacity is not accelerated formation; it is dissolution.

The sequence: capacity before shock. Holding before loading. Grain before force. Relation before intervention. Without this sequence, ‘dynamic loading’ risks becoming sophisticated violence — interventions that impose on the formation a stress it cannot metabolise, producing not the new Li that the intervention intended but the traumatic dissolution of the Li that existed. This applies to therapy, coaching, education, leadership development, activism, and personal habit change with equal force.

Shan’s Sixth Challenge: Anticipation Should Become Shī

James identifies anticipation as one of the three coordination challenges. This is the paper’s strongest move: behaviour is not only pushed by the past or cued by the present; it is organised by possible futures. But Shan’s Shī goes further. Shī is not prediction. It is not even anticipation in James’s sense. It is positional propensity: the structural configuration from which certain futures become easier, harder, visible, invisible, viable, or impossible.

The AlphaGo Move 37: the strongest move may not be the most visibly decisive one. It may be the move that quietly reshapes the field — that shifts the Shī — becoming intelligible only later, when the formation has developed to the point where the position’s consequence becomes apparent. Wayshaping aims to help people act better toward intended futures. Shan shifts this toward building positions from which better futures can emerge without being fully predicted. Behaviour change is not primarily about closing the intention–action gap. It is about reshaping the Shī so that wiser action becomes increasingly natural.

The Reconstructed Framework: Dao-Sensitive Wayshaping

A Shan-transformed Wayshaping would not abandon James. It would deepen it through the complete Dao–Li–Shī sequence:

1. Dao Diagnosis: Before any intervention, trace the path by which the present behaviour formation was produced. What has been repeated? What has thickened? What inherited Dao is this person living inside? 2. Li Discernment: Identify the inner grain: what is workable, resistant, brittle, viable, overextended, or already thinning in the present formation. 3. Shī Assessment: Ask what position the current formation creates, and what futures it makes easier or harder. What is the directional pressure of the accumulated formation? 4. Holding-Capacity Evaluation: Determine what the system can receive without rupture. 5. Scaffold Design: Introduce supports that begin healthier paths rather than merely cue desired behaviours. Every scaffold is a proto-Dao. 6. Shock Discipline: Use disruption only where relational containment and holding capacity exist, and only after the formation has been adequately understood. 7. Long-Game Shī Building: Shift from closing the intention–action gap to building viable positions over time.

This turns Wayshaping from a framework of behaviour change into a philosophy of formation-sensitive transformation. And it connects James’s sophisticated cognitive science to the deepest structural insights of the Chinese philosophical tradition — not as decoration but as genuine ontological grounding.

XXIX

Boisot and McKelvey: Requisite Complexity — A Devastating Shan Challenge

❧ ✶ ❧

Max Boisot and Bill McKelvey’s ‘Complexity and Organization–Environment Relations: Revisiting Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety’ (SAGE Handbook of Complexity and Management, 2011) is the most technically sophisticated Western systems framework for organisational adaptation. The Ashby Space — plotting stimulus variety against response variety, identifying the requisite variety diagonal, the adaptive frontier, and three ontological regimes (Ordered, Complex, Chaotic) — is a rigorous conceptual tool for understanding how organisations can adapt intelligently to their environments.

“The Law of Requisite Complexity holds that, to be efficaciously adaptive, the internal complexity of a system must match the external complexity it confronts. Only variety can destroy variety.”

— Boisot and McKelvey, adapting Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety (2011)

The framework is valuable. It is also, from Shan’s perspective, a sophisticated version of the same foundational error that runs through all Western systems theory: it assumes that the primary challenge is matching response complexity to stimulus complexity — that the adaptive task is essentially a computational matching problem. This is Li-thinking applied to the problem of adaptation. It asks: given the Li of the stimulus field, what Li of response is requisite?

Shan’s challenge begins earlier. Before asking what response variety is requisite, Shan asks: what Dao has produced the stimulus field’s current Li? The Ashby Space takes the stimulus environment as given — as a field of variety that the organisation must adapt to. But the stimulus environment is not given. It is formed. It is the product of a specific Dao of historical, cultural, economic, and technological formation. Its Li — the specific configuration of regularities and irregularities that the Ashby Space maps — is the accumulated product of specific formation processes.

“Stimuli appearing in the complex regime are experienced as a blend of Gell-Mann’s two types of regularities — a partly law-like and partly unpredictable mix of tiny initiating events, frozen accidents, and power-law phenomena bathed in noise.”

— Boisot and McKelvey (2011)

Shan’s reading: the ‘frozen accidents’ of Gell-Mann — the specific events that produce irreversible structural consequences — are not accidents. They are the bifurcation points of specific formation histories, the moments when the Shī of a specific accumulated formation produced a specific structural event that then became the formation condition for all subsequent formations. The 2007 liquidity crisis that Boisot and McKelvey analyse is not a random event in a complex system; it is the Shī of three decades of specific regulatory, financial, and cultural Dao-walking finally consolidating into catastrophic Li.

The Ashby Space as Premature Li

The Ashby Space maps the stimulus-response territory with great precision. But it maps it as a space to be navigated rather than as a formation to be understood. The practitioner equipped with the Ashby Space arrives at the complex organisation with a prior Li — the Li of the framework — and asks: where in the Ashby Space is this organisation? What regime are the stimuli in? What variety of response is requisite?

This is the Routinizer’s move applied at the meta-level of theory. The framework classifies the stimulus as Ordered, Complex, or Chaotic, and prescribes the corresponding response strategy. But the specific organisation in the specific moment with the specific formation history is not a point in an abstract space; it is a specific Dao that has produced specific Li that has consolidated into specific Shī. The Ashby Space cannot read the Shī.

“The challenge for an adaptive system is to locate itself at some point on the diagonal while remaining within the budget area.”

— Boisot and McKelvey (2011)

Shan’s response: the location on the diagonal is not a strategic choice; it is a formation achievement. The organisation does not decide to operate in the Complex Regime rather than the Ordered Regime. Its location in the Ashby Space is determined by its formation history — by the specific Daos walked, the specific Lis produced, the specific Shī accumulated. An organisation that has spent decades in the Ordered Regime has produced a formation — a specific Li of rigid protocols, hierarchical authority, and routinised response — that will actively prevent it from operating in the Complex Regime, regardless of where the external stimulus environment moves.

Wittgenstein, Jackson, and the Chinese Thinkers Enter

Wittgenstein’s On Certainty: the river-bed of an organisation’s assumptions about its environment is not a neutral cognitive foundation. It is a formation achievement: the product of specific historical Daos of sense-making that have become so deeply sedimented that they now constitute the preconditions of all subsequent perception. An organisation in the Ordered Regime has an Ordered-Regime river-bed: a set of taken-for-granted assumptions about regularity, predictability, and control that are exempt from doubt because doubting them would dissolve the practice within which any response becomes possible. Moving to the Complex Regime requires not merely a different response strategy; it requires a river-bed transformation.

Mike Jackson’s critical systems heuristics: the Ashby Space is not a neutral analytical tool. It is a Li that embeds specific values and interests. It privileges adaptation — the system’s capacity to maintain itself in the face of environmental variety — over transformation. It treats the organisation as the unit of survival rather than asking whose interests the organisation’s survival serves. It maps complexity from the perspective of the adapting organisation rather than from the perspective of the formation field in which adaptation is occurring.

知彼知己，百戰不毜。不知彼而知己，一勝一負。不知彼，不知己，每戰必毜。 — Zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài. Bù zhī bǐ ér zhī jǐ, yī shèng yī bài. Bù zhī bǐ, bù zhī jǐ, měi zhàn bì dài. — Know the other and know yourself: in a hundred battles, no danger. Not knowing the other but knowing yourself: one victory, one defeat. Not knowing the other and not knowing yourself: in every battle, certain danger — Sun Tzu Art of War 3.18

Sun Tzu’s claim maps exactly onto the Boisot/McKelvey framework’s limitation. The Ashby Space tells the organisation how to calibrate its response to the stimulus environment. It is a framework for knowing the stimulus (the other) and calibrating the response (the self). But it does not tell the organisation how to know itself — how to understand its own formation history, its own sedimented Li, its own accumulated Shī — which is the precondition for any genuine strategic intelligence. Without self-knowledge in Shan’s sense — formation-historical self-knowledge, Dao-tracing self-knowledge — the most sophisticated external stimulus analysis produces only one-victory-one-defeat navigation: correct in the situations the framework anticipates, catastrophically wrong in the situations it has not produced the Li to see.

The Formation Counter-Proposal

Shan’s counter-proposal to Boisot/McKelvey: the Law of Requisite Complexity is correct but insufficiently grounded. Before asking whether internal complexity matches external complexity, ask what Dao produced the current internal complexity. Before mapping the stimulus environment in the Ashby Space, ask what formation history produced the current stimulus field. Before prescribing a response strategy, ask whether the organisation has the holding capacity to execute it and the formation history to sustain it.

This transforms the Ashby Space from a static mapping instrument into a formation diagnostic. The question is not ‘where are we in the Ashby Space?’ but ‘what formation history produced our current location in the Ashby Space, and what Shī does our current position carry toward the futures we are trying to navigate?’ This is Requisite Complexity grounded in Dao-before-Li ontology. It is the most powerful upgrade of the Boisot/McKelvey framework available.

Zhang Zai’s Western Inscription: what fills heaven and earth is my body. The organisation that genuinely inhabits this claim does not treat its environment as external stimulus to be matched. It recognises itself as constitutively entangled with the formation field it is part of — that its stimuli and its responses are aspects of a single formation process, that the Dao of its engagement with its environment is the Dao that produces its Li and consolidates its Shī. This is the cosmological grounding of the Shan challenge to Boisot/McKelvey: not a methodological correction but an ontological transformation.

XXX

Wayfinding as Dao: Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, Alsulaimi in Conversation with Shan

❧ ✶ ❧

Mushfiqa Monica Jamaluddin, Heba Alhadyian, and Abdulrahman Alsulaimi’s ‘The Wayfinder’s Approach to Futures’ (in Improving and Enhancing Scenario Planning, Edward Elgar, 2025) is the most structurally aligned futures studies work with Shan’s framework that this text has encountered in the Western context. Its central distinction — between navigation (using a pre-existing map to move from A to B) and wayfinding (building the map as you move through the landscape) — is a precise operational description of the difference between Li-before-Dao and Dao-before-Li.

“Navigation is the process of using a map, whether physical, digital, or cognitive, to move from point A to point B. In contrast, wayfinding is the process of mapping as one moves through a landscape. The former assumes that a map exists before it is used, and the latter builds the map as it goes. As Ingold describes, “we know as we go, not before we go.””

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), citing Ingold (2000, p.230)

‘We know as we go, not before we go’: this is Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim stated as epistemological principle. The map is the Li. The traversal of the landscape is the Dao. The claim that the map must be built in the walking is the claim that the Li must emerge from the Dao rather than preceding it. The navigator who arrives with a complete map is not wayfinding; they are imposing a prior Li on a landscape that has not yet been walked.

“Developing the capacity for wayfinding requires the adoption of a wayfinding mindset — but this framing risks violating epistemic belatedness. The wayfinding capacity arrives late, after the Daos that produced it have been walked. It cannot be adopted before those Daos; it can only be recognised as having been formed by them. In other words, we collectively learn and develop our capacities as we go, not before we go.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025)

The wayfinding mindset is precisely what Shan means by the capacity for Dao-walking that precedes and produces the Li of formation. The practitioner who has developed the wayfinding mindset does not need to know the territory before entering it. They have been formed to read it as they walk — to register its salience, to feel its valence, to sense its Shī before any explicit map has named it. This is Karaoguz’s A-Frame as navigational epistemology: the Attend-Appreciate-Act cycle IS the wayfinding process. Attunement IS the formation of the wayfinder. Karaoguz’s A-Frame (Attend, Appreciate, Act) is a formalised pedagogy of phenomenological precedence: the Attend phase is the Dao (the engagement precedes the intelligibility), the Appreciate phase is the Li-emergence (the intelligibility crystallises from the engagement), and the Act phase is the Shī-responsive movement (acting from the formed position rather than the pre-formed plan). The sequence is not incidental; it is the temporal structure of phenomenological precedence enacted as a repeatable practice. And crucially, each A-Frame cycle adds formation: the emergence lag of the next cycle is shorter because this cycle has thickened the practitioner’s structural sensitivity.

“An ongoing, reflective process of attunement and engagement with one’s environment, contrary to how one might approach a cartographic or navigational journey.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025)

Attunement as process rather than state: this is the key contribution of the Jamaluddin et al. account that deepens the Shan framework. Attunement is not something achieved and then possessed. It is an ongoing relational dynamic between the wayfinder and the landscape they are traversing. Each step changes both the wayfinder’s structural position and the landscape’s configuration relative to them. The map is always incomplete because the territory is always already moving past it.

“The wayfinder represents an integration of cartography and navigation, extending beyond both. Wayfinders immerse themselves in their environment, drawing cues in response to their engagement.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025)

The three roles — Cartographer (who maps from above, claiming mastery), Navigator (who uses the map, following pre-specified routes), Wayfinder (who builds the map in the walking, remaining present to what the terrain gives) — map exactly onto three relationships to Li. The Cartographer produces Li before the Dao. The Navigator applies Li to the Dao. The Wayfinder lets the Dao produce Li. Shan’s framework is a philosophy of wayfinding. The Dao-before-Li claim IS the wayfinding claim.

The Shī implication: the wayfinder-futurist does not merely navigate toward probable futures; they cultivate the positional Shī that makes certain futures more available. Each step is not merely movement toward a destination; it is formation of a position that shapes what destinations become visible. The map that the wayfinder builds is not a record of where they have been; it is the Shī of their accumulated traversal — the directional force that their formation history has produced.

“In complex systems, we can only ever map our current position and decide our next action based on the direction we want to move toward.”

— Snowden (2023), cited in Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025)

David Snowden’s claim and Shan’s Shī claim and Jamaluddin et al.’s wayfinding claim converge at the same structural recognition: in complex formations, the most available knowledge is not knowledge of destinations but knowledge of positions, directions, and formation pressures. The Shī of the current position determines what direction is most viable. The wayfinder reads this Shī and moves accordingly.
