This is not surrender to determinism; it is the highest form of strategic intelligence: the art of reading what the formation is already tending toward and aligning one’s movement with that tendency rather than against it.

❧ ✶ ❧
❧ ✶ ❧

Deepened Dialectical Encounter: The Full Architecture of the Wayfinding Chapter in Collision with Shan

What follows is the full analytical expansion of the encounter between Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi’s ‘The Wayfinder’s Approach to Futures’ (Chapter 4, pp. 73–95, in Crawford and Wright (eds.), Improving and Enhancing Scenario Planning: Futures Thinking, Edward Elgar Publishing, first published 13 February 2025, ISBN 9781035310579) and Shan’s complete body of work. Every claim extracted from the chapter is quoted exactly from the text as provided. Every Shan response is drawn from the verified body of work assembled in this paper. The collision is structural, not merely thematic.

I. Bibliographic Correction and Full Publication Record

The main text of this paper has previously referred to the Jamaluddin et al. chapter as published in ‘2025.’ This is correct. The confirmed publication record: Mushfiqa Monica Jamaluddin, Heba Alhadyian, and Abdulrahman Alsulaimi, ‘The Wayfinder’s Approach to Futures,’ Chapter 4 (pp. 73–95), in Megan M. Crawford and George Wright (eds.), Improving and Enhancing Scenario Planning: Futures Thinking, Cheltenham: Edward Elgar Publishing, published 13 February 2025. Print ISBN: 9781035310579; Electronic ISBN: 9781035310586 (Elgaronline). The PDF provided by the user shows a download date of 04/03/2025, confirming the 2025 publication. The Strathclyde University research repository lists this as Cheltenham 2024 (pre-publication record); the authoritative Elgar date is February 2025. This paper uses 2025 throughout.

II. The Navigation–Wayfinding Distinction: Full Structural Collision

The chapter’s most architecturally consequential claim is its distinction between navigation (map-using) and wayfinding (mapping-as-one-moves), articulated through the Ingold epistemology of knowing-as-we-go. The full chapter passage:

“Navigation is the process of using a map, whether physical, digital, or cognitive, to move from point A to point B. In contrast, wayfinding is the process of mapping as one moves through a landscape. The **former assumes that a map exists before it is used, and the latter builds the map as it goes. As Ingold describes, ‘we know as we go, not before we go’ (Ingold, 2000, p. 230).”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 78 — citing Ingold, The Perception of the Environment (2000, p. 230)

Three Ingold passages are required to understand the full structural convergence with Shan. The first is the one the chapter cites (pp. 229–230). The second, at p. 220, is the one the chapter does not cite but which carries the decisive structural claim:

“Wayfinding is understood as a skilled performance in which travelers, whose powers of perception and action have been fine-tuned through previous experience, ‘feel their way’ towards their goal, continually adjusting their movements in response to an ongoing perceptual monitoring of their surroundings.”

— Tim Ingold, The Perception of the Environment (2000, p. 220) [VERIFIED: confirmed verbatim in multiple scholarly sources]

The third, at p. 242, is the passage most directly convergent with Shan’s attunement account:

“But above all, wayfinding depends upon the attunement of the traveller’s movements in response to the movements, in his or her surroundings, of other people, animals, the wind, celestial bodies, and so on. Where nothing moves there is nothing to which one can respond.”

— Tim Ingold, The Perception of the Environment (2000, p. 242) [VERIFIED: confirmed verbatim in PMC article, DOI 10.1186/s40798-021-00326-6]

These three Ingold passages constitute a structural triad that maps exactly onto Shan’s Dao-before-Li sequence. The knowing-as-we-go (pp. 229–230) maps onto the ontological priority of Dao: the path precedes the pattern. The fine-tuning through experience (p. 220) maps onto Shan’s formation theory: the capacity to walk the Dao is itself a formation achievement produced by prior Daos — you can only feel your way through a terrain if your formation has produced the sensitivity to read its signals. The attunement of movements (p. 242) maps onto Shan’s cadence, resonance, and salience account: the wayfinder reads the formation field through the attuned response of a practitioner whose specific formation has produced the specific perceptual capacities required. The chapter uses Ingold’s first passage and underuses the second and third. The depth of the convergence with Shan is therefore greater than the chapter itself articulates.

“Dao precedes Li, not the other way around. This is not a semantic preference. It is a question of ontological precedence. The path must open before its inner grain can appear. Intelligibility does not come first. The path does. Mutual generation does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’, Cynefin Co (May 14, 2026)

The precise challenge Shan brings that the chapter does not fully address: the chapter presents the navigation-wayfinding distinction as a professional and cognitive choice — a matter of stance, of how futurists relate to their field. Shan insists that Dao-before-Li is not a choice. It is the structure of all formation. Every practitioner’s engagement with a complex field was already a Dao-before-Li process. The question is only whether they attended to it. The futures practitioner who ‘adopts a wayfinding mindset’ is not doing something genuinely new; they are beginning to notice what was already structurally happening. This is a deepening, not a correction — but it shifts the chapter’s framing from a mindset that can be adopted to a structural dynamic that can be recognised and attended to.

III. Lynch’s Imageability as Li-Before-Dao: The Structural Critique

The chapter draws on Lynch to establish the importance of imageability and legibility for the futures field. The key Lynch definitions as cited:

“that quality in a physical object which gives it a high probability of evoking a strong image in any given observer” [imageability] — and “the ease with which its parts can be recognized and can be organized into a coherent pattern” [legibility]

— Kevin Lynch, The Image of the City (1960), pp. 9 and 2–3 — as cited in Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 78

Both Lynch definitions assume that Li is a property of the object — that imageability belongs to the formation field and legibility is an intrinsic quality of the cityscape that the observer reads. Shan’s framework refuses this. Li is not a property of the formation; it is a relational achievement of the practitioner-formation encounter. The imageability of a city is not fixed; it is the specific grain of the city as produced by the specific Dao of the specific practitioner’s engagement with it. The image that a Chinese-Scottish bilingual researcher produces of Edinburgh is not the same image as the one a local urban planner produces — not because one is more accurate than the other but because they have walked different Daos through the same terrain and produced different Li from the same formation field. Lynch’s public image — the aggregate of individual images — is Li; but it is Li produced by the accumulated Daos of the city’s inhabitants, not a property of the city itself.

The chapter acknowledges Lynch’s limits: ‘it is limited in its cognitivist approach’ and ‘the focus is on the mental or cognitive image an individual holds of a city, to the exclusion of the embodied experience’ (p. 79). Shan’s framework supplies the structural account of why the embodied experience is not merely a supplement but the generative mechanism. The embodied engagement — the walking of the Dao — is what produces the Li that Lynch calls the image. The cognitivist approach captures the Li (the image) without the Dao (the walk) that produced it. This is the same error as the navigator’s: possessing the map without having walked the terrain.

IV. The Three Types and Their Structural Counterparts in Shan

“1. The Cartographer: who moves across a landscape, and, taking a bird’s eye view, sketches out the features of the environment as fixed locations in space. 2. The Navigator: who uses a map sketched out **by a cartographer to match waypoints on the map with physical coordinates, making their way from point A to point B. 3. The Wayfinder: steps into the environment, pauses to orient themselves and identify directionality, takes a few steps forward, pauses to orient in the new place, listens for familiar birdsong, feels the warmth from the sun, and adjusts course to move forward again.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 80

Shan’s structural analysis maps these three types onto three relationships to Dao and Li. The Cartographer produces Li before walking the current Dao: they impose a pattern-interpretation on the terrain from a bird’s-eye position that the terrain has not generated. The map encodes a prior Li that was itself produced by a prior Dao — the cartographer’s own previous traversal, or the accumulated traversals of earlier practitioners — but is now being applied to terrain that may have changed or that has a different grain than the inherited Li encodes.

“Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Dao: A Path Repeated Over Time Becomes Pattern’ (Substack, April 2026)

The Navigator applies the inherited Li. They do not make the error of claiming mastery; they follow the map faithfully. But they trust the map more than the terrain. When the terrain departs from the map — when the actual formation field produces Li that the prior map does not encode — the navigator either does not notice (the departure is invisible through the lens of prior Li) or discounts it (the departure seems like noise rather than signal). This is premature legibility: the Li of the prior map is applied before the Dao of the current terrain has been walked.

The Wayfinder does not arrive without a formation. Shan’s account is that the wayfinder’s capacity is not a virtue of openness or attitude; it is the product of a specific formation history that has produced the specific perceptual sensitivities required to read the specific terrain. The birdsong is a directional signal to the wayfinder whose formation has produced the sensitivity to read it as such. To a practitioner without that formation, it is irrelevant background noise. The wayfinding capacity is formation-specific. It cannot be adopted; it must be grown.

The chapter identifies a risk for veterans specifically:

“The role of the cartographer is important and tricky. Veterans of the field may come to view themselves as the map-makers. While their contributions are invaluable in shaping the landscape and supporting its legibility, this subtle but crucial shift in identity risks a disconnection from the pursuit of mapping, generating rigidity within the field and blocking the flow and evolution of the field.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 81

Shan’s structural precision: the veteran who has shifted from wayfinder to cartographer has inverted the Dao-Li sequence in their own self-understanding. They believe they have the Li; they believe their formation is complete. Shan’s mutual generation framework insists that the formation is never complete: the Li that the current Dao has produced becomes the starting condition for the next Dao, which will produce new Li that the current Li cannot predict. The veteran who believes their map is complete has confused the crystallised Li of their accumulated Daos with the actual grain of the ongoing formation field. The map is always already out of date.

V. Heuristics, Satisficing, and the Formation Theory of the Adaptive Toolbox

The chapter’s heuristics argument is grounded in the Simon-Gigerenzer architecture. The key claims, verbatim from the chapter:

“Ecological rationality means that a given decision is in alignment with the structural properties of the environment, or the context, in which it occurs; it is a ‘rationality that is defined by its fit with reality’ (Gigerenzer & Todd, 1999).”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 86

“In complex systems, we can only ever map our current position and decide our next action based on the direction we want to move toward.”

— David Snowden (2023), cited in Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 88

Snowden’s formulation and Shan’s Shī claim converge at the same structural recognition: in complex formations, the most important knowledge is not knowledge of destinations but knowledge of positions, directions, and formation pressures. The Shī of the current position determines what direction is most viable. But Shan’s Shī concept adds something the Snowden formulation does not have: it asks what positional force has been built by the accumulated Dao-walks of the practitioner and the field. The direction is not chosen; it is felt — as the directional pressure of a formed position. The wayfinder reads the Shī of their accumulated traversal and moves accordingly.

Shan’s three challenges to the heuristics architecture, all involving the ontology of precedence. First: Gigerenzer’s adaptive toolbox is Li. Simon’s satisficing is itself an acknowledgement of epistemic belatedness: the ‘good enough’ decision is good enough precisely because the full Li of the situation has not yet emerged from the Dao of engagement—the emergence lag has not resolved. Satisficing is the epistemically honest response to epistemic belatedness. Bayesian optimisation is the epistemically dishonest response: it demands the full Li before the Dao has been walked. And Gigerenzer’s adaptive toolbox is Li. The ecologically rational heuristics are the patterns of response that specific Daos of engagement with specific domain types have produced. The toolbox contains the crystallised Li of prior formation. It does not contain the Dao that built it, and therefore does not account for the formation sequence required to deploy it correctly. The practitioner who has not walked the Dao of a specific type of situation cannot reliably select the ecologically rational heuristic for it. Domain recognition is itself a formation achievement. You must have walked enough of this terrain to recognise its grain before you can select the heuristic that fits it.

“Li is the inner grain that makes the jade workable in some directions and resistant in others. It is not merely abstract logic, but the grain through which something becomes recognisable.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’, Cynefin Co (May 14, 2026)

Second: the feeling of ‘home’ in the chapter’s housing example (Table 4.1, p. 87) is not a bypass of rationality; it is a formation-adequate Li-reading. The specific structural resonance between the practitioner’s formation history and the specific grain of this specific space — what Shan would call the attunement of relational fields — is what produces the feeling. It is a direct perception of Li-match. The rational analysis of size, price, amenities, and location is an attempt to replicate analytically what the formation-adequate practitioner reads directly. Gigerenzer is right that the heuristic outperforms the analysis; Shan explains why: the heuristic is the Li; the analysis is an attempt to reconstruct the Li from the outside.

Third: the chapter’s Savage argument (large worlds preclude optimal rationality) establishes why ecological rationality is necessary. But it does not establish what produces ecological rationality in a specific practitioner in a specific domain. Shan’s holding capacity analysis provides this: the practitioner who has built sufficient formation in a domain — who has walked enough of the domain’s Daos to develop genuine holding capacity for its complexity — is the practitioner whose heuristics will be ecologically rational in that domain. Without the formation, the heuristics will be confident but wrong: the practitioner will apply the heuristic of a familiar domain to an unfamiliar one and mistake the confidence of recognition for the truth of fit.

“The system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The point is not simply that one step comes before another, but that prior formation makes further complexity possible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’ (Substack, May 2026)

VI. The Direction–Not–Destination Synthesis: Catmull, Snowden, and Shan on Shī

“the future is not a destination — it is a direction”

— Ed Catmull and Amy Wallace, Creativity, Inc. (2014, p. 361), cited by Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 88

The Catmull-Wallace formulation is elegant and structurally convergent with Shan’s Shī account. If the future is a direction rather than a destination, then futures practice is formation-building rather than prediction. The practitioner orients by their formation, reads the Shī of their accumulated position, and moves in the direction that the formation makes most viable. There is no terminal Li waiting to be reached; there is only the ongoing Dao whose walking produces new Li that shapes new direction.

The synthesis: Catmull provides the insight that direction supersedes destination. Snowden provides the operational frame: map position, decide next action based on direction. Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi embed both in the wayfinding framework. Shan provides the structural account of what direction means: the Shī of the accumulated formation, the positional force built by the specific Daos walked, the directionality that is felt rather than chosen by the practitioner whose formation has produced genuine structural attunement. Direction is not a preference; it is a formation achievement.

“A path repeated over time becomes pattern. Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Dao: A Path Repeated Over Time Becomes Pattern’ (Substack, April 2026)

Direction-keeping requires that the practitioner know which Daos they have inherited, which they are walking, and what Li those Daos are producing. The capacity to maintain direction in a complex formation field is the product of a specific formation history. It cannot be maintained by orientation alone; it requires the formation intelligence that the accumulated walk has produced. This is what the wayfinder’s pausing and listening and adjusting actually is: the ongoing reading of the Shī of the current position, the sense of where the formation’s own tendency is pointing, the feel of the grain that makes certain moves workable and others costly.

VII. The Ethical Layer: Dao Transparency and the Politics of Li-Production

“We must question who controls the map-making, who navigates using the maps, and how we can transcend this dichotomy to reclaim autonomy in the field. The wayfinding perspective suggests a collaborative model where everyone engages in both map-making and map-using. This approach calls for a conscious effort to preserve storytelling and recognize the impact of our journeys on the broader narratives of the field.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 90

Who controls the map-making controls the Li of the field. Shan’s structural account of this problem: the veteran cartographers of a field have encoded their specific Daos into the field’s accumulated Li. The newcomer who enters the field inherits that Li without the Dao that produced it. They receive the pattern; the path is invisible. The ethical question is not only who makes the maps but whether the Daos that produced those maps are sufficiently transparent that newcomers can trace them, walk them, and thereby develop the formation sensitivity required to produce genuinely new Li rather than merely applying the inherited patterns.

The chapter’s positionality section is an enactment of this transparency. By disclosing their connection to the University of Houston, their status as relative newcomers, their independent self-funding, and their transdisciplinary orientation, the authors make their Daos visible. They are saying: here is the formation that produced this Li. This is the ethical practice Shan’s framework requires: not the pretence of formation-independent authority but the explicit acknowledgement of the Daos that produced the specific Li being offered. Positionality statements are Dao-transparency declarations.

“For both audiences, the journey is ongoing and reflective, emphasizing a process-orientation.”

— Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi (2025), p. 91

Process-orientation as the chapter’s closing ethical commitment is structurally convergent with Shan’s account of the ongoing nature of all genuine formation. The practitioner is never finished forming. The Li they have produced is never the final Li. A futures field that stops walking its Dao — that crystallises its Li into fixed cartographic representations without continued traversal — has begun the collapse trajectory that Shan describes in ‘Nothing Collapses in One Move.’ The collapse does not announce itself; it manifests first as the smooth, unquestioned circulation of prior Li; it deepens as the field’s formation-sensitivity narrows; it becomes visible only when the crisis is already well advanced.

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. The formation becomes critical long before the visible crisis. What you see at the moment of collapse was forming for months, years, decades in the invisible substrate.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Nothing Collapses in One Move’ (Substack, April 2026)

VIII. What the Wayfinding Chapter Gives Shan — and What Shan Gives the Chapter

The Jamaluddin, Alhadyian, and Alsulaimi chapter gives Shan’s framework six things it needs. (1) A vocabulary for three epistemological stances — cartographer, navigator, wayfinder — that operationalises Dao-before-Li at the professional level of futures practice. (2) The Simon-Gigerenzer architecture of ecological rationality as the Western philosophical infrastructure for the claim that formation-adequate responses outperform optimal-rational responses in complex, large-world contexts. (3) The Savage small-world/large-world framing as a structural argument for why the futures field cannot achieve Bayesian optimality and why this is a feature, not a bug. (4) An explicit ethics of map-making that names the power dimensions of Li-production in professional communities. (5) The de Certeau account of the temporal dimension of orientation as the structural explanation of how practitioners locate themselves in formation histories. (6) The positionality framework as a model of Dao-transparency that could be adopted across the field.

Shan’s framework gives the chapter six things it needs. (1) The ontological grounding for the wayfinding/navigation distinction: not as mindset preference but as structural sequence written into the formation dynamics of all complex systems. (2) The formation theory that explains what makes wayfinding capacity possible — the Dao-walk is the formation that produces the Li-reading capacity, and without that walk, the mindset remains aspirational rather than structural. (3) The Li concept as the account of what the wayfinder reads: not a property of the terrain but a relational achievement of the practitioner-formation-field encounter. (4) The holding capacity analysis explaining why formation sequence cannot be shortcutted by attitude or reflection alone. (5) The Shī concept as the structural account of what the wayfinder orients toward: the positional force of the accumulated formation, the directional tendency of the field, the grain that makes certain moves workable and others costly. (6) The mutual generation framework explaining how Dao and Li interact without collapsing into each other: the formation produces the pattern, the pattern enables the next formation, and neither can serve as a fixed foundation for the other.

❧ ✶ ❧

Shan’s Seventh Challenge: Intention Remains Too Central

James criticises simplistic intention-based models, but the intention–action gap still organises the paper. Even when reframed as a coordination problem, intention remains the problem’s anchor. Shan would ask whether this is already too Western, too cognitive, too individualistic, too explicit. Dao does not begin with intention. It begins with movement under constraint. A path forms because something traverses a landscape repeatedly. The path may precede any explicit intention. Indeed, intention itself may be a late-arriving Li: an articulation that appears after the body, field, and relation have already begun moving.

“A path becomes a path only through repeated walking. This is as true of ideas as it is of ground. The conceptual paths that feel most natural are the ones that have been walked most often, by the most people, across the longest time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (Substack, April 2026)

The deep Shan critique: James has not fully escaped the intention frame. A Dao-first behavioural theory would begin not with ‘I intend X but do Y’ but with: Given this field, these constraints, these relations, these repetitions, and this inherited path, what movements have become available, natural, costly, shameful, invisible, or impossible? That is a more radical starting point. The Dao was walking before the intention arrived to name it.

Shan’s Eighth Challenge: Relation Precedes Dynamics

“Dynamics do not happen in a void. They presuppose a relational condition within which movement becomes possible, transmissible, and intelligible. Relation precedes dynamics.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (Substack, May 2026)

James is relational, but Shan is more radically relational. James says behaviour emerges from brain-body-environment dynamics. Shan says dynamics themselves presuppose a relation-bearing field. Motion only becomes consequential when relation makes it matter. Her formula: Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time. In James, relation often appears as part of the dynamic system. In Shan, relation is the condition for dynamics becoming dynamics at all.

The practical consequence: a behavioural intervention does not fail only because the scaffold is wrong, the stress is wrong, or the affordance is wrong. It may fail because the relation-bearing field is absent. The same advice lands differently depending on trust. The same scaffold works differently depending on dignity. The same shock transforms or traumatises depending on relational containment. The same habit change plan succeeds or fails depending on whether the person feels recognised. Wayshaping needs a prior diagnostic of relational field quality. Before intervention: relation. Before dynamics: relation. Before realignment: relation.

Shan’s Ninth Challenge: Wayshaping Needs a Theory of Language

Shan’s framework is deeply concerned with language as field-generative. A behaviour-change framework does not merely describe change — it shapes what practitioners can perceive. If a practitioner says ‘resistance’ they see obstruction. If they say ‘misalignment’ they see coordination failure. If they say ‘low motivation’ they see insufficient drive. If they say ‘path inheritance’ they see formation. If they say ‘holding capacity’ they see viability. If they say ‘grain’ they see workability.

“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6

Wayshaping’s Wittgensteinian blind spot: the terms ‘scaffold’, ‘shock’, ‘alignment’, ‘self-collective’, and ‘dynamic loading’ are not neutral instruments. They are interfaces that make some things visible and hide others. They generate a world in which certain formations are perceivable and others are not. Shan’s demand: Wayshaping must examine how its own vocabulary creates its own perceptual world. The Li of the framework must be examined with the same formation-tracing rigor that the framework applies to the formations it analyses.

Shan’s Tenth Challenge: The Ethics of Non-Intervention

James is careful. It rejects predictability fantasies and admits models are only maps. But Wayshaping is still oriented toward shaping. Shan asks for the art of knowing when not to shape. If Dao precedes Li, and if Li must be discovered through the path, then not acting too soon is not passivity. It is the highest discipline.

“为学日益，为道日搏。搏之又搏，以至於無為。”

Sometimes the right move is not scaffold. Sometimes the right move is not shock. Sometimes the right move is not realignment. Sometimes the right move is to dwell, trace, listen, thicken perception, and wait until the grain appears. This is not anti-practical. It is deeper practicality. It is Cook Ding’s knife: the cut happens only because the grain has already been perceived — this is phenomenological precedence enacted at the level of ethical practice. The practitioner who intervenes before the grain has been read does not help the formation; they rupture it. The intervention-before-Li is a violation of emergence lag: the formation has not yet produced the Li that would make intervention formation-adequate. Premature intervention does not merely fail; it actively forecloses the Dao that would have produced the Li it was trying to bypass. This is Shan’s tenth and most fundamental challenge to Wayshaping: the art of formation-sensitive transformation begins with the discipline of non-premature intervention. 悖论: The most powerful intervention is often the one that does not yet happen. The Dao must be walked. The Li will appear.

Fuller’s Tensegrity: The Physics of Relational Integrity

❧ ✶ ❧

“‘The word tensegrity is an invention: it is a contraction of tensional integrity.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics Dictionary

Tensional integrity: the phrase does not merely name a structural type. It announces an ontological reversal. The dominant structural imaginary of Western engineering is compressional — things hold together because their elements push against each other in rigid chains of contact. Tensegrity refuses this. The structure holds because tension — distributed, continuous, non-local — connects every element to every other simultaneously. There are no rigid chains. There is only the continuous field of relational holding. Shan reads this as a structural metaphor for her entire framework: relational dynamics is the tensegrity of meaning, of formation, of practice. Coherence is not achieved by elements locking against each other. It is achieved by the continuous distribution of relational force through the whole.

“‘The integrity of the whole structure is invested in the finitely closed, tensional-embracing network of the system.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.02–03

Finitely closed, tensional-embracing: the structure is not open at its edges — the tension network closes around the whole, making every point a structural participant. This is the physics of what Shan calls the relational field that precedes dynamics. The field is not a background against which events occur; it is a tensionally closed network whose specific topology determines what events are possible. Nothing happens outside the network. Nothing happens to the network from without. Every perturbation is a change in the distribution of tension within the closed whole. This is why nothing collapses in one move: the dissolution of structural integrity is always the progressive failure of the tension network, always distributed, always prior to the visible event.

“‘All structures, properly understood, from the solar system to the atom, are tensegrity structures.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.04

All structures. The cosmological scope of the claim is not rhetorical. Fuller is making an ontological claim about the deep structure of physical reality: the universe maintains its coherence not through compression but through the omnitensional integrity of distributed relational force. Shan’s parallel claim: all formation — from the neonatal gut forming around the first feeding to the organisation developing its strategic capacity over decades — is a tensional-integrity process. The specific Li of any specific formation is the specific topology of its tensional network. What Zhu Xi calls the cosmic Li, Fuller calls omnitensional integrity. What Shan calls the relational field, Fuller calls the closed tensional-embracing network. The physics and the philosophy converge on the same structural recognition.

“‘Each of the chemical elements is a pattern integrity. Each individual is a pattern integrity.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Pattern integrity: the element or the individual does not exist as a substance — but Fuller’s pattern-integrity claim contains a hidden structural asymmetry that his framework does not fully address. The pattern integrity of the carbon atom is the Li of the Dao that produced it through stellar nucleosynthesis: the specific formation history of cosmic matter at a specific temperature under specific pressure constraints. The pattern (Li) is real and stable; but it is structurally asymmetrical with the process (Dao) that produced it. Fuller tells us what the pattern is; Shan asks what walked it into being. The pattern cannot reverse-engineer its own formation — the structural asymmetry is written into the direction of time itself. — a thing with fixed properties — but as a pattern of relationships held in coherent form. The carbon atom is not a particle; it is a specific topology of relational forces whose specific pattern makes it carbon rather than nitrogen or oxygen. The individual human being is not a substance; they are a specific pattern of relational formation — biological, psychological, cultural, linguistic — whose specific topology makes them who they are. Shan’s self-collective (via the Wayshaping challenge) is precisely this: not a substance with properties but a pattern integrity whose coherence is maintained through the distribution of relational tension across all its constituent formations.

“‘You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

This is the strategic principle of Shan’s entire project, stated in design theory terms. Fighting the existing model — arguing against the Li-before-Dao assumption, polemicising against the management frameworks that apply prior patterns to unwalked formations — reinforces the existing model by treating it as the primary reference. The new model that makes the old obsolete: a framework so structurally adequate to the actual, so clearly grounded in genuine formation rather than imposed Li, that the old model loses its grip not through refutation but through irrelevance. Relational dynamics is not an argument against the old models. It is the new model. Walk the Dao. Let the Li appear. The obsolescence follows.

“‘Integrity is the essence of everything successful. If humanity does not opt for integrity, it is through ignorance, which is humanity’s greatest challenge.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Integrity as the essence of success: not strategy, not intelligence, not resources, not timing — integrity. The structural claim: what succeeds is what holds together under pressure, what maintains the distribution of relational tension through the whole even when specific elements are stressed, what does not fracture at the point where the load is concentrated. The ignorance claim is the most structurally interesting: the failure of integrity is not primarily moral failure but epistemic failure. The practitioner who does not know that tension is the great integrity — who tries to build through compression, who tries to impose rather than follow the grain — produces structures that fracture. The correction is not better intentions. It is the formation of structural attunement: the Dao-walk that produces the Li of genuine integrity.

“‘All the categories of creatures act individually as special-case and may be linearly analyzed, but the entire generalized system is non-linearly and synergetically operative.’”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §1005.53

Special-case versus generalized system: the individual element can be analysed linearly; the whole operates nonlinearly and synergetically. This is Shan’s coupling claim applied to Fuller’s structural physics. Each element of the formation can be traced, described, characterised. But the formation as a whole — the Dao that produces Li through the specific nonlinear interaction of all elements simultaneously — cannot be reconstructed from linear analysis of the parts. Synergy: the whole exhibits properties that none of the parts possesses. The Li that emerges from the Dao-walk is synergetic: it could not have been predicted from analysis of the formation’s components. Move 37 is synergetic. The Empty City Stratagem is synergetic. The formation that holds under pressure is synergetic. This is why Dao must precede Li: only the nonlinear whole produces the emergent pattern.

Wittgenstein’s Tractatus: The Limit of the Sayable and the Grain of the Real

“‘The world is everything that is the case. The world is the totality of facts, not of things.’”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 1–1.1

The world is facts, not things. This is the Tractatus’s most decisive opening move: the primary reality is not substances but states of affairs — not what exists but what obtains. Things exist only as the nodes of possible fact; they have no reality independent of their potential participation in states of affairs. Shan reads this as a structural alignment with her relational-precedes-dynamics claim: what is primary is not the elements but the relational field in which elements participate. The world as the totality of facts is the world as a relational structure. Things are not prior to relations; relations are prior to things. The element has its character — its Li — only through its participation in the formation that constitutes it.

“‘The picture is a model of reality. To the objects correspond in the picture the elements of the picture.’”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 2.12–2.13

The picture theory of meaning: language pictures reality by sharing its logical form. The proposition has the same relational structure as the state of affairs it depicts. This is the Tractatus’s Li claim: the logical form of language is the Li of reality, and adequate language is language whose structure matches the structure of what it describes. Shan’s challenge: the logical form of the Chinese philosophical vocabulary for Dao, Li, and Shī is not the same as the logical form of Western analytical philosophy. The two linguistic pictures do not share the same structural form. This means that translation between them is not a mapping of one Li onto another; it is the encounter of two different formation traditions whose specific Lis are structurally different, and whose collision produces something neither could depict alone.

“‘Es ist klar, dass sich die Ethik nicht aussprechen lässt. Ethics cannot be put into words.’”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.421

Ethics cannot be put into words: not because ethics is arbitrary or subjective but because ethical value — like logical form, like what shows itself — is a structural feature of reality that exceeds any propositional representation. Shan’s formation ethics shares this structure: the ethical quality of a practitioner’s relationship to the formation they navigate cannot be fully stated in any code or principle. It shows itself in the quality of the engagement — in whether the practitioner approaches the formation with genuine attunement or with a prior Li they are determined to confirm. This is why Cilliers’ critique of premature Li is ethical as well as epistemological: imposing a prior pattern on an unwalked formation is an ethical violation that no propositional code can adequately characterise.

“‘My propositions are elucidatory in this way: he who understands me finally recognizes them as senseless, when he has used them — as steps — to climb up beyond them.’”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 6.54–7

The ladder to be thrown away: the Tractatus is a self-consuming artefact. It makes propositional claims in order to demonstrate that no propositional claims can capture what it is trying to show. Shan’s framework has the same structure. The Dao-before-Li claim is itself a Li — a named pattern produced by a specific formation. The relational dynamics vocabulary is a set of concepts that, if held too tightly, becomes the very premature Li it warns against. The correct relationship to Shan’s framework is the ladder relationship: use it to climb. Recognise it as provisional. Let the Dao it points toward exceed it. And then — like Wittgenstein’s ladder, like the actual ox after Cook Ding’s nineteenth year — let it dissolve into the formation it was always pointing toward.

“‘Philosophy is not a theory but an activity. The object of philosophy is the logical clarification of thoughts.’”

— Wittgenstein, Tractatus 4.112

Philosophy as activity: not the production of doctrines but the practice of clarification. Shan’s essays enact this claim structurally. They do not produce a theory of Dao and Li and Shī. They practice the clarification of thought about formation, about what precedes what, about the structure of the relationship between path and pattern. The essays are Dao-walks: they produce Li through the act of traversal. Each essay is a formation act. The Li that appears — the clarification achieved — is downstream of the specific Dao of that specific essay’s specific intellectual traversal. This is why the essays cannot be summarised without loss: the summary is a Li without the Dao that produced it.

Philosophical Investigations: Forms of Life and the Grammar of Practice

“‘The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life.’”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §23

Language as activity within a form of life: this is Shan’s bilingual formation claim stated as philosophical principle. The Chinese speaker and the English speaker do not have access to two different sets of meanings; they inhabit two different forms of life within which language functions differently, within which different things are sayable and different things show themselves. The translation problem that Shan’s work navigates is not a translation problem; it is a form-of-life problem. The Chinese character 道 does not translate into English because no single English word inhabits the same form of life. The translation that Shan performs across her essays is the slow, patient formation of a new form of life — a bilingual intellectual practice within which ‘Dao’ gradually acquires the depth of use that makes it genuinely available rather than merely decorative.

“‘It is not only agreement in definitions but also (odd as it may sound) in judgments that we call agreement in form of life.’”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §241–242

Agreement in form of life: not just agreement about what words mean but agreement in how to respond, in what matters, in what requires justification and what does not. The practitioner who shares Shan’s form of life — who has walked enough of the same Dao, who has been formed to find certain things salient and certain responses natural — understands the essays immediately, not through decoding but through resonance. The practitioner who has not walked that Dao finds the essays interesting but somehow elusive. This is not a failure of clarity; it is the structure of formation-dependent understanding. The Dao must be walked before the Li can be genuinely shared. Agreement in form of life is the highest form of genuine intellectual alignment.

“‘What is your aim in philosophy? To show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.’”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §309

The fly-bottle: the philosophical fly is trapped not by external constraint but by its own confused picture of how things are. It keeps flying against the glass because it cannot see that the glass is glass — that the constraint is the Li of its own formed perception rather than a feature of external reality. The way out is not to smash the glass but to show the fly how it got in — to trace the Dao by which the confusing picture was formed, to illuminate the inherited path that now presents itself as the only possible way of seeing. This is exactly Shan’s therapeutic project. The management practitioner trapped in the Li-before-Dao assumption is not stupid; they are inside a fly-bottle. The relational dynamics framework is the gesture that shows the way out.

“‘If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: This is simply what I do.’”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §217

Bedrock: the point at which justification runs out and practice stands on itself. Shan’s Dao-walk reaches its own bedrock: the formation of the practitioner who has walked long enough that the Li of the formation field shows itself without requiring justification — who acts from structural attunement rather than from explicit reasoning. Cook Ding after nineteen years has reached bedrock. The knife finds the hollow not because of reasoning but because of formation. His spade is turned: not by ignorance but by the depth of his formation, which has taken him beyond the domain where explicit justification is the appropriate mode of knowing. This is not anti-intellectual; it is the deepest possible achievement of intellectual formation.

“‘What we do is bring words back from their metaphysical to their everyday use.’”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §116

From metaphysical to everyday use: the philosophical therapy. When ‘Dao’ is lifted out of its everyday formation context and made into a metaphysical principle, it loses the specific gravity of its use and becomes something that can travel smoothly through management training programmes and corporate vision statements. Shan’s counter-move is to return the term to its embodied, formation-specific, practice-embedded use — to show what ‘Dao’ does in the specific context of complexity navigation, in the specific encounter between a bilingual practitioner and the formation field of Chinese international students in Edinburgh seminars. The everyday use is the heavy use, the use with friction and resistance, the use that produces Li through the Dao of genuine engagement. The metaphysical use is the smooth use, the use that travels too easily, the use that warns of premature Li.

“‘A philosophical problem has the form: “I don’t know my way about.”’”

— Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §123

I don’t know my way about: disorientation as the form of philosophical problems. The practitioner who does not know their way about is the practitioner who has arrived in a formation field with a prior Li that no longer maps onto the actual terrain. The categories of the map do not match the features of the landscape. The framework explains but does not illuminate. The concept is clear but does not grip the real. This is not stupidity; it is the condition of any practitioner whose existing Li has reached the edge of its formation. The way forward is the Dao: walk the actual terrain, let the new Li emerge from the actual formation, re-form the map through genuine traversal. Philosophical disorientation is the signal that a new Dao is needed.

On Certainty: The River-Bed of Formation

“‘It might be imagined that some propositions, of the form of empirical propositions, were hardened and functioned as channels for such empirical propositions as were not hardened but fluid.’”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty §96

Hardened propositions as channels: the river-bed metaphor before it is named. Some beliefs harden into the formation structure that makes all other beliefs possible. They do not function as propositions that can be doubted or confirmed; they function as the channels that give doubtable and confirmable propositions their shape. Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim has this structure: it is not itself a hypothesis to be tested but a channel that determines what counts as evidence, what formations are visible, what Li is available for reading. The hardened channel is the formation’s deepest Li — the grain that was laid down first and that now gives direction to all subsequent formation.

“‘The river-bed of thoughts may shift. But I distinguish between the movement of the waters on the river-bed and the shift of the bed itself.’”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty §97

River-bed shifting: the most important claim in On Certainty for the dynamics of formation change. The hardened propositions — the bedrock of the practitioner’s formation — are not permanent. They can shift. But the shift is not the ordinary movement of thought along the channel; it is the transformation of the channel itself, the restructuring of what functions as the precondition of all subsequent thought. Cook Ding’s river-bed shifted in the third year of his practice: the whole-ox perception — the hardened channel that made all previous knife-work possible — dissolved, and a new channel formed, one that made the articulations of the actual ox visible for the first time. This is the most profound transformation available in the Dao-walk: the shift of the river-bed itself.

“‘The world-picture is the inherited background against which I distinguish between true and false.’”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty §94

The inherited background: this is Shan’s inherited Dao, the path already formed when the practitioner arrives. The world-picture is not chosen; it is the condition within which choice becomes possible. The Chinese scholar who enters the Edinburgh seminar has a world-picture within which certain forms of oral participation are natural and certain are impossible. The Edinburgh seminar itself has a world-picture within which certain forms of participation count as contribution and certain do not. The collision of world-pictures is not a problem to be solved by better translation; it is the specific Dao that Shan walked for the duration of her PhD research and that produced the specific Li of the relational dynamics framework.

“‘At the core of all well-founded belief lies belief that is unfounded.’”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty

Unfounded foundation: the deepest level of the formation is not justified by anything prior to it; it is the precondition of justification itself. This is not scepticism; it is the structural recognition that every formation has a ground that is the product of its specific Dao rather than the consequence of its explicit reasoning. The unfounded foundation is the most-formed thing: the formation that has been walked the longest, that has hardened into the deepest channel, that requires the most Dao-transformation to shift. Shan’s claim that the relational field precedes dynamics is itself unfounded in this sense: it is the formation ground of the relational dynamics framework, the channel that gives all subsequent analysis its shape, the bedrock where the spade is turned.

“‘If you tried to doubt everything you would not get as far as doubting anything. The game of doubting itself presupposes certainty.’”

— Wittgenstein, On Certainty

The game of doubting presupposes certainty: radical scepticism is self-refuting. Every act of questioning presupposes a formation that makes the question possible — a language, a context, a set of inherited practices within which questioning is a recognisable activity. Shan’s anti-premature-Li argument has exactly this structure: the practitioner who arrives with a prior Li is not wrong to have formation; they are wrong to mistake their formation for certainty about this specific formation field. The correction is not the abandonment of formation but the cultivation of the structural sensitivity to recognise when the existing Li is no longer adequate to the actual Dao — when the certainty that presupposes the questioning has itself become the object of questioning.

Heidegger: Questioning as Dao-Walking

“‘Questioning builds a way. We would be advised, therefore, above all to pay heed to the way, and not to fix our attention on isolated sentences and topics.’”

— Martin Heidegger, “The Question Concerning Technology”

Questioning builds a way: this is the most direct Western philosophical statement of the Dao-before-Li claim. The question does not arrive at an answer that pre-existed the questioning; it builds the path along which an answer becomes possible. Heidegger’s instruction to pay heed to the way rather than fixing attention on isolated sentences is exactly Shan’s instruction to trace the Dao rather than applying the Li. The isolated sentence — the extracted quotation, the decontextualised principle, the framework applied without the prior formation walk — is always a Li without its Dao. The way must be attended to. The questioning must be walked. The answer is the grain of the path, not the destination that precedes it.

Prigogine: Irreversibility, Entropy, and the Arrow of Formation

“‘Only when a system behaves in a sufficiently random way may the difference between past and future, and therefore irreversibility, play an essential role.’”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

Sufficient randomness as the condition of irreversibility: only in genuinely complex systems — systems that are far enough from equilibrium, that have enough internal variety, that cannot be fully specified by their current state — does the arrow of time play an essential role. Shan’s formation field is such a system: it is not a closed mechanical system whose future state follows deterministically from its current state, but a genuinely complex, far-from-equilibrium formation whose Li emerges from the specific, historically irreversible Dao of its specific engagement with its specific conditions. The Dao’s irreversibility is the Li’s guarantee of novelty.

“‘The main character of any living system is openness.’”

— Ilya Prigogine

Openness as the main character of living systems: not closure, not self-sufficiency, not independence from environment, but continuous exchange with the formation field that sustains the living system’s far-from-equilibrium organisation. Shan’s Dao is the specific mode of openness of the formation: the direction and character of the exchange between the practitioner and the formation field, the specific way in which the practitioner’s formation receives and metabolises the formation field’s inputs. A closed formation — one that has shut down its openness to the actual, that confirms only what its existing Li predicts — has ceased to be genuinely living in Prigogine’s sense. It is drifting toward equilibrium. Toward thermodynamic death.

“‘The real is only one realization of the possible.’”

— Ilya Prigogine

One realisation of the possible: this is the adjacent possible stated as ontology. The actual Li of the actual formation is one specific crystallisation from the field of all possible Lis that the formation conditions made available. The bifurcation point — the moment of maximum sensitivity to perturbation, the far-from-equilibrium crisis — is the moment when the greatest range of possible Lis is available, when the smallest specific perturbation determines which possible world becomes actual. Move 37 was one realisation of the possible. The practitioners who could not see it were not stupid; they were accessing a different set of realisable possibles. AlphaGo’s different formation produced a different adjacent possible. The real is always the specific — never the necessary.

“‘Classical science, the mythical science of a simple, passive world, belongs to the past.’”

— Ilya Prigogine, Order Out of Chaos

The simple, passive world: the world of classical mechanics, in which every state follows deterministically from prior states, in which the observer stands outside the observed, in which time is reversible and the arrow of formation has no ontological significance. This world belongs to the past as a description of physical reality. But as a model of organisational and human formation, it persists with remarkable tenacity in management theory, in behaviour-change frameworks, in complexity tools that promise to map the formation field before entering it. Shan’s framework is the equivalent of Prigogine’s revolution applied to human and organisational formation: the formation field is not simple, not passive, not predictable from its current state. The Dao must be walked. The Li will appear in the walking.

Kauffman: Order for Free and the Biosphere of Formation

“‘The complex whole may exhibit properties that are not readily explained by understanding its parts.’”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe

Properties not explained by the parts: this is the anti-reductionist claim that Fuller names synergy and Shan names the emergent Li of the Dao-walk. The Li of a complex formation cannot be reconstructed from analysis of its components because it is a property of the whole configuration — of the specific nonlinear interaction of all elements simultaneously. This is why the Ashby Space cannot read Shī: it analyses components and their varieties, but Shī is a property of the whole formation that no component-level analysis can access. The whole is not the sum of parts. The Li is not the summary of the Dao’s individual steps. The pattern of the path is not visible from any point along the path.

“‘This web of life, the most complex system we know of in the universe, breaks no law of physics yet is not derivable from physics.’”

— Stuart Kauffman

Not derivable from physics: even though life obeys every physical law, the specific forms it takes — the specific Lis of specific organisms, ecosystems, and evolutionary trajectories — are not derivable from the underlying physics. The higher-level organisation has genuine causal efficacy that is not reducible to its physical substrate. Shan’s framework applies this principle to human formation: the Li of a specific organisational formation is not derivable from the biology of its members, the economics of its environment, or the sociology of its context, even though it is constrained by all three. The formation is genuinely emergent. The Dao that produces it is genuinely creative. The Li that appears is genuinely new.

Holland: Emergence and the Building Blocks of Formation

“‘Emergence is the notion that the whole is more than the sum of its parts.’”

— John Holland, Emergence: From Chaos to Order

More than the sum of parts: the most compressed statement of the emergent Li claim. When specific formation elements interact under specific constraints in a specific Dao, what emerges is not predictable from any prior analysis of those elements. Holland’s building blocks: complex systems build themselves from simple rules applied locally, and the complexity that emerges from local interaction exceeds any prior specification of it. Move 37 is a building-block emergence: the local interaction of board positions, strategic principles, and game states produced a specific configuration whose global significance — whose Shī — was invisible to human formation but visible to a system formed through a different Dao. The emergence is real. The sum was wrong before the whole appeared.

Snowden: Cynefin, Coherence, and the Limits of the Map

“‘We manage the emergence of beneficial coherence within attractors within boundaries. And we manage by starting with small probes.’”

— David Snowden

Managing emergence rather than managing outcomes: this is Shan’s holding-capacity argument stated as complexity practice. The practitioner does not specify the Li in advance and then implement it; they cultivate the formation conditions — the attractors, the boundaries — within which beneficial coherence can emerge from the formation field’s own Dao. Small probes: not large interventions premised on prior knowledge of the Li that should appear, but minimal perturbations that generate feedback, that allow the formation field to reveal its own grain, that walk the Dao before naming the Li. The Cynefin framework’s Complex domain is exactly Shan’s formation territory: the domain where probe-sense-respond replaces sense-analyse-respond, where the Li is downstream of the Dao, where the formation must be encountered before it can be mapped.

Bateson: The Pattern That Connects and the Ecology of Formation

“‘What is the pattern which connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all four of them to me?’”

— Gregory Bateson, Mind and Nature (1979)

The pattern that connects: Bateson’s most famous question, and the one that most directly parallels Shan’s Li. The metapattern is not the pattern of any specific formation but the structural principle that makes diverse formations recognisable as instances of the same kind. The crab and the lobster share a metapattern not because they are similar but because the specific Daos that produced them have produced Lis that are structurally capable of mutual recognition. This is resonance as ontological recognition: the metapattern is the structural reality that the resonance reveals. The practitioner formed to read metapatterns can see the common Li of formations that appear, on the surface, entirely different. This is the foundation of genuine comparative thought.

“‘Information is any difference that makes a difference.’”

— Gregory Bateson

Information as difference that makes a difference: the most precise available definition of what Shan means by the formation field’s salience structure. Not all differences make differences; only those differences that the formation is structured to respond to register as information. What registers depends entirely on the specific Li of the specific formation — on the specific attunement that the specific Dao has produced. The practitioner who cannot see Move 37 is not receiving less information than AlphaGo; they are receiving the same physical signals with a different formation that makes different differences make differences. Salience is not a property of stimuli; it is a relational property of the encounter between a specific formation and a specific formation field.

Luhmann: Social Systems and the Formation of Meaning

“‘Society is a self-organizing system that produces its own elements by means of its own elements.’”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1995)

Self-producing elements: Luhmann’s social autopoiesis claim. The organisation does not receive its elements from its environment and then organise them; it produces its elements — its communications, its meanings, its structural distinctions — through its own operation. This is Shan’s relational-field claim stated as social systems theory: the formation field constitutes itself through its own formation processes. The Dao produces the Li that shapes the next Dao. The system produces the elements that it uses to produce itself. There is no external source of Li; there is only the specific formation history of the specific system’s specific Dao. This is why the practitioner who imposes an external Li on an organisation is not helping it; they are introducing foreign elements into a self-producing system whose coherence depends on its own formation history.

Meadows: Systems, Leverage, and the Patience of Formation

“‘The world is a complex, interconnected, finite, ecological-social-psychological-economic system. We treat it as if it were not, as if it were divisible, separable, simple, and infinite.’”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)

Treating the complex as simple: this is the Li-before-Dao error stated as systems pathology. We treat the complex system as if it were divisible — as if its components could be analysed separately and their interactions then simply added. As if it were separable — as if the formation field could be cleanly bounded and the elements within it fully specified. As if it were simple — as if the formation had a fixed Li that prior analysis could reveal. As if it were infinite — as if the system’s capacity to absorb interventions had no limit. Shan’s holding-capacity concept is the correction to the infinite assumption: every formation has a Dynamic Maximum Tension, a limit to what it can absorb. The practitioner who treats the formation as if it had no limits produces rupture, not transformation.

Whitehead: Process and the Creativity of Formation

“‘Process is fundamental.’”

— Whitehead, Process and Reality

Process is fundamental: the three most compressed words in Whitehead’s philosophy, and the claim that most directly grounds Shan’s Dao-before-Li ontology. If process is fundamental, then the formation is prior to the formed. The Dao is prior to the Li. The actual occasion — the specific process of formation in the specific moment — is the primary unit of reality; the formed Li is the record of that process, not the substance that preceded it. Whitehead’s process ontology and Shan’s relational dynamics framework share the same ontological structure: both refuse the primacy of static substance, both insist on the primacy of the formation process, both locate genuine creativity in the specific, historically contingent, irreversible process of actual formation rather than in any prior principle or cosmic essence.

Shan: The Essays — Dialectical Voltage Under Each Quote

“Participation is the visible surface of a deeper relational field, shaped by linguistic, cultural, and epistemic formations that precede and exceed the moment of speaking.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Iceberg Model of Oral Participation, Revisited” (May 2026)

The visible surface and the deeper relational field: this is the foundational claim of the iceberg model and the structural principle that organises all of Shan’s work. What appears in the seminar room — who speaks, when, how, with what confidence — is never the primary phenomenon. It is the crystallised surface of a formation field that was shaped before anyone entered the room: by the student’s linguistic formation, by the cultural epistemology that determines what counts as contribution, by the specific history of this student’s formation in two educational traditions simultaneously. The practitioner who sees only the visible surface and intervenes at the level of participation norms is working on the Li without walking the Dao. The relational field precedes the dynamics.

The four-part sequence: Dao before Li, path before pattern, grain before intelligibility, exploration before explanation. Each pair makes the same claim in a different register. Dao/Li: the formation process precedes the named pattern. Path/Pattern: the traversal precedes the map. Grain/Intelligibility: the structural reality precedes the conceptual grasp of it. Exploration/Explanation: the genuine encounter with the actual precedes the framework that explains the actual. All four pairs are descriptions of the same ontological sequence, approached from the perspectives of philosophy, geography, material science, and epistemology simultaneously. The four together constitute the most compressed possible statement of what the relational dynamics framework claims about the structure of formation.

“Coupling does not abolish sequence. It makes sequence harder to see. If we want to understand how a complex system works, we need both.’”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence” (May 2026)

Two ways of seeing the same structural claim: the Chinese philosophical vocabulary (Dao/Li) and the Western complexity vocabulary (relation/dynamics) are two different formation traditions that have independently arrived at the same structural recognition. This is not incidental. It is evidence that the recognition is genuine: when radically different Daos produce convergent Lis, the convergence is evidence of structural reality rather than cultural preference. Shan’s bilingual practice is the specific Dao that makes this convergence visible. Only a practitioner formed simultaneously in both traditions can see what their specific convergence demonstrates. This is the unique contribution that Shan’s formation makes possible.

“The move that finally loses the game is often not the move that truly lost it. It only makes the loss visible.”

— Alice Jing Shan, “Nothing Collapses in One Move” (April 2026)

Makes the loss visible: collapse and its cause are separated in time. The move that appears to lose the game — the visible crisis, the final failure — is the moment when the Shī of accumulated formation finally crystallises into irreversible consequence. The game was lost earlier, in the formation of the position that made the losing move’s consequence unavoidable. This is the structural principle that transforms Shan’s nothing-collapses-in-one-move claim into a practical diagnostic tool: look upstream of the visible crisis. Ask what Dao was walked that produced the Shī that made the crisis available. The post-mortem that looks only at the final move is looking at the Li without the Dao.

“‘What began as 围棋 in Chinese travelled through Japanese, was compressed into “Go” in English, fused with AI into AlphaGo, and returned to Chinese as a dog. A trans-species level of reverse culture shock.’”

— Alice Jing Shan, “AlphaGo’s Move 37” (April 2026)

The cross-cultural journey of a game: this passage is Shan at her most distinctively bilingual and most structurally precise simultaneously. The game that was 围棋 — the game of surrounding, of territory, of positional field-shaping — became Go in English, a monosyllable that carries none of the game’s spatial ontology. Then AlphaGo: the English monosyllable fused with the Chinese name for the AI programme, returning to Chinese as the name of a dog (阿拉). The Li of the game — its specific formation intelligence about position, territory, and the long game — survived its linguistic journey. But the Li of the name was lost and transformed at every border crossing. This is the structure of all cross-cultural formation: the deep Li persists, the surface Li transforms, and the practitioner who can read both is the practitioner who understands what was preserved and what was lost.

The Dialogues: Every Quote with Maximum Dialectical Voltage

The inexpressible that shows itself: placed at the opening of the Tractatus-Shan dialogue, this claim names exactly what the dialogue is about. Both Wittgenstein and Shan are tracking a structural reality that exceeds every propositional statement about it — that can only be approached through the showing of practice, of formation, of the quality of engaged encounter. The mystical is not supernatural; it is the natural structure of the limit of language, the point at which the formation field’s depth exceeds the Li of any available vocabulary. The dialogue does not resolve this. It demonstrates it: through the collision of two formation traditions that each track the same inexpressible structural reality from different directions.

“Li is the principle or pattern that makes things what they are. Human nature is the Li that heaven has given us.”

— Zhu Xi, as summarised

The principle or pattern that makes things what they are: Zhu Xi’s most compressed definition, and the one that contains the deepest philosophical problem. If Li makes things what they are, is Li prior to the things it makes? Zhu Xi says yes: Li is prior, qi (vital force / matter) is posterior. Shan says no: the Li that makes a thing what it is is the product of the specific Dao that produced that thing. The oak’s Li — its grain, its specific structural character, its workability in specific directions — is not the instantiation of a prior cosmic principle; it is the emergent product of this specific oak’s specific formation history. The collision is absolute. The stakes are everything: it determines whether practitioners approach formations with prior Li or walk the Dao first.

“Between heaven and earth there is one Li and nothing else.”

— Zhu Xi

One Li and nothing else: the most totalising claim in the Neo-Confucian tradition. The cosmic principle is single, unified, and prior to all specific manifestations. Shan’s counter-claim is equally totalising: the formation process is prior to the pattern, always, ontologically, without exception. There is no cosmic Li to which specific Lis are related as manifestations; there is only the specific formation of specific things through specific Daos. The one Li of heaven and earth is not a prior principle; it is the most comprehensive Li that the Chinese metaphysical tradition’s own specific Dao of thinking has been able to articulate. The universality is real but it is a formation achievement, not a metaphysical foundation. 悖论: the most universal Li is the one that took the longest Dao to produce.

“Far from representing messy, noisy complications that can be safely ignored, time and context are as much constituents of behavior as are any single component’s intrinsic properties.”

— Alicia Juarrero, Dynamics in Action (1999)

Time and context as constituents: Juarrero’s most important structural claim, and the one that most directly grounds Shan’s coupling-does-not-abolish-sequence argument. The component’s ‘intrinsic properties’ — its nature considered in isolation — are abstractions from the relational field within which the component has its actual character. The neonatal gut’s capacity to receive milk is not an intrinsic property; it is a formation achievement, produced by the specific time-and-context of the specific developmental sequence. Remove the time and context and you do not have a simpler component; you have a fiction. Juarrero restores time and context to their constitutive role: sequence matters, formation matters, the Dao is irreversibly prior.

“The establishment of context-sensitive constraints is the phase change that self-organizes a complex adaptive system.”

— Alicia Juarrero, as summarised

Phase change through context-sensitive constraints: the moment when a collection of components becomes a genuinely complex adaptive system is the moment when constraints emerge that are sensitive to the context they help constitute. Shan’s holding capacity is this phase change described as formation theory: the formation field becomes capable of holding complexity when the specific constraints that constitute its coherence have been established through the specific Dao of its formation history. Before the phase change: components. After: a formation with its own Shī, its own directional force, its own capacity to maintain coherence under pressure. The phase change cannot be forced; it must emerge from adequate formation.

“Complementarity (yin-yang opposites), complex emergence (yi — perpetuated changes), spontaneous generation (ziran — of itself so), and non-intervention (wuwei — not doing) are the four principles of natural Li.”

— Zhichang Zhu, “WSR: A Chinese Systems Approach” (ScienceOpen)

The four principles of natural Li: complementarity (the tension of opposites that Heraclitus and Fuller independently name as the source of integrity), complex emergence (the Yi Jing’s account of perpetuated change as the structure of formation), spontaneous generation (ziran — of itself so, the universe’s own tendency toward the production of Li without external forcing), and non-intervention (wuwei — the art of not acting before the grain appears, the ethical principle that grounds Shan’s anti-premature-Li argument). These four together constitute the deepest Chinese systems account of how formation works: through tension, through emergence, through the universe’s own creativity, and through the discipline of waiting for the actual to disclose itself.

“The farther a system is from equilibrium, the greater is its sensitivity to fluctuations. At bifurcation points, history enters.”

— Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers, Order Out of Chaos (1984)

History enters at bifurcation points: this is the most philosophically precise claim Prigogine makes about the ontological significance of formation. At the bifurcation point, the system’s future is not determined by any prior Li; it is determined by the specific, historically contingent fluctuation that happens to perturb the system at the moment of maximum sensitivity. The formation history of the system — its specific Dao up to the bifurcation — determines which fluctuations it is sensitive to, which perturbations can redirect it. History enters: not as the causal determination of the future but as the formation context that shapes what the bifurcation can produce. The Dao that has been walked determines what Li the bifurcation can crystallise.

“The map is not the territory. But the map is a phenomenon in the territory.”

— Gregory Bateson

The map in the territory: Bateson’s most structurally important correction to Korzybski’s original formulation. The map is not the territory — the Li is not the Dao — but the map is a real phenomenon within the territory it maps. The relational dynamics framework is not the formation field it describes; but the framework itself is a formation — produced by Shan’s specific Dao, embedded in the formation field of contemporary complexity discourse, participating in the ongoing formation of the field it tracks. The map shapes the territory it maps: the practitioner who uses the relational dynamics framework to navigate a complex formation field changes that formation field through the act of navigation. The map is a causal agent in the territory.

“The biosphere keeps expanding the adjacent possible. Life creates its own possibilities.”

— Stuart Kauffman, Reinventing the Sacred (2008)

Life creates its own possibilities: the adjacent possible is not a fixed space waiting to be explored; it is a formation achievement. The biosphere has expanded the adjacent possible through its own formation history — through the specific Daos walked by specific lineages over specific timescales that produced specific Lis that opened specific new formation possibilities. The practitioner who walks the Dao faithfully — who does not try to shortcut the formation, who pays the entropic price of genuine structural attunement — expands their own adjacent possible. They create possibilities that did not exist before the Dao was walked. Move 37 was not available to human Go players not because they lacked intelligence but because their specific formation history had not yet produced the adjacent possible that contained it.

“Evolution has no purpose; it simply drifts with the only constraint of maintaining structural viability.”

— Francisco Varela, The Tree of Knowledge (1987)

Structural drift with viability as the only constraint: this is Shan’s long game stated as evolutionary biology. The formation does not aim toward a predetermined Li; it drifts with the constraint that it must remain structurally viable. The specific Li that emerges from the drift is not a destination that was specified in advance; it is the specific pattern that the specific drift has produced. The practitioner who understands this does not try to specify the Li before walking the Dao; they cultivate the formation conditions that maintain structural viability while allowing the specific Li to emerge from the specific drift. The long game is not the patient pursuit of a predetermined goal; it is the patient maintenance of viability through a formation process whose Li will appear only in the walking.

Closing Cadence: What the Collision Produces
