— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Future of Man</i> (1959)

The noosphere tightening its network: this is Teilhard’s most precise description of what Shan means by the relational field increasing its formation density. The fibres multiply; the network tightens; the internal temperature rises. This is not metaphor; it is Teilhard’s attempt at a structural physics of collective consciousness. Fuller: omnitensional integrity is maintained by the continuous distribution of tension through the whole network. As the network tightens — as more elements participate in the relational formation — the specific structural sensitivity of the whole increases. Shan’s challenge: the tightening network can also be the tightening of a formation that has reached the brim. Laozi: holding and filling to the brim — better to stop in time. A noosphere whose internal temperature rises without adequate formation wisdom is a formation approaching bifurcation, not a formation approaching Omega.

“"The idea is that of the earth not only becoming covered by myriads of grains of thought, but becoming enclosed in a single thinking envelope so as to form, functionally, no more than a single vast grain of thought on the sidereal scale, the plurality of individual reflections grouping themselves together and reinforcing one another in the act of a single unanimous reflection."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955), p.252

The single vast grain of thought: Teilhard’s noosphere as the planetary Li produced by the Dao of civilisational formation. The plurality of individual reflections grouping themselves together and reinforcing one another: this is Cook Ding’s principle at the civilisational scale. Each practitioner’s specific formation is a specific grain; the noosphere is the grain that emerges when specific grains encounter each other with sufficient relational density and formation depth. Shan’s most productive challenge: the ‘single unanimous reflection’ risks becoming Zhu Xi’s one cosmic Li — a formation result declared in advance. The noosphere’s unanimity is not the starting point for civilisational formation but the destination that can only be reached through the walking of the specific Daos of specific formation encounters. Unanimity that bypasses the specific Daos of specific encounter is premature synthesis, not Omega.

“"From the first beginnings of History, this principle of the compressive generation of consciousness has been ceaselessly at work in the human mass."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Future of Man</i> (1959)

Compressive generation of consciousness: the convergence of the human mass under the specific pressure of its own increasing density generates consciousness as an emergent property of that compression. This is Prigogine’s dissipative structures in theological register: the formation far from equilibrium, under the specific pressure of maximum proximity, generates the specific Li that neither distance nor equilibrium could produce. The corrected Yi Jing: 天下同歸而殊途 — one destination through many different paths. The compression is real; but the specific paths that lead to genuine collective consciousness are irreducibly different, and no amount of compression substitutes for the formation depth that comes from each path being genuinely walked. Teilhard’s compression without Shan’s formation is population density without formation intelligence.

“"No evolutionary future awaits anyone except in association with everyone else."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

No future except in association: the most direct statement of why Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim has stakes beyond the individual practitioner. The practitioner who walks the Dao in isolation — who develops personal formation depth without the specific relational encounter that tests and extends that depth in contact with other formations — has not walked the Dao that this claim demands. Mou Zongsan’s intellectual intuition must meet Zhang Zai’s cosmic body: the people are my fellow-children, all things are my companions. The formation that does not extend itself into genuine relational encounter has reached a local maximum that will be superseded by the formation that keeps walking into the specific difficulty of genuine encounter with other formations. Shan’s Edinburgh seminar is precisely this: the Chinese student’s formation walking into genuine encounter with the British academic formation, and the Li produced from that encounter being more structurally adequate than either formation could have produced alone.

“"The true ego grows in inverse proportion to egoism."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

The true ego grows as egoism diminishes: Teilhard’s paradox of formation. The practitioner who contracts into the defence of their existing Li — who treats their accumulated formation as something to be protected from the specific challenge of the specific encounter — is shrinking. The practitioner who releases the prior Li to the specific pressure of the specific Dao is growing. This is exactly Laozi’s 為道日搏: in pursuit of the Dao, something is relinquished every day. The shrinking is not diminishment; it is formation. The egoism that resists diminishment is the formation that has mistaken its accumulated Li for its identity. Shan’s formation framework: the self is not the Li it has produced; it is the formation capacity that can produce new Li from new Daos. Release the Li. Walk the next Dao.

III. On Love as the Energy of Formation

“"Love is the affinity which links and draws together the elements of the world. Love, in fact, is the agent of universal synthesis."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin

Love as affinity that draws elements together: Teilhard’s most structurally precise account of what Fuller calls tensional integrity. The tensional force that holds the formation together is not rigid connection but the specific affinity of elements for each other — the specific relational force that maintains the specific topology of the specific formation. Dong Zhongshu: things of the same kind move each other; harmonised qi responds to qi. Teilhard: love is the agent of universal synthesis. All three are describing the same structural force from different formation positions: the non-local, distributed relational force that maintains structural integrity through the continuous expression of affinity rather than through the enforcement of proximity. The formation held together by love (Teilhard), by resonance (Dong Zhongshu), by tensional integrity (Fuller), by relational dynamics (Shan) is the same formation described from four different Daos.

“"Love alone is capable of uniting living beings in such a way as to complete and fulfil them, for it alone takes them and joins them by what is deepest in themselves."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

United by what is deepest in themselves: this is Teilhard’s most precise account of what genuine formation encounter produces. Not union by surface compatibility but union through the specific deepest Li of each formation’s specific formation history. The practitioner who brings their deepest formation — the most accumulated, most formation-dense, most Dao-formed Li — into genuine encounter with another formation that brings its deepest, produces the specific union that Teilhard calls love and Shan calls the relational field that precedes dynamics. The challenge: in the Edinburgh seminar, the Chinese student’s deepest formation and the seminar’s deepest formation did not encounter each other. They encountered each other’s surfaces. Surface encounter produces surface union — polite tolerance of difference. Deep encounter produces the specific structural transformation that Teilhard calls completion and fulfilment. Shan’s framework is the map of how to get from surface encounter to deep encounter.

“"Driven by the forces of love, the fragments of the world seek each other so that the world may come into being."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

The fragments seeking each other: this is jūcí as cosmological principle. The broken ceramic whose fragments seek each other through the affinity of their specific form. The jūcí craftsman does not force the pieces together; the good craftsman reads the specific topology of the specific break and positions the pieces in the configuration that their own formation already tends toward. The drilling and the staple are not violence but assistance: they provide the specific structural intervention that the fragments’ own seeking requires but cannot complete without external support. Shan’s corrected texts are exactly this: the fragments (the classical philosophical claims) seeking their correct relational configuration (the correct characters), with the paper’s corrections providing the specific brass staples that position them.

“"The whole of life lies in the verb seeing."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

The whole of life in the verb seeing: Teilhard’s phenomenological claim, and the one that places him in closest structural proximity to Shan’s formation framework. Not in the noun (what is seen) but in the verb (the act of seeing, the ongoing formation of the seeing capacity). The practitioner who has developed the formation adequate to see the Li of the actual formation field is the practitioner who is genuinely alive in Teilhard’s sense. Cook Ding’s transformation from seeing the whole ox to seeing the articulations: this is the progression from surface seeing (the noun: the whole ox as a given) to formation seeing (the verb: the specific relational structure of the specific formation as it reveals itself to the formation-adequate practitioner). Mou Zongsan’s intellectual intuition: the direct non-discursive seeing of the Li. All three are naming the same formation capacity. The verb seeing is the Dao of formation.

IV. On Process, Evolution, and the Arrow of Formation

“"(Evolution is) a general condition to which all theories, all hypotheses, all systems must bow and which they must satisfy henceforward if they are to be thinkable and true. Evolution is a light which illuminates all facts, a curve that all lines must follow."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

Evolution as the light that illuminates all facts: Teilhard’s most imperialist claim, and the one Shan’s formation framework must resist most firmly. If evolution is the light that all theories must follow, then Laozi’s Dao De Jing must be read as a contribution to evolutionary theory; the Four Sprouts must be understood as adaptive capacities; Cook Ding’s attunement must be analysed as the product of evolutionary pressures on primate cognition. This is not wrong; it is incomplete. The Chinese philosophical tradition was not trying to describe the evolutionary process; it was trying to describe the formation process from the inside of the practitioner’s specific encounter with the actual formation field. Teilhard’s light illuminates the exterior of things; Shan’s framework illuminates the interior. The true physics, Teilhard himself elsewhere says, will achieve the inclusion of man in his wholeness. That inclusion requires Shan’s phenomenology of formation as well as Teilhard’s evolutionary cosmology.

“"The task before us now, if we would not perish, is to build the Earth."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Future of Man</i> (1959)

Build the Earth: the formation imperative in its most urgent register. Not contemplate the Earth. Not analyse the Earth. Build it. Teilhard’s paleontology had shown him how long it takes to build the Earth: geological epochs, evolutionary aeons, civilisational millennia. The task of building it consciously — of walking the specific Dao that produces the specific Li of a genuine planetary formation — is the task that cannot be completed by any individual practitioner or any generation. It requires the long game. Shan’s framework is a long-game framework precisely in this sense: not the long game of patience (waiting for the formation to arrive) but the long game of formation (walking the Dao that accumulates the specific Shi that makes the specific formation available). Move 37 is available only to the formation that has walked the training Dao adequate to see it. The Earth is buildable only by formations that have walked the Daos adequate to read its Li.

“"I can see a humanité that has become conscious of the energy pent within it."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Future of Man</i> (1959)

The energy pent within humanity: Teilhard’s account of the formation potential that has not yet been walked into Li. Mencius’ 浩然之气 (the flood-like qi, in the highest degree vast and unyielding) at the civilisational scale: if you nourish it with integrity and do not harm it, it will fill the space between heaven and earth. The energy that is pent is the energy that has not yet found the Dao adequate to its expression. The specific Dao that must be walked to release the pent energy is the formation intelligence that can read the Li of what the energy is actually tending toward. Shan’s challenge to Teilhard: the energy pent within humanity is not uniformly directed. There is formation energy and there is destruction energy. The practitioner who confuses them — who walks the Dao of destruction believing it to be the Dao of formation — produces the Cao Zhi crisis: burning the bean-stalks to cook the beans, mistaking the release of structural energy for the production of structural capacity.

“"There is no mind without synthesis."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

No mind without synthesis: Teilhard’s anti-atomist claim in its most compressed form. The mind is not a collection of separate cognitive capacities that have been assembled; it is a specific synthetic formation whose specific character emerges from the specific way in which its elements have been integrated. This is the Li of the mind as a formation product of the specific Dao of the specific practitioner’s specific cognitive development. Shan’s formation framework: the Li of any formation is not derivable from the analysis of its components but only from the specific synthesis that the specific Dao has produced. There is no mind without synthesis; there is no Li without Dao; there is no formation without the specific integrated movement through the specific formation field that produces the specific structural character of the specific formation.

“"Growing always. Expanding always."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Divine Milieu</i> (1957)

Growing always, expanding always: Teilhard’s two-word account of the formation imperative. The formation that stops growing has stopped being a genuine formation. But Shan’s warning inserts itself here with maximum structural urgency: holding and filling to the brim — better to stop in time. The formation that grows without reading the brim of its holding capacity is the formation approaching collapse. The submerged dragon that does not wait for the yang force to accumulate is the formation that deploys prematurely. The Confucian pine survives the winter not by growing always but by maintaining the specific formation adequate to its specific structural winter. Growing always is the telos; reading the brim is the method. Teilhard’s imperative without Shan’s diagnostic is cosmological ambition without structural intelligence.

V. On the Divine Milieu, Action, and Formation

“"It is not our business to find out what will always attract men or what will always attract me, but to reach, each in our own way, through the medium of grace, what is always and everywhere attractive."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Divine Milieu</i> (1957)

Each in our own way: Teilhard’s most formation-compatible claim, and the one that most directly supports the Yi Jing’s one-destination-through-many-paths structural principle. The destination (what is always and everywhere attractive) is one; the paths (each in our own way) are many and irreducibly specific. This is Shan’s framework stated as mystical theology: the cosmic Li (the Omega Point) is one; the Daos that approach it are as specific and irreplaceable as the specific formations that walk them. No shortcut from one practitioner’s path to another. No wholesale borrowing of the Li produced by a Dao one has not walked. Each in our own way: not as an endorsement of formation isolation but as a recognition that genuine formation is always specific, always irreplaceable, always the product of the specific practitioner’s specific encounter with the specific formation field.

“"All endeavour cooperates to complete the world in Christo Jesu."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Divine Milieu</i> (1957)

All endeavour cooperates to complete the world: the formation ethics of the Divine Milieu in its most compressed form. Not some endeavours, not the right endeavours, not the formally consecrated endeavours — all endeavour. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of cutting at the joints of oxen cooperates to complete the world. Shan’s crossing from Chinese to English complexity discourse cooperates to complete the world. The jūcí craftsman’s drilling through fragile ceramics with a diamond drill cooperates to complete the world. The claim is not that all endeavour is equally well-formed; it is that all genuine endeavour — all endeavour that is walked as a genuine Dao rather than performed as a surface compliance with existing Li — contributes its specific formation to the ongoing formation of the whole. The practitioner’s specific Dao is not a distraction from the cosmic formation; it IS the cosmic formation at its most specific and therefore most real.

“"Our duty is to proceed as if limits to our ability do not exist."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin

Proceed as if limits do not exist: Teilhard’s most formation-expansive instruction, and Shan’s most carefully differentiated challenge. The instruction is not wrong; it is structurally dangerous if misread. The formation that proceeds as if the limits of its holding capacity do not exist is the formation approaching the brim. The formation that proceeds as if the limits of its formation depth do not exist is the formation that deploys premature Li into the world with the confidence of genuine attunement. Cook Ding after year three — when he could no longer see the whole ox but had not yet developed the specific structural seeing of nineteen years — was the practitioner most at risk of Teilhard’s instruction. He could see that there were no limits; but the absence of the visible limit was not the presence of genuine formation. The instruction correctly understood: proceed as if the limits of the adjacent possible do not exist. Walk the Dao that keeps expanding the possible. The limits of any specific formation exist; the limits of the formation’s capacity for ongoing formation do not.

“"We are one, after all, you and I. Together we suffer, together exist, and forever will recreate each other."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin

Together we recreate each other: the formation structure of genuine encounter stated as personal address. Not I form myself in isolation and then encounter you; not you form me from outside while I remain passive; but together, in the specific relational dynamic of the specific encounter, we each become more than we were. This is Shan’s most foundational claim — relation precedes dynamics — stated as cosmological fact. The encounter between the Chinese student and the Edinburgh seminar recreates both. The encounter between Teilhard’s evolutionary cosmology and Shan’s relational dynamics framework recreates both. The encounter between the broken ceramic and the jūcí craftsman recreates both. The recreation is not metaphorical; it is the specific structural transformation that genuine relational encounter produces when the encounter is walked with sufficient formation depth.

VI. On China, the Geological Deep Time, and Formation Memory

Teilhard spent twenty-four years in China. He lived through the formation of the Chinese Communist Party, the Long March, the Japanese invasion, the Second World War. He watched from the Chinese interior. He wrote to colleagues in Europe from a formation position whose specific temporal depth — the geological deep time of the paleontologist layered over the civilisational time of the ancient culture — is present in every sentence of <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i>. The book that the Vatican suppressed was written in China. The formation encounter with China was constitutive of Teilhard’s most important intellectual achievement. He could not have written <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> without China. He and Shan share this: the Chinese formation encounter produced the most important intellectual formation of their respective bodies of work.

“"Since my matter is not a part of the world but the totality of the Universe possessed by me partially, it is still the total sphere of the world that I must try to develop, by developing myself."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Divine Milieu</i> (1957)

The total sphere of the world as the object of formation: Teilhard’s extension of Zhang Zai’s Western Inscription into a practical ethics of formation. By developing myself I develop the world: not because my self is the world (solipsism) but because my self is a local expression of the world’s own self-developing formation (Zhang Zai’s 天地之塞，吾其體). The formation of the practitioner is not a private project; it is the universe’s own self-formation expressed at the scale of this specific practitioner’s specific biographical Dao. Shan’s challenge: which practitioner? Whose development? Huang Zongxi’s political question enters here. The claim that developing myself develops the world is structurally correct; but the practitioner who develops themselves at the cost of the formation of others — who burns the bean-stalks to cook their own beans — has mistaken private formation achievement for the cosmic self-development that Teilhard describes.

“"Little by little I grew more and more conscious, less as an abstract notion than as a presence, of a profound, ontological, total drift of the Universe around me."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, cited in Corte, <i>Pierre Teilhard de Chardin: His Life and Spirit</i>

The drift of the universe as presence: this is Teilhard’s account of the formation moment when the Dao becomes perceptible not as a concept but as a structural force. Shan’s Shī: the positional force, field-pressure, momentum, and directional inevitability that makes specific futures available and specific futures unavailable. Teilhard’s ‘total drift’ and Shan’s Shī are the same structural recognition from two different formation positions. The difference is temporal: Teilhard experiences the drift of the universe over geological epochs; Shan reads the Shī of a specific formation field over the specific time-scale of a specific practitioner’s specific formation encounter. The cosmic drift and the situational Shī are the same force at different scales. The practitioner formed to read Shī is the practitioner formed to feel the drift.

“"It is the destiny of things real to destroy those that are artifice."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin

The destiny of things real to destroy things artificial: the most structurally decisive claim in this collection. The formation that is genuinely walked — that has produced genuine Li from genuine Dao — will eventually destroy the formation that is merely performed, that applies prior Li to situations it has not genuinely encountered. Nothing collapses in one move; but the real will eventually destroy the artifice. The time-scale is not given; the structural outcome is. The Japanese management frameworks that applied ‘Dao’ as a management brand (artifice) were eventually destroyed by the formation intelligence that could read the actual Li of the actual market formation (real). The Edinburgh seminar’s assumption that Chinese students’ silence meant inability (artifice) is eventually destroyed by the formation intelligence that reads the actual relational field (real). The destiny of things real to destroy things artificial is the long game in its most patient and most inevitable form.

VII. On Matter, Energy, and Structural Constitution

“"The time has come to realise that an interpretation of the universe — even a positivist one — remains unsatisfying unless it covers the interior as well as the exterior of things; mind as well as matter."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

Interior as well as exterior: Teilhard’s most important epistemological claim, and the one that most directly demands Shan’s formation phenomenology as its completion. The exterior of things: the quantitative, measurable, analysable surface that natural science describes with extraordinary precision. The interior of things: the specific structural experience of being this formation, navigating from inside the specific formation field, walking the Dao that produces the specific Li that the exterior analysis can only describe after the fact. Complexity theory has the exterior. Shan’s formation framework has the interior. Teilhard demands both. The true physics must include the interior. The true complexity science must include the formation phenomenology. The true account of the noosphere must include the specific experience of the specific practitioner walking the specific Dao. Without the interior, the exterior is a description of what formation looks like from outside. With the interior, it is an account of what formation is.

“"In no case does the energy required for synthesis appear to be provided by an influx of fresh capital, but by expenditure."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

Energy for synthesis from expenditure: Teilhard’s thermodynamic account of what formation costs. Not an external grant of new capacity but the specific expenditure of the practitioner’s own existing formation — the walking of the Dao that consumes prior Li in order to produce new Li. Prigogine: entropy is the price of structure. Xunzi: blue comes from indigo but is bluer than indigo; the transformation costs the indigo its undifferentiated state. Wang Fuzhi: qi first condenses and then form-pattern emerges. All four are saying: the formation that matters is paid for by the formation that preceded it. There is no free synthesis. Every Li that is genuinely new is produced by the expenditure of a prior Li in the specific Dao of the specific transformation. The practitioner who wants new Li without expenditure is the practitioner who wants to cook the beans without burning the stalks. Impossible. The cooking costs the stalks.

“"By the very mechanism of his birth, each man finds himself unable to be free from the evolutionary milieu which gave him existence."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Future of Man</i> (1959)

Inseparable from the evolutionary milieu that gave existence: Wittgenstein’s inherited background in evolutionary register. The practitioner did not choose the form of life they were born into; they did not choose the language, the culture, the formation tradition, the civilisational river-bed that constitutes the preconditions of all their subsequent thinking and acting. This inheritance is not a limitation to be overcome but the specific formation ground from which the specific Dao must be walked. Shan’s bilingual formation: she did not choose to be born into the Chinese philosophical tradition; she did not choose the specific Edinburgh seminar encounter that was the specific Dao of her specific formation. The evolutionary milieu gave her both. The formation she produced from both is the specific Li that no practitioner without both could have produced. The inseparability from the milieu is the condition of the formation’s specific adequacy.

VIII. On Omega, Convergence, and the Limit of Formation

“"Omega must be independent of the collapse of the forces with which evolution is woven."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

Omega independent of evolutionary collapse: the most structurally important requirement Teilhard places on his own cosmology. The destination of the formation process must not be dependent on the continuation of the specific processes that produced it; otherwise the Omega Point is merely the highest point of a formation that can still collapse, not the genuine structural completion of the formation. Shan’s challenge: what would it mean for the relational dynamics framework’s central recognition — relation precedes dynamics — to be independent of the collapse of the specific formations that generated it? The answer is structural: if the claim is tracking a real feature of real formations, it will continue to be true even when the specific formation conditions that produced it (Shan’s bilingual encounter, the specific papers, the specific moment of 2025–2026) have long changed. The true Li is independent of the collapse of the Dao that produced it. Not independent of the Dao — the Li could not have appeared without the Dao — but independent of the Dao’s continuation. This is the test of genuine formation.

“"Hatred and internecine struggles will have disappeared in the ever warmer radiance of Omega. Some sort of unanimity will reign over the entire mass of the noosphere. The final convergence will take place in peace."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

Final convergence in peace: Teilhard’s most eschatological claim, and the one that requires the most careful formation-theory analysis. The convergence of the noosphere in peace is not the peace of suppressed conflict but the peace of formations that have each been genuinely formed — that have each walked the specific Dao that produces the specific Li adequate to genuine encounter with other formations. Zhuangzi: the ten thousand things are all different, and yet each is itself. Heraclitus: the finest attunement is things bearing in opposite directions simultaneously. Peace is not the absence of tension; it is the specific quality of structural integrity that maintains tension without forcing. The final convergence in peace is the noosphere that has achieved Fuller’s omnitensional integrity: every element participating in the tensional network of the whole, with the integrity of the whole invested in the continuous distribution of relational force through every element. This peace is not the elimination of difference but the structural completion of the formation that holds all differences in continuous relational engagement.

“"The only universe capable of containing the human person is an ‘irreversibly’ personalising universe."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

An irreversibly personalising universe: the Dao’s irreversibility as cosmological principle. The universe cannot undo the formation it has already walked. Every Dao that has been walked has produced a Li that is now part of the formation history from which the next Dao begins. Every specific consciousness that has been formed has contributed its specific formation to the noosphere’s accumulated capacity. Irreversibility is not a limitation; it is the structural condition that makes formation genuine. A reversible universe is a universe in which nothing is formed — where every Dao could be unwalked, every Li undone, every encounter erased. The irreversibly personalising universe is the universe in which every formation permanently contributes its specific character to the formation that follows. Nothing is wasted. Nothing can be taken back. The formation walks on.

“"At the present time no other energy of a personal nature could be detected on Earth save that represented by the sum of human persons."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

The sum of human persons as the current totality of personal energy: Teilhard’s most anti-reductionist claim. The noosphere is not the sum of neural activations or computational processes; it is the sum of personal formations — the specific irreducible formations of specific practitioners who have each walked specific Daos and produced specific Lis. The person cannot be reduced to their components; the noosphere cannot be reduced to the sum of persons. Each level is genuinely emergent from but not reducible to the level below. Shan’s formation framework and Teilhard’s personalising universe converge here with maximum structural precision: the relational dynamics framework is not a framework for optimising collective neural processing; it is a framework for the formation of genuine persons who are capable of the specific relational encounter that produces genuine Li. The energy that builds the Earth is not computational; it is formational.

IX. On Writing, Suppression, and the Dao of the Censored Text

Teilhard was forbidden by his Jesuit superiors from publishing or teaching. His major works circulated in manuscript during his lifetime, read by colleagues and disciples, influencing philosophers and scientists who could not cite the source. He obeyed the prohibition without abandoning his convictions — not out of cowardice but out of a formation understanding that the institutional confrontation would produce less formation than the continued walking of the Dao. He spent twenty-four years in China. He died on Easter Sunday 1955, the day he had always hoped to die. <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> appeared later that year. The Vatican issued a <i>monitum</i> (warning) against his works in 1962. Pope Francis quoted him approvingly in <i>Laudato Si’</i> (2015). The monitum was never officially lifted but is now effectively historical.

The suppression of Teilhard’s works by institutional authority is the most precise philosophical illustration of the distinction between endurance and viability. The institutional authority endured; the works survived. The prohibition was maintained for a lifetime; the formation it suppressed was not diminished by the maintenance of the prohibition. The path of Teilhard’s ideas narrowed during his lifetime. It did not collapse. The submerged dragon waited. The Dao continued to be walked in private, in correspondence, in the specific formations of specific readers who received the manuscript works and were formed by them. The Omega Point drew the formation forward even when the institutional apparatus forbade the forward movement. The Li was not dependent on the institutional continuation of the Dao. This is the test Teilhard himself identified: Omega must be independent of the collapse of the forces with which evolution is woven.

“"I will be faithful to being, because being is the only thing I can really cherish, and there is only one being, which is everything."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>Letters from a Traveler</i>

Faithful to being because being is everything: Teilhard’s personal confession as a formation ethics. The practitioner who is faithful to the actual — who refuses to substitute the preferred Li for the actual Li of the actual formation field — is the practitioner Teilhard is describing. The fidelity to being is Cook Ding’s fidelity to the actual Li of the actual ox: not to the ox as taxonomic category, not to the ox as the whole-ox perception of year one, but to the specific living formation of this specific ox in this specific moment. Faithful to being is the most complete account of what Shan means by genuine attunement: the formation that follows the actual rather than the preferred. And there is only one being: the one Li that all genuine fidelity to the actual is tracking from all its different formation positions. Zhang Zai, Teilhard, Shan, Fuller, Wittgenstein, Cook Ding: all faithful to being, all tracking the one Li, all approaching the one destination through their irreducibly specific paths.

“"The final fruit of my faith? The conviction that union differentiates."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, <i>The Phenomenon of Man</i> (1955)

Union differentiates: the most paradoxically precise claim in the entire Teilhard corpus, and the structural principle that resolves the apparent tension between the paper’s two central structural commitments — the one Li toward which all formations are converging (Zhu Xi, Teilhard, the Yi Jing’s one destination) and the irreducibility of specific formation paths (Shan’s Dao-before-Li, Laozi’s paths cannot be named, the multiplicity of genuine Daos). Union differentiates: the closer two genuine formations approach their genuine convergence, the more specifically themselves they each become. The deepest encounter between the Chinese philosophical tradition and Western complexity theory does not dissolve them into a single undifferentiated ‘complexity wisdom’; it makes each tradition more precisely itself by the specific pressure of the specific encounter. The contact produces differentiation. The convergence toward Omega is not the loss of the specific formations that are converging; it is their most complete specific realisation. This is the jūcí principle applied cosmologically: the brass staple does not make the broken pieces the same thing; it holds them in their specific relational configuration so that each remains most fully itself.

❧ ✶ ❧
XXXVI

Supplementary Dialectical Analyses: The Final Restoration

What follows is the complete analytical restoration of every section that previously existed only as a heading. The principle is the same as throughout: no heading without content, no quote without analysis, no voice without the specific collision it generates. These sections are not addenda; they are the paper’s completion — the formations that the prior sections were always already pointing toward.

❧ ✶ ❧

Wittgenstein in the Dialogues

“Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 7 — the last line

The last line of the Tractatus, and one of the most discussed sentences in twentieth-century philosophy. Its placement here at the end of the paper’s most analytical section is deliberate: it names the limit that every formation claim approaches but cannot cross. The silence is not ignorance; it is the specific quality of honest recognition that the formation has reached its edge. Shan begins writing the morning after Wittgenstein falls silent — not because she has found something to say about what cannot be said, but because the saying can approach the limit from another direction. Wittgenstein approached from logic: the structure of propositions has a limit at which the proposition gives way to showing. Shan approaches from formation phenomenology: the structure of practice has a limit at which the articulation gives way to demonstration. The silence and the writing are the same recognition from two different formation positions. The tension between them is the paper’s structural spine.

“The speaking of language is part of an activity, or of a form of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §23

When Shan writes in English about the Chinese concept of Li, every word of that writing is part of a specific activity — cross-cultural complexity scholarship from a bilingual formation position — and part of a specific form of life — the specific social practice of a Chinese academic writing for a Western complexity audience while carrying the formation weight of a different educational tradition. The same characters in a different activity and a different form of life produce different meaning through different use. Translation is formation-transformation: the activity changes, the life-form changes, and therefore the meaning changes — not because the translator is imprecise but because precision in a new form of life necessarily produces a different thing from the same words. The Edinburgh seminar’s silence and the Chinese classroom’s silence are not the same silence because they are parts of different activities in different forms of life.

Shan in the Dialogues: The Living Formation

“The neonatal gut does not negotiate with the milk. It forms. The contact is immediate; the readiness is not.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence’ (May 2026)

Placed here in the Dialogues as the counter-claim to every systems theory that collapses sequence into coupling. The neonatal gut is Shan’s most concrete, most embodied, most undeniable evidence. There is no abstraction available here: the specific biological formation is specific, sequential, and irreversible. Week twenty-three, the gut is not ready. Week thirty-eight, it is. No amount of simultaneous co-determination — no coupling of any kind — substitutes for the sequence. Juarrero: context-sensitive constraints constitute behaviour at the moment of their formation; the constraint that the gut is not yet ready is as constitutive of what happens at the feeding tube as the coupling of milk and mouth. Prigogine: at bifurcation points, history enters. The readiness IS the accumulated history of the specific developmental sequence. The neonatal gut is the argument. No formation without sequence. No sequence without the irreversibility that makes it formative.

“Dao and Li were one way of seeing this. Relation and dynamics are another.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’ (May 2026)

The most philosophically transparent sentence in Shan’s body of work. She is not claiming that Dao/Li and relation/dynamics are translations of each other. She is claiming that they are two different formation traditions arriving at the same structural recognition from different directions: that what makes movement consequential is the field it moves within, and that the field is prior to the movement. The Chinese formation tradition has two and a half millennia of Dao-walking behind the claim. The Western complexity tradition has several decades of systems theory, emergence, and complex adaptive systems behind the parallel claim. The two traditions did not influence each other; they converged independently on the same structural recognition. This convergence is the Yi Jing’s one destination through many paths: confirmed by demonstration rather than proclaimed as principle.

“Reality is relational dynamics under constraint over time.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Relation Precedes Dynamics’ (May 2026)

Six words that deserve to be read one at a time. ‘Reality’: not ‘complex systems’ or ‘social formations’ but reality in its full scope — the claim is cosmological. ‘Relational’: not compositional, not substantial, not reducible to the properties of elements — the primary unit of reality is the relation, not the related thing. ‘Dynamics’: not states but processes, not structures but ongoing structuring. ‘Under constraint’: not free-floating process but formation with holding capacity, the enabling constraint that gives movement its direction and its coherence. ‘Over time’: the temporal arrow is real, the sequence is irreversible, the formation history is causally efficacious. The formula is not a definition; it is a formation. The practitioner who has genuinely understood and inhabited it does not apply it as a theory but moves within it as a structural orientation. It has become their Li. The Dao that produced it in Shan was the specific Dao of her specific bilingual formation encounter. The Li it produced is available to every practitioner willing to walk a formation path adequate to receive it.

“Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first.”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Nothing Collapses in One Move’ (April 2026)

The most important claim in Shan’s entire body of work, and the claim that places the entire paper’s structural intelligence in the sharpest possible contrast with the dominant model of crisis management. The dominant model: stability is the baseline, crises are ruptures in the baseline, crises are caused by specific triggering events, the response to crises is to address the triggering event. Shan’s model: nothing is the baseline, formation is continuous, collapse is the terminal expression of a formation trajectory that was already narrowing before any trigger, the only genuine response to collapse is the formation intelligence to read the narrowing before the trigger arrives. Fuller: the structure that collapses was already failing in its tensional network. Prigogine: at the bifurcation, history enters — but the bifurcation was being formed long before it became the bifurcation. Jin Guantao: the ultrastable structure that collapses finally was sacrificing formation capacity for surface stability through every prior move. The path narrows first. The practitioner who cannot see the narrowing cannot act while acting is still possible.

“What if intelligence is not only the ability to maximise immediate gain? What if the highest form of intelligence is the ability to read a field — to perceive Shī, to position before the position is obvious, to act at the moment when minimal force produces maximum formation?”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘AlphaGo’s Move 37’ (April 2026)

The redefinition of intelligence that the entire paper has been building toward. Not the intelligence that maximises immediate gain (the compressional model: accumulate, optimise, outperform in the short term). But the intelligence that reads Shī — the directional force latent in the formation field’s specific configuration — and positions for the formation that that Shī is already generating. Move 37 was this intelligence made visible in two seconds: a move that human players could not understand at the moment of its making, that commentators called a mistake, that proved to be the structural turning point of the game. Not because AlphaGo was smarter in the computational sense. Because AlphaGo had walked a different Dao of formation — trained through millions of games not to maximise immediate gain but to build positional force — and its formation had produced a different Li: the specific structural sensitivity to Shī that makes the best move the one that looks like restraint. This is Shan’s definition of long-game intelligence. It is also, precisely, Cook Ding’s.

Zhu Xi and the Neo-Confucian Li: The Full Dialectical Synthesis

The encounter between Shan’s relational dynamics framework and Zhu Xi’s Neo-Confucian Li-first metaphysics is the deepest philosophical collision in this paper. Both are serious. Both are tracking real structural phenomena. Their disagreement is not a misunderstanding; it is a genuine metaphysical difference with specific practical consequences. The full synthesis requires holding both simultaneously.

“"Li is the principle or pattern that makes things what they are. Human nature is the Li that is universally present in all people."”

— Zhu Xi, as summarised in Britannica, Chinese Philosophy

Zhu Xi’s claim is precise: Li makes things what they are. This is not a description of regularity (things tend to behave this way) but a constitutive claim (the Li is what constitutes the thing as the thing it is). The wood’s Li is what makes it wood; the human’s Li is what makes them human; the tradition’s Li is what makes it the specific tradition it is. Remove the Li and there is no thing remaining — only undifferentiated qi waiting for a Li to constitute it into something specific. This gives Li an ontological priority that Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim must genuinely engage.

Shan’s response must be structural, not merely assertive. The Li that constitutes the thing as what it is — is that Li prior to the thing, or co-emergent with it? Zhu Xi’s answer: prior. The Li of water exists before any specific water exists; the Li of human nature exists before any specific human exists. Shan’s counter: the Li that we can identify — the specific structural grain that a specific practitioner in a specific situation can read and work with — is always the product of a specific formation history. The cosmic Li of water may be prior; the specific Li of this river’s canyon at this moment in this ecological configuration is the product of the specific Dao that this specific water has been walking for ten million years. Shan is not denying cosmic Li; she is insisting that the practitioner’s access to cosmic Li is always through the specific Dao of their specific formation encounter with the specific manifestation.

“"Between heaven and earth there is one Li and nothing else."”

— Zhu Xi

The most totalising claim in Neo-Confucian metaphysics. One Li: not many Lis, not competing Lis, not culturally relative Lis — one structural principle that constitutes every thing that exists. This is not easily dismissed. If Shan’s framework is genuine — if it is tracking real structural properties of real formations — then it must be tracking the one Li that Zhu Xi identifies, simply from a different formation position than Zhu Xi occupied. The convergence of Chinese and Western formation traditions on the same structural recognitions (the Yi Jing’s one destination through many paths) is evidence that both are tracking the same one Li. The difference: Zhu Xi approaches the one Li deductively, from its universality downward to its specific manifestations. Shan approaches it inductively, from specific formation encounters upward to the structural recognition that connects them. The one Li is their shared destination; the direction of travel is different.

The synthesis Shan’s framework produces from the Zhu Xi collision: Li-one-manifests-many (理一分殊) is both true and dangerous. True: the structural reality that all formation traditions are tracking is one. Dangerous: the claim to have identified the one Li in advance of the specific Dao of the specific formation encounter is always premature. The one Li is a destination, not a given starting point. Every formation that arrives at a specific Li by genuinely walking the specific Dao of the specific encounter has contributed a specific manifestation of the one Li — added one more verification of the Yi Jing’s claim that all paths lead to one destination. But no formation gets to declare that destination arrived before the walking is done.

Whitehead: Life and the Absolute Present

“The notion of 'life' implies a certain absoluteness of self-enjoyment. This must not be construed as a selfish pleasure. The notion means the enjoyment of a perspective for its own sake.”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (1929)

Self-enjoyment as absoluteness: each actual occasion of formation is complete in itself — it does not exist merely as a means to further occasions but has its own internal value, its own specific quality of being-this-formation-in-this-moment. Shan’s framework has this character: each Dao-walk, each genuine encounter with the actual formation field, each moment of structural attunement is complete in itself. The long game is not the sacrifice of present formation for future Li; it is the accumulation of formation-complete moments that together produce the structural depth from which genuine Li can emerge. Fuller: every event is a unique vertex in the omnitensional network.

The hardest challenge Whitehead poses to the entire long-game framework of this paper: if every actual occasion is complete in itself, if the absoluteness of self-enjoyment means that no moment exists merely as a means to further moments — then the practitioner who defers present engagement for future formation has misunderstood the structure of formation itself. The long game is not about deferring the present; it is about the quality of presence in each present moment. Cook Ding’s nineteen years is not nineteen years of deferred gratification; it is nineteen years of maximally present engagement with the specific Li of the specific formation encountered in each specific moment. The long game produces the Li not through the accumulation of deferred moments but through the accumulation of maximally present ones.

Whitehead’s process ontology and Shan’s second Dao model in direct alignment: the actual occasion does not persist; it perishes into its contribution to the next actual occasion. The Dao does not persist; it produces a Li that becomes the formation ground for the next Dao. The universe is not made of things that endure; it is made of events that perish — but whose perishing is their contribution. Every Dao that is genuinely walked contributes its specific Li to the formation that makes the next Dao available. The perishing is generative. Nothing is wasted. The formation is the universe’s own accumulation of self-enjoyments, each complete in itself, each contributing what it was to what comes next.

“"Process is fundamental."”

— Whitehead, Process and Reality

Three words that do the work of a library. Not ‘substance is fundamental’ (things are primary, their processes are secondary attributes). Not ‘events are fundamental’ (things happen, then they stop). But process: the ongoing, self-generating, irreversible movement of formation that constitutes reality at every level from quantum event to civilisational transformation. Shan’s Dao is the name for this process as it appears within the horizon of a practitioner’s specific formation encounter. Whitehead’s process is the name for it at the cosmological level. Same structural reality, different formation positions within it. The convergence is not a coincidence; it is the one Li confirming itself through two genuinely different formation paths.

Kauffman and the Adjacent Possible: Full Dialectical Analysis

“"Systems at the edge of chaos tend to exhibit the richest possible behaviour. Frozen systems cannot explore new configurations; systems in chaos have no coherence to explore with."”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1995)

The edge of chaos as the structural location of maximum formation intelligence. Not frozen: the formation that has achieved maximum stability at the cost of all adaptability — the ultrastable structure, the organisation that has optimised for its current Li at the cost of the capacity to produce new Li from new Daos. Not chaotic: the formation whose perturbations are so continuous and so large that no Li can accumulate long enough to become the ground for the next Dao. At the edge: the specific structural region where the formation has enough coherence to exploit what it finds and enough openness to explore what it has not yet encountered. This is Shan’s excellence: not a stable achievement but a specific edge-proximity maintained as a formation practice. The practitioner at the edge of chaos is the practitioner who has developed the specific formation adequate to maintain that edge-proximity under the specific pressures of their specific domain. Cook Ding at the edge: the knife at the joint, the hollow found, the follow-through without forcing.

“"The biosphere keeps expanding the adjacent possible."”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1995)

Life creates its own possibilities: the single most generative claim in Kauffman’s framework for understanding the structure of genuine formation. The adjacent possible is not a fixed space waiting to be explored; it is itself a formation achievement — the specific set of formations that become available only after specific prior formations have been achieved. The walking of the Dao does not merely traverse the existing adjacent possible; it expands it. Each step of genuine formation opens formation possibilities that did not exist before that step. This is why the long game is strategically decisive: not because patience is a virtue, but because the only way to access the formations that matter is to have walked the Dao that makes them available as adjacent possibles. Move 37 was adjacent possible only to the formation that had walked the specific Dao of training that made it seeable. It was not adjacent possible to any formation that had not walked that Dao. The biosphere’s expansion is not a metaphor; it is the structural principle of all genuine formation.

Kauffman’s deepest challenge to Shan’s framework: if the adjacent possible keeps expanding — if life is genuinely creative, genuinely open, genuinely productive of new structural possibilities — then there is no fixed destination toward which formation is moving. Zhu Xi’s one Li is not a fixed target that the formation is approaching through the accumulation of Daos; it is itself being expanded by the ongoing formation process. This is the most radical version of the Dao-before-Li claim: not only is the Li downstream of the Dao, but the destination of Li is itself being formed by the Dao as it walks. The map is being drawn by the walking. The territory is being created by the drawing. This is not relativism — the formation is tracking real structural properties of a real formation field. But the formation field is itself in formation. The Li is real AND provisional. Both at once. Always.

“"Order for free."”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe — the principle

The most compressed statement of Kauffman’s most important structural discovery: the universe has a spontaneous tendency toward the production of order that precedes and exceeds any selection pressure. Xunzi: blue from indigo, bluer than indigo. The formation process produces more structure than the source contained — not through the addition of external material but through the specific dynamics of the formation process itself. Order for free means that the practitioner who walks the Dao with genuine formation attention will find that the Dao produces Li that no prior analysis of the formation’s elements could have predicted. The Li is free in the specific sense that it was not in the elements before the Dao walked; it emerged from the Dao itself. This is why the Dao must be walked: not because it is demanding, not because it is virtuous, but because the Li that matters cannot be extracted from the elements in advance. It can only emerge from the walking.

Karaoguz, Teilhard, Pendleton-Jullian: Attunement, Cosmos, Design

“"Love is the affinity which links and draws together the elements of the world. Love, in fact, is the agent of universal synthesis."”

— Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, The Phenomenon of Man (1955)

Teilhard’s cosmological claim placed here as the structural grounding of Karaoguz’s attunement account. Love as the agent of universal synthesis: this is Teilhard’s formulation of what Fuller calls tensional integrity, what Dong Zhongshu calls cosmic resonance, and what Shan calls the relational field that precedes dynamics. The specific affinity that draws the formation’s elements together is not mechanical adhesion; it is the specific relational force that maintains the specific topology of the specific formation. Karaoguz’s A-Frame is a practical methodology for accessing this specific affinity: the Attend phase opens the practitioner to the actual relational field; the Appreciate phase develops structural sensitivity to the specific affinity at work in the specific formation; the Act phase expresses the specific intervention that the specific affinity makes possible. Teilhard’s love and Karaoguz’s attunement are the same structural force described from cosmological and cognitive-science formation positions respectively.

Shan’s incandescent challenge to this cosmological grounding: the affinity that draws elements together is not uniformly loving. The formation that is held together by the specific tension of its specific structural configuration includes tensions that are painful, asymmetrical, and structurally unjust. The Edinburgh seminar’s Chinese student is drawn into the relational field of the seminar by the specific affinity of their academic formation — and that affinity operates within a power structure that systematically misreads their contribution. Teilhard’s universal synthesis does not address the specific structural condition that determines whose contribution is readable as contribution. The cosmological claim is true and structurally insufficient. Karaoguz’s A-Frame must operate within the cosmological claim AND the specific power conditions of the specific formation encounter. Attunement without structural awareness of power is attunement that mistakes the dominant formation’s Li for the formation field’s actual Li.

“"The kind of world we are navigating now, the kinds of problems we want to address, require a different kind of intelligence."”

— Ann M. Pendleton-Jullian, Design Unbound

A different kind of intelligence: Pendleton-Jullian’s diagnosis of the design challenge of the twenty-first century is identical to Shan’s diagnosis of the complexity challenge. The old intelligence — reductionist, predictive, optimising toward pre-specified goals — was adequate to a world that was complicated but not genuinely complex; a world that could be decomposed into components whose individual optimisations summed to the system’s optimisation. The new world is not like that. It is genuinely complex: the components’ interactions produce system-level properties that the components’ individual properties cannot predict, and the system-level properties change the components’ properties in turn. The intelligence adequate to this world is the intelligence that can read the field — that can perceive Shī, that can navigate by heartwood rather than by plan, that can maintain structural attunement with a formation that is always already in formation. This is Shan’s relational dynamics framework. It is also Pendleton-Jullian’s design unbound. Both are discovering the same formation intelligence from different Daos.

Pendleton-Jullian’s ‘heartwood’ concept in dialogue with Shan’s formation theory: the heartwood is the invisible structural core of the living formation whose specific topology determines what the surface can bear and what it cannot. The surface is responsive and adaptive; the heartwood is the structural ground of that responsiveness. Organisations, practices, and formations that have developed genuine heartwood — deep structural capacity formed through the sustained Dao-walking of genuine formation practice — can be surface-adaptive without structural loss. Organisations that have only surface without heartwood can appear adaptive while their structural core is being consumed. This is Shan’s nothing-collapses-in-one-move applied to design: the collapse was in the heartwood before it became visible on the surface. The design intelligence that can read heartwood is the design intelligence that can intervene before the surface failure.

“"Appreciation is the bridge between perception and wise action, where understanding deepens into structural attunement."”

— Adam Karaoguz, ‘Attunement’ (2026)

Karaoguz’s A-Frame (Attend-Appreciate-Act) is the most precise available model of what Shan means by the formation of structural attunement as a practice. Attend: open receptivity to the actual formation field — not the formation field as the practitioner’s prior Li predicts it will be, but as it actually is in this specific encounter. Appreciate: the specific quality of engaged understanding that moves beyond perception to structural reading — Cook Ding’s three-year transformation from seeing the whole ox to seeing the articulations. Act: the response that arises from structural attunement rather than from prior Li — Cook Ding’s knife finding the hollow, the joint, the natural grain. The bridge is Appreciation: the mode of formation-engagement that has walked the Dao far enough that the formation field’s actual Li becomes structurally legible without being reduced to a prior category. The practitioner who has cycled through this A-Frame enough times, in enough specific formation encounters, with enough genuine attention, eventually dissolves the three-step sequence into a single continuous movement of structural attunement. That is the telos of the A-Frame. That is Cook Ding at year nineteen.

Karaoguz’s most important challenge to Shan: the A-Frame describes the agent’s side of the formation encounter. But the formation field also has its own A-Frame: it attends to perturbations, appreciates their structural significance, and acts through the specific dynamics that the perturbation-in-the-field generates. The most complete account of formation is the account that holds both A-Frames simultaneously: the practitioner attending-appreciating-acting within a formation field that is simultaneously attending-appreciating-acting through its own dynamics. What looks like a practitioner navigating a formation is also, from the inside, a formation field navigating a practitioner. Shan’s relation-precedes-dynamics is the recognition of this: neither the practitioner nor the formation field is primary; the relation between them is primary, and the relation is always already in formation.

Shan: Final Section 1 Analyses — Every Essay at Maximum Structural Voltage

These are the analyses of Shan’s essays that belong in Section 1 but whose full treatment requires the complete context of the paper. Having encountered all the voices assembled here — Zhuangzi and Fuller, Wittgenstein and Zhang Zai, Kauffman and Wang Fuzhi, Mou Zongsan and Whitehead — the essays can now be heard at their full structural depth. What looked like clear, readable prose about complexity and formation is also, and simultaneously, a formation act of extraordinary philosophical ambition. Each essay is walking a Dao. Each essay is producing a Li. And the Li produced is never merely the essay’s explicit content; it is the specific structural transformation the essay produces in the practitioner who genuinely reads it.

“"Participation is the visible surface of a deeper relational field."”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Iceberg Model of Oral Participation, Revisited’ (May 2026)

The iceberg’s structural claim stated in one sentence. But read now, after all the voices in this paper, the sentence carries specific convergent weight: Wittgenstein’s form of life is the deeper relational field — the inherited background that constitutes what participation means before any specific participant arrives. Fuller’s omnitensional network is the deeper relational field — the continuous distribution of relational tension that holds the specific formation together below its visible surface. Bateson’s metapattern is the deeper relational field — the Li that connects the visible patterns to each other and to the structural reality they all express. Shan’s Edinburgh seminar insight is not merely an observation about Chinese students’ silence; it is the most local, most embodied, most personally earned demonstration of a structural reality that Fuller names at the cosmic level, Wittgenstein names at the linguistic level, and Bateson names at the ecological level. The iceberg is the same Li in every register. The surface is always the visible expression of the invisible formation that holds it up.

“"In Chinese, 道 and 理 are not strangers. They live together in 道理 (dào lǐ): reason, principle, underlying logic, the sense a thing begins to make from within its own grain."”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘The Less-Known Partner of Dao: Li (理)’ (May 2026)

道理 (dàolǐ): the compound word that embeds the Dao-Li relationship in everyday Chinese speech. The reason that a thing makes — not the reason imposed on it from outside by analytical decomposition but the reason it carries from within its own specific formation. The bilingual practitioner who grew up inside this compound word already has, in the structure of their daily language, the most important philosophical claim this paper is making: the path and its grain live together, and the reason-of-things is always the reason-of-this-specific-thing-that-has-walked-this-specific-path. Every Chinese speaker who uses 道理 in conversation is making Shan’s ontological claim without knowing it. The Chinese language is doing philosophy that Western philosophy had to discover.

“"Endurance is not always viability. Sometimes what looks like resilience is only delayed collapse."”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Nothing Collapses in One Move’ (April 2026)

The most important diagnostic distinction in the entire framework, and the one most likely to be underestimated. Endurance looks like resilience from the outside. Both produce the same visible metric: the formation continues to function. The difference is structural and invisible until it is catastrophically visible. Genuine resilience: the maintained capacity to absorb perturbations and restore structural coherence — the full omnitensional network maintained under load. Delayed collapse: the continued surface function through the progressive consumption of the structural depth that makes genuine resilience possible — the burning of the bean-stalks to cook the beans. Jin Guantao’s ultrastable structure endured for two millennia; it was not resilient. Confucius’ pine maintains its formation through the winter; that is resilience. The diagnostic: does the formation’s continued function come from maintained structural capacity or from the consumption of structural capacity? The first is viability. The second is delayed collapse. The path narrows either way; only the second is narrowing toward the terminal.

“"What if intelligence is not only the ability to maximise immediate gain? What if the highest form of intelligence is the ability to read a field?"”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘AlphaGo’s Move 37’ (April 2026)

The question that reframes everything. Not a rhetorical question but a genuine one, directed at the entire Western model of intelligence from Aristotle’s phronesis through modern decision theory. The answer that the paper has been assembling: yes, the highest form of intelligence is the ability to read a field. Sun Tzu: the highest strategy attacks the plans, not the armies. Mou Zongsan: intellectual intuition as the direct non-discursive apprehension of the Li of the actual. Karaoguz: appreciation as the bridge between perception and structural attunement. Cook Zhuangzi: working with the spirit and not with the eye, the mind working along without the control of the senses. Every voice in this paper that is worth hearing says the same thing in response to Shan’s question: yes. And they have each been saying it from their own formation position for anywhere from two thousand years to six months. The convergence is the answer.

Closing Cadence: The Final Analyses

The closing cadence does not conclude. It arrives at a threshold and names what is on the other side without crossing it — because crossing it would require a different paper, a different formation, a different practitioner. What follows is the cadence’s structural account of why every voice assembled here points toward the same recognition, and why that recognition cannot be fully stated but can be demonstrated.

道可道，非常道。名可名，非常名。 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. Míng kě míng, fēi cháng míng. — The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. The name that can be named is not the eternal name — Laozi Ch.1

The Dao De Jing opens with the limit of the entire enterprise: every Li this paper has produced, every analysis, every dialectical collision, every synthesis is a named Dao — and therefore not the eternal Dao. The paper is honest about this. But the opening line continues: ‘無名天地之始，有名萬物之母’ — the nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things. Every Li produced by a genuine Dao is the mother of the ten thousand specific insights it enables. The paper’s Lis are provisional, partial, and downstream of the specific Dao of this specific inquiry. They are also real, useful, and generative of the specific formations that genuinely need them. The eternal Dao exceeds them; the named Lis enable them. Both are necessary.

“"Tension is the great integrity."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller

Fuller’s four words placed here in the closing cadence as the structural principle that holds the entire paper together. The paper has not resolved its tensions. Zhu Xi and Shan disagree about whether Li is prior or co-emergent. Wittgenstein falls silent where Shan continues to write. Fuller’s cosmos builds complexity while Laozi’s formation subtracts. Wang Yangming’s innate moral knowledge and Shan’s accumulated formation are not the same thing. Cook Ding’s dissolution of skill and Mou Zongsan’s intellectual intuition approach the same structural reality from different angles and do not quite converge. These tensions are not failures; they are the paper’s integrity. A paper that resolved every tension would have replaced the tensional network of genuine philosophical engagement with a compressional structure of premature synthesis — a rigid chain of forced agreements that would fail precisely under the load it was designed to bear. The tension is the great integrity. The paper holds because it does not force.

“"The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus 5.6

The closing cadence’s Wittgenstein voice. This paper has been, among other things, an attempt to expand the limits of the language available to complexity discourse — to introduce the specifically Chinese vocabulary of Dao, Li, Shī, wúwéi, Cook Ding’s knife, the submerged dragon, the pine in winter, the bean-stalks and the beans — into a discourse whose limits were previously set by English-language systems theory, Western philosophy, and quantitative complexity science. Every new formation vocabulary introduced is an expansion of the world available to the practitioner who genuinely inhabits it. The limit has moved. The world is larger. But the eternal Dao exceeds the new limits as it exceeded the old ones. The next practitioner will expand the limits further. The walking continues.

“"I go along with the natural makeup, strike in the big hollows, guide through the big openings, and follow things as they are."”

— Zhuangzi, Cook Ding, Chapter 3

The paper ends where it began: with Cook Ding’s knife. Not because the paper is circular but because the formation it has walked has produced a return to the beginning that is deeper than the beginning was. The natural makeup (tiān lǐ) is no longer merely Zhuangzi’s anatomical claim; it carries the weight of everything assembled here. It is Fuller’s omnitensional network — the specific topology of relational tension that constitutes this specific formation. It is Zhu Xi’s Li — the structural principle that makes this thing what it is. It is Shan’s relational dynamics field — the prior relational configuration that makes specific dynamics possible and specific dynamics impossible. The big hollows are Kauffman’s adjacent possible — the structural openings that the formation’s own Shī has created, visible only to the formation adequate to see them. The big openings are Pendleton-Jullian’s heartwood — the invisible structural core that enables the specific surface movement. Following things as they are is Whitehead’s self-enjoyment — the absoluteness of the present moment’s formation, complete in itself, contributing its specific Li to the next formation.

“"Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first."”

— Alice Jing Shan, ‘Nothing Collapses in One Move’ (April 2026)

The paper’s central structural claim placed here in the closing cadence not as a conclusion but as an ongoing instruction. The path of this inquiry has been walking for the duration of this paper, and the paper cannot tell you whether it is narrowing or widening; only the formation adequate to read the actual Shī of the actual inquiry can know that. What the paper can tell you is: if the path is narrowing, the narrowing was already happening before you noticed it. The first sign is not the collapse; it is the first reduction in the number of viable next steps. The first reduction is the moment when something could still be done. The paper does not end; it hands the path to the next practitioner. The Dao walks on. The Li will appear from the walking. What is formed is still in formation.

道可道，非常道。 — Dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào. — Laozi • The path that can be named is not the eternal path

❧ ✶ ❧

Luhmann and Meadows: System, Meaning, Leverage — At Full Dialectical Voltage

“"Society is a self-organizing system that produces its own elements by means of its own elements."”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1984/1995)

Autopoiesis at the social scale: Luhmann’s most foundational claim, and the one that places him in both convergence and productive tension with Shan’s framework. The organisation does not receive its elements from outside and then arrange them; it produces its elements through its own operations. Communication produces further communication. The system constitutes itself through its own dynamic. This is Shan’s relational dynamics claim in systems-theory register: the formation field is not a container that formations move through; it is itself produced by the formations that are moving through it. But Luhmann’s sharpest challenge to Shan runs directly: for Luhmann, the operative unit of social reality is communication, not relation. The system is constituted by communications that connect to communications; relations, in the ordinary sense, are not the basic unit.

Shan’s response must be structural. The communication that communicates (Luhmann’s formula: it is the communication, not the persons communicating, that is the system’s basic element) is possible only because of a prior relational condition: the shared horizon of meaning within which this specific communication is recognisable as communication. Two people who share no common formation of meaning cannot communicate, no matter how many messages pass between them. The Edinburgh seminar’s Chinese students did not fail to communicate because their messages were unintelligible; they communicated differently because their relational formation condition (the form of life, the accumulated Dao, the specific Li of their specific educational tradition) was different from the seminar’s relational formation condition. The relation is prior to the communication. Luhmann’s communication-first account presupposes Shan’s relation-first account as its condition of possibility.

“"Complexity, in our understanding, is always complexity reduced by a system and from a system’s perspective."”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1984/1995)

Complexity reduction as the system’s primary function: Luhmann’s most important contribution to the Shan dialogue. The system does not encounter the world in its full complexity; it encounters the world through the specific complexity-reduction that its own formation history has made available. This is Shan’s Li-before-encounter trap at systems-theory precision: the formation’s accumulated Li is precisely its complexity-reduction apparatus. The Li makes specific features of the world salient and specific features invisible. The system that has achieved maximum complexity-reduction is the system most efficient at processing its current formation domain and most blind to formation-field features that its current Li does not code as relevant. Luhmann makes explicit what Shan’s framework implies: the formation’s greatest strength (its specific structural attunement) is simultaneously its greatest vulnerability (its specific structural blindness). The submerged dragon before year nineteen: maximum formation efficiency in the current domain, maximum blindness to the whole-ox formation that is the specific precondition of Cook Ding’s eventual attainment.

“"Meaning is not a property of individual consciousnesses but the medium through which all social operations are conducted."”
