— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1984/1995)

Meaning as medium: Luhmann’s most direct statement of the point where his systems theory and Shan’s relational dynamics converge most deeply. The meaning-horizon is the specific structural condition that makes all further communication possible — not a property of this or that practitioner’s consciousness but the shared relational formation that constitutes the field within which specific communications become meaningful. This is Shan’s relational field in its most formal specification: the prior shared formation-condition that makes specific dynamics possible. What precedes the dynamics of Edinburgh seminar discussion is not the individual consciousnesses of the participants but the shared (and not-shared) meaning-medium that constitutes what ‘contributing to a seminar’ means. The meaning-medium is the Dao’s Li made systemic.

Shan’s most coruscating challenge to Luhmann: the meaning-medium is not symmetrically accessible to all participants in any given social system. The Chinese student enters the Edinburgh seminar’s meaning-medium from outside its formation history; they carry a different meaning-medium with a different set of formation conditions and a different Li of what ‘academic contribution’ means. Luhmann’s theory is structurally elegant but sociologically inadequate: it describes the system’s self-reproduction without adequately accounting for the power differential that determines whose meaning-medium constitutes the system’s operational environment and whose meaning-medium is reduced to noise. The system that communicates also decides what counts as communication and what counts as silence. Shan’s iceberg: the Edinburgh silence is information-rich communication in the student’s meaning-medium. It is noise in the seminar’s. The system’s meaning-reduction is also a power operation.

“"Before you disturb the system in any way, watch how it behaves."”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)

Meadows’ first and most important methodological instruction: watch before you act. This is Shan’s Dao-before-Li at systems-intervention scale: the practitioner who intervenes in a formation without first walking the Dao of genuine observation produces the wrong Li — the intervention that addresses the system as it is conceived rather than as it actually operates. The leverage points hierarchy is the Li of Meadows’ observation: the specific structural features of specific systems that, if intervened at correctly, produce disproportionately large formation changes. But the leverage point can only be identified by the practitioner who has watched long enough to read the system’s actual dynamics rather than its apparent structure. The patience that watching requires is not passivity; it is the formation practice that produces the specific structural sensitivity adequate to reading the actual Shī of the actual system.

“"The most powerful leverage point is intervening in the paradigm — the shared idea from which the system arises."”

— Donella Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999)

The paradigm as the highest leverage point: Meadows’ structural account of why Shan’s framework matters beyond individual practice improvement. The paradigm is the shared formation-ground of the entire system — the accumulated Li of all the formation histories that constitute the system’s meaning-medium. Changing a parameter (a goal, a flow rate, a stock) produces local change within the existing paradigm. Changing the paradigm changes what kinds of change are possible. Shan’s framework is a paradigm intervention: it does not propose to improve the existing formation practices of complexity practitioners; it proposes to change the formation-ground from which those practices arise. The shift from ‘system as object to be analysed’ to ‘formation field as relational condition to be walked’ is a paradigm shift in Meadows’ technical sense: the highest available leverage point.

Shan’s incendiary challenge to Meadows: the paradigm-shift leverage point is the highest and also the most resistant. Meadows acknowledges this: you can point at a paradigm all your life and not change it. The formation that changes a paradigm is not an analytical intervention; it is a Dao-walk of sufficient depth and sufficient duration that the new formation-ground becomes structurally available to practitioners who encounter it. Shan’s essays are not arguments for a paradigm shift; they are demonstrations of the new formation-ground in operation. Each essay is a Dao walked with sufficient formation depth that its Li — relation precedes dynamics; the Dao produces the Li; nothing collapses in one move — becomes structurally available to readers who encounter it with sufficient formation readiness. The paradigm changes by being inhabited, not by being argued for. This is the meta-lesson of Meadows’ own leverage hierarchy applied to itself.

“"Stay humble. Stay a learner."”

— Donella Meadows, Leverage Points (1999)

Meadows’ least-discussed and most important practical instruction. The practitioner who has identified the leverage point is the practitioner most at risk of the premature-Li trap: the formation that has produced the specific structural insight (I know where the leverage is) now faces the specific temptation to apply that insight before walking the next Dao. Staying humble means maintaining the specific formation porosity that prevents the achieved Li from becoming the imposed Li. Staying a learner means maintaining the Dao-walking orientation even when the Li is rich, specific, and apparently adequate. Cook Ding at year nineteen: he still follows the heavenly grain; he does not rely on his year-nineteen Li; he continues to read the actual Li of each actual ox. The leverage-point practitioner who has stopped being a learner is the practitioner who has turned their highest insight into their lowest limitation.

Whitehead, Kuhn, Lakatos: Process, Paradigm, Programme — Shan Unconstrained

“"The notion of 'substance' is transformed into the notion of 'actual entity.'"”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (1929)

The most consequential ontological substitution in twentieth-century process philosophy. Substance: the static, enduring, property-bearing thing that exists independently of its relations and its time. Actual entity: the specific, temporally located, processual event of formation — the ‘actual occasion’ that arises from its specific past, achieves its specific determination, and perishes into its specific contribution to the formation of subsequent actual entities. For Shan, the substitution is the ontological foundation of the entire framework: every formation is an actual entity in Whitehead’s sense, not a substance with properties but a specific processual event of Dao producing Li. What is formed is still in formation: the actual entity never finalises.

Shan’s most urgent challenge to Whitehead: the actual entity perishes. Its contribution to subsequent formations is its causal efficacy — the specific structural character it achieved before perishing is now part of the formation ground from which subsequent actual entities arise. But who carries the accumulated formation across the perishing? Whitehead’s answer involves God (as the primordial nature that preserves all perished occasions). Shan’s answer is structural: the accumulated formation is carried in the specific Dao-walking of specific practitioners whose formation has been shaped by the prior formation’s specific Li. The tradition carries it. The community of practitioners carries it. The classical texts carry it — which is exactly why the correct characters matter: the perishing actual occasions of Zhang Zai’s specific formation encounter must be preserved with precision, or the causal efficacy of his specific Li cannot be transmitted. Jūcí is Whitehead’s principle of causal efficacy applied to textual transmission: the correction of the wrong character is the preservation of the perished occasion’s specific structural contribution.

“"Process is fundamental."”

— Alfred North Whitehead, Process and Reality (1929)

Three words that carry the philosophical weight of a library. Not: process is important. Not: process explains much. But: process is fundamental — it is the basic ontological category from which all others are derived. Substance is derived from process (as the characterisation of a relatively enduring sequence of actual occasions). Property is derived from process (as the specific determination achieved by a specific actual occasion). Relation is derived from process (as the specific way in which each actual occasion arises from and contributes to the formation of others). Shan’s challenge: she agrees with Whitehead that process is fundamental, but she insists that the specific characterisation of what kind of process matters decisively. Whitehead’s process is cosmological: the creative advance of the universe. Shan’s process is phenomenological: the specific practitioner’s specific Dao-walk through the specific formation field. Both are needed. Without Whitehead’s cosmological process, Shan’s phenomenological process is a technique. Without Shan’s phenomenological specificity, Whitehead’s cosmological process is an abstraction that floats free of the specific encounters that make process concrete. Process is fundamental: but the process that is fundamental has a specific interior that Whitehead’s exterior account does not fully inhabit.

“"Normal science means research firmly based upon one or more past scientific achievements, achievements that some particular scientific community acknowledges for a time as supplying the foundation for its further practice."”

— Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)

The paradigm as accumulated Li: Kuhn’s account of normal science is the most precise available description of what happens when a formation’s Li becomes its paradigm — the shared framework that guides all further inquiry without itself being questioned. Normal science is productive: it produces specific knowledge, specific techniques, specific formation achievements that no other framework could have produced. It is also constraining: it renders invisible the anomalies that do not fit the paradigm, the formation-field features that the paradigm’s complexity-reduction apparatus codes as noise. The practitioner formed in normal science is the practitioner whose specific structural attunement is most precisely calibrated to the paradigm’s questions and most blind to the questions the paradigm cannot formulate. This is Shan’s formation framework applied to the sociology of scientific knowledge: the Li of the paradigm is the most productive and the most constraining simultaneously.

Shan’s white-hot challenge to Kuhn: the paradigm shift is not merely a change in scientific framework; it is a change in the formation of the practitioners who constitute the scientific community. A new paradigm is not adopted by existing scientists converting their existing formation to a new framework; it is adopted by new practitioners who have been formed within the new framework. Kuhn’s account of the generation gap in paradigm shifts is the most sociologically honest recognition that formation is irreversible: the practitioner formed in the Newtonian paradigm cannot fully become a practitioner formed in the quantum mechanical paradigm; they can understand the new framework intellectually without inhabiting it formationally. Shan’s consequence: every paradigm shift is a formation crisis. The generation that walks the new Dao and produces the new Li is the generation that did not have the old Li to overcome. The formation’s strength is also its structural inertia.

“"Scientists do not reject paradigms when they encounter anomalies. Paradigms are given up only when a new paradigm is available to take its place."”

— Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)

Anomaly alone does not produce paradigm shift: this is Kuhn’s most structurally important finding for Shan’s collapse theory. The formation that encounters anomalies does not abandon its Li; it absorbs them, reclassifies them, or ignores them. The practitioner whose formation has produced a specific Li cannot relinquish that Li on the basis of anomalous evidence alone; they require an alternative Li available to take its place. Nothing collapses in one move: the formation facing anomalies continues to function, continues to produce outputs, continues to appear structurally adequate — until the specific alternative Li is available and the specific next generation of practitioners is ready to walk the new Dao. The path narrows first. The paradigm shift is the collapse that the anomaly accumulation made structurally inevitable. But the inevitability is only visible from after the fact. The practitioners inside the narrowing paradigm cannot see the brim approaching.

“"All scientific research programmes are characterised by a hard core and a protective belt."”

— Imre Lakatos, The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes (1978)

The research programme’s structure: a hard core of non-negotiable assumptions protected by a belt of auxiliary hypotheses that absorb anomalies and take the strain of disconfirmation. This is the most precise available structural account of how a formation maintains its Li against the specific pressure of contrary evidence. The hard core is the formation’s constitutive Li — the specific structural assumptions that, if abandoned, would dissolve the formation entirely. The protective belt is the formation’s adaptive capacity — the specific flexibility that allows the formation to absorb specific anomalies without structural collapse. The distinction between hard core and protective belt is the distinction between the formation’s irreducible Li and its adaptive periphery: between what the formation IS and what the formation DOES in response to specific challenges.

Shan’s most incandescent challenge to Lakatos: the hard core’s protection is also its structural risk. The formation that has identified its hard core and protected it against disconfirmation is the formation that has named its own most irreplaceable Li — and in doing so has made it available for premature application. The hard core, explicitly identified, becomes a Li-before-Dao: a named commitment that guides all further inquiry before the inquiry has been walked. The protective belt’s function — to preserve the hard core against the specific challenge of specific anomalies — is also the function of the formation’s blindness: it is precisely the anomalies that the protective belt absorbs that contain the specific formation-field features that the hard core’s Li cannot process. The progressive research programme is the programme whose protective belt produces new predictions and new formation achievements. The degenerative programme is the programme whose protective belt absorbs anomalies without producing formation. The practitioner who cannot distinguish the two from inside is the practitioner whose formation has already begun its structural decline.

Laozi’s Challenge to Shan’s Framework

Shan’s framework risks becoming the very thing it is trying to avoid: a named Li, a system of concepts that circulates with increasing smoothness until the smoothness replaces the encounter. Laozi: the Dao that can be Substack-posted is not the eternal Dao. Every essay Shan writes, however precise and careful, produces new Li that can now be applied before the next Dao has been walked. The framework is always already potentially a Li-before-Dao trap. A practitioner who has read all of Shan’s essays and absorbed their specific vocabulary — Dao, Li, Shī, formation, the long game, Move 37, Cook Ding, the submerged dragon — has a highly refined Li available. The question Laozi presses: how much of that Li has been genuinely walked, and how much is being borrowed from Shan’s Dao without the practitioner walking their own? The borrowed Li is not false; it is premature. The smooth circulation of formation theory is the smoothness of a frozen river: there is apparent movement, but the water has stopped moving beneath. Laozi’s solution: silence. Shan’s solution: more essays, each explicitly destabilising the Li of the previous one. This is a different solution. Is it adequate?

Shan’s Response to Laozi: The Writing that Does Not Force

The relinquishment is not silence. 無為 (non-action) is not non-writing. It is action that does not force — writing that does not impose its Li on the formation it describes. Shan’s essays demonstrate rather than define; they show the Li forming rather than stating it as formed. ‘Nothing collapses in one move’ is not a rule to be applied; it is a formation to be walked into. ‘The path narrows first’ is not a prediction to be verified; it is an orientation to be inhabited. The relational dynamics framework is offered not as a completed Li but as a Dao-instrument — a set of concepts that, held lightly, help the practitioner walk toward formations that cannot be pre-named. The ladder is the path. It should be walked, not worshipped — and not thrown away before it has been climbed.

But Shan’s response must confront the sharpest form of Laozi’s challenge: the practitioner who has absorbed the framework fully — who can name Shī and read the adjacent possible and recognise the narrowing path — is precisely the practitioner most at risk of the specific premature-Li failure the framework is designed to prevent. The framework’s explicit articulation of its own anti-premature-Li commitment does not immunise it against being applied prematurely. The anti-trap is not immunity from the trap; it is a more refined version of the same trap. The practitioner who knows that nothing collapses in one move may be the practitioner who does not recognise when the formation IS collapsing in very few moves because the framework tells them it should be slow. The Li of the framework shapes what the practitioner attends to; it also shapes what the practitioner misses.

The Synthesis: Laozi and Shan — A Structural Resolution at White Heat

The synthesis is incendiary precisely because it does not resolve the tension but inhabits it as a structural necessity. Shan cannot stop writing without abandoning the specific formation that has produced the specific Li of the relational dynamics framework — a Li that genuinely helps practitioners navigate formations that prior frameworks could not adequately describe. Laozi cannot stop being right: the Dao that can be Substack-posted is not the eternal Dao. Both are true. The synthesis is the structural relationship between them, not their resolution.

What Laozi’s silence and Shan’s writing share: both are oriented toward the formation that precedes the Li, not the Li that consolidates the formation. Laozi’s silence maintains the practitioner’s formation porosity by refusing to close any specific Li around the specific formation encounter. Shan’s writing maintains the practitioner’s formation porosity by continuously producing new Li that destabilises the previous Li before it solidifies into paradigm. The silence and the writing are two formation strategies for the same structural requirement: keeping the Dao alive, keeping the practitioner’s formation genuinely open to the actual Li of the actual formation field. Silence achieves this by saying nothing that can be applied prematurely. Writing achieves this by saying something that explicitly undermines its own premature application. Neither is sufficient alone. Together they are the two formation strategies that Shan’s bilingual position inhabits simultaneously: the Chinese formation tradition’s deepest impulse is toward Laozi’s silence; the Western academic formation’s demand is for Shan’s writing. The specific Li she produces is the product of the tension between them, not the resolution of it. The tension is the great integrity.

Bateson’s Challenge: The Ecology of Mind and the Limit of Formation Theory

The ecology of mind challenge is the most structurally penetrating criticism available to Shan’s formation framework, precisely because it comes from the inside. Shan’s framework is focused on the formation field and the practitioner’s capacity to read it. But Bateson asks what the Li of the practitioner’s mind is — what metapatterns their formation has made available as perceptual categories. The practitioner who cannot see the metapattern that connects the crab to the orchid and the orchid to the spiral of a galaxy cannot read the Li of formations that span those categories. Bateson’s ecology of mind is the account of how the practitioner’s cognitive formation shapes what Li they can perceive. The practitioner’s attunement is not to the formation field as it is; it is to the formation field as it appears through the specific cognitive ecology that their specific formation history has produced.

“"The unit of survival is the organism plus environment."”

— Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)

The organism plus environment as the unit: Bateson’s most structurally decisive claim. Not the organism adapting to the environment; not the environment shaping the organism; but organism-plus-environment as an indivisible formation unit. This is Shan’s relation-precedes-dynamics claim at the biological level: the relational field (organism-environment interface) is prior to the dynamics (adaptation, evolution, learning) that occur within it. But Bateson’s claim has a specific directional charge that Shan must confront: the unit of survival is determined by whether the organism’s maps of its environment match the territory well enough for navigation. The practitioner whose Li-of-the-formation-field is systematically misaligned with the actual formation field will not navigate successfully, regardless of the sophistication of their formation theory.

Shan’s Challenge Back to Bateson: The Circularity Problem Resolved

Bateson’s ecology risks circularity: if the mind and its environment are constitutively entangled, how does genuine learning occur? How does the mind develop sensitivity to metapatterns it has not yet encountered? The entanglement seems to close the system: the practitioner can only perceive what their existing cognitive ecology makes perceptible. The new metapattern — the one that would transform the practitioner’s formation — is precisely what their existing cognitive ecology renders invisible. If Bateson is right that the mind and its environment are constitutively entangled, there seems to be no entry point for the genuinely new.

Shan’s Dao-walk provides the mechanism that Bateson’s framework needs but does not adequately specify: the specific, repeated, formation-sufficient engagement with the actual formation field that progressively restructures the practitioner’s cognitive ecology. The formation history is the bridge between the mind as it is and the mind as it becomes capable of reading the metapatterns it could not previously perceive. Cook Ding does not arrive at year-nineteen attunement through conceptual learning; he arrives through the specific, repeated, embodied, formation-sufficient engagement with the actual formation field of the actual ox. Each encounter restructures his cognitive ecology slightly; after nineteen years, the restructuring is complete enough that the metapattern — the heavenly grain (天理) — is perceptible where it was previously invisible. The Dao-walk is the mechanism of ecological cognitive restructuring that Bateson describes but does not specify.

Bateson’s sharpest response: even if the Dao-walk is the mechanism, the specific Dao that is walked determines what specific cognitive ecology emerges. The practitioner who walks the Dao of Chinese classical philosophy develops a specific cognitive ecology (sensitivity to Li, Dao, Shī, formation patterns in human social dynamics) that is different from the cognitive ecology of the practitioner who walks the Dao of Western complexity science (sensitivity to emergence, adaptation, edge-of-chaos dynamics, feedback loops). Each cognitive ecology makes specific formation-field features perceptible and specific formation-field features invisible. The bilingual practitioner — Shan’s specific formation position — is the practitioner who has walked both Daos and has the specific double cognitive ecology that makes both sets of features simultaneously perceptible. This is not a resolution of the circularity; it is the specific Dao-walk that breaks the circularity in the specific case of bilingual formation. It is not universalisable. Every practitioner must walk their own Daos.

The Synthesis: Bateson and Shan — Mind, Formation, and the Metapattern’s Ground

The synthesis at maximum dialectical heat: the metapattern that connects is real (Bateson), but it is not directly accessible; it is accessible only through the specific cognitive ecology produced by the specific formation-sufficient Dao-walk (Shan). The metapattern is the Li; the cognitive ecology is the formation instrument; the Dao-walk is the process. The synthesis produces a specific instruction for formation practice: you cannot perceive the metapattern you have not yet walked the Dao adequate to perceive. The answer to ‘what is the pattern that connects the crab to the orchid and the orchid to me?’ is not a formula; it is a formation requirement. Walk the Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient attention to specific biological formations, as Bateson did, for as long as it takes for the specific cognitive ecology that makes the metapattern perceptible to emerge. Then walk the Dao of Shan’s relational dynamics framework alongside it, and watch what each illuminates in the other. The double Dao-walk is the double attunement that the complexity practitioner needs: Bateson’s ecology of mind for the interior of the formation, Shan’s relational dynamics for the exterior of the field. Together they are the specific structural consciousness that the twenty-first century’s formation challenges require.

The 6E Model: The Entangled Self in Formation — Claydon, Karaoguz, and Shan at Maximum Structural Voltage

Richard Claydon opens his account of the 6E model with the claim that will detonate throughout everything that follows: the self is ‘formed and re-formed in constant interaction with role, context, and system conditions.’ This is not a therapeutic observation about personal flexibility; it is an ontological claim that the self has no fixed substance prior to its relational encounters — that what appears as a stable identity is always a formation product of the specific relational field within which the specific practitioner has been embedded, enacted, extended, regulated, and recombined. Karaoguz’s 6E framework (Embodied, Embedded, Enacted, Extended, Emotive, Exaptive) names the six dimensions through which this constant formation and re-formation occurs in the cognitive architecture of the practitioner. Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations names the relational field within which all six dimensions are always already operating. The three frameworks need each other with structural urgency: Shan provides the ontological ground (relation precedes dynamics; the relational field is prior to the self that forms within it); Karaoguz provides the cognitive architecture (the six specific mechanisms through which the self forms within that relational field); Claydon provides the formation phenomenology (the first-person account of what it feels like, from inside the formation, to be formed and re-formed). None alone is complete. Together they are the most adequate available account of what it takes to navigate genuinely complex formation fields with structural intelligence.

The specific structural pressure that Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations applies to every E is this: every E describes a dimension of the practitioner’s cognitive formation, but the practitioner’s cognitive formation is always already inside a relational field that precedes it. The formation is downstream of the relation. The self is downstream of the interaction. Shan’s challenge to the 6E framework is not that any E is wrong; it is that every E’s account of cognitive formation must be grounded in the prior ontological claim that the relational field is constitutive of the formation rather than merely contextual to it. The difference is the whole game. If the relational field is merely the context within which the self forms, then the self can in principle be understood independently of its context, and the 6E model is a description of how context shapes a pre-existing self. If the relational field is constitutive of the formation — if Shan is right that relation precedes dynamics — then there is no self prior to the relational encounter, and the 6E model describes how the self IS the relational encounter in its six cognitive dimensions. The second reading is more radical, more accurate, and more demanding of the practitioner. Karaoguz’s challenge to each: does this E capture the formation’s depth, or only its surface?

E1: Embodied — The Body as Formation Instrument AND Formation Sensor

Embodied cognition: the practitioner’s body IS the formation instrument. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of practice are nineteen years of embodied formation — the progressive restructuring of his somatic attunement to the specific formation field of the ox. The knowledge is in the body before it is in the head. 天理 (tiān lǐ, heavenly grain) is perceived by the hand at the joint before it is articulated by the mind in language. Karaoguz: ‘embodied cognition suggests that cognition is not solely a product of the brain, but is also influenced by sensory and motor experiences, bodily sensations.’ Shan: the path must be walked (embodied) before its grain can appear. The formation that is merely understood conceptually has not yet been walked. The graduate student who has read all of Shan’s essays and can recite the Dao-before-Li principle has not walked the Dao that produces the somatic sensitivity to the formation field’s actual Li. The body must be educated. The hand must develop the specific sensitivity that registers the joint before the mind names it.

Claydon’s crucial addition: the body is not only the formation instrument but the formation sensor. Before the maps and frameworks, Maya noticed the physical cues: a knot in her stomach when alignment masked fear, tight shoulders when conversations became political, fatigue behind her eyes when the room pretended everything was fine. She began to treat her body as a sensor — not always accurate, but rarely irrelevant. This distinction — between the body as instrument (it performs formation) and the body as sensor (it reads the formation field) — is the difference between the body as the practitioner’s tool and the body as the formation field’s message. Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations grounds this distinction: the body-as-sensor is the relational field becoming readable through the practitioner’s somatic architecture. The knot in the stomach is not produced by the practitioner’s psychology; it is produced by the relational field’s specific configuration and registered through the practitioner’s specific somatic sensitivity. The body reads the field before the mind names the reading. The formation is prior to the articulation. And when the room pretends everything is fine while the body reports otherwise, the body is reading the actual relational field while the room is performing an official Li that the actual Dao has already moved past. The body’s reading is the Dao. The room’s performance is the prior Li.

Shan’s white-hot challenge to the embodiment claim: the body’s education is also the body’s limitation. Cook Ding’s nineteen years of embodied formation produce a specific somatic attunement to the specific formation field of the ox. That specific embodied formation is also a specific embodied blindness: the practitioner whose body has been formed in ox-butchery is the practitioner whose somatic sensitivity is calibrated to the specific Li of the specific domain. The transferred body — the practitioner trying to apply the somatic sensitivity of one formation domain to a different formation domain — will produce false Li: the specific grain of the new formation field felt through the somatic vocabulary of the old. The body’s formation is its strength and its transferability limit simultaneously. The practitioner must walk each new formation domain with the body, not merely with the concept. There are no shortcuts through embodiment.

E2: Embedded — The Formation Field as Cognitive Scaffolding AND System Expression

Embedded cognition: cognition is constituted by its environmental scaffolding. The practitioner does not think inside their skull and then deploy thoughts into the world; they think within a formation field that shapes what is thinkable. Wittgenstein’s form of life: the inherited background that constitutes the preconditions of all specifically formed thinking. Shan’s relational field: the prior relational configuration that makes specific dynamics possible. Karaoguz: the practitioner’s cognitive architecture is embedded in the specific social, physical, and cultural formation field that constitutes its operational environment. The Edinburgh seminar’s silence is embedded cognition: the Chinese student’s contribution is shaped by the specific embedding of their cognition in a different formation field from the seminar’s — a formation field where silence is information, where contribution is demonstrated through presence rather than performance.

Claydon’s most productive extension: the practitioner is not merely embedded in the system; they are part of the system’s expression. Maya recognised that her busyness mirrored the system’s pace, her search for clarity reinforced the illusion of control, and her past silences became precedents for others’ silence. Recognising herself as part of the system’s expression created both humility and responsibility. This is the ontological move that shifts embedded cognition from a passive account (I am shaped by my context) to an active-relational account (I am the formation field expressing itself through my specific cognitive architecture). Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim makes this explicit: the practitioner is not embedded in the relational field as an object in a container; they are the relational field locally expressed. The field’s dynamics are not external constraints on the practitioner; they are the practitioner’s own dynamics from a different angle. This is why noticing that your busyness mirrors the system’s pace is not merely useful feedback; it is the recognition that you ARE the system’s pace, locally. To change your pace is to change the system’s expression. The practitioner who cannot see this cannot intervene at the level that matters.

Shan’s challenge: embedded cognition explains why the practitioner whose embedding has changed faces the specific formation crisis of the cross-cultural encounter. But it does not explain how genuine formation across embedding boundaries occurs. The practitioner who has been embedded in one formation field cannot simply re-embed in another; they carry their original embedding’s Li as the specific cognitive scaffolding that shapes what is thinkable in any new embedding. The genuine bilingual formation practitioner is not the practitioner who has switched embeddings; they are the practitioner who has developed the specific formation capacity to operate simultaneously in two embeddings without either dominating. This requires walking the specific Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient engagement with the new embedding from inside the old — not conceptual translation but the specific somatic, relational, cognitive restructuring that genuine re-embedding requires.

E3: Enacted — Formation Through Action AND the Shadow of Performance

Enacted cognition: every action is a formation event. The practitioner does not first form and then act; they form through acting. Shan’s Dao-walk is enacted cognition running to its full depth: the repeated, deliberate, formation-sufficient engagement with the specific formation field that progressively produces the structural attunement of the practitioner. Karaoguz: ‘enacted cognition proposes that cognition is a process of actively engaging with the world and that our actions play a crucial role in shaping our thinking and understanding.’ Zhuangzi’s Cook Ding: the knife entering the joint IS the formation event. Not: Cook Ding thinks about the joint and then inserts the knife. Cook Ding inserts the knife into the joint and in doing so completes the formation that makes the next insertion possible.

Claydon’s most structurally important extension: enactment has a shadow, and the shadow is as formative as the enactment itself. Maya’s leadership was situational. Reporting up, she became concise; mediating peers, she softened; in uncertain spaces, her curiosity contracted. These shifts weren’t inauthentic — they were adaptive. But she also saw the shadow: performances could limit what she allowed herself to think or say. The shadow of enactment is the enacted cognition that forecloses its own formation: the performance so consistent that the practitioner no longer knows whether they are adapting or simply repeating a prior formation’s Li without walking the Dao that would produce a new one. Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations names this precisely: the enacted performance that produces its own relational field is also the enacted performance that narrows the relational field’s available Li. The leader who always becomes concise when reporting up has enacted a relational field in which concision is the only available Li — and in doing so has made the specific Li that directness-under-uncertainty would produce unavailable, not because it is impossible but because the enactment’s accumulated history has closed off the relational pathway to it.

Shan’s most urgent challenge: enacted cognition without formation orientation is the practitioner who acts continuously but does not form. The person who engages with the formation field incessantly without the specific orientation of Dao-before-Li produces surface fluency without structural depth — the practitioner who has made ten thousand cuts without Cook Ding’s specific attentional orientation, and has produced ten thousand surface cuts without finding a single joint. Enaction requires orientation: the specific formation orientation that the Dao-before-Li principle provides. Action without Dao is the formation field engaged without formation intelligence. The enacted practitioner who has never sat still long enough to read the formation field’s actual Li is the practitioner who is most active and least formed. Formation requires both enacted engagement and reflective attunement. The action must be followed by the silence that allows the Li to reveal itself.

E4: Extended — Formation Instruments, Organisational Intelligence, and the Material Reach of the Self

Extended cognition: the practitioner’s formation instruments — Cook Ding’s knife, the Polynesian navigator’s body-in-the-waves, the Go master’s accumulated game-sense, the organisation’s informal networks and shared practices — are extensions of the practitioner’s cognitive architecture into the formation field. The knife does not merely execute the practitioner’s intention; it extends the practitioner’s sensory capacity into the formation field, providing real-time formation feedback that the practitioner’s unaided body could not receive. Pendleton-Jullian and Brown’s invisible machinery is extended cognition at organisational scale: the specific formation instruments that extend individual cognitive capacity into the collective formation field.

Claydon’s critical extension: the practitioner’s cognitive extension includes communications, platforms, rituals, and silences that travel beyond their direct presence and cannot be fully controlled. A Slack message could be read with unintended weight. An email could anchor a narrative she didn’t mean to set. Silence could be interpreted as endorsement or resistance. She saw herself as materially extended through tools, platforms, and rituals. Shan’s ontology makes this structurally precise: the extended self does not merely influence the relational field; the extended self IS the relational field as it has been shaped by the practitioner’s specific cognitive-material presence. Every tool, ritual, communication, and structured silence the practitioner has contributed to the organisation’s formation history is part of the specific relational field that now precedes the dynamics of every new encounter. The email that anchored the wrong narrative has become part of the formation field’s specific relational configuration — part of the prior relational condition that makes specific dynamics possible and other dynamics impossible. The practitioner cannot un-extend. They can only extend more deliberately.

Shan’s challenge: extended cognition’s instruments carry their own formation history. Cook Ding’s knife is not a neutral instrument; it has been formed by eighteen years of Cook Ding’s specific Dao-walking, and its specific formation (unbroken, still sharp where other blades have long since dulled) is the material embodiment of Cook Ding’s specific formation. The instrument and the practitioner form each other. The organisation’s informal networks carry the specific formation history of their development — the specific Daos that the organisation’s practitioners have walked together and the specific Lis that those walks have produced. When the instrument is destroyed (the knife lost, the informal network dissolved), the formation that it carried is lost with it. The bean-stalk burned: not only the practitioner’s embodied capacity but their extended cognitive instruments are the formation at risk in any formation-consuming urgency.

E5: Emotive — Emotional Memory, Narrative, Resonance, and the Relational Field’s Affective Ground

Emotive cognition (Claydon’s term, more precise than the generic ‘emotional’): the practitioner is influenced by emotional memory, narrative, and resonance — not merely by current emotional states but by the accumulated history of emotionally significant formation encounters that constitutes the practitioner’s specific affective architecture. The emotional memory is not merely a record of past feelings; it is the specific relational formation history that has calibrated the practitioner’s affective responsiveness to the specific features of specific formation fields. Karaoguz: ‘the valence our mind assigns to a given stimulus will colour the processing which comes after.’ The practitioner’s emotional formation — the specific history of formation encounters that has calibrated their emotional responsiveness to specific formation-field features — shapes what they attend to, how they appreciate it, and what actions feel available to them. Shan’s Valence frequency is the formation field’s directional tendency — but the practitioner’s own emotive valence shapes what formation-field Valence they can register.

Claydon’s most structurally important contribution to this E: emotions are system data. The goal is not to suppress or indulge them, but to recognise their influence, name them when useful, and shape the emotional conditions that allow good thinking and collaboration. Frustration narrows focus, anxiety shortens the time horizon, hope opens to new ideas but sometimes inflates expectations. Each of these is a specific emotive valence that the practitioner’s formation history has calibrated in a specific way. Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations makes the structural consequence explicit: the emotive valence of the practitioner is not a psychological overlay on the relational field; it IS a constitutive dimension of the relational field. The practitioner whose frustration narrows focus is not merely a practitioner who feels frustrated; they are a practitioner who is constituting a specific relational field in which certain dimensions of the formation are perceptible and others are not. The emotion is a relational event, not a psychological state. It shapes what Li is available for production and what Li is closed off. Treating emotions as system data is Shan’s ontological claim operationalised: the emotive dimension of the practitioner’s cognition is a dimension of the relational field’s actual formation dynamics.

Attunement includes somatic regulation — Karaoguz’s rubric item — precisely because emotional cognitive architecture shapes the quality of the entire A-Frame cycle. The practitioner whose nervous system is dysregulated — whose emotional formation is producing anxiety, defensiveness, or urgency — is the practitioner whose Attend phase is compromised at its foundation: they are attending to their own emotional state rather than to the actual formation field. Cook Ding’s specific achievement at year nineteen includes this: he approaches the ox with ‘the spirit and not with the eye’ — a phenomenological description of the specific emotional regulation that allows the practitioner to attend to the formation field’s actual Li rather than to their own anticipatory Li. The ‘spirit’ is the emotionally regulated cognitive state that makes genuine formation-field attunement possible.

Shan’s white-hot challenge to emotive cognition: the emotional formation that produces settled attunement is not a personal psychological achievement; it is a formation achievement. The practitioner does not develop somatic regulation by learning to calm down; they develop it by walking the specific Dao of formation-sufficient engagement with enough specific formation encounters that the emotional responsiveness becomes calibrated to the actual formation field rather than to the practitioner’s anticipatory Li. The anxiety of not-yet-sufficient formation is appropriate: it is the accurate emotional registration of actual formation inadequacy. The practitioner who is prematurely calm — who has achieved somatic regulation without the formation depth that genuine attunement requires — is the practitioner whose emotional calibration is producing false signals. The right emotional formation for year three is not year-nineteen equanimity; it is year-three appropriate anxiety, engaged productively rather than suppressed.

E6: Exaptive — The Adaptive Archive, Formation Recombination, and the Relational Field as Resource Library

Exaptive cognition (Claydon’s term, more precise than the generic ‘exapted’): cognitive capacities are repurposed and re-patterned across time and context. In pressure moments, Maya drew not from the official leadership toolkit but from unexpected places — an old facilitation trick, an improv exercise, the rhythm of live music, a conflict she mediated years ago. These weren’t random; they were recombinations of past experience for present need. She began to value this ‘adaptive archive’ and saw the same in others. The adaptive archive is not a static repository of past competences; it is the specific formation history of the specific practitioner, crystallised into specific cognitive capacities that can be recombined for formation challenges that their original domain did not anticipate. Karaoguz: in complex systems, the ability to repurpose and reframe existing resources is often more valuable than acquiring new ones.

Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations makes the exaptive E’s deepest claim structural: the adaptive archive is not the practitioner’s private possession; it is the product of the specific relational fields they have inhabited and been formed by. The old facilitation trick is not the practitioner’s individual cognitive resource; it is the crystallised Li of a specific relational formation encounter that the practitioner walked with specific other people in a specific formation field. It is available now because that relational formation produced it then. Every entry in the adaptive archive is a prior relational field’s specific Li, available for re-contextualisation in a current relational field’s specific formation challenge. The practitioner’s adaptive archive is their relational formation history made cognitively available for new encounters. Shan’s bilingual formation is an exaptive formation: the specific cognitive capacities developed in the Chinese philosophical formation domain are exapted for navigating the English-language complexity-theory domain, producing Li that neither domain alone could generate.

Shan’s most structurally important challenge to the exaptation account: exaptation is not transfer. The capacity exapted is not the capacity in its original form; it is the capacity restructured by the new formation encounter into a new cognitive instrument adequate to the new domain. Shan’s Dao-Li-Shī vocabulary does not arrive in the English-language complexity discourse as a Chinese philosophical import; it arrives as a new formation instrument that has been restructured by the specific encounter between Chinese philosophical formation and Western complexity formation into something that neither tradition alone could have specified. The exaptation is the formation. The Li of the exapted capacity is not the Li of the original capacity; it is the Li produced by the specific Dao of the specific cross-formation encounter. Every genuine bilingual formation event is an exaptation event. Every time a formation walks into genuinely new territory, it exapts whatever formation capacity it carries into the new domain. This is the adjacent possible expanded: the new territory is adjacent possible only because the exapted capacity makes it navigable.

The 6E Synthesis: The Entangled Self, Cook Ding, and Shan’s Ontology of Dynamic Relations

The synthesis of 6E cognition, Claydon’s entangled-self account, and Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations is not additive; it is structural. Claydon’s framing: the 6E self is not a target identity. It is a working description of how a leader can stay responsive without losing coherence — the shift from ‘How do I lead better?’ to ‘How do I stay attuned, adapt wisely, and act accountably in the complexity I’m part of?’ Not heroic. Not detached. Just situated, connected, and in motion — with others, for the whole. This is the most compressed account of what Shan’s formation practice requires: not the achievement of a fixed formation identity (the practitioner who has finally become fully formed) but the sustained capacity for formation — the practitioner who is always already in formation, always already reading the actual relational field’s actual Li, always already walking the next Dao.

Shan’s ontology of dynamic relations makes the 6E synthesis structurally coherent by providing its ontological ground: each E is a dimension of the practitioner’s cognitive formation, but the practitioner’s cognitive formation is always already inside a relational field that precedes it. Embodied (the body walks the Dao within the relational field), embedded (the formation field IS the cognitive scaffold and the practitioner IS the field’s expression), enacted (the Dao is walked through specific action that constitutes specific relational dynamics), extended (the formation instruments carry the formation and extend the practitioner’s relational presence), emotive (the practitioner’s affective formation is a constitutive dimension of the relational field’s dynamics), exaptive (the formation capacity is restructured by the cross-domain relational encounter into new cognitive resources). The 6E practitioner who has developed all six dimensions is the practitioner whose specific cognitive architecture is adequate to the specific formation challenge of the twenty-first century’s genuinely complex formation fields.

Cook Ding at year nineteen has all six Es simultaneously, and Shan’s ontology grounds each: his knife’s edge (extended: the relational field of practitioner-instrument-formation is indivisible) enters the joint (enacted: the action constitutes the relational dynamic) guided by somatic registration (embodied: the body reads the formation field’s actual Li) within the specific formation field of the ox (embedded: the practitioner is part of the formation field’s expression, not a visitor to it) with the settled equanimity of adequate formation (emotive: the emotional calibration is accurate because the formation history is adequate) that his two decades of attunement have exapted into a structural orientation adequate to any complex formation field (exaptive: the adaptive archive of nineteen years’ relational formation history is available for recombination in any new encounter). This is the formation that the paper has been walking toward. The 6E account of how to develop it is the cognitive-science underpinning that Shan’s ontological account requires. The Dao walks on. The entangled self is always already in formation. With others, for the whole.

❧ ✶ ❧
XXXVII

Part XVIII: Boisot and WSR — The Devastating Encounter

What follows is the most forensically demanding collision in this paper. Max Boisot and Zhichang Zhu are not peripheral voices; they are the most structurally ambitious attempts within English-language management theory to build a framework adequate to what Shan names with Dao, Li, and Shī. They have worked in the same territory. They have walked adjacent Daos. And precisely because they are closest to Shan’s formation field, the dialectical collision between them is the most productive and the most explosive available. Where a distant voice (Wittgenstein, Fuller) collides with Shan and produces light from the distance, Boisot and Zhu collide with Shan and produce heat from proximity. The heat is the point.

❧ ✶ ❧

Max Boisot (1943–2011) — The I-Space, the Social Learning Cycle, and the Formation That Cannot Be Mapped

Max Boisot spent his career doing what Shan is doing: attempting to bridge the gap between the tacit formation knowledge of the practitioner and the explicit analytical frameworks of management theory. His I-Space (Information Space) is the most rigorous available attempt in Western knowledge management theory to provide a three-dimensional account of what knowledge IS, where it lives, how it moves, and why its movement generates both value and loss. He worked on China — explicitly, empirically, over decades. He understood that Chinese institutional formations (fiefs, clans) occupied specific positions in the I-Space that Western institutional analysis had systematically misread. He died in 2011, the framework still alive and still inadequate. The inadequacy is not failure; it is the specific form of his formation’s specific Dao coming closest to the Li it could not quite name. Shan names it. The collision is incandescent.

The I-Space: Three Axes, One Fundamental Error

“"The more easily data can be structured and converted into information, the more diffusible it becomes. The less data that has been so structured requires a shared context for its diffusion, the more diffusible it becomes."”

— Max Boisot, Knowledge Assets (1998)

The I-Space’s two axioms, stated with exemplary precision. The first: codification increases diffusibility. The second: decreased context-dependency increases diffusibility. Together they constitute the I-Space’s structural logic: the movement of knowledge from tacit, context-embedded, slowly-diffusing formation (Cook Ding’s nineteen years) toward abstract, context-independent, rapidly-diffusing explicit knowledge (a management textbook summarising Cook Ding in four bullet points) is the movement from maximum formation depth to maximum diffusion range. Boisot’s framework is built on this movement. And this is precisely where Shan’s challenge becomes incendiary.

The fundamental error is not empirical but ontological: Boisot’s three axes (codification, abstraction, diffusion) are axes of what happens TO knowledge AFTER it has been produced by a formation. They are not axes of the formation process itself. The I-Space maps the Li after it has been produced by the Dao; it does not map the Dao that produces the Li. This is not a minor omission. The formation that produces Cook Ding’s specific structural attunement to the specific Li of the specific ox occupies NO POSITION in the I-Space because it is not yet codifiable, not yet abstractable, not yet diffusible. It is in the process of formation. The I-Space has no coordinate for the submerged dragon; the submerged dragon is, by definition, not yet at any position that the I-Space’s axes can specify. The framework that cannot locate the most important phase of the formation process — the Dao-walk itself, before any Li is produced that could be positioned in the I-Space — is the framework that has arrived at the party after the formation.

“"Codification constitutes a selection from competing perceptual and conceptual alternatives, and this selection is often conflict-laden. Higher codification economizes on data-processing resources, but it also results in lost flexibility and options. It fossilizes hard-won skills, and thus also deskills skilled craftspeople."”

— Max Boisot, Knowledge Assets (1998), p.47

Boisot’s most honest moment — and his most devastating self-indictment. He sees it: codification deskills. The formalisation of Cook Ding’s attunement into a management framework that can be taught in two days deskills the specific formation that the nineteen years produced. But Boisot draws no structural conclusion from this acknowledgement. He notes it, moves past it, and continues building the I-Space as though the acknowledged loss were a minor implementation detail rather than a structural indictment of the entire project. Shan cannot let this pass.

The deskilling that codification produces is not an unfortunate side-effect; it is the I-Space’s constitutive condition. The I-Space requires that knowledge be codifiable to be positioned within it. But the Li that matters most — the specific structural attunement of the specific practitioner who has walked the specific Dao of their specific formation domain — is precisely the Li that loses its essential character in the process of codification. It is not merely that codification loses some richness; it is that the specific Li of formation IS the richness that codification eliminates. The I-Space is a framework that systematically removes from view the very knowledge it claims to be managing. The map has expelled the territory from the map.

“"Economizing on data-processing resources involves moving away from the uncodified end and towards the codified end of the scale, from the inarticulate towards the articulate, from the complex towards the simple. Data-processing economies are by no means an unmixed blessing. A price is paid in terms of lost flexibility, of options sacrificed."”

— Max Boisot, Knowledge Assets (1998) — from The Information Space chapter

A price is paid: Boisot’s thermodynamic formulation of what Shan calls the Cao Zhi crisis. The bean-stalks burned to cook the beans: the formation’s tacit structural depth (the options and flexibility that the uncodified position in the I-Space represents) is consumed in the process of producing the explicit, abstract, diffusible Li that can be managed as a knowledge asset. The price is structural: not merely some richness lost in translation but the specific formation capacity that enables further formation from the current Li. The organisation that has codified all its knowledge assets has maximised its diffusion range and eliminated its formation depth. It can teach everything it knows and learn nothing new from what it knows.

Shan’s most explosive challenge: the price Boisot acknowledges is not a tax on the transaction; it is the destruction of the production facility. The practitioner whose formation is codified has not merely paid a tax on their knowledge; they have converted the specific structural attunement that makes their knowledge generative into a static asset whose value declines as the formation field moves on. The I-Space models this movement as an S-curve (the Social Learning Cycle). But the S-curve is the trajectory of a specific Li’s diffusion and eventual impaction into practice — it is not the trajectory of the Dao that produces the next Li. Between each cycle of the SLC, there is a Dao-walk that the I-Space does not model. The SLC is a sequence of Li-positions in the I-Space; it is not the Dao that connects them. Boisot has modelled the visible Li but missed the invisible Dao.

The Social Learning Cycle: Six Phases, One Missing Phase

Boisot’s Social Learning Cycle (SLC) proposes six phases through which knowledge moves in the I-Space: Scanning (insights from diffused data) → Problem-Solving (codification of insights) → Abstraction (generalisation of codified insights) → Diffusion (sharing with a target population) → Absorption (application producing new tacit learning) → Impacting (embedding in concrete practices). The cycle is elegant and genuinely useful. It is also missing its most important phase.

“"The SLC consists of four phases: a scanning phase, in which insights are extracted from generally available data; a problem-solving phase; an abstraction phase; and a diffusion phase."”

— Max Boisot, paraphrased from Knowledge, Organization, and Management (2013)

The missing phase: the formation phase. Between Absorption (new tacit learning) and Scanning (insights from diffused data), the SLC assumes a seamless transition — as if the absorption of the previous cycle’s knowledge automatically produces the scanning readiness for the next cycle’s insights. But this transition is not seamless; it is the Dao-walk. The practitioner who has absorbed the previous cycle’s Li must walk a new Dao in order to develop the specific formation sensitivity that makes the next cycle’s scanning genuinely productive rather than merely the application of the previous cycle’s Li to new data. Without the formation phase, the SLC is a recycling of existing Li rather than the production of genuinely new Li. The cycle spins; the formation moves.

Cook Ding’s nineteen years in Boisot’s framework: year one corresponds to the Absorption phase of a prior cycle. Years two through eighteen are the formation phase that the SLC does not model. Year nineteen is the moment when genuine Scanning readiness is achieved — when the specific structural attunement to the specific formation domain is sufficient that new insights can be extracted from the formation field’s actual Li rather than from the practitioner’s prior Li. The SLC jumps from Absorption to Scanning in one step. Cook Ding’s formation takes seventeen years in that step. Boisot’s framework collapses the Dao into a transition between two I-Space positions. The Dao is the whole game. The transition is the point.

Fiefs, Clans, Bureaucracies, Markets: The I-Space’s Political Economy

“"China’s rapid economic development is being accomplished through a system of industrial governance and transaction that differs from Western experience. The limited extent of codification of information in China and its communal property rights and organization of economic transactions suggest that decentralization from the former state-command system is giving rise to a distinctive institutional form—network capitalism."”

— Max Boisot and John Child, Administrative Science Quarterly (1996)

Boisot and Child’s 1996 paper on China is the most empirically grounded application of the I-Space framework, and the one that most directly intersects with Shan’s formation domain. The I-Space’s four institutional types — fiefs (uncodified, undiffused), clans (uncodified, diffused), bureaucracies (codified, undiffused), markets (codified, diffused) — map onto Chinese institutional formations with genuine analytical precision. The clan-based trust networks of Chinese business (guānxi, 关系) are structurally fief-to-clan formations: operating through personal relationship and embodied trust rather than through the codified contracts of Western market capitalism. Boisot and Child’s framework makes this visible in a way that standard Western institutional economics cannot.

Shan’s challenge: the I-Space’s analysis of guanxi as a clan formation — uncodified, diffused through personal networks, structurally resistant to abstraction and codification — is accurate as a description of the Li of Chinese relational formations. But it systematically misreads the specific formation depth that produces guanxi as a structural achievement. Guanxi is not merely a lower position on the codification axis that will eventually move toward the codified upper region as China develops. It is the specific Li produced by a specific Dao of relational formation-building that has no equivalent in the codified, abstractable, diffusible Li of Western market capitalism. The I-Space reads guanxi as a developmental stage that precedes full codification. Shan reads it as a specific formation achievement that produces specific structural capacities that codification destroys rather than supersedes. The framework that reads guanxi as pre-modern is the framework that has not walked the Dao of guanxi formation. Boisot and Child spent years in China. They still read guanxi with the I-Space’s axes. The axes precede the encounter. The Li precedes the Dao. The map precedes the territory.

The Paradox of Value: Boisot’s Most Productive Provocation

“"Structuring knowledge increases its utility and value but simultaneously enhances its reproducibility, which makes it easier for competitors to imitate and thereby reduces its scarcity value."”

— Max Boisot, Knowledge Assets (1998) — the Paradox of Value

The Paradox of Value is Boisot’s deepest insight and his most direct route to Shan’s framework. The formation that codifies its knowledge increases its utility (more practitioners can use it) while reducing its value (it is now reproducible by competitors). The strategic problem of knowledge management is exactly this: how to codify enough to be useful without codifying so much that the formation’s specific competitive advantage disappears into the diffuse public domain. Boisot’s framework treats this as a management challenge to be navigated strategically. Shan’s framework reveals it as an ontological condition to be understood structurally.

The Paradox of Value is real. It is also inadequate as a description of what is actually at stake. The practitioner’s specific formation attunement — Cook Ding’s knife at the joint, the navigator’s body in the waves, the bilingual scholar’s structural sensitivity to formations that neither language can name alone — is not a competitive advantage to be protected from diffusion. It is a formation achievement that cannot be diffused because it cannot be fully codified. The paradox that Boisot describes is the paradox of explicit knowledge; it is not the paradox of the Li that genuine formation produces. The genuine Li’s irreducibility is not a strategic asset; it is the structural condition of formation itself. You cannot codify the submerged dragon. You can only walk the Dao that produces it. The Paradox of Value protects nothing that matters from diffusion, because the formation that matters cannot be diffused.

Shan’s Wake-Up Call to Boisot: What the I-Space Cannot See

The I-Space is a framework of extraordinary analytical power applied to the wrong object. It applies to Li; it does not apply to Dao. It maps knowledge positions; it does not map formation processes. It models diffusion; it does not model walking. These are not minor limitations; they are structural conditions of what the I-Space is. A map of where Li ends up is not the same as an account of how Li is produced. The I-Space is the geology of formation-knowledge products; it is not the formation process that produced them.

Boisot’s framework acknowledges its own limitation at exactly the points where Shan’s framework begins: the loss of richness in codification; the price paid in options sacrificed; the deskilling of craftspeople; the transition from Absorption to Scanning that the SLC models as a single step. At every point where Boisot says ‘a price is paid’ or ‘flexibility is lost’ or ‘context is required’, Shan’s framework provides the structural account of what is happening and why. The I-Space tells you that Cook Ding’s attunement is positioned at the low-codification, low-abstraction, low-diffusion corner of the cube. Shan tells you what it took to get there and why getting there is the whole game. Both are needed. Neither alone is adequate.

The most explosive structural challenge: Boisot’s framework cannot model the Edinburgh seminar’s silence because silence has no position in the I-Space. Silence is neither codified nor uncodified; it is the refusal of the codification-abstraction-diffusion axis as the frame for what is happening. The Chinese student’s silence is a specific formation response to a specific relational configuration whose Li cannot be captured by any position on any of the I-Space’s three axes. The I-Space is a framework of explicit signals; Shan’s framework is a framework of the formation field that produces and interprets signals. The formation field is prior to any specific signal it generates. Boisot starts from the signal. Shan starts from the field. The difference is the whole game.

Zhichang Zhu and the WSR Framework — Three Li, One Missing Dao

Zhichang Zhu’s WSR (Wuli-Shili-Renli) framework is the most ambitious Chinese-origin systems methodology in the English-language literature. It takes seriously what Western systems thinking has systematically neglected: that systems problems have a human dimension (人理, renli) that is not reducible to technical constraints (wuli) or methodological choices (shili). Zhu has spent decades insisting, against the grain of Western systems theory, that the principles governing human relations (人理) constitute a distinct and irreducible dimension of any systems intervention. He is right. And his framework is still inadequate in ways that Shan must name with surgical precision — not to diminish it but to complete it.

WSR’s Three Li: The Framework in Full

“"WSR contends that wuli (regularities in objective existence), shili (ways of seeing and doing), and renli (patterns underlying human relations) constitute a differentiated whole that conditions systems projects."”

— Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu, Knowing Wuli, Sensing Shili, Caring for Renli (2000)

WSR’s three Li are three modes of structural engagement with the same formation field. Wuli: the objective regularities — the physical, institutional, and technical constraints that constitute the formation field’s material structure. Shili: the ways of seeing and doing — the cognitive-methodological orientation of the practitioner toward the formation field. Renli: the principles governing human relations — the specific relational ethics of the specific human encounter within the formation field. The three together constitute, WSR claims, the complete account of any systems intervention’s relevant dimensions.

Shan’s first structural challenge to WSR: the three Li are not a complete account of any systems intervention because they are all Li. They are all downstream of the Dao that produced them. The wuli of a specific formation field — its objective regularities — is the specific Li that the specific formation history of that formation field has produced from the specific Dao of its specific development. The shili of the practitioner — their ways of seeing and doing — is the specific Li that their specific Dao-walk has produced. The renli of the specific human encounter — the principles underlying the specific human relations in the specific context — is the specific Li of the specific relational formation history of the specific people in the specific cultural and institutional context. WSR has three Li and no Dao. The framework that names three forms of pattern without naming the formation process that produces them is the framework that arrives at the party after the formation has already occurred.

“"WSR 2.0 redefines wuli as characteristics and regularities of objective existence, shili as means and methods for knowing and doing, and renli as principles and norms that guide collective actions toward higher purpose."”

— Zhichang Zhu, WSR 2.0 (2), Systems Research and Behavioral Science (2022)

WSR 2.0’s redefinitions are genuine advances. The shift from ‘regularities in objective phenomena’ (WSR 1.0) to ‘characteristics and regularities of objective existence’ (WSR 2.0) is the difference between a law-of-nature reading of wuli and a formation-sensitive reading: wuli is not the timeless regularities of physics but the specific regularities of this specific formation’s specific material existence. The shift from ‘ways of seeing and doing’ to ‘means and methods for knowing and doing’ is modest. The shift from ‘patterns underlying human relations’ to ‘principles and norms that guide collective actions toward higher purpose’ is significant: renli becomes explicitly teleological, oriented toward a purpose that exceeds the specific transaction.

Shan’s challenge to WSR 2.0’s higher purpose: whose higher purpose? The renli of the Edinburgh seminar guided collective actions toward the higher purpose of academic dialogue and scholarly formation. The Chinese student’s renli guided their contribution toward the higher purpose of the specific relational ethics of their specific cultural formation — the renli of showing respect through attentive presence rather than competitive performance. Both are renli. Both are orienting collective actions toward higher purposes. They are not the same renli, and WSR 2.0 provides no mechanism for resolving the collision between them. The framework identifies that renli exists; it does not identify whose renli governs when multiple renlis conflict. This is not a minor gap; it is the precise location of every formation injustice that the framework is supposed to help navigate.

The Three Verbs: WSR’s Hidden Formation Theory

“"The WSR core injunction: 知物理 (zhī wùlǐ), 想事理 (sèn shílǐ), 怀人理 (guān rénlǐ) — Knowing wuli, Sensing shili, Caring for renli."”

— Jifa Gu and Zhichang Zhu, WSR (2000) — the core injunction

The three verbs are WSR’s hidden formation theory, and they are more philosophically important than the three nouns. Zhī (knowing): the epistemological stance toward wuli is cognitive — systematic, analytical, propositional. Sèn/sí (sensing): the epistemological stance toward shili is attuned — requiring the formation that makes situational complexity sensible without explicit analysis. Guān/huái (caring/carrying): the epistemological stance toward renli is ethical — not a method applied to human relations but a formation orientation that makes human relations constitutive of the practitioner’s structural position. The three verbs perform three different formation depths. Knowing is available to any analytically competent practitioner. Sensing requires formation. Caring requires character.

Shan’s most productive challenge: the three verbs assume that the practitioner can switch between them as cognitive modes. You know wuli, you sense shili, you care for renli. But the practitioner’s capacity to sense shili is not a mode they can switch into; it is the product of a specific formation history that has produced the specific structural sensitivity to the specific formation field’s shili. The practitioner who has not walked the Dao that produces shili-sensitivity cannot simply decide to ‘sense shili’ any more than Cook Ding in year one can simply decide to ‘see the articulations rather than the whole ox.’ WSR’s methodological framework assumes that the three verbs are available as options; Shan’s formation framework reveals that they are achievements. The framework names the destination; it does not provide the map for the Dao that must be walked to arrive there.

The Edinburgh Seminar Through WSR: What the Framework Reveals and Conceals

The Edinburgh seminar’s silence is a perfect test case for WSR’s analytical power and its structural limits. Applied to the seminar, WSR’s three Li would produce the following analysis: the wuli of the seminar (its institutional structure, power hierarchy, assessment format, scheduling, physical space) creates specific constraints on participation; the shili of the seminar (its cognitive methodology — active verbal contribution as the primary form of intellectual engagement) produces specific ways of seeing and doing that advantage certain formation histories; the renli of the seminar (the principles governing the relationships between supervisor, lecturer, and students in a British academic context) determines what relational formations are recognised as legitimate contributions.

This is a genuinely useful WSR analysis. It names the three dimensions of the formation field that are producing the participation pattern Shan observed. But it does not go deep enough. The WSR analysis treats the wuli, shili, and renli of the seminar as given formation conditions that constrain behaviour. It does not ask: what is the specific Dao that produced the specific wuli, shili, and renli of the British academic seminar? And what is the specific Dao that produced the specific wuli, shili, and renli of the Chinese educational formation that the students carried into the seminar? And what happens when these two formation histories — these two accumulated Daos, each with their specific Li of wuli, shili, and renli — encounter each other in the specific formation space of the seminar? WSR names the Li of each; it does not model the Dao-encounter that makes the collision structurally productive rather than merely structurally oppressive.

Zhu’s Wake-Up Call: The Framework That Cannot Walk

Zhu’s WSR framework is a methodology for applying three Li to a specific formation field. It tells the practitioner: knowing this wuli, sensing this shili, caring for this renli. It does not tell the practitioner how to develop the formation depth that makes genuine sensing and genuine caring possible rather than merely methodological gestures toward sensing and caring. WSR is a framework for practitioners who are already formed. For the practitioner who is not yet formed — who has not yet walked the Dao that produces the specific structural sensitivity to the specific formation field’s shili; who has not yet developed the specific relational character that makes genuine renli-caring possible rather than methodologically performed — WSR provides a vocabulary without a formation path. It names where the practitioner should be without specifying the Dao that must be walked to get there.

The sharpest possible challenge: WSR’s methodological process — its stages of inquiry (understand client desires, clarify system objectives, select methods, implement, evaluate) — is a rational, systematic, analytically navigable process. The practitioner who follows WSR’s methodological process will produce a wuli-shili-renli analysis of the specific formation field. But the quality of that analysis is entirely dependent on the formation depth that the practitioner brings to each of the three verbs. The WSR method cannot produce formation depth; it can only deploy what the practitioner already has. The methodologically correct WSR analysis conducted by a practitioner with shallow formation depth will produce a shallow analysis dressed in the three-Li vocabulary. The formation is the analysis.
