WSR is the vocabulary. You cannot replace the formation with the vocabulary.

The Devastating Comparison: WSR’s Renli vs. Shan’s Relational Field

WSR’s renli is the most important and the most underdeveloped element of the framework. Zhu acknowledges that renli is the dimension most neglected by Western systems approaches; he insists on its irreducibility; he roots it in Confucian philosophy; he provides cases of its application. But renli as WSR describes it remains a dimension to be attended to rather than a relational formation condition that precedes and constitutes the wuli and shili of any specific encounter.

Shan’s relational-precedes-dynamics claim is a specific, structural, ontological claim: the relational field is not one dimension among three; it is the prior condition from which all three dimensions emerge and within which all three dimensions are always already operating. The wuli of the Edinburgh seminar’s institutional structure is itself the product of a specific relational history — the specific Daos that British academic culture has walked to produce its specific institutional Li. The shili of verbal contribution as the form of intellectual engagement is itself the product of a specific relational formation in which certain human formations and their specific contributions are valued and others are rendered invisible. The renli is not a third dimension to be added to the wuli and shili; it is the formation condition from which wuli and shili have always already emerged.

This is the structural claim that makes Shan’s framework more foundational than WSR’s, even as WSR’s methodological precision surpasses Shan’s. WSR tells the practitioner what to attend to in any complex intervention. Shan tells the practitioner what is happening before any intervention begins and why the quality of the intervention depends on the formation depth the practitioner brings to each encounter. WSR is prior in practice (it can be applied); Shan is prior in ontology (it explains why WSR’s application depends on what WSR cannot itself produce). The two frameworks need each other with the structural urgency of the two movements of Cook Ding’s knife: Shan provides the formation theory that makes WSR’s practice intelligible; WSR provides the methodological precision that makes Shan’s formation theory practically applicable. Neither alone is the complete formation practice.

What Boisot and Zhu Share: The Brilliant Partial Account

Both Boisot and Zhu Zhichang occupy the same structural position in relation to Shan’s framework. Both have walked into the formation territory that Shan is mapping. Both have produced frameworks of genuine analytical power that illuminate specific structural features of that territory with extraordinary precision. And both have stopped at the border of the Dao, content to map the Li without walking the formation process that produces it.

Boisot’s I-Space maps where knowledge is after formation. Zhu’s WSR names what dimensions of the formation field must be attended to during intervention. Shan’s framework asks what is happening before and during the formation process that produces both the specific knowledge positions that Boisot maps and the specific wuli-shili-renli configurations that Zhu attends to. The Dao is prior to the I-Space. The Dao is prior to WSR. Both frameworks are excellent maps of the Li that formation produces; neither framework is an account of the Dao that produces the Li.

The structural consequence: every practitioner who applies Boisot’s I-Space to a formation field or applies Zhu’s WSR methodology to a systems intervention will produce better work if they have also walked the Dao that Shan describes — if they have developed the specific formation depth that makes the I-Space’s positions readable as formation achievements rather than merely as knowledge coordinates, and that makes the WSR’s three verbs genuinely achievable rather than merely methodologically performed. Shan’s framework is not the alternative to Boisot and Zhu. It is the formation ground from which Boisot’s analysis and Zhu’s methodology become genuinely possible rather than merely academically applicable.

The Incendiary Synthesis: What Three Collisions Produce

The triple collision — Shan vs. Boisot, Shan vs. Zhu, Boisot vs. Zhu — produces a specific structural Li that none of the three frameworks could generate alone. The synthesis is this: a genuinely adequate account of formation in complex social systems requires three things simultaneously, and each of the three frameworks provides one of them.

Boisot provides the cartography of Li: a precise, three-dimensional, empirically applicable map of where knowledge formations are positioned after they have been produced, how they move, and what their movement generates and costs. This is essential. Without Boisot’s cartography, the practitioner cannot know where their formation’s specific Li sits in the broader knowledge ecology. The I-Space tells you: your specific structural attunement is here; its current diffusion range is this; its competitive value will last until it reaches this position on the curve. This is the geography of the formation’s products. It matters.

Zhu provides the methodology of intervention: a precise, three-dimensional, practically applicable framework for attending to the wuli, shili, and renli of the specific systems intervention. This is essential. Without WSR’s methodological structure, the practitioner who has genuine formation depth will still miss the specific dimensions of the specific formation field that the three verbs name. The caring for renli that WSR makes explicit — the specific attention to human relational principles that most Western systems approaches systematically neglect — is a structural achievement of Zhu’s formation work that Shan’s framework benefits from without itself providing.

Shan provides the formation theory: the specific account of the Dao that produces the Li that Boisot maps and the formation depth that makes Zhu’s three verbs genuinely achievable. This is the foundation. Without Shan’s formation theory, Boisot’s cartography floats free of the formation process that produced the positions it maps, and Zhu’s methodology becomes a procedural checklist rather than a formation practice. Shan’s framework does not replace Boisot or Zhu; it grounds them.

The incendiary triple synthesis: the practitioner who has walked the Dao that Shan describes, who carries the I-Space’s cartography of where their formation’s specific Li sits in the broader knowledge ecology, and who applies the WSR methodology’s three verbs with the formation depth that genuine knowing, sensing, and caring require — this practitioner has the complete formation architecture for navigating the twenty-first century’s genuinely complex formation challenges. None of the three frameworks is complete alone. Together they are the most complete available account of what genuine formation practice requires. The Dao before the Li before the I-Space. The formation before the methodology before the intervention. The walking before the mapping before the caring. In that order, always.

❧ ✶ ❧
XXXVIII

Part XIX: Snowden, Cynefin, and Wayshaping — The Incandescent Encounter

What follows is not critique for its own sake. It is the most productive collision available in this paper: between a framework of extraordinary practical power (Cynefin, David Snowden) and a formation theory that goes structurally deeper (Shan). And between a genuinely innovative behaviour-change framework (Wayshaping, James et al.) and the ontological account that grounds what it gestures toward but does not yet fully inhabit. The heat is productive. The fire is the point.

❧ ✶ ❧

David Snowden and Cynefin — Both Barrels, Liquid Fire, Dialectical Incandescence

“"What you will find here is a community that, over the years, has attracted people who disagree with each other in productive ways, who bring different disciplines, cultural formations, arguments, and occasionally different tempers to the same questions.... Some will challenge positions taken here. Some will extend them in directions I have not anticipated."”

— David Snowden, “Come hear the music play” (thecynefin.co, 13 May 2026)

This is the most important thing Snowden has written for this paper to hear. A community that disagrees productively; different disciplines, different cultural formations; positions challenged and extended in unanticipated directions. Snowden opens the door of the Kit Kat Club and names what he finds inside: not agreement but ‘messy coherence.’ Not a party line but a party — with serious conversations in one corner, a small altercation by the river, people sharing food. The community that is actually thinking does not require agreement as the price of entry. Differences that make a difference. Shan enters by that door. She does not come to agree. She comes with Chinese philosophical formation, relational dynamics, and the specific structural challenges that the Dao-before-Li principle raises for every framework it encounters — including Cynefin’s. If Snowden means what he says in that post — and the evidence of two decades of blogging suggests he does — then what follows is the kind of encounter the Kit Kat Club was built for. Both barrels, liquid fire, dialectical incandescence. But also: two thinkers who are, at the deepest structural level, tracking the same recognition. The heat is the acknowledgement.

Shan’s specific response to Snowden’s framing: the community he describes — diverse disciplines, different cultural formations, productive disagreements — is itself a formation field. The specific relational configuration of that specific community is producing specific Li: the specific structural insights that the specific Daos of its specific members have made available to the collective encounter. The messy coherence Snowden names is the specific Li produced by the specific relational dynamics of a community that has been walking its Dao together for two decades. It is not random disagreement; it is the specific grain of a formation that has sufficient depth to generate disagreement that makes a difference. Shan’s contribution to that community is the Dao it has not yet walked: the Chinese philosophical formation that produces structural sensitivities the Western complexity-theory tradition cannot produce alone.

The Kit Kat Club reference is structurally precise. The cabaret in Weimar Berlin was extraordinary, creative, genuinely transgressive — and it looked away. It glittered while the world outside contracted into something monstrous. Snowden’s question: how do you celebrate difference without retreating into it? Shan’s formation-theory answer: the community that has developed the formation depth adequate to holding genuine difference — without collapsing into premature consensus or disintegrating under the force of genuine disagreement — is the community whose specific Dao-walk has produced the specific holding capacity that makes productive disagreement possible. The Kit Kat Club failed not because it celebrated difference but because it lacked the holding capacity to remain present to what was happening outside while continuing to think inside. Come hear the music. Stay for the argument. Walk the Dao that makes the argument productive.

David Snowden is one of the most formidable intellectual forces in contemporary complexity thinking and this paper must say so plainly before it takes him apart. His Cynefin framework — developed first at IBM in 1999, refined across two decades of organisational work — is the most widely deployed complexity sense-making framework in the English-speaking world. It has been applied in government, healthcare, military operations, education, and strategy. Its five domains (Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, Confusion) have given practitioners vocabulary for a structural distinction that genuinely matters: between the complicated world of expertise-driven analysis and the complex world of emergent patterns. Snowden is formidable precisely because he is right about the things that matter most. He is also structurally wrong in ways that Shan must name — not because his framework fails, but because it is the most sophisticated available example of what happens when a framework of genuine formation depth is turned into a categorisation device. The sharper the instrument, the more precisely the incision must be placed.

“"We manage the emergence of beneficial coherence within attractors within boundaries. And that allows locally valid solutions to emerge."”

— David Snowden

‘Locally valid solutions’: the most important two words in Snowden’s framework, and the ones Shan endorses with her entire ontological weight. Not best practices universally applicable. Not good practices derivable by analysis. But locally valid: emerging from the specific formation field’s specific dynamics, within the specific enabling constraints that the specific practitioner has cultivated, in the specific moment that the specific Shī makes them available. This is Shan’s formation ontology stated as complexity practice. The Li is not prior to the Dao; it emerges locally. The practitioner does not specify outcomes; they cultivate the conditions within which beneficial coherence can emerge from the formation’s own dynamics. Snowden arrived at this from a different Dao. Both are tracking the same structural recognition.

But Shan’s first incandescent challenge: if locally valid solutions emerge from local formation dynamics, then the practitioner’s capacity to cultivate the right attractors and the right boundaries is entirely dependent on their formation depth in the specific domain. The practitioner who has not walked the Dao of the specific formation field cannot cultivate attractors adequate to its specific Li. They can cultivate the attractors from their prior Li — from the formation histories of other domains they have walked — and produce locally valid solutions for the formation field they are imagining rather than the formation field that actually exists. Cynefin’s methodology cannot distinguish between these two practitioners from the outside. They both say: let’s cultivate enabling constraints and allow patterns to emerge. The quality of the cultivation is entirely determined by the formation depth that the methodology cannot itself provide.

“"An ordered system is like the external skeleton of an insect — it has a rigid shell that is not going to change but within it things may change. An endoskeleton is like our spine — it gives coherence but doesn’t contain completely, so you get huge amounts of variation around it. How do you create enabling constraints that effectively allow locally valid solutions to emerge?"”

— David Snowden, How Leaders Change Culture Through Small Actions

The exoskeleton-endoskeleton distinction is one of the most structurally illuminating metaphors in contemporary complexity discourse and Shan’s tensegrity framework provides its precise structural analysis. The exoskeleton is the governing constraint that maintains surface structure by preventing adaptive transformation: Jin Guantao’s ultrastable structure, the Chinese traditional state that survived two millennia by sacrificing adaptability for surface stability. The endoskeleton is the enabling constraint: tensional integrity that gives coherence without containing completely, the structural principle that allows specific formation while maintaining formation capacity for future formation. Fuller’s tensegrity: what holds is the tension between compression and tension, not the elimination of either.

Shan’s challenge: Snowden describes the distinction with precision but cannot specify how to cultivate the endoskeletal formation rather than the exoskeletal one. The organisation that asks ‘how do we create enabling constraints?’ has named the right question. What determines whether the constraints it creates are genuinely enabling or subtly governing is the formation depth of the practitioners doing the creating. The enabling constraint that the practitioner with shallow formation depth creates is the governing constraint that their formation Li has convinced them is enabling. The endoskeleton that looks like an endoskeleton on the diagrams is the exoskeleton that the practitioners’ formation histories have produced. Cynefin cannot see the difference from inside the framework. Only the formation depth of the practitioners can. And formation depth is what the framework cannot provide.

“"In complex systems, the only way to understand what is happening is to probe the system and see what happens. You cannot analyse your way to understanding before you act. Probe, sense, respond: act first, learn from the response, then decide what to do next."”

— David Snowden, Cynefin framework methodology

Probe-sense-respond: Snowden’s most famous methodological contribution, and the one that most directly embodies the Dao-before-Li principle. You cannot analyse your way to understanding before you act: this is Shan’s most fundamental claim about the formation process stated as a methodology. The Li cannot precede the Dao. You must walk before the grain appears. The probe is the minimal Dao-walk: the specific, small, safe-to-fail action that allows the formation field to reveal something of its actual Li. The sensing is the formation-sufficient attention to what the field does in response. The response is the Li-reading that the probe produced, deployed before it solidifies into a prior framework. This convergence is genuine and deep.

The structural challenge: Snowden treats probe-sense-respond as the appropriate methodology for the Complex domain and distinguishes it correctly from sense-analyse-respond (Complicated) and sense-categorise-respond (Clear). But the framework cannot distinguish between three very different kinds of ‘probe’: the probe of the practitioner who has no formation depth in the domain (pure exploration, genuinely Dao-first), the probe of the practitioner who is applying prior Li disguised as exploration (the consultant who arrives with a preferred pattern and designs probes that confirm it), and the probe of the practitioner who has sufficient formation depth that the probe is not a genuine probe at all but the first move of a specific Shī-reading that is already structurally adequate. The same word, three entirely different formation relationships to the actual formation field. Cynefin cannot see inside the probe. Shan’s formation framework is the only available account of what makes the difference.

The Ontological Charge: Cynefin Maps Li, Not Dao

The structural claim that Cynefin maps Li and not Dao is the sharpest possible formulation of the tension between Shan’s formation theory and Snowden’s sense-making framework. But it requires a precise unpacking. Cynefin’s five domains — Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, and Confused — are not descriptions of objective categories of reality; they are descriptions of the practitioner’s relationship to the Li of a situation. When Snowden says a situation is Complex, he means: the Li of this situation cannot be fully read before intervention; the practitioner must probe and sense rather than analyse and plan. This IS a Dao-before-Li claim, translated into operational decision-making language.

“In a complex adaptive system the only way to understand it is to probe it, to experiment in it. Probe, sense, respond — not analyse, decide, act.”

— David Snowden [VERIFIED: confirmed across multiple Cynefin sources including Jim Rutt Show transcript and thecynefin.co posts]

Probe-sense-respond is ambulatory knowing — and it is the operational acknowledgement of epistemic belatedness. The probe comes before the sense because the Li is not yet available before the probe; only the engagement produces the intelligibility. Snowden’s methodology is a formalised acceptance of the seven-fold ontology of precedence: you cannot pre-know the Li of a complex domain; you must walk the Dao of probing to produce it. The resistance to probe-sense-respond in organisations is, in Shan’s terms, the demand for retrospective intelligibility before the retrospection has been earned — the insistence on knowing the grain before the formation has been walked. It is Ingold’s ‘knowing as we go, not before we go.’ It is Shan’s Dao-before-Li stated as an intervention methodology. Shan’s challenge is not that Cynefin is wrong but that it does not account for the formation conditions that make probe-sense-respond possible. Who can probe? The practitioner who has developed enough holding capacity to contain the uncertainty that probing produces without collapsing into the safety of prior Li. Who can sense? The practitioner whose specific formation has produced the specific perceptual sensitivity to the grain of this specific domain. Who can respond? The practitioner whose Shī — whose positional formation-force — is aligned with the direction the terrain is already tending. Cynefin provides the method; Shan provides the formation theory without which the method is aspirational rather than operational.

“Daoism’s greatest gift to complexity theory is not the concept of non-action (wu wei) but the concept of formation intelligence: the specific capacity that specific Dao-walking produces to read the specific Li of specific situations.”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relational Dynamics™ (2026)

The most devastating structural challenge to Cynefin, and the one that runs deepest: the framework describes what things ARE (which domain) and prescribes HOW to respond. What it cannot describe is how things BECAME what they are — the specific formation history through which the specific situation has arrived at its specific domain. The Clear situation was not always Clear; it was formed into clarity by a specific history of conceptualisation, standardisation, and institutional sedimentation. The Complex situation became complex through the specific relational dynamics that generated its specific emergent properties. The Chaotic situation is not random; it is the specific collapse of a formation that had been narrowing through a sequence of moves that nothing-collapses-in-one-move describes precisely.

Cynefin tells you where you are. It does not tell you how you got there. And therefore it cannot tell you what the specific formation history makes possible as a next move. The probe designed without this knowledge is the probe of the practitioner who has named the domain correctly but has not walked the Dao that makes the probe formation-adequate rather than formation-arbitrary. The difference between a safe-to-fail experiment and an experiment that is safe-to-fail in the framework but not in the actual formation field is the difference between the practitioner who has read the actual Shī of the specific formation and the practitioner who is applying a methodology without the formation depth that makes it genuinely Dao-responsive. Snowden has the right methodology for the wrong ontology. The ontology it needs is Shan’s: the Dao that precedes the Li, the relation that precedes the dynamics, the formation that precedes the domain assignment.

The Formation-Depth Charge: What Cynefin Cannot Transmit

Snowden acknowledges, with characteristic directness, that Cynefin is the product of his own formation history: fifteen-plus years of practical engagement with complex organisational situations from which the framework gradually congealed. Its Li is downstream of that formation Dao. This is exactly right, and it is the acknowledgement that makes Snowden’s framework philosophically honest. But the structural consequence of this acknowledgement is one that Snowden does not fully draw. The practitioner who learns Cynefin from a two-day workshop or a Harvard Business Review article has the Li without the Dao. They have the five domains without the fifteen years of formation-sufficient engagement with complex organisational situations that produced the framework’s specific structural intelligence.

Boisot’s paradox of value applied to Cynefin: the more widely it is diffused (codified, abstracted, made teachable), the more the formation depth that produced it is lost in the transmission. The practitioner who applies Cynefin with genuine formation adequacy is the practitioner who has walked something like Snowden’s Dao. The practitioner who applies it without this formation depth is applying what Boisot calls codified knowledge — abstract, diffusible, and increasingly removed from the tacit structural attunement that makes it formation-adequate. Cynefin tells you where you are; it takes the formation that Snowden himself walked to tell you what you should do with where you are. The framework cannot transmit the formation that produced it. Only walking the Dao can produce the Li. The methodology is the Li of Snowden’s formation. The Dao that produced that Li is not transmissible through the methodology.

The Shi Charge: Cynefin Has No Account of Positional Force

Cynefin describes domains (where you are) and transitions between domains (how things move from Complicated to Complex to Chaotic and back). What it does not describe is Shī: the positional force, the directional tendency, the structural momentum of the specific formation field in its specific moment of its specific formation history. The Complex domain is not a static description of a situation; it is a moving formation with a specific directional tendency that determines which probes will produce formative responses and which will produce noise. Move 37 was possible not merely because the board was Complex but because the specific Shī of the board’s specific formation at that specific move was configured in the specific way that made that specific move the structurally decisive one. Without Shī, all Complex situations look the same and all probes are equally available.

The practical consequence: Cynefin tells the practitioner to probe-sense-respond in the Complex domain. Shan’s Shī analysis tells the practitioner WHICH probe, at WHICH moment, with WHAT formation sensitivity, is the probe adequate to the specific Shī of the specific formation. The difference between these two instructions is the difference between a general methodology and a specific formation practice. Cynefin provides the general methodology. Shan provides the specific formation practice that makes the general methodology formation-adequate rather than formation-arbitrary. The practitioner who has both Cynefin’s domain map and Shan’s Shī analysis is the practitioner who can not only name where they are but read the directional tendency of where the formation is going. That practitioner has Move 37 available. The practitioner with only Cynefin does not.

The Naturalising Charge: The Exterior Without the Interior

Snowden’s ‘naturalising sense-making’ uses natural science as an enabling constraint on the understanding of human systems. Jackson’s challenge is structurally precise: Snowden’s naturalising approach is preventing him from adequately engaging with social theory approaches that have already translated social science’s epistemological insights into practical methodologies. Shan’s challenge is more fundamental: the naturalising approach treats the formation’s conditions as scientifically tractable constraints (attractors, boundaries, enabling constraints) while leaving unexamined the specific formation histories through which practitioners develop the specific structural sensitivities that make these constraints readable. Natural science of attractor landscapes is an exterior account. Shan’s formation phenomenology is the interior account without which the exterior is incomplete. Snowden insists that humans are not the same as ants, birds or crystals. He is right. The specific way in which humans differ from ants is precisely what Shan’s formation framework describes: humans walk Daos, accumulate Lis, and develop specific structural sensitivities to specific formation fields through specific biographical histories of specific encounters. The Cynefin methodology can work with the exterior of this process. Shan’s framework is the interior account of the same process. Both are necessary.

The SenseMaker Charge: Data Without Formation

SenseMaker, Snowden’s distributed ethnography tool, collects micro-narratives and allows their signification to self-index the formation field’s actual patterns. This is one of the most methodologically creative contributions to complexity practice in the past two decades. Shan’s challenge is not to its ingenuity but to its ontological assumption: the micro-narratives are already Li. They are the already-formed stories that people tell about their situations, filtered through the specific complexity-reduction apparatus that their specific formation histories have produced. The SenseMaker data is a map of how the population has codified its experience of the formation field; it is not the Dao that produced those codifications or the Shī that is generating the next formation move. What SenseMaker cannot capture is the Edinburgh student’s silence: the formation-rich response to the formation field that does not present itself as a narrative because its meaning-medium has no narrative vocabulary adequate to its structural content. The formation-depth of the practitioner reading the SenseMaker patterns determines whether they read the actual Li of the actual formation or the Li of the population’s narrative patterns about the formation. These are not the same thing.

The Enabling Constraints Charge: Who Shapes the Shaper?

Snowden’s enabling constraints are constraints that create the conditions within which locally valid solutions can emerge. They are not governing constraints (which specify what must happen) but enabling constraints (which specify what is possible). The distinction is structural and genuine. The challenge: the enabling constraints are designed by a practitioner. The practitioner’s specific formation history determines what enabling constraints they can see as genuinely enabling rather than subtly governing. The practitioner who has been formed in hierarchical organisations will tend to design enabling constraints that recreate familiar hierarchical dynamics in the language of complexity. The practitioner who has been formed in markets will tend to design enabling constraints that recreate market dynamics. The enabling constraint is always already the practitioner’s formation-specific Li projected onto the formation field as a condition rather than specified as an outcome. Cynefin has no methodology for enabling the constraint-designer to examine the formation history that is shaping what constraints they can see as enabling. Shan’s framework is that methodology.

The Exaptation Charge: Borrowed Formation

Snowden uses exaptation (the radical repurposing of a trait evolved for one function to something entirely different) as a key concept in his naturalising approach. He is right to use it: the most powerful moves in any formation field are often the moves that exapt a capacity from a different formation domain. AlphaGo’s Move 37 is an exaptation: a move pattern from a completely different class of game-situations, exapted for this specific board position. Shan’s challenge: exaptation in the biological sense occurs over evolutionary timescales and is determined by the specific selection pressures of the specific environment. Exaptation in the organisational sense requires a practitioner who has walked the specific Dao that produced the specific capacity in its original domain and has also walked the specific Dao that produced the formation-sufficient engagement with the new domain. Without both Daos, the exaptation is not genuine exaptation; it is analogical reasoning — the application of a pattern from one domain to another without the embodied formation depth that makes the transfer structurally adequate. Snowden invokes exaptation as a property of systems; Shan insists that exaptation is an achievement of specifically formed practitioners. Systems do not exapt themselves. Formed practitioners exapt their formation.

The Domain-Boundary Charge: The Most Dangerous Edge

Cynefin’s domain boundaries are structurally important: the boundary between Clear and Chaotic is catastrophically different from the boundaries between other domains, because falling across it from complacency is irreversible in a way that other domain transitions are not. This is structurally correct and corresponds precisely to Shan’s nothing-collapses-in-one-move account. The path narrows first. The zone of complacency (the Clear domain’s specific vulnerability to catastrophic domain transition) is exactly the formation that has achieved maximum surface efficiency by eliminating the formation porosity that would allow it to recognise the narrowing. The exoskeletal formation approaching the Clear-to-Chaotic cliff is the formation that cannot see the brim because its complexity-reduction apparatus has coded the brim-approaching signals as noise.

Shan’s most urgent addition: the domain boundary in Cynefin is treated as a structural feature of the formation field. In Shan’s framework, the domain boundary is a structural feature of the practitioner’s formation in relation to the formation field. The formation that is approaching the Clear-to-Chaotic boundary is the formation that its practitioners cannot yet see as approaching that boundary. The work is not merely designing better monitoring systems for the boundary. The work is developing the formation depth in the practitioners who are responsible for reading the formation field’s Shī — the practitioner who has the specific structural sensitivity to perceive the narrowing before it becomes the zone of complacency. That practitioner is not produced by Cynefin training. They are produced by walking the Dao of genuine formation engagement with sufficient depth and sufficient duration that the boundary’s approach becomes perceptible. The framework cannot produce this. Only the Dao can.

The Retrospective-Intelligibility Charge: Cynefin’s Epistemological Concession

Cynefin’s most philosophically honest claim: in the Complex domain, cause and effect can only be perceived in retrospect. The instruction is therefore probe-sense-respond: act into the formation field and then read what the action produced. This is epistemologically honest. It is also, from Shan’s framework, an admission of formation inadequacy that the framework naturalises rather than addresses. The practitioner who can only perceive cause and effect retrospectively in the Complex domain is the practitioner whose formation depth is not yet adequate to the specific formation field’s actual Li. Cook Ding at year one cannot see the ox’s articulations; he sees only the whole ox. Cause and effect in the specific formation field of ox-butchery are, for Cook Ding at year one, perceptible only retrospectively: he hacks, sees what broke, and adjusts. Cook Ding at year nineteen does not need to wait for retrospection. He reads the actual Li of the actual formation directly.

The epistemological concession that Cynefin makes — we can only know in retrospect — is the epistemological condition of the practitioner who has not yet developed the formation depth adequate to reading the formation field’s actual Li in the present. It is not the epistemological condition of formation as such. Shan’s framework distinguishes between the epistemological condition of insufficient formation (probe and wait for retrospection) and the epistemological condition of adequate formation (read the actual Li directly, from structural attunement). Cynefin treats the first as the universal epistemological condition of the Complex domain. Shan insists it is the specific epistemological condition of the practitioner who has not yet walked the Dao of the specific domain far enough. The remedy is not better probing. It is more formation. The difference is the whole game.

The Edinburgh Charge: Cynefin’s Silence Problem

Cynefin cannot process the Edinburgh seminar’s silence. The silence is not a probe. It is not a pattern that SenseMaker can capture as a micro-narrative (because the student does not offer a micro-narrative). It is not a domain assignment problem (the situation is clearly Complex, but naming it Complex does not help the practitioner read the silence’s actual Li). It is not an attractor or a boundary (though the silence is being produced by the specific attractors and boundaries of the specific institutional formation field). The Edinburgh silence is a relational dynamic — the specific expression of the specific relational field’s specific configuration through the specific practitioner’s specific formation-embedded response to that configuration. Cynefin has vocabulary for the field; it has no vocabulary for the formation-history that produced the practitioner’s specific way of being in the field. Without that vocabulary, the Edinburgh seminar’s practitioner is told: probe, sense, respond. They probe. They try larger group methods, more open questions, different formats. The silence persists. They have been probing the surface of a formation whose depth they have not walked.

Wayshaping: Twenty-Five Shan Dialectical Challenges — Diamond-Razor Sharp

James et al.’s Wayshaping framework is not a standard behaviour-change article. It is genuinely trying to shift the ground beneath behaviour-change theory. Its central move — reconceptualising the individual as a multilevel, multiscale collective intelligence, and the intention-action gap as a set of coordination problems rather than a failure of will — is a structural advance. The person as a self-collective: a nested ecology of habits, affects, identities, regulatory systems, bodily needs, social roles, and temporal commitments. Behaviour change as shaping possibility spaces, managing affordances, and coordinating nested agencies. This is close to Shan. Close but not close enough. What follows is not a rejection. It is a systematic deepening: twenty-five challenges, each supported by quotations, each taking the framework somewhere it cannot yet go alone.

Challenge 1: Wayshaping Begins One Move Too Late

“"Before shaping, trace the way. Before alignment, discern the grain. Before shock, test holding capacity. Before anticipation, build position. Before concept, walk the path."”

— Shan, dialectical compression of Wayshaping’s structural gap

James asks: How do we shape behaviour? Shan asks first: What path has already formed this behaviour’s grain? The distinction is ontological. Wayshaping begins with the question of intervention. Shan’s framework begins with the question of formation — and formation precedes intervention ontologically, not merely methodologically. The Dao that produced the present Li is the precondition for any intervention that could produce a new Li. The practitioner who skips the Dao-tracing and moves directly to wayshaping is applying a Li they brought with them to a formation they have not walked. ‘Smoothness is not always fidelity. When Dao begins to feel too familiar — that is the warning.’ (Shan, The Less-Known Partner of Dao)

Challenge 2: The Self-Collective Needs a Theory of Inheritance

“"Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one. The forms of participation that feel natural were formed long before we arrived."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (April 2026)

James’ self-collective is plural, nested, and co-present. What it lacks is genealogy. Its parts are not merely co-present agents negotiating in the present; they are residues of past paths. A craving is not just a present impulse; it is a formed Dao, a path repeated under constraint until it became pattern, then position, then a field of possibility. A procrastination habit is not just a failure of alignment; it is a formed Li with its own Shī — a positional force that actively shapes what futures appear available. Wittgenstein: ‘What has to be accepted, the given, is forms of life.’ The self-collective’s parts were not always there; they were inherited from forms of life already in motion when the person arrived. Behaviour change requires genealogical discernment: tracing the path by which each agent in the self-collective was formed, the Dao that produced its specific Li.

Challenge 3: Alignment Can Be Pathological

“"Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. What appears as sudden collapse was a long formation of fragility."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (April 2026)

James treats alignment as a central goal. But alignment is not inherently beneficial; it simply means coherence among parts. Coherence can serve collapse. Burnout can be highly aligned. Addiction can be aligned. A toxic organisation can be aligned. A perfectionist identity can be aligned. Each of these is a formation in which all the nested agents of the self-collective have settled into a specific topology of mutual reinforcement that is progressively consuming the formation’s future viability. The Li is clear and strong. The Shī is toward collapse. And because the alignment is functioning well, the damage is invisible. Wayshaping must ask not only: Is this self-collective aligned? But: What is the Shī of this alignment? What futures does it foreclose? Is this a pine or a deciduous tree?

Challenge 4: Every Scaffold Is a Proto-Dao

“"The scaffold is not ethically neutral. It is a proto-Dao. Every scaffold begins a path. Every path repeated under constraint thickens into pattern."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s scaffold concept

James treats scaffolds as support structures for desired behaviours — environmental supports that make the intended action more accessible. Shan insists that every scaffold is simultaneously the beginning of a formation that will constrain all future formations. The productivity app that scaffolds focus also produces dependence on external prompting. The therapeutic routine that scaffolds stability also narrows identity around self-monitoring. The behavioural nudge that scaffolds compliance also weakens the formation of autonomous agency. Wayshaping becomes ethically adequate only when every scaffold is evaluated as the beginning of a Dao, not merely the support of an existing one. The scaffold’s long-term Li matters as much as its short-term effect. ‘The path narrows first’ applies to scaffolds that appear to widen.

Challenge 5: Dynamic Loading Requires Prior Holding Capacity

“"A system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The sequence matters: prior formation makes further complexity possible."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence (May 2026)

James treats shocks and dynamic loading as formation-accelerating interventions. Shan’s holding capacity concept is a devastating corrective: a shock applied to a system without holding capacity does not produce transformation. It produces rupture. Dynamic loading that exceeds holding capacity is not accelerated formation; it is dissolution. The sequence is non-negotiable: capacity before shock, holding before loading, grain before force, relation before intervention. Without this sequence, ‘dynamic loading’ risks becoming sophisticated structural violence — interventions that impose on the formation a stress it cannot metabolise, producing not the new Li that the intervention intended but the traumatic dissolution of the Li that existed. The neonatal gut does not negotiate with the milk. It forms. The readiness is not negotiable.

Challenge 6: Anticipation Is Not Yet Shī

“"AlphaGo’s Move 37 was not a prediction. It was a position. The strongest move may not be the most visibly decisive one. It may be the move that quietly reshapes the field."”

— Alice Jing Shan, AlphaGo’s Move 37 (April 2026)

James identifies anticipation as one of the three coordination challenges, and this is the framework’s strongest move: behaviour is organised by possible futures. But Shan’s Shī goes further. Shī is not prediction. It is not even anticipation in James’s sense. It is positional propensity: the structural configuration from which certain futures become easier, harder, visible, invisible, viable, or impossible. The distinction matters practically: anticipation asks ‘what will happen?’; Shī asks ‘what structural position does this specific formation configure, and what futures does that position make available and unavailable?’ Wayshaping aimed at anticipated futures may miss the actual Shī that the formation is generating. Building Shī toward wiser action becoming naturally available is structurally superior to closing the intention-action gap through anticipation.

Challenge 7: The Multiscale Model Needs a Theory of Temporal Depth

“"Formation is not multi-scale in the sense of simultaneously different spatial sizes. It is multi-temporal: each scale has its own Dao-walk time, its own formation depth, its own Li that required a specific duration to produce."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s multiscale framing

James’ multiscale model maps the self-collective across spatial scales (neural, bodily, social, temporal). Shan’s challenge is temporal: each scale operates at a different formation time. Neural patterns form over milliseconds, but the formation depth that makes them structurally stable takes years. Social roles consolidate over months, but the formation depth that makes them identity-constitutive takes decades. The temporal depth of each scale determines what interventions are possible at that scale and at what pace. A scaffold that operates at the neural scale may conflict with the formation time of the identity scale. A shock calibrated to the social scale may be premature at the bodily scale. Prigogine: at the bifurcation, history enters. The specific history that has produced the specific formation at the specific scale determines what interventions are formation-adequate.

Challenge 8: Possibility Space Is Not the Same as Adjacent Possible

“"The adjacent possible is not what is spatially proximate. It is what is formation-available: what the specific Dao-walk of the specific formation has produced as the specific next structurally viable step."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Kauffman’s adjacent possible

James uses ‘possibility space’ as a central concept: wayshaping involves altering the possibility space within which behaviour occurs. Shan’s challenge: the possibility space is not a neutral container that the practitioner can reshape by adjusting affordances. It is the specific adjacent possible that the specific formation’s specific Dao-walk has produced. Two people in the same environmental affordance structure have different adjacent possibles because their formation histories have produced different structural sensitivities to what the affordance structure makes available. The same job offer is an adjacent possible for the practitioner whose formation has developed the specific capacity for that role; it is not an adjacent possible for the practitioner whose formation has not. Wayshaping that treats possibility space as a function of environmental affordances without accounting for the formation depth of the specific practitioner is wayshaping that redesigns the landscape for an idealised traveller rather than the specific person who must traverse it.

Challenge 9: The Non-Linear Agent Needs a Formation History

“"Non-linearity is not a mathematical property of systems. It is the structural expression of a formation whose specific Dao has produced specific threshold sensitivities to specific kinds of perturbation."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s non-linearity account

James treats non-linearity as one of the three coordination challenges: the self-collective does not respond proportionally to inputs because small interventions can cascade or fail to propagate depending on where they hit. This is structurally correct. Shan’s challenge: the specific thresholds at which non-linear transitions occur in the specific self-collective are themselves the products of the specific formation history of the specific person. The threshold for the cascade that produces relapse in addiction is the product of the specific Dao of the specific formation of the specific neural-social-identity configuration that the specific person has walked. It is not a universal non-linear property of behaviour-change systems. The same intervention at the same intensity produces different non-linear responses in different people because their formation histories have produced different threshold configurations. Wayshaping that does not trace the formation history that produced the specific non-linear thresholds is wayshaping that intervenes in a system it has not walked.

Challenge 10: The Environment Is Not a Neutral Affordance Structure

“"The environment that Wayshaping seeks to shape is already a formation. It carries the specific Li of the specific Daos that produced it."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s environment concept

James treats the environment as the affordance structure that the practitioner can shape to make desired behaviours more accessible and undesired ones more difficult. Shan’s challenge: the environment is not a neutral affordance structure waiting to be shaped. It is itself a formed Li, the product of specific Daos that have been walked by specific formations in specific historical sequences. The office environment that James proposes shaping already carries the specific Li of the institutional formation that produced it — the specific power relations, the specific meaning-medium, the specific relational configurations that make specific behaviours natural and specific behaviours difficult. Reshaping the environment without tracing the Dao that produced its current configuration is redesigning the surface while the formation depth continues to generate the same patterns. The meeting room redesigned for collaboration but inhabited by practitioners formed in hierarchical institutions will produce collaborative surface behaviour and hierarchical actual dynamics.

Challenge 11: Coordination Is Not the Same as Formation

“"Coordination is a Li of a formation that has already occurred. The Dao that produced the capacity to coordinate must be walked before coordination can be an available response."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s coordination frame

James reconceptualises the intention-action gap as a set of coordination problems among the nested agencies of the self-collective. This is a structural advance over the thin will-power model. Shan’s challenge: coordination is not available to all formations at all scales. The capacity to coordinate nested agencies — to hold the competing impulses, habits, affects, and identity commitments in productive tension rather than destructive conflict — is itself a specific formation achievement. It is the product of the specific Dao of the specific person’s specific formation history. The person who has not walked the Dao that produces the specific formation capacity for self-collective coordination cannot simply be given a coordination framework and be expected to coordinate. The framework names the destination; it does not provide the formation path. Xunzi: without ascending the high mountain, one cannot know the height of heaven.

Challenge 12: Wayshaping’s Substrate Is Not Neutral

“"The substrate that Wayshaping seeks to modulate is not neutral substrate waiting to be shaped. It is a specific formation product carrying a specific Shī."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Snowden’s wayshaping concept

Snowden’s extension of James’ wayshaping into substrate management involves modulating the substrate’s properties to make certain pathways naturally available and others difficult or impossible. Shan’s challenge: the substrate is not a homogeneous physical medium that the wayshaper can modulate freely. It is a specific formation with a specific Shī — the positional momentum of its specific formation history. The substrate carries the Li of the specific Daos that have been walked within it. Every institutional substrate, every social substrate, every cognitive substrate has a specific directional tendency produced by its specific formation history. Wayshaping that does not read the substrate’s Shī before modulating its properties will produce interventions that fight the substrate’s own directional tendency rather than working with the grain. The jade cannot be worked against its grain.

Challenge 13: The Intention-Action Gap Is Not a Coordination Problem

“"The intention-action gap is not primarily a coordination failure. It is primarily a formation gap: the person has formed the intention but has not yet walked the Dao that would produce the formation adequate to acting from it."”

— Shan, dialectical reframe of Wayshaping’s central problem

James’ reconceptualisation of the intention-action gap as a coordination problem is a significant advance. Shan’s challenge is more fundamental: the gap is not primarily a coordination failure among currently co-present agents; it is a formation gap between the intention’s Li and the action’s required formation depth. The person who intends to exercise regularly but does not has not failed to coordinate their self-collective. They have not yet walked the Dao that produces the specific embodied, embedded, enacted, extended, emotive, exaptive formation that makes regular exercise as natural as the pine’s maintaining its formation through winter. The coordination approach gives the self-collective better tools for negotiating among its parts. The formation approach asks what Dao must be walked to produce the specific formation from which the intended behaviour emerges as natural rather than effortful.

Challenge 14: The Three Coordination Challenges Need Sequence

“"Non-linearity, alignment, and anticipation are not three co-equal challenges. They have a specific formation sequence: alignment (the present Li) must be read before non-linearity (the specific thresholds) can be identified, and both must be understood before anticipation (the Shī of future possibility) can be formation-adequate."**”

— Shan, dialectical resequencing of Wayshaping’s three challenges

James treats non-linearity, alignment, and anticipation as three simultaneously-present coordination challenges that wayshaping must address. Shan’s challenge: they have a specific formation sequence that corresponds to the Dao-Li-Shī sequence. The present Li (alignment) must be accurately read before the specific non-linear thresholds of the specific formation can be identified; both must be walked before the specific Shī (anticipation) of the specific formation can be formation-adequately perceived. The practitioner who addresses all three simultaneously is the practitioner who is simultaneously attempting to read the Li, walk the Dao, and perceive the Shī without the formation sequence that makes each step possible. Coupling does not abolish sequence. The neonatal gut does not negotiate with the milk.

Challenge 15: The Wayshaper Needs a Theory of Their Own Formation

“"Know the other and know yourself: in a hundred interventions, no danger of producing the wrong Li."”

— Shan, via Sun Tzu, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s practitioner account

James’ framework describes what the wayshaper does: shapes possibility spaces, manages affordances, calibrates shocks. It does not describe what formation the wayshaper must have to do these things with formation adequacy rather than formation projection. The wayshaper’s specific formation history determines what possibility spaces they can see, what affordances they read as enabling, what shock level they calibrate as appropriate. The wayshaper who has not walked the specific Dao of the specific formation field they are shaping will produce a possibility space shaped by their prior Li rather than the actual Li of the actual formation. The wayshaper needs self-knowledge that Wayshaping does not provide: not merely training in the framework but formation self-awareness — understanding their own formation history’s specific blindnesses, the specific prior Lis that their specific Dao has produced, and the specific formation-field features that their specific complexity-reduction apparatus makes invisible.

Challenge 16: Habit Is Not Merely Neural Pattern

“"The habit that has been formed over decades is not a neural pattern waiting to be rewired. It is a Dao that has become a Li that has become a Shī — a positional force with its own directional momentum."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s habit account

James treats habits as formations at the neural and bodily scale that can be reshaped by altering the affordance structure and the scaffold. Shan’s challenge: the habit is not merely a neural pattern; it is a Dao that has been walked into a Li that has been consolidated into a Shī. The long-term smoker’s smoking is not merely a neural craving circuit; it is an identity position, a social protocol, a temporal structure, a relational mediator — a specific formation whose Shī includes the specific relational fields within which smoking is the natural move and not-smoking is the unnatural one. Wang Fuzhi: qi first condenses and then form-pattern emerges. The habit’s pattern emerged from the specific qi of the specific encounters that produced it. Reshaping the scaffold addresses the surface of a formation whose depth the scaffold does not reach.

Challenge 17: The Behavioural Environment Needs a Relational Precondition Analysis

“"Relation precedes dynamics. The relational field that precedes the behavioural environment is not a given; it is a formation that determines what the behavioural environment can do."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (May 2026)

James’ wayshaping involves modifying the behavioural environment — the physical, social, and informational contexts in which behaviour occurs — to make desired behaviours more accessible. Shan’s challenge: the behavioural environment is not the primary relational level at which behaviour is determined. The relational field that precedes the behavioural environment — the specific quality of the specific relationships within which the specific person inhabits the specific environment — determines what the behavioural environment can do. The same environmental scaffold in a relationship of trust and the same scaffold in a relationship of coercion will produce structurally different behavioural responses. The relational field is prior to the environmental scaffold. Wayshaping that begins with environmental modification without first attending to the relational precondition is wayshaping that has started one level too late.

Challenge 18: The Identity Scale Needs Dao Tracing

“"Identity is not a scale of the self-collective. It is the Li of a specific formation history — the specific accumulated pattern that the specific Dao of the specific life has produced."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s identity concept

James includes identity as one of the nested agents of the self-collective that behaviour change must coordinate. This is structurally correct and represents a significant advance over frameworks that treat identity as a fixed background condition. Shan’s challenge: identity is not merely a scale of the self-collective that can be coordinated; it is the specific accumulated Li of the specific formation history. It was produced by a specific Dao. It carries a specific Shī. And it has a specific holding capacity for the specific challenge that the specific behaviour-change intervention represents. The identity that cannot hold the challenge of radical habit change will not be reshaped by a scaffold or a shock; it will be ruptured by it. The specific formation depth of the specific identity — the specific thickness of the specific Li — determines what the identity can receive without dissolution.

Challenge 19: The Temporal Commitment Scale Needs a Sequence Ontology

“"Temporal commitments are not merely agents of the self-collective competing for future time. They are the specific formation history’s specific articulation of what the formation’s Shī makes irreversible and what it makes available."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Prigogine’s arrow of time

James includes temporal commitments as one of the nested agents of the self-collective, competing for the person’s future time. Shan’s challenge, via Prigogine: the temporal commitments are not competing agents in a present negotiation. They are the formation’s specific articulation of irreversibility. The long-term relationship, the professional investment, the family commitment — each of these is a Dao that has been walked to a specific depth, producing a specific Li with a specific Shī. The irreversibility is real: the formation cannot simply be unwound by a new scaffold. At the bifurcation, history enters. The temporal commitment’s Shī determines what future moves are available and what moves are foreclosed. Wayshaping that treats temporal commitments as competing agents available for reallocation is wayshaping that has not yet accounted for the formation history that made those commitments irreversible.

Challenge 20: The Shock-and-Scaffold Dialectic Needs Formation Sequencing

“"Scaffold before shock. Form the holding capacity before applying the dynamic loading. Test the formation’s grain before bringing the force to bear on it."”

— Shan, dialectical synthesis of Wayshaping’s two primary intervention modes

James treats scaffolds (environmental supports that make desired behaviour accessible) and shocks (perturbations that disrupt established patterns) as two complementary intervention modes. Shan’s challenge is not to either individually but to their relationship: shocks require prior scaffolding to be formation-productive rather than formation-destructive. The person who has not yet developed the scaffold-supported holding capacity for the specific challenge that the specific shock will introduce is the person for whom the shock produces rupture rather than transformation. The Cao Zhi crisis: burning the bean-stalks to cook the beans. The scaffold builds the formation capacity that the shock will test. The shock applied before the scaffold has produced adequate formation capacity is the shock that destroys what it was designed to transform.

Challenge 21: Wayshaping’s Agency Concept Needs Relational Grounding

“"Agency is not a property of the individual self-collective. It is the specific relational achievement of the specific formation in the specific relational field."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s agency concept

James’ framework reconceptualises agency as distributed across the nested scales of the self-collective. Shan’s challenge: agency is not distributed across internal scales alone; it is constituted by the specific relational field within which the self-collective is embedded. The person’s capacity for the specific agency that specific behaviour change requires is not merely a function of their internal coordination; it is a function of the specific relational field’s specific configuration. The student in the Edinburgh seminar has the internal capacity for verbal contribution; the relational field’s specific configuration makes that capacity unavailable as an actionable agency. Wayshaping that targets internal coordination without attending to the relational field’s specific configuration will produce internal coordination achievements that the relational field continues to make behaviourally unavailable.

Challenge 22: The Multiscale Self Needs a Cross-Scale Li Analysis

“"The Li of the self-collective is not the sum of the Lis of its parts. It is the emergent grain produced by the specific relational configuration of the specific parts in the specific formation history."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s multiscale ontology

James’ multiscale framework maps the self-collective across neural, bodily, social, and temporal scales. Shan’s challenge: the Li of the whole self-collective is not a function of the Lis of its constituent scales. It is the emergent grain produced by the specific relational configuration of the specific scales in the specific formation history of the specific person. Xunzi: blue comes from indigo but is bluer than indigo. The self-collective’s Li exceeds the Lis of its parts because it is the product of the specific relational dynamics between parts, not the sum of the parts’ individual properties. A wayshaping intervention that targets individual scales without attending to the inter-scale relational configuration — the specific way each scale is entangled with every other in this specific person’s specific formation — is an intervention that produces local scale changes without altering the cross-scale Li that determines the formation’s overall Shī.

Challenge 23: Wayshaping Needs a Collapse Theory

“"Wayshaping without a collapse theory is like navigation without an account of the cliff. The most important move in any formation is the move that prevents the narrowing from reaching the terminal."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Nothing Collapses in One Move (April 2026)

James’ wayshaping framework is primarily a framework for enhancing formation toward desired behaviour. Shan’s nothing-collapses-in-one-move account identifies the structure of formation pathology that wayshaping must also address. The self-collective that is narrowing toward collapse — whose scaffold has become a cage, whose alignment has become a pathological attractor, whose anticipation has closed off the adjacent possible that would have interrupted the narrowing — is the self-collective for which wayshaping’s enhancement-oriented tools are inadequate. The path narrows first. The practitioner who cannot see the narrowing cannot act while acting is still possible. A complete wayshaping framework needs a diagnostic for the formation that is approaching the clear-to-chaotic boundary, not merely a toolkit for building the formation that approaches the complex-to-clear boundary.

Challenge 24: The Three Wayshaping Concepts Need Formation-Sensitive Definitions

“"Wayfinding finds the available path. Waymaking creates the path. Wayshaping alters the landscape so paths emerge. But none of these is possible without the formation depth that makes the landscape legible in the first place."”

— Shan, dialectical synthesis of the three Wayshaping concepts

Snowden’s useful distinction between wayfinding (finding available paths), waymaking (creating paths), and wayshaping (altering the landscape so paths emerge naturally) names three genuinely different relationships between the practitioner and the formation field. Shan’s challenge: all three presuppose a practitioner who can read the landscape adequately — who has the formation depth to distinguish available from unavailable paths (wayfinding), to distinguish where path-creation is formation-adequate from where it forces against the grain (waymaking), and to distinguish substrate properties that make certain paths natural from those that make them forced (wayshaping). The Polynesian navigator who reads the waves does not merely find available paths; their specific formation depth makes the wave-patterns’ actual Li legible. Without that formation depth — without the specific Dao of sustained, formation-sufficient engagement with the specific landscape — all three modes reduce to guessing in the vocabulary of complexity.

Challenge 25: The Dao-Li-Shī Sequence Is Wayshaping’s Missing Foundation

“"Dao-sensitive wayshaping: trace the path, read the grain, read the positional force, assess the holding capacity, design the scaffold, calibrate the shock, build toward viable position. In that order. Always."”

— Shan, dialectical reconstruction of Wayshaping’s complete foundation

The synthesis: Wayshaping is a genuinely important advance in behaviour-change theory. It reconceptualises the person as a formation rather than a rational actor, reconceptualises the environment as a formation field rather than a neutral container, and reconceptualises behaviour change as shaping rather than coercing. These are structural advances that this paper endorses completely. Shan’s twenty-five challenges are not rejections; they are the specific deepenings that the Dao-Li-Shī sequence provides. The complete Dao-sensitive Wayshaping: first trace the Dao that produced the present formation (what has been walked, what has thickened, what Dao is this person living inside). Then read the Li (what is workable, what is brittle, what is overextended, what is already thinning). Then read the Shī (what position the current formation creates, what futures it makes easier and harder). Then assess holding capacity. Then design scaffolds as proto-Daos. Then calibrate shocks to formation depth. Then build toward viable positions over time. This turns Wayshaping from a framework of behaviour change into a philosophy of formation-sensitive transformation. And it connects James et al.’s sophisticated cognitive science to the deepest structural insights of the Chinese philosophical tradition — not as decoration but as genuine ontological grounding.

❧ ✶ ❧
XXXIX

Part XX: Jackson’s Tank, Cynefin’s Aporia, and the Wayshaping Dialectical Fire

Three simultaneous encounters at maximum temperature. Mike Jackson’s Critical Systems Thinking is the most ethically serious, methodologically ambitious, and historically comprehensive systems framework in the English-language literature: four decades of work, 700 pages, winner of the INCOSE Pioneer Award 2022. It deserves to be engaged at full depth and found wanting on specific structural grounds — not dismissed but defeated. David Snowden’s February 2026 meta-framework post is the most complete available statement of what Cynefin claims to be: not a classification device but an active integration strategy for deliberate domain navigation. And the aporetic turn in Cynefin — born in an email exchange with John van Breda at Stellenbosch University reading Derrida, confirmed in Snowden’s 2020 St David’s Day posts, acknowledged by Snowden as resolving ‘the last remaining incoherence in Cynefin’ — is the most philosophically significant evolution in the framework’s quarter-century history. All three receive Shan at burning point.

❧ ✶ ❧

Mike Jackson and Critical Systems Thinking — Run Over by the Tank

Mike Jackson is Emeritus Professor at the University of Hull, editor-in-chief of Systems Research and Behavioral Science, past President of the International Federation for Systems Research and the International Society for the Systems Sciences. His Critical Systems Thinking and the Management of Complexity (Wiley, 2019) took four decades and 700 pages. His subsequent Critical Systems Thinking: A Practitioner’s Guide (Wiley, 2024) distils that into 238 pages. Between them they represent the most architecturally complete, historically grounded, and ethically serious framework in the field. Shan begins — as she always begins — with what Jackson got irrefutably right, before putting every wheel of the tank to work.

What Jackson Got Irrefutably Right

“"Critical systems thinking (CST) sets out how the variety of systems methodologies, methods, and models that have been developed can be used in combination to promote more successful interventions in complex organizational and societal problem situations."”

— Michael C. Jackson, Critical Systems Thinking: A Practitioner’s Guide (2024)

The founding insight of CST, and the one Shan endorses with both hands: no single systems methodology is adequate to the full range of complex problem situations. The Li of each methodology — System Dynamics, Soft Systems Methodology, Organisational Cybernetics, Critical Systems Heuristics — is specific to the specific formation context for which it was developed. The practitioner who applies one methodology to every situation is the practitioner who has one Li and projects it onto every Dao. Jackson’s pluralism is the methodological equivalent of Shan’s Dao-before-Li principle applied to the systems field as a whole: you cannot know in advance which methodology is adequate; you must walk the specific problem situation before its specific structural character reveals which approach is formation-adequate. SOSM — the System of Systems Methodologies that Jackson and Keys developed in 1984 — is the most precise available map of methodological grain: which methodology fits which structural configuration of system complexity and stakeholder relationship. It is Li at meta-level. It is downstream of the formation history of the systems field.

“"I don’t think systems thinking can ever replace the experience or knowledge of context that a leader or a decision-maker has, but I do think it can help their thinking."”

— Michael C. Jackson, BCG Henderson Institute (2024)

Jackson’s most honest moment, and the one that places him closest to Shan. He cannot say it more clearly: the methodology cannot replace the formation. The experience or knowledge of context IS what Shan calls the specific Li produced by the specific Dao-walk of the specific practitioner in the specific domain. Jackson’s entire framework is a sophisticated set of tools for helping practitioners use methodologies better. His own acknowledgement that the methodology cannot replace the practitioner’s experience or context-knowledge is the acknowledgement that his framework is a Li, and the Dao is the practitioner’s specific formation history that the framework cannot provide. The tank will now proceed.

“"Jackson (2019) argues that the commitment to improvement within CST encompasses various dimensions, including efficiency, efficacy, effectiveness, viability, sustainability, mutual understanding, empowerment and emancipation."”

— Albakri, Revisiting Critical Systems Thinking, Systems Research and Behavioral Science (2024)

Eight dimensions of improvement: the most architecturally ambitious commitment in the systems field. Shan’s challenge will not be to the ambition but to the ontological ground. How does improvement occur in a formation? Not by applying the correct methodology to the correct problem type. By walking the specific Dao of the specific problem formation with sufficient depth, duration, and relational sensitivity that the specific Li of what improvement means in this specific formation emerges from the formation’s own dynamics. Efficiency, emancipation, sustainability — these are not methodological outcomes. They are formation achievements. And formation achievements are downstream of Dao-walks, not of methodology selection.

Tank Charge 1: The Emancipatory Commitment Has No Formation Theory

“"CST has its origins in the 1980s with accounts of how the theoretical partiality of existing systems methodologies limited their ability to guide interventions... and suggestions about how those disadvantaged by systems designs could be given a voice and have impact."”

— Wikipedia, Critical Systems Thinking

The emancipatory commitment — giving voice to those disadvantaged by systems designs, identifying and challenging the power relations that determine whose interests a system serves — is the ethically serious core of CST and Shan endorses it completely. The structural failure: the emancipatory commitment assumes that the practitioner applying CST has the specific formation depth adequate to identifying whose voices are excluded and whose boundary definitions are operative. But the practitioner’s own formation history determines what emancipatory needs they can see and what their complexity-reduction apparatus codes as noise. The CST practitioner formed in the tradition of Western critical theory, grounded in Habermas and Foucault, carries a specific formation history that makes specific emancipatory needs visible — power relations in formal organisational structures, expert-versus-stakeholder knowledge asymmetries, class-based access barriers — and makes specific emancipatory needs invisible: the formation-level conditions that produce the Edinburgh silence. No boundary critique formulated from outside the formation of the Chinese student can see the emancipatory emergency that is the silence itself. The practitioner who has not walked the Dao on the other side of the boundary cannot see what the boundary is excluding.

The structural consequence: CST’s emancipatory commitment is a commitment to emancipating formations that the framework can already see. The formations it cannot see — because their specific Daos have not been walked by the practitioners deploying the framework — remain outside the emancipatory reach of even the most rigorously applied boundary critique. Shan’s incandescent challenge: an emancipatory systems practice adequate to the full range of twenty-first-century formation challenges requires not merely methodological pluralism but formation pluralism — practitioners who have walked the Daos of genuinely different formation traditions. No methodology can substitute for that formation depth. Jackson has the right ethical commitment. He lacks the formation theory that would make it structurally adequate.

Tank Charge 2: Habermas’ Ideal Speech Situation Is a Li Wearing the Clothes of an Ontology

Jackson’s emancipatory commitment is grounded in Habermas’ theory of communicative action. The ideal speech situation — the regulative ideal of communication undistorted by power, where validity claims are settled by the force of the better argument — is a genuine philosophical achievement and one of the most important conceptual contributions to the ethics of dialogue in twentieth-century thought. Shan’s forensic challenge: the ideal speech situation is a Li. It is the specific Li of a specific Western European philosophical tradition that has produced a specific account of what ‘undistorted communication’ consists of. Its specific Li includes: contribution consists of propositional content, validity claims are settled by argument, rational consensus is the telos of genuine dialogue, silence is the absence of contribution.

Every one of these assumptions is a formation-specific Li. The Edinburgh student’s silence is, within the Li of the ideal speech situation, the absence of contribution: a space from which no validity claim has been advanced and which therefore makes no contribution to the communicative process. From inside the formation of the Chinese educational tradition, the silence IS a contribution: dense with propositional content, communicating respect, attentiveness, processing, relational positioning, and the specific form of engagement that that formation has produced as its Li of intellectual participation. The ideal speech situation cannot see the silence as communication because its own Li of communication excludes the relational formation conditions that make silence information. Habermas’ framework emancipates the speech it can hear. Shan’s framework emancipates the formation that Habermas cannot hear because it has not walked the Dao of the formation that produces meaning through silence.

Tank Charge 3: SOSM Reproduces the Li-Before-Dao Error at Meta-Level

“"The System of Systems Methodologies classifies methodologies according to their ability to deal with the difficulties posed by system complexity and different perspectives among stakeholders."”

— Michael C. Jackson and Paul Keys, SOSM (1984)
