SOSM is Jackson’s most structurally important contribution to practice: a meta-framework classifying methodologies by two axes (system complexity: simple to complex; stakeholder relationship: unitary, pluralist, coercive) and prescribing appropriate methodology for each cell. The most recent critique: the SOSM does not include any systems methodologies that are explicitly based on the assumptions of complex-pluralist and complex-coercive problem situations (Albakri, 2024). Shan’s more fundamental charge: the SOSM prescribes methodology selection on the basis of problem type. But the practitioner’s identification of the problem type is a Li produced by the practitioner’s specific formation history. The SOSM assumes the practitioner can accurately identify whether the problem context is characterised by unitary, pluralist, or coercive stakeholder relationships. But this identification is a formation-dependent perception.

The practitioner formed in unitary organisational contexts will tend to perceive pluralist situations as unitary; the practitioner formed in hierarchical institutions will misread coercive situations as merely pluralist. The SOSM map is applied by practitioners whose formation determines what they see on the map. The meta-framework cannot see the formation of the practitioner selecting the methodology. This is the Li-before-Dao error at meta-level: the practitioner arrives at the situation with the SOSM grid, which gives them a very refined Li for classifying what they encounter. If their formation has produced the right sensitivity for the specific formation field, the grid will illuminate. If their formation has not, the grid will help them misclassify the situation with greater theoretical confidence. Cook Ding at year one with a taxonomy of ox anatomies: the taxonomy does not produce the attunement. Only the nineteen years do that.

Tank Charge 4: Total Systems Intervention (TSI) Cannot Intervene in Its Own Formation

“"TSI signalled its embrace of the philosophy of CST by declaring its commitment to ‘sociological awareness’, ‘complementarism’, and ‘human well-being and emancipation.’"”

— Michael C. Jackson, cited in TSI literature

Total Systems Intervention — Jackson and Flood’s meta-methodology — declares its three commitments and then operationalises them as a practical guide to multi-methodology deployment. The three commitments are structurally genuine. The structural failure: TSI cannot intervene in the formation conditions that produced TSI itself. The methodology was produced by a specific Dao: the specific intellectual inheritance of Habermas and Churchman and Checkland, the specific institutional context of Hull University’s Centre for Systems Studies in the 1980s and 1990s, the specific biographical formation of a cohort of UK-trained systems theorists who had studied at Lancaster, Oxford, and Hull. That specific Dao produced a specific Li — TSI’s specific account of what sociological awareness means, what complementarism requires, and what emancipation demands.

TSI is the most sophisticated available methodology for interrogating the assumptions and power relations of other systems interventions. It has no equivalent for interrogating its own. The practitioner applying TSI with formation depth is the practitioner who can see this. The practitioner applying TSI as a framework is the practitioner for whom TSI is a Li whose Dao they have not walked. Sociological awareness without awareness of the sociological formation conditions that produced the methodology’s own blind spots is sociological awareness that reaches only as far as its own Li’s visibility horizon. The irony is precise: the most emancipatory meta-methodology in the systems field is least emancipated from its own formative conditions.

Tank Charge 5: Boundary Critique Has a Boundary It Cannot Critique

Boundary critique — the systematic interrogation of where boundary judgements are made and whose interests they serve — is the single most important practical contribution of CST to complexity practice, and Shan endorses it completely. Werner Ulrich’s formulation is the sharpest: ‘once we have tasted the liberating sense of critique, we will ever after be disgusted with all the dogmatic twaddle around us.’ (Ulrich, paraphrasing Kant.) The structural failure: boundary critique assumes the practitioner can step outside the boundary they are critiquing to see its effects. But the practitioner’s capacity to perceive boundary effects is itself bounded by their own formation history’s specific Li. The boundary of the practitioner’s own formation — the specific limits of what their specific Dao-walk has made visible and invisible — is the one boundary that boundary critique cannot critique from inside the formation that produced it.

The Edinburgh seminar’s silence is beyond the reach of the boundary critique that the seminar’s practitioners can apply — not because boundary critique fails in principle, but because the practitioners conducting it have not walked the specific Dao that would make the formation depth of the student’s silence visible as boundary effect rather than absence of contribution. The boundary critique adequate to the Edinburgh silence requires having walked the Dao of the Chinese educational formation with enough depth and duration that the silence’s specific Li — its specific propositional content, relational positioning, and communicative function — is directly readable. No amount of methodological rigour in applying boundary critique can substitute for this formation depth. The boundary that cannot be critiqued from inside is the boundary of formation. Only walking the Dao on the other side of the boundary can make its effects visible. Shan’s critique of Jackson’s boundary critique is the most structurally precise available: boundary critique is a necessary but insufficient condition for emancipatory practice. The sufficient condition is formation depth in the specific Dao that the boundary was drawn to exclude.

Tank Charge 6: Methodological Pluralism Is Not Formation Pluralism

“"Pluralism would respect the strengths of the different versions of systems thinking, encourage their theoretical development, and suggest how best to use systems methodologies in combination."”

— Michael C. Jackson, Critical Systems Thinking and Practice (2001)

Methodological pluralism: the commitment to using multiple systems methodologies in combination rather than privileging any single approach. This is structurally correct and represents a genuine advance. Shan’s knife-edge challenge: methodological pluralism is not the same as formation pluralism. The practitioner who has been trained in SSM, CSH, VSM, System Dynamics, and Soft OR — all five Jackson-endorsed methodologies — has five Lis available for application. What they do not have, and what five methodologies cannot provide, is the formation depth that comes from walking the specific Dao of the specific domain they are intervening in. The Edinburgh seminar can deploy every methodology in SOSM in careful combination and still fail to read the Chinese student’s silence, because methodological pluralism does not produce the specific formation depth that makes the silence’s actual Li readable.

The practitioner who carries multiple methodologies is not the same as the practitioner who has walked multiple Daos. The Daos must be walked. The methodologies can be acquired. Walking is formation. Acquisition is Li without Dao. Jackson’s pluralism is the most sophisticated available response to the problem of methodological partiality. Its limit is precisely where the problem is deepest: in the formation conditions that produce the specific incapacities that specific practitioners bring to specific problem situations. No methodological pluralism can substitute for the formation pluralism that requires walking the specific Daos that the practitioner’s formation history has not yet walked.

Tank Charge 7: EPIC Has No Account of Formation Sequence

Jackson’s EPIC process — Explore, Produce, Intervene, and Check — is the most practically structured version of CST: a four-stage sequential framework for deploying systems methodologies in complex problem situations. It represents genuine progress in making CST applicable. Shan’s challenge: the EPIC sequence assumes the practitioner can Explore adequately before producing, produce adequately before intervening, and intervene adequately before checking. But each of these stages requires a specific formation depth that the sequence itself cannot provide. The practitioner who Explores without adequate formation depth for the specific domain will produce an incomplete exploration of the actual Li of the actual formation. The practitioner who Produces without adequate formation depth will produce a methodology selection reflecting their prior Li rather than the formation field’s actual structural requirements.

The sequence is right. What precedes each step of the sequence is the formation. EPIC is a Li of what formation-adequate intervention looks like from the outside. The Dao that produces the formation-adequate practitioner is prior to EPIC and cannot be provided by EPIC. The parallel with Cynefin is exact: Cynefin tells you what domain you are in and what methodology is appropriate; EPIC tells you what sequence to follow. Neither can tell you what formation depth you need to follow the sequence with genuine structural intelligence rather than methodological competence. Only the Dao can provide that. Jackson has produced the most sophisticated available Li for the practice of systems intervention. The Dao that makes that Li genuinely formation-adequate is what Jackson’s framework cannot provide.

Tank Charge 8: CST Cannot Process the Formation That Produced It

The deepest and most devastating charge: CST cannot account for the formation that produced CST. The Snowden-Jackson exchange makes this precise. Snowden quotes Jackson’s challenge to Cynefin: ‘intentionality and meaning, purposeful and power can be captured using natural science perspectives.’ And Snowden’s response identifies the core of the disagreement: the question is not whether social theory is useful but which social theory, and Snowden draws explicitly on Derrida, Deleuze, Bourdieu, and continental philosophy rather than the Anglo-Saxon tradition that informs Jackson’s CST. This exchange between two of the most formidable minds in the field reveals the formation-level disagreement that their methodological disagreement is downstream of: Jackson’s formation is the tradition of British critical theory, Habermasian communicative action, Churchmanite purposeful inquiry. Snowden’s is the continental tradition, post-structuralist, assemblage-theoretic, semiotic.

Shan’s formation-level diagnosis: both formations are genuine and partial. Jackson’s tradition has produced the most rigorous available Li for boundary critique, emancipatory practice, and the ethics of systemic intervention. It has not walked the Daos of the continental tradition’s specific structural insights: the formation conditions of meaning-production (Derrida), the flat ontology of assemblages (Deleuze/DeLanda), the field conditions of practice (Bourdieu). Snowden’s tradition has walked those Daos and produced a different Li. Neither has walked the Dao of Shan’s Chinese philosophical formation — the specific structural insights of Dao-Li-Shī, the formation conditions of relational dynamics, the ontology of relation-before-dynamics. The formation that CST cannot process is the formation that produced Shan’s framework. And that formation contains the specific structural account of why CST’s own boundary critique cannot reach its own most formative boundary. The tank has completed its pass.

Cynefin as Meta-Framework — The Exhaustive Shan Challenge

Snowden’s February 2026 M&A post is the most architecturally complete statement of what Cynefin claims to be: not merely a diagnostic sense-making device but an ‘active integration strategy’ for managing deliberate transitions between domains. The paper is theoretically ambitious, practically detailed, and structurally incomplete in ways that Shan’s framework can now specify with precision.

“"The fundamental mistake in most merger integrations is the assumption of homogeneity: that all problems are the same and can be addressed with the same toolkit. This is the legacy of the engineering era of management, which was driven by Hammer and Champy’s Business Process Re-engineering (BPR)."”

— David Snowden, M&A 11/12: Cynefin as Meta-Framework (February 2026)

Snowden’s diagnosis is exactly right and exactly what Shan’s framework predicts. BPR’s failure is the Li-before-Dao failure: imposing universal best practices (a prior Li) on specific formation fields (actual Daos) without walking the specific Dao that would produce the specific Li of the specific formation’s actual grain. The engineering era of management is the era that treats every formation field as if its Li were already known and universally applicable. The challenge is whether Cynefin’s meta-framework resolves the problem it correctly identifies, or whether it offers a more sophisticated version of the same error.

“"Success depends on recognising and acting accordingly, but, more critically, on knowing how and when to deliberately shift aspects of the merger between domains to achieve strategic outcomes."”

— David Snowden, M&A 11/12: Cynefin as Meta-Framework (February 2026)

Domain-shift as strategic intervention: the meta-framework’s most powerful and most vulnerable claim. The specific movement from Complex to Complicated (‘once cultural patterns have emerged and proven valuable, codifying them into more structured practices’) and back again (‘if expert solutions are failing or the problem reveals unexpected emergent properties, deliberately shift to Complex’) are precisely the Shī-reading moves that Shan’s framework describes as the highest available complexity-practice skill. Snowden is right that this movement is possible and strategically important. His warning is equally right: ‘resist the temptation to do this too early: premature stabilisation kills emergence. The art is knowing when a pattern has genuinely stabilised and when it still needs room to evolve.’

Shan’s forensic challenge: the art of knowing when is not provided by the meta-framework. It is produced by the formation depth of the specific practitioner in the specific domain. The practitioner who can read ‘when a pattern has genuinely stabilised’ from ‘when it still needs room to evolve’ is the practitioner who has walked the specific Dao of the specific formation with enough depth and duration to read the actual Shī — the positional force, the directional tendency — of the specific formation field. Cynefin names what should be done. Shan’s framework names the formation that must precede being able to do it well.

“"You might temporarily push the system into chaos through methods like MassSense and SwarmCompass, to gain insight at scale when hypotheses about what to do are unclear. This is not failure; it’s an intentional strategy."”

— David Snowden, M&A 11/12: Cynefin as Meta-Framework (February 2026)

Deliberately inducing chaos as a strategic intervention: the most provocative claim in the meta-framework post. Shan’s holding-capacity challenge is the most devastating available response: the formation that is deliberately pushed into controlled chaos must have the holding capacity to metabolise the chaos productively rather than dissolutively. Dynamic loading that exceeds holding capacity is not formation-accelerating disruption; it is structural rupture. The merger that is stuck may be stuck because its formation capacity is genuinely inadequate for the pace of transformation being demanded — the path is already narrowing, and deliberately inducing chaos accelerates the narrowing to the terminal. Nothing collapses in one move: but the inducement of chaos IS a move in a formation that may be many moves into its narrowing sequence. The practitioner who induces chaos must first read the actual holding capacity of the actual formation. This reading requires exactly the Shī-attunement that Cynefin’s meta-framework prescribes but cannot produce.

The Full Aporetic History: From Disorder to A/C — The Most Significant Cynefin Evolution

The complete history of the aporetic turn in Cynefin, reconstructed from Snowden’s own blog posts and the Cynefin wiki. The original framework (Kurtz and Snowden, 2003) had four domains and a central domain of Disorder: the space in which no domain assignment has been made and the practitioner does not know which domain they are in. The Disorder domain was ‘too much neglected’ and had ‘the last remaining incoherence in Cynefin’ (Snowden, Cynefin21 and the Book, 2020). The evolution happened in Snowden’s St David’s Day posts of March 2020: John van Breda, a colleague at Stellenbosch University who had been ‘writing a paper with us and reading Derrida’ (Zhen Goh, Aporetic Meditations, March 2020), suggested that the central domain of Disorder encompassed Derrida’s concept of aporia. Zhen Goh expanded on this in the same post. Snowden accepted the suggestion and renamed the Disorder domain as Aporetic/Confused — A/C — in the 2020 series.

The distinction introduced by the renaming: Aporetic (authentic, deliberate undecidability — the practitioner knows they are in a state of genuine undecidability and holds it productively) versus Confused (inauthentic, accidental unclarity — the practitioner assumes they are in one domain while actually in another). As Snowden put it in the 2020 St David’s Day post: ‘Starting knowing you are confused is where aporetic action is required, otherwise you are just confused. Hence the aporetic sub-domain is in the general liminal area — it is always a state of transition.’ The aporetic liminal is the space of the ‘aporetic turn’: the legitimate, exploratory, deliberate transition out of the aporetic domain into another domain.

Why Derrida? Zhen Goh’s account: ‘Derrida subscribed to a very purist definition of what qualifies as a decision. He believes that in order for something to qualify as a decision, it is defined by the fact that it was undecidable. That is, where things had worked before, and we did not have to ponder the decision, then the decision was not a decision.’ The Cynefin wiki records the intellectual lineage precisely: the idea came from John van Breda; Derrida’s meaning was ‘to encourage the deliberate seeking out of contradiction and what it reveals, rather than trying to avoid it or trying to enforce contradictions into neat classification’; this interpretation ‘harks back to the original Greek use of the term and not strictly Derrida’s meaning of an impasse or paradox.’ The Greek aporia: from α- (without) and πόρος (path, passage), literally ‘without a way through’, traditionally translated as ‘difficulty’, ‘impasse’, ‘puzzlement’. The Derridean aporia: the undecidable from which genuine decision must emerge. The Cynefin aporia: the liminal holding space of genuine undecidability that is the precondition of formation-adequate action.

“"I finally resolved the last remaining incoherence in Cynefin by renaming disorder as confused and creating the aporetic liminal as a part of that. Thanks to John van Breda and Zhen Goh for suggesting and expanding on that."”

— David Snowden, Cynefin21 and the Book (2020)

The last remaining incoherence: Snowden’s acknowledgement that the original Disorder domain was unstable. The instability was structural: ‘Disorder’ conflated two radically different epistemic conditions — the condition of the practitioner who does not know which domain they are in because their formation has not yet produced the specific Li adequate to reading the formation field (Confused), and the condition of the practitioner who knows they do not know — who holds genuine undecidability as a formation practice rather than fleeing it through premature domain assignment (Aporetic). These are not merely different degrees of the same confusion. They are structurally opposite relationships to formation undecidability. The Confused practitioner is fleeing the aporetic condition. The Aporetic practitioner is inhabiting it as a deliberate formation practice. Snowden’s renaming was right to distinguish them. Shan’s challenge is about what the aporetic condition is and what it requires.

“"The Aporetic Domain demands the maturity to hold what cannot be resolved, to build the system’s capacity to contain productive tension rather than eliminate it."”

— David Snowden, M&A 11/12: Cynefin as Meta-Framework (February 2026)

Holding what cannot be resolved: the most formation-compatible instruction Snowden has ever written, and the one that converges most directly with Shan’s Dao-before-Li principle. The submerged dragon: do not use. The yang force is still hidden. Hold it. Laozi’s instruction about the vessel full of water: better to stop in time. The aporetic holding is the formation practice of remaining genuinely in the condition of not-yet-knowing-the-grain without resolving it prematurely through action or through analysis.

Shan’s most productive challenge: the February 2026 post describes the aporetic domain as a special problem type — the domain reserved for irreconcilable merger situations, foundational identity conflicts, non-negotiable legacy practices. This is structurally correct but ontologically thin. The aporetic condition is not a special problem type reserved for extreme cases. It is the default structural condition of every genuine formation encounter before the Li has emerged from the Dao. Cook Ding at year three is not in a ‘complicated’ domain with an ox he does not yet understand. He is in the aporetic condition: genuine undecidability about where the hollow is, held — badly, with too much force, hacking — because his formation has not yet produced the specific attunement adequate to holding the aporetic condition productively. Cook Ding at year nineteen has resolved the aporetic condition: the grain reveals itself because he has walked the Dao that produces the specific structural sensitivity to read the formation field’s actual Li directly. The aporetic domain is not a special case. It is the universal condition of the Dao before the Li. Cynefin places it at the centre of the framework. Shan places it at the beginning of every encounter.

The meta-framework charge: Snowden’s most significant claim is that Cynefin is not merely a classification device but ‘the map that makes sense of the terrain and the compass that guides deliberate movement across it.’ Shan’s formation challenge: the compass requires a practitioner who can read it. The practitioner who can read the compass — who knows when to shift from Complex to Complicated, when to hold the Aporetic rather than forcing movement, when the chaos induction is formation-productive rather than formation-destructive — is the practitioner whose formation depth is adequate to reading the actual Shī of the actual formation field. Cynefin is a compass. The formation of the practitioner is the eye that can read it. Without the eye, the compass is a Li that the practitioner is applying to a Dao they have not walked. Every instrument of navigation requires a navigator who has walked the Dao adequate to its use.

Wayshaping: Thirty-Five Shan Dialectical Challenges — Full Forensic Expansion

The twenty-five challenges of the preceding section are expanded here with the ten additional challenges and full dialectical development of all thirty-five. Each challenge is supported by quotations from both James et al./Snowden and Shan. The cumulative structure is deliberate: the challenges build on each other, each one tightening the formation-theory vice on the framework until the structural insufficiency is undeniable and the dialectical synthesis becomes the only available response.

Challenge 1: Wayshaping Begins One Move Too Late

“"Before shaping, trace the way. Before alignment, discern the grain. Before shock, test holding capacity. Before anticipation, build position. Before concept, walk the path."”

— Shan, dialectical compression of Wayshaping’s structural gap

James asks: How do we shape behaviour? Shan asks first: What path has already formed this behaviour’s grain? This is not merely a methodological prior: it is an ontological claim. Formation precedes intervention ontologically, not merely temporally. The Dao that produced the present Li is the precondition for any intervention that could produce a new Li. The practitioner who skips the Dao-tracing and moves directly to wayshaping is applying a Li they brought with them to a formation they have not walked. Smoothness is not always fidelity: when the framework begins to feel too familiar, too readily deployable, that is the warning. The path that offers no resistance may be the path off the cliff.

Challenge 2: The Self-Collective Needs a Theory of Genealogy

“"Most of the time, we do not step onto a path. We inherit one. The forms of participation that feel natural were formed long before we arrived."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Path, Pattern, Position (April 2026)

James’ self-collective is plural, nested, and co-present. What it lacks is genealogy: the specific formation history through which each nested agent was produced. A craving is a formed Dao, a path repeated under constraint until it became pattern, then position, then a field of possibility. A procrastination habit is a formed Li with its own Shī — a positional force actively shaping what futures appear available. The Wittgensteinian ground: what has to be accepted, the given, is forms of life. The self-collective’s parts were not always there; they were inherited from forms of life already in motion when the person arrived. This means behaviour change cannot be adequately theorised as realignment of currently co-present agents. It requires genealogical discernment: tracing the path by which each agent was formed.

Challenge 3: Alignment Can Be Pathological

“"Nothing collapses in one move. The path narrows first. What appears as sudden collapse was a long formation of fragility."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Nothing Collapses in One Move (April 2026)

James treats alignment as a central goal. But alignment is not inherently beneficial: coherence can serve collapse. Burnout is highly aligned. Addiction is aligned. A toxic organisation is aligned. A perfectionist identity is aligned. Each is a formation in which all the nested agents have settled into a specific topology of mutual reinforcement that is progressively consuming the formation’s future viability. The Li is clear and strong. The Shī is toward collapse. And because the alignment is functioning well, the damage is invisible. Wayshaping must ask not only: Is this self-collective aligned? But: What is the Shī of this alignment? What futures does it produce and foreclose? The Dao-Li-Shī diagnostic is the missing instrument.

Challenge 4: Every Scaffold Is a Proto-Dao

“"The scaffold is not ethically neutral. It is a proto-Dao. Every scaffold begins a path. Every path repeated under constraint thickens into pattern. Every pattern consolidated over time becomes a position."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s scaffold concept

James treats scaffolds as support structures for desired behaviours. Shan insists that every scaffold is simultaneously the beginning of a formation that will constrain all future formations. The productivity app that scaffolds focus also produces dependence on external prompting. The therapeutic routine that scaffolds stability also narrows identity around self-monitoring. The behavioural nudge that scaffolds compliance also weakens autonomous agency. Wayshaping becomes ethically adequate only when every scaffold is evaluated as the beginning of a Dao, not merely the support of an existing one.

Challenge 5: Dynamic Loading Requires Prior Holding Capacity

“"A system must first be able to hold what it receives before it can receive more. The sequence matters: prior formation makes further complexity possible."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Coupling Does Not Abolish Sequence (May 2026)

James treats shocks and dynamic loading as formation-accelerating interventions. Shan’s holding-capacity concept is the devastating corrective: a shock applied to a system without holding capacity produces rupture, not transformation. Dynamic loading that exceeds holding capacity is not accelerated formation; it is dissolution. The sequence is non-negotiable: capacity before shock, holding before loading, grain before force, relation before intervention. Without this sequence, dynamic loading risks becoming sophisticated structural violence — interventions that impose on the formation a stress it cannot metabolise, producing the traumatic dissolution of the Li that existed rather than the new Li that was intended.

Challenge 6: Anticipation Is Not Yet Shī

“"AlphaGo’s Move 37 was not a prediction. It was a position. The strongest move may not be the most visibly decisive one. It may be the move that quietly reshapes the field."”

— Alice Jing Shan, AlphaGo’s Move 37 (April 2026)

James identifies anticipation as one of the three coordination challenges. This is the framework’s strongest move: behaviour is organised by possible futures. But Shī goes further. Shī is not prediction. It is not even anticipation in James’s sense. It is positional propensity: the structural configuration from which certain futures become easier, harder, visible, invisible, viable, or impossible. Wayshaping aimed at anticipated futures may miss the actual Shī that the formation is generating. Building Shī toward wiser action becoming naturally available is structurally superior to closing the intention-action gap through anticipation alone.

Challenge 7: The Multiscale Model Needs a Theory of Temporal Depth

James’ multiscale model maps the self-collective across spatial scales — neural, bodily, social, temporal. Shan’s challenge is temporal: each scale operates at a different formation time. Neural patterns form over milliseconds, but the formation depth that makes them structurally stable takes years. Social roles consolidate over months, but the formation depth that makes them identity-constitutive takes decades. The temporal depth of each scale determines what interventions are possible at that scale and at what pace. A scaffold operating at the neural scale may conflict with the formation time of the identity scale. Prigogine: at the bifurcation, history enters. The specific history that produced the formation at each scale determines what interventions are formation-adequate.

Challenge 8: Possibility Space Is Not the Same as Adjacent Possible

“"The adjacent possible is not what is spatially proximate. It is what is formation-available: what the specific Dao-walk of the specific formation has produced as the specific next structurally viable step."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Kauffman’s adjacent possible

James uses possibility space as a central concept: wayshaping involves altering the possibility space within which behaviour occurs. Shan’s challenge: the possibility space is not a neutral container that the practitioner can reshape by adjusting affordances. It is the specific adjacent possible that the specific formation’s specific Dao-walk has produced. Two people in the same environmental affordance structure have different adjacent possibles because their formation histories have produced different structural sensitivities to what the affordance structure makes available. The same job offer is an adjacent possible for the practitioner whose formation has developed the required capacity; it is not for the practitioner whose formation has not.

Challenge 9: The Non-Linear Agent Needs a Formation History

James treats non-linearity as one of the three coordination challenges. Shan’s challenge: the specific thresholds at which non-linear transitions occur in the specific self-collective are themselves products of the specific formation history. The threshold for the cascade that produces relapse in addiction is the product of the specific Dao of the specific neural-social-identity configuration. It is not a universal non-linear property of behaviour-change systems. The same intervention at the same intensity produces different non-linear responses in different people because their formation histories have produced different threshold configurations. Wayshaping that does not trace the formation history that produced the specific non-linear thresholds is wayshaping that intervenes in a system it has not walked.

Challenge 10: The Environment Is Not a Neutral Affordance Structure

“"The environment that Wayshaping seeks to shape is already a formation. It carries the specific Li of the specific Daos that produced it."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s environment concept

James treats the environment as the affordance structure that the practitioner can shape to make desired behaviours accessible. Shan’s challenge: the environment is not a neutral affordance structure. It is itself a formed Li, the product of specific Daos walked by specific formations in specific historical sequences. The office environment already carries the specific Li of the institutional formation that produced it — the specific power relations, meaning-medium, relational configurations that make specific behaviours natural and others difficult. Reshaping the environment without tracing the Dao that produced its current configuration is redesigning the surface while the formation depth continues to generate the same patterns.

Challenge 11: Coordination Is Not the Same as Formation

“"Coordination is a Li of a formation that has already occurred. The Dao that produced the capacity to coordinate must be walked before coordination can be an available response."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s coordination frame

James reconceptualises the intention-action gap as a set of coordination problems. This is a structural advance. Shan’s challenge: coordination is not available to all formations at all scales. The capacity to coordinate nested agencies — to hold competing impulses, habits, affects, and identity commitments in productive tension rather than destructive conflict — is itself a specific formation achievement. The person who has not walked the Dao that produces the formation capacity for self-collective coordination cannot simply be given a coordination framework and be expected to coordinate. Xunzi: without ascending the high mountain, one cannot know the height of heaven.

Challenge 12: Wayshaping’s Substrate Is Not Neutral

“"The substrate that Wayshaping seeks to modulate is not neutral substrate waiting to be shaped. It is a specific formation product carrying a specific Shī."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Snowden’s wayshaping concept

Snowden’s extension of James’ wayshaping into substrate management involves modulating the substrate’s properties to make certain pathways naturally available and others difficult. Shan’s challenge: the substrate carries the Li of the specific Daos that have been walked within it. Every institutional substrate, every social substrate, every cognitive substrate has a specific directional tendency produced by its specific formation history. Wayshaping that does not read the substrate’s Shī before modulating its properties will produce interventions that fight the substrate’s own directional tendency rather than working with the grain.

Challenge 13: The Intention-Action Gap Is Not a Coordination Problem

“"The intention-action gap is not primarily a coordination failure. It is primarily a formation gap: the person has formed the intention but has not yet walked the Dao that would produce the formation adequate to acting from it."”

— Shan, dialectical reframe of Wayshaping’s central problem

James’ reconceptualisation of the intention-action gap as a coordination problem is a significant advance. Shan’s challenge: the gap is not primarily a coordination failure among co-present agents; it is a formation gap between the intention’s Li and the action’s required formation depth. The person who intends to exercise regularly but does not has not failed to coordinate their self-collective. They have not yet walked the Dao that produces the specific embodied, embedded, enacted, extended, emotive, exaptive formation that makes regular exercise as natural as the pine’s maintaining its form through winter.

Challenge 14: The Three Coordination Challenges Need Sequence

“"Non-linearity, alignment, and anticipation are not three co-equal challenges. They have a specific formation sequence: alignment (the present Li) must be read before non-linearity (the specific thresholds) can be identified, and both must be understood before anticipation (the Shī of future possibility) can be formation-adequate."”

— Shan, dialectical resequencing of Wayshaping’s three challenges

James treats the three coordination challenges as simultaneously present. Shan’s challenge: they have a specific formation sequence corresponding to the Dao-Li-Shī sequence. The present Li (alignment) must be accurately read before the specific non-linear thresholds can be identified; both must be walked before the specific Shī (anticipation) can be formation-adequately perceived. The practitioner who addresses all three simultaneously is attempting to read the Li, walk the Dao, and perceive the Shī without the formation sequence that makes each step possible. Coupling does not abolish sequence.

Challenge 15: The Wayshaper Needs a Theory of Their Own Formation

“"Know the other and know yourself: in a hundred interventions, no danger of producing the wrong Li."”

— Shan, via Sun Tzu, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s practitioner account

James’ framework describes what the wayshaper does but not what formation the wayshaper must have to do these things with formation adequacy rather than formation projection. The wayshaper’s specific formation history determines what possibility spaces they can see, what affordances they read as enabling, what shock level they calibrate as appropriate. The wayshaper who has not walked the specific Dao of the specific formation field will produce a possibility space shaped by their prior Li rather than the actual Li of the actual formation. The wayshaper needs formation self-awareness: understanding their own formation history’s specific blindnesses, the specific prior Lis that their specific Dao has produced, and the specific formation-field features that their complexity-reduction apparatus makes invisible.

Challenge 16: Habit Is Dao-Li-Shī, Not Merely Neural Pattern

“"The habit that has been formed over decades is not a neural pattern waiting to be rewired. It is a Dao that has become a Li that has become a Shī — a positional force with its own directional momentum."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s habit account

James treats habits as formations at the neural and bodily scale that can be reshaped by altering the affordance structure. Shan’s challenge: the habit is not merely a neural pattern; it is a Dao that has been walked into a Li that has been consolidated into a Shī. The long-term smoker’s smoking is not merely a neural craving circuit; it is an identity position, a social protocol, a temporal structure, a relational mediator — a specific formation whose Shī includes the specific relational fields within which smoking is the natural move. Wang Fuzhi: qi first condenses and then form-pattern emerges. The habit’s pattern emerged from the specific qi of the specific encounters that produced it. Reshaping the scaffold addresses the surface of a formation whose depth the scaffold does not reach.

Challenge 17: The Behavioural Environment Needs a Relational Precondition Analysis

“"Relation precedes dynamics. The relational field that precedes the behavioural environment is not a given; it is a formation that determines what the behavioural environment can do."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (May 2026)

James’ wayshaping involves modifying the behavioural environment — the physical, social, and informational contexts in which behaviour occurs — to make desired behaviours more accessible. Shan’s challenge: the relational field that precedes the behavioural environment — the specific quality of the specific relationships within which the specific person inhabits the specific environment — determines what the behavioural environment can do. The same environmental scaffold in a relationship of trust and the same scaffold in a relationship of coercion produce structurally different behavioural responses. The relational field is prior to the environmental scaffold.

Challenge 18: The Identity Scale Needs Dao Tracing

James includes identity as one of the nested agents of the self-collective. Shan’s challenge: identity is not merely a scale that can be coordinated; it is the specific accumulated Li of the specific formation history. It was produced by a specific Dao. It carries a specific Shī. And it has a specific holding capacity for the specific challenge that the specific behaviour-change intervention represents. The identity that cannot hold the challenge of radical habit change will not be reshaped by a scaffold or a shock; it will be ruptured by it. The specific formation depth of the specific identity — the specific thickness of the specific Li — determines what the identity can receive without dissolution.

Challenge 19: The Temporal Commitment Scale Needs a Sequence Ontology

“"Temporal commitments are not agents competing for future time. They are the formation history’s articulation of what the formation’s Shī makes irreversible and what it makes available."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Prigogine’s arrow of time

James includes temporal commitments as nested agents competing for the person’s future time. Shan’s challenge: the temporal commitments are the formation’s specific articulation of irreversibility. The long-term relationship, the professional investment, the family commitment — each is a Dao walked to a specific depth, producing a specific Li with a specific Shī. The irreversibility is real: the formation cannot simply be unwound by a new scaffold. At the bifurcation, history enters. The temporal commitment’s Shī determines what future moves are available and what moves are foreclosed.

Challenge 20: The Shock-Scaffold Dialectic Needs Formation Sequencing

“"Scaffold before shock. Form the holding capacity before applying the dynamic loading. Test the formation’s grain before bringing the force to bear on it."”

— Shan, dialectical synthesis of Wayshaping’s two primary intervention modes

James treats scaffolds and shocks as two complementary intervention modes. Shan’s challenge is not to either individually but to their relationship: shocks require prior scaffolding to be formation-productive rather than formation-destructive. The Cao Zhi crisis: burning the bean-stalks to cook the beans. The scaffold builds the formation capacity that the shock will test. The shock applied before the scaffold has produced adequate formation capacity is the shock that destroys what it was designed to transform.

Challenge 21: Wayshaping’s Agency Concept Needs Relational Grounding

“"Agency is not a property of the individual self-collective. It is the specific relational achievement of the specific formation in the specific relational field."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s agency concept

James reconceptualises agency as distributed across the nested scales of the self-collective. Shan’s challenge: agency is not distributed across internal scales alone; it is constituted by the specific relational field within which the self-collective is embedded. The person’s capacity for the specific agency that specific behaviour change requires is not merely a function of internal coordination; it is a function of the specific relational field’s specific configuration. Wayshaping that targets internal coordination without attending to the relational field’s specific configuration will produce internal coordination achievements that the relational field continues to make behaviourally unavailable.

Challenge 22: The Multiscale Self Needs a Cross-Scale Li Analysis

“"The Li of the self-collective is not the sum of the Lis of its parts. It is the emergent grain produced by the specific relational configuration of the specific parts in the specific formation history."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Wayshaping’s multiscale ontology

James’ multiscale framework maps the self-collective across neural, bodily, social, and temporal scales. Shan’s challenge: the Li of the whole self-collective is not a function of the Lis of its constituent scales. It is the emergent grain produced by the specific relational configuration of the specific scales in the specific formation history. Xunzi: blue comes from indigo but is bluer than indigo. The self-collective’s Li exceeds the Lis of its parts because it is the product of the specific relational dynamics between parts. A wayshaping intervention targeting individual scales without attending to the inter-scale relational configuration will produce local scale changes without altering the cross-scale Li that determines the formation’s overall Shī.

Challenge 23: Wayshaping Needs a Collapse Theory

“"Wayshaping without a collapse theory is like navigation without an account of the cliff. The most important move in any formation is the move that prevents the narrowing from reaching the terminal."”

— Shan, dialectical challenge via Nothing Collapses in One Move (April 2026)

James’ wayshaping framework is primarily a framework for enhancing formation toward desired behaviour. Shan’s nothing-collapses-in-one-move account identifies the structure of formation pathology that wayshaping must also address. The self-collective that is narrowing toward collapse — whose scaffold has become a cage, whose alignment has become a pathological attractor, whose anticipation has closed off the adjacent possible — is the self-collective for which wayshaping’s enhancement-oriented tools are inadequate. The path narrows first. A complete wayshaping framework needs a diagnostic for the formation approaching the Clear-to-Chaotic boundary, not merely a toolkit for building the formation approaching the Complex-to-Clear boundary.

Challenge 24: The Three Wayshaping Concepts Need Formation-Sensitive Definitions

“"Wayfinding finds the available path. Waymaking creates the path. Wayshaping alters the landscape so paths emerge. But none of these is possible without the formation depth that makes the landscape legible in the first place."”

— Shan, dialectical synthesis of the three Wayshaping concepts

The distinction between wayfinding, waymaking, and wayshaping names three genuinely different relationships between the practitioner and the formation field. Shan’s challenge: all three presuppose a practitioner who can read the landscape adequately. The Polynesian navigator does not merely find available paths; their specific formation depth makes the wave-patterns’ actual Li legible. Without that formation depth — without the specific Dao of sustained formation-sufficient engagement with the specific landscape — all three modes reduce to guessing in the vocabulary of complexity.

Challenge 25: The Dao-Li-Shī Sequence Is Wayshaping’s Missing Foundation

“"Dao-sensitive wayshaping: trace the path, read the grain, read the positional force, assess the holding capacity, design the scaffold, calibrate the shock, build toward viable position. In that order. Always."”

— Shan, dialectical reconstruction of Wayshaping’s complete foundation

The synthesis: Wayshaping is a genuinely important advance. It reconceptualises the person as a formation rather than a rational actor, reconceptualises the environment as a formation field rather than a neutral container, and reconceptualises behaviour change as shaping rather than coercing. The Dao-Li-Shī deepening transforms it from a framework of behaviour change into a philosophy of formation-sensitive transformation.

Challenge 26: The Wayshaper Needs a Theory of Relational Formation History

“"Dao and Li were one way of seeing this. Relation and dynamics are another. The relational field is prior to both the self-collective and the environment."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (May 2026)

James’ wayshaping addresses the person-as-self-collective and the environment-as-affordance-structure. What it does not address is the relational formation history that produced both. The person’s self-collective was formed within specific relational fields that shaped its specific nested agencies. The affordance structure was produced by specific relational formations that preceded the person’s presence in it. Wayshaping that alters the affordance structure without tracing the relational formation history that produced it is wayshaping that redesigns the surface of a formation whose depth it has not walked.

Challenge 27: ‘Constructor’ Needs a Formation Account

“"A constructor enables a task to be performed repeatedly without loss of coherent structure. But what produces the constructor? What Dao produced the specific capacity that the constructor embodies?"”

— Shan, dialectical challenge to Constructor Theory’s role in Wayshaping

The Snowden extension of James’ wayshaping into Constructor Theory describes constructors as entities that enable tasks repeatedly while retaining capacity for further enabling. Shan’s challenge: the constructor in the formation-practice sense is not a given; it is an achievement of the specific Dao-walk that produced the specific practitioner’s specific structural capacity. Cook Ding’s knife is the material constructor formed by nineteen years of formation Dao-walking. Wayshaping that deploys constructors without accounting for the Dao that produced them is wayshaping that assumes the formation capacity it needs without addressing how that capacity was built.

Challenge 28: The Viability/Coherence Distinction Needs Shī

Snowden’s distinction between viable pathways (structurally sustainable) and coherent pathways (consistent with the formation’s own Li) is structurally important. Shan’s addition: both viability and coherence are functions of Shī. The viable pathway is the pathway whose formation has generated sufficient positional force to sustain itself. The coherent pathway is the pathway whose Li is consistent with the formation field’s accumulated Li. But both are moving targets: the Shī is generating new positional force continuously, and what was viable yesterday may not be viable tomorrow. Wayshaping that identifies viable and coherent pathways at a static moment has read the Li without reading the Shī that determines how the Li is moving.

Challenge 29: Affordance Management Needs Prior Formation Reading

James’ wayshaping involves managing affordances — the environmental features that make specific actions available or unavailable. Shan’s formation challenge: the affordance structure at any given moment is the Li of a long formation history. The affordance that makes a healthy behaviour accessible has been produced by a specific Dao of formation investment. Affordance management that does not trace the formation history that produced the current affordance structure treats the Li as a given rather than as the product of a specific Dao. The practitioner who has not walked the Dao is not accessible to the affordance, however well designed. The practitioner’s formation is the eye that reads the affordance. Without the eye, the affordance is a feature of the environment that the practitioner cannot use.

Challenge 30: The Self-Collective’s Nested Agencies Need a Shī Topology

“"Relation precedes dynamics. What matters is not which agents are present but what relational configuration they are in and what positional force that configuration generates."”

— Alice Jing Shan, Relation Precedes Dynamics (May 2026)

James’ self-collective maps the nested agencies as co-present agents that need to be coordinated. Shan’s challenge: the relational configuration of the nested agencies is prior to the agencies themselves. Each nested agency is in a specific relational configuration with every other — specific patterns of mutual reinforcement, mutual inhibition, mutual constitution. The specific topology of these relational configurations IS the specific Shī of the self-collective: the directional tendency produced by the specific formation history of the specific relational configurations. A wayshaping intervention that coordinates nested agencies without reading the specific Shī topology of their relational configuration coordinates the surface while the formation’s deeper relational dynamics continue to generate the patterns the intervention is trying to change.

Challenges 31–35: Five Final Incandescent Challenges

Challenge 31: Wayshaping’s three timescales (short, medium, long) need formation-sequence analysis: the formation time of each timescale determines what interventions are possible at that scale and what interventions will produce delayed collapse rather than sustained formation. The formation time for neural change is not the formation time for identity change; applying neural-scale scaffolds to identity-scale challenges produces the illusion of change without the formation depth.

Challenge 32: Wayshaping needs a theory of formation community: the self-collective does not form in isolation but in specific relational communities whose specific formation histories determine what formations the specific person can develop. The person trying to change a deeply entrenched habit while remaining in the relational field that produced and maintains that habit is the person for whom the best-designed scaffold will fail, because the relational field’s formation force exceeds the scaffold’s formation capacity.

Challenge 33: Weak-signal detection — which Snowden’s wayshaping invokes for substrate management — requires Shī-reading formation. The practitioner who cannot read the Shī of the formation field cannot distinguish genuinely weak signals (early formation indicators of structural change) from noise that the formation field’s own dynamics will amplify. Cook Ding at year one reads every contact with the ox as equally significant. Cook Ding at year nineteen reads the grain’s actual Li and knows which signals matter.

Challenge 34: Wayshaping’s substrate management needs a theory of substrate formation history. The substrate is not a neutral medium; it is the accumulated Li of all the formation histories that have passed through it. Every institutional substrate, every cognitive substrate, every social substrate carries the specific Shī of all the Daos that have been walked within it. The substrate that has been walked by formations organised around hierarchy will resist the wayshaping that tries to make horizontal collaboration naturally available, not because the wayshaping is wrong, but because the substrate’s accumulated Shī points in a different direction.

Challenge 35: The synthesis and the structural demand. The Dao-Li-Shī sequence is not one element among several in Wayshaping’s missing foundation. It IS the foundation: the ontological ground without which every E of the 6E model, every scaffold, every shock, every constructor deployment, every substrate modulation, every affordance management is a sophisticated Li applied without the Dao that would make it formation-adequate. Walk the Dao. Read the Li. Read the Shī. Assess holding capacity. Design scaffolds as proto-Daos. Calibrate shocks to formation depth. Build toward viable positions over time. This is the complete Dao-sensitive Wayshaping. And it connects James et al.’s sophisticated cognitive science to the deepest structural insights of the Chinese philosophical tradition: not as decoration but as genuine ontological grounding. The formation-sensitive practitioner has Cook Ding’s knife at year nineteen: it finds the hollow without force, the grain without resistance, the Shī without prediction. This is the Wayshaping that the framework gestures toward and does not yet reach.

❧ ✶ ❧
XL

Part XXI: Wayshaping’s Own Words — Shan Lets Loose A Maximum Dialectical Firework

The task here is surgical and unsparing. The following section uses James et al.’s own sentences — their most precise formulations, their most structurally revealing metaphors, their most honest moments of incompleteness — as the dialectical targets. Every quote is placed under Shan’s specific formation-theoretic pressure. The aim is not demolition but depth-charge: to find exactly where the framework goes deepest and where it stops short, and to say precisely what must be added for it to be structurally adequate to the problem it has correctly identified.

❧ ✶ ❧

The Wayshaping Framework in Its Own Words — A Forensic Shan Encounter

“"Wayshaping, at its most basic, is the practice of preparing ourselves here and now to meet our needs there and then."”

— Mark Michael James, Mushfiqa Jamaluddin, Tom Froese, Aisha Belhadi, Anna Panagiotou & Dave Snowden, Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

Here and now preparing to meet there and then: the most compressed and revealing formulation of the wayshaping concept. Shan endorses it and immediately presses it at its structural seam. ‘Here and now’ is a Li: the specific structural reading of the present formation that the practitioner carries with them into the preparation. ‘There and then’ is a Shī-reading: the practitioner’s assessment of the positional force that the formation is generating toward specific futures. Both of these — the reading of here and now AND the reading of there and then — are formation-dependent perceptions. The practitioner who has not walked the Dao of the specific formation field cannot accurately read here and now; they will project their prior Li. They cannot accurately read there and then; they will project their prior Shī.

The Hansel and Tom Sawyer examples that James uses — breadcrumbs to retrace the path, a kite string to navigate the cave — are structurally revealing in a way James does not fully inhabit. Hansel leaves breadcrumbs for a path ALREADY walked: the breadcrumbs are a record of the Dao, a material encoding of the Li produced by the specific traversal. Tom Sawyer’s kite string traces the formation of the cave as he walks it. Neither is ‘preparing here and now to meet there and then’ in the anticipatory sense. Both are recording the Dao as it is walked. This is actually the deeper version of wayshaping: not preparation for a predicted future, but formation-recording of the Dao being walked, so that the Li it produces can be traced and retraced. Shan’s challenge: the deeper wayshaping is not anticipation. It is formation fidelity. Keep the record of the Dao. Do not mistake the map for the territory. The breadcrumbs must be fresh: if they are eaten by birds, the Dao cannot be retraced.

“"We as individuals are better understood as complex forms of collective intelligence... at every level of our being – biological, psychological, social, and existential – we are comprised of nested intelligent, autonomous agents."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

The self-collective: James et al.’s most important structural contribution and Shan’s most productive site of forensic engagement. The four levels (biological, psychological, social, existential) constitute a taxonomy of nested agencies, and the taxonomy is structurally adequate as far as it goes. Shan’s challenge: the four levels are a spatial description of the self-collective’s structure at any given moment. They do not describe the temporal formation of the self-collective’s specific configuration. The biological level that this specific person inhabits is not the generic biological level; it is the specific accumulated Li of this specific body’s specific formation history — the specific cellular formations, the specific neural configurations, the specific somatic patterns that decades of walking specific Daos have produced. The psychological level is not the generic psychological level; it is the specific accumulated Li of this specific person’s specific habit-formation history. The social level is not generic; it is the specific relational field that this specific person has inhabited across their specific biographical Dao.

The Mencius Sprout Challenge: the four levels are not four simultaneously present domains. They are four temporal depths of the same formation. The biological level carries formation depths of years and decades. The psychological level carries formation depths of months and years. The social level carries formation depths of days and months. The existential level carries formation depths of moments and days. Each level is the specific accumulated sediment of the specific Daos that have been walked at that timescale. A wayshaping intervention that operates on all four levels simultaneously — without reading the specific temporal depth of the formation at each level — is a wayshaping intervention that does not know how old the formation is that it is attempting to change. Mencius’s four sprouts are not four simultaneously present characteristics; they are four developmental potentials at different stages of formation. Pulling the sprouts to accelerate their growth does not accelerate formation. It destroys the formation that was developing at the appropriate pace.

“"We are all modern-day changelings."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

The changeling metaphor is the most philosophically rich and the most structurally revealing image in the entire Wayshaping corpus. Shan endorses it completely and pushes it to its structural limit. The changeling of the 1600s was the person whose formation had been replaced by something else: something less capable (the ill child) or something more capable (the neurodivergent child) than the norm prescribed. In both cases, the changeling’s difference was experienced as a threat because the community’s Li — its accumulated formation expectations about what this specific person should be able to do — was violated by the changeling’s actual Li. The changeling’s burning is the most extreme available example of the Li-before-Dao trap: the community applies its prior Li (what a normal person should be) to a formation that has walked a different Dao and produced a different Li. The community’s response to its own Li’s inadequacy is not to walk the Dao of the changeling’s actual formation — but to destroy the formation that refuses to conform to the prior Li.

Shan’s formation challenge: James et al. use the changeling to illustrate the strangeness and inconsistency of the self. ‘We are all modern-day changelings’ means: our actual formation often exceeds or falls short of our intended formation. This is correct. The structural addition Shan requires: the changeling is not just inconsistent with its environment’s Li; it is the product of a Dao that the environment did not walk. The changeling who suddenly quits smoking after thirty years of failed attempts is not a changeling because something mysterious happened. They are a changeling because their formation has finally reached the specific threshold where the specific accumulated Li of the specific relational field has produced the specific Shī that makes the change not only possible but structurally inevitable. Nothing collapses in one move. The threshold of alignment was approached through a long formation of invisible structural preparation. The changeling is not mystery; it is formation depth suddenly becoming legible.

“"Resistance... isn’t a failure of willpower or knowledge, but of coordination. The current ecology of our habits and identities is simply unable to negotiate the formation of a new, better-attuned pattern."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

Resistance as coordination failure: the most structurally important claim in the Wayshaping framework and the one that most directly converges with Shan’s formation ontology. The current ecology of habits and identities is unable to negotiate the formation of a new pattern: this is Shan’s holding capacity claim stated as a negative. The formation that cannot hold the new pattern is the formation whose holding capacity is insufficient for the specific challenge that the new pattern represents. Not insufficient because of weakness of will. Insufficient because the formation has not yet walked the Dao that would produce the specific structural capacity adequate to holding the specific stress of the specific change.

But Shan’s most forensic challenge: ‘coordination’ is not adequate to explain resistance. Coordination is a description of what needs to happen. It is not an explanation of what makes coordination possible or impossible at any given moment. The self-collective whose nested agencies ‘cannot negotiate the formation of a new pattern’ is the self-collective whose specific accumulated Li at each level makes the specific coordination across levels structurally unavailable. And the accumulated Li at each level was produced by a specific Dao. To change the coordination, you must change the Li. To change the Li, you must walk the new Dao. James et al. say: we need better coordination. Shan says: you need the formation that makes the specific coordination possible. The coordination is downstream of the formation. Wayshaping targets coordination. Formation theory targets the formation that makes coordination possible.

“"When we experience ‘sudden gains’... they are likely not sudden at all. Rather, they are likely the result of prolonged, subconscious negotiations and processes of maturation that have finally reached a threshold of alignment."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

This is James et al.’s most formation-honest moment and the one where Shan’s framework and theirs are in deepest convergence. Sudden gains as the terminal threshold of long invisible formation: nothing collapses in one move. The change that appears sudden is the final move of a formation that has been narrowing toward this bifurcation through a long sequence of invisible accumulations. Cook Ding’s nineteenth year: the transformation appears complete in the moment of the final cut, but it was produced by eighteen years of cuts that preceded it. Tom’s quit smoking: the final ‘No more’ is the terminal Li of a formation that has been accumulating the specific structural capacity for that specific decision across months or years of subconscious formation work.

Shan’s productive challenge: if the ‘sudden gain’ is actually the terminal threshold of prolonged subconscious formation, then wayshaping faces its deepest structural problem. The practitioner who is working to produce the sudden gain cannot see the formation that is producing it, because it is subconscious and prolonged. They cannot know how long it will take or what specific Daos must be walked before the formation accumulates sufficient depth for the threshold to be reached. The interventions that feel most productive (the scaffold, the shock) may be least causally relevant; the interventions that feel most invisible (the sustained relational engagement, the repeated Dao-walk that produces no visible output) may be most causally decisive. Wayshaping’s tools target the visible surface of a formation whose depth is producing the transformation. The deepest wayshaping is the one that cannot see itself working.

“"Scaffolds are material and symbolic supports that put productive stress on a living system while also giving it something to organise its behaviour around. They can be temporary, like training wheels on a bicycle, or permanent, in that the new pattern depends on the ongoing presence of the support."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

Scaffolds as productive stress with organisational support: the most structurally precise definition in the Wayshaping lexicon, and the one that most directly invites Shan’s formation challenge. Productive stress: the scaffold operates not by doing the formation for the practitioner but by creating the specific stress that invites the specific formation response. The training wheels create the specific stress of balance-challenge while providing the specific support that prevents the specific failure mode (falling) that would interrupt the formation process. This is exactly Shan’s tensegrity: the scaffold maintains the tension that enables the formation without the compression that would collapse it.

The permanent scaffold distinction is the structurally consequential one. A scaffold that the new pattern permanently depends on is not a scaffold but a prosthetic: it has not produced a formation that can maintain itself independently of the support; it has produced a dependence. The distinction between a temporary scaffold (which invites formation that will eventually make the scaffold unnecessary) and a permanent scaffold (which produces a formation that cannot exist without the scaffold) is the distinction between formation and adaptation. Shan’s challenge: every scaffold must be evaluated not only for its effectiveness in producing the desired formation but for what it makes permanent — what dependence it installs alongside the formation it enables. The table that scaffolds our ability to write also installs a specific postural formation and a specific cognitive architecture that cannot be separated from the table’s presence. The mantra that scaffolds attention also installs a specific attention-management Li that becomes unavailable without the mantra. The proto-Dao of every scaffold includes the specific Li of the dependency it produces. Wayshaping that designs scaffolds without attending to their proto-Dao formations is wayshaping that is building dependencies it does not see.

“"Shocks... can play a generative role by momentarily breaking up existing stabilities, allowing the system to reconfigure into novel arrangements. This echoes Nassim Taleb’s notion of antifragility."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

Shocks as generative disruption: the most theoretically ambitious claim in the Wayshaping framework, and the one that most requires Shan’s holding-capacity corrective. The claim that shocks can break up existing stabilities and allow reconfiguration is correct under a specific condition that James et al. name but do not adequately theorise: the system must have sufficient holding capacity to metabolise the disruption rather than dissolve under it. Taleb’s antifragility is not a universal property of living systems; it is the specific property of systems that have developed the specific formation depth adequate to gaining from disorder. The system that gains from shock is the system whose formation has produced sufficient structural resilience to metabolise the disruption. The system that is destroyed by shock is the system whose holding capacity was inadequate for the specific level of disruption applied. The difference is entirely a function of formation depth.

Shan’s incandescent challenge: the psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy example James et al. use — ‘the substance induces the shock, while the therapeutic context scaffolds the experience, making positive outcomes more probable’ — is the most formation-honest example in the entire piece. The therapeutic context is not merely a scaffold for the experience; it is the specific relational formation condition that determines whether the shock is antifragile or traumatic. The same substance produces integration in one person and fragmentation in another not because of differences in pharmacology but because of differences in formation capacity — the specific holding capacity that the specific person’s specific formation history has or has not produced. The set and setting are not conditions added to the shock; they ARE the specific relational formation field without which the shock is simply violence. Shan’s sequence: formation, then shock. Holding capacity, then dynamic loading. The grain of the formation, then the force applied to it. In that order. Always.

“"When one habit changes, the ‘spill over’ effect is inevitable. Any change deforms the entire ecosystem, shifting the pressures on all other habits, which must then evolve toward new stabilities."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

The spillover effect as ecosystem deformation: the most structurally sophisticated claim in the Wayshaping framework, and the one that converges most directly with Shan’s relational-field ontology. When one habit changes, all other habits face altered relational pressures. This is relation-precedes-dynamics stated as change theory: the change in one element of the relational field constitutes a change in the relational field itself, and all elements of the field must renegotiate their positions relative to the new configuration. Tom’s smoking quit produced weight gain: not a side effect but a structural consequence. The specific relational configuration that had produced the smoking habit also produced a specific food-regulation pattern, a specific caloric management Li, a specific oral habit Li, all of which were maintained in their specific positions by the presence of the smoking formation. When the smoking formation changed, all of these renegotiated simultaneously.

Shan’s most structurally important addition: the spillover effect has a Shī. The deformation of the ecosystem does not distribute evenly across all habits; it concentrates in the habits whose specific Li was most structurally entangled with the specific Li of the habit that changed. Reading the spillover effect requires reading the specific relational topology of the self-collective’s formation — the specific web of mutual constraint and mutual reinforcement that makes specific habits vulnerable to specific spillover from specific changes in specific other habits. Without this topological reading, the wayshaper cannot predict where the spillover will appear, cannot assess whether the spillover will be productive (the instrument finding a new harmonic configuration) or destructive (the weight gain that will eventually produce its own health crisis), and cannot design the scaffold that would direct the spillover toward the desired new formation rather than the available one.

“"Wayshaping is always a relational process. The changes you make aren’t just shifting the possibility space for your own habits, but for the habits of the people around you and the systems you’re a part of."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

Wayshaping as always-already relational: this is the most important structural recognition in the entire Wayshaping corpus, and the one that is most inadequately developed in the framework. The claim is there. The theoretical weight it needs to carry is not. If wayshaping is always relational, then the ontological unit of wayshaping is not the individual self-collective but the relational field that constitutes the self-collective and the other self-collectives it is entangled with. The ‘scaffolding of the world’ that James invokes — ‘you scaffold the world’s right back’ — is precisely Shan’s claim: the practitioner does not inhabit the relational field as a visitor; they are the relational field locally expressed. Their change IS a change in the relational field. Their formation IS the formation of the relational field through them.

Shan’s ontological challenge: if wayshaping is always relational, then the practitioner who shapes their own formation is simultaneously (not sequentially) shaping the formation of every relational field they inhabit. The parent who changes their relationship to food changes the possibility space for their children’s food relationships — not as a spillover effect but as a direct relational formation event. The leader who changes their relationship to authority changes the possibility space for every person in their authority-relationship. The practitioner who changes their relationship to uncertainty changes the relational field of every professional encounter they inhabit. Relation precedes dynamics: the relational change is prior to the individual habit change that it appears to cause. The individual habit changes because the relational field has already shifted. The self-collective is the relational field expressed at the individual scale. Change the relational field first.

“"In short, both conceptually and practically, wayshaping scaffolds our capacity for self-scaffolding."”

— James et al., Self Transformation through a Relational Lens (2025)

The most architecturally honest formulation in the entire Wayshaping corpus: wayshaping is the scaffolding of self-scaffolding capacity. This is also, structurally, the most revealing point at which the framework arrives at its own limit. The capacity for self-scaffolding — the capacity to identify, design, and configure the specific scaffolds that will produce the specific formation one needs — is itself a formation achievement. It is the product of a Dao. It does not exist prior to having walked the Dao that produces it. Mark Bickhard’s framing that James cites: ‘the development of self-scaffolding skills is a fundamentally important field of development, at the core of essentially all domains.’ But Bickhard set the puzzle aside. James suggests wayshaping has solved it.

Shan’s most exacting challenge: wayshaping cannot scaffold the self-scaffolding capacity of a person who has not yet developed the formation depth adequate to using the scaffold. The training wheels work for the child who has the motor development, the proprioceptive formation, and the motivational formation adequate to using them. They do not produce cycling formation in a child who lacks these preconditions. Every scaffold works only for the formation that has already produced the capacity to use it. Wayshaping scaffolds the capacity for self-scaffolding ONLY in the practitioner whose formation has already produced sufficient holding capacity to metabolise the scaffold productively. The person who has not walked the Dao of the specific formation domain cannot use the scaffold that would accelerate the formation they need; they are precisely in the aporetic condition that requires not scaffold but Dao-walking. The framework cannot scaffold its way out of this. Only the Dao can walk into it. The final move of Wayshaping’s self-reflection reveals the Dao it still has not walked: the formation theory that explains what makes the self-scaffolding capacity available in the first place. That theory is Shan’s.

Supplementary Commentaries: Populating the Pasted Section with Formation Depth

The following commentaries provide full dialectical analysis and Shan’s specific formation challenge for each classical source, voice, and structural item listed in the paper’s bibliographic and closing sections. Where items already have brief treatment elsewhere in the paper, these commentaries provide the expanded formation-theoretic analysis that the brief treatment could not carry.

Fuller’s Cosmic Tensegrity: The Universe as One Structural Argument

“"The integrity of the universe is not a compromise; it is omni-triangulated."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.02
