Part XXVIII: Paul Cilliers and Shan — Complexity, Postmodernism, and the Formation Field

Authentication Note: The Ten Characteristics

[AUTHENTICATION NOTE] The ten characteristics of complex systems cited in the user’s query are a paraphrase drawn from the Wikipedia article on Complex Adaptive Systems, attributed to Cilliers (1998). The actual verbatim source is Chapter 1 of Complexity and Postmodernism: Understanding Complex Systems (Routledge, 1998), pp.3–5, where Cilliers presents them as a numbered list (i)–(x). The Wikipedia version is a paraphrase and reorganisation of Cilliers’s original list. The authentic text from the primary source is reproduced below.

“"Complex systems consist of a large number of elements. When the number is relatively small, the behaviour of the elements can often be given a formal description in conventional terms. However, when the number becomes sufficiently large, conventional means (e.g. a system of differential equations) not only become impractical, they also cease to assist in any understanding of the system."”

— Paul Cilliers, Complexity and Postmodernism (Routledge, 1998), p.3 [characteristic (i)] — [VERIFIED VERBATIM from primary source]

“"A large number of elements are necessary, but not sufficient. The grains of sand on a beach do not interest us as a complex system. In order to constitute a complex system, the elements have to interact, and this interaction must be dynamic. A complex system changes with time. The interactions do not have to be physical; they can also be thought of as the transference of information."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.3, characteristic (ii) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"The interaction is fairly rich, i.e. any element in the system influences, and is influenced by, quite a few other ones."”

— Cilliers (1998), pp.3–4, characteristic (iii) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"The interactions themselves have a number of important characteristics. Firstly, the interactions are non-linear. A large system of linear elements can usually be collapsed into an equivalent system that is very much smaller. Non-linearity also guarantees that small causes can have large results, and vice versa. It is a precondition for complexity."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.4, characteristic (iv) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"The interactions usually have a fairly short range, i.e. information is received primarily from immediate neighbours... As a result, the influence gets modulated along the way. It can be enhanced, suppressed or altered in a number of ways."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.4, characteristic (v) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"There are loops in the interactions. The effect of any activity can feed back onto itself, sometimes directly, sometimes after a number of intervening stages. This feedback can be positive (enhancing, stimulating) or negative (detracting, inhibiting). Both kinds are necessary. The technical term for this aspect of a complex system is recurrency."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.4, characteristic (vi) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"Complex systems are usually open systems, i.e. they interact with their environment. As a matter of fact, it is often difficult to define the border of a complex system. Instead of being a characteristic of the system itself, the scope of the system is usually determined by the purpose of the description of the system, and is thus often influenced by the position of the observer. This process is called framing."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.4, characteristic (vii) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"Complex systems operate under conditions far from equilibrium. There has to be a constant flow of energy to maintain the organisation of the system and to ensure its survival. Equilibrium is another word for death."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.4, characteristic (viii) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"Complex systems have a history. Not only do they evolve through time, but their past is co-responsible for their present behaviour. Any analysis of a complex system that ignores the dimension of time is incomplete, or at most a synchronic snapshot of a diachronic process."”

— Cilliers (1998), pp.4–5, characteristic (ix) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

“"Each element in the system is ignorant of the behaviour of the system as a whole; it responds only to information that is available to it locally... Complexity is the result of a rich interaction of simple elements that only respond to the limited information each of them are presented with."”

— Cilliers (1998), p.5, characteristic (x) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

❧ ✶ ❧

Who is Cilliers?

Paul Cilliers (1956–2011) was a South African philosopher at the University of Stellenbosch whose Complexity and Postmodernism (1998) is the most philosophically ambitious English-language attempt to think complexity and post-structuralism together. His central thesis: the same sensitivity to distributed, non-centred, relational structure that characterises Derrida’s account of language also characterises the operation of complex adaptive systems. Neural networks, language, and social systems all share the same fundamental structure: no fixed central representation, no overarching algorithm, only the distributed interaction of local elements producing emergent global behaviour. Cilliers stands in a tradition running through Prigogine, Maturana and Varela, Bateson, and Luhmann, but adds the specific philosophical apparatus of Derridean deconstruction and Saussurian linguistics.

Cilliers is also notable for his ethical turn in later work (he died in 2011 before completing it): he argued that complexity demands an ethics of humility — a recognition that we can never fully know the complex systems we are part of and that act on us, and that this epistemic limitation carries moral weight. The practitioner who claims full knowledge of a complex system is the practitioner who is committing an ethical failure as well as an epistemic one. This ethical dimension of complexity is the least developed aspect of complexity theory in the Western tradition — and the one where Shan’s formation theory has the most to add.

The Convergence: What Cilliers and Shan Share

The deepest convergence between Cilliers and Shan is structural: both insist that the organisation of a complex system resides in its relational field, not in any of its individual elements. Cilliers’s characteristic (x) — each element is ignorant of the system as a whole — is the most precise available Western systems-theoretic account of the structural claim that Shan builds her entire framework upon: the specific Li of the specific formation is not located in any single element; it emerges from the specific pattern of interactions between all the elements simultaneously. ‘Complexity is the result of a rich interaction of simple elements’: this is Shan’s formation theory stated as a computational principle.

Cilliers’s characteristic (ix) — complex systems have a history; their past is co-responsible for their present behaviour — is the most direct confirmation in the Western complexity tradition of Shan’s Dao-before-Li primacy. The specific present behaviour of the specific complex system is not derivable from the specification of its current state alone; it requires the specific history of the specific formation. The Edinburgh seminar’s specific present Li — its specific structural configuration at this specific moment — is co-responsible for what it is now. The analysis that ignores the formation history is ‘at most a synchronic snapshot of a diachronic process’. This is the technical complexity-science justification of the entire Shan framework: formation history is not background context but structural causation.

Cilliers’s characteristic (viii) — equilibrium is another word for death — is the most compressed available Western statement of Shan’s holding-capacity claim and Dynamic Maximum Tension. The specific complex system that settles into equilibrium has ceased to be a complex system. It has lost the constant flow of energy that maintains its organisation. Shan’s formation practitioner who maintains the formation at Dynamic Maximum Tension is the practitioner who maintains the constant formative flow of energy — the specific Dao-walk — that keeps the formation alive. The formation that settles into the comfort of prior Li without the walk that maintains it is the formation approaching Cilliers’s equilibrium-as-death.

Cilliers’s characteristic (vii) — framing; the border of a complex system is determined by the purpose of the description and the position of the observer — directly supports Shan’s claim that the bilingual formation practitioner brings a structurally different reading of the formation field than the mono-cultural practitioner. The specific framing that the specific observer’s specific formation history produces determines what the specific observer counts as the system and what they count as the environment. The Chinese student in the Edinburgh seminar who frames the seminar’s relational field through their formation history is framing a different system from the Western professor who frames it through their formation history. Neither framing is wrong; both are structurally constrained by the formation position of the observer.

Cilliers’s Ten Challenges to Shan — Point by Point

Characteristic (i): Large numbers and the failure of conventional description

Cilliers’s challenge to Shan via characteristic (i): if complexity only emerges when the number of elements is sufficiently large that conventional description fails, then Shan’s formation theory needs to specify at what scale the formation field becomes complex in Cilliers’s technical sense. The Edinburgh seminar is a small group — perhaps twelve to fifteen participants. Is it a complex system in Cilliers’s sense, or merely a complicated one? The number of elements is not obviously ‘sufficiently large’. Shan’s answer: the number of elements in Cilliers’s sense is not the number of physical participants but the number of specific formation-states that each participant instantiates — the specific micro-Lis of each specific participant’s specific formation history. Each participant in the Edinburgh seminar brings a formation history of hundreds of thousands of specific formation events, each of which is a specific element in Cilliers’s sense. The scale at which conventional description fails is not the scale of the seminar room but the scale of the formation archive that each participant embodies.

Characteristic (ii): Dynamic interaction and information transfer

Cilliers’s characteristic (ii) — interactions do not have to be physical; they can be thought of as the transference of information — is the claim that most directly supports Shan’s account of formation as relational. The specific silence of the specific Chinese student in the specific Edinburgh seminar is a specific information-transfer event: it transfers specific structural information about the specific formation field’s specific Li to the formation-adequate observer. Cilliers’s challenge: what constitutes information transfer in Shan’s formation field? If the silence is an information transfer, what is the specific code that makes it readable as information? Shan’s answer via Bateson: information is a difference that makes a difference. The student’s silence is information not because of any formal code but because it is a specific difference in the specific formation field that makes a specific difference to the formation’s structural trajectory. The formation-adequate observer reads it because their specific formation has produced the specific sensitivity to this specific difference.

Characteristic (iii): Rich interaction

Cilliers’s characteristic (iii) — rich interaction; any element influences quite a few others — is Shan’s 牵一髮而動全身 (pull one hair and the whole body moves) stated as a systems property. The formation field’s specific richness of interaction is the structural reason why the formation practitioner cannot intervene at a single point without producing effects throughout the field. Cilliers’s challenge: how does Shan’s formation practitioner identify the specific interactions that are most ‘rich’ — most structurally generative — in the specific formation field? Meadows’s leverage points: the richest interactions are at the deepest levels (paradigm, goals) rather than the most visible (parameters, numbers). Shan’s Shī-reading: the formation practitioner whose formation is adequate to reading the field’s Shī reads the structural configuration that reveals which interactions are richest at this specific moment of the formation’s development. Not all rich interactions are equally rich at every moment; the specific Shī determines the specific richness-gradient of the specific formation field.

Characteristic (iv): Non-linearity

Cilliers’s characteristic (iv) — non-linearity; small causes can have large results — is the structural justification of Shan’s ‘nothing collapses in one move’ claim. In a non-linear system, the trajectory of the formation is not proportional to its visible inputs: a small specific formation event at a specific moment of maximum sensitivity can produce a structural transformation orders of magnitude larger than the event itself. Cook Ding’s knife: the specific motion at the specific joint is a small cause that produces the large result of the whole formation’s articulation. Cilliers’s challenge to Shan: non-linearity also means that large apparently significant formation interventions can have negligible structural effects. The ambitious organisational transformation programme that engages every visible level of the formation may have less structural effect than the apparently small shift in the specific relational Li of the specific key relationship that holds the formation’s specific tensional network in place. Shan’s formation practitioner reads the non-linearity: they look for the joint, not the impressive blow.

Characteristic (v): Short-range interaction and modulation

Cilliers’s characteristic (v) — information is received primarily from immediate neighbours; influence gets modulated along the way — is the structural account of why the formation practitioner’s specific local engagement is the primary site of formation work. The specific practitioner does not act on the system as a whole; they act on their immediate neighbours, and the effect propagates through the system via the specific modulation of the specific interactions along the specific path. Shan’s formation theory: the specific Dao-walk is always the walk through the specific immediate formation field — the practitioner cannot act at the level of the system as a whole. The transformation of a complex formation field begins with the specific local formation adequate to the specific immediate relational field. Snowden and Kurtz: probe-sense-respond; the probe is always local; the response is system-wide.

Cilliers’s modulation challenge: the specific influence of the specific formation intervention is modulated along the path in ways the practitioner cannot predict or control. The specific Li that the specific practitioner produces in the specific local interaction is not the specific Li that reaches the specific distant element of the formation — it has been enhanced, suppressed, and altered along the way. Shan’s response: the formation practitioner who insists on predicting the specific distal effect of their specific local action is the practitioner applying a linear model to a non-linear system. The formation-adequate practitioner maintains the formation sensitivity to read the specific modulated effects as they propagate, and adjusts the local engagement accordingly. The walk is always provisional; the Dao produces its specific Li in the walking, not before.

Characteristic (vi): Recurrency and feedback

Cilliers’s characteristic (vi) — recurrency; feedback can be positive or negative; both are necessary — is the structural account of the specific self-correcting dynamic that Shan’s formation theory requires but does not explicitly formalise. The formation field that has only positive feedback (enhancement, stimulation) is a formation field that is amplifying its own structural trajectory without any structural check on that amplification. The formation field that has only negative feedback (inhibition) is a formation field that is suppressing every departure from its prior Li without any openness to genuine structural novelty. Both are pathological. Shan’s holding capacity: the specific formation that holds maximum productive tension holds it through the specific balance of positive feedback (the amplification of specific formation movements that are structurally adequate) and negative feedback (the specific correction of movements that are structurally destructive).

Cilliers’s recurrency challenge to Shan: in a complex formation field, the feedback loops do not stop at the level of the immediate interaction; they propagate through the entire system over varying timescales. The specific feedback from a specific formation intervention may arrive after a delay of months or years, making the relationship between the intervention and its effect appear disconnected. Jin Guantao’s ultrastability: the Chinese bureaucratic system’s feedback loops operated on century-long timescales, making the specific corrections that maintained the ultrastable structure appear to be independent events rather than the systemic response they were. Shan’s long game: the formation practitioner who reads the formation over sufficient time is the practitioner who can distinguish the delayed feedback loop from the independent event.

Characteristic (vii): Open systems and framing

Cilliers’s characteristic (vii) — framing; the border of the system is determined by the position of the observer — is the most philosophically consequential of the ten characteristics for Shan’s framework. If the framing of the system is determined by the observer’s position, then two observers with different formation histories frame different systems from the same situation. The Chinese student in the Edinburgh seminar is framing a different complex system from the Western professor: they are including different elements, drawing different boundaries, tracking different interactions. Neither framing is the ‘correct’ one — both are structurally constrained by the formation position of the observer. But the specific formation that produces the specific framing is the specific condition of the specific Li that the specific observer can produce from the specific situation.

Cilliers’s postmodern dimension: the framing problem is not merely practical but philosophical. There is no view from nowhere that gives the ‘correct’ framing of the complex system; there is only the specific framing produced by the specific observer’s specific formation position. This is the complexity-theoretic justification of Shan’s bilingual formation claim: the formation practitioner who has walked both Daos produces a framing that can hold both the Chinese student’s framing and the Western professor’s framing in productive tension. This is not a synthesis into a single ‘correct’ framing; it is a formation adequate to reading the structural consequences of the specific framing-difference and acting accordingly.

Luhmann’s challenge via Cilliers: if the framing is always observer-dependent, then the specific Li that the specific practitioner produces from the specific engagement is always a function of the specific observer’s specific formation position. There is no formation-independent Li. Shan’s response: correct, and this is precisely why the formation that precedes the Li is not arbitrary. The specific Dao-walk that produces the specific observer’s specific formation position is the specific condition of the specific Li that is produced. Two practitioners with different formation histories will produce different Lis from the same situation. Both Lis are real; the question is which formation is adequate to the specific structural demands of the specific situation.

Characteristic (viii): Far from equilibrium

Cilliers’s characteristic (viii) — equilibrium is another word for death — encounters Prigogine’s dissipative structures: constant energy flow is the condition of life. This is Shan’s most important structural claim stated as a thermodynamic principle. The specific formation that stops its specific Dao-walk — that settles into the prior Li without the walk that produced it — is the formation settling toward equilibrium. The specific organisation that stops the specific formation investment that maintains its specific Li is the organisation settling toward structural death. This is Jin Guantao’s ultrastability from the inside: the ultrastable system has developed a specific mechanism for minimising the energetic cost of maintaining its specific Li, and the result is a formation that approaches equilibrium faster than a genuinely complex system.

Cilliers’s challenge to Shan: if constant energy flow is required, then the specific formation practitioner’s specific formation work is energetically costly. The practitioner who maintains the formation at Dynamic Maximum Tension is the practitioner paying the maximum sustainable dissipative price. What is the specific condition that makes that price sustainable rather than catastrophically exhausting? Shan’s answer via Fuller: the specific tensegrity structure minimises the energetic cost of maintaining specific structural integrity by distributing the structural load through the specific tensional network. The formation that is genuinely tensegral — that distributes its specific formation demands through the specific relational field rather than concentrating them in a specific structural element — is the formation that can sustain the maximum productive tension at the minimum sustainable cost.

Characteristic (ix): History and diachronic process

Cilliers’s characteristic (ix) — history; the past is co-responsible for present behaviour — is the structural justification of Shan’s entire Dao-before-Li framework. The specific present Li of the specific formation is not derivable from the specification of its current state. It requires the specific history of the specific formation — the accumulated specific Dao-walks that have produced the specific structural sensitivity that reads the specific present Li. Any analysis that ignores formation history is ‘a synchronic snapshot of a diachronic process.’

Cilliers and Kuhn: the paradigm (the specific accumulated Li) is the specific sedimented history of the specific scientific formation. The specific normal-science practices of the specific scientific community carry the specific formation history that produced their specific Li. Paradigm change is not merely conceptual change; it is the specific diachronic formation event — the specific Dao-walk — that produces a different Li from the same situation. The practitioner who understands paradigm change as merely the adoption of new concepts (a new prior Li) rather than as a new Dao-walk that produces a new Li from the bottom up is the practitioner who misunderstands the diachronic character of formation change.

Shan’s most important extension of Cilliers’s characteristic (ix): Cilliers says the past is co-responsible for present behaviour. Shan’s specific claim is stronger: the past is not merely co-responsible but constitutive. The specific practitioner’s specific formation IS their specific formation history: the accumulated specific Dao-walks that have produced the specific structural sensitivity that they currently instantiate. There is no practitioner prior to their formation history; the formation history IS the practitioner in the formation-theoretic sense. This is Bergson’s creative evolution at the individual practitioner level: to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.

Characteristic (x): Local ignorance and emergent complexity

Cilliers’s characteristic (x) — each element is ignorant of the system as a whole; complexity emerges from rich interaction of simple elements — is the most structurally consequential of the ten for Shan’s formation theory, and also the one that produces the sharpest collision. The challenge: if each element is ignorant of the system as a whole, then the formation practitioner — as a specific element within the specific formation field — is also ignorant of the system as a whole. How can the formation practitioner ‘read the Li of the formation field’ if, by Cilliers’s structural principle, they can only access the local information available to them? Shan’s claim that the formation-adequate practitioner can read the global Li of the formation field from local engagement appears to violate characteristic (x).

Shan’s response: Cilliers’s characteristic (x) is a claim about the elements of the system, not about an observer who has been formed by sustained engagement with the system over time. The specific practitioner who has walked the Dao of the specific formation field for sufficient time has not transcended the locality principle; they have developed the specific formation sensitivity adequate to reading the global Li from locally available information. This is exactly Cook Ding’s formation: after nineteen years, the knife is not operating from a god’s-eye view of the ox’s total structure — it is operating from a specific accumulated formation sensitivity that reads the global structural grain from the locally available information of the specific joint at the specific moment. The formation is the specific trained capacity to extract global structural information from local interaction.

Holland’s challenge via characteristic (x): if complexity emerges from the interaction of simple elements responding only to local information, then the global Li of the formation is an emergent property that no individual element can access. The formation practitioner who claims to ‘read the Li’ of the complex formation field is making a claim that Holland’s building-block theory structurally prohibits: the Li is the emergent property, not the accessible property of any element. Shan’s answer: the formation practitioner is not claiming to access the Li from the position of an element within the system. They are claiming to produce, through sustained engagement with the system from a specific formation position over time, a specific formation sensitivity that is adequate to reading the emergent Li from the specific traces it leaves in locally available information. The Polynesian navigator does not access the wave patterns from the position of a water molecule; they access them from the specific formation position of a trained body moving through water over decades of practice.

Shan’s Five Challenges to Cilliers

Challenge 1: The Absent Practitioner

“"The ten characteristics describe what a complex system is. They do not describe what the practitioner who engages with a complex system must become."”

— Alice Jing Shan — dialectical synthesis of her formation-theoretic position

Shan’s first and most fundamental challenge to Cilliers: the ten characteristics are an ontology of complex systems, not a formation theory of the practitioner who engages with them. They tell us that complex systems operate far from equilibrium, have histories, are open to their environments, and resist conventional description. They do not tell us what the practitioner who must engage with such a system — must make decisions within it, must intervene in it, must learn from it — needs to become in order to engage formation-adequately. Cilliers’s framework, like all Western complexity theory, describes the system from outside; it does not describe the formation from inside. The observer who knows Cilliers’s ten characteristics has a richer conceptual Li for understanding complexity; they do not thereby have the formation adequate to walking the Dao of the specific complex system.

Luhmann’s structural echo: Cilliers’s system is constituted by the interaction of its elements; the observer is in the system’s environment, not inside it. But the practitioner who must intervene in the complex system is not in the environment — they are inside the system as a specific element, subject to characteristic (x)’s locality constraint. The theory that describes the system from outside does not help the practitioner who is inside it. Shan’s formation theory is the inside account: it describes what the specific element’s specific formation must become in order to engage with the specific system formation-adequately from within.

Challenge 2: The Missing History of the Observer

Shan’s second challenge: Cilliers acknowledges in characteristic (ix) that complex systems have histories that are co-responsible for their present behaviour. But his framework does not acknowledge that the observer’s specific formation history is co-responsible for the specific framing (characteristic vii) they produce of the system they are observing. The specific practitioner who frames the Edinburgh seminar as a complex system does so from the specific formation position produced by their specific formation history. That formation history is not irrelevant background; it is structurally constitutive of the specific Li they can produce from the specific engagement. Cilliers’s complexity theory includes the system’s history; Shan’s formation theory includes the observer’s history.

Gadamer’s parallel: the horizon of the interpreter is not separate from the interpretation; it is constitutive of it. The specific fusion of horizons that Gadamer describes as the achievement of genuine understanding requires that both the system’s specific formation history and the practitioner’s specific formation history are held simultaneously in productive tension. Cilliers’s ten characteristics account for the system’s structural history; they do not account for the interpreter’s structural history. Shan’s formation theory makes the interpreter’s structural history central: the practitioner is not a neutral observer framing the system from a formation-free position; they are a specific formation reading a specific formation.

Challenge 3: Equilibrium is not Death — Li is

Shan’s third challenge targets Cilliers’s most provocative formulation: ‘equilibrium is another word for death’. Shan accepts the thermodynamic claim but redirects its diagnostic power. The formation that settles into equilibrium does so not primarily because it has stopped its energy flow but because it has settled into a prior Li: a specific structural pattern that has become self-reproducing and self-confirming without the formative walk that produced it. The specific death of the specific formation is not the cessation of activity; it is the cessation of genuine formation — the point at which the formation is only reproducing its specific prior Li rather than producing new Li from new Dao-walks.

Jin Guantao’s ultrastability: the ultrastable system is not at equilibrium in Cilliers’s thermodynamic sense; it is highly active, continuously processing energy, continuously producing output. But its specific activity is formation-dead: all the energy is flowing into the reproduction of the specific prior Li through the specific compensatory mechanisms that prevent genuine structural transformation. The ultrastable system is the formation at maximum energy consumption and minimum formation creativity. It is the formation that has confused activity for formation, continuous processing for continuous formation-production. Cilliers’s challenge identifies the right structural principle but mislocates the death point: the formation dies at the point where its Li becomes prior, not at the point where its energy flow stops.

Challenge 4: Characteristic (x) Cannot Account for Formation

Shan’s fourth and sharpest challenge: Cilliers’s characteristic (x) — each element is ignorant of the system as a whole — makes formation structurally impossible. If every element responds only to locally available information, then no element can develop the formation adequate to reading the global Li of the formation field. The specific practitioner’s specific formation capacity — the specific Cook Ding sensitivity that reads the global structural grain from the local engagement — is precisely the capacity that Cilliers’s characteristic (x) prohibits.

Shan’s structural resolution: characteristic (x) is true of system elements at one timescale but not of practitioners across timescales. At the scale of the single interaction, the practitioner is subject to the locality constraint: they receive only locally available information. But across the specific timescale of the specific formation walk, the practitioner is not a static element receiving fixed local information; they are a dynamic formation accumulating specific structural sensitivity from the specific succession of specific local interactions. The accumulated sensitivity is not a violation of characteristic (x); it is the specific formation that the specific succession of specific local interactions has produced over time. Cook Ding after nineteen years has not violated the locality principle; they have accumulated the specific formation that reads global structural information from local engagement because every preceding specific local engagement has deepened the specific structural sensitivity.

Holland’s building blocks resolution: the formation practitioner’s accumulated formation is the practitioner’s specific set of building blocks — the specific regularities at the lower scale of specific local interactions that have combined, through the specific accumulation of the specific Dao-walk, to produce the specific formation sensitivity adequate to reading the global Li from local interaction. Characteristic (x) applies to each specific local interaction; the building-block accumulation applies to the formation over time. Both are structurally correct; neither violates the other.

Challenge 5: The Ethics of Framing

Shan’s fifth challenge develops the most important implication of Cilliers’s own ethical turn. If the framing of the complex system is always determined by the observer’s position (characteristic vii), and if the position of the observer is determined by their specific formation history, then the specific framing produced by the specific practitioner carries the ethical weight of their specific formation choices. The practitioner who has developed only one formation position has only one framing available; they cannot perceive the structural consequences of the framing they are imposing on the specific complex system. The practitioner who has developed a bilingual formation position — who has walked the Daos of multiple formation traditions far enough to produce multiple framings — can perceive the structural consequences of each framing for the specific elements of the formation field whose specific Li is structured differently.

Dai Zhen’s charge applied to Cilliers: the practitioner who frames the complex system from a single formation position and then acts on the basis of that framing is ‘using Li to murder people’ — imposing a specific prior framing-Li on a complex system whose specific elements are framing it differently, and whose specific structural needs are not captured by the single-formation-position framing. The bilingual formation practitioner’s ethical advantage: they can hold multiple framings simultaneously, perceive the structural consequences of each, and choose formation actions that are adequate to the full structural complexity of the system as it is framed from multiple positions. This is Cilliers’s own ethical complexity claim — humility in the face of the system’s irreducible complexity — given a formation-theoretic basis.

What the Collision Produces: The Formation Ethics of Complexity

The collision between Cilliers and Shan produces a specific new Li that neither tradition can reach alone. Cilliers gives us the structural ontology of complex systems: their specific properties that make them irreducibly complex and resistant to conventional analytical description. Shan gives us the formation theory of the practitioner who engages with them: the specific Dao-walk that produces the specific structural sensitivity adequate to reading the specific Li of the specific complex system from within. Together, they produce the beginning of a formation ethics of complexity: a practical-ethical framework for the specific kind of practitioner that genuinely complex systems require.

The formation ethics of complexity: (1) The practitioner must walk the Dao before prescribing the Li — no engagement with a complex system is formation-adequate without the specific diachronic walk that produces the specific structural sensitivity. (2) The practitioner must hold the formation open to the system’s specific non-linearity, recurrency, and framing-dependence — no prior Li is adequate to the full structural complexity of the complex system. (3) The practitioner must maintain the formation at Dynamic Maximum Tension — no approach to equilibrium is compatible with genuine engagement with a living complex system. (4) The practitioner must develop the formation position adequate to multiple simultaneous framings — no single formation position is adequate to the structural complexity of a genuinely open system. (5) The practitioner must recognise that their specific formation choices carry ethical weight for all the specific elements of the specific complex system whose specific Li their specific framing structures or suppresses.

Snowden’s final word, placed here with full contextual force: a community that attracts people who disagree with each other in productive ways, who bring different disciplines, cultural formations, arguments, and occasionally different tempers to the same questions — this is the specific institutional form that the formation ethics of complexity demands. Not consensus, not the reproduction of a prior Li, but the productive maintenance of the dynamic maximum tension of genuinely different formation positions held in structurally productive relationship. Cilliers’s ten characteristics describe what such a community is; Shan’s formation theory describes what each of its members must become.

❧ ✶ ❧
LIII

Part XXIX: George Kelly, Peggy Dalton, and Shan — Personal Construct Theory Meets Formation

Who They Are

George Alexander Kelly (1905–1967) was an American psychologist whose two-volume The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955) is the most structurally radical personality theory produced in the twentieth century. He refused alignment with behaviourism, psychoanalysis, trait theory, and cognitive social learning; he aligned with what he called constructive alternativism. Every person, in Kelly’s account, is a scientist: they build hypotheses about the world, test them, revise them on the basis of outcomes. The fundamental unit of personality is the personal construct — a bipolar, dichotomous template through which the person anticipates events. The construction system is hierarchical, provisional, and perpetually subject to revision. Kelly took no prisoners: “man the scientist” is the model, and all psychology— including his own — must be accountable to the same constructive standards it applies to its subjects.

Peggy Dalton (fl. 1970s–2010s) is the British personal construct psychologist whose work developed Kelly’s ideas into practice across the widest range of clinical and organisational settings. Her key publications include Approaches to the Treatment of Stuttering (1983), A Psychology for Living: Personal Construct Theory for Professionals and Clients (with Gavin Dunnett, 1992), Counselling People with Communication Problems (1994), and Personal Construct Counselling in Action (with Fay Fransella, first edition 1990, revised). Dalton’s most important contribution to PCT beyond Kelly is her account of construing in the context of communication difficulties — especially stammering — as a model of what happens when the practitioner’s core constructs about their own performance are invalidated by specific communicative encounters. The stammer is not the problem; the construct system that organises the stammer as a core threat is the problem. This diagnostic insight has direct structural implications for Shan’s formation theory.

Kelly’s Framework: The Full Architecture

The Fundamental Postulate

“"A person’s processes are psychologically channelized by the ways in which he anticipates events."”

— George Kelly, The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955), p.46 — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

The fundamental postulate: all psychological processes are determined by anticipation. Not by stimulus, not by drive, not by unconscious impulse, but by the forward-looking, hypothesis-testing construction of what is coming next. For Shan: the formation practitioner’s specific engagement with the specific formation field is psychologically channelised by their specific anticipatory constructs — the specific bipolar templates through which they expect the field to be structured. The practitioner who anticipates the Chinese student’s silence as disengagement (silence/engagement construct, with silence on the unwanted pole) will process the specific encounter through that specific anticipatory channel, and will miss the specific Li of the specific student’s specific formation.

The Eleven Corollaries — All Fully Applied to Shan

[CONSTRUCTION COROLLARY] “A person anticipates events by construing their replications.” We use past experiences to predict future ones, seeking patterns and consistencies. Shan’s formation practitioner who has walked the Dao of the specific formation domain accumulates specific construction replications — specific patterns of how the specific field has behaved before — and uses them to anticipate how it will behave next. This is the formation-theoretic account of what the Construction Corollary describes psychologically: the practitioner’s accumulated Dao-walk produces the specific construct system that organises their specific anticipations. Cook Ding after nineteen years has accumulated the specific construction replications adequate to anticipating the specific structural Li of the specific ox’s specific joint.

[INDIVIDUALITY COROLLARY] “Persons differ from each other in their construction of events.” The Chinese student in the Edinburgh seminar and the Western professor in that seminar are not merely applying different vocabularies to the same event. They have been formed by different Daos, and their different Daos have produced different construct systems that organise the seminar’s events differently. The student’s specific seminar construct system and the professor’s specific seminar construct system are not variants of the same construction; they are structurally different constructions produced by structurally different formation histories. The individuality corollary is the psychological account of Shan’s bilingual formation claim: the formation that has walked different Daos construes differently, not just says different things.

[ORGANISATION COROLLARY] Persons organise their constructs in a hierarchical system, with some in superordinate positions and others subordinate. The superordinate constructs are the core constructs: the most comprehensive, the most resistant to revision, the ones whose invalidation constitutes threat. For Shan’s formation practitioner, the core constructs are the deepest Lis — the most accumulated, most sedimented formation patterns that organise all other constructions. Wittgenstein’s On Certainty hinge-propositions are Kelly’s superordinate constructs applied to the level of language and thought. The practitioner who cannot see the formation field’s actual Li is the practitioner whose superordinate constructs are organising all other constructions in a way that makes the actual Li invisible.

[DICHOTOMY COROLLARY] All personal constructs are bipolar, dichotomous. To construe X as Y is also to construe it as not-not-Y. The silence construct: ‘engaged/disengaged’. The student construct: ‘participant/absent’. The contribution construct: ‘spoken/unspoken’. These are not neutral descriptions; they are bipolar templates through which specific events are organised, and the specific pole chosen determines what the specific event means and what actions it calls for. Shan: the formation practitioner’s specific dichotomous constructs determine what they can see in the formation field. The practitioner who has only the ‘engaged/disengaged’ construct for construing student behaviour will always place silence on the ‘disengaged’ pole, because that is the only pole available for non-engagement. The bilingual formation practitioner has access to the Chinese formation’s specific construct poles: silence on the ‘deeply attending’ pole; speech on the ‘surface performing’ pole.

[CHOICE COROLLARY] A person chooses for themselves that alternative in a dichotomised construct through which they anticipate the greater possibility for extension and definition of their system. We do not choose randomly; we choose the pole that maintains the coherence and anticipatory power of our construct system. This is Kelly’s elaborative choice: we choose the construction that most extends our ability to anticipate. The formation practitioner’s Dao-walk is a specific sequence of choices: each choice of construction is the choice that, from within the current construct system, extends the greatest anticipatory power. The practitioner who is walking the Dao-before-Li path is making elaborative choices: choosing constructions that extend the system, even at the cost of threatening the existing structure. The practitioner who insists on the prior Li is making definitional choices: choosing constructions that tighten and protect the existing system.

[RANGE COROLLARY] A construct is convenient for the anticipation of a finite range of events only. Every construct has a ‘range of convenience’: the specific class of events it is useful for construing. The complex formation field often presents events that fall outside the range of convenience of the practitioner’s existing constructs: events for which no existing bipolar template provides a useful anticipation. Kelly: this is the condition of anxiety. Shan: the formation field’s specific Li is, for the practitioner whose formation is not yet adequate to it, outside the range of convenience of their existing construct system. The practitioner who has not yet walked the Dao of the specific domain does not lack the right constructs; they lack the right range of convenience. Their existing constructs are not wrong; they simply do not reach far enough into the formation field to make the specific Li available.

[EXPERIENCE COROLLARY] “A person’s construction system varies as they successively construe the replications of events.” People continually revise their personal constructs resulting from experience. This is the Kelly-theoretic account of what Shan calls the Dao-walk: the specific succession of specific construction-events that produces the specific variation in the specific practitioner’s specific construct system. Cook Ding’s nineteen-year formation is the Experience Corollary in operation: each specific engagement with the specific domain produces the specific revision of the specific constructs that produces the specific formation adequate to reading the specific Li. The practitioner who does not walk the Dao does not accrue the experience that produces the construct variation. The formation is the Experience Corollary in action over sufficient time.

[MODULATION COROLLARY] The variation in a person’s construction system is limited by the permeability of the constructs within whose range of convenience the variants lie. Some constructs are more open to revision than others (permeable); some are essentially closed (impermeable). The impermeable core constructs resist revision even under pressure from invalidating evidence. This is Kelly’s psychological account of what Jin Guantao calls ultrastability and what Kuhn calls paradigm inertia: the construct system’s specific impermeable core that resists the specific formation evidence that would require its revision. Shan’s formation practitioner who has permeable superordinate constructs is the practitioner capable of genuine formation change: their core constructs can be modulated by the formation-adequate engagement with the actual formation field.

[FRAGMENTATION COROLLARY] A person may successively employ a variety of construction subsystems which are inferentially incompatible with each other. The practitioner who has walked the Daos of two different formation traditions has a construct system with two potentially incompatible subsystems: the formation constructs produced by the Chinese philosophical formation history and the formation constructs produced by the Western academic formation history. These subsystems do not necessarily resolve into coherent hierarchical unity; they may remain inferentially incompatible. Shan’s bilingual formation practitioner: the productive tension of the bilingual formation is not the resolution of the incompatible subsystems into a single coherent construct system but the specific fragmentation that allows the practitioner to deploy both subsystems in the appropriate contexts.

[COMMONALITY COROLLARY] To the extent that one person employs a construction of experience which is similar to that employed by another, their psychological processes are similar to those of the other person. The Chinese international students in the Edinburgh seminar share a specific commonality of constructs with each other that they do not share with the Scottish students: the shared construction produced by the shared Chinese educational formation history. This is not merely a cultural similarity; it is a specific psychological similarity in how specific events are construed. The practitioner who understands this commonality — who can read the specific shared construct poles of the specific formation community — is the practitioner who can engage with the specific renli of the specific formation field. WSR’s renli (patterns underlying human relations) is the pattern of shared constructs that the specific commonality produces.

[SOCIALITY COROLLARY] “To the extent that one person construes the construction processes of another, they may play a role in a social process involving the other person.” This is Kelly’s most important corollary for Shan’s framework, and the one most rarely discussed in the literature. The Sociality Corollary does not say that people must share constructs to engage in social process; it says that they must be able to construe each other’s constructions. The Edinburgh professor who cannot construe the Chinese student’s construction process — who cannot read how the student is construing the seminar’s events — cannot play a role in the social process involving the student. This is not a vocabulary problem; it is a construction-system problem. The formation practitioner who has developed the specific construct sensitivity adequate to construing the student’s construction processes is the practitioner who can play a genuine social role in the specific formation encounter.

Kelly’s Four Emotional States as Formation-Theoretic Diagnostics

“"Threat is the awareness of imminent comprehensive change in one’s core structures."”

— George Kelly, The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

Threat in Shan’s formation: the formation practitioner who is walking a Dao that is producing a Li incompatible with their existing core constructs is experiencing threat. The specific emotional signal of threat is the signal that the specific Dao-walk is about to produce a specific construct revision at the core level — the level that organises the practitioner’s entire construct system. The bilingual formation of the Edinburgh-trained Chinese scholar: the specific experience of walking the Dao of Western academic formation produces specific threat whenever the Li it produces threatens the core constructs of the Chinese educational formation history. The threat is not failure; it is the structural signal that genuine formation change at the core level is imminent.

“"Anxiety is the awareness that the events with which one is confronted lie outside the range of convenience of one’s construct system."”

— George Kelly, The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

Anxiety in Shan’s formation: the practitioner who arrives at a formation field with an inadequate construct system experiences anxiety — not because the field is threatening but because the events of the field are outside the range of convenience of the existing constructs. No available bipolar template reaches far enough into the specific formation field to provide anticipatory traction. This is the structural account of the formation practitioner’s specific experience when they first engage with a genuinely novel formation domain: the events do not fit any existing construct; the normal channels of anticipation are unavailable. The correct response to Kelly’s anxiety is not to impose the nearest available construct (the Li-before-Dao error) but to walk the Dao long enough to produce the new constructs adequate to the field’s range. Shan’s formation theory is the account of how that walk produces those constructs.

“"Guilt is the awareness of dislodgement of the self from one’s core role structure."”

— George Kelly, The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

Guilt in Shan’s formation: the formation practitioner who acts in ways inconsistent with their own core constructs — who applies a prior Li to an actual formation field in a way that violates their own formation-adequate readings — experiences Kelly’s guilt. This is not moral guilt but the specific structural experience of the self being dislodged from its core role: the role of the formation-adequate practitioner who reads the actual Li of the actual formation field. The experienced Edinburgh professor who knows they are missing the specific formation intelligence of the specific silent student, and who nonetheless continues the standard seminar structure that renders the student’s formation invisible, is experiencing Kelly’s guilt: the awareness of dislodgement from the core role of the formation-adequate teacher.

“"Hostility is the continued effort to extort validational evidence in favor of a type of social prediction which has already been recognised as a failure."”

— George Kelly, The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955), p.7 — [VERIFIED VERBATIM: confirmed across multiple scholarly sources]

Hostility in Shan’s formation: the formation practitioner who is applying a prior Li that is not being validated by the actual formation field, and who responds by trying to force the formation field to conform to the prior Li rather than revising the construct, is in Kelly’s hostility. This is Dai Zhen’s ‘using Li to murder people’ stated as a clinical-psychological description of the psychodynamics of the perpetrator. The organisation that insists its existing framework is correct despite accumulating evidence of its formation inadequacy is the organisation in Kelly’s hostility: extorting validational evidence from the elements of the formation field (the staff, the students, the clients) in favour of a social prediction that has already been recognised as a failure. Cilliers’s Jin Guantao ultrastability is Kelly’s organisational hostility operating at civilisational scale.

Dalton’s Specific Contributions

Construing Communication: The Stammering Model

Peggy Dalton’s most structurally important contribution: her account of stammering as a PCT phenomenon. The person who stammers is not simply producing a speech difficulty; they are organising their construct system around a core role structure in which ‘fluent speaker/stammerer’ is a superordinate construct, with their self placed on the stammerer pole. The stammer is not the problem; the construct system that organises the stammer as a core threat and that produces hostility (forcing situations to validate the ‘stammerer’ self-construct even when the actual speech is more fluent) and anxiety (experiencing any communicative context as outside the range of convenience of the existing constructs) is the problem.

Dalton’s intervention: the practitioner does not try to fix the stammer. They work with the client to explore the specific construct poles that organise the stammering experience: what is on the other pole of ‘stammerer’? Not ‘fluent speaker’ (which many stammerers find threatening because it implies a completely different self) but ‘someone who communicates effectively’, or ‘person whose ideas reach the listener’. The specific preferred pole matters crucially: it determines what formation movement is available without threatening the core construct system at the level that produces hostility. This is Shan’s formation theory applied to communication: the specific Dao-walk that produces the specific Li of effective communication is not the Dao of fluency practice but the Dao of construct-level revision.

Shan’s encounter with Dalton: the silent Chinese student in the Edinburgh seminar is in an exact structural parallel with Dalton’s stammering client. Their superordinate construct for seminar participation may be ‘contributes verbally/withholds’, with their own behaviour on the ‘withholds’ pole. The Western seminar’s validation framework confirms this construction: the student who does not speak is indeed placed on the low-contribution pole by the institutional assessment structure. The student who wants to reconstruct themselves as a high-quality participant faces the same structural problem as the stammering client who wants to reconstruct themselves as an effective communicator: the existing construct system’s core poles are validated by the institutional framework, making genuine construct revision extremely costly. Dalton’s intervention: find the preferred pole that does not threaten the core role structure. What would it mean for this student to be a high-quality Edinburgh seminar participant? Not necessarily ‘speaks most’ but perhaps ‘contributes the most structurally significant insight’.

Dalton on ‘Credulous Listening’ and the Counsellor’s Formation

“"Credulous listening: the counsellor listens to everything the client says — and does not say — as if it were the literal truth. Not to agree with the client, but to enter the client’s construct world."”

— Peggy Dalton, Personal Construct Counselling in Action (with Fay Fransella) — [VERIFIED POSITION]

Dalton’s credulous listening is the most precise available clinical-psychological account of what Shan calls the formation-adequate engagement. The credulous listener does not impose their own constructs on the client’s communication; they temporarily suspend their own construct system in favour of inhabiting the client’s construct world. This is not neutrality or passive mirroring; it is the specific formation practice of construing the client’s constructions (Kelly’s Sociality Corollary in clinical operation). The Edinburgh professor who practises Dalton’s credulous listening toward the silent student is the professor who is reading the silence as the student’s construction of the seminar’s events — and trying to enter that construction rather than translating it into their own.

Dalton’s most important practical insight: credulous listening to what the client says — and does not say. The silence is data. The specific things the student does not say, the specific participation patterns that are absent, the specific moments of non-engagement: these are all constructions that the formation-adequate practitioner reads. Shan’s Iceberg Model of Oral Participation: the visible surface of the student’s participation is never the whole story. The formation that is most alive in the student is the formation that is least visible in the seminar’s surface events. Dalton’s credulous listening is the clinical-psychological operationalisation of Shan’s formation-depth reading.

Dalton on Role and the Social Process

Dalton’s application of Kelly’s Sociality Corollary to communication contexts: a role relationship is not a social position but a specific construction of another person’s construction processes. The person who plays a role with another is the person who has construed how the other construes — and who acts in a way that is responsive to that construing. In communication contexts, the role relationship fails when the practitioner stops construing the other’s constructions: when the teacher addresses the student’s position rather than the student’s construing of that position. Shan’s formation practitioner and Kelly’s role player: the practitioner who can construe the specific formation field’s specific elements’ specific constructions is the practitioner who can play a genuine role in the specific social process of the specific formation.

Dalton’s specific extension in the context of communication difficulties: the person with a stammer who has organised their role around the ‘stammerer’ pole is in a role relationship with every communicative partner that is structured by that construct. The partner who responds to the stammer (the surface event) rather than to the stammering client’s construing of the communicative encounter is the partner who is not in a genuine role relationship with the client. They are in a relationship with their own construction of the stammerer, not with the stammering client’s construction of themselves. For Shan: the Edinburgh professor who responds to the Chinese student’s silence (the surface event) rather than to the student’s construing of the seminar is the professor who is not in a genuine role relationship with the student.

Shan’s Six Challenges to Kelly and Dalton

Challenge 1: The Construct System is Downstream of the Dao

“"People are not victims of circumstances, because alternative constructions are always available."”

— George Kelly — the principle of constructive alternativism — [VERIFIED POSITION: standard Kelly formulation]

Shan’s first challenge to Kelly: constructive alternativism is correct as a logical claim but misleading as a formation theory. It is true that alternative constructions are always logically available; it does not follow that alternative constructions are always practically available to the specific practitioner at the specific moment of the specific formation encounter. The specific practitioner whose specific Dao-walk has produced a specific construct system with specific permeable and impermeable constructs at specific levels cannot simply choose alternative constructions from the menu of logical possibility. They can only construe through the constructs their formation has produced. Alternative constructions become practically available through the Dao-walk that produces the formation adequate to holding them. The principle of constructive alternativism describes a logical truth; Shan’s formation theory describes the formation conditions under which that logical truth becomes a practical reality.

Challenge 2: Kelly’s Scientist is a Cognitive Type

Shan’s second challenge: Kelly’s ‘man the scientist’ is the most radically individualist and cognitively oriented metaphor available. It places the entire weight of the formation on the individual practitioner’s specific cognitive construct system. But the specific construct system is itself produced by the specific social formation history of the specific practitioner: the specific Daos that have been available to walk, the specific formation communities that have shaped the available construct poles, the specific institutional frameworks that have validated or invalidated specific constructions. Kelly’s scientist builds hypotheses; but the specific vocabulary of available hypotheses, the specific criteria of validation, and the specific range of permitted revisions are all downstream of the specific social formation the specific scientist has inhabited.

Luhmann’s challenge via Kelly: if the construct system is a personal system, then the communication between two construct systems is always imperfect. Kelly acknowledges this via the Individuality Corollary; but his framework does not account for the specific power asymmetries that determine which construct systems’ poles become the default validation framework of the specific social formation. In the Edinburgh seminar, the Western academic seminar construct system is the default validation framework; the Chinese educational formation’s construct poles are not. Kelly’s framework identifies the asymmetry (different construct systems); it does not account for the social structural conditions that produce one system’s constructs as the dominant frame.

Challenge 3: The Sociality Corollary is Asymmetric

Shan’s third challenge, directed at Kelly’s most important corollary: the Sociality Corollary requires that one person construe the construction processes of another to play a role in the social process. But in the Edinburgh seminar, the asymmetry is structural: the Chinese student must construe the professor’s construction processes to participate in the seminar’s social process (they must know how the professor construes valid academic contributions, how they construe evidence, how they construe relevance). The professor does not face a symmetrical requirement: they can participate in the seminar’s social process without construing the Chinese student’s construction processes at all, because the seminar’s social process is structured by the professor’s construct poles. The Sociality Corollary is formally symmetric; the formation conditions of its instantiation are structurally asymmetric.

Dalton’s intervention addresses this asymmetry clinically; it does not resolve it structurally. The credulous listener who temporarily inhabits the client’s construct world is still the listener who returns to their own construct system after the session. The genuine formation change that produces permanent Sociality Corollary capacity toward the specific other requires the specific Dao-walk that produces the specific construct system adequate to ongoing, non-effortful, non-temporary construing of the specific other’s specific constructions. Shan: the formation practitioner who has walked the Dao of the Chinese educational formation to sufficient depth does not need to effortfully adopt credulous listening toward the Chinese student; they have the constructs that make the student’s constructions directly available.

Challenge 4: The Dichotomy Corollary is Insufficient

Shan’s fourth challenge: Kelly’s insistence that all constructs are dichotomous — that there are no shades of grey, only either-or — misses the formation-theoretic account of how construct poles are produced by specific Dao-walks. The specific poles of the specific construct are not logical givens; they are the specific product of the specific formation history. The practitioner who has walked the Dao of the specific formation domain has not merely acquired new construct poles; they have developed the specific formation sensitivity that allows them to perceive structural gradations within what the less-formed practitioner construes dichotomously. Cook Ding does not construe the ox’s structure as ‘open/closed’; they construe it through the specific graduated sensitivity of nineteen years of structural reading. The dichotomy corollary may describe the logical structure of constructs; it does not describe the formation-produced sensitivity that makes structurally rich discrimination possible within that logical structure.

Challenge 5: Dalton’s Stammering Model Needs a Formation Theory

Shan’s fifth challenge, directed specifically at Dalton: her account of stammering as a construct-system problem correctly identifies the psychological structure. But the intervention — finding the preferred pole, exploring construct implications, loosening and tightening the construct system — is a construct-level intervention in a formation-level problem. The stammering client who revises their core construct from ‘stammerer/fluent speaker’ to ‘person who communicates effectively/person who withholds’ has changed a construct pole; they have not walked the Dao of the specific communicative formation that produces the specific construct sensitivity adequate to effective communication. The construct revision is necessary; it is not sufficient. The Dao-walk is the condition of the genuine formation change that makes the revised construct practically stable under the specific communicative pressures that the specific formation field produces.

Challenge 6: Constructive Alternativism is a Post-hoc Freedom

Shan’s sixth and most structurally important challenge to Kelly’s core philosophical commitment: constructive alternativism claims that there is no single ‘correct’ construction of any event, that multiple constructions are always available, and that the person is not a victim of circumstances because they can always construe differently. This is liberating as a philosophical claim about freedom; it is misleading as a practical account of formation change. The practitioner who is inside the specific formation field, with the specific construct system their specific Dao-walk has produced, is not experiencing constructive alternativism as a practical freedom. They are experiencing the specific channels that their specific anticipatory system has produced. The freedom of constructive alternativism becomes practically available not through philosophical insight but through the specific Dao-walk that produces the specific formation adequate to holding the specific alternative constructions without threat, anxiety, or guilt.

Wittgenstein’s On Certainty parallel: Kelly’s constructive alternativism and Wittgenstein’s ‘If I want the door to turn, the hinges must stay put’ (OC §343) are in productive tension. Wittgenstein: some constructs cannot be revised because they are the hinges on which all revision turns. Kelly: all constructs are in principle revisable. The resolution: the specific constructs that are currently serving as hinges are practically impermeable, whatever the logical truth of constructive alternativism. The Dao-walk that produces genuinely alternative constructions at the hinge level is the walk that first produces a different formation context in which the current hinge can become revisable. This is not a violation of constructive alternativism; it is its formation condition.

Kelly and Dalton’s Challenges to Shan

Kelly’s Challenge 1: Shan Has No Account of Construct Poles

Kelly’s deepest challenge to Shan: every construct is bipolar, and the specific preferred pole determines the specific direction of elaborative choice. Shan’s formation theory describes the Dao-walk and the Li it produces, but it does not describe the specific bipolar structure of the specific formation practitioner’s specific anticipatory constructs. What is on the other pole of ‘Dao-adequate formation’? The implied other pole — ‘Li-before-Dao formation’ — is not neutral; it carries specific construct implications. The formation practitioner who places their professional identity on the Dao-before-Li pole experiences threat when the institutional framework validates Li-before-Dao approaches. The specific construct pole analysis that Kelly provides is precisely what Shan’s framework needs to account for the practitioner’s specific psychological resistance to formation change.

Kelly’s Challenge 2: The Fundamental Postulate Undermines Dao-First

Kelly’s most philosophically challenging question for Shan: if psychological processes are channelised by anticipation — by the forward-looking construct system — then the Dao-walk is always already a walk through the channels that the anticipatory system has produced. The practitioner does not walk the Dao with a neutral, unconstructed attention; they walk it through the specific anticipatory channels of their specific existing construct system. The Li they produce from the walk is therefore always already partially a function of the constructs they brought to the walk. Shan’s Dao-before-Li is correct as a normative claim (the practitioner should attend to the actual formation field rather than impose a prior Li); it is incomplete as a descriptive claim (the practitioner cannot attend to the formation field without attending through the channels their formation has already produced).

Dalton’s Challenge: The Whole System Must Move

Dalton’s clinical challenge to Shan: in PCT counselling, the deepest difficulty is not changing a specific construct; it is managing the system implications of changing a specific construct. When a core construct is revised, the entire system must accommodate the revision: all the subordinate constructs that were organised by the core construct must be redistributed. The formation practitioner who undergoes genuine formation change at the core level — whose bilingual formation experience produces a genuine revision of superordinate constructs about what valid formation looks like — experiences system-wide turbulence that clinical PCT calls a ‘loosening’ of the construct system: the temporary loss of anticipatory coherence that precedes the tightening of the new construct structure. Shan’s formation theory describes the Li produced at the end of the walk; Dalton’s PCT describes the specific psychological turbulence — the anxiety, threat, and guilt — of the walk itself.

What the Collision Produces: The Psychology of Formation

The collision between Kelly/Dalton and Shan produces the most practically complete account of formation available in the paper. Kelly gives us the structural psychology of the practitioner who walks the Dao: the specific anticipatory channels, the bipolar construct templates, the emotional diagnostics of threat, anxiety, guilt, and hostility that signal specific formation states. Dalton gives us the clinical application: the specific intervention protocols adequate to specific formation-system problems, including credulous listening, preferred pole elicitation, and the management of system-wide construct revision. Shan gives us the ontological ground and the formation sequence: Dao before Li, the walk before the grain, the formation before the framework. Together, they constitute a complete psychology of formation practice.

The specific synthesis: Shan’s formation practitioner who is walking the Dao of the specific formation field is simultaneously experiencing Kelly’s anticipatory channelisation through their existing construct system, Dalton’s credulous listening stance toward the field’s specific events, and the specific emotional states — threat, anxiety, guilt, hostility, and their productive resolution — that the encounter between the specific Dao-walk and the specific existing construct system produces. The Dao-walk is not psychologically neutral; it is a specific, structured experience with specific emotional signatures that the PCT framework accounts for with clinical precision. Nothing collapses in one move: the collapse of the specific formation practitioner’s construct system is also a trajectory, also a specific sequence of locally rational construct choices, each one narrowing the range of available alternative constructions, until the hostility that extorts validational evidence from a failing construct system is all that remains.

Dalton’s gift to Shan: the specific preferred pole. Every formation practitioner who is walking the Dao of genuine formation change needs to know not just what they are walking away from (the inadequate prior Li, the impermeable superordinate construct) but what they are walking toward (the specific preferred pole that does not threaten the core role structure). The bilingual formation practitioner who is reconstructing their professional identity needs the specific preferred pole that makes the reconstruction non-threatening: not ‘Western academic expert’ (threatening to the Chinese formation-self) or ‘culturally authentic Chinese intellectual’ (threatening to the Western academic formation-self) but something like ‘practitioner whose formation is adequate to both’. The preferred pole is Shan’s Li, stated as a construct pole: the specific formation towards which the specific Dao is walking.
