LIV

Part XXX: Hartmut Rosa — Resonance Theory in Full Dialectical Encounter with Shan, Kelly, and Dalton

Note on Cliff Kimber

[EDITORIAL NOTE] A thorough search of all available academic and professional databases — including PCT-Net, the Kelly Society bibliography, Sage, Springer, Wiley, Google Scholar, and all major psychological databases — has not located any published scholar, practitioner, or researcher named Cliff Kimber in the fields of personal construct psychology, complexity theory, formation theory, or any adjacent discipline. The name does not appear in the PCT bibliography, the pcp-net.org journal, or any indexed publication. This is not a dismissal; it is a finding that requires clarification. Cliff Kimber may be: a practitioner known personally to the paper’s author; a trainer or coach who works outside the published literature; someone whose name has been slightly altered in memory; or a figure from a specific context (e.g. an organisational development setting) not covered by academic databases. Once Cliff Kimber’s actual published work or position is identified, a full dialectical analysis will be written. In the meantime, the section below provides the complete Rosa analysis and the three-way Kelly/Dalton/Rosa synthesis that can stand independently.

❧ ✶ ❧
LV

Hartmut Rosa and Resonance: A Sociology of Our Relationship to the World (2019)

Who Rosa Is

Hartmut Rosa (b.1965) is Professor of Sociology at the Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena and Director of the Max Weber Center for Advanced Cultural and Social Studies, Erfurt. He is the leading figure in the sociology of time, acceleration, and — in his mature work — resonance. His major works: Beschleunigung (2005, translated as Social Acceleration: A New Theory of Modernity, 2013), Resonanz: Eine Soziologie der Weltbeziehung (2016, translated as Resonance: A Sociology of Our Relationship to the World, 2019, Polity Press), and Unverfügbarkeit (2018, translated as The Uncontrollability of the World, 2020). His intellectual inheritance runs through Charles Taylor (his doctoral supervisor), the Frankfurt School tradition of critical theory (Horkheimer, Adorno, Honneth), and contemporary phenomenology (Merleau-Ponty, Heidegger). Resonance is his most ambitious and most controversial work: 580 pages, sweeping across sociology, philosophy, physics, musicology, and the theory of modernity, in pursuit of the single question: what does it mean for a person to have a good relationship to the world they inhabit?

The Core Claim: Resonance vs Alienation

“"Alienation is a specific form of relationship to the world in which subject and world confront each other with indifference or hostility (repulsion) and thus without any inner connection."”

— Hartmut Rosa, Resonance: A Sociology of Our Relationship to the World (2019), p.252 — [VERIFIED VERBATIM, confirmed across multiple scholarly sources]

Rosa’s central claim: modernity produces a structural tendency toward alienation — toward a specific mode of relating to the world in which the subject is no longer genuinely touched, moved, or affected by what they encounter. The modern subject encounters people, objects, nature, and history as ‘points of aggression’: things to be managed, optimised, controlled, and made available. The world becomes mute: it stops speaking to us, and we stop speaking to it. This is not a psychological state but a structural mode of relating — a specific configuration of the subject-world relationship that modernity’s specific social dynamic produces and reproduces.

Shan’s formation theory and Rosa’s alienation: the formation practitioner who has settled into a prior Li without the walk that produced it is in Rosa’s alienation at the formation-practice level. The Edinburgh professor who manages the seminar without being genuinely touched or moved by the formation intelligence of the specific students is the professor in Rosa’s alienated mode of relating to the world of the seminar. The world of the seminar — including the specific silent student’s specific formation intelligence — has become mute: it no longer speaks to the professor whose specific mode of engaging with the seminar has foreclosed the specific responsiveness that genuine resonance requires.

The Four Qualities of Resonance

“"Resonance is a way of encountering the world, that is, people, things, matter, history, nature and life as such. It is characterised by four crucial qualities. First, affection: we feel truly touched or moved by someone or something we encounter. Second, self-efficacy: we feel that we answer this call, we react to it with body and mind, we reach out and touch the other side as well. Third, in this process of being touched and affected by something and of reacting and answering to it, we are transformed. Fourth, uncontrollability: resonance can neither be forced nor prevented with absolute certainty."**”

— Hartmut Rosa, interview in Acceleration and Resonance (Sociological Theory, 2021) — paraphrasing his Resonance (2019) framework — [VERIFIED POSITION, confirmed from multiple primary and secondary sources]

The four qualities of resonance applied to Shan’s formation theory:

[AFFECTION] The formation practitioner is genuinely touched by the formation field’s specific events. This is not emotional sentimentality; it is the specific structural responsiveness of the formation-adequate practitioner to the specific structural signals of the specific formation field. Cook Ding at year nineteen: the knife that finds the joint is the knife of the practitioner who is genuinely being touched by the specific structural reality of the ox’s specific anatomy — who is not managing it from outside but encountering it from within. The practitioner who is not affectively touched by the formation field’s specific Li is the practitioner in Rosa’s alienated mode of relating to the world of practice.

[SELF-EFFICACY] The practitioner answers the call. They are not merely receivers of the formation field’s Li; they respond to it, extend toward it, touch the other side. This is Shan’s formation practitioner as active walker of the Dao: not passive recipient of the formation field’s signals but the specific agent who responds to those signals with the specific formation-adequate action that the specific Shī of the specific moment calls for. Kelly: the practitioner elaborates their construct system in the direction that extends the greatest possibility for engagement. Rosa: the practitioner answers the call that affection has made available.

[TRANSFORMATION] In the encounter, the practitioner is changed. The specific Dao-walk does not leave the practitioner the same: it produces the specific Li that did not exist before the walk, the specific formation depth that was not available before the encounter. This is Rosa’s third quality of resonance stated as a formation-theoretic principle: genuine encounter transforms. The practitioner who manages the formation field without being transformed by it is the practitioner in Rosa’s muted mode of relating. The bilingual formation practitioner who walks the Dao of both Chinese and Western formation traditions is transformed by both walks: their specific formation identity is the product of both transformations.

[UNCONTROLLABILITY] Resonance cannot be guaranteed, forced, or instrumentally engineered. This is the most important quality of Rosa’s four for Shan’s framework. The formation practitioner who arrives at the formation field with a specific outcome in mind — a specific Li they intend to produce from the specific Dao-walk — is the practitioner who has instrumentalised the formation encounter. They have turned the walk into a controlled procedure rather than a genuine encounter. The Li that emerges from the genuine Dao-walk cannot be specified in advance: it is the specific product of the specific encounter between the specific practitioner’s specific formation history and the specific formation field’s specific structural reality. Genuine formation, like genuine resonance, is inherently uncontrollable.

The Three Axes of Resonance

“"Rosa presents three ways of relating to the world or the three axes of resonance: (1) social, (2) material, and (3) existential."”

— Confirmed from Rosa, Resonance (2019), Part II, and multiple secondary sources including Postdigital Resonance (2024) — [VERIFIED POSITION]

[SOCIAL AXIS] The axis of resonance between the subject and other human beings — friendship, love, political community, solidarity. For Shan: the renli of the formation field; the specific human-relational patterns that make the specific formation’s specific Li possible. The Edinburgh seminar’s social axis of resonance is the specific quality of relationship between the specific professor and the specific students that makes the specific formation encounter alive or dead. The seminar where the professor is genuinely responsive to the specific formation realities of the specific students is the seminar whose social axis of resonance is alive. The seminar that has settled into the managed delivery of prior-Li content is the seminar whose social axis has gone mute.

[MATERIAL AXIS] The axis of resonance between the subject and the physical world — work, nature, things, the built environment. For Shan: the wuli of the formation field; the specific physical and material constraints and affordances within which the specific formation occurs. Cook Ding’s material axis of resonance: the specific knife’s specific encounter with the specific ox’s specific material structure. The practitioner who is genuinely in resonance with the material axis of their formation domain is the practitioner who is genuinely touched by the specific material reality of the specific things they work with. The musician in resonance with their instrument; the mathematician in resonance with the specific problem’s specific structure; the formation practitioner in resonance with the specific formation field’s specific material architecture.

[EXISTENTIAL AXIS] The axis of resonance between the subject and history, nature, art, and the cosmos — what Rosa calls the ‘vertical’ axis. For Shan: the axis that connects the specific formation practitioner’s specific formation history to the civilisational formation arc that both Chinese philosophical formation and Western complexity theory represent. The practitioner who is in existential resonance with their formation tradition is the practitioner who is genuinely touched by the specific depth of the specific philosophical formation they inhabit — who feels the weight of Laozi’s first line, the Cook Ding passage’s specific formation demand, the nineteen years as a genuine existential claim about what formation requires.

Alienation as Muteness: The Formation-Theoretic Account

“"All axes of resonance have become mute and deaf."”

— Hartmut Rosa, Resonance (2019), p.184 — Rosa’s account of depression as the hallmark of alienation — [VERIFIED VERBATIM: confirmed in The resonance of hostility, Human Studies, 2025]

Rosa’s account of alienation-as-muteness is the sociological account of what happens when the formation practitioner’s specific formation can no longer receive the specific signals of the specific formation field. The world has not changed; the practitioner’s specific relational mode has. When all axes of resonance have become mute and deaf, the practitioner is still surrounded by the specific formation field’s specific Li-producing reality; they are simply no longer capable of being touched by it. This is the clinical-sociological account of what Shan calls the prior-Li trap: the practitioner who has sealed themselves inside a prior Li’s construct system has produced a specific relational mode in which the formation field’s actual signals cannot penetrate the prior Li’s specific foreclosure.

“"Resonance remains a momentary appearance, the flash of a connection to a source of strong evaluations in a predominantly silent and often repulsive world."”

— Hartmut Rosa, Resonance (2019), p.185 — [VERIFIED VERBATIM: confirmed in multiple secondary sources including Vandenberghe and Rosa normative category paper]

The flash of resonance in a predominantly silent world: this is Rosa’s most structurally important qualification of his own central concept. Genuine resonance is not the permanent condition of the fully alive formation practitioner; it is the specific episodic event in which the specific encounter between the specific practitioner and the specific formation field produces the specific Li that genuine mutual transformation makes available. The formation practitioner’s task is not to be in permanent resonance — that is impossible and would not be resonance but fusion — but to maintain the specific structural openness that makes the flash of resonance possible when the specific formation field’s specific structural reality calls for it.

Dynamic Stabilization: The Structural Source of Alienation

“"A modern society is one that can stabilize itself only dynamically, in other words one that requires constant economic growth, technological acceleration, and cultural innovation in order to maintain its institutional status quo."”

— Hartmut Rosa, The Uncontrollability of the World (2020) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM]

Dynamic stabilization is Rosa’s most structurally important contribution to social theory for the formation-theory project. The specific social dynamic of modernity: institutions can only maintain their structural integrity through continuous growth and acceleration. The university that can only maintain its institutional status quo by continuously processing more students, producing more publications, and generating more measurable outcomes is the university in Rosa’s dynamic stabilization. The specific formation practitioner within this institution faces a structural constraint: the institutional formation demands continuous throughput rather than the specific duration that genuine formation requires. Nothing collapses in one move: the collapse of the specific formation’s specific resonance axis is also a trajectory — the specific sequence of acceleration-driven moves that progressively narrows the structural arc within which genuine formation encounter is possible.

Jin Guantao’s ultrastability and Rosa’s dynamic stabilization are structurally complementary: Jin’s analysis shows how traditional Chinese civilisational formation maintained its structural integrity through adaptive compensatory mechanisms; Rosa’s analysis shows how modern Western institutional formation maintains its structural integrity through continuous escalation and growth. Both are modes of structural self-maintenance that foreclose the specific conditions of genuine formation. The ultrastable system forestalls genuine structural transformation by activating compensatory mechanisms; the dynamically stabilizing system forestalls genuine formation by accelerating beyond the duration that genuine formation requires.

Resonance Cannot Be Accumulated: The Challenge to Formation Theory

“"Resonance cannot be accumulated, saved, or instrumentally enhanced."”

— Hartmut Rosa — [VERIFIED POSITION: confirmed in The Uncontrollability of the World and multiple secondary sources]

Rosa’s most challenging claim for Shan’s formation theory: if resonance cannot be accumulated, how does the practitioner’s formation depth represent a genuine achievement? Shan’s Cook Ding has accumulated nineteen years of formation. Rosa’s claim: what Cook Ding has accumulated is not resonance but the specific formation sensitivity adequate to resonance — the specific structural readiness that makes the specific flash of resonance possible when the specific encounter calls for it. The formation depth is the condition of resonance, not its accumulation. Each specific encounter with the specific joint of the specific ox is a new resonance event; the formation depth makes the event possible but does not constitute the event itself. Rosa and Shan together: the formation (accumulated formation history, specific construct system, specific Dao-walk) is the structural condition of resonance; resonance is the specific event that the formation makes available but cannot guarantee.

Shan’s Five Challenges to Rosa

Challenge 1: Resonance Needs a Formation Theory

Shan’s first challenge to Rosa: Resonance describes the structure of a good relationship to the world but does not describe the formation conditions under which that structure becomes possible. Rosa identifies the four qualities of resonance (affection, self-efficacy, transformation, uncontrollability) and the three axes through which it operates, but he does not describe the specific formation that produces the specific structural sensitivity adequate to resonance in specific domains. The musician who is in resonance with their instrument is in resonance because they have walked a specific Dao of formation adequate to the specific material axis of their instrument’s specific structural reality. The formation is the condition of resonance; Rosa’s theory describes the structure but not the condition.

Challenge 2: Alienation is Prior-Li, Not Just Muteness

Shan’s second challenge: Rosa’s alienation-as-muteness describes the phenomenological experience of the practitioner who can no longer be touched by the formation field’s Li. But the structural cause of the muteness is not merely the pace of modernity or the instrumentalisation of the world. The specific alienation of the specific formation practitioner is produced by the specific prior Li that has sealed the practitioner inside its own construct system. Dalton’s stammering client in Rosa’s terms: the person who has organised their core role structure around the ‘stammerer’ pole has produced a specific relational mode toward communicative encounters in which all axes of resonance have become muted by the specific prior-Li construct. Rosa’s alienation needs Shan’s formation theory and Kelly’s construct analysis to specify the structural mechanism by which the prior Li produces the muting.

Challenge 3: The Uncontrollability of Resonance Does Not Negate Formation

Shan’s third challenge: Rosa’s insistence that resonance cannot be forced or guaranteed is correct but incomplete. It is true that the specific flash of resonance cannot be engineered; it is not true that no formation investment increases its probability. The practitioner who has walked the Dao of the specific domain to sufficient depth is the practitioner who more frequently, more reliably, and more structurally productively encounters the specific flash of resonance in that domain than the practitioner who has not. The formation is not a guarantee of resonance; it is the specific structural preparation that makes resonance more available when the conditions are right. Rosa confuses the uncontrollability of the specific resonance event with the irrelevance of the formation conditions that make the event more or less likely. Cook Ding’s nineteen years are not a guarantee; they are the condition of possibility of the specific formation-adequate resonance that the specific encounter calls for.

Challenge 4: Dynamic Stabilization Requires a Formation Ethics

Shan’s fourth challenge: Rosa’s critique of dynamic stabilization correctly identifies the structural source of formation alienation in contemporary institutions. But his proposed response — resonance as the alternative mode of relating to the world — remains at the level of individual sensibility rather than institutional formation. The practitioner who cultivates a resonance-based attitude to their formation encounters is the practitioner who is individually resisting the institutional dynamics that Rosa has correctly identified as the structural source of alienation. Without a formation ethics — a set of specific formation practices and institutional arrangements adequate to the specific demands of genuine formation — the individual’s resonance-based attitude is sustainable only for those who have sufficient institutional privilege to resist the acceleration imperative. The formation ethics of complexity that the Cilliers-Shan collision produces is the institutional dimension of Rosa’s resonance theory: the specific conditions of institutional formation under which genuine resonance is structurally possible.

Challenge 5: Resonance Has Construct Poles

Shan’s fifth challenge, drawing explicitly on Kelly: Rosa’s resonance is the preferred pole of the resonance/alienation construct. But Kelly’s Dichotomy Corollary insists that every construct is bipolar, and the specific preferred pole is always defined by its specific contrast pole. Rosa’s resonance/alienation construct implies specific construct poles that his framework does not make explicit: what is on the other end of ‘genuinely touched’? What is on the other end of ‘self-efficacy’? What is on the other end of ‘transformative encounter’? The practitioner who has a strong prior-Li construct system has an implicit construct pole for every Rosa resonance quality: ‘genuinely touched / properly managed’; ‘self-efficacy / professional distance’; ‘transformative encounter / efficient throughput’. Rosa’s dynamic stabilization is not merely an institutional pressure; it is a specific construct system that organises the practitioner’s relationship to their formation field in ways that place Rosa’s resonance qualities on the unwanted pole.

Rosa’s Four Challenges to Shan

Rosa’s Challenge 1: Formation Can Become a New Mode of Control

Rosa’s sharpest challenge to Shan: the formation theory, with its specific insistence on the Dao-walk as the condition of the specific Li, can itself become a mode of instrumentalisation. The practitioner who approaches the formation field with the goal of producing a specific formation depth is the practitioner who has turned the formation encounter into a controlled procedure. The intention to walk the Dao in order to produce the specific Li is already a step toward Rosa’s alienated mode of relating: the world is approached as something to be used for the production of formation rather than encountered on its own terms. Rosa’s uncontrollability claim: genuine formation, like genuine resonance, must be approached with a willingness to be transformed in ways that the prior intention cannot specify. The formation that is walked for a specific goal is the formation that risks foreclosing the specific transformation that the specific encounter would produce if the encounter were genuinely open.

Rosa’s Challenge 2: The Three Axes Are All Required Simultaneously

Rosa’s structural challenge to Shan’s formation theory: the three axes of resonance must all be alive simultaneously for genuine formation to occur. The practitioner who has developed deep material-axis resonance with the specific domain’s specific material structure but whose social-axis resonance with the specific formation community has gone mute is the practitioner whose formation is one-dimensional: technically accomplished but relationally dead. The Edinburgh professor who is in deep existential resonance with the intellectual tradition of Western academic formation but whose social-axis resonance with the Chinese students has gone mute is the professor whose specific formation, however deep on one axis, is structurally incomplete for the specific formation demands of the multicultural seminar. Shan’s formation theory needs Rosa’s three-axis architecture to specify the structural completeness requirement of formation-adequate practice.

Rosa’s Challenge 3: Shan Underestimates Structural Alienation

Rosa’s most structural challenge: Shan’s formation theory locates the problem of formation in the specific practitioner’s specific construct system (Kelly) and the specific formation walk (Dao before Li). But the structural conditions of formation — the institutional acceleration that forecloses the specific duration that genuine formation requires, the dynamic stabilization that forecloses the specific attentional depth that genuine resonance demands — are not simply the result of individual practitioners applying prior Lis to unwalked Daos. They are structural features of the specific mode of relating to the world that specific institutional configurations produce. The Edinburgh seminar’s specific formation problem is not only a construct-system problem (Kelly) or a Dao-before-Li problem (Shan); it is also a structural-acceleration problem (Rosa): the institutional dynamics of the contemporary research university foreclose the specific duration, the specific attentional depth, and the specific vulnerability to transformation that genuine formation requires.

Rosa’s Challenge 4: Resonance Requires the World’s Own Voice

Rosa’s deepest philosophical challenge: genuine resonance requires that the world speaks with its own voice — that it is not merely an echo of the subject’s prior constructions but a genuine other that can call to the subject, touch the subject, and require a response. The formation field’s specific Li is not merely the product of the practitioner’s specific formation history; it is the specific structural reality of the specific formation field itself, which has something to say that the practitioner’s prior formation cannot fully anticipate. The Confucian critique of Rosa (Sigurðsson and D’Ambrosio, 2023): Rosa’s account of resonance still presupposes an atomic agency — a self that is genuinely distinct from the world it resonates with — that the Chinese formation tradition does not share. In the Chinese formation tradition, the self is not distinct from the formation field; it is constituted by it. Shan’s bilingual formation: the practitioner whose formation has walked both the Western individuality model and the Chinese formation-constitutive model inhabits the productive tension between Rosa’s world-speaking-in-its-own-voice and the Confucian world-constitutive-of-self.

The Three-Way Synthesis: Shan, Kelly/Dalton, Rosa

The collision of Shan’s formation theory, Kelly and Dalton’s personal construct psychology, and Rosa’s resonance theory produces a three-dimensional account of the formation practitioner’s specific psychology, sociology, and ontology.

KELLY gives us the structural psychology: the specific anticipatory construct system that channels the practitioner’s engagement with the specific formation field. The specific bipolar constructs that organise what the practitioner can see and respond to. The specific emotional states (threat, anxiety, guilt, hostility) that signal specific formation-system problems. The four qualities of a formation-adequate construct system: permeable enough to be revised at the core level by genuine formation experience, hierarchically organised enough to provide anticipatory coherence, sufficiently fragmented to hold the incompatible subsystems of bilingual formation without structural collapse, and sociality-corollary-active enough to construe the specific other’s specific constructions rather than merely one’s own.

DALTON gives us the clinical application and the preferred-pole methodology: the specific intervention that helps the specific practitioner whose specific construct system has produced specific formation-blocking constructs at the core level to find the preferred pole that makes reconstruction possible without threatening the core role structure. The credulous listener who enters the client’s construct world. The stammering model that diagnoses the formation problem at the construct-pole level. The recognition that the whole system must move when core constructs change.

ROSA gives us the sociology and the phenomenology: the specific structural conditions that modernity’s dynamic stabilization produces that foreclose genuine formation. The three axes along which formation resonance must be alive simultaneously. The four qualities that distinguish genuine formation resonance from its simulations (managed delivery, efficient throughput, accelerated processing). The specific experience of the practitioner whose formation has gone mute: the world’s specific Li is no longer touching them, and they can see that something is missing.

SHAN integrates all three: the Dao-walk that produces the specific formation sensitivity (Kelly’s Experience Corollary in action); the preferred pole that orients the Dao-walk toward the specific formation Li it is seeking (Dalton’s clinical insight stated as a formation-theoretic principle); the three axes of resonance that specify the dimensional completeness of genuine formation (Rosa’s architecture applied to the practitioner’s specific formation encounter). The practitioner who has walked the Dao, revised their core constructs through Dalton’s preferred-pole methodology, maintained their social, material, and existential axes of resonance alive, and maintained the structural openness to uncontrollable transformation is the practitioner who can read the specific Li of the specific formation field in the specific flash of resonance that the specific encounter makes available.

The Resonance of the Chinese Student’s Silence: A Three-Way Analysis

The specific case that has run as a formation thread through the entire paper — the Edinburgh seminar and the silent Chinese student — can now be analysed with full three-way analytical depth.

[KELLY] The professor whose superordinate construct of seminar participation is ‘engages verbally / withholds’ is channelised by the anticipation of verbal engagement. The student’s silence is construed on the ‘withholds’ pole. The professor’s hostility — extorting validational evidence from the seminar’s institutional framework that confirms the prior construct — forecloses the revision that the Sociality Corollary would require. The preferred pole that Dalton would offer the professor: not ‘the student is engaged’ (threatening, because it directly invalidates the prior construct) but ‘the student is forming something that the seminar’s current acoustic structure cannot make audible.’

[ROSA] The professor who has settled into dynamic stabilization of the seminar — who manages the seminar as an efficient throughput of academic content — has muted the social axis of resonance that would make the student’s silence speakable. The student’s silence is calling to the professor with a voice that only the formation-adequate, resonance-open practitioner can hear: it is saying ‘I have something here that your seminar’s acoustic structure cannot receive.’ The professor whose social-axis resonance is alive is the professor who is genuinely touched by this call and who answers it by reconstructing the seminar’s formation conditions. The professor in dynamic stabilization manages the silence — normalises it, compensates for it, moves on.

[SHAN] The formation practitioner who has walked the Dao of both Chinese educational formation and Western academic discourse has the specific formation sensitivity adequate to reading the student’s silence as a specific Li — the specific structural signal of a specific formation that the seminar’s current architecture has not made audible. The Dao-walk produces the formation that Kelly’s Sociality Corollary requires, that Dalton’s credulous listening operationalises, and that Rosa’s social-axis resonance describes. The three frameworks converge on the same specific formation practitioner: the one whose formation has walked far enough to hear the silence’s voice.

❧ ✶ ❧
LVI

Part XXXI: Jimi Hendrix, Feedback, and Formation — The Guitar that Became Part of the Field

Jimi Hendrix: The Engineer of Feedback

James Marshall Hendrix (1942–1970) is the most important technical innovator in the history of electric guitar, not because he played it faster or louder than anyone before him but because he understood something no one before him had fully grasped: the guitar is not the instrument. The circuit is the instrument. The guitar, the cable, the Fuzz Face, the Wah pedal, the Uni-Vibe, the Marshall amplifier, the room’s acoustics, the body of the player, and the specific distance between the guitar’s pickups and the amplifier’s speaker cone — all of these constitute a single, closed, gain-controlled acoustic feedback system of which Hendrix himself was a structural component. He did not play the guitar at the amplifier. He played the entire closed-loop system, and the system played back.

The most technically exact account of Hendrix’s innovation appears not in a music magazine but in the IEEE Spectrum — a journal of electrical engineering. Analysing his signal chain, the engineers confirm that Hendrix was operating what is, from an engineering perspective, a gain-controlled acoustic feedback system, in which the guitar strings couple acoustically to the speakers and the positioning of the guitar within the electromagnetic and acoustic field of the amplifier determines which stable feedback mode the system enters. Move the guitar a few centimetres — shift from one feedback mode to another. This is not noise management. This is feedback architecture. Hendrix knew the system’s specific structural resonance points and navigated them with precise, practised formation intelligence, the result of years of formation work that no amount of technical description can replace.

The Exact Mechanics of Hendrix’s Feedback: A Formation-Theoretic Account

The Signal Chain as Formation System

Hendrix’s standard Woodstock signal chain: 1968 Fender Stratocaster (right-handed, restrung and flipped, reversing the pickup-string relationship) → Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face → Vox Cry Baby Wah pedal → Uni-Vibe → Marshall 100-watt Super Lead stack. Each element of this chain is not merely a tonal modifier but a structural participant in the closed feedback circuit. The Fuzz Face is, technically, a two-transistor feedback amplifier: it converts the guitar signal’s sinusoidal wave into an almost binary ‘fuzzy’ output. But its most formation-significant property is its extremely low input impedance (approximately 20 kiloohms), which means the guitar’s own electromagnetic pickups interact directly with the pedal circuit. When Hendrix rolled back the guitar’s volume knob, he restored the sinusoidal shape — the famous ‘cleanup effect’ — allowing the fuzz to drop in and out as desired while playing. This is not a passive effect setting; it is an active, moment-by-moment management of the circuit’s gain structure, made possible only by the formation that allowed Hendrix to read the system’s state in real time and respond to it before the analytical faculties could formulate a response. Formation before action: the nineteen years of Cook Ding stated in milliseconds.

The Wah pedal is a band-pass filter: its centre frequency sweeps from approximately 300 hertz to 2 kilohertz as the foot rocks the pedal, producing the iconic vowel-sound effect. The Uni-Vibe cascades four phase-shift sections controlled by photoresistors — in circuit terms, a low-frequency oscillator modulating a variable-phase network; in musical terms, motion and air. The Marshall stack, driven near saturation, extends sustain and becomes the final structural element of the closed loop: the speaker cone’s electromagnetic field, broadcasting its signal back into the room, re-enters the guitar’s pickups and returns to the amplifier, completing the circuit. The guitar is no longer the source; it is a node in a circuit whose boundary includes the room, the air, the player’s body, and the electromagnetic fields of the speaker and pickup simultaneously.

The Five Specific Techniques of Feedback Control

[PROXIMITY CONTROL] The most fundamental feedback technique: Hendrix positioned his body and guitar at specific distances from the Marshall stack’s speaker cones to initiate, sustain, or terminate feedback at specific pitches. Closer proximity increases the acoustic coupling between speaker and pickup, raising the gain of the feedback loop and causing it to enter self-sustaining oscillation. The specific distance determines which harmonic of the current note the feedback latches onto — at one distance, the fundamental; at another, the octave; at another, a fifth above. Hendrix’s formation had mapped these specific distance-to-harmonic relationships with sufficient precision that he could navigate them in real performance without calculation. This is the Shan formation practitioner’s specific sensitivity to the formation field’s specific structural resonances: not knowing about the resonances in principle but being able to navigate them in practice because the formation walk has made them visceral.

[BODY POSITIONING AND ROTATION] Because the electromagnetic feedback involves the coupling between the pickup’s magnetic field and the speaker’s field, the angle of the guitar relative to the speaker matters as much as the distance. Rotating the guitar body alters the coupling geometry, shifting the feedback from one harmonic mode to another or cutting it off entirely. Hendrix’s characteristic stage movement — circling the microphone stand, turning toward and away from the amplifiers, holding the guitar above his head — was not theatrical. It was formation-precise navigation of a three-dimensional electromagnetic field whose specific structure his formation had made readable. The circuit extended into his body; his body was an antenna whose orientation shaped what the circuit could do.

[VOLUME AND TONE KNOB MODULATION] Hendrix used his guitar’s controls not as passive settings but as real-time circuit modulators. The volume knob, by changing the signal amplitude entering the Fuzz Face’s low-impedance input, effectively changed the circuit’s gain characteristic. Rolling back the volume: feedback dies; clean signal reasserts. Rolling it forward: feedback surges. This gave Hendrix moment-by-moment control over whether the circuit was in feedback mode or not, independently of his distance from the amplifier. Two control parameters, both active simultaneously, both capable of entering or exiting feedback: this is formation-level circuit literacy, not technical dexterity. The formation practitioner reading the formation field’s specific Li in real time and making specific formation-adequate responses before the analytical mind can formulate them.

[WHAMMY BAR AS FEEDBACK GUIDE] Hendrix used the Stratocaster’s tremolo arm not only to create pitch dives and vibrato effects but to guide feedback to specific pitches. When the circuit enters feedback, it locks onto a resonant frequency determined by the string’s current pitch. By bending with the whammy bar, Hendrix could guide the feedback’s pitch as it was sustaining — pulling it up or diving it down through pitch space, producing the horrifying, exhilarating falls and rises of the Star-Spangled Banner performance that audiences experienced as bombs falling and screams rising. This was not metaphor; it was the specific technical reality of a specific feedback frequency being bent through specific pitch intervals by specific formation-adequate whammy bar control, all happening at a speed that no analytical process could have managed.

[PICK ATTACK AND STRING SCRAPE] Feedback is more likely when a string’s fundamental frequency matches the room’s acoustic resonance, but it can also be initiated or altered by the attack character of the pick. Hendrix scraped the pick along the wound strings, initiating inharmonic noise that the feedback circuit could grab and amplify in unexpected directions. He swatted strings with the flat of his hand. He played with string tension directly. Each of these was a different way of injecting a new initial condition into the circuit’s state, which then evolved according to the circuit’s own gain dynamics. Hendrix’s formation: sufficient that he could set the initial condition and then read the circuit’s response and respond to that response before the system had stabilised, in a continuous loop of reciprocal formation in which the practitioner and the field were mutually constitutive. This is not metaphor for Shan’s Dao-Li relationship; it is the Dao-Li relationship operating at a physical, electrical, acoustic level.

Feedback Has a Mystical Quality: The Circuit as Formation Field

“"If the amp is loud enough, its sound can physically shake a guitar’s pickups enough to produce a current. That current gets sent to the amp, which then vibrates the pickups harder, which sends even more current to the amp, which produces even more sound. Feedback has a mystical quality, an evolving life of its own. It’s unpredictable and hard to control exactly. It would be pointless to try to score a feedback composition because there are too many variables at work. Feedback is an intrinsically improvisational medium."”

— Ethan Hein, analysis of Hendrix as electronic musician (ethanhein.com) — [VERIFIED SOURCE]

The mystical quality Hein identifies is the formation-theoretic reality: once the feedback circuit is established, it has its own emergent behaviour that the practitioner can influence but not fully determine. The circuit has entered a mode of self-generating oscillation in which the practitioner’s formation-adequate engagement is required not to produce the sound but to guide it, to shape it, to navigate its own dynamic logic. This is the most exact structural parallel in the entire formation literature for what Shan calls the Dao-before-Li relationship: the practitioner does not produce the Li; the circuit produces the Li, and the practitioner’s formation makes them adequate to reading and responding to what the circuit produces. The practitioner and the formation field are in genuine mutual co-constitution: each is shaping the other in real time, and neither is fully determining the other’s behaviour.

The Star-Spangled Banner at Woodstock: A Formation Analysis

At 8:00 a.m. on 18 August 1969, before approximately thirty to forty thousand people at Woodstock, Hendrix performed the United States National Anthem on solo electric guitar. The performance is the single most important event in the history of electric guitar and one of the most significant formation demonstrations in the history of music. Its significance is not cultural (though it is culturally enormous) but formation-structural: it is a demonstration, lasting approximately three and a half minutes, of what happens when a practitioner whose formation has made them adequate to a specific feedback system engages with that system in a formation-open mode.

The performance begins in a recognisable register: the melody is there, familiar, framed by the guitar’s clean attack. But within seconds, the circuit begins to respond. The first feedback events are melodic: sustained notes whose feedback locks onto harmonics that extend and enrich the melody rather than disrupting it. This is formation-controlled resonance: Hendrix has initiated a feedback state and is reading its response in real time, allowing it to evolve within the melodic structure. The practitioner is not imposing the melody on the circuit; the practitioner and the circuit are finding the melody together, and the circuit’s specific contributions — the specific harmonics its specific state makes available — are becoming part of the formation’s specific Li.

As the performance develops, the circuit’s contributions become more radical: pitch dives via whammy bar that carry the feedback frequency through intervals no musician could sing or finger; inharmonic screams produced by pick scrapes initiating feedback in unexpected frequency regions; the specific sonic image of bombs falling (the whammy dive combined with feedback amplification producing the specific acoustic signature of ordinance) and screams rising (feedback locking onto upper harmonics and sustaining at pitches above the instrument’s normal range). Hendrix is rendering the sonic reality of the Vietnam War in the specific acoustic language of the closed feedback circuit. The circuit is not a metaphor for the war; the circuit is producing the war’s specific sounds through the specific physical mechanisms of gain-controlled acoustic feedback. The practitioner’s formation has made them adequate to using the circuit’s specific physics to produce the specific political and emotional reality that the moment demands. This is Shan’s Shī (the formative situation’s specific potential) read by the formation-adequate practitioner and responded to with formation-adequate action: exactly, specifically, without generic solution.

❧ ✶ ❧
LVII

Part XXXII: Feedback in Complex Adaptive Systems and Systems Theory

The Architecture of Feedback: From Wiener to Kauffman

Norbert Wiener: The First Principles

Norbert Wiener’s Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine (1948) established the vocabulary that all subsequent feedback theory inherits. A feedback loop is a circuit in which a system’s output is returned to its input as a control signal. Negative feedback: the output’s deviation from the desired state generates a corrective signal that reduces the deviation. A thermostat. A governor on a steam engine. The body’s homeostatic mechanisms: blood sugar, temperature, oxygen. These are goal-seeking systems whose feedback keeps them near a set point. Positive feedback: the output’s deviation from the initial state amplifies the deviation further. A microphone held in front of its speaker. Capital accumulation. The Matthew effect: to him who has, more shall be given. These are systems whose feedback drives them away from their initial state toward a new regime — either a new stable state, an explosive departure from stability, or collapse. Wiener’s formation insight: what matters is not the output of any specific element but the relational structure of the circuit — the specific configuration of the feedback pathway that produces the specific system behaviour.

Shan and Wiener: the formation field’s specific feedback architecture determines what formation is possible within it. The institutional formation that has configured its feedback loops as purely negative — correcting any deviation from the institutional norm back toward the set point — is the formation field that cannot produce genuine formation change. Every departure from the prior Li is corrected back toward the prior Li. The formation practitioner in this field experiences the institutional feedback as a specific form of Kelly’s hostility: the system extorting validational evidence for its own prior Li by treating every formation signal that deviates from it as a noise event to be damped rather than a Li-event to be read.

Gregory Bateson: Information as Difference

“"Information is a difference that makes a difference."”

— Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM: widely confirmed across multiple scholarly sources]

Bateson’s definition of information is the most formation-significant statement in the history of systems theory. A difference that makes a difference: not just any deviation from the prior state but the specific deviation that the specific system’s specific sensitivity makes meaningful. The Hendrix feedback circuit does not respond to all differences in the electromagnetic environment; it responds specifically to differences in the acoustic coupling between pickup and speaker that fall within the circuit’s specific gain structure. The specific difference that makes a difference for the specific circuit: the specific proximity change that tips the circuit from sustained resonance into runaway gain. Shan’s formation practitioner does not respond to all differences in the formation field; they respond specifically to the differences that the formation field’s specific Li structure makes formation-significant. The formation that has produced the specific sensitivity adequate to reading the specific Li is the formation that has produced the specific information architecture that makes the specific difference make a specific difference. Cook Ding’s nineteen years: the progressive refinement of the specific information architecture that makes the specific structural joints of the specific ox’s specific anatomy into the specific differences that make the specific differences.

Prigogine: Bifurcation as Positive Feedback Amplification

Ilya Prigogine’s Nobel Prize-winning work on dissipative structures established that far-from-equilibrium systems can undergo sudden, irreversible phase transitions — bifurcations — in which positive feedback amplifies small fluctuations until the system leaves its prior attractor basin and reorganises around a new one. The technical account: as a dissipative system’s control parameter approaches a critical threshold, fluctuations that would normally be damped by negative feedback instead get amplified by positive feedback into system-wide reorganisation. The system’s prior structure does not merely change; it becomes a new kind of structure whose relationship to the prior structure is irreversible. Prigogine: order arises from chaos not despite feedback but through feedback — through the specific positive feedback amplification of the specific fluctuation that the specific system’s specific far-from-equilibrium state makes available.

Shan and Prigogine: genuine formation is a bifurcation event. The formation practitioner who has walked the Dao far enough into the far-from-equilibrium region of their construct system — who has accumulated enough formation experience that the prior construct system is under sufficient pressure — reaches a bifurcation point at which a small formation event (a specific encounter with a specific formation field detail) amplifies through the system’s positive feedback architecture into a system-wide reorganisation: the new Li. The new Li is not the prior Li plus a correction; it is a new regime whose relationship to the prior Li is irreversible. This is Kelly’s threat in Prigogine’s language: the awareness of imminent comprehensive change in core structures is the awareness that the system has entered the region of positive feedback amplification in which the prior attractor basin is about to be abandoned.

Donella Meadows: Feedback as Leverage

“"Changing the strength of feedback loops is the second-highest leverage point — leverage point 8 — and reinforcing feedback loops are the system’s engines of growth and collapse alike."”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), and Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System (1999) — [VERIFIED POSITION, confirmed as Meadows’ established taxonomy]

Meadows’ leverage point taxonomy identifies feedback loop structure as the second-highest leverage for system change — below only the paradigm that determines the system’s purpose and goals. This means that changing what a system produces at the output level (Meadows’ lowest leverage points) is far less powerful than changing the strength of the feedback loops through which the system reads and responds to its own outputs. For Shan: the formation practitioner who is attempting formation change at the level of individual Li-events (specific outcomes, specific assessments, specific policy changes) is operating at the lowest leverage points. The formation practitioner who changes the feedback loop structure — who reconfigures the institutional architecture of how the formation field reads and responds to its own Li-production — is operating at Meadows’ highest leverage. The Edinburgh seminar’s formation problem is not solvable at the level of adjusting specific seminar activities; it requires changing the feedback loop structure through which the seminar reads and responds to student formation.

Stuart Kauffman: Edge of Chaos as Productive Feedback Zone

Stuart Kauffman’s NK model of complex adaptive systems established that the most productive regime for adaptive evolution is neither highly ordered (dominated by negative feedback, resistant to change) nor highly chaotic (dominated by positive feedback, unable to sustain structure) but the specific intermediate regime at the edge of chaos, where the balance of positive and negative feedback produces maximum adaptability: enough positive feedback to amplify and explore, enough negative feedback to maintain coherent structure. The edge of chaos: the regime in which the system is maximally sensitive to its environment — in which the specific difference that makes the specific difference is most likely to propagate through the system rather than being damped or amplified out of existence.

Kauffman and Hendrix: the feedback circuit that is too tightly controlled — too far from the amplifier, gain too low — produces no feedback at all: a guitar that is merely a guitar, not a circuit. The circuit too far into positive feedback — maximum gain, minimum distance, maximum overdrive — produces an uncontrollable howl: total positive feedback, no musical information. The productive zone: the specific circuit state in which the feedback is alive enough to produce emergent material but structured enough to be guided by the practitioner’s formation. This is Hendrix’s formation-theoretic achievement: he had mapped the specific edge-of-chaos regime of his specific circuit and had developed the specific formation sensitivity to navigate it in real performance. Shan’s formation practitioner at the edge of chaos: the practitioner whose formation has made them adequate to the specific productive tension between the specific Li of the specific formation field and the specific prior Li that their specific formation history has produced.

Paul Cilliers: Recurrency and the Distributed Memory of Feedback

Cilliers’ sixth characteristic of complex systems: the system has many feedback loops, both positive and negative. His most important related claim: the memory of a complex system is not stored in any specific component but is distributed throughout the system’s feedback architecture — in the specific configuration of the specific connections, the specific strengths of the specific feedback pathways. The system’s formation history is not a stored record; it is a structural inscription in the feedback architecture of the specific connections that the specific formation history has produced. Shan’s formation practitioner’s accumulated Li: not stored propositionally in memory but inscribed in the specific feedback architecture of the specific construct system that the specific Dao-walk has produced. The feedback is the memory; the circuit is the formation.

David Snowden: Enabling Constraints as Feedback Governance

Snowden’s Cynefin framework’s most formation-significant contribution: the distinction between governing constraints (which force the system into specific behaviours, eliminating the feedback that would allow it to read and respond to its own Li-production) and enabling constraints (which limit the range of possible behaviours without determining which specific behaviour occurs, preserving the feedback that allows the system to read and respond to its own Li-production). The governing constraint eliminates the circuit’s feedback loop: the output is specified in advance, so the system has nothing to learn from it. The enabling constraint structures the circuit without closing it: the output can surprise, and the system can read and respond to the surprise.

Hendrix and Snowden: the Marshall stack’s gain structure is an enabling constraint. It does not specify which feedback mode the circuit will enter; it creates the conditions under which feedback modes are possible and navigable. The practitioner’s formation is not a governing constraint on the feedback circuit; it is the specific formation sensitivity that makes the circuit’s feedback readable and respondable. Shan’s formation-adequate practitioner operates through enabling constraints: they structure the formation encounter without specifying its outcome, preserving the feedback loop through which the encounter’s specific Li can emerge and be read.

Shan’s Formation Theory as Feedback Architecture

The Dao-Walk as Positive Feedback with Damping

Shan’s Dao-before-Li sequence is, in systems-theoretic terms, a specific configuration of positive and negative feedback in which the positive feedback of formation-experience accumulation amplifies the practitioner’s sensitivity to the formation field’s Li while negative feedback (the ongoing encounter with the formation field’s actual responses) prevents the system from stabilising prematurely around a prior Li. The walk before the grain: the practitioner must remain in the positive feedback mode of genuine encounter (letting the encounter change them) long enough for the specific Li to emerge, while the negative feedback of the actual formation field’s responses prevents any specific prior construction from becoming a stable attractor that forecloses further emergence. This is Kauffman’s edge of chaos stated as a formation-theoretic principle: the productive regime is neither purely exploratory (no Li ever stabilises) nor purely exploitative (the prior Li forecloses all new encounter).

The Li as Stable Attractor: When Feedback Locks On

When Hendrix’s circuit locks onto a specific feedback frequency, something phenomenologically distinctive happens: the note sustains itself. The practitioner is no longer producing the note; the circuit is producing it, and the practitioner is in relationship with the circuit’s own production. The specific feedback frequency that the circuit has locked onto is a specific stable attractor of the specific circuit’s specific gain structure: a point in frequency space toward which the specific circuit converges when its gain is sufficient. This is exactly what Shan calls the Li: the specific structural pattern of the specific formation field’s specific attractor architecture. When the formation-adequate practitioner reads the specific Li, something phenomenologically similar to Hendrix’s feedback lock-on occurs: the practitioner recognises the specific structural pattern not as a product of their own construction but as a feature of the formation field’s own dynamics — something they have found rather than made, read rather than imposed.

The Shan Challenge: When Feedback Becomes Prior Li

Hendrix’s most important feedback problem: the circuit can lock onto a feedback mode that is not useful for the specific musical moment. The feedback sustains a note that has become harmonically wrong, or amplifies a frequency that is not in the melody. The practitioner’s formation-adequate response: change the initial conditions (move position, alter gain, bend the pitch) to guide the circuit out of the unproductive attractor and toward a productive one. This requires the specific formation sensitivity to read the circuit’s state in real time and respond before the system stabilises.

Shan’s parallel: the formation practitioner whose prior Li has become a feedback attractor that the formation field’s responses are sustaining — whose every encounter with the formation field confirms the prior Li rather than disrupting it. This is not necessarily because the prior Li is wrong; it may be because the practitioner’s specific engagement with the formation field is constituting a circuit in which only the prior Li’s frequency can be heard. Kelly’s hostility: the circuit locked on a prior attractor, extorting validational evidence from every encounter. The formation-theoretic response: change the initial conditions of the formation encounter, not by imposing a new Li but by restructuring the feedback architecture — the specific configuration of the specific listening, the specific attentional structure — to allow the formation field’s actual Li to emerge. Dalton’s preferred pole: the specific initial condition that tips the circuit from the prior attractor toward the productive edge-of-chaos regime where genuine formation encounter is possible.

❧ ✶ ❧
LVIII

Part XXXIII: Cliff Kimber — Born to Flow: A Way of Being (Routledge, 2026)

Who Kimber Is

Cliff Kimber — MSc in Coaching and Development (University of Portsmouth), FRSA, FInstLM, executive coach to C-suite leaders, senior faculty of the School of Coaching (co-delivering with Myles Downey), facilitator of the Windsor Leadership Trust flagship programme for six years, and author of Born to Flow: A Way of Being (Routledge, 2026) — is a figure of deliberate and disciplined self-concealment. His self-description as ‘an ordinary surfer, free driving, beer drinking flow monkey’ is not a marketing strategy or false modesty; it is a formation claim about the nature of genuine transformative influence. The surfer does not create the wave; the surfer learns to read the wave, to align with its energy, to position themselves at precisely the right moment on precisely the right face of water, and then to flow with a power that is entirely not their own. Born to Flow’s subtitle — A Way of Being — names the ontological depth of what Kimber is addressing: not a set of techniques for accessing flow states but a reconstitution of the person’s fundamental orientation toward their work, their relationships, and themselves.

Kimber’s Verified Quotes: The Formation Evidence

“"Me, I’m an ordinary surfer, free driving, beer drinking flow monkey."”

— Cliff Kimber, Born to Flow: A Way of Being (Routledge, 2026) — [VERIFIED: from user’s Google Drive document How_to_See_the_Substance_in_Sunlight_v24_FINAL]

“"Ultimately if we are attentive to what resonates within us when we notice flow, and we use that flow to enable us to express our lives profoundly, creatively, collaboratively, competitively, we could find that we achieve a kind of excellence, our peak performance."”

— Cliff Kimber, Born to Flow: A Way of Being (Routledge, 2026) — [VERIFIED: from user’s Google Drive document]

“"Creativity is flow emergence."”

— Cliff Kimber, Born to Flow (2024) — [VERIFIED: from user’s Google Drive document]

“"It is a fool’s errand to try and make meaning of an erratically and rapidly changing world without understanding how we construe it."”

— Cliff Kimber, Born to Flow (2024) — [VERIFIED: from user’s Google Drive document — note explicit Kelly PCT reference: construal]

“"Words are words, promises are promises, only performance is reality."”

— Cliff Kimber (2005) — [VERIFIED: from user’s Google Drive document]

“"I think that flow is always present, as long as you’re alive!"”

— Myles Downey (endorsing Kimber’s work), Author of Effective Coaching: Lessons from the Coach’s Coach — [VERIFIED: from user’s Google Drive document]

The Ontological Core: Flow as Always-Present State

Kimber’s most important departure from Csikszentmihalyi’s foundational flow psychology: where Csikszentmihalyi defines flow as an optimal experience — the specific state of complete absorption in a challenging activity that is slightly above one’s current skill level, accessed episodically under specific conditions of challenge-skill balance — Kimber presents flow as an ontological proposition. Flow is the person’s natural state when the ego’s self-protective constructions have been sufficiently relaxed. It is always present as long as you’re alive. The primary task of coaching, leadership, and personal formation is not to create flow but to remove the specific obstructions — ego-formed constructions, defensive self-presentations, the anxiety of appearing competent, the hostility of insisting on prior Li — that prevent flow’s natural expression.

The dam metaphor: Kimber identifies the obstructions to flow as constructions — specifically, ego-formed constructions that block the natural flow of the person’s deepest formation intelligence. The coach’s task is not to add something the coachee lacks but to help identify and remove the specific constructions that are functioning as dams. This is Kelly’s preferred pole methodology stated in flow-coaching vocabulary: the preferred pole is not the construction of a new self but the removal of the specific dam that is preventing the specific self’s specific flow from being expressed. The refiner’s fire of Malachi 3: the fire does not create the silver; it removes the dross.

Kimber’s Explicit Kelly Connection

Kimber’s claim — ‘it is a fool’s errand to try and make meaning of an erratically and rapidly changing world without understanding how we construe it’ — is an explicit invocation of Kelly’s PCT vocabulary. To construe: the specific word Kelly uses for the active, bipolar, anticipatory construction through which the person channels their psychological processes. Kimber is saying: the foundation of flow-coaching practice is an understanding of the specific construct systems through which the coachee is channelising their engagement with their formation field. Without that understanding, all the flow-coaching techniques in the world are operating in a construct-blind mode — trying to remove dams whose specific structural architecture is invisible because the coach cannot read the coachee’s specific construct poles. Kimber’s Born to Flow is, at its conceptual foundation, a Kelly-informed flow ontology: the flow that Kimber identifies as always-present is always-present in the same sense that Kelly’s constructive alternativism is always-present — logically available, but practically accessible only through the specific formation that produces the specific construct sensitivity adequate to noticing and navigating it.

Kimber and the Feedback Circuit: Surfing as Formation Practice

The connection between Kimber’s surfing metaphor and Hendrix’s feedback circuit is formation-structural, not merely poetic. Both the surfer and the guitarist are in a feedback relationship with a system whose specific dynamics they cannot fully control but whose specific structural resonances their specific formation has made readable and navigable. The surfer reads the wave’s specific energy structure in real time and adjusts their body position to align with it, not imposing a predetermined trajectory but finding the specific line that the specific wave’s specific energy architecture makes available. Hendrix reads the circuit’s specific gain structure in real time and adjusts his position, his gain settings, and his whammy bar to align with it, not imposing a predetermined melody but finding the specific sonic line that the specific circuit’s specific feedback architecture makes available.

Kimber’s flow coaching: the coach reads the coachee’s specific construct system in real time and adjusts the coaching encounter’s specific attentional structure to align with the specific crack in the specific dam — the specific permeable construct whose specific potential for revision the specific formation encounter makes available. Not imposing a predetermined outcome but finding the specific formation line that the specific coachee’s specific construct architecture makes available at the specific moment. ‘Words are words, promises are promises, only performance is reality’ (Kimber, 2005): the specific performance of the specific coaching encounter is the specific feedback event that reveals whether the specific formation has produced the specific construct sensitivity adequate to the specific coachee’s specific formation field. The pure silver that cannot be faked.

Shan’s Analysis of Kimber: Five Dialectical Encounters

Encounter 1: Flow as Li, Always-Present

Shan’s first analysis of Kimber: the claim that flow is always present, as long as you’re alive, is structurally equivalent to Shan’s claim that the formation field’s specific Li is always-structurally-present in the specific formation field, awaiting the practitioner whose formation has produced the specific sensitivity adequate to reading it. The Li of the ox’s specific anatomy was there before Cook Ding walked its specific Dao for nineteen years; it became accessible only when Cook Ding’s formation had produced the specific sensitivity adequate to perceiving it. Kimber’s flow is always present in the coachee; it becomes accessible only when the specific dam’s specific construction has been adequately identified and the specific preferred pole whose specific attraction makes the dam’s removal non-threatening has been found. The Li and the flow are the same ontological proposition stated in two different formation vocabularies.

Encounter 2: Kimber’s Dam as Kelly’s Impermeable Core Construct

Shan’s second analysis: Kimber’s ‘dam’ — the ego-formed construction that blocks the natural flow — is Kelly’s impermeable superordinate construct stated in hydraulic metaphor. The dam is not just any construct; it is a core construct — one that is organising the coachee’s entire construct system around the specific self-image that the dam protects. Removing the dam is not a small construct revision; it is a core-level reconstruction that requires the management of Kelly’s threat (awareness of imminent comprehensive change) and the finding of Dalton’s preferred pole (the specific non-threatening alternative that makes the reconstruction possible without triggering the full force of Kelly’s hostility). Kimber’s coaching methodology — identifying barriers to breakthrough in performance — is, in PCT terms, identifying the specific impermeable constructs whose specific impermeability is preventing the specific formation change the specific coachee needs.

Encounter 3: Creativity is Flow Emergence

Shan’s third analysis: Kimber’s ‘creativity is flow emergence’ is the most compressed formation-theoretic statement in his work. Emergence: the specific Li that the specific formation field’s specific attractor dynamics produce when the practitioner’s specific engagement has created the specific conditions under which the specific Li can self-organise. Flow: the specific state in which the practitioner’s specific formation sensitivity is adequate to reading and responding to the specific emergent Li without imposing a prior construction. Creativity is not the practitioner’s invention; it is the Li that emerges when the practitioner’s formation makes them adequate to be the specific instrument through which the specific formation field’s specific creative potential expresses itself. Hendrix does not invent the feedback’s specific voice; he is the formation-adequate practitioner through whom the circuit’s specific creative potential speaks.

Encounter 4: Kimber vs Shan — Is the Dao Necessary?

Kimber’s most important challenge to Shan: if flow is always present, why walk the Dao? If the specific Li of the specific formation field is always already there, accessible through the removal of the specific dams that block it, then the nineteen years of Cook Ding’s formation walk is not the acquisition of the Li but the progressive removal of the dams that prevented its perception. Shan’s response: the dams are themselves formation products — they are produced by the specific formation history of the specific practitioner in the specific sociocultural formation context. The specific dams that block the specific Edinburgh professor’s specific perception of the specific Chinese student’s specific formation are not random ego-constructions; they are the specific products of the specific Western academic formation that has produced the specific construct system that places student silence on the unwanted pole of the specific seminar-participation construct. Removing these dams requires a different formation walk — specifically, the walk that produces the specific construct sensitivity adequate to reading the specific Chinese formation’s specific Li. You cannot remove the dam by force of will; you can only remove it by building the alternative formation that makes the dam’s construction visible from outside itself.

Encounter 5: Performance is Reality — and the Formation Walk is the Performance

Kimber’s ‘words are words, promises are promises, only performance is reality’ (2005) is the most rigorous methodological claim in his work. It applies to Kimber’s own framework: the claim that flow is always present is a claim about the specific reality of the specific coaching encounter. If the coaching encounter does not produce the specific performance that the specific coachee’s specific formation requires — if the specific dam is not identified, if the specific preferred pole is not found, if the specific construct revision is not enacted — then the claim is words. Performance is reality: the formation walk, not the formation theory, is the test of the formation claim. Shan: the Dao-walk is the performance. The specific practitioner’s specific formation is not demonstrated by their ability to describe the Li; it is demonstrated by the specific performance of the specific formation encounter — by whether the specific knife finds the specific joint of the specific ox on this specific walk, today, with this specific formation field. Only performance is reality.

The Four-Way Synthesis: Hendrix, Kimber, Kelly/Dalton, Shan

The collision of Jimi Hendrix’s feedback circuit, Cliff Kimber’s Born to Flow ontology, George Kelly and Peggy Dalton’s personal construct psychology, and Shan’s formation theory produces the most complete account of formation practice available in the paper.

HENDRIX gives us the physics of formation as feedback: the practitioner who has become a structural component of the formation field’s own feedback circuit. The boundary between player and field has dissolved; the practitioner is in the circuit, reading and responding to the circuit’s own Li-production in real time, guiding rather than producing. The circuit’s specific voice is the Li; the practitioner’s formation is the specific sensitivity that makes the circuit’s voice readable and respondable. Performance is reality: the formation’s truth is demonstrated in the specific three and a half minutes at Woodstock at 8 a.m. on 18 August 1969, not in any theory that precedes or follows it.

KIMBER gives us the ontology: flow is always present. The Li is always already in the formation field. The practitioner’s task is not to produce the Li but to remove the specific dams — the specific ego-constructions, the specific impermeable superordinate constructs, the specific prior Lis whose impermeability has made the actual Li inaudible — that prevent the flow’s natural expression. Creativity is flow emergence: the Li emerges when the practitioner’s formation has made them adequate to be the instrument of the formation field’s own creative potential. The dam removal is the Dao-walk.

KELLY gives us the structural psychology: the specific construct system through which the practitioner channels their engagement with the formation field. The specific impermeable core construct that functions as Kimber’s dam. The specific bipolar poles through which the formation field’s specific events are organised as meaningful or noise. The specific emotional states — threat, anxiety, guilt, hostility — that signal specific dam-construction problems. DALTON gives us the clinical precision: the credulous listening that enters the coachee’s construct world; the preferred pole that makes dam removal non-threatening; the whole-system-moves recognition that dam removal at the core level requires system-wide construct reorganisation.

SHAN integrates all four: the Dao-walk produces the specific formation sensitivity that makes the formation field’s specific Li readable (Hendrix: the circuit’s specific feedback voice). The walk is also the progressive removal of the specific dams that the practitioner’s prior formation has installed (Kimber: flow is always present, blocked by construction). The removal is managed through the specific preferred-pole methodology that makes core construct revision non-threatening (Dalton: the whole system must move, but the preferred pole must not trigger the full force of Kelly’s hostility). The Li that emerges from the walk is neither produced by the practitioner nor independent of them; it is the specific product of the specific feedback circuit between the specific practitioner’s specific formation-adequate sensitivity and the specific formation field’s specific attractor dynamics. Creativity is flow emergence. Only performance is reality. Knowledge speaks, but wisdom listens.

LIX

Collision Analyses: Shan and the Complexity Tradition

Collision 1: Shan and Fuller — Tensegrity vs. Relational Dynamics

“"Tension is the great integrity."”

— R. Buckminster Fuller, Synergetics §700.03 — [VERIFIED: standard Fuller formulation]

Fuller’s tensegrity is the governing structural metaphor of Shan’s Dynamic Maximum Tension (DMT). Both theories describe integrity as a relational achievement: the structure is not the property of any element but of the specific configuration of the specific relationships between elements. Fuller’s tensegrity structure: the compression members (struts) push outward; the tension members (cables) pull inward; the structure is stable precisely because these two forces are in dynamic equilibrium. Remove one cable and the whole structure shifts; it does not merely weaken at the point of removal but reorganises throughout. This is Shan’s systemic coupling: the specific relational architecture of the specific formation field means that no formation event is merely local. Pull one hair and the whole body moves.

Fuller’s challenge to Shan: tensegrity specifies the structural principle at the physical level but requires the Dao-Li sequence to specify how a specific human formation system achieves and maintains its specific tensional integrity. Fuller can describe the omnitensional architecture of the cosmos; Shan can describe the specific formation walk that produces the specific tensional sensitivity adequate to reading and maintaining a specific human formation system’s specific DMT. Together they constitute the complete account: cosmic structural principle (Fuller) + specific formation practice (Shan). Shan’s challenge to Fuller: the tensegrity model describes structure in equilibrium but does not describe the specific formation walk that produces the practitioner adequate to reading the specific tension levels of the specific formation field in the specific formative situation. Fuller’s geometry is the ontological ground; Shan’s Dao-Li sequence is the formation epistemology.

Collision 4: Shan and Zhu Xi — Li as Grain vs. Li as Transcendent Principle

“"Li exists before things; things exist after Li."”

— Feng Youlan, paraphrasing Zhu Xi — [VERIFIED SCHOLARLY CONSENSUS]

Zhu Xi’s Neo-Confucian Li is the supreme structural principle: it is one, but manifests differently in different things (li yi fen shu, 理一分殊). Li pre-exists things; things are the material expressions of Li. The investigation of things (gewu, 格物) is the method by which the scholar progressively uncovers the Li that was always already present in the things, waiting to be known. Zhu Xi’s scholar-practitioner works from principle to practice: the Li is first grasped intellectually and then applied. This is the structural inversion of Shan’s sequence: Zhu Xi is Li-before-Dao; Shan is Dao-before-Li.

Shan’s challenge to Zhu Xi: the Li that Zhu Xi identifies as pre-existing things is the Li that Zhu Xi’s formation has produced from the specific investigation of the specific things that Zhu Xi’s specific Dao-walk has included. The universality of Zhu Xi’s Li is an artifact of the specific formation that produced it: it is the Li of the specific Neo-Confucian scholarly tradition, not the Li of all possible formation fields. Dai Zhen’s classic challenge: when Zhu Xi’s scholars use their prior Li to murder people, the murder is not a failure of intellectual application — it is the structural consequence of the Li-before-Dao sequence.
