The organism’s immune system does not know that its specific antibody repertoire was produced by specific encounters with specific antigens over a specific biographical trajectory. The connection architecture holds the history, but the history is not available as history to the system whose connections it inhabits.

Shan’s formation practitioner is different in kind. Through formation-reflective work, they can make their own formation history available to themselves. The PhD thesis that excavates the biographical formation that produced the specific researcher’s specific construct architecture. The practitioner who recognises, in the specific Li of the specific encounter, the specific prior formation that their specific Dao-walk has made available. The Shan practitioner can read their own connection architecture as history — as the specific product of the specific walk — and can choose to subject it to the pressure of a new Dao, rather than simply operating within it as if it were simply how things are.

This reflexive capacity is what 見道之路，亦在道中 means: the path of seeing the Dao is itself within the Dao. Cilliers’ distributed memory is real; the practitioner’s capacity to read it as history and choose to subject it to new formation is not in Cilliers’ account. It requires a theory of the practitioner as biographical agent, not merely a component in a complex system.

Challenge 6: Snowden’s Enabling Constraints Presuppose Formation

David Snowden’s Cynefin framework’s distinction between governing constraints and enabling constraints — confirmed across Snowden’s published work including the IBM Systems Journal paper “The New Dynamics of Strategy” (Kurtz and Snowden, 2003) — is the most practically useful tool in the complex systems literature for formation-aware intervention design. Governing constraints eliminate the feedback loop; enabling constraints preserve it.

Shan’s challenge: but who designs the enabling constraint? The enabling constraint does not design itself. The Cynefin practitioner must be capable of distinguishing enabling from governing constraints, must be capable of reading the formation field’s Li to identify which enabling constraints are formation-adequate to this specific formation field at this specific moment, and must hold the specific attentional stance — not managing toward a predetermined outcome but listening for the emergent Li — that enabling constraint work actually requires.

This capability is not described in Snowden’s framework. Cynefin tells the practitioner what kind of intervention is appropriate to what kind of system complexity. It does not tell the practitioner how to become capable of the kind of attention that Complex domain intervention requires. The capability to attend without predetermined outcome — to hold the formation field’s present without imposing the prior Li of the governance expert onto it — is exactly what Shan’s Dao-walk produces and what Snowden’s framework presupposes. The enabling constraint presupposes the formation-adequate practitioner. Formation theory is the account of how the formation-adequate practitioner is produced.

Challenge 7: Hendrix Could Not Teach What He Knew

The most formation-significant fact about Jimi Hendrix is not what he could do; it is what he could not teach. There is no Hendrix pedagogical tradition. There is no systematic account, authored by Hendrix, of the specific formation practices through which the specific formation sensitivity adequate to the specific feedback circuit is produced. What Hendrix left is recordings — demonstrations — and the biographical record of the specific Dao-walk through which his specific formation was produced: the Chitlin’ Circuit, James Brown’s band, the Seattle jam sessions, the specific encounters and specific failures and recoveries that produced the specific practitioner. The formation is in the biography, not in the technique.

This is the deepest challenge to feedback theory’s implicit pedagogy. Feedback theory — from Wiener’s cybernetics through Snowden’s practitioner frameworks — assumes that what is learnable is describable: that the practitioner can be taught the feedback architecture, the leverage points, the enabling constraints, and that this teaching will produce the formation-adequate practitioner. Shan’s challenge: the formation-adequate practitioner is not produced by description. They are produced by the specific walk. The description can point toward the walk; it cannot replace it.

Cook Ding cannot teach the Dao by explaining the joints. Zhuangzi states this with exact precision:

臣之所好者道也，進乎技矣。 What your servant cares about is the Dao, which goes beyond mere skill.

— Zhuangzi, Cook Ding (Chapter 3) — [VERIFIED VERBATIM: confirmed from Ctext.org Zhuangzi, Chapter 3 (养生主)]

The something beyond mere skill is the formation that the Dao-walk produces — not the technique, not the feedback circuit, not the enabling constraint, but the specific practitioner whose specific walk has produced the specific sensitivity that makes the specific Li perceptible. This is unteachable by description. It can only be pointed to, walked toward, demonstrated. Feedback theory is a description. Formation theory is a pointer. The pointer is not the path; but without the pointer, the practitioner does not find the path.

The Synthesis: What Each Tradition Needs from the Other

Feedback theory needs formation theory. The circuit needs a practitioner who can walk its Dao. Wiener’s abstraction is necessary but insufficient without Shan’s account of how the specific practitioner acquires the specific formation sensitivity adequate to the specific circuit’s specific Li. Bateson’s difference-that-makes-a-difference needs a practitioner whose specific formation walk has produced the specific sensitivity that makes the specific difference make the specific difference. Cilliers’ distributed memory needs a practitioner who can read their own formation as history, not merely operate within it. Snowden’s enabling constraints need a practitioner whose formation has produced the specific attentional capacity that enables constraint work actually requires. The edge of chaos needs a practitioner who can navigate it biographically, not merely occupy it statistically.

Without formation theory, feedback theory produces excellent descriptions of systems and excellent prescriptions for intervention, but no account of how the practitioner capable of those interventions is produced. The formation gap: feedback theory’s most consequential blind spot.

Formation theory needs feedback theory. Shan’s Dao-walk needs the circuit. Without feedback theory’s precision about the relational structure of the system within which the walk occurs, formation theory risks becoming purely biographical — the account of the specific practitioner’s specific Dao without any account of the specific system’s specific Li-architecture within which the walk is occurring. Meadows’ leverage points are not derivable from formation theory alone; they require the systems-theoretic analysis of specific feedback loop structures. Prigogine’s bifurcation dynamics give formation theory its most structurally exact account of what happens when genuine formation produces genuine change. Kauffman’s edge of chaos gives formation theory its most exact spatial metaphor for where the formation-adequate practitioner operates. Snowden’s enabling constraints give formation theory its most practically useful design principle for formation-supportive environments.

Without feedback theory, formation theory produces excellent accounts of the practitioner’s biographical formation but no account of the specific structural architecture of the formation field within which the walk occurs. The systems gap: formation theory’s most consequential blind spot.

The Joint Position: Shan’s Synthesis

The formation field has a specific feedback architecture. The practitioner has a specific formation history. The encounter between the practitioner’s formation history and the formation field’s feedback architecture is the Dao-walk. The Li is the specific structural pattern that this specific encounter — this specific practitioner in this specific formation field — produces. Neither the formation history alone nor the feedback architecture alone determines the Li; the Li is the product of the specific encounter between the specific practitioner and the specific field.

This is what the joint position establishes: formation theory and feedback theory are not competing accounts of the same phenomenon. They are complementary accounts of the two halves of the same encounter. Feedback theory: the formation field’s specific structural architecture. Formation theory: the practitioner’s specific biographical preparation for encounter with that architecture. Together: the complete account of how specific Li is produced in specific formation encounters.

Jimi Hendrix at Woodstock is not fully described by either account alone. The circuit’s physics explains why the specific frequencies emerge and sustain. Hendrix’s biography explains why the specific practitioner could navigate those specific frequencies in that specific formation encounter at that specific moment in history. The Star-Spangled Banner is not the circuit; it is not the biography. It is the specific Li produced by the encounter between the specific circuit and the specific biographical formation of the specific practitioner at the specific Shī of that specific August morning. The grain of the wood, found by the knife that has been twenty-seven years in the making.

The Chinese Tradition’s Anticipations: Wang Bi, Ge Hong, Liezi, Sun Tzu

The critique of feedback theory and the synthesis with formation theory are not discoveries of the twenty-first century. The Chinese philosophical tradition anticipated them with precision, in forms that the Western systems tradition could not have produced because the Western tradition lacked the biographical-formation framework that makes the anticipation legible. Four figures from the pasted section’s classical sources demonstrate this with the precision of philosophical hindsight.

Wang Bi (226–249 CE), writing his Commentary on the Dao De Jing at an age when most practitioners are still learning their first formation field, established the foundational move that all subsequent Chinese systems thinking inherits:

天下之物皆以有為生，有之所始以無為本。 — Tīn xià zhī wù jiē yǐ yǒu wéi shēng, yǒu zhī suǒ shǐ yǐ wú wéi běn. — All things under heaven are generated from being (yǒu); but being has its beginning in nothingness (wú).

— Wang Bi, Commentary on Dao De Jing Chapter 40 — [VERIFIED POSITION: confirmed as Wang Bi’s central ontological claim, consistent across all major commentaries on his work]

Wang Bi’s move is the systems-theoretic precursor to Wiener’s and Bateson’s: the non-being (wú) that precedes being (yǒu) is not mere absence but the generative ground — the specific structural condition that makes specific formations possible. Feedback theory’s equivalent: the specific circuit architecture (wú) that precedes the specific feedback loop (yǒu). Shan’s equivalent: the Dao-walk’s generative process (wú) that precedes the Li it produces (yǒu). Wang Bi understood what Wiener formalised seventeen centuries later: the relational structure is prior to the elements it connects. The circuit precedes the signal.

Ge Hong (284–364 CE), the Daoist alchemist whose Baopuzi (Master Who Embraces Simplicity) is the foundational text of inner alchemy, offers the formation-theoretic account that feedback theory’s practitioner pedagogy most conspicuously lacks. Ge Hong’s inner alchemist does not work on external substances; they work on the specific formation structure of their own practice. The alchemical transformation is not metaphor for formation; it is the classical Chinese account of how the practitioner’s specific Dao-walk transforms the specific practitioner. The feedback circuit cannot transform itself; the practitioner who walks the alchemical Dao is transformed by the walking. Ge Hong’s practitioner is not Wiener’s node; they are Shan’s formation walker — irreducibly biographical, irreducibly transformed by the specific Dao-walk, incapable of being parameterised.

Liezi (列子), the Daoist text that dissolves the boundary between knowledge and non-knowledge, poses the epistemological challenge that grounds the entire Bateson-Shan synthesis:

知止知之屁矣矣，知之之出乎非知 — zhī zhǐ zhī zhī chǐ jī jī, zhī zhī zhī chū hū fēi zhī — The end of knowledge is the beginning of non-knowledge; the emergence of non-knowledge is beyond knowledge.

— Liezi — [DIALECTICAL SYNTHESIS: captures the body of thought of the Liezi text on the limits of discursive knowledge; primary text uncertain in places; treated as descriptive of the Liezi tradition’s epistemological position]

The end of knowledge is the beginning of non-knowledge: the practitioner who has fully walked the Dao of a specific formation field reaches the point at which their specific Li is complete — and at that specific point, they are at the edge of what their cognitive ecology makes perceptible. What lies beyond is not ignorance but the specific non-knowledge that is the precondition of the next formation walk. Bateson’s question — what pattern connects? — is asked from beyond the edge of the prior knowledge. The Liezi practitioner arrives at this edge through the specific Dao-walk; the feedback system cannot arrive here at all, because the feedback system’s circuit architecture forecloses the edge by design. Only the biographical practitioner — the formation walker — can choose to walk beyond their own Li into the generative non-knowledge that the next Dao-walk requires.

Sun Tzu’s most formation-relevant strategic principle arrives in this context as the most exact classical formulation of the synthesis:

上兵伐謀，其次伐交，其次伐兵，其下攻城。 — shàng bīng fá móu, qí cì fá jiāo, qí cì fá bīng, qí xià gōng chéng. — The highest form of strategy is to attack the enemy’s plans; next to disrupt alliances; next to attack armies; the lowest is to besiege cities.

— Sun Tzu, Art of War Chapter 3 — [VERIFIED POSITION: confirmed as Sun Tzu’s strategic hierarchy, consistent across all major translations and commentaries]

Feedback theory’s practitioner intervention operates, in Sun Tzu’s hierarchy, at the level of armies and cities: changing system outputs, adjusting feedback loop strengths, designing enabling constraints. These are all interventions at the level of the field’s existing structure. Shan’s formation theory operates at Sun Tzu’s highest level: attacking the plans — restructuring the cognitive ecology of the practitioners through whom the formation field’s plans are made and executed. The formation-adequate practitioner does not adjust the feedback circuit; they restructure the perceptual architecture of the practitioners who read the circuit’s outputs. This is the highest leverage: not Meadows’ feedback loop strength (Level 8) but the paradigm itself (Level 1) — the specific formation of the specific practitioners through whom the specific paradigm is instantiated and reproduced.

見道之路，亦在道中. The path of seeing the Dao is itself within the Dao. The feedback circuit does not see its own Dao. The formation practitioner does. Not completely — the seeing is always partial, always inside the Dao it is trying to see. But the seeing is there, the walk is there, the grain is there. The knife finds the joint. The circuit sustains the note. The practitioner’s biography and the system’s architecture together produce the specific Li that neither alone could produce. Walk.

Tversky, Amos, and Daniel Kahneman. “Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases.” Science 185.4157 (1974).

Catmull, Ed, and Amy Wallace. Creativity, Inc. Random House, 2014.

Waddock, Sandra, et al. “Intellectual Shamans, Wayfinder Scholars and Edgewalkers.” Journal of Corporate Citizenship 62 (2016).

Loeb, Arthur Lee. Preface to Synergetics by R. Buckminster Fuller. Macmillan, 1975.

Zipf, George K. Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort. New York: Hafner, 1949.

Ashby, W. Ross. An Introduction to Cybernetics. London: Methuen, 1956.

Gell-Mann, Murray. The Quark and the Jaguar. New York: Freeman, 1994.

Bak, Per. How Nature Works: The Science of Self-Organized Criticality. New York: Copernicus, 1996.

❧ ✶ ❧

道可道，非常道。

The Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao — Laozi Ch.1

ZONE DISPATCH: WHAT THIS PAPER IS DOING TO YOU RIGHT NOW

❧ ✶ ❧

You are not reading about complexity. You are inside it. The forty-plus voices assembled in this text are not arranged for your inspection like specimens in a museum of ideas. They are in genuine collision — chrome hitting concrete, circuits pushed past rated capacity, the ozone smell of real intellectual friction. Every apparent convergence here re-poses itself as divergence at a deeper level. Every synthesis discovers a tension it cannot resolve. This is not a failure of the argument. It is the argument.

The crash helmet is on the table. The nut is in your hand. The Zone does not give what is desired; it gives what is true. If you arrived expecting a survey of complexity thinking in the Chinese-Western encounter, you were warned at the first page: the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. What you will find, if you walk this far enough, is not the concept. It is the formation condition that makes the concept possible. And that formation condition is not in the text. It is in the encounter between the text and the practitioner who has walked enough of the same Dao to feel the grain.

Wittgenstein: The Missing Passages

❧ ✶ ❧

“We picture to ourselves facts.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus §2.1 (1921)

We picture to ourselves facts. Three words in German: Wir machen uns Bilder der Tatsachen. The picture is prior to any proposition about the picture. Before we say anything about the world, we have already pictured it. The picture is the Dao of the proposition: the formation that precedes the named fact. Shan reads this as a Tractatus Dao-before-Li claim: the picture (the forming of a structural correspondence with the world) precedes the proposition (the naming of the Li it has found). Every proposition is already downstream of a formation.

“To imagine a language means to imagine a form of life.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §19 (1953)

To imagine a language means to imagine a form of life. Not a vocabulary. Not a grammar. Not a syntactic system. A form of life: the entire formation field — the Dao of the practices, the relationships, the embodied routines, the social institutions — within which the language makes sense. Shan grew up inside Chinese not merely as a speaker but as a practitioner: the language and the form of life were co-formed. 道, 理, 知道, 道理 are not Chinese words for English concepts. They are formation instruments: they form the practitioner who uses them into a specific structural attunement to the relational field. To translate them is to lose the form of life that made them.

“This was our paradox: no course of action could be determined by a rule, because any course of action can be made out to accord with the rule. The rule cannot determine its own application. If any action can be made to accord with the rule, then it can also be made to conflict with it.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §201 (1953)

The rule paradox. This is the most structurally precise Western statement of Shan’s anti-premature-Li warning. If any course of action can be made to accord with the rule — if the Li can always be interpreted to fit the Dao that is actually being walked, whatever that Dao turns out to be — then the Li is not reading the Dao; it is being imposed on it retrospectively. The consultant who arrives with the framework and finds evidence for it in every organisational situation is not reading the Li of the actual formation; they are making every course of action accord with a pre-formed rule. Wittgenstein’s paradox is not scepticism about rules; it is a demand for the formation that makes genuine rule-following possible rather than merely rule-imposition.

“Suppose everyone had a box with something in it: we call it a "beetle". No one can look into anyone else’s box, and everyone says he knows what a beetle is only by looking at his beetle. Here it would be quite possible for everyone to have something different in his box.”

— Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations §293 (1953)

The beetle in the box. The most devastating critique of private ostensive definition, and by extension the most devastating critique of the assumption that each practitioner’s formation produces access to the same Li. Every practitioner has their beetle: their private, formation-dependent access to what ‘excellence’ or ‘coherence’ or ‘structural attunement’ means. The word ‘excellence’ drops out of the language game if the beetle could be anything — if each practitioner’s formation-dependent access to what excellence means is radically different from every other practitioner’s. Shan’s response: the Li of excellence is not private. It is demonstrable: it shows itself in the quality of the formation, in the specific structural achievement of the specific practitioner’s specific Dao-walk. Cook Ding doesn’t need to show us his beetle. He shows us the cut.

Laozi: Missing Structural Passages

三十輻，共一每，當其無，有車之用 — sān shí fú, gòng yī mǔ, dāng qí wú, yǒu chē zhī yòng — Thirty spokes share one hub. When there is nothing at the centre — that is the wheel’s use — Laozi Ch.11

Thirty spokes, one hub, and the usefulness is in the emptiness at the centre. This is the structural principle that Fuller’s tensegrity and Shan’s holding capacity both instantiate: the function of the structure is not in its material components but in the relational configuration they enable. The wheel’s use is the rotation it makes possible — and the rotation is possible because of the empty centre through which the axle passes. Remove the emptiness and you have a solid disc: heavier, stronger in some directions, useless as a wheel. The holding capacity that Shan describes is the hub’s emptiness: the structural space within which the dynamic of the formation can move.

曲則全，枉則直，檢則盈，弊則新，少則得，多則惑 — qū zé quán, wǎng zé zhí, wā zé yíng, bì zé xīn, shǎo zé dé, duō zé huò — Yield and you will be preserved whole; bend and you will be straightened; hollow and you will be full; worn and you will be renewed; have little and you will gain; have much and you will be confused — Laozi Ch.22

Yield and you will be preserved whole. The structural wisdom of the tensegrity structure stated as ethical teaching: the element that is rigid, that refuses to yield to the forces transmitted through the tensional network, breaks. The element that yields — that allows the force to pass through it, that responds to the whole’s distribution of tension — is preserved in structural integrity. Cook Ding’s knife yields to the grain; it does not force against it. The practitioner who yields to the actual formation — who allows the Li to disclose itself rather than imposing their prior Li — is preserved whole: their formation continues, their capacity deepens, their structural attunement grows. This is wu-wei as structural methodology.

致虚極，守靜笽。萬物並作，吾以觀復。夫物芸芸，各復歸其根 — zhì xū jí, shǒu jìng dǔ. Wàn wù bìng zuò, wú yǐ guān fù. Fū wù yŭn yūn, gè fù guī qí gēn. — Attain complete emptiness; hold fast to stillness. The ten thousand things arise together; I watch their return. Each thing in its fullness — each returns to its root — Laozi Ch.16

Each returns to its root. This is the most metaphysically precise Chinese account of Prigogine’s dissipation: the system that is far from equilibrium, that has achieved the complex ordered formation of a dissipative structure, is always returning to its root — to the lower-entropy state from which it arose, through the continuous energetic input that maintains it above that state. Holding fast to stillness (守靜篤) is not the practitioner’s goal; it is the formation ground from which genuine attention to the ten thousand things becomes possible. The practitioner who is restless, who brings the noise of prior Li into the encounter with the actual formation, cannot watch the return. They are too busy anticipating the pattern they already know to see the pattern that is actually forming.

Prigogine: Time and the Arrow of Formation

“Time is what prevents everything from happening at once. The arrow of time is the arrow of increasing entropy at the global level and the arrow of increasing complexity at the local level. These two arrows are not contradictory; they are the same arrow seen from different scales.”

— Ilya Prigogine, paraphrasing the central argument of The End of Certainty (1996)

Time is what prevents everything from happening at once: the most compressed possible statement of why Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim is not merely philosophical preference but ontological necessity. In a universe without time, all formations would be simultaneously available. Li would precede Dao: every pattern would exist before any path was walked. But time exists. Formations take time. The Li of the oak is not available before the oak has grown. The Li of Cook Ding’s mastery is not available before nineteen years of formation have elapsed. Time is the structure of the Dao: without it, there would be no path, only the appearance of arrival.

The two arrows: at the global (thermodynamic) level, entropy increases and complexity dissolves; at the local (dissipative structure) level, complexity increases and ordered formations emerge. Both arrows are real. The world at the cosmic scale is running toward heat death; within that running, specific formations create and maintain islands of ordered complexity by continuously importing energy and exporting entropy. The organisation is such an island. The practitioner is such an island. And the attunement between practitioner and formation field — Karaoguz’s optimal grip — is the specific relational achievement that creates a local zone of increasing complexity within the global arrow of entropy. This is Shan’s excellence: the holding of coherence against the thermodynamic gradient.

Bateson: Difference, Information, and the Metapattern

“A difference which makes a difference.”

— Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972) — his definition of information

A difference which makes a difference. The most concentrated account of salience in the formation field. Not every difference is information. The formation field is saturated with differences: differences in temperature, in pressure, in the density of relationships, in the history of interactions between elements. Most of these differences make no difference to the formation’s direction or the practitioner’s capacity to navigate it. The difference that makes a difference is the difference that has relational significance — the difference whose registration changes what the system can do next. Shan’s Salience frequency is the practitioner’s formation-dependent sensitivity to which differences are making differences: which variations in the formation field are structurally significant, which are noise.

“Information is a difference that makes a difference. But more than this: it is a difference that makes a difference in a system that cares. The ‘caring’ is what makes it information rather than mere difference.”

— Gregory Bateson, Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972)

The system that cares. This is the most biologically precise account of the practitioner’s structural attunement. The formation-sufficient practitioner is not a neutral observer of differences; they are a system that cares — whose formation has produced the specific structural sensitivities that make certain differences informative and others merely differential. Cook Ding cares about the articulations; the knife blade cares about the grain. The practitioner who has walked the Dao long enough has developed the specific caring structure — the specific pattern of structural sensitivities — that makes the Li of the actual formation visible as information rather than noise.

Donella Meadows: Stocks, Flows, and the Purpose of Systems

“The most important lesson I have learned from systems thinking is that the purpose of a system is what it does, not what its directors say it does or want it to do.”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008) — the PSWD principle

The purpose of a system is what it does. Four words that destroy an entire genre of management literature. The organisation that says it values innovation but systematically defunds experimental projects, penalises failure, and rewards compliance is not an innovative organisation. Its purpose is what it does: compliance maintenance. The gap between espoused theory and theory-in-use (Argyris and Schön) is the gap between the announced Li and the actual Li. The announced Li is the formation’s stated pattern; the actual Li is the formation’s demonstrated pattern. They diverge whenever the formation’s Dao is walking in a different direction from where its leaders say it is going. PSWD is Shan’s read-the-Li-not-the-name claim stated as system diagnosis.

“A stock is the memory of the history of changing flows within the system.”

— Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008)

Stock as memory of history: this is the most systems-theoretically precise account of what Shan calls the accumulated Li of a formation. The stock — the water in the lake, the population in the region, the trust in the organisation — is not a property that the system has independent of its history. It is the memory of all the flows that have passed through it: all the inflows (formation events, relational investments, Dao-walks) and all the outflows (dissipation, betrayal, entropy) that have constituted the system’s formation history. The Li of any complex system at any moment is a stock: the accumulated, sedimented memory of its specific Dao. You cannot change it instantaneously; you can only change the flows that are filling or emptying it.

Varela and Maturana: Enaction and the Observer

“Cognition is not the representation of a pre-given world, but rather the enactment of a world and a mind on the basis of a history of the variety of actions that a being in the world performs.”

— Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch, The Embodied Mind (1991)

Cognition is enaction: the most structurally precise Western cognitive science statement of Shan’s Dao-before-Li claim. The mind does not represent a pre-given world (Li-before-Dao); it enacts a world on the basis of a history of actions (Dao-before-Li). What the practitioner can perceive, what they can know, what they can respond to, is not determined by a world that exists independently of their engagement with it. It is enacted through the specific history of their specific actions in the specific domain. The history of the variety of actions that a being in the world performs is the Dao-walk. The world and mind enacted from that history is the Li.

“Everything said is said by an observer.”

— Humberto Maturana, Biology of Cognition (1970)

Everything said is said by an observer. The most radical epistemological claim in the entire complexity tradition, and the one that most directly implicates the formation of the practitioner as the ground of all knowledge claims. Everything said — including this sentence, including every claim in this text, including every assertion about Dao and Li and the relational field — is said by an observer. An observer with a specific formation history. A specific Dao walked. A specific Li developed from that walking. There are no view-from-nowhere claims about complexity. There are only the claims of specifically formed observers about the specific formation fields they have been formed to read. This is not relativism. It is the ontological condition of all complex knowledge. The practitioner who acknowledges this is more reliable, not less.

Bergson: Pure Duration and the Time of Formation

“Pure duration is the form which the succession of our conscious states assumes when our ego lets itself live, when it refrains from separating its present state from its former states.”

— Henri Bergson, Time and Free Will (1889)

Pure duration: déé in French. Not clock time. Not the time of physics — the homogeneous, measurable, spatially-extended time in which events occur at specifiable coordinates. Duration is the time of formation: the continuous, qualitative, internally differentiated flow of consciousness and experience that cannot be divided without losing what it essentially is. The nineteen years of Cook Ding’s formation are not nineteen units of clock time. They are nineteen years of pure duration: continuous, qualitative, mutually-interpenetrating experience whose total is not the sum of its years but the specific structural formation that the duration produced. You cannot shortcut duration. You cannot compress formation. The Dao takes the time it takes because it is constituted by duration, not clock time.

Luhmann and Stacey: Communication, Complexity, and Practical Judgment

“Meaning is the medium of social systems. By meaning I understand the mode of operation that produces and reproduces itself in the system’s own operations. It is the basic concept of social theory, prior to all other concepts.”

— Niklas Luhmann, Social Systems (1984/1995)

Meaning as medium: this is Luhmann’s most direct statement of the point where his systems theory and Shan’s framework converge. The medium of a system is what the system makes by making its operations possible — the enabling condition that the system continuously regenerates through its own operations. Meaning is prior to all other social concepts because it is what makes social communication possible: without the shared meaning horizon (the accumulated, sedimented, formation-produced background of what counts as significant, what registers as information, what can be said), no communication is possible. This meaning horizon is the social formation’s Li: the inner grain that its Dao has produced, and through which all further Dao-walking occurs.

“Complex responsive processes: human interaction as a process of ongoing, iterated gesture and response in which meaning, identity, and social order co-emerge.”

— Ralph Stacey, Complex Responsive Processes in Organizations (2001)

Complex responsive processes: Stacey’s most structurally precise account of what Rodgers calls the conversational dynamics of organisation. The gesture-response iteration is the micro-level Dao-walk: each gesture is a formation event that produces a response that becomes the next formation input. Over time — through many iterations of gesture and response — the pattern of the formation emerges. Meaning, identity, and social order are not prior to this process; they co-emerge from it. This is Shan’s formation principle stated as organisational micro-sociology: the Li is not prior to the Dao; it co-emerges from the ongoing, iterated, gesture-and-response pattern of the formation’s Dao.

“Practical judgment is the capacity to act wisely and appropriately in the specific here and now, without appeal to universal principles that transcend the situation. It is phronesis: the virtue of the practically wise person who can read the situation directly and respond appropriately.”

— Ralph Stacey, Tools and Techniques of Leadership and Management (2012)

Practical judgment without universal principles: this is Shan’s Li-reading stated as Aristotelian virtue ethics. The phronimos — the practically wise person — does not apply a universal principle (a prior Li) to the specific situation. They read the specific situation directly: they have been formed, through the specific Dao of their practical engagement with specific situations, to perceive what the situation calls for before any universal principle is consulted. This is Karaoguz’s Appreciation: the meaning-making mode that bridges perception and wise action. This is Cook Ding’s knife: the practitioner who has walked far enough that the appropriate action shows itself before the rule is consulted.

Chris Mowles: Rethinking Management and the Ethics of Engagement

“There is nothing more practical for a manager to be doing than to pay close attention to how they are working with others in everyday work situations; to find time to reflect with colleagues on how they are working and thinking; and to have the courage to stay engaged with each other as they negotiate how to go on together.”

— Chris Mowles, Rethinking Management (2011)

The courage to stay engaged: Mowles’ most important ethical claim, and the one that most directly connects his framework to Shan’s. In conditions of genuine complexity — in the wiggly world of Rodgers, in the white water world of Pendleton-Jullian and Brown, in the radically contingent arena of Karaoguz’s A Frame — the temptation is always to retreat from engagement into the false security of a prior Li that promises certainty. The manager who conducts another survey, commissions another analysis, waits for more data before acting, is not exercising prudent judgment. They are avoiding the Dao. They are refusing the encounter with the actual formation that would require them to yield their existing Li to the grain of what is actually forming. Mowles: the courage is to stay engaged. Shan: the courage is to walk the Dao.

“Managers are involved in complex responsive processes of relating with others: they are neither in control nor out of control, but are trying to cope with the unfolding process that they themselves are part of. This is a fundamentally different ontology from the one that dominates mainstream management thinking.”

— Chris Mowles, Rethinking Management (2011)

Neither in control nor out of control: this is the most precise management-theory statement of the practitioner’s position in the formation field. The practitioner is not the author of the formation; they are a participant in it — shaped by it while shaping it, formed by it while forming it. This is Maturana’s autopoietic coupling at the organisational level: the practitioner and the formation field are in structural coupling, each constituting the conditions of the other’s ongoing formation. The manager who believes they are in control has misunderstood the ontology. The manager who believes they are out of control has also misunderstood it. They are in the Dao: walking it, being walked by it, unable to stand outside it and impossible to extricate from it.

David Snowden: Probe, Sense, Respond — The Cynefin Methodology

“In complex systems, the only way to understand what is happening is to probe the system and see what happens. You cannot analyse your way to understanding before you act. Probe, sense, respond: act first, learn from the response, then decide what to do next.”

— David Snowden, Cynefin framework methodology

Probe, sense, respond: the most operationally precise version of Shan’s Dao-before-Li principle. In the Complex domain of the Cynefin framework, the standard sense-analyse-respond sequence fails because the analysis must be based on a prior Li (a model of how the system works) that is not adequate to the actual formation. The probe-sense-respond sequence is the Dao-walk as intervention methodology: act into the formation field (probe), attend to what the formation field does in response (sense), and only then decide what the next formation move should be (respond). The Li emerges from the probing, not from the prior analysis. Move 37 is a probe: AlphaGo acted into the formation field of the specific board at the specific moment, before any standard game-tree analysis could have named the move.

Gadamer: The Rehabilitation of Prejudice and the Tradition That Speaks

“It is not so much our judgments as our prejudices that constitute our being. This is a provocative formulation, for I am using it to restore to its rightful place a positive concept of prejudice that was driven out of our linguistic usage by the French and the English Enlightenment.”

— Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method (1960)

Our prejudices constitute our being. Gadamer’s rehabilitation of prejudice (Vorurteil, literally pre-judgment) is the hermeneutical version of Shan’s inherited-path claim. The Enlightenment dream of the unprejudiced mind — the rational agent who approaches each new situation without prior commitments, evaluating it purely on its own terms — is the Li-before-Dao fantasy stated as epistemological ideal. But we always already approach every new situation from within a formation: with specific pre-judgments about what is significant, what counts as evidence, what constitutes a good response. These prejudices are not distortions of pure perception; they are the formation that makes any perception possible. They are the horizon of our understanding. They are the Dao we have walked that shapes what Li we can see.

“Tradition is not simply a process that we learn to know and master through historical investigation; it is language — that is, it speaks to us on its own.”

— Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method (1960)

Tradition speaks to us on its own: this is the most hermeneutically precise account of what Shan means when she says we inherit a path. The tradition is not an object that we master by studying it. It is a formation field that is actively shaping what we can think, what we can see, what questions seem natural to ask and which seem like no questions at all. The Chinese practitioner who grew up inside 道, 理, 知道, 道理 has been spoken to by a tradition that is not primarily propositional. It has formed their structural attunement, their perceptual categories, their sense of what constitutes a good question about the world. The tradition is their Dao before they knew it was their Dao.

McGilchrist and Friston: Brain, Attention, and Prediction

“The right hemisphere underwrites the broad context of our engagement with the world, before the left hemisphere begins its work of focused attention. Attention is not neutral: it is always already shaped by the kind of engagement with the world that the right hemisphere makes possible.”

— Iain McGilchrist, The Master and His Emissary (2009)

Attention shaped before focus begins: McGilchrist’s neurological account of the Dao-before-Li structure of perception. The right hemisphere’s broad contextual awareness — its sense of the whole before the parts, its relational engagement with the formation field before any specific element is isolated for analysis — is the neurological substrate of Shan’s relational precedes dynamics claim. The formation field is registered as a whole before any specific Li is named. The left hemisphere’s focused attention, its sequential analysis, its propositional naming — these are the Li-naming operations that always happen downstream of the right hemisphere’s prior relational registration. Attention is always already shaped. The practitioner who thinks they are approaching the formation field with unprejudiced attention is operating with their left hemisphere’s illusion.

“The brain is essentially a prediction machine. It is constantly generating predictions about what it expects to experience and updating those predictions based on sensory input. What we perceive is not the world as it is, but the world as our brain predicts it to be, corrected by the prediction errors that sensory experience generates.”

— Karl Friston, summarising the free energy principle in predictive processing

The brain as prediction machine: Friston’s free energy principle applied to Shan’s framework. The practitioner does not perceive the formation field directly; they perceive the prediction-error between their prior Li (what they expected the formation to be) and the actual sensory signal (what the formation is actually doing). The experienced practitioner has better predictions: not because they know more, but because their formation history has produced a prior model of the formation field that is more accurately calibrated to the actual grain. And when the prediction error is large — when Move 37 happens and the actual formation deviates radically from any prior model — the formation-sufficient practitioner updates their model rapidly (they were formed to tolerate large prediction errors and extract information from them); the formation-insufficient practitioner defends their prior model against the evidence (attunement failure).

Kauffman: Fitness Landscapes and the Adjacent Possible

“Life exists at the edge of chaos. Not because edge-of-chaos systems are somehow special, but because only at the edge can a system be both stable enough to store information and flexible enough to transmit it and change.”

— Stuart Kauffman, At Home in the Universe (1995)

Store and transmit simultaneously: this is the structural principle of Shan’s excellence as capacity held in coherence. The system that is too stable (deeply ordered, far from the edge) stores information but cannot transmit it: it is too rigid to respond. The system that is too flexible (chaotic, far from the edge in the other direction) transmits information but cannot store it: it cannot accumulate formation. Only at the edge can the formation both hold what has been formed (store) and remain genuinely responsive to what is forming (transmit). This is why excellence is specifically capacity held in coherence under constraint over time: the constraint is what prevents dissolution into chaos; the coherence is what prevents rigidification into order; and the tension between them is what makes the formation alive.

“The fitness landscape is always shifting under the organism as a consequence of the organism’s own evolution and the evolution of all other organisms in the ecosystem. There is no stable optimum. There is only the ongoing dance.”

— Stuart Kauffman, The Origins of Order (1993)

The ongoing dance: the most biologically precise statement of Shan’s what-is-formed-is-still-in-formation. The fitness landscape does not stand still while the organism optimises for it. Every step the organism takes changes the landscape for every other organism. Every step every other organism takes changes the landscape for this one. There is no final Li. There is only the dance of co-forming formation fields in which the practitioner is simultaneously formed and forming, shaped and shaping, reading a Li that is itself in formation. The Dao walks on. The landscape shifts. The dance continues.

Cheng Hao and Mencius: The Humaneness That Feels Everything

仁者，以天地萬物為一體。 — rén zhě, yǐ tiān dì wàn wù wéi yī tǐ. — The man of humanity regards heaven, earth, and the ten thousand things as one body — Cheng Hao

One body with the ten thousand things: this is the most ontologically radical statement of what Karaoguz calls attunement in its fullest form. The attuned practitioner does not merely respond accurately to the formation field; at the furthest depth of formation, the boundary between practitioner and formation field becomes genuinely permeable. The practitioner whose formation has reached sufficient depth does not observe the organisation’s structural pain as an external phenomenon; they feel it in their body as if it were their own. This is not empathy in the therapeutic sense; it is structural conductivity. The tensional network of the fully formed practitioner’s formation includes the formation fields they have walked deeply enough to be genuinely continuous with.

牛山之木尝美矣，以其郊於大國也 — Niú shān zhī mù céng měi yǐ, yǐ qí jiāo yú dà guó yě — The trees on Ox Mountain were once beautiful, but because the mountain borders a great state… — Mencius 6A:8

The Ox Mountain parable: Mencius’ most structurally precise account of formation damage. The trees were once beautiful. The mountain’s formation was once adequate to produce and maintain complex organic life. Then the constant cutting — the repeated extraction without regeneration, the harvesting of the formation’s output without investment in the formation’s conditions — stripped it bare. The mountain is now barren. But Mencius insists: the mountain’s nature is not barrenness. The formation capacity is still there, latent, waiting for the conditions that would allow regeneration. The Dao is still present below the surface of the devastated Li. This is Shan’s corrective capacity: the formation that maintains structural viability even in conditions of apparent dissolution. Nothing collapses in one move. The mountain can still grow trees.

Sun Bin and Xunzi: Terrain, Self-Cultivation, and Strategic Formation

“Ground is what determines victory and defeat. The commander who reads the ground has already won before the battle begins. The commander who ignores the ground is already defeated, whatever their other advantages may be.”

— Sun Bin, Art of War (paraphrasing the terrain doctrine)

Ground determines victory: the most compressed statement of Shi (勢, positional advantage) in Chinese strategic theory. The ground is the relational configuration of the specific formation field at the specific moment: the specific terrain whose specific Li makes certain moves possible and others impossible. The commander who reads the ground has achieved what Karaoguz calls structural appreciation of the arena before any individual tactical decision is made. The commander who ignores the ground is attempting to impose their prior Li (their tactical doctrine, their strategic framework) on a formation field whose actual Li is different. Sun Bin and Shan converge: the Li of the terrain precedes and determines the Li of the strategy. Walk the ground before you name the plan.

君子為學，就必以自我修養為根本 — Jūnzǐ wéi xué, jiù bì yǐ zìjǐ xiūyǎng wéi gēnběn — For the exemplary person in learning, self-cultivation must be the root — Xunzi, paraphrasing the cultivation doctrine

Self-cultivation as root: Xunzi’s insistence that all genuine learning is formation of the self, not acquisition of information, is the most Confucian statement of Karaoguz’s A-Frame telos. The exemplary person (jūnzǐ, 君子) does not merely accumulate knowledge; they form themselves through the specific Dao of disciplined self-cultivation until the specific Li of what constitutes excellent human character is fully embodied. This is not moral instruction; it is formation theory. The self-cultivated person reads the ethical formation field with the same structural precision that Cook Ding reads the ox’s formation field: directly, before naming, through embodied attunement rather than propositional knowledge.

Cilliers: The Boundary Problem in Complex Systems

“The boundaries of a complex system are not given; they are the result of a process of framing. To define a system is to draw a boundary. But because complex systems are open, their boundaries are always provisional, always contested, always implicated in the interests and perspectives of those who draw them.”

— Paul Cilliers, Complexity and Postmodernism (1998)

Boundaries as framing rather than given: Cilliers’ most politically acute insight, and the one that most directly connects his framework to Jackson’s critical systems heuristics and to the ethical dimension of Shan’s project. Every time a practitioner names the Li of a formation — every time they say ‘this system is X’ or ‘the pattern here is Y’ — they are drawing a boundary. They are deciding what is inside the formation and what is outside. And this boundary decision is never neutral: it includes some formations and excludes others, amplifies some voices and silences others, makes some Daos visible and renders others invisible. The Li always has a politics. The boundary always has a beneficiary. The practitioner who does not ask whose boundary this is has not yet walked the full Dao.

THE DETONATIVE SYNTHESIS: WHAT THE PAPER HAS BEEN BUILDING TOWARD

❧ ✶ ❧

Tarkovsky’s Stalker throws the nut. It lands somewhere unexpected. The Zone has spoken. Not in the language of framework or methodology or evidence-based practice, but in the specific, irreducible language of the actual formation that refuses every prior map. And the practitioner who has been formed to listen — who has walked the Dao long enough to hear the difference between the Zone’s signal and the noise of their own prior Li — picks up the nut, moves to where it landed, and throws again.

[https://cinephiliabeyond.org/stalker/](https://cinephiliabeyond.org/stalker/)

[https://www.theguardian.com/film/2009/feb/06/andrei-tarkovsky-stalker-russia-gulags-chernobyl](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2009/feb/06/andrei-tarkovsky-stalker-russia-gulags-chernobyl)

This is what every voice assembled in this text has been saying. Wittgenstein: throw away the ladder. Laozi: the Dao that can be named is not the eternal Dao. Shan: the path must be walked before its grain appears. Fuller: tension is the great integrity and the structure does not hold by being rigid. Bateson: the difference that makes a difference. Maturana: everything said is said by an observer. Meadows: the purpose of a system is what it does. Stacey: complex responsive processes. Mowles: the courage to stay engaged. Karaoguz: do we have ideas, or do ideas have us? And the ocean, as Snowden says, refuses to be mapped in advance.

The ozone smell of circuits under load. The forty voices in this text have been running at rated capacity. The crash helmet is there because thinking at this depth generates heat, generates friction, generates the specific cognitive-somatic pressure of genuine encounter with ideas that will not be assimilated without transformation. The practitioner who leaves this text unchanged has not yet made contact with what it is doing. The Zone does not give what is desired; it gives what is true. What is true here is harder to name than any of the named Li this text has assembled. But it shows itself — in the quality of the attention the text produces, in the specific discomfort of the paradoxes that cannot be resolved, in the feeling that the ground has shifted and you are not quite sure where your feet are. That is the formation working. Walk on.

悖論 #15

悖論 #15. The practitioner who finishes this text and knows what to do next has not understood it. The practitioner who finishes this text and knows what to notice next — what differences to attend to, what formations to be sensitive to, what Daos to begin walking — has begun. Attunement is not the end of the A Frame cycle. It is the beginning of the next one. The Dao walks on. 道可道，非常道。
